articles.title: Darling, Your Shark Can't Swim Here: Ole Miss Brings an Oceanless Mascot and the 108th-Ranked Defense to Austin
articles.byline: Caro Whitfield, The Texas Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 7 Ole Miss (5-1) at No. 19 Texas (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium, ABC
articles.text:
Well, hello, y'all. Caro Whitfield, coming to you from the Forty Acres, where the Tower glows burnt orange after a win and the coffee comes with a side of perspective. I bring rodeo-queen polish and a consultant's brain to every Saturday, and darling, this week needs both.

This week I owe you two things: an honest board meeting about last Saturday, and a very warm Texas welcome for our guests from Oxford, Mississippi. Warm like an 85-degree kickoff. Warm like a branding iron. Pull up a chair.

Part 1: The Board Meeting Nobody Wanted

Let's do the hard part first, because this is an honest house. Florida beat us 27-24 at DKR last Saturday, in front of 103,989 people. That's our second straight three-point loss, after the 27-24 loss to Oklahoma at the Cotton Bowl. We are 4-2. I have filed the paperwork. I have called an emergency meeting with myself. Hypothetically, heads rolled.

And it started so beautifully. Raleek Brown ran 32 yards for a touchdown early in the first quarter. Gianni Spetic hit a 38-yard field goal. Then Ryan Niblett fielded a punt and took it 63 yards to the house, the third punt-return touchdown of his career, and we led 17-3 in the second quarter. I was already drafting the press release.

Then the Gators did the one thing a consultant hates most: they slowed the meeting down. Tramell Jones Jr., in his first career start, threw two touchdowns to Lacota Dippre, one with 18 seconds left before the half and one to finish a 15-play drive that ate eight minutes of the third quarter. Florida held the ball for 38:11. We went 2-for-10 on third down. That's not a slump, darling. That's a bad quarterly report.

Patrick Durkin's 28-yard field goal gave Florida its first lead, and Jadan Baugh's 11-yard run made it 27-17. But I want you to remember what came next, because it's the moment I'm holding onto. On fourth down, Arch Manning escaped a sack and found Emmett Mosley V for 62 yards. That set up his 9-yard touchdown pass to Cam Coleman with 4:21 left. Manning finished 14 of 20 for 173 yards, a touchdown and no interceptions. Florida sacked him five times, and the last one forced a fumble on our final possession. That's football. It stings.

The defense still showed up in full formal wear. Justin Cryer made 11 tackles. Colin Simmons had eight tackles, four tackles for loss and a sack, and he left in the fourth quarter with what AP called an apparent ankle injury. Now we have real news, and it isn't the news I wanted. Wednesday's SEC availability report lists Colin as doubtful for the Ole Miss game with a high ankle sprain, and backup pass rusher Richard Wesley is out. You don't replace a young man like that with a memo. We pray for both of those young men, we pray for a quick and full recovery, and we ask the rest of this defense to stand up tall. That's all there is to say.

Now, perspective. This same team beat Ohio State 24-23 and won 20-17 at Tennessee. In those two wins the defense allowed 40 points combined. The bones are good. The quarter was bad. We do not panic in October.

Part 2: Welcome to Austin, Rebels. Mind the Bats.

Saturday night, 7:30 Eastern, on ABC, No. 7 Ole Miss comes to DKR. It's our first meeting as SEC members, Texas leads the series 6-2, and it's the Rebels' first trip to Austin since 2013.

I'll be gracious first, because Mama raised me right. Ole Miss beat No. 13 Missouri 31-3 last Saturday, and it was impressive. Trinidad Chambliss threw three touchdowns and ran for another. Kewan Lacy ran for 122 yards and the Rebels put up 498 yards. They held Missouri to 39 rushing yards on 26 carries. Well done, darlings. Truly.

Now let me tell you about the rest of the roster.

Who to Watch

Trinidad Chambliss, quarterback: 1,676 passing yards, 14 touchdowns, four interceptions. He's the real thing, and Mama didn't raise a liar. Our pass rush needs to find him early and often.

Deuce Alexander, receiver: 35 catches, 523 yards, five touchdowns. Our secondary should know where he is on every snap.

The Ole Miss defense: 390 yards allowed a game, 108th in FBS. Opponents gain 236.5 passing yards a game against it, which ranks 104th. And on third down, opponents convert 44 of every 100 times, 118th in the country. Darling, I've seen tighter security at a lemonade stand.

Here's the part I find delicious. Pete Golding was Ole Miss's defensive coordinator before he got promoted to head coach. The defense now ranks 108th in yards allowed. I'm not saying anything. I'm just reading the stat sheet out loud.

And the Rebels hold the ball for 26:59 a game, 131st in FBS. They score fast, sure, and they've scored on every one of their red zone trips, first in the nation. Credit where due. But then their defense is right back on the field, wondering who booked such a short break.

Texas's Defense vs. the Rebel Offense

This is the main event. Ole Miss throws for 290.7 yards a game, 13th in FBS, and scores 37.5 points a game. Our defense allows 272.5 yards a game overall (12th in FBS), 166.2 passing yards (12th) and 17.8 points (29th). Rasheem Biles leads us with 48 tackles and two interceptions. Somebody's streak gives on Saturday night, y'all. I know which side I'm on.

On the other side, Manning has 11 touchdowns this year, Ryan Wingo has 26 catches for 345 yards, and Smothers has 289 rushing yards. Our offense ranks 93rd in yards, and I won't pretend otherwise. But we're about to meet a defense that ranks 104th against the pass. You don't need a consultant for that math, though I'm happy to draw you a chart.

The Road Problem

AP pointed out that Ole Miss is 25-1 at home since 2023. Gorgeous number. Frame it. Hang it in the Grove. Now look at the 2026 road trips: the Rebels won at Vanderbilt, then went to Gainesville and lost 52-28 to Florida.

Yes, the same Florida that beat us. Here's the difference, darling: Florida, with a quarterback in his first career start, needed a whole Saturday to squeeze past us by three. Against Ole Miss, the Gators hung 52 on the board. We lost a negotiation. Ole Miss lost the whole building.

A Brief History Seminar

Ole Miss has been in the SEC since 1932. Its last SEC title came in 1963, under Johnny Vaught. In the 32 years the league had divisions, the Rebels never reached the SEC Championship Game. Texas joined the league in 2024 and played in that game in year one. We lost it 22-19 in overtime to Georgia, and I'm still upset, but at least we found the stadium. Thirty-two years, darling. Somebody hand Oxford a map.

And bless their hearts, the Rebels' last coach, Lane Kiffin, left for LSU on Nov. 30, 2025, two days after the Egg Bowl, with a playoff run still ahead. To be fair, Golding stepped in and took that team to the playoff semifinal, where it lost 31-27 to Miami in the Fiesta Bowl, and this year Ole Miss beat Kiffin's LSU 32-24. I respect the comeback story. I just prefer ours, especially when it ends in a Texas win.

Tower Talk: A Tale of Two Towns

Every football weekend is really a town weekend, and darling, I've been waiting all week for this one.

Austin. It's the capital of Texas. Its official slogan is "The Live Music Capital of the World." It's home to SXSW and Austin City Limits. At sunset, about 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats pour out from under the Ann W. Richards Congress Avenue Bridge over Lady Bird Lake. Texas Parks and Wildlife calls it the largest urban bat colony in the world, and the bats don't fly south until early November. That means our visitors get the full show. We'll have 1.5 million bats in the sky and a stadium with more than 100,000 seats. Then, after a win, the UT Tower glows burnt orange, and Bevo, our actual living, breathing longhorn steer, looks over the evening with deep approval.

Oxford. Now, I adore a charming town, and Oxford is charming. The Square is lovely. Square Books is a real treasure. William Faulkner lived there, and I respect a man who wrote sentences longer than some Ole Miss defensive stands. But consider the branding. The founders named the town after Oxford, England, to promote it as a center of learning. Darling, borrowing a more famous town's name is like showing up to the gala in somebody else's gown.

The 2020 census counted 25,416 people in Oxford. Last Saturday's crowd at DKR was 103,989. Our losing crowd was about four Oxfords. Even Oxford's Wikipedia entry introduces the town by how far it is from Memphis: 75 miles.

Then there's the Grove: about 10 shaded acres of tents, fine china and, I'm told, chandeliers. Hanging chandeliers. Outdoors. I'm a rodeo queen, darling, and even I think that's a lot of sparkle for a tailgate. Out here we light a whole Tower.

And the mascot. In 2017 the university made the Landshark its official mascot, and Tony the Landshark debuted in 2018. A shark. In the North Central Hills of Mississippi. Oxford's entire water area is about 0.09 square miles. Ole Miss has since de-emphasized Tony on game days. I understand. He's probably looking for an ocean. We'll leave a kiddie pool out on Lady Bird Lake for him. The bats will keep him company.

One sincere note, because I'm a lady. Ole Miss's campus speed limit is 18 miles per hour in honor of Archie Manning, who wore No. 18 there. Oxford slows the traffic down to honor that family. In Austin, we honor it by giving Archie's grandson the football. Everybody loves the Mannings, darling. We just have the current model.

The Final Word

Here's how I see it. Ole Miss has a terrific quarterback, a perfect red zone record and a defense ranked 108th in yards. Texas has a top-12 defense, a home crowd the size of four Oxfords, a chip on its shoulder from two three-point losses, and a quarterback who answered on fourth down last Saturday when it got ugly. The Rebels hold the ball for less time than almost anybody in America. On Saturday night, our defense would love to hand it back to them early and often.

Come early. Watch the bats. Stay for the Tower. Hook 'em, y'all.

My call: Texas Longhorns 30, Ole Miss Rebels 24.

articles.title: Roll Tide, and I Mean That as a Threat: Two Losses, One Grudge, and the Aggies Walk Right Into Bryant-Denny
articles.byline: Mary-Kathryn 'MK' Strickland, The Alabama Fanatic
articles.matchup: Texas A&M (4-3) at No. 13 Alabama (5-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Bryant-Denny Stadium, ABC
articles.text:
Well, hello, darlings. Pull up a chair, put your napkin in your lap, and sit up straight, because Mama is not in a giggly mood this week. This is Mary-Kathryn Strickland, MK to my friends, coming to you from Tuscaloosa, where the water oaks are turning, the porch lights are on, and the whole town has spent seven days quietly staring at the wall.

I grew up on horseback, darling, and the first thing a horse teaches you is this: when you get thrown, you do not sit in the dirt writing poetry about it. You dust off your jodhpurs and you get right back on. So let's talk about getting thrown, and then let's talk about the Aggies, who are about to learn what it feels like to visit a barn full of riders in a very bad mood.

Part 1: The Night Knoxville Got Loud

I will be honest, because honesty is good manners. Tennessee beat us 26-10 at Neyland Stadium last Saturday, in front of 101,915 people and one very large amount of orange. A week earlier, Georgia beat us 20-17 at Bryant-Denny. According to the AP, that's the first time Alabama has lost consecutive regular-season games since 2007. I had to sit down when I read that. Then I had to stand back up, because a lady doesn't stay down.

The first half was a field goal festival, and not the kind with funnel cakes. Tennessee kicker Cooper Ranvier hit four field goals before halftime, from 29, 33, 41 and 34 yards. Our quarterback, Keelon Russell, scored our only touchdown on a 19-yard run in the second quarter, and Conor Talty drilled a 42-yarder with five seconds left in the half. We went into the locker room down just 12-10, which, considering we had 93 yards of offense at the break, was a small miracle and a credit to our defense.

Then the second half happened. DeSean Bishop ran for 159 yards and two touchdowns for the Vols, 95 of those yards after halftime, and their fourth-quarter drive lasted nine minutes and 32 seconds. Nine minutes, darling. I have attended entire debutante receptions shorter than that drive.

The numbers are not pretty, and I won't dress them up. We had 201 yards, only 54 on the ground. We were 2 of 13 on third down. We turned it over four times, two fumbles and two interceptions. Russell finished 19 of 29 for 147 yards. Rico Scott caught four passes for 54 yards. Our captain, receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams, missed the game, which the AP said was due to several injuries including a concussion. We wish him a full recovery, and that's all I'll say about that.

But I watched the defense, and I want you to see what I saw. Caleb Woodson made 11 tackles. Bray Hubbard made 10. Yhonzae Pierre had a sack and two quarterback hurries, and Ivan Taylor picked off a pass. That group spent 35 minutes on the field and still held Tennessee to 347 yards. When your offense hands the ball back four times, that's what keeping your dignity looks like.

Coach's Brain

Here's the maxim my granddaddy taught me at the supper table, and I'll repeat it perfectly because I always do: "You don't learn much from a win, but a loss will teach you the whole hymnal." We have now had two lessons in a row. I'd like to graduate.

And don't forget what this team was a month ago. We beat Florida State 50-36. We won at Kentucky 45-17, and Kentucky is ranked 12th right now. We beat South Carolina 49-18 and won at Mississippi State 56-23. We still score 39.3 points a game, 12th in FBS. The bones are good, darling. The last two Saturdays were a bad hair day, not a new hairstyle.

Part 2: Howdy, Aggies. Wipe Your Boots.

Saturday at 3:30 Eastern on ABC, Texas A&M comes to Bryant-Denny. The Tide is 5-2 and No. 13 in the AP poll. The Aggies are 4-3 and 1-3 in the SEC.

Now, I'll be gracious first, because that's how I was raised. The Aggies beat The Citadel 41-0 last Saturday. Jamarion Morrow ran for three first-half touchdowns, KJ Edwards ran for 116 yards, and Aaron Gregory caught two touchdown passes. It was their second shutout of the year, and the AP said it's the first time since 1993 they've posted two in one season. Lovely. Truly. The Citadel arrived at 2-5, but a shutout is a shutout, and I'll send a nice card.

Now let me tell you about the rest of the Aggie season. They lost at home to Kentucky 31-21. They lost at LSU 35-6. They lost at Missouri 27-6. In those last two SEC road trips, the Aggies scored a combined 12 points. Darling, I've seen more offense at a garden club meeting about azaleas.

Who to Watch

Marcel Reed, A&M quarterback: 1,227 yards, seven touchdowns, six interceptions, and 55.7 completions for every 100 throws. The Aggie passing game averages 195.7 yards a game, 103rd in FBS. Pierre leads our pass rush with 3.5 sacks, and I'd love for him to introduce himself early.

The A&M defense: This is the real thing, and I respect it. It allows 306.6 yards a game, 29th in FBS, and only 164.1 passing yards a game, 10th. Opponents convert just 29.8 of every 100 third downs, 11th in the country. Ray Coney leads them with 36 tackles. Our offense needs to stay ahead of the chains and stop handing out free gifts.

Keelon Russell, our quarterback: 1,746 yards, 12 touchdowns, four interceptions, and a 67.5 completion rate on the season. One bad night in Knoxville doesn't erase that.

Trae'shawn Brown, running back: 313 yards and five touchdowns. Our run game has to show up, because 54 yards won't do it twice.

Caleb Woodson, linebacker: 53 tackles, team high. The man is everywhere, like a mother at a wedding.

The Honest Part

I'm not hiding the warts. Our pass defense allows 230.9 yards a game, 101st in FBS, and the AP preview says opponents have scored on 95.7 of every 100 red-zone trips against us, 134th in the country. That has to get fixed, starting Saturday. The good news is that the Aggie passing game is 103rd. Somebody's weakness gives first, and it's not going to be ours in front of 100,077 of our closest friends.

A Brief History Seminar

Alabama leads this series 13-3, according to CollegeFootballData.com. The last two meetings were both four-point wins for the Tide: 24-20 in Tuscaloosa in 2022 and 26-20 in College Station in 2023. Yes, the Aggies won 41-38 in 2021. I remember. I've moved on. Mostly.

And while we're doing history, the Aggies' last conference championship came in 1998, back in the Big 12. That was so long ago, darling, that most of their current fans were not yet born. Alabama claims 18 national championships. We are not the same kind of family reunion.

Debutante Ball: A Tale of Two Towns

Tuscaloosa. They call it the Druid City because of the water oaks folks have been planting along downtown streets since the 1840s. It sits on the Black Warrior River, which is about the most Alabama name a river could ever have. The 2020 census counted 99,600 people, and on a fall Saturday it feels like double that. Before kickoff, our players take the Walk of Champions, the brick plaza from University Boulevard to the north end zone. Our band was founded in 1912 and is the largest student organization at the university. And after the game, the original Dreamland barbecue joint, opened in 1958 in the Jerusalem Heights neighborhood, is waiting with ribs and white bread, which is all a girl needs. Our mascot is Big Al, an elephant, officially recognized by the university in 1979. A large, dignified animal. Fitting.

College Station. Now, College Station is a sweet town, and I mean that. But darling, the median age there is 22.5, according to the census numbers. That's not a city. That's a dormitory with a zip code. The Aggies do have Kyle Field, which seats 102,733 and is the largest stadium in the SEC. I'll give them that. It's a beautiful big house. It just hasn't hosted a conference championship celebration since 1998.

blocks.text: Well, hello, darlings. Pull up a chair, put your napkin in your lap, and sit up straight, because Mama is not in a giggly mood this week. This is Mary-Kathryn Strickland, MK to my friends, coming to you from Tuscaloosa, where the water oaks are turning, the porch lights are on, and the whole town has spent seven days quietly staring at the wall.

I grew up on horseback, darling, and the first thing a horse teaches you is this: when you get thrown, you do not sit in the dirt writing poetry about it. You dust off your jodhpurs and you get right back on. So let's talk about getting thrown, and then let's talk about the Aggies, who are about to learn what it feels like to visit a barn full of riders in a very bad mood.
Part 1: The Night Knoxville Got Loud

I will be honest, because honesty is good manners. Tennessee beat us 26-10 at Neyland Stadium last Saturday, in front of 101,915 people and one very large amount of orange. A week earlier, Georgia beat us 20-17 at Bryant-Denny. According to the AP, that's the first time Alabama has lost consecutive regular-season games since 2007. I had to sit down when I read that. Then I had to stand back up, because a lady doesn't stay down.

The first half was a field goal festival, and not the kind with funnel cakes. Tennessee kicker Cooper Ranvier hit four field goals before halftime, from 29, 33, 41 and 34 yards. Our quarterback, Keelon Russell, scored our only touchdown on a 19-yard run in the second quarter, and Conor Talty drilled a 42-yarder with five seconds left in the half. We went into the locker room down just 12-10, which, considering we had 93 yards of offense at the break, was a small miracle and a credit to our defense.

Then the second half happened. DeSean Bishop ran for 159 yards and two touchdowns for the Vols, 95 of those yards after halftime, and their fourth-quarter drive lasted nine minutes and 32 seconds. Nine minutes, darling. I have attended entire debutante receptions shorter than that drive.

The numbers are not pretty, and I won't dress them up. We had 201 yards, only 54 on the ground. We were 2 of 13 on third down. We turned it over four times, two fumbles and two interceptions. Russell finished 19 of 29 for 147 yards. Rico Scott caught four passes for 54 yards. Our captain, receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams, missed the game, which the AP said was due to several injuries including a concussion. We wish him a full recovery, and that's all I'll say about that.

But I watched the defense, and I want you to see what I saw. Caleb Woodson made 11 tackles. Bray Hubbard made 10. Yhonzae Pierre had a sack and two quarterback hurries, and Ivan Taylor picked off a pass. That group spent 35 minutes on the field and still held Tennessee to 347 yards. When your offense hands the ball back four times, that's what keeping your dignity looks like.
Coach's Brain

Here's the maxim my granddaddy taught me at the supper table, and I'll repeat it perfectly because I always do: "You don't learn much from a win, but a loss will teach you the whole hymnal." We have now had two lessons in a row. I'd like to graduate.

And don't forget what this team was a month ago. We beat Florida State 50-36. We won at Kentucky 45-17, and Kentucky is ranked 12th right now. We beat South Carolina 49-18 and won at Mississippi State 56-23. We still score 39.3 points a game, 12th in FBS. The bones are good, darling. The last two Saturdays were a bad hair day, not a new hairstyle.
Part 2: Howdy, Aggies. Wipe Your Boots.
Saturday at 3:30 Eastern on ABC, Texas A&M comes to Bryant-Denny. The Tide is 5-2 and No. 13 in the AP poll. The Aggies are 4-3 and 1-3 in the SEC.

Now, I'll be gracious first, because that's how I was raised. The Aggies beat The Citadel 41-0 last Saturday. Jamarion Morrow ran for three first-half touchdowns, KJ Edwards ran for 116 yards, and Aaron Gregory caught two touchdown passes. It was their second shutout of the year, and the AP said it's the first time since 1993 they've posted two in one season. Lovely. Truly. The Citadel arrived at 2-5, but a shutout is a shutout, and I'll send a nice card.

Now let me tell you about the rest of the Aggie season. They lost at home to Kentucky 31-21. They lost at LSU 35-6. They lost at Missouri 27-6. In those last two SEC road trips, the Aggies scored a combined 12 points. Darling, I've seen more offense at a garden club meeting about azaleas.
Who to Watch

Marcel Reed, A&M quarterback: 1,227 yards, seven touchdowns, six interceptions, and 55.7 completions for every 100 throws. The Aggie passing game averages 195.7 yards a game, 103rd in FBS. Pierre leads our pass rush with 3.5 sacks, and I'd love for him to introduce himself early.

The A&M defense: This is the real thing, and I respect it. It allows 306.6 yards a game, 29th in FBS, and only 164.1 passing yards a game, 10th. Opponents convert just 29.8 of every 100 third downs, 11th in the country. Ray Coney leads them with 36 tackles. Our offense needs to stay ahead of the chains and stop handing out free gifts.
Keelon Russell, our quarterback: 1,746 yards, 12 touchdowns, four interceptions, and a 67.5 completion rate on the season. One bad night in Knoxville doesn't erase that.

I'm not hiding the warts. Our pass defense allows 230.9 yards a game, 101st in FBS, and the AP preview says opponents have scored on 95.7 of every 100 red-zone trips against us, 134th in the country. That has to get fixed, starting Saturday. The good news is that the Aggie passing game is 103rd. articles.title: Woooo, Pig, Here Comes the Data: The Hogs Snapped a 14-Game SEC Skid, Took a Well-Earned Nap, and Now Missouri Is Coming to the Ozarks
articles.byline: Bubba Fayette-Dorsey, The Arkansas Fanatic
articles.matchup: Arkansas (3-4): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: No. 22 Missouri (5-2) at Arkansas, Sat., Oct. 31, Razorback Stadium, Fayetteville
articles.text:
WOOOOOOOO, PIG! SOOIE!

Sorry, folks. Reflex. I call the Hogs before every stat, and it turns out I also call 'em before every sentence when I'm happy. And friends, I am happy. I'm Bubba Fayette-Dorsey, a grade-school science teacher from up in the Ozarks, and I spend my weekdays explaining the water cycle to fourth graders and my weekends explaining Razorback football to anybody who'll stand still.

This week, my fourth graders got a bonus lesson. It's called "How to End a Streak." Pull up a hay bale.

Part 1: The Night the Skid Ended

WOOOO, PIG! Arkansas 31, Vanderbilt 21, Saturday night in Nashville.

And folks, here's why I'm hollering. According to the AP, that win snapped Arkansas's 14-game Southeastern Conference losing streak. Our first SEC win since 2024. Fourteen straight. I had started measuring that streak in school years. I had students graduate from the fourth grade during it. Okay, that's just one grade, but it felt longer.

Here's how it went down. Vanderbilt scored first, on a 4-yard run with 13 seconds left in the first quarter. Then in the second quarter, defensive back Joker Johnson stepped in front of a pass and took it 25 yards for a touchdown. SOOIE! That's a man who reads a quarterback like a fourth grader reads the lunch menu: fast, and with purpose.

Vandy went back up 14-7, and then Cam Settles scored from 11 yards out with 38 seconds left in the half to tie it. In the third quarter, our quarterback, KJ Jackson, ran in from eight yards, the Commodores tied it again, and then Settles scored his second touchdown, from three yards, with nine seconds left in the quarter. 28-21.

And then the play of the night. With 3:46 left, Vanderbilt drove to our 29. On second-and-12, Miguel Mitchell intercepted the pass. WOOOO! Max Gilbert drilled a 39-yard field goal with 24 seconds left, and the streak was over.

Jackson completed 21 of 31 passes for 251 yards with no interceptions, and he ran for 58 yards and that touchdown. We ran for 187 yards as a team, spreading it around five different runners, as the AP put it. Settles had 45 yards and two scores, and Braylen Russell added 51 yards. Antonio Jordan caught five passes for 74. On defense, Ja'Quavion Smith made 10 tackles and Mitchell had a sack to go with his interception. We didn't turn it over once and held the ball for 33:47.

Hog Call Science Corner

Every week I explain one thing like I would to my class. This week: momentum. An object in motion stays in motion. For 14 straight SEC games, our object was not in motion. Saturday night, Joker Johnson applied an outside force, 25 yards' worth, and now we're rolling. That's Newton's first law, kids. Isaac Newton never called the Hogs, but I like to think he would have.

The Honest Lab Report

A good scientist reports all the data, even the ugly results. WOOOO, PIG, here comes the ugly data. We're 3-4 and 1-3 in the SEC. We lost at Utah 43-10, to Georgia 45-17 and at Texas A&M 34-7, and we lost 24-17 to Tennessee, which just beat Alabama by 16. We score 21 points a game and give up 26.7. Those numbers have room to grow, like a bean sprout on a windowsill.

Part 2: This Week, Nap Time. Next Week, Missouri.

WOOOO, PIG! Here's the honest schedule note: Arkansas has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. The Hogs get a week to rest, heal, and, I hope, watch the Vanderbilt tape a few dozen times just to feel good about themselves. I know I will.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, No. 22 Missouri comes to Razorback Stadium in Fayetteville. Kickoff time hasn't been announced as I write this. Halloween in the Ozarks, folks. I'll be in costume. I'm going as a stat sheet.

Now, I'll be neighborly first. Missouri is 5-2. It's unbeaten at home, the AP noted, beat Florida 45-17 and Texas A&M 27-6, and it was ranked 13th until last week. Its running back, Jamal Roberts, has 867 rushing yards and eight touchdowns. Its quarterback, Austin Simmons, has thrown for 1,773 yards with 14 touchdowns and two interceptions. Daeden Hopkins has seven sacks. That's a good football team, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But let me show you some data from last Saturday. WOOOO, PIG!

Missouri lost 31-3 at Ole Miss. Three points. Roberts, who had run for more than 200 yards in each of his previous two games, ran 20 times for 39 yards. Missouri as a team ran for 39 yards on 26 carries. And when the Tigers had first-and-goal at the Ole Miss 2, they lost yards twice, threw an incomplete pass and then missed a 23-yard field goal. Friends, I have fourth graders who can get a pencil sharpened faster than Missouri got that ball across the goal from the 2.

And that wasn't their only road trouble. Missouri also lost at Mississippi State 31-24. So the Tigers are unbeaten at home and 1-2 away from it. Guess where they're playing on Oct. 31? Not at home, folks. Here. In the Ozarks. On Halloween. Spooky.

Who to Watch

WOOOO, PIG! KJ Jackson, our quarterback: 1,444 yards, seven touchdowns, four interceptions on the season, and coming off his cleanest SEC night.

Chris Marshall, receiver: 43 catches for 633 yards, our leader.

Ja'Quavion Smith: 48 tackles, our leader. Quincy Rhodes Jr.: three sacks.

Jamal Roberts, Missouri running back: 867 yards. Ole Miss just showed the world how to slow him down. We've got two weeks to take notes.

Cayden Lee, Missouri receiver: 47 catches for 678 yards and five touchdowns.

A Brief History Seminar

I'll be honest: Missouri leads the series 13-4, according to CollegeFootballData.com, and has won the last four meetings. That's a streak, folks, and if there's one thing the Hogs just proved, it's that streaks end. Ask Vanderbilt.

Ozark Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Fayetteville. The 2020 census counted 93,949 of us, and Fayetteville is the most populous city in Northwest Arkansas. We sit in the Boston Mountains, part of the Ozarks, and when the leaves turn at the end of October, there's no prettier place on God's green earth. Dickson Street is the best-known entertainment district in Arkansas. Our track and cross country teams have won so much that folks call Fayetteville the "Track Capital of the South." Razorback Stadium seats 76,212. Our live mascot, Tusk, rides up from a family farm in Dardanelle, a two-hour trip, for every home game. And Arkansas claims the 1964 national championship, when the Hogs were the only major team to go 11-0. Then there's the Hog call itself, which got its "Sooie" back in the 1920s. Hundred-year-old tradition, folks. Older than some of the hills, almost.

Columbia, Missouri. Now, Columbia's a nice college town. I'll say it. But Wikipedia says folks there used to call it the "Athens of Missouri," and now it's "more commonly called 'CoMo.'" Friends, they went from Athens to CoMo. That's like a science fair project that started as a volcano and ended as a potato battery.

They're very proud of the Missouri School of Journalism, founded in 1908. Great school. Real history. So I've got a story for those student reporters, free of charge, and the headline writes itself: "Missouri Scores Three Points in Oxford." Run it above the fold, kids.

Missouri calls itself the Show-Me State, so let's do it. Show me, Missouri. Show me a touchdown from the 2. We'll wait.

And their mascot, Truman the Tiger, is named after President Harry S. Truman. That's a fine man to name a tiger after. Our mascot is a real hog named Tusk. Truman is a costume. Tusk is a hog. Science says the hog wins.

The Last Hog Call

Here's my hypothesis, and I've tested it all week. We just ended a 14-game streak. We have two weeks to prepare. Missouri is coming off a game where it ran for 39 yards and scored three points, it's 1-2 on the road, and it's coming to the Ozarks on Halloween, where the leaves are orange, the stadium is red and the noise is a hundred years old.

Results pending, kids. But I like this experiment.

WOOOOOOOO, PIG! SOOIE! Razorbacks!

articles.title: War Eagle, Bless Their Hearts: Auburn Just Toppled No. 1 Georgia, and Now the Other Tigers Want a Turn
articles.byline: Lacey Bellamy, The Auburn Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 18 LSU (5-2) at Auburn (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, noon ET, Jordan-Hare Stadium, ABC
articles.text:
Well, hey there, Auburn family. It's Lacey Bellamy, and I am writing to you from a porch swing on the Plains with a glass of sweet tea, a voice that is completely gone, and a little bit of toilet paper still stuck in my hair. Do not ask me how. Actually, you know exactly how.

Because on Saturday afternoon, in Athens, Georgia, inside the hedges, in front of 93,033 people wearing red and black, our Auburn Tigers beat the No. 1 team in the country. I have been reenacting the final drive in my living room ever since, and yes, in my version, I'm the one who kicks the field goal. In heels. Through a hurricane.

Part 1: The Day the Hedges Wilted

Let me set the scene, because this one deserves a proper telling.

It did not start pretty, darlin'. Georgia scored on its first two possessions, a 15-yard Dwight Phillips Jr. run and a 24-yard pass from Gunner Stockton to Lawson Luckie, and it was 14-0 before most of us had found our seats. I'll be honest, I had a moment. I said a little prayer. Then I said, "Lacey, you've seen worse. You've seen Iron Bowls."

And then Auburn scored the next 24 points.

Our first touchdown came on a trick play that I will be describing to my grandchildren. Byrum Brown pitched to receiver Christian Neptune, and Neptune threw a touchdown pass to Keshaun Singleton. It was Neptune's second completion of the season, and both of them have gone for touchdowns. A perfect career, sugar. That young man should never throw again, just to protect the record.

Then Brown hit Chas Nimrod for a 9-yard score to tie it. Alex McPherson drilled a 49-yard field goal before the half, and we led 17-14. Brown ran it in from five yards out in the third quarter, and it was 24-14 in Athens. I was standing on my coffee table.

Georgia came back, because Georgia is good. A 42-yard field goal, then a 94-yard, 13-play drive to tie it at 24 with 2:58 left. And then, with 58 seconds remaining and Georgia driving, Stockton fumbled on a run from our 46, and safety Sylvester Smith-Reed fell on it at the Auburn 44. A roughing-the-passer penalty on Georgia helped us along, and McPherson kicked a 34-yard field goal as time expired. Auburn 27, Georgia 24.

Byrum Brown was magnificent. He ran 26 times for 115 yards and a touchdown and completed 15 of 26 passes for 150 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions. We outrushed Georgia 192 to 113 and didn't turn it over once. Jeremiah Cobb added 61 yards on the ground. On defense, Elijah Melendez had nine tackles, a sack and an interception, and AnQuon Fegans picked off a pass too.

And, oh, the streaks we broke. The AP said it ended Georgia's nine-game winning streak over Auburn, and its 53-game winning streak against unranked teams. It was also the second straight week that the No. 1 team lost to an unranked opponent, and the AP says that hadn't happened in consecutive weeks since October 1990. Our first-year coach, Alex Golesh, has us believing again. War Eagle, bless their hearts.

Toomer's Corner Report

You know where I was Saturday night. Since 1962, Auburn folks have celebrated big wins by rolling the trees at Toomer's Corner with toilet paper, and on Saturday night those live oaks looked like they'd been through a very joyful snowstorm. If you came by and saw a woman in a sundress throwing a roll with her eyes closed and a tear on her cheek, no, you didn't.

Part 2: Here Come the Other Tigers

Now, Saturday at noon Eastern on ABC, No. 18 LSU comes to Jordan-Hare. We're 4-2 and 2-2 in the SEC. They're 5-2 and 2-2.

I'll be sweet first, because my mama raised me on a porch. LSU is good, y'all. Last Saturday they beat Mississippi State 31-0 in Baton Rouge. Sam Leavitt went 31 of 38 for 289 yards and four touchdowns, his first game of the season without an interception. Jackson Harris caught two of those touchdowns. Their offense averages 504 yards a game, seventh in FBS, and their defense allows only 256.6 yards a game, fourth in the country. Those are real numbers, and I respect them.

Now, let me tell you about the rest.

Two weeks ago, LSU lost 35-34 in overtime at Kentucky. Earlier this year, they lost at Ole Miss 32-24. On the road in the SEC this season, LSU is 0-2, sugar. They're about to visit the loudest village on the plains, and I hope they packed earplugs and a hankie.

And bless their hearts, their quarterback had thrown eight interceptions in LSU's first six games, and the AP said he was the only FBS quarterback intercepted in every one of his team's games before Saturday. I'm not saying a thing. I'm just reading the newspaper out loud, which my mama says is not gossip if it's printed.

Who to Watch

Byrum Brown, our quarterback: 1,202 passing yards, eight touchdowns, and a team-high 459 rushing yards with five more scores on the ground. He's 235 pounds of pure Plains, and LSU's run defense is about to meet him personally.

Keshaun Singleton, receiver: 32 catches for 367 yards, our leader. Also the proud owner of a touchdown catch thrown by a wide receiver, which is the most Auburn sentence I've ever typed.

Sam Leavitt, LSU quarterback: 1,784 yards, 14 touchdowns, eight interceptions. Our secondary has two interceptions from Saturday and would love a few more.

Dilin Jones, LSU running back: 567 yards on 128 carries.

The clock. Here's the honest part. The AP preview says we're 134th in FBS in time of possession at 26:54 a game, and LSU is 19th at 32:55. We were flagged 11 times for 85 yards on Saturday, and we average 68 penalty yards a game, 111th. We can't do that twice in a row against a defense this good. But you know what we did do on Saturday? We beat the best defense we'll see all year by running straight at it.

A Brief History Seminar

LSU leads the series 33-23-1, according to CollegeFootballData.com. The last time these two met at Jordan-Hare, in 2022, LSU won 21-17. The 2021 game in Baton Rouge, though? Auburn 24, LSU 19. And in 2020, at Jordan-Hare, Auburn won 48-11. I have reenacted that one at three family weddings.

Here's the fact I love most. Auburn claims nine national championships and has produced three Heisman Trophy winners: Pat Sullivan, Bo Jackson and Cam Newton. Our stadium is named for Shug Jordan, who won more games than any coach in Auburn history, and Cliff Hare, who played on Auburn's very first football team. When his name went up in 1973, it was the first stadium in the country named for an active coach.

Porch Talk: A Tale of Two Towns

Auburn. They call us the Loveliest Village on the Plains, from Oliver Goldsmith's poem "The Deserted Village": "Sweet Auburn! Loveliest village of the plain." The 2020 census counted 76,143 of us, and every one of them knows where Toomer's Corner is. Before every home game, a golden eagle and a bald eagle perform the War Eagle Flight at Jordan-Hare, which seats 88,043. People ask me why our battle cry is an eagle when our team is the Tigers and our mascot is Aubie the Tiger. Darlin', we have more than one good thing going. It's called abundance.

Baton Rouge. Now, I love Baton Rouge. It's the state capital, it sits on a bluff above the Mississippi River, and the food is a gift from the Lord. But the name, y'all. Baton Rouge means "red stick," after a red-painted post early French explorers found marking a boundary on the bluff. Their whole city is named after a stick. Auburn is named after a poem. I'm just pointing out who reads.

And they're very proud of the "Earthquake Game," when the roar of the crowd at Tiger Stadium registered on a seismograph on campus. You know who they were playing? Auburn. In 1988. We have been making Baton Rouge shake for almost four decades, sugar. We're happy to do it again from our place.

Their mascot is a live tiger named Mike. Mike VII no longer comes to the stadium on game days. I understand completely. I wouldn't want to see an Auburn game in person either, if I were an LSU tiger. Our eagles, on the other hand, fly right into the stadium. Brave birds.

And one more, because I can't help myself. Baton Rouge has 227,470 people, and Tiger Stadium seats 102,321. They built a stadium for half the town, then told everybody to arrive at night. Here on the Plains, kickoff is at noon. Bring your sunglasses, Tigers. The village is wide awake.

The Last Word

Here's how I see it. LSU is talented, and its defense is no joke. But we just went to Athens, fell behind 14-0, and walked out with a win over No. 1 and a pocketful of broken streaks. Byrum Brown runs like a freight train with good manners, our defense took the ball away twice from the best team in America, and Jordan-Hare at noon is going to be loud enough to register on somebody's seismograph.

Roll the corner, darlin'. Or at least keep the toilet paper handy. War Eagle!

My call: LSU Tigers 28, Auburn Tigers 22.

articles.title: That Play Had Scales: A First-Time Starter Tamed the Longhorns in Austin, and Now the Gators Get a Week to Study the Bulldog in Its Natural Habitat
articles.byline: Dax Marchetti, The Florida Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 20 Florida (5-2): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Florida vs. No. 5 Georgia (6-1), Sat., Oct. 31, Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Atlanta
articles.text:
(whispering) Here, in the burnt-orange grasslands of central Texas, a remarkable thing has occurred.

A young quarterback, making the first start of his college career, has crept into a stadium holding 103,989 Longhorns. The herd does not notice him at first. It scores 17 of the first 20 points. It grows comfortable. And then, slowly, patiently, over 38 minutes and 11 seconds of possession...

(full volume) THE GATOR STRIKES!

Sorry. I'm Dax Marchetti. I minored in herpetology, I classify every opponent as a species, and I've been narrating Florida football in a nature-documentary whisper since before it was socially acceptable. It still isn't. I do it anyway.

That play had scales, friends. Let's go to the tape.

Part 1: Field Notes From Austin

Florida 27, No. 7 Texas 24. Saturday, Oct. 17, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium.

Let me set the scene, because the context makes it sweeter. We started 4-0 under first-year coach Jon Sumrall and climbed as high as No. 8 in the AP poll. Then we lost 45-17 at Missouri and 38-19 at home to South Carolina. Our defense, the AP noted, ranked last in the SEC. Our starting quarterback, Aaron Philo, was hurt. And so we went to Austin with Tramell Jones Jr. making his first career start.

And for a while, the documentary looked like it was about to get sad. Raleek Brown ran 32 yards for a Texas touchdown on the opening drive, Gianni Spetic added a field goal, and Ryan Niblett returned a punt 63 yards for a score. 17-3, Texas, in the second quarter.

But observe, friends, the patience of the apex predator.

Patrick Durkin had already hit a 45-yard field goal. Then, with 18 seconds left in the half, Jones found Lacota Dippre for a 7-yard touchdown. 17-10. In the third quarter, the Gators went on a 15-play drive that took eight minutes off the clock, and Jones hit Dippre again, this time from 8 yards out. 17-17. Durkin's 28-yarder gave us our first lead, and then Jadan Baugh broke outside for an 11-yard touchdown. 27-17.

Texas answered with a touchdown with 4:21 left. And then, on Texas's final possession, Myles Graham got to Arch Manning and forced a fumble. It was our fifth sack of the day. Game over.

The AP called it the program's first road win over a top-10 opponent since 2012. Fourteen years, friends. In that time, I finished a herpetology minor and filled three field notebooks. The Gators were overdue.

The Habitat Report

Jones completed 22 of 35 passes for 155 yards and two touchdowns, with no interceptions, and ran 10 times for 41 yards. Baugh carried 25 times for 91 yards and the score, Eric Singleton Jr. caught seven passes for 43, and Durkin made both field goals. We didn't turn the ball over once.

But the defense, friends. The defense. The group that ranked last in the conference held Texas to 272 yards. Graham led us with seven tackles to go with his sack and forced fumble. LJ McCray had a sack and a half and 2.5 tackles for loss. After the first two Texas drives, the AP noted, the defense was excellent, allowing one first down on the Longhorns' first three drives of the second half. We held the ball for 38:11. Texas had it for 21:49. That's not a football game. That's a crocodile waiting at the riverbank.

Part 2: The Open Week, and the Bulldog Ahead

(whispering) And now, the predator rests.

Florida has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. That's the honest schedule note. The Gators get a week to heal, and I get a week to update my Field Guide to Opponents.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, we play No. 5 Georgia at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, with kickoff listed for 3:30 p.m. Eastern. That's right. Atlanta. The rivalry has called Jacksonville home since 1933, but with Jacksonville's stadium under renovation, it moves to Atlanta this year and to Tampa next year. Which means the Okefenokee Oar, the student-government trophy carved from a 1,000-year-old cypress from the swamp that straddles the state border, is coming to Atlanta, too.

The Reptile Index: Georgia

Every week I classify the opponent. This week, I've had to think hard.

Georgia's mascot is a bulldog. A mammal. Not a reptile. And yet, this Georgia team has the qualities of a saltwater crocodile: large, powerful, and very difficult to dislodge from a riverbank. The Bulldogs are 6-1, they score 43 points a game, and they allow 15.9. Their defense gives up 91.4 rushing yards a game. Gunner Stockton has thrown for 1,570 yards with 16 touchdowns and four interceptions. Raylen Wilson leads them in tackles, with 44, and in sacks, with four. Respect the crocodile.

But I am a scientist, and science requires that we observe recent behavior. And last Saturday, friends, the crocodile was surprised.

Auburn walked into Sanford Stadium and beat No. 1 Georgia 27-24 on a field goal as time expired. Georgia led 14-0, and then Auburn scored the next 24 points. The Bulldogs had three turnovers, including a Stockton fumble with 58 seconds left while driving for a potential go-ahead field goal. They committed three personal fouls, the AP noted. Auburn outrushed them 192 to 113. And the loss ended Georgia's 53-game winning streak against unranked teams.

Fifty-three. That's a long time for an apex species to go without a surprise. But nature always finds a way.

Who to Watch

Jadan Baugh, our running back: 763 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns on 135 carries. Thirteen, friends. That is a creature that finds the end zone the way a gator finds a warm rock.

Tramell Jones Jr., quarterback: one start, one road win over a top-10 team, zero interceptions. That's a perfect field record.

Dallas Wilson, receiver: our leader with 29 catches for 403 yards and three touchdowns.

Myles Graham: 48 tackles, the team lead, plus the play of the season. Jayden Woods: 4.5 sacks, our leader.

Gunner Stockton, Georgia quarterback: 16 touchdowns, and four interceptions, two of them last Saturday. Our secondary will want to be in that neighborhood.

The History Section

I'll be honest, as a scientist must be. CollegeFootballData.com's count has Georgia ahead in the series, 58-44-2, and the Bulldogs have won the last five meetings. Last year's game was 24-20. That's a long dry season. But dry seasons end, friends. Ask the Longhorns.

Swamp Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Gainesville. Our home ground had 141,085 residents at the 2020 census, the most populous city in North Central Florida. Just south of town sits Paynes Prairie, 21,000 acres of wilderness where, I can tell you from personal field research, actual alligators live. Gatorade was invented right here in the 1960s to help refresh the Florida football team. Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers came out of Gainesville. And on Saturdays we play in Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, which holds 88,548, making it the largest stadium in Florida. Steve Spurrier named it the Swamp in 1992 because, as he explained, a swamp is where Gators live, and it's hot and sticky and can be dangerous. We've won three national championships, in 1996, 2006 and 2008, and produced three Heisman winners: Spurrier, Danny Wuerffel and Tim Tebow.

Athens, Georgia. Now, Athens is a lovely town. Great music scene. R.E.M. came from there, and the B-52's, and they're very proud of it, as they should be.

But I have to share a field observation. In Athens, at the corner of South Finley and Dearing Streets, there's a famous oak called the "Tree That Owns Itself." Sometime between 1820 and 1832, its owner deeded the tree ownership of itself and the land around it. Friends, I've studied many species, and I've never seen one that confident. A tree, with a deed. The tree standing there now is an offspring of the original, so even the tree has a backup. Georgia's run defense could have used one when Auburn ran for 192 yards on it.

And their stadium is famous for its privet hedges, planted because roses wouldn't grow well in Athens's climate. Friends, roses wouldn't grow there. Gators, on the other hand, can live just about anywhere. Including Atlanta, on Oct. 31.

The Final Narration

(whispering) The predator rests this week. It studies. It waits. And on the last day of October, in a dome in Atlanta, it will rise once more from the water...

(full volume) AND THE GATOR... STRIKES!

That play had scales. Go Gators.

Texas had it for 21:49. That's not a football game. That's a crocodile waiting at the riverbank.
Part 2: The Open Week, and the Bulldog Ahead
(whispering) And now, the predator rests.
Florida has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. That's the honest schedule note. The Gators get a week to heal, and I get a week to update my Field Guide to Opponents.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, we play No. 5 Georgia at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, with kickoff listed for 3:30 p.m. Eastern. That's right. Atlanta. The rivalry has called Jacksonville home since 1933, but with Jacksonville's stadium under renovation, it moves to Atlanta this year and to Tampa next year. Which means the Okefenokee Oar, the student-government trophy carved from a 1,000-year-old cypress from the swamp that straddles the state border, is coming to Atlanta, too.
The Reptile Index: Georgia
Every week I classify the opponent. This week, I've had to think hard.

Georgia's mascot is a bulldog. A mammal. Not a reptile. And yet, this Georgia team has the qualities of a saltwater crocodile: large, powerful, and very difficult to dislodge from a riverbank. The Bulldogs are 6-1, they score 43 points a game, and they allow 15.9. Their defense gives up 91.4 rushing yards a game. Gunner Stockton has thrown for 1,570 yards with 16 touchdowns and four interceptions. Raylen Wilson leads them in tackles, with 44, and in sacks, with four. Respect the crocodile.
But I am a scientist, and science requires that we observe recent behavior. And last Saturday, friends, the crocodile was surprised.

Auburn walked into Sanford Stadium and beat No. 1 Georgia 27-24 on a field goal as time expired. Georgia led 14-0, and then Auburn scored the next 24 points. The Bulldogs had three turnovers, including a Stockton fumble with 58 seconds left while driving for a potential go-ahead field goal. They committed three personal fouls, the AP noted. Auburn outrushed them 192 to 113. And the loss ended Georgia's 53-game winning streak against unranked teams.
Fifty-three. That's a long time for an apex species to go without a surprise. But nature always finds a way.
Who to Watch
Jadan Baugh, our running back: 763 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns on 135 carries. Thirteen, friends. That is a creature that finds the end zone the way a gator finds a warm rock.
Tramell Jones Jr., quarterback: one start, one road win over a top-10 team, zero interceptions. That's a perfect field record.
Dallas Wilson, receiver: our leader with 29 catches for 403 yards and three touchdowns.
Myles Graham: 48 tackles, the team lead, plus the play of the season. Jayden Woods: 4.5 sacks, our leader.
Gunner Stockton, Georgia quarterback: 16 touchdowns, and four interceptions, two of them last Saturday. Our secondary will want to be in that neighborhood.
The History Section

I'll be honest, as a scientist must be. CollegeFootballData.com's count has Georgia ahead in the series, 58-44-2, and the Bulldogs have won the last five meetings. Last year's game was 24-20. That's a long dry season. But dry seasons end, friends. Ask the Longhorns.
Swamp Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Gainesville. Our home ground had 141,085 residents at the 2020 census, the most populous city in North Central Florida. Just south of town sits Paynes Prairie, 21,000 acres of wilderness where, I can tell you from personal field research, actual alligators live. Gatorade was invented right here in the 1960s to help refresh the Florida football team. Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers came out of Gainesville. And on Saturdays we play in Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, which holds 88,548, making it the largest stadium in Florida. Steve Spurrier named it the Swamp in 1992 because, as he explained, a swamp is where Gators live, and it's hot and sticky and can be dangerous. We've won three national championships, in 1996, 2006 and 2008, and produced three Heisman winners: Spurrier, Danny Wuerffel and Tim Tebow.
Athens, Georgia. Now, Athens is a lovely town. Great music scene. R.E.M. came from there, and the B-52's, and they're very proud of it, as they should be.

But I have to share a field observation. In Athens, at the corner of South Finley and Dearing Streets, there's a famous oak called the "Tree That Owns Itself." Sometime between 1820 and 1832, its owner deeded the tree ownership of itself and the land around it. Friends, I've studied many species, and I've never seen one that confident. A tree, with a deed. The tree standing there now is an offspring of the original, so even the tree has a backup. Georgia's run defense could have used one when Auburn ran for 192 yards on it.

And their stadium is famous for its privet hedges, planted because roses wouldn't grow well in Athens's climate. Friends, roses wouldn't grow there. Gators, on the other hand, can live just about anywhere. Including Atlanta, on Oct. 31.
The Final Narration
(whispering) The predator rests this week. It studies. It waits. And on the last day of October, in a dome in Atlanta, it will rise once more from the water...
(full volume) AND THE GATOR... STRIKES!
That play had scales. Go Gators.

articles.title: Album Review: Auburn Scratched the Record in Athens, the Dawgs Get a Week in the Studio, and the Gators Are Booked for a Show in Atlanta
articles.byline: Thaddeus 'Thad' Okafor-Brandt, The Georgia Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 5 Georgia (6-1): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Georgia vs. No. 20 Florida (5-2), Sat., Oct. 31, Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Atlanta
articles.text:
Some records you put on, and you know by the second track you're in for something great. Some records skip.

Saturday, the record skipped.

I'm Thad Okafor-Brandt. I spun indie rock on college radio in Athens for years before I figured out that a good defensive call sheet reads exactly like a good set list: open strong, build tension, save the big one for the end. I review every Georgia game like an album, and every album gets a verdict. Some weeks, that's a joy. This week, it's a growth opportunity.

Track one on the set list: honesty.

Part 1: Album Review, "Auburn 27, Georgia 24"

Here's the liner-notes version. Auburn beat us 27-24 at Sanford Stadium on a 34-yard field goal by Alex McPherson as time expired. We were ranked No. 1 for exactly one week. The AP poll now has us at No. 5.

Side A opened like a classic. On the very first play, Gunner Stockton went into the turf helmet-first and had to come out. So Ryan Puglisi came in and completed all three of his passes, including a 41-yarder to Craig Dandridge Jr., and Dwight Phillips Jr. finished the drive with a 15-yard touchdown run. Stockton came back on the next possession and threw a 24-yard touchdown pass to tight end Lawson Luckie. 14-0, Georgia. I was already writing "instant classic" in the margin.

And then the album went somewhere I didn't expect. Auburn scored the next 24 points. Its first touchdown came on a trick play, a 24-yard pass from receiver Christian Neptune. Byrum Brown, Auburn's 235-pound quarterback, wore our defense down with his legs, running 26 times for 115 yards. Our defense was on the field for 45 plays in the first half, the AP noted. Auburn outrushed us 192 to 113.

Side B is where it got dramatic. Peyton Woodring hit a 42-yard field goal, and then Stockton led a 13-play, 94-yard drive starting at our own 6, finishing it with a 4-yard touchdown pass to London Humphreys. Tied at 24 with 2:58 left. That drive is the best track on the record, and I'll defend it forever.

Then the hidden track nobody wanted. We got the ball back and drove to the Auburn 46, and Stockton lost a fumble with 58 seconds left. A roughing-the-passer penalty helped set up McPherson's kick. Auburn's sideline emptied onto the field.

The Credits

Stockton completed 22 of 34 passes for 272 yards with two touchdowns and two interceptions, and coach Kirby Smart said afterward that Stockton played through a stinger in his throwing shoulder. Respect. Dandridge caught four passes for 88 yards, Talyn Taylor four for 64. Phillips ran for 68 yards on 10 carries. Raylen Wilson had 10 tackles and a sack, and Chris Cole added 10 tackles.

The AP noted three turnovers and three personal fouls, and the loss ended our nine-game winning streak over Auburn and our 53-game run against unranked opponents. Fifty-three straight. That's a career-spanning box set. It's okay for a box set to end.

The Verdict

Half a classic. A brilliant opening, a gorgeous comeback track, and a final song that I'll be skipping on future listens. Every great band has an album like this one. The good ones learn from it.

The Discography So Far

We're 6-1 and 4-1 in the SEC. We beat Tennessee State 63-3 and Western Kentucky 70-20, won at Arkansas 45-17, then beat Oklahoma 41-13 and Vanderbilt 38-14. Then, one week before the Auburn game, we won 20-17 at Alabama. We score 43 points a game and allow 15.9. One skipped record doesn't erase a discography.

Part 2: The Studio Week, Then Atlanta

Georgia has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. That's the honest schedule note. The Dawgs get a week in the studio to remix, rest and heal.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, we play No. 20 Florida at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, with kickoff listed for 3:30 p.m. Eastern. The rivalry has lived in Jacksonville since 1933, but with Jacksonville's stadium under renovation, it's in Atlanta this year and in Tampa next year. A Georgia-Florida game, in Georgia's capital city. I don't make the rules, friends. I just enjoy the venue.

Let me be gracious first, because a good critic gives credit. Florida won 27-24 at No. 7 Texas last Saturday, with quarterback Tramell Jones Jr. throwing two touchdown passes in his first career start. Its defense sacked Arch Manning five times and held the ball for more than 38 minutes. That's a real performance, and the Gators earned it.

Now, the full discography, because a critic listens to the whole catalog. Florida started 4-0 and climbed to No. 8 in the AP poll. Then it lost 45-17 at Missouri and 38-19 at home to South Carolina. Before the Texas game, the AP noted, Florida's defense ranked last in the SEC. For the season, the Gators allow 28.3 points a game. We allow 15.9.

Gainesville gave the world Tom Petty, and friends, I'd never start a feud with Tom Petty. But a 4-0 start, followed by two blowout losses? That's "Free Fallin'." I'm just reading the track list.

Who to Watch

Gunner Stockton, our quarterback: 1,570 yards, 16 touchdowns and four interceptions this season. He played through a stinger and still led a 94-yard tying drive. That's a headliner.

Raylen Wilson: leads us in tackles, with 44, and sacks, with four. He's the bass player. You don't always notice him, but nothing works without him.

Dwight Phillips Jr.: our leading rusher, 348 yards on 47 carries.

Jadan Baugh, Florida running back: 763 yards and 13 touchdowns. Our defense allows 91.4 rushing yards a game, and this will be the matchup of the afternoon.

Myles Graham, Florida linebacker: 48 tackles and the forced fumble that ended the Texas game.

The Back Catalog

CollegeFootballData.com's count has Georgia leading the series 58-44-2, and we've won the last five meetings: 34-7, 42-20, 43-20, 34-20 and, last year, 24-20. Five straight. That's what we call a greatest-hits collection.

Liner Notes: A Tale of Two Towns

Athens. The 2020 census counted 127,315 people in the Classic City, and the 2020 book "Cool Town" describes Athens as the model of 1980s indie culture. R.E.M., the B-52's, Widespread Panic and Drive-By Truckers all came out of here, and there are commemorative plaques on the sidewalk in front of the Georgia Theatre and the 40 Watt Club. Sanford Stadium holds 93,033, and its privet hedges have surrounded the field since the first game in 1929. The idea came from a Georgia athletic official who loved the roses at the Rose Bowl, but roses don't suit our climate, so we planted hedges, and a legend took root. Uga, our English bulldog, has belonged to the Seiler family of Savannah since 1956. He travels with the team and stays in the team hotel in his own room. And Georgia claims national titles from 1980, 2021 and 2022, with back-to-back College Football Playoff championships.

Gainesville. Now, Gainesville is a fine town. But here's a fun liner note. Gatorade was invented in Gainesville in the 1960s to help refresh the Florida football team. Friends, they had to invent a whole new drink just to survive their own home games. Steve Spurrier named the stadium the Swamp in 1992, and he explained that a swamp is hot and sticky and can be dangerous. That's the official mission statement. Hot, sticky and dangerous. In Athens, our mission statement is a hedge. You can sit next to a hedge without breaking a sweat.

And there's a 21,000-acre wilderness called Paynes Prairie on the south side of Gainesville. I hear alligators live there. That's the thing about the Gators: their natural habitat is a prairie south of town. Their unnatural habitat, until the Texas game, was the bottom of the SEC defensive rankings.

Encore

Here's my final note. A great band doesn't break up after one skipped record. It goes back to the studio, listens to the tape, fixes the bridge and comes back louder. We have a week in the studio. We have a quarterback who plays through stingers, a defense that allows 15.9 a game and a five-game streak in this rivalry. And on Oct. 31, in Atlanta, we get to play the encore.

Track nine on the set list: blitz. Go Dawgs.

articles.title: Pedigree Tells: Kentucky Is 6-1, Tied for First in the SEC, and the Commodores Are Sailing a Landlocked Boat Into Lexington
articles.byline: Rhett Abernathy-Coyle, The Kentucky Fanatic
articles.matchup: Vanderbilt (3-4) at No. 12 Kentucky (6-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, Kroger Field, SEC Network
articles.text:
Good evening, friends, and welcome to the paddock. Rhett Abernathy-Coyle here, writing from a fence rail on a horse farm off Versailles Road, where the October grass is still somehow blue if you squint, the Keeneland fall meet is in full swing, and I am wearing my lucky seersucker for the seventh straight week, because I do not mess with a streak.

And friends, what a streak it is. Your Kentucky Wildcats are 6-1. We're 4-1 in the SEC. We're ranked 12th in the country. And after Saturday night, the AP says we're tied for first place in the Southeastern Conference with Georgia. I had to read that sentence out loud to my mare, Lady Bluegrass, just to hear how it sounded. She nodded. She knows pedigree.

Part 1: Four Interceptions in Norman

Kentucky 21, Oklahoma 13, at Memorial Stadium in Norman, in front of 83,218 Sooner fans who came in feeling awfully good about themselves after beating then-No. 1 Texas the week before.

I won't sugarcoat the first three quarters, because a good horseman tells the truth about a slow start. We scored on our opening drive, a 67-yard march capped by Kenny Minchey's 2-yard touchdown pass to Willie Rodriguez. Then Oklahoma's defense held us to 76 yards and four punts on our next five drives. Tate Sandell kicked two field goals, John Mateer hit Rocky Beers for a 20-yard touchdown right before half, and we trailed 13-7 late in the third quarter. The horse was in the back of the pack, friends. Mud on the silks.

And then the closer kicked in.

Ty Bryant intercepted Mateer, the first of his two interceptions on the night. Minchey took us 44 yards in seven plays and found Rodriguez again, this time from 12 yards out, and Adam Zouagui's extra point made it 14-13 early in the fourth. Then, with 1:17 left, Jordan Castell stepped in front of a pass and took it 41 yards to the house. Ballgame. Castell had two interceptions, Bryant had two, and the Wildcats picked off Oklahoma four times. Four. That's not a defense, friends. That's a pickpocket convention.

Minchey finished 21 of 28 for 158 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Rodriguez caught five passes for 38 yards and both scores. Nic Anderson led us with 48 receiving yards. On defense, Grant Godfrey made 15 tackles, Elijah Barnes made 10, and Tavion Gadson had 1.5 sacks. We gained only 230 yards, and I'll own that. But we won the turnover battle 4-0, and in this family, that's what we call breeding.

The Bloodline Report

A good breeder looks at the whole record, not just one race. So here it is. That was our fifth straight win. Before Norman, we won 35-34 at South Carolina and then beat LSU 35-34 in overtime at Kroger Field. Earlier, we won at Texas A&M 31-21. Our only loss came to Alabama, 45-17, back on Sept. 12. Will Stein, our first-year head coach, came over from Oregon in December, and this team plays like it has never once heard that Kentucky is supposed to be a basketball school.

Now, the honest part, because pedigree also means knowing your flaws. The AP preview says we're dead last in FBS in third-down conversions, at 29.1 of every 100 tries. Last, friends. Our pass defense allows 249.7 yards a game, 116th. But we're third in FBS in turnover margin at +11, and our quarterback has thrown 13 touchdowns and one interception. We make our living stealing the ball and never giving it back. It is not pretty. It is a mudder. It wins.

Part 2: The Commodores Come to Lexington

Saturday night, 7:30 Eastern, SEC Network, Kroger Field. No. 12 Kentucky hosts Vanderbilt.

Now, I'll be gentlemanly first. Vanderbilt has beaten us two years running: 20-13 here in Lexington in 2024 and 45-17 in Nashville in 2025. I remember both. My mare remembers both. We do not forget a race we lost. Respect where it's due, Commodores.

But let's look at this year's form.

Vanderbilt is 3-4 and 0-4 in the SEC. It lost to Arkansas 31-21 at home last Saturday, and that snapped the Razorbacks' 14-game SEC losing streak. Friends, Arkansas hadn't won an SEC game since 2024, and the Commodores ended that drought for them, in Nashville, on a Saturday night. That's not a loss. That's a charitable donation. Before that, Ole Miss beat Vanderbilt 52-17 in Nashville, and Georgia won 38-14 in Athens.

To be fair, Jared Curtis threw for 274 yards against Arkansas, and Junior Sherrill caught eight passes for 99 yards and a touchdown. Sherrill leads Vanderbilt with 41 catches for 628 yards on the season. He is the real thing, and our secondary needs to know where he is.

Who to Watch

Kenny Minchey, our quarterback: 1,552 yards, 13 touchdowns, one interception and a 68.4 completion rate. One interception in seven games. That's a horse that doesn't throw a shoe.

C.J. Baxter, running back: 484 yards on 87 carries and eight touchdowns, our leader on the ground.

Kenny Darby, receiver: 34 catches for 436 yards and three touchdowns.

Our ball hawks: Castell and Bryant, two interceptions each on Saturday. Vanderbilt has a turnover margin of -6, 126th in FBS, and Curtis has thrown seven interceptions this season with two more on Saturday. I like this matchup the way I like a filly on a fast track.

The Vanderbilt run defense: The AP said the Commodores allowed 196 rushing yards to Ole Miss and 170 to Arkansas the last two weeks. Their run defense ranks 79th. Our backs should be licking their chops.

A Brief History Seminar

Kentucky leads the all-time series 49-42-4, according to CollegeFootballData.com. So we're ahead, but these two have been running neck and neck for a long, long time. We'd like to stop their two-race winning streak, please and thank you.

Bluegrass Paddock: A Tale of Two Towns

Lexington. They call us the Horse Capital of the World, and we earned it, thanks to hundreds of horse farms, the Kentucky Horse Park, The Red Mile and Keeneland, which runs live races in April and October and hasn't changed much since it opened in 1936. Keeneland hosted the 2015 Breeders' Cup, when American Pharoah won the Classic. The 2020 census counted 322,570 people in Lexington, the second-most populous city in Kentucky, and every one of them can tell a thoroughbred from a quarter horse at 50 paces. Rupp Arena is downtown, Kroger Field holds about 61,000, and on a crisp October Saturday night, the whole Bluegrass is blue.

Nashville. Now, I adore Nashville. Music City. The Grand Ole Opry. The Ryman. It's a wonderful place to visit. But friends, the Nashville Scene once counted 33 bachelorette parties on Lower Broadway in less than two hours on a Friday night, and said the real number was probably higher. Thirty-three in two hours. That's not a downtown. That's a bridal conveyor belt.

They also call Nashville the "Athens of the South," and they built a full-size replica of the Parthenon in Centennial Park to prove it. Friends, when your city needs a copy of an ancient Greek temple to feel smart, I gently suggest you just read a book.

And then there's their stadium. FirstBank Stadium seats 35,000 after a renovation that took it down from 40,350. It is officially the smallest stadium in the SEC. They renovated it and made it smaller. I've seen horse barns with more ambition. Last Saturday's crowd was 35,000. Our crowd will be bigger, louder and much more blue.

Here's how this race sets up. Kentucky has won five straight, takes the ball away like it's in the rulebook, and has a quarterback who doesn't give it back. Vanderbilt has lost four straight SEC games, hands the ball over more than almost anybody in the country, and just watched Arkansas end a 14-game skid on its home field. We'll play at night, at home, with a share of first place at stake and two years of Vandy wins in the back of our minds.

Pedigree tells, friends. Saddle up. Go Big Blue.

My call: Kentucky Wildcats 33, Vanderbilt Commodores 23.

blocks.text: Good evening, friends, and welcome to the paddock. Rhett Abernathy-Coyle here, writing from a fence rail on a horse farm off Versailles Road, where the October grass is still somehow blue if you squint, the Keeneland fall meet is in full swing, and I am wearing my lucky seersucker for the seventh straight week, because I do not mess with a streak.

And friends, what a streak it is. Your Kentucky Wildcats are 6-1. We're 4-1 in the SEC. We're ranked 12th in the country. And after Saturday night, the AP says we're tied for first place in the Southeastern Conference with Georgia. I had to read that sentence out loud to my mare, Lady Bluegrass, just to hear how it sounded. She nodded. She knows pedigree.
Part 1: Four Interceptions in Norman
Kentucky 21, Oklahoma 13, at Memorial Stadium in Norman, in front of 83,218 Sooner fans who came in feeling awfully good about themselves after beating then-No. 1 Texas the week before.

I won't sugarcoat the first three quarters, because a good horseman tells the truth about a slow start. We scored on our opening drive, a 67-yard march capped by Kenny Minchey's 2-yard touchdown pass to Willie Rodriguez. Then Oklahoma's defense held us to 76 yards and four punts on our next five drives. Tate Sandell kicked two field goals, John Mateer hit Rocky Beers for a 20-yard touchdown right before half, and we trailed 13-7 late in the third quarter. The horse was in the back of the pack, friends. Mud on the silks.
And then the closer kicked in.

Ty Bryant intercepted Mateer, the first of his two interceptions on the night. Minchey took us 44 yards in seven plays and found Rodriguez again, this time from 12 yards out, and Adam Zouagui's extra point made it 14-13 early in the fourth. Then, with 1:17 left, Jordan Castell stepped in front of a pass and took it 41 yards to the house. Ballgame. Castell had two interceptions, Bryant had two, and the Wildcats picked off Oklahoma four times. Four. That's not a defense, friends. That's a pickpocket convention.

Minchey finished 21 of 28 for 158 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Rodriguez caught five passes for 38 yards and both scores. Nic Anderson led us with 48 receiving yards. On defense, Grant Godfrey made 15 tackles, Elijah Barnes made 10, and Tavion Gadson had 1.5 sacks. We gained only 230 yards, and I'll own that. But we won the turnover battle 4-0, and in this family, that's what we call breeding.
The Bloodline Report

A good breeder looks at the whole record, not just one race. So here it is. That was our fifth straight win. Before Norman, we won 35-34 at South Carolina and then beat LSU 35-34 in overtime at Kroger Field. Earlier, we won at Texas A&M 31-21. Our only loss came to Alabama, 45-17, back on Sept. 12. Will Stein, our first-year head coach, came over from Oregon in December, and this team plays like it has never once heard that Kentucky is supposed to be a basketball school.

Now, the honest part, because pedigree also means knowing your flaws. The AP preview says we're dead last in FBS in third-down conversions, at 29.1 of every 100 tries. Last, friends. Our pass defense allows 249.7 yards a game, 116th. But we're third in FBS in turnover margin at +11, and our quarterback has thrown 13 touchdowns and one interception. We make our living stealing the ball and never giving it back. It is not pretty. It is a mudder. It wins.
Part 2: The Commodores Come to Lexington
Saturday night, 7:30 Eastern, SEC Network, Kroger Field. No. 12 Kentucky hosts Vanderbilt.

Now, I'll be gentlemanly first. Vanderbilt has beaten us two years running: 20-13 here in Lexington in 2024 and 45-17 in Nashville in 2025. I remember both. My mare remembers both. We do not forget a race we lost. Respect where it's due, Commodores.
But let's look at this year's form.

Vanderbilt is 3-4 and 0-4 in the SEC. It lost to Arkansas 31-21 at home last Saturday, and that snapped the Razorbacks' 14-game SEC losing streak. Friends, Arkansas hadn't won an SEC game since 2024, and the Commodores ended that drought for them, in Nashville, on a Saturday night. That's not a loss. That's a charitable donation. Before that, Ole Miss beat Vanderbilt 52-17 in Nashville, and Georgia won 38-14 in Athens.

Kenny Minchey, our quarterback: 1,552 yards, 13 touchdowns, one interception and a 68.4 completion rate. One interception in seven games. That's a horse that doesn't throw a shoe.
C.J. Baxter, running back: 484 yards on 87 carries and eight touchdowns, our leader on the ground.
Kenny Darby, receiver: 34 catches for 436 yards and three touchdowns.
