articles.title: That's a Whole Roux of a Defense, Cher: LSU Brings the Gumbo to the Plains, and Auburn's Eagle Might Want to Look Away
articles.byline: Celestine 'Cece' Thibodeaux, The LSU Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 18 LSU (5-2) at Auburn (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, noon ET, Jordan-Hare Stadium, ABC
articles.text:
Bonjour, Tiger fans! Ça va? It's Cece Thibodeaux, coming to you from a folding chair outside Tiger Stadium, where the smoke from forty tailgate pots is still hanging in the air like a lovely purple-and-gold fog. My crawfish étouffée is resting, my notebook is open, and my spice rack is fully stocked, because we have a defense to rate and a road trip to plan.

Last Saturday, the Tigers did something I haven't seen since I was a little girl licking the spoon in Mamère's kitchen. They shut out an SEC team. And this Saturday, we go to Auburn, where the other Tigers are feeling very proud of themselves. Cher, let's cook.

Part 1: The Shutout Gumbo

LSU 31, Mississippi State 0. In front of 102,321 people at Tiger Stadium, which is the stadium's full capacity, because of course it was.

The AP says it was LSU's first shutout of an SEC opponent since a 45-0 win at Mississippi State in 2007. You know what happened in 2007, cher? LSU won the national championship. I'm not saying. I'm just setting the table.

Let me walk you through the recipe.

The roux: Sam Leavitt. He completed 31 of 38 passes for 289 yards and four touchdowns, and he threw no interceptions. The AP pointed out it was his first turnover-free game of the season. He fed nine different receivers. That's not a passing game, cher, that's a church potluck where everybody brought something.

The trinity: the touchdowns. Eugene Wilson III caught a 10-yard touchdown early in the first quarter. Jackson Harris caught a 27-yarder later in the first and a 17-yarder in the second, and it was 21-0 at the half. Scott Starzyk kicked a 26-yard field goal in the third, and Malik Elzy caught a 6-yard touchdown with 31 seconds left in the quarter. Harris finished with six catches for 85 yards before leaving in the third quarter with what the AP called an apparent lower left leg injury. We're praying for him and waiting on real news.

The seasoning: Dilin Jones. He ran 18 times for 84 yards, including a 21-yard run on which his helmet came right off. He added eight catches for 58 yards.

The pot lid: the defense. Mississippi State got inside our 40 five times. All five drives ended on failed fourth downs, one of them at our 6. The Bulldogs went 0 for 5 on fourth down. TJ Dottery made 12 tackles, Davhon Keys had 10 with 1.5 for loss, Jordan Ross had a sack and 2.5 tackles for loss, and Ty Benefield picked off a pass. To be fair and kind, Mississippi State was playing without its starting quarterback and top running back, and their young quarterback was making his first start. We wish them health. We still shut them out.

The Week Before

I won't pretend the week before didn't happen. We lost 35-34 in overtime at Kentucky, and we dropped 12 spots in the AP poll for it. Earlier this year, we lost 32-24 at Ole Miss. Both on the road. Both close. Both stung like a hot pepper you thought was a green bean. But this team answered, and that's what a good gumbo does: it tastes even richer the second day.

Part 2: Off to the Plains

Saturday at noon Eastern on ABC, No. 18 LSU visits Auburn at Jordan-Hare Stadium. We're 5-2 and 2-2 in the SEC. Auburn is 4-2 and 2-2.

Now, I'll be gracious, because Mamère is watching from heaven with a wooden spoon. Auburn beat No. 1 Georgia 27-24 in Athens last Saturday on a field goal as time expired. Byrum Brown ran for 115 yards and threw a touchdown, and Auburn didn't turn it over. That was a beautiful win, cher, and I sent them a little praline in my heart.

But then I opened the stat sheet.

The Spice Scale

Every week I rate the other team's defense on my scale, from "bland" all the way to "Saturday night in Death Valley." Here's Auburn's.

The Auburn defense allows 371 yards a game, 87th in FBS. It gives up 228 passing yards a game, 96th. It allows 143 rushing yards a game, 74th. And against Georgia, it allowed 440 yards and 327 through the air.

On the spice scale, cher, that is a mild boudin. It has some flavor. It has a little kick. But you could feed it to a toddler and nobody would cry.

Our defense, on the other hand? It allows 256.6 yards a game, fourth in FBS. It allows 88.3 rushing yards a game, 11th, and opponents convert just 30.6 of every 100 third downs, 14th. In the red zone, opponents score on 70.6 of every 100 trips, 13th. That's a whole roux of a defense, cher. That's Saturday night in Death Valley, even at noon.

Who to Watch

Sam Leavitt, our quarterback: 1,784 yards, 14 touchdowns, 70.1 completions for every 100 throws. If he keeps the ball as clean as he did last week, Auburn's 96th-ranked pass defense is in for a long lunch.

Dilin Jones, running back: 567 yards on 128 carries and five touchdowns.

Jackson Harris, receiver: 27 catches for 456 yards and five touchdowns. We'll wait on official word about his leg.

Byrum Brown, Auburn quarterback: 1,202 passing yards and a team-high 459 rushing yards. He's big and he runs hard. Our run defense, 11th in the country, has been looking forward to meeting him.

The clock. The AP preview says Auburn ranks 134th in FBS in time of possession, at 26:54 a game. We're 19th at 32:55. Auburn also averages 68 penalty yards a game, 111th. If we hold the ball like a pot of red beans on a Monday, slow and steady, that Auburn defense is going to be very tired by the fourth quarter.

A Brief History Seminar

LSU leads the series 33-23-1, according to CollegeFootballData.com. In the most recent meeting, in 2023, LSU won 48-18 in Baton Rouge. The last time we went to Jordan-Hare, in 2022, we won 21-17.

And LSU claims four national championships: 1958, 2003, 2007 and 2019. Our coach, Lane Kiffin, has been here since November 2025, and he already has us shutting out SEC teams. Somebody hand him a bowl of gumbo.

Bayou Kitchen: A Tale of Two Towns

Baton Rouge. Our capital city sits on a bluff above the Mississippi River, and it's the home of the Louisiana State Capitol, which at 450 feet and 34 stories is the tallest state capitol in the United States. We don't build small, cher. The 2020 census counted 227,470 people, and on a Saturday night it feels like all of them are at the stadium. Tiger Stadium seats 102,321, it's the second-largest stadium in the SEC, and the Sporting News once named "Saturday Night in Death Valley" and our tailgating the top tradition in college football. Our mascot, Mike the Tiger, is a real, live tiger who lives in a habitat right on campus. A real tiger, cher. We don't do metaphors.

Auburn. Now, Auburn is a sweet little town. Very lovely. But listen to this. Auburn's nickname, "the Loveliest Village on the Plains," comes from Oliver Goldsmith's poem. The name of that poem? "The Deserted Village." Cher, they named their town after a poem about a deserted village, and then they're surprised we're coming to visit.

The 2020 census counted 76,143 people in Auburn. That's a nice crowd for a crawfish boil. And Jordan-Hare seats 88,043, so the stadium has more seats than the town has people. I respect that. That's Louisiana thinking.

And then there's the confusion. Their team is the Tigers. Their official mascot is Aubie the Tiger. But their battle cry is "War Eagle," and they fly an eagle before games. Wikipedia literally says the War Eagle cry has "often led to outside confusion as to Auburn's official mascot." Cher, if Wikipedia is confused, imagine how the eagle feels. Over here, our tiger is a tiger. Our tiger knows he's a tiger.

Their big celebration is wrapping the oak trees at Toomer's Corner in toilet paper after wins. I love a tradition. But in Baton Rouge, when we win, we feed people. Auburn decorates a tree like it's a bathroom. Different cultures, cher.

And I'll remind Auburn, sweetly, about the 1988 Earthquake Game, when the roar at Tiger Stadium registered on a seismograph on campus. The opponent that day? Auburn. We have literally moved the earth on these folks. We'll try to keep it to a rumble on the Plains.

The Last Word

Here's my recipe. Start with a defense ranked fourth in the country. Add a quarterback who just threw four touchdowns without a single turnover. Stir in a team that holds the ball for almost 33 minutes a game against one that holds it for 27. Simmer at noon on the Plains. Season generously with Death Valley attitude.

Auburn had a wonderful Saturday, cher. But one great Saturday is a beignet. We're bringing the whole gumbo pot.

Geaux Tigers!

My call: LSU Tigers 28, Auburn Tigers 22.

articles.title: Ring It If You Mean It: The Sooners Make Their First Trip Ever to Starkville, and Their Offense Is Running on Pony Power
articles.byline: Wade Pettus, The Mississippi State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Oklahoma (3-3) at Mississippi State (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Davis Wade Stadium, SEC Network
articles.text:
Well. Evenin', folks. Wade Pettus here, poultry science graduate, Air Raid enthusiast, and the proud owner of a cowbell that has better football sense than most of the people on television. I'm writin' to you from the tailgate of my truck outside the feed store in Starkville, with a stack of receipts I've been drawin' plays on all week and a bell in my lap that has been very, very quiet since Saturday.

I'll explain the quiet. Then I'll explain why it's about to get loud.

Part 1: A Long Afternoon in Baton Rouge

LSU 31, Mississippi State 0. At Tiger Stadium, in front of 102,321 people, most of 'em in purple.

I won't dress that up. A farmer tells you the truth about the crop. LSU's quarterback, Sam Leavitt, completed 31 of 38 passes for 289 yards and four touchdowns. It was 21-0 at halftime and 31-0 after three quarters. And the AP said it was LSU's first shutout of an SEC team since 2007.

Here's what you need to know, though. We went into that game without our starting quarterback, Kamario Taylor, and our top running back, Da'Marion "Fluff" Bothwell. We wish them both a quick and full return, and that's all I'll say about that. So second-year quarterback Parker Puckett made his first career start in Death Valley, which is a little like learnin' to drive on the interstate at rush hour.

And you know what? The young man moved the ball. Puckett drove us inside the LSU 40 five separate times. Five. Every one of those drives ended on a failed fourth down, including one from the LSU 6. We went 0 for 5 on fourth down. Puckett finished 16 of 26 for 121 yards and ran 11 times for 40 more, with a 33-yard run that made my bell twitch. Kolin Wilson ran for 71 yards. We actually outrushed LSU, 170 to 90. Jett Jefferson made eight tackles, Tyler Lockhart made seven, and Marcus Williams had a sack and two tackles for loss.

Cowbell Rating

I rate plays from one ring to five. Puckett's 33-yard run: three rings. Our run defense holdin' LSU to 90 rushing yards: four rings. Five fourth-down trips with nothin' to show for it: no rings, and I'm not sure the bell's speaking to me. And two straight losses by 30-plus, after Alabama beat us 56-23 two weeks before the LSU game: the bell has asked for some quiet time.

But here's the bigger crop report. Before those two, we were 4-0. We beat UL Monroe 62-13, won at Minnesota 38-13, won at South Carolina 41-34 and beat Missouri 31-24. Missouri is ranked 22nd right now. This team can play.

Part 2: The Sooners Come to Starkville

Saturday at 3:30 Eastern, on SEC Network, Oklahoma comes to Davis Wade Stadium. We're 4-2 and 2-2 in the SEC. The Sooners are 3-3 and 1-2.

And folks, according to CollegeFootballData.com's records, these two programs have never played each other. Not once. So this is the very first time the Sooners get to hear a Davis Wade cowbell up close. I'd tell 'em to bring earplugs, but honestly, they ought to experience it raw. It's educational.

There's also a good storyline here. Our coach, Jeff Lebby, was Oklahoma's offensive coordinator before he came to Starkville in November 2023. So he knows the Sooners. I'd imagine the Sooners know him too. Should be a fun family reunion, and he's bringin' the bells.

Now, I'll be gracious first, because my mama raised me in a church pew. Oklahoma's defense is the real thing. The AP preview says it allows 260.7 yards a game, fifth in FBS, and 151.3 passing yards a game, sixth. Opponents convert only 25.6 of every 100 third downs, second in the country. And two Saturdays ago, the Sooners beat then-No. 1 Texas 27-24. Respect. Real respect.

Now let's talk about the Sooner offense. I'll go slow, so everybody can follow along.

Oklahoma averages 311.5 yards a game, 126th in FBS. It runs for 92.5 yards a game. That ranks 136th in FBS. Folks, that's the bottom of the feed bin. Our cowbell runs for more than that on a good Saturday. The Sooners score 21.3 points a game, 113th. And their turnover margin is -8, 134th in the country. Last Saturday, against Kentucky, they threw four interceptions in a 21-13 loss at home.

Ag Science Hour: The Schooner Problem

Here's an agricultural observation. Oklahoma's official mascot is the Sooner Schooner, a little covered wagon pulled by two white ponies named Boomer and Sooner. Ponies, folks. Not horses. Not mules. Not a tractor. Ponies. And their running game ranks 136th. I'm not sayin' the two things are related. I'm sayin' a poultry scientist notices patterns.

Who to Watch

Anthony Evans III, our receiver: 47 catches for 614 yards and five touchdowns, our leader. He caught seven more passes last week. Oklahoma's pass defense is sixth in the nation, so this is the matchup of the day.

Kamario Taylor, quarterback: 1,450 yards, 17 touchdowns, four interceptions before missing the LSU game. We'll wait for official word on who plays.

Our run game: We average 176.5 rushing yards a game, and even without Bothwell we ran for 170 at LSU. Oklahoma's run defense is 31st, which is good, but it's not the wall its pass defense is.

John Mateer, Oklahoma quarterback: 1,308 yards, nine touchdowns and seven interceptions, including three last week. Our defense would like to go two for two in that department.

The honest part: Our pass defense allows 264.8 yards a game, 127th in FBS, and we average 70.7 penalty yards a game, 118th. We've got to clean up the flags and keep the Sooners in front of us. Mateer threw for 270 yards last week. Nobody's sleepin' on that.

Golden Triangle Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Starkville. The 2020 census counted 24,360 of us, and every single one owns a cowbell. Starkville is the largest city in the Golden Triangle. It was founded in 1831 and was first called Boardtown, after a mill that made clapboards, before it was renamed for Revolutionary War general John Stark. Mississippi State was founded here in 1878 as the state's land-grant university. Our stadium, Davis Wade, opened in 1914 and is the second-oldest stadium in FBS. It seats 60,311, and on Saturday it'll sound like 600,000. Mississippi State's official tradition materials say cowbells started showin' up at games in the late 1930s and early '40s, and they've survived every attempt by opponents and rule books to quiet 'em down since. You cannot stop a cowbell, folks. You can only hope to contain it.

Norman. Now, Norman's a fine town. It had 128,026 people in the 2020 census, it's the third-largest city in Oklahoma, and their stadium seats 80,126. But listen to how the town got its name. It was named for Abner Norman, a 23-year-old surveyor from Kentucky. So it's a whole city named after a young fella who was just measurin' the land. In Starkville we name things after generals.

And then there's the Sooners nickname itself. Wikipedia explains that the original Sooners were folks who hid out and jumped into the Oklahoma land run early, stakin' their claims hours before the legal start. So the whole team is named after folks who couldn't wait their turn. I've got nothin' against enthusiasm. But on our farm, if you go before the bell, you start over. And around here, we've got a whole stadium full of bells.

Last thing. Their mascot wagon is a replica of the covered wagons settlers used in the 1889 land rush. Folks, they're still driving a wagon from 1889. We got a stadium from 1914, which makes ours the modern one.

The Last Ring

Here's how I see it. Oklahoma has a terrific defense and an offense that ranks 126th. We have a run game that just outrushed LSU with a backup quarterback, a receiver with 614 yards, and 60,000 people who will be ringin' from the opening kickoff until the last snap. The Sooners have never heard it in person. They're gonna remember the first time.

Ring it if you mean it, folks. I mean it. Hail State.

My call: Oklahoma Sooners 25, Mississippi State Bulldogs 24.

articles.title: Show Me the Tape: Missouri Takes Its Open Week After a Rough Night in Oxford, and the Hogs Are Still Celebrating Beating Vanderbilt
articles.byline: Delphine Arceneaux-Moss, The Missouri Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 22 Missouri (5-2): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Missouri at Arkansas (3-4), Sat., Oct. 31, Razorback Stadium, Fayetteville
articles.text:
Ba-da-da-DUM. Ba-da-da-DUM.

That's my news ticker, darling, and it means I have breaking news. Ready? Here it is: Missouri does not play this Saturday.

I know. Shocking. Stop the presses. I'm Delphine Arceneaux-Moss, reporting from a corner booth at Shakespeare's Pizza in downtown Columbia, where I've filed this story with a reporter's notebook, a slice of pepperoni and the steely calm of a woman who has watched the Ole Miss tape four times. I break news, I break down blitzes, and this week I'm going to break down exactly how we get back to winning. Show me the tape.

Part 1: The Oxford Dispatch

Ba-da-da-DUM. Breaking news: Ole Miss 31, Missouri 3.

I'm a journalist. I report what happened, even when I'd rather write a feature about the weather. So here's the lede: we went to Vaught-Hemingway Stadium ranked 13th, and we came home with three points.

And it began so promisingly, darling. Blake Craig kicked a 27-yard field goal in the first quarter, and for about two and a half minutes, Missouri led No. 9 Ole Miss on the road. I filed a draft headline. I deleted it later. Trinidad Chambliss threw three touchdown passes before halftime, and it was 21-3 at the break. He ran for a fourth score in the fourth quarter.

The moment I'll replay in my head, though, came in the second quarter. We had first-and-goal at the Ole Miss 2. Two consecutive runs lost yardage, a pass to the end zone fell incomplete, and Craig missed a 23-yard field goal. The AP called it a missed opportunity to keep pace. I'd call it the turning point of the whole story, and I'm a stickler for accurate headlines.

The run game never got going. Jamal Roberts came in with two straight 200-yard games and ran 20 times for 39 yards. As a team, we ran 26 times for 39. Ole Miss ran for 257.

Show Me the Tape: What Went Right

A fair reporter shows both sides, so here's the good news, and there was some. Austin Simmons threw for 339 yards, completing 25 of 44. Donovan Olugbode caught nine passes for 127 yards. Linebacker Nicholas Rodriguez made 13 tackles, the AP singled him out, and he leads us with 76 for the season. And Brunno Reus punted seven times for 297 yards, a long of 56, with two downed inside the Ole Miss 20. When your punter is in the AP story for the right reasons, the rest of the team owes him a nice lunch.

The Season So Far

We're 5-2 and 2-2 in the SEC, and the AP poll has us at No. 22. We beat Arkansas-Pine Bluff, won at Kansas 38-21, beat Troy, then beat Florida 45-17 and Texas A&M 27-6. The AP noted we're unbeaten at home. Our only other loss came at Mississippi State, 31-24. Coach Eli Drinkwitz led Missouri to back-to-back 10-win seasons and top-25 finishes in 2023 and 2024. This team has a foundation. Saturday was a bad edition, not a bad newspaper.

Part 2: Open Week, Then the Ozarks

Ba-da-da-DUM. Breaking news, part two: Missouri has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. The team gets a week to rest and heal, and I get a week to edit.

Then, on Saturday, Oct. 31, we go to Fayetteville to play Arkansas at Razorback Stadium. Kickoff time hasn't been announced yet. A Halloween road trip into the Ozarks. Spooky, darling. But I've seen the tape, and I'm not scared.

Let me be gracious first, because my editor taught me fairness. Arkansas beat Vanderbilt 31-21 last Saturday on the road. Joker Johnson returned an interception 25 yards for a touchdown, Miguel Mitchell intercepted a late pass, and quarterback KJ Jackson threw for 251 yards without a turnover. Good for them. Truly.

Now, the context paragraph, which every good story needs.

That win snapped Arkansas's 14-game SEC losing streak, according to the AP. It was the Razorbacks' first SEC win since 2024. Ba-da-da-DUM. Breaking news: Arkansas beat Vanderbilt. Hold the front page. The Hogs are 3-4 and 1-3 in the SEC. Earlier this season they lost at Utah 43-10, to Georgia 45-17 and at Texas A&M 34-7. They score 21 points a game and allow 26.7. We score 31.1 and allow 19.6.

Who to Watch

Jamal Roberts, our running back: 867 yards and eight touchdowns on 167 carries this season. One quiet night in Oxford doesn't erase 800 yards. Arkansas allows 144.7 rushing yards a game, and I expect him to remind everyone who he is.

Austin Simmons, quarterback: 1,773 yards, 14 touchdowns, two interceptions. Fourteen to two, darling. That's an accuracy rate I'd want in a fact-checker.

Cayden Lee, receiver: 47 catches for 678 yards and five touchdowns, our leader.

Daeden Hopkins: seven sacks. KJ Jackson should keep his head on a swivel.

Chris Marshall, Arkansas receiver: 43 catches for 633 yards, the Hogs' leader. He's the one our secondary needs to fact-check all afternoon.

A Brief History Seminar

Missouri leads the series 13-4, according to CollegeFootballData.com, and we've won the last four meetings: 29-27 in 2022, 48-14 in 2023, 28-21 in 2024 and 31-17 last year in Fayetteville. That's a four-year streak, and in my newsroom, streaks are stories. This one's ours.

Show Me the Town: A Tale of Two Towns

Columbia. The 2020 census counted 126,254 people here. Folks used to call it the "Athens of Missouri," and now it's just CoMo, because we're efficient. Missouri is recognized by the NCAA and, per Wikipedia, even Trivial Pursuit as the birthplace of Homecoming, which traces back to the 1911 game against Kansas. The Missouri School of Journalism opened on Sept. 14, 1908, and in 1921 it offered the world's first master's degree in journalism. On game day, look to the north end zone of Faurot Field, where the rock "M," built by freshmen from leftover stadium rocks, has stood since Oct. 1, 1927. Our mascot, Truman the Tiger, named for President Harry S. Truman, has won the national college mascot competition several times, most recently in 2024. And Shakespeare's Pizza, founded right here, is the unofficial fuel of journalism students.

Fayetteville. Now, Fayetteville is lovely, nestled in the Boston Mountains of the Ozarks. But here's my detective report. Folks call Fayetteville the "Track Capital of the South," because Arkansas's track and cross country teams win so often. Ba-da-da-DUM. Breaking news: the most successful athletes in Fayetteville are the ones who run away.

Their live mascot, Tusk, lives on a family farm in Dardanelle and makes a two-hour trip to Fayetteville for every home game. Darling, even the mascot commutes. I'd like to request an interview with Tusk, because he's the only Razorback with a longer streak of showing up than the SEC losing streak they just ended.

And then there's the Hog call. Grown adults, in a stadium, yelling "Woo, Pig! Sooie!" at the top of their lungs. It's a beloved tradition, I'm told, and it got its "Sooie" in the 1920s. That means Arkansas fans have been calling the pigs for a hundred years. I'll say this: the pigs always come. The SEC wins took a little longer.

Final Edition

Here's my closing paragraph, and I've fact-checked it twice. Missouri had one bad night. We have a running back with 867 yards, a quarterback with a 14-to-2 ratio, a defense that holds teams to 19.6 points a game, and a two-week head start on our Halloween homework. Arkansas just ended a streak. We'd like to keep ours.

That's the news. I'm Delphine Arceneaux-Moss. Show me the tape. M-I-Z!

On game day, look to the north end zone of Faurot Field, where the rock "M," built by freshmen from leftover stadium rocks, has stood since Oct. 1, 1927. Our mascot, Truman the Tiger, named for President Harry S. Truman, has won the national college mascot competition several times, most recently in 2024. And Shakespeare's Pizza, founded right here, is the unofficial fuel of journalism students.

Fayetteville. Now, Fayetteville is lovely, nestled in the Boston Mountains of the Ozarks. But here's my detective report. Folks call Fayetteville the "Track Capital of the South," because Arkansas's track and cross country teams win so often. Ba-da-da-DUM. Breaking news: the most successful athletes in Fayetteville are the ones who run away.

Their live mascot, Tusk, lives on a family farm in Dardanelle and makes a two-hour trip to Fayetteville for every home game. Darling, even the mascot commutes. I'd like to request an interview with Tusk, because he's the only Razorback with a longer streak of showing up than the SEC losing streak they just ended.

And then there's the Hog call. Grown adults, in a stadium, yelling "Woo, Pig! Sooie!" at the top of their lungs. It's a beloved tradition, I'm told, and it got its "Sooie" in the 1920s. That means Arkansas fans have been calling the pigs for a hundred years. I'll say this: the pigs always come. The SEC wins took a little longer.
Final Edition

Here's my closing paragraph, and I've fact-checked it twice. Missouri had one bad night. We have a running back with 867 yards, a quarterback with a 14-to-2 ratio, a defense that holds teams to 19.6 points a game, and a two-week head start on our Halloween homework. Arkansas just ended a streak. We'd like to keep ours.
That's the news. I'm Delphine Arceneaux-Moss. Show me the tape. M-I-Z!

articles.title: Boomer! (You Say Sooner.): Oklahoma Rides Into Starkville for the First Time Ever, and Somebody Please Hand Out Earplugs
articles.byline: Savannah Redbird-Lowe, The Oklahoma Fanatic
articles.matchup: Oklahoma (3-3) at Mississippi State (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Davis Wade Stadium, SEC Network
articles.text:
Boomer!

I said, BOOMER!

There it is. I heard you say "Sooner" from all the way out here on the prairie. Hey, y'all, it's Savannah Redbird-Lowe, former rodeo princess, current full-time Sooner, and a woman who reads a defense the way I used to read a barrel pattern: three turns, no wasted motion, and don't you dare knock one over.

This week I'm writing from the bleachers of a little practice arena outside Norman, where the October wind is doing that thing where it rearranges your hair for free. It's been a two-sided week, darlin'. One weekend we beat No. 1. The next weekend, we tipped a barrel. So let's talk about both, and then let's go to Starkville, a place no Sooner team has ever played.

Part 1: Four Barrels Down

Kentucky 21, Oklahoma 13, at home in Norman, in front of 83,218 people.

I'll be honest, because a rodeo princess doesn't fib about her times. We led most of the night. After Kentucky scored on its first drive, our defense held the Wildcats to 76 yards and four punts on their next five possessions. Tate Sandell drilled a 44-yard field goal. Then John Mateer found tight end Rocky Beers for a 20-yard touchdown with 30 seconds left in the half, and we led 10-7. Sandell added a 26-yarder in the third, and it was 13-7. I was standing up in my boots.

And then the barrels started falling. Kentucky intercepted us four times. Ty Bryant's first interception set up a Kentucky touchdown that made it 14-13 early in the fourth quarter. Then, with 1:17 to go, Jordan Castell returned an interception 41 yards for a touchdown. That was the night.

Mateer threw for 270 yards and a touchdown. Isaiah Sategna III caught eight passes for 83 yards, and Manny Choice caught five for 98. And our defense was terrific. Jake Kreul had 2.5 sacks and three tackles for loss, Owen Heinecke and Kip Lewis each made eight tackles, and we held Kentucky to 230 yards. You hold an SEC team to 230 yards, you ought to win. We just have to quit handing out free gifts.

Schooner Ride: The Week Before

Now let me remind everybody what happened one week earlier, because a princess always shows her best ride first. On Oct. 10, at the Cotton Bowl, Oklahoma beat then-No. 1 Texas 27-24. The AP noted that the No. 1 team then lost again the next week, too, when Auburn beat Georgia, the first time the No. 1 team had lost in consecutive weeks since October 1990. We started that trend, darlin'. You're welcome, college football.

That's this team. When we hold onto the ball, we can beat anybody in America.

Part 2: First Trip to Starkville

Saturday at 3:30 Eastern on SEC Network, we head to Davis Wade Stadium to play Mississippi State. We're 3-3 and 1-2 in the SEC. The Bulldogs are 4-2 and 2-2.

According to CollegeFootballData.com's records, the Sooners and Bulldogs have never played each other. First time ever. And there's a twist: Mississippi State's head coach, Jeff Lebby, used to be Oklahoma's offensive coordinator. He knows us. He knows our songs. He might even know the words to "Boomer Sooner." I hope he hums along.

Now, I'll be gracious, because Mama raised me with manners and a curry comb. Mississippi State started 4-0, with wins at South Carolina and over Missouri. Its offense averages 454.3 yards a game, 22nd in FBS, and Anthony Evans III has 47 catches for 614 yards. And the Bulldogs have been without starting quarterback Kamario Taylor and top running back Da'Marion Bothwell; we wish them both well and a full recovery.

But then I read the rest of the program.

The last two weeks, Mississippi State lost 56-23 at home to Alabama and 31-0 at LSU. That's two straight losses by more than 30. The Bulldog pass defense gives up 264.8 yards a game, 127th in FBS. It allows 28.5 points a game, 111th. And Mississippi State averages 70.7 penalty yards a game, 118th. Darlin', that's a lot of yellow laundry for one afternoon.

Who to Watch

Our defense: It allows 260.7 yards a game, fifth in FBS, and 151.3 passing yards, sixth. Opponents convert just 25.6 of every 100 third downs, second in the country. In the red zone, opponents score only 66.7 of every 100 times, sixth. This is the best barrel racer in the arena, and it doesn't knock anything over.

John Mateer, quarterback: 1,308 yards, nine touchdowns and a 65.1 completion rate. The interceptions are the one thing I'd fix with a magic wand. Against a pass defense that ranks 127th, he doesn't need to force anything. Just ride the pattern.

Isaiah Sategna III, receiver: 33 catches for 414 yards, our leader.

Lloyd Avant, running back: 267 yards on 60 carries. I'll be honest: our run game averages 92.5 yards a game, 136th in FBS. But Mississippi State's defense just gave up 289 passing yards to LSU, so maybe this is a throw-it-around kind of Saturday.

Anthony Evans III, the Bulldogs' top receiver: 614 yards. Our sixth-ranked pass defense would like a word with him.

A Brief History Seminar

Oklahoma claims seven national championships: 1950, 1955, 1956, 1974, 1975, 1985 and 2000. We have seven Heisman Trophy winners and 50 conference championships. Mississippi State has won one SEC championship, in 1941. Darlin', we won 14 straight conference titles from 1946 to 1959. We've had seasons with more trophies than Starkville has stoplights. I'm kidding about the stoplights. Mostly. I haven't counted.

Prairie Talk: A Tale of Two Towns

Norman. The 2020 census counted 128,026 people in Norman, the third-largest city in Oklahoma. Our campus has a Gothic-inspired style that Frank Lloyd Wright called "Cherokee Gothic," and our stadium, which seats 80,126, is known as the Palace on the Prairie. And our official mascot, the Sooner Schooner, is a scaled-down replica of the Conestoga wagons used by settlers around the Land Rush of 1889. It's pulled by two white ponies named Boomer and Sooner, and it first rolled onto Owen Field in 1964. Name a cuter mascot. You can't. I'll wait.

Starkville. Now, Starkville is charming, and I mean it. But it had 24,360 people in the 2020 census. Norman is more than five times bigger. Our stadium alone holds more than three Starkvilles.

And the town's history! Starkville was first called Boardtown, because a nearby mill made clapboards. They named the town after lumber, darlin'. Then they renamed it to honor a Revolutionary War general. Honestly, I liked Boardtown. It had honesty.

Their stadium, Davis Wade, opened in 1914, and it's the second-oldest in FBS. I respect my elders. I just wonder whether the bleachers creak in time with the cowbells.

Oh, the cowbells. Mississippi State fans have been ringing cowbells at games since roughly the late 1930s, and Wikipedia says the tradition has survived repeated attempts to quiet it down. Y'all, I grew up around livestock. I know exactly what a cowbell is for. It's so you can find the cow. And after the last two Saturdays, I think the Bulldogs might be ringing them to find their offense.

The Last Barrel

Here's how I see it. We have a top-five defense, a pass defense that ranks sixth, and a team that beat No. 1 two weeks ago. They have a pass defense that ranks 127th and two straight blowout losses. All we have to do is hold on to the football and ride a clean pattern. Three turns, no knockdowns, and a fast time home.

Now, one more time, all together.

Boomer!

(You say Sooner.)

My call: Oklahoma Sooners 25, Mississippi State Bulldogs 24.

articles.title: Hotty Toddy, and Hand Me the Footnotes: Ole Miss Brings a Perfect Red Zone and a Novel's Worth of Offense to a Texas Team That Keeps Losing by Three
articles.byline: Langston Fairbanks, The Ole Miss Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 7 Ole Miss (5-1) at No. 19 Texas (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium, ABC
articles.text:
Gentle reader, permit me a moment. I am seated on a bench on the Square in Oxford, Mississippi, in a seersucker suit that is frankly too light for late October, with a cup of coffee, a well-thumbed paperback from Square Books, and the warm, contented glow of a man whose football team just held a ranked opponent to three points. The courthouse clock is chiming. The leaves are turning. And somewhere, I like to imagine, the ghost of Mr. Faulkner is reading the box score and nodding.

I am Langston Fairbanks. My takes, I'm told, run long. I prefer to think of them as novels with a kickoff. So settle in, refill your cup, and let us begin, as all great Southern stories do, with a triumph and a journey west.

Part 1: The Missouri Chapter

Ole Miss 31, Missouri 3, at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium, before 67,510 of the faithful.

The story opened, as tragedies sometimes do, with a small misfortune: Missouri kicked a 27-yard field goal in the first quarter, and for about two and a half minutes we trailed 3-0. Then Trinidad Chambliss turned the page. He hit Caleb Odom for a 10-yard touchdown, then Horatio Fields for 21 yards in the second quarter, then Caleb Cunningham for 17 more before halftime. It was 21-3 at the break, and the AP observed that Missouri never seriously threatened again.

Chambliss finished 20 of 36 for 241 yards and three touchdowns, with no interceptions, and he ran in a fourth from five yards out in the fourth quarter. Lucas Carneiro added a 38-yard field goal. But the true protagonists of this chapter were the running backs. Kewan Lacy ran 16 times for 122 yards, and Makhi Frazier ran 15 times for 101. Ole Miss gained 498 yards, 257 of them on the ground.

And then there was the defense, which deserves its own epilogue. Missouri came in with Jamal Roberts, who had run for more than 200 yards in each of his previous two games. He finished with 39 yards on 20 carries. Missouri as a team ran 26 times for 39 yards. Will Echoles had a sack, two pass breakups and a quarterback hurry. Sharif Denson led us with nine tackles. Landon Barnes intercepted a pass. And when Missouri had a first-and-goal at our 2 in the second quarter, it lost yardage twice, threw an incomplete pass and missed a 23-yard field goal. Gentle reader, that is what literary critics call a reversal of fortune.

The Grove Novel, Abridged

The AP noted that Ole Miss is 25-1 at home since 2023. Our record this year: wins over Louisville, Charlotte, LSU, Vanderbilt and Missouri, and a single blemish, a 52-28 loss at Florida in September that I have chosen to regard as an experimental chapter. Every great author has a chapter he'd rather revise. Ours is set in Gainesville.

Part 2: The Journey West

Saturday night, 7:30 Eastern, on ABC, No. 7 Ole Miss visits No. 19 Texas. The AP says it's the first meeting between these two as SEC members and the Rebels' first trip to Austin since 2013. Texas leads the series 6-2.

Allow me to be gracious, as a Southern gentleman must. Texas's defense is excellent. It allows 272.5 yards a game, 12th in FBS, and 166.2 passing yards, also 12th. Rasheem Biles leads the Longhorns with 48 tackles and two interceptions. And earlier this season, Texas beat Ohio State 24-23. That is a fine paragraph in anyone's book.

But let us read on.

Texas has lost two straight games, each by three points. Oklahoma beat the Longhorns 27-24 at the Cotton Bowl, and then Florida beat them 27-24 in Austin, with a quarterback making his first career start. A first career start, gentle reader. The Gators held the ball for 38 minutes and 11 seconds, and Texas went 2 for 10 on third down. Florida sacked Arch Manning five times. That is not a plot twist. That is a recurring theme.

The Texas offense averages 361.3 yards a game, 93rd in FBS. It runs for 134.5 yards a game, 103rd. Its leading rusher, Daylan Smothers, has 289 yards. Our Lacy has 352, and he and Frazier combined for 223 against Missouri alone. I footnote this without comment. All right, with a little comment.

Who to Watch

Trinidad Chambliss, our quarterback: 1,676 yards, 14 touchdowns, four interceptions and a 67.6 completion rate. He plays with the confidence of a man who has already read the last page.

Deuce Alexander, receiver: 35 catches for 523 yards and five touchdowns, our leader.

Kewan Lacy, running back: 352 yards and five touchdowns on 62 carries, 122 of them last week.

The red zone: The AP preview says Ole Miss has scored on every one of its red-zone trips this season, first in the nation. Texas's red-zone defense ranks 57th, allowing scores on 81.3 of every 100 trips. Gentle reader, once we cross the 20, we write "The End."

The honest footnote: I am a man of letters, and letters must be truthful. Our defense allows 390 yards a game, 108th in FBS, and opponents convert 44 of every 100 third downs, 118th. We also hold the ball just 26:59 a game, 131st. But a novelist would tell you that a short chapter, written well, is the most powerful kind. We score fast. We'd simply like to give our defense a slightly longer intermission.

A Brief History Seminar

Ole Miss's football heritage needs no introduction, but I shall provide one anyway, as is my custom. The campus speed limit is 18 miles per hour in honor of Archie Manning, who wore No. 18 for the Rebels. Every car in Oxford slows down to honor the great man. Saturday, his grandson will be playing for the other side. We wish young Arch well, sincerely, and we will be honoring the family the only way a gracious host can: by reminding everyone that No. 18 is ours.

Grove Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Oxford. The Grove is about 10 acres of shaded oaks in the heart of campus, and on game day it fills with tents, lace, fine china, sterling silver and, yes, chandeliers. The Columbia Missourian once called it "the mecca of tailgating in American sports," and I've never heard a Missouri fan say anything nicer about anything of ours. William Faulkner bought Rowan Oak in 1930 and lived there until his death in 1962. You can still visit. Square Books anchors the Square, the courthouse watches over everything, and Vaught-Hemingway, which seats 64,038, is the largest stadium in Mississippi. And before every home game, our team walks through the Grove under the Walk of Champions arch, built in 1998. Oxford is small, gentle reader. So is a sonnet.

Austin. Now. Austin is a large and energetic city, and I mean that in the most complimentary way available to a man of my upbringing. The 2020 census counted 961,855 people there. Its unofficial motto, printed on bumper stickers and T-shirts all over town, is "Keep Austin Weird." Gentle reader, in Oxford, we do not need to print an instruction to be interesting on a T-shirt. We simply are.

Austin is also the home of about 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats, which live under the Congress Avenue Bridge and fly out every evening at dusk. Texas Parks and Wildlife calls it the largest urban bat colony in the world. That is a magnificent natural spectacle. It is also, by my count, the only stadium crowd in Austin that reliably shows up before kickoff and leaves in an orderly fashion.

And Wikipedia describes something called "Old Austin," a time when the city was smaller, more bohemian and, I quote, "better known for its lack of traffic." So even Austin misses the version of Austin that had less traffic. In Oxford, our traffic is governed by an 18-mile-per-hour speed limit and a deep personal respect for a quarterback. Austin's is governed by Interstate 35 and, I gather, a great deal of patience.

Their mascot, Bevo, is a live longhorn steer, and their Tower glows burnt orange after victories. Both are lovely. We would be delighted to see the Tower stay its regular color on Saturday night. It's a handsome building. It looks distinguished in white.

Epilogue

Here, then, is the shape of my novel. Ole Miss arrives with an offense that scores 37.5 points a game, a quarterback who hasn't thrown an interception in two weeks, a red zone that converts every time, and a defense that just held a ranked team to three points. Texas arrives with a fine defense and two consecutive three-point losses, the second at home to a quarterback making his first start. The bats will fly at dusk. The Rebels will follow.

Hotty Toddy, and pass the footnotes.

My call: Texas Longhorns 30, Ole Miss Rebels 24.

Landon Barnes intercepted a pass. And when Missouri had a first-and-goal at our 2 in the second quarter, it lost yardage twice, threw an incomplete pass and missed a 23-yard field goal. Gentle reader, that is what literary critics call a reversal of fortune.
The Grove Novel, Abridged

The AP noted that Ole Miss is 25-1 at home since 2023. Our record this year: wins over Louisville, Charlotte, LSU, Vanderbilt and Missouri, and a single blemish, a 52-28 loss at Florida in September that I have chosen to regard as an experimental chapter. Every great author has a chapter he'd rather revise. Ours is set in Gainesville.
Part 2: The Journey West

Saturday night, 7:30 Eastern, on ABC, No. 7 Ole Miss visits No. 19 Texas. The AP says it's the first meeting between these two as SEC members and the Rebels' first trip to Austin since 2013. Texas leads the series 6-2.

Allow me to be gracious, as a Southern gentleman must. Texas's defense is excellent. It allows 272.5 yards a game, 12th in FBS, and 166.2 passing yards, also 12th. Rasheem Biles leads the Longhorns with 48 tackles and two interceptions. And earlier this season, Texas beat Ohio State 24-23. That is a fine paragraph in anyone's book.
But let us read on.

Texas has lost two straight games, each by three points. Oklahoma beat the Longhorns 27-24 at the Cotton Bowl, and then Florida beat them 27-24 in Austin, with a quarterback making his first career start. A first career start, gentle reader. The Gators held the ball for 38 minutes and 11 seconds, and Texas went 2 for 10 on third down. Florida sacked Arch Manning five times. That is not a plot twist. That is a recurring theme.

The Texas offense averages 361.3 yards a game, 93rd in FBS. It runs for 134.5 yards a game, 103rd. Its leading rusher, Daylan Smothers, has 289 yards. Our Lacy has 352, and he and Frazier combined for 223 against Missouri alone. I footnote this without comment. All right, with a little comment.
Who to Watch
Trinidad Chambliss, our quarterback: 1,676 yards, 14 touchdowns, four interceptions and a 67.6 completion rate. He plays with the confidence of a man who has already read the last page.
Deuce Alexander, receiver: 35 catches for 523 yards and five touchdowns, our leader.
Kewan Lacy, running back: 352 yards and five touchdowns on 62 carries, 122 of them last week.

The red zone: The AP preview says Ole Miss has scored on every one of its red-zone trips this season, first in the nation. Texas's red-zone defense ranks 57th, allowing scores on 81.3 of every 100 trips. Gentle reader, once we cross the 20, we write "The End."

The honest footnote: I am a man of letters, and letters must be truthful. Our defense allows 390 yards a game, 108th in FBS, and opponents convert 44 of every 100 third downs, 118th. We also hold the ball just 26:59 a game, 131st. But a novelist would tell you that a short chapter, written well, is the most powerful kind. We score fast. We'd simply like to give our defense a slightly longer intermission.
A Brief History Seminar

Ole Miss's football heritage needs no introduction, but I shall provide one anyway, as is my custom. The campus speed limit is 18 miles per hour in honor of Archie Manning, who wore No. 18 for the Rebels. Every car in Oxford slows down to honor the great man. Saturday, his grandson will be playing for the other side. We wish young Arch well, sincerely, and we will be honoring the family the only way a gracious host can: by reminding everyone that No. 18 is ours.
Grove Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Oxford. The Grove is about 10 acres of shaded oaks in the heart of campus, and on game day it fills with tents, lace, fine china, sterling silver and, yes, chandeliers. The Columbia Missourian once called it "the mecca of tailgating in American sports," and I've never heard a Missouri fan say anything nicer about anything of ours. William Faulkner bought Rowan Oak in 1930 and lived there until his death in 1962. You can still visit. Square Books anchors the Square, the courthouse watches over everything, and Vaught-Hemingway, which seats 64,038, is the largest stadium in Mississippi. And before every home game, our team walks through the Grove under the Walk of Champions arch, built in 1998. Oxford is small, gentle reader. So is a sonnet.

Austin. Now. Austin is a large and energetic city, and I mean that in the most complimentary way available to a man of my upbringing. The 2020 census counted 961,855 people there. Its unofficial motto, printed on bumper stickers and T-shirts all over town, is "Keep Austin Weird." Gentle reader, in Oxford, we do not need to print an instruction to be interesting on a T-shirt. We simply are.

Austin is also the home of about 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats, which live under the Congress Avenue Bridge and fly out every evening at dusk. Texas Parks and Wildlife calls it the largest urban bat colony in the world. That is a magnificent natural spectacle. It is also, by my count, the only stadium crowd in Austin that reliably shows up before kickoff and leaves in an orderly fashion.

And Wikipedia describes something called "Old Austin," a time when the city was smaller, more bohemian and, I quote, "better known for its lack of traffic." So even Austin misses the version of Austin that had less traffic. In Oxford, our traffic is governed by an 18-mile-per-hour speed limit and a deep personal respect for a quarterback. Austin's is governed by Interstate 35 and, I gather, a great deal of patience.

Their mascot, Bevo, is a live longhorn steer, and their Tower glows burnt orange after victories. Both are lovely. We would be delighted to see the Tower stay its regular color on Saturday night. It's a handsome building. It looks distinguished in white.
Epilogue

Here, then, is the shape of my novel. Ole Miss arrives with an offense that scores 37.5 points a game, a quarterback who hasn't thrown an interception in two weeks, a red zone that converts every time, and a defense that just held a ranked team to three points. Texas arrives with a fine defense and two consecutive three-point losses, the second at home to a quarterback making his first start. The bats will fly at dusk. The Rebels will follow.
Hotty Toddy, and pass the footnotes.
My call: Texas Longhorns 30, Ole Miss Rebels 24.

articles.title: Cue the Music: The Vols Walk Into Williams-Brice, Where the Bass Drops, the Press Box Shakes and Rocky Top Isn't Even Their Fight Song
articles.byline: Beaumont 'Beau' Cheraw, The South Carolina Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 11 Tennessee (6-1) at South Carolina (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Williams-Brice Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Bum. Bum. Bum. BUMMMMM.

That's me humming the opening of "Also sprach Zarathustra," the theme from "2001: A Space Odyssey," which is how every segment of mine begins, because it's how every great Saturday in Columbia begins. I'm Beau Cheraw, a Columbia boy, a former drumline snare, and a man who can feel the low notes of that song start in his ankles and travel all the way up to his hat.

And friends, it's time to turn the music back on. We've had two weeks to think about our last game, and for once, that was a pleasant way to spend two weeks. Now No. 11 Tennessee comes to town. Lights down. Bass up. Cue the music.

Part 1: The Open Week, and the Swamp Before It

South Carolina had an open date last Saturday, Oct. 17. I spent it the way any responsible fan would: rewatching our last game, which happened on Oct. 10 in Gainesville. Let me tell you about it, because I've watched it enough to narrate it in my sleep. My wife says I do.

South Carolina 38, Florida 19, at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, in front of 90,311 people.

It started rough. Florida scored on a 59-yard pass on its first drive. But with 12 seconds left in the first quarter, LaNorris Sellers hit Nyck Harbor for a 15-yard touchdown. Malik Orsan added a 37-yard field goal, and Sellers found Mazeo Bennett Jr. for a 12-yard touchdown before halftime. Then came a 45-minute lightning delay that stretched the break. And friends, after that halftime, we came out of the tunnel like the bass had just dropped.

In the third quarter, Sellers threw a 26-yard touchdown to Donovan Murph and then plunged in from a yard out. In the fourth, he hit Lex Cyrus for 21 yards. Sellers finished 23 of 35 for 279 yards and four touchdowns, no interceptions, and he ran for a fifth. The AP called it his best performance in nearly two years. Harbor caught four passes for 83 yards. Vicari Swain and Justin Okoronkwo each intercepted a pass, and Dylan Stewart had a sack and, per the AP, forced two fumbles. We didn't turn it over once.

It was our first win in Gainesville since 2014. And it snapped an eight-game SEC losing streak that went back to September 2025. I had been holding my breath since then, friends. I can breathe now. I can also hum.

Garnet Gospel: The Honest Part

We're 3-3 and 1-3 in the SEC. We lost to Mississippi State 41-34, at Alabama 49-18 and to Kentucky 35-34, and the AP pointed out we'd blown four significant leads in five SEC games before the Florida win. That hurt. But we're also 13th in FBS in yards, at 474.7 a game, and 10th in rushing, at 232.3 a game. We score 37.7 points a game, 18th. This offense can play with anybody. On Oct. 10, it finally finished.

Part 2: Here Come the Vols

Saturday at 3:30 Eastern, on ESPN, No. 11 Tennessee visits Williams-Brice Stadium. The Vols are 6-1. We're 3-3.

I'll be gracious first, because my mama sang in the choir and she'd know. Tennessee is good. It beat Alabama 26-10 last Saturday, and DeSean Bishop ran for 159 yards and two touchdowns. Bishop has 837 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns this season. The Vols defense allows 14.7 points a game, ninth in FBS, and 159.3 passing yards a game, eighth. That's real.

Now let's talk about the rest of the song.

The Tennessee passing game averages 188 yards a game, 110th in FBS. Against Alabama, the Vols scored four field goals in the first half. Four. Every time they got close, the music stopped and somebody had to kick. The AP called the quarterback position "a work in progress." Their leading passer this season, Faizon Brandon, has 697 yards. George MacIntyre started Saturday. Friends, I know a band in search of a lead singer when I hear one.

And here's a number I like. Earlier this season, Texas came to Neyland and beat Tennessee 20-17. Then Texas lost to Oklahoma and Florida. So the Vols lost at home to a team that has since lost two in a row. I'm just reading the liner notes.

Who to Watch

LaNorris Sellers, our quarterback: 1,338 yards, 12 touchdowns, four interceptions. He's coming off five touchdowns and two weeks of rest. That's a man who's had time to warm up his voice.

Matthew Fuller, running back: 485 yards and five touchdowns on 81 carries. Our run game ranks 10th in the country.

Nyck Harbor, receiver: 17 catches for 278 yards, our leader. Tennessee's pass defense is eighth in FBS, so this is the headliner matchup.

DeSean Bishop, Tennessee running back: 837 yards and 10 touchdowns. Our run defense ranks 25th, allowing 103.7 a game, and it has to be at its best.

The honest part: Our pass defense allows 237.2 yards a game, 107th. And the AP preview says opponents score on 93.8 of every 100 red-zone trips against us, 122nd. Tennessee's red-zone offense is sixth. We have to make the Vols kick. They seem to enjoy it anyway.

Entrance Ratings

I rate every stadium entrance, kindly, on a scale of one to "2001." Tennessee's is good. Their band forms a giant T, Smokey runs in, and the team storms the field. I give it a solid seven. It's a fine entrance. But ours has subwoofers.

And Tennessee's Vol Walk? Wikipedia says coach Johnny Majors came up with it after a 1988 game at Auburn, when he saw Auburn's Tiger Walk. Friends, the Vol Walk is a remake. I love a good remake. But it's a remake.

A Brief History Seminar

Tennessee leads the series 29-11-2, according to CollegeFootballData.com. But I'd like to direct your attention to the last time the Vols came to Williams-Brice, in 2022. South Carolina 63, Tennessee 38. Sixty-three points. I still have the scoreboard picture as my phone background. Tennessee won 41-20 in Knoxville in 2023, and I'll accept that, because I'm a gracious host. But this game is in Columbia.

Soda City Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Columbia. We're the capital of South Carolina, founded in 1786 as the state's first planned capital city. The 2020 census counted 136,632 people. Folks shorten our name to "Cola," which is why we're called Soda City. Three rivers meet here, the Broad and Saluda forming the Congaree, and Congaree National Park is right down the road. Williams-Brice holds 77,559 people, and when "2001" plays, the subwoofers under the scoreboard shake the whole place. During a game in 2001, ESPN announcers said they had to shout to hear each other in the press box. Then there's "Sandstorm" before kickoff and after touchdowns, often enough to make the press box noticeably shake. And behind the south end zone sit 22 old cabooses on an unused railroad track, the Cockaboose Railroad, the most unique tailgate in America. Cocky, our mascot since 1980, makes his entrance at the climax of "2001." Bum. Bum. Bum.

Knoxville. Now, Knoxville is a lovely town, and I mean it. The Great Smoky Mountains are right there. But their most famous landmark is the Sunsphere, a 266-foot tower with a gold glass ball on top, built for the 1982 World's Fair. Friends, the World's Fair was 44 years ago. Their skyline's headliner is a souvenir from 1982. In Columbia, we play 1982 too, but only when it's "2001."

And "Rocky Top." I respect "Rocky Top." It's one of Tennessee's official state songs. But Wikipedia says it isn't even Tennessee's official fight song. That's "Down the Field." So the Vols' band plays a song that isn't their fight song, over and over, all game long. Friends, that's like going to a concert where the band never plays its own hit. We know our song. Ours starts with a timpani.

The Last Note

Here's my setlist. Tennessee has a great running back and a strong defense. But its passing game is 110th in the country, it kicked four first-half field goals last week, and its quarterback room is still holding auditions. We're rested, we're healthy enough to sing, our offense is top-15 in the country, and we're coming home to a stadium that makes press boxes shake.

Lights down. Bass up. Cue the music. Forever to thee.

My call: Tennessee Volunteers 29, South Carolina Gamecocks 27.

articles.title: Cue the Banjo: The Vols Just Ran Over Alabama, and Now They're Headed to Columbia, Where the Train Cars Don't Move and the Music Needs Subwoofers
articles.byline: Earl 'Rocky Top' Haskew, The Tennessee Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 11 Tennessee (6-1) at South Carolina (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Williams-Brice Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Plink-a-plink-a-plink-a-PLANG.

That's my banjo, friends, and it's a little out of tune on purpose, because I'm still shaking from Saturday. Howdy from the porch of a cabin up toward the Smokies, where the leaves on the ridge are turning the exact shade of orange God intended for them. I'm Earl Haskew. Folks call me Rocky Top. I used to snap the football for a living, and now I play banjo before every stat, because a good number deserves a good intro.

And brother, have I got some good numbers this week.

Part 1: Third Saturday in October, Indeed

Plink-a-plink. Tennessee 26, Alabama 10.

At Neyland Stadium, in front of 101,915 people, which is the stadium's official capacity, so every last seat had a Vol in it, give or take a few folks in crimson who had a quiet ride home.

The first half was a kicker's clinic. Cooper Ranvier drilled field goals from 29, 33, 41 and 34 yards. Four field goals before halftime, friends. As a former long snapper, I wept. Those were beautiful snaps. I'd know. We led 12-10 at the break. Not pretty, but a long snapper never asks for pretty. He asks for points.

Then DeSean Bishop took over the afternoon. He had 64 rushing yards at halftime and 95 more after it, finishing with 159 yards and two touchdowns on 32 carries. His 5-yard touchdown in the third quarter made it 19-10. And then, friends, came the best drive of the season: nine minutes and 32 seconds in the fourth quarter, ending with Bishop scoring from five yards out again. Nine and a half minutes. Alabama's offense spent that whole drive on the bench, probably reading the program.

George MacIntyre completed 21 of 31 passes for 197 yards, and Mike Matthews caught seven passes for 85. We held the ball for 35:44.

Plang. Now the defense. Alabama finished with 201 yards and 54 rushing yards, and it went 2 for 13 on third down. We forced four turnovers. Kayin Lee and Dejuan Lane each intercepted a pass, Jeremiah Telander had two sacks, and Amare Campbell made eight tackles. The AP said Alabama has now lost consecutive regular-season games for the first time since 2007, and Tennessee has won three of its last five against Alabama, all at home, after 15 straight losses in the series.

Fifteen straight, friends. I remember every one of 'em. Now look at us.

Smoky Mountain Stories: Why We Run Through the T

Every home game, our band forms a giant T, with its base at the entrance to the locker room in the north end zone. Smokey, our bluetick coonhound, runs in, and the whole team storms through the T to the roar of 100,000-plus Vols fans. Coach Doug Dickey started that tradition in the 1960s, along with the Power T logo and the checkerboard end zones, which first appeared in 1964. When the checkerboards are painted and the T is formed, God's in His heaven and all's right in Knoxville.

The Honest Verse

I won't pretend we're perfect, because the banjo knows when you're lying. Texas beat us 20-17 at Neyland back in September. And the AP called our quarterback spot "very much a work in progress." Faizon Brandon leads us in passing with 697 yards and seven touchdowns, MacIntyre started Saturday, and our passing game ranks 110th in FBS. But we run for 217.1 yards a game, 19th in the country, and we've won three straight. That'll do.

Part 2: Headed to Columbia

Plink-a-plink. Saturday at 3:30 Eastern on ESPN, No. 11 Tennessee visits South Carolina at Williams-Brice Stadium. We're 6-1. They're 3-3.

Now, I'll be neighborly first. The Gamecocks are coming off an open week, and two Saturdays ago they won 38-19 at Florida. LaNorris Sellers threw four touchdowns and ran for another. Their offense averages 474.7 yards a game, 13th in FBS, and they run for 232.3 a game, 10th. That's a real offense, and we'll respect it.

But let's tune up the rest of the song.

Before that Florida win, South Carolina had lost eight straight SEC games, going back to September 2025. The AP said the Gamecocks had blown four significant leads in their previous five SEC games. They lost 49-18 at Alabama, the same Alabama we just held to 10 points. They lost to Mississippi State. They lost to Kentucky. Friends, that's a lot of verses about heartbreak, and not one of 'em on the banjo.

Who to Watch

Plang. DeSean Bishop, our running back: 837 yards and 10 touchdowns on 139 carries, coming off 159 against Alabama. He's the main melody.

Mike Matthews, receiver: 29 catches for 481 yards and three touchdowns, our leader.

That's my banjo, friends, and it's a little out of tune on purpose, because I'm still shaking from Saturday. Howdy from the porch of a cabin up toward the Smokies, where the leaves on the ridge are turning the exact shade of orange God intended for them. I'm Earl Haskew. Folks call me Rocky Top. I used to snap the football for a living, and now I play banjo before every stat, because a good number deserves a good intro.
And brother, have I got some good numbers this week.
Part 1: Third Saturday in October, Indeed
Plink-a-plink. Tennessee 26, Alabama 10.
At Neyland Stadium, in front of 101,915 people, which is the stadium's official capacity, so every last seat had a Vol in it, give or take a few folks in crimson who had a quiet ride home.

The first half was a kicker's clinic. Cooper Ranvier drilled field goals from 29, 33, 41 and 34 yards. Four field goals before halftime, friends. As a former long snapper, I wept. Those were beautiful snaps. I'd know. We led 12-10 at the break. Not pretty, but a long snapper never asks for pretty. He asks for points.

Then DeSean Bishop took over the afternoon. He had 64 rushing yards at halftime and 95 more after it, finishing with 159 yards and two touchdowns on 32 carries. Alabama's offense spent that whole drive on the bench, probably reading the program.

articles.title: Howdy, and Let Me Yell This: The Aggies Roll Into Tuscaloosa, Where the Elephants Are Nervous and the Tide Is Going Out
articles.byline: Colt Wendeborn, The Texas A&M Fanatic
articles.matchup: Texas A&M (4-3) at No. 13 Alabama (5-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Bryant-Denny Stadium, ABC
articles.text:
HOWDY! That's not me shouting at you, friend. That's the official greeting of Texas A&M University, and if you're going to read a column by an Aggie, you're going to get greeted properly. I'm Colt Wendeborn, petroleum engineering grad, lifelong member of the 12th Man, and a man who has never once explained a tradition without then explaining the tradition behind the tradition.

This week we have a lot to explain. We just had a perfect Saturday at Kyle Field, and now we head east to Tuscaloosa, where a famous program is having the strangest October it's had in almost two decades. So sit up straight, stand when it's time to stand, and let me yell this.

Part 1: FORTY-ONE TO NOTHING

Texas A&M beat The Citadel 41-0 last Saturday at Kyle Field, in front of 101,052 people. I'll be honest about the opponent, because that's the Aggie way. The Citadel came in 2-5 and is a good, proud program at the FCS level. But a shutout is a shutout, and this one did exactly what our team needed it to do.

We scored a touchdown on all four of our first-half drives. FOUR FOR FOUR. Jamarion Morrow, who came into the day with one rushing touchdown all season, punched in three of them, from four yards, one yard and one yard. That's six yards combined, folks, scored with the efficiency of a man parallel parking a pickup on the first try. Sandwiched in there, Marcel Reed hit Aaron Gregory for a 37-yard touchdown. We led 28-0 at halftime.

Reed finished 8 of 13 for 130 yards, a touchdown and no interceptions, then handed the second half to the backups. Brady Hart threw a 12-yard touchdown to Gregory in the fourth quarter, and David Olano added field goals from 23 and 20 yards. KJ Edwards ran 13 times for 116 yards, 8.9 a carry. Gregory caught six passes for 94 yards and two touchdowns. TK Norman added five catches for 88. We gained 501 yards and didn't turn it over once.

And the defense? The Citadel finished with 183 yards and 43 passing. Tawfiq Byard made seven tackles with 1.5 for loss, and Ray Coney added seven more. The AP says it's our second shutout of the year, after 50-0 over Missouri State in the opener, and the first time since 1993 that A&M has posted two shutouts in one season. I'll yell that one: NINETEEN NINETY-THREE.

Tradition Explainer: Why We Stand

Here's why you'll see every Aggie student standing the whole game Saturday. In 1922, at the Dixie Classic, coach Dana X. Bible realized one more injury would leave him without a backfield player to send in, so he called a sophomore basketball player named E. King Gill down from the stands to suit up and stand ready. He never had to go in. But he was ready. Ever since, the student body stands for the entire game to show it's ready, too. That's the 12th Man. Now you know. And now you know why we're tired on Sunday.

The Honest Report

I'm an engineer, so I deal in tolerances, and I'll tell you where we're out of spec. We're 4-3 and 1-3 in the SEC. Kentucky beat us 31-21 at Kyle Field. We lost at LSU 35-6 and at Missouri 27-6. Our offense averages 356.9 yards a game, 97th in FBS, and our passing game averages 195.7 a game, 103rd. That is what it is. But the Citadel game showed what happens when the big guys up front get a push: 264 rushing yards. That's the blueprint.

Part 2: Tuscaloosa, We Have Arrived

Saturday, 3:30 Eastern, ABC, Bryant-Denny Stadium. Alabama is No. 13 in the AP poll and 5-2. We are 4-3. Nobody outside College Station expects much from us. Good. We like it that way.

Let me be gracious, because my mama is reading. Alabama beat Florida State 50-36, won at Kentucky 45-17 and scores 39.3 points a game, 12th in FBS. Keelon Russell has thrown for 1,746 yards with 12 touchdowns and four interceptions. Caleb Woodson leads the Tide with 53 tackles. Those are good football players.

Now. Let's discuss the last two weeks in Tuscaloosa.

Georgia beat Alabama 20-17 at Bryant-Denny. Then Tennessee beat Alabama 26-10 in Knoxville. According to the AP, that's the first time the Tide has lost consecutive regular-season games since 2007. TWO THOUSAND SEVEN. Against Tennessee, Alabama gained 201 yards, ran for 54, went 2 of 13 on third down and turned it over four times. The Vols' fourth-quarter touchdown drive lasted nine minutes and 32 seconds. Folks, the elephants are nervous.

Who to Watch

Our defense vs. their passing game. We allow 164.1 passing yards a game, 10th in FBS, and 306.6 yards a game overall, 29th. Opponents convert just 29.8 of every 100 third downs against us, 11th in the country. Alabama just went 2 of 13 on third down in Knoxville. I'm not saying the math is simple. I'm saying the math is friendly.

Ray Coney, linebacker: 36 tackles, our team leader. Marco Jones: two sacks, our leader there. Somebody needs to say howdy to Russell early, and politely, and often.

Marcel Reed, quarterback: 1,227 yards, seven touchdowns. He needs to be efficient, the way he was against The Citadel, and let the run game carry the freight.

KJ Edwards, running back: 317 yards on 47 carries this year, and 116 of those came last Saturday. Alabama allows 107 rushing yards a game, 30th, so this is a real test.

The red zone. This is the one I've circled in red pen. The AP preview says Alabama's defense allows opponents to score on 95.7 of every 100 red-zone trips, 134th in FBS. If we get inside the 20, history says we come home with points. Our kicker, Olano, didn't miss last Saturday. Bring him.

A Brief History Seminar

I'll be honest: Alabama leads the series 13-3, according to CollegeFootballData.com, and the last two meetings were four-point Tide wins. But I'll remind everybody about 2021, when the Aggies upset No. 1 Alabama 41-38 at Kyle Field. The 12th Man stood for that whole game, and some of us are still standing.

And here's a fact I just enjoy. Before this month, Alabama hadn't lost two straight regular-season games since 2007. The Aggies would be delighted to help the Tide find out what three feels like.

Twelfth Man Report: A Tale of Two Towns

College Station. The 2020 census counted 120,511 people in College Station, and since 2021 Texas A&M has enrolled the largest student body in the United States. Kyle Field seats 102,733, the largest stadium in the SEC and the largest in Texas. The night before a home game, at midnight, we hold Midnight Yell Practice, where the 12th Man practices its yells and sings the War Hymn, led by five student Yell Leaders and the Fightin' Texas Aggie Band. Then there's Northgate, the district just north of campus with restaurants, churches and a whole lot of maroon, and Reveille, our Rough Collie, who holds the rank of Cadet General with five silver diamonds as the highest-ranking member of the Corps of Cadets. She outranks me, she outranks you, and she outranks everybody in Tuscaloosa.

Tuscaloosa. Now, Tuscaloosa is a pretty town on the Black Warrior River. I like it. But I need to share a number. The 2020 census counted 99,600 people in Tuscaloosa. College Station: 120,511. So when Alabama folks talk about visiting the little college town in Texas, friends, our little college town is bigger than theirs.

They call Tuscaloosa the Druid City, which sounds mysterious and ancient until you learn it's named after the water oaks planted downtown since the 1840s. It's a tree nickname, folks. That's like calling College Station "Pecan Town" and expecting folks to be scared.

And I want to discuss the branding. The team is the Crimson Tide. The mascot is an elephant named Big Al. The river is the Black Warrior. That's three completely different themes, like a wedding where the bride chose nautical, the groom chose safari and the caterer chose medieval. I respect it. I just can't explain it, and I can explain anything.

And I've been told their players walk to the stadium on the Walk of Champions, a brick plaza at the north end zone. It's a lovely plaza. Lately, friends, it has been seeing a little more walking than championing.

The Final Yell

Here's how I see it. We have a top-10 pass defense. They're coming off a night with 201 yards and four turnovers. They're nervous in the red zone. We're healthy on the ground. And every Aggie in Bryant-Denny will be standing from the opening kickoff to the last snap, because that's who we are. We don't sit down. We especially don't sit down in Tuscaloosa.

Gig 'em, and HOWDY.

My call: Alabama Crimson Tide 32, Texas A&M Aggies 20.

Texas A&M's defense allows 164.1 passing yards a game, 10th in FBS, and opponents convert only 29.8 of every 100 third downs, 11th.
The AP preview says Alabama allows opponents to score on 95.7 of every 100 red-zone trips, 134th in FBS. Colt has circled it in red pen.
The 12th Man tradition dates to the 1922 Dixie Classic, when E. King Gill came down from the stands to stand ready, and the student body stands for every game.
Tuscaloosa had 99,600 people in the 2020 census. College Station had 120,511. The little college town in Texas is bigger.
Kyle Field seats 102,733, the largest stadium in the SEC, and Texas A&M has enrolled the largest student body in the United States since 2021.
Crimson Tide, an elephant mascot and the Black Warrior River: three themes, one wedding, and not even Colt can explain it.
