articles.title: That's a Hit Single, Y'all: Vanderbilt Takes Its Guitar to Lexington, Where the Horses Are Famous and Third Down Goes to Die
articles.byline: Penelope 'Pippa' Ashcroft, The Vanderbilt Fanatic
articles.matchup: Vanderbilt (3-4) at No. 12 Kentucky (6-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, Kroger Field, SEC Network
articles.text:
Hey, y'all, it's Pippa Ashcroft, tuning my guitar on a bench in Centennial Park, right in front of the Parthenon, because when your heart's a little bruised, you go sit next to the most dramatic building in Tennessee. I'm an economics student by day and a songwriter by night, and every week I write a country song about the Commodores. Some weeks it's a stadium anthem. This week, darlin', it's a slow one in a minor key.

But here's the thing about country music: the sad songs are always the setup for the comeback single. So let's get through verse one, and then let's talk about Lexington, where the chorus is going to be a whole lot louder.

Part 1: The Ballad of a Saturday Night

Arkansas 31, Vanderbilt 21, at FirstBank Stadium, in front of a full house of 35,000.

And it started like a hit. With 13 seconds left in the first quarter, Sedrick Alexander punched in a 4-yard touchdown run, and we led 7-0. In the second quarter, after Arkansas tied it, Jared Curtis threw a gorgeous 24-yard touchdown to Junior Sherrill, and we led 14-7 with under two minutes to go in the half. I was already humming the chorus.

Then the record skipped.

The Razorbacks' first touchdown came on a 25-yard interception return by Joker Johnson. Then Cam Settles scored with 38 seconds left before halftime to tie it at 14. In the third quarter, KJ Jackson ran in from eight yards, Makhilyn Young answered with a 3-yard touchdown run to tie it at 21, and then Settles scored again with nine seconds left in the quarter. In the fourth, Curtis drove us to the Arkansas 29 with 3:46 left, and Miguel Mitchell intercepted him on second-and-12. Max Gilbert added a 39-yard field goal, and that was the song.

Curtis threw for 274 yards and a touchdown, with two interceptions. Sherrill caught eight passes for 99 yards. Alexander had 57 rushing yards and a score, plus 40 receiving yards. On defense, Bryan Longwell made 13 tackles with 1.5 for loss. But the AP pointed out the hard part: Arkansas ran for 187 yards, Ole Miss ran for 196 against us the week before, and the run defense has to get fixed.

And yes, I know. That loss snapped Arkansas's 14-game SEC losing streak. We're very generous people in Nashville. We're a hospitality town.

Game-Day Song: "Fourth-Quarter Blues (Second-and-Twelve)"

Well, we had it at fourteen, I was singin' in the stands,
Had a Sherrill touchdown ringin' and a hot dog in my hands,
Then a Razorback came flyin' like a freight train off the track,
And second-and-twelve took my Saturday back.

That's a hit single, y'all. A sad one. But a hit.

The Honest Verse

We're 3-4 and 0-4 in the SEC. We beat Austin Peay, Delaware and NC State, 35-31. Then we lost at Auburn 21-15, at Georgia 38-14, at home to Ole Miss 52-17 and at home to Arkansas. The AP preview says our turnover margin is -6, 126th in FBS, and we score 23.6 points a game. Those aren't great numbers. But I'm an economist, and I know a down cycle isn't the whole story.

Part 2: Off to Horse Country

Saturday night at 7:30 Eastern, on SEC Network, we go to Kroger Field to play No. 12 Kentucky.

Now, I'll be gracious first, because my mama taught me manners and a G chord on the same afternoon. Kentucky is 6-1 and tied for first in the SEC, and it beat Oklahoma 21-13 in Norman last Saturday by intercepting four passes. Kenny Minchey has thrown 13 touchdowns and one interception all year. That's real, y'all. I tip my cowboy hat.

And let's remember who has won this game the last two years. Vanderbilt beat Kentucky 20-13 at Kroger Field in 2024 and 45-17 in Nashville in 2025. That's two straight, darlin'. We know the way to Lexington. We've got the directions saved on the phone.

The Kentucky Stat Sheet, Set to Music

Here's where I start strumming a little faster.

The AP preview says Kentucky is dead last in FBS in third-down conversions, at 29.1 of every 100 tries. Last. Out of everybody. On third down, Kentucky's offense is a song with no bridge.

The Kentucky pass defense allows 249.7 yards a game, 116th in FBS. Its defense overall allows 377 yards a game, 95th, and 25.9 points a game, 92nd. Last Saturday in Norman, the Wildcats won with 230 yards. Four interceptions bailed them out, and I respect a defense that takes the ball away. But 230 yards won't win every week, and Curtis and Sherrill have been waiting for a secondary that ranks 116th.

Who to Watch

Junior Sherrill, our receiver: 41 catches for 628 yards and four touchdowns, and he's coming off eight catches for 99 yards. Kentucky's pass defense is 116th. You do the math, sugar. I'm an economist, so I already did.

Jared Curtis, quarterback: 1,242 yards and six touchdowns. He throws a lovely deep ball, and he needs to keep it out of the other team's hands on Saturday, because Kentucky is third in FBS in turnover margin at +11.

Sedrick Alexander, running back: 270 yards on 61 carries and five touchdowns.

Kentucky's C.J. Baxter: 484 rushing yards and eight touchdowns. Our run defense needs to tackle like it's the last song of the night and everybody wants to go home happy.

A Brief History Seminar

Kentucky leads the series 49-42-4, according to CollegeFootballData.com. Ninety-five games, friends, and it's that close. That's not a rivalry. That's a duet.

Music Row Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Nashville. We're Music City, and we've been Music City since 1950, when a WSM radio announcer named David Cobb said on air that the sounds listeners were hearing were coming from "Music City, U.S.A." The Grand Ole Opry started here in 1925. The Ryman was home to the Opry until 1974. Lower Broadway, Second Avenue and Printer's Alley are packed with music clubs and honky-tonks. The 2020 census counted 689,447 people, the 20th-most populous city in America. And we're also called the Athens of the South, because by the 1850s Nashville was the first Southern city to set up a public school system. That's why there's a full-size replica of the Parthenon in Centennial Park. We didn't just say we were smart. We built the receipt.

Lexington. Now, Lexington is a beautiful town. Rolling hills, white fences, horse farms everywhere. It's known as the Horse Capital of the World. And honestly? That's the problem. The most famous athletes in Lexington have four legs. Keeneland has live races every April and October. The football team plays in October too. Guess which one the town dresses up for.

And then there's basketball. The Kentucky men's basketball program has won eight national championships and was the first program to reach 2,000 wins. Rupp Arena is downtown. Football in Lexington is what you do in the fall while you wait for basketball season. It's the opening act, darlin'. And I love an opening act. I've been one.

Then there's their stadium name. Kroger Field. Y'all, they named their football stadium after a grocery store. I don't hate it. I just think it's funny to drive all the way to Lexington to play football in the produce aisle. I'll grab a gallon of milk on the way out.

The Last Song

Here's the setlist. Kentucky's offense is last in the country on third down. Its pass defense is 116th. Vanderbilt has a receiver with 628 yards and two straight wins in this series. Yes, we need to stop the run, and yes, we need to hold on to the football. But this is Nashville, and Nashville writes comebacks for a living.

Every great album has a track nine that nobody expects to be the single. Saturday night in Lexington, that's us.

Anchor down, y'all.

My call: Kentucky Wildcats 33, Vanderbilt Commodores 23.

articles.title: I've Crunched the Numbers, and the Numbers Say Orange: The Illini Survived East Lansing, Rested Up, and Now Oregon Has to Come Find Champaign on a Map
articles.byline: Margery Vandermolen, The Illinois Fanatic
articles.matchup: Illinois (3-3) vs. Oregon (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 3 p.m. EDT, Gies Memorial Stadium, Champaign (BTN)
articles.text:
Good morning, class. Please take out a pencil, and if you have a slide rule, even better. I have mine right here. It belonged to my father, who taught agricultural economics for 31 years, and it has never once been wrong about the soybean harvest or the need for a two-point stop.

I'm Margery Vandermolen. I grew up between a cornfield and Memorial Stadium, and I color-code my notes in orange and blue, which my neighbors find charming and my accountant finds alarming.

Today's lesson: how to survive overtime, and what to do with a bye week. Orange you glad it's Saturday? Let's begin.

Part 1: Review of the Overtime Problem

Our last game was two Saturdays ago, Oct. 10, at Spartan Stadium. Illinois 38, Michigan State 37, in overtime. We had last Saturday off, and the doctors in my household agree that my blood pressure needed the week.

Let's chart the first half, because it was a beautiful curve on my graph. Ethan Moczulski kicked a 40-yard field goal. Katin Houser threw a 5-yard touchdown pass to Aidan Laughery and then ran one in from two. Moczulski added kicks of 35 and 38 yards. We scored on our first five drives, the AP noted, and led 23-7 midway through the third quarter.

Now, class, a graph that goes straight up forever is a graph somebody drew wrong. In the third quarter, Houser hurt his hand making a tackle on an interception return. Michigan State scored twice. Then Michael Clayton II, who'd never thrown a college pass before, stepped in and threw a 14-yard touchdown to Collin Dixon, and Laughery ran in the two-point conversion. 31-17.

Then the part of the lesson I'll call "a teachable moment." With 3:27 left, coach Bret Bielema went for it on fourth-and-1 at our own 33. We were stuffed. Michigan State tied it with 1:17 left. Overtime.

On the first play of overtime, Clayton threw a 25-yard touchdown to Hudson Clement. Michigan State answered with a touchdown and went for two and the win. The pass fell incomplete. Illinois wins, 38-37. I've never been so happy to see a ball hit the grass.

The Grade Book

Houser was 20 of 29 for 194 yards with a touchdown pass and a rushing score before the injury. Clayton completed six of eight for 88 yards and two touchdowns in his first passing action. Clement caught six passes for 105 yards. Moczulski made all three field goals. James Kreutz made 15 tackles and a sack. We committed two penalties all day.

The hard part of the grade: Houser broke a bone in his hand, and Bielema said he'd be out for a considerable amount of time, according to the AP. I wish him a quick recovery, and I'm told he's a fine young man.

Season-to-Date

We're 3-3 and 1-2 in the Big Ten. We beat UAB and Southern Illinois, lost 31-27 to Duke and 24-17 to Purdue at home, lost 42-19 at Ohio State, and won at Michigan State. We score 31.8 points a game. On the Purdue loss, I'll only say I've graded tougher exams.

Part 2: This Saturday, Oregon Comes to Champaign

Saturday, Oct. 24, at 3 p.m. Eastern, Oregon visits Gies Memorial Stadium. BTN has it.

Let me be fair, because a good teacher shows all her work. Oregon is 4-2 and 2-1 in the Big Ten. It won at USC 41-27, and its defense ranks third in FBS on third downs, allowing conversions only 25.9 of every 100 times. Matayo Uiagalelei has six sacks. Under coach Dan Lanning, the Ducks went 13-0 in the 2024 regular season. That's a serious program.

And now, the data the Ducks would like to leave out of the slide deck.

Oregon lost at home to UCLA, 17-15, and lost at Oklahoma State. On Saturday night against Nebraska, the Ducks had 91 yards of offense when they went to the bench for a new quarterback. Third-stringer Brock Thomas had started. Their regular starter, Dante Moore, has been out with a concussion since Sept. 26. Dylan Raiola came off the bench and won the game with 28 seconds left, going 11 of 18 for 59 yards in the fourth quarter. Oregon's rushing offense ranks 97th in FBS, according to the AP.

Class, when both teams have a quarterback question, the tiebreaker is home field. And I've crunched the numbers. The numbers say orange.

Now, in fairness, I must show you our weak spot, too: our red-zone defense ranks 137th in FBS, allowing scores on every single trip, per the AP preview. Every trip. That's a perfect score, and it's the only perfect score I'd like us to stop getting. Our defense allows 27.8 points a game. If we can keep Oregon out of the red zone, our chances improve considerably.

Who to Watch

Collin Dixon, receiver: 47 catches, 608 yards, nine touchdowns. Our most reliable variable.

Aidan Laughery, running back: 391 yards. Oregon allows 111.7 rushing yards a game.

Hudson Clement, receiver: six catches for 105 yards and the overtime winner at Michigan State.

Michael Clayton II: two touchdown passes in his first career passing action. Please consult your slide rule.

Matthew Bailey: 41 tackles, our leader. James Kreutz: 15 tackles at Michigan State.

Matayo Uiagalelei, Oregon defensive end: six sacks. Protect the quarterback, whoever he is.

Evan Stewart, Oregon receiver: 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns.

History Lesson

Oregon leads the series 3-1, according to CollegeFootballDigest, and won the last meeting, 38-9 in Eugene in 2024. Our lone win came in 1970, 20-16, here in Champaign. It's been a while. Not as long as it takes to grow an oak tree, but longer than corn.

Field Trip: A Tale of Two Towns

Champaign. Population 88,302 at the 2020 census, sharing the University of Illinois with its twin city, Urbana. Our campus is home to the Morrow Plots, the oldest continuously used experimental agricultural fields in the country, and the undergraduate library was built underground so it wouldn't cast shadows on the corn. Class, we built a library underground for corn. That's devotion. Memorial Stadium, completed in 1923, has 200 columns on its east and west sides, and 183 of them carry the name of an Illinois alum who died in World War I. A 12-foot statue of Red Grange, who once scored five touchdowns in a single game here, stands outside. The fight song is "Oskee Wow-Wow." Say it out loud. You feel better already.

Eugene, Oregon. Eugene is a lovely town of 176,654, nestled in the Willamette Valley. It's called "Track Town, USA," and Nike got its start there, founded by an Oregon runner, Phil Knight, and his coach, Bill Bowerman. Oregon football wears a different uniform combination nearly every week, thanks to that Nike partnership. Class, a team that can't decide what to wear on a Saturday is a team that needs a checklist, and I'd be happy to provide one.

And here's a footnote I discovered in my research. According to Wikipedia, the Eugene area has the highest grass pollen counts in the United States. Olympic runners have flown in by helicopter to avoid it. So when the Ducks come to Champaign, they'll be breathing clean prairie air for the first time all season. In fact, the only allergy they'll suffer from in Champaign is orange.

Closing Remarks

Here's my summary for the test. We're rested, we're at home, and we have a receiver with nine touchdowns. Oregon is coming off a 17-14 win in which its offense mustered 91 yards before the fourth quarter, and it's still sorting out its quarterbacks. Our red-zone defense needs to show up, and if it does, this will be a close finish worth staying for.

I've crunched the numbers. Oskee-wow-wow!

My call: Oregon Ducks 34, Illinois Fighting Illini 24.

If we can keep Oregon out of the red zone, our chances improve considerably.
Who to Watch
Collin Dixon, receiver: 47 catches, 608 yards, nine touchdowns. Our most reliable variable.
Aidan Laughery, running back: 391 yards. Oregon allows 111.7 rushing yards a game.
Hudson Clement, receiver: six catches for 105 yards and the overtime winner at Michigan State.
Michael Clayton II: two touchdown passes in his first career passing action. Please consult your slide rule.
Matthew Bailey: 41 tackles, our leader. James Kreutz: 15 tackles at Michigan State.
Matayo Uiagalelei, Oregon defensive end: six sacks. Protect the quarterback, whoever he is.
Evan Stewart, Oregon receiver: 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns.
History Lesson

Oregon leads the series 3-1, according to CollegeFootballDigest, and won the last meeting, 38-9 in Eugene in 2024. Our lone win came in 1970, 20-16, here in Champaign. It's been a while. Not as long as it takes to grow an oak tree, but longer than corn.
Field Trip: A Tale of Two Towns

Champaign. Population 88,302 at the 2020 census, sharing the University of Illinois with its twin city, Urbana. Our campus is home to the Morrow Plots, the oldest continuously used experimental agricultural fields in the country, and the undergraduate library was built underground so it wouldn't cast shadows on the corn. Class, we built a library underground for corn. That's devotion. Memorial Stadium, completed in 1923, has 200 columns on its east and west sides, and 183 of them carry the name of an Illinois alum who died in World War I. A 12-foot statue of Red Grange, who once scored five touchdowns in a single game here, stands outside. The fight song is "Oskee Wow-Wow." Say it out loud. You feel better already.

Eugene, Oregon. Eugene is a lovely town of 176,654, nestled in the Willamette Valley. It's called "Track Town, USA," and Nike got its start there, founded by an Oregon runner, Phil Knight, and his coach, Bill Bowerman. Oregon football wears a different uniform combination nearly every week, thanks to that Nike partnership. Class, a team that can't decide what to wear on a Saturday is a team that needs a checklist, and I'd be happy to provide one.

And here's a footnote I discovered in my research. According to Wikipedia, the Eugene area has the highest grass pollen counts in the United States. Olympic runners have flown in by helicopter to avoid it. So when the Ducks come to Champaign, they'll be breathing clean prairie air for the first time all season. In fact, the only allergy they'll suffer from in Champaign is orange.
Closing Remarks

Here's my summary for the test. We're rested, we're at home, and we have a receiver with nine touchdowns. Oregon is coming off a 17-14 win in which its offense mustered 91 yards before the fourth quarter, and it's still sorting out its quarterbacks. Our red-zone defense needs to show up, and if it does, this will be a close finish worth staying for.
I've crunched the numbers. Oskee-wow-wow!
My call: Oregon Ducks 34, Illinois Fighting Illini 24.

articles.title: Bless Your Yards Per Play: The Hoosiers Lost by a Toe, and Now It's Off to the Big House to See Whether Michigan Has Settled on a Quarterback
articles.byline: Mallory Penhallow, The Indiana Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 6 Indiana (6-1) at Michigan (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. EDT, Michigan Stadium, Ann Arbor (FOX)
articles.text:
Good morning, America. I'd like to thank the judges.

I'm Mallory Penhallow, former Miss Monroe County runner-up, and I'll tell you what I learned on the pageant circuit: you can lose by an inch and still hold your head high. I know, because I lost Miss Monroe County by roughly one baton twirl. And Saturday, my Hoosiers lost to Ohio State by roughly one left toe.

I've updated the 40-tab efficiency model. I've had my cry. My mascara is back in place. Let's talk football, darlings.

Part 1: The Talent Portion Went Sideways

Ohio State 19, Indiana 15. Saturday, Oct. 17, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, the first top-five game ever played there, according to the AP.

Here's the context, and it matters. Indiana came into this game as the defending national champions, on a 22-game winning streak and with 19 straight wins at home, the two longest active streaks in FBS. Coach Curt Cignetti hadn't lost a home game in three seasons. That's not a run, sweetheart. That's a reign.

And the reign ended on the white paint.

We fell behind 19-7 when Ohio State hit a 38-yard touchdown pass on fourth-and-1 early in the fourth quarter. Then Josh Hoover, back from a right arm injury of his own, led a 75-yard drive, finishing it with a 19-yard touchdown pass to Nick Marsh and a two-point conversion pass to Turbo Richard. 19-15, with 10:30 left.

Hoover got one more chance and moved us into scoring range fast. With 1:02 left, Marsh was wide open, racing for the front corner of the end zone. He caught it. The fireworks went off. And his left foot had come down on the white paint. Out of bounds. Ohio State ran out the clock.

Cignetti called it a tough one to swallow, and I'm with him. I've swallowed it. It went down like a pageant-week rice cake.

The Scorecard

Pageant answer: it's the explosives, darling, and we had them. Hoover threw for 296 yards and the touchdown with no interceptions. Charlie Becker caught nine passes for 165 yards. Amare Ferrell intercepted two passes. Tyrique Tucker and Rolijah Hardy made eight tackles each, and the defense held Ohio State to 78 rushing yards and Jeremiah Smith to four catches.

The deductions? Two fumbles lost early in the third quarter, after the AP says we'd gone 1,487 snaps without losing one since the 2025 opener. Hoover's was his first turnover of the season. And Nico Radicic missed two field goals. Add those up and the toe doesn't matter. That's what stings.

The Résumé

We're 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big Ten, and the AP poll has us at No. 6. We beat North Texas, Howard and Western Kentucky by a combined 145-16, then Northwestern 29-23, then won at Rutgers 47-15 and at Nebraska 20-17. We score 36.6 points a game and allow 12.9, fourth-best in FBS. Last season ended with a 16-0 record and the program's first national championship. One judge's bad night does not change the crown.

Part 2: A Visit to the Big House

Saturday, Oct. 24, at noon Eastern, we play Michigan at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on FOX.

Now, I'm a pageant girl. I open with a compliment. Michigan's defense is outstanding. It allows 256.5 yards a game, third in FBS, and 16.2 points. Troy Bowles has 50 tackles and John Henry Daley has four sacks. Michigan won 21-18 over Penn State on Saturday, and Tommy Carr came off the bench to run for the clinching touchdown, on the same field where his grandfather Lloyd Carr coached a national champion. That's a lovely story. I'd give it a sash.

And now, the interview portion.

Michigan benched its starting quarterback, Bryce Underwood, at halftime on Saturday. He has six interceptions this season and five touchdown passes. First-year coach Kyle Whittingham wasn't ready to say who'd start against us, according to the AP. So, darling, Michigan doesn't know who its quarterback is. I do. Ours is Josh Hoover, with 18 touchdowns and zero interceptions. Zero. That's what we call a flawless walk.

The AP's preview numbers are, how shall I say, a challenging talent portion. Michigan's offense ranks 125th in FBS in yards per game, 125th in passing and 105th in scoring, at 22.7 points. Its red-zone defense ranks 118th, allowing scores on 92.9 of every 100 trips. Michigan averages 65.8 penalty yards a game, 104th. We average 30.7, third in the country. And the Wolverines needed Saturday's win to avoid starting 0-3 in Big Ten play for the first time since 1967.

Bless their yards per play.

Miss Congeniality

Every week I award my Miss Congeniality sash to the opponent I've teased the hardest. This week it goes to the Michigan quarterback room, which has two contestants and no winner. Wear it proudly, gentlemen. It matches the maize.

Who to Watch

Josh Hoover, our quarterback: 1,660 yards, 18 touchdowns, zero interceptions.

Charlie Becker, receiver: 39 catches for 694 yards and eight touchdowns.

Turbo Richard, running back: 643 yards and six touchdowns on 87 carries. Michigan allows 89.7 rushing yards a game, so this is the matchup to watch.

Tobi Osunsanmi: seven sacks. Isaiah Jones: 52 tackles, our leader. Our defense allows 75.4 rushing yards a game, fourth in FBS.

Tommy Carr, Michigan quarterback: five of seven passing for 47 yards Saturday, plus 36 rushing yards and the clinching score.

JJ Buchanan, Michigan receiver: 27 catches for 482 yards and four touchdowns.

The History Portion

I'll be honest, because honesty is a pageant value. Michigan leads the series 62-11, according to CollegeFootballData.com. But we won the last meeting, 20-15 in Bloomington in 2024. The AP says if we win Saturday, it'll be our first back-to-back wins over Michigan since 1958 and 1959. I've been waiting 67 years. Well, my family has.

Hometown Pageant: A Tale of Two Towns

Bloomington. The 2020 census counted 79,168 of us, and we were the setting for the Academy Award-winning 1979 movie "Breaking Away," about four Bloomington teenagers and our Little 500 bicycle race. Our town sits on southern Indiana limestone, and in 2005 coach Terry Hoeppner installed a limestone boulder called "The Rock" in the north end zone. It's now Hep's Rock, a tribute to him, and it sits on the stadium's east concourse. Memorial Stadium seats 53,524 and has been home since 1960. Cignetti drove the pace car at the Indianapolis 500 in May, and a five-time IndyCar champion, Alex Palou, did the pregame IndyCar drive on Saturday. We're a cycling town, a racing town and, as of last January, a championship town.

Ann Arbor. Ann Arbor is a lovely town, darling, nicknamed "Tree Town." It's also called "A-squared," and as a woman who runs a 40-tab efficiency model, I'd like to point out that A-squared is the only math Michigan's passing game has figured out this year. Their offense ranks 125th in passing yards. A squared. A times A. Michigan's quarterbacks, sadly, are still working on A.

Michigan Stadium holds 107,601, the largest stadium in the United States. When they announce the attendance, the PA announcer traditionally thanks fans for being part of the largest crowd watching a football game anywhere in America. Sweetheart, that's 107,601 people who will all get to watch Josh Hoover throw to Charlie Becker. We'd like to thank them for coming.

Crowning Moment

Here's my final answer, and I'd like world peace and a road win, in that order. We lost a heartbreaker by a toe. We have the better quarterback situation by a mile, the better defense by every number in my model and a coach who has never had a losing season as a head coach. Michigan has a great defense and a question mark under center.

Pageant answer: it's the explosives, darling. Go Hoosiers.

My call: Indiana Hoosiers 28, Michigan Wolverines 16.

articles.title: A Good Punt Is a Love Letter: The Hawkeyes Held Washington to Minus-3 Rushing Yards, Rested Up, and Now Head North to Bring the Pig Home Again
articles.byline: Orrin Kalvelage, The Iowa Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 15 Iowa (5-1) at Minnesota (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. EDT, Huntington Bank Stadium, Minneapolis (FS1)
articles.text:
Pull up a chair on the porch. Not that one, the one with the cushion. There's coffee in the pot and the corn's mostly in, so we have time.

I'm Orrin Kalvelage. I grew up on a farm outside Iowa City, I haven't missed a home opener since I was old enough to sit still, and I own exactly one black-and-gold sweater. My wife says I should buy a second one. I say a man who changes sweaters is a man who's asking for trouble.

Now, some folks come to football for the touchdowns. I come for the defense, the field position, and the punts. A good punt is a love letter to your defense, and Iowa writes a lot of mail.

Part 1: Friday Night in Seattle

Our last game was a Friday night, Oct. 9, at Husky Stadium. Iowa 41, Washington 24. We had last week off, which gave me time to rewatch it twice and write the defense a thank-you card.

Let me tell you what our defense did, because I've been telling everybody at church and they've started sitting farther away. Washington ran the ball 25 times and finished with minus-3 yards rushing. Minus three. You could lose more yards than that walking backward to the mailbox. The Huskies punted on each of their first five drives and gained 14 yards on their first 18 plays. Our boys had six sacks and nine tackles for loss. Cam Buffington had two sacks and Preston Ries had two more.

Now, the offense. Kamari Moulton ran for a career-high 208 yards on 26 carries, including a 56-yard touchdown run in the first quarter. That came one week after Ohio State held him to 27 yards, and the AP said he played like a young man with a chip on his shoulder. Jeremy Hecklinski, starting in place of the injured Hank Brown, completed 14 of 19 passes for 202 yards and three touchdowns. He threw two to tight end DJ Vonnahme, from 20 and 24 yards, and one to Reece Vander Zee from eight. Caden Buhr kicked field goals of 51 and 27 yards, and we led 27-0 before Washington scored.

And Boston Everitt punted four times for a 42-yard average, with three of them inside the 20. Three love letters, folks. Washington got each one in the mail.

It was Iowa's first win in the Pacific Time Zone since the 2019 Holiday Bowl, according to the AP. I stayed up late for it. My cows did not appreciate it the next morning.

The Season So Far

We're 5-1, 2-1 in the Big Ten, and No. 15 in the AP poll. We beat Northern Illinois 40-0, Iowa State 16-13, and Northern Iowa 55-0. We won 20-19 at Michigan. Then Ohio State came to Kinnick and beat us, 31-14. I won't sugarcoat it. The Buckeyes were better that day, and we'll learn from it.

Our defense allows 14.5 points per game, eighth in the country, and 84.7 rushing yards a game, seventh, according to the AP. That's the kind of number I'd frame and hang next to the barn door.

Part 2: Up North for Floyd

Saturday, Oct. 24, at 3:30 p.m. Eastern, we visit Minnesota at Huntington Bank Stadium. FS1 has it. And the winner takes home Floyd of Rosedale, the 98-pound bronze pig.

Let me be neighborly first. Minnesota is 4-2 and 2-1 in the Big Ten, and coach P.J. Fleck's team won at Washington, 27-24, and beat Michigan, 20-14, in Minneapolis. The Gophers' pass defense ranks ninth in FBS, allowing 159.7 yards a game, and opponents convert only 30.9 of every 100 third downs against them. Quarterback Drake Lindsey has thrown for 1,335 yards and nine touchdowns. TJ Bush Jr. has four sacks. Maverick Baranowski has 45 tackles. Those are real players, and I respect them.

Now, the less neighborly part. Minnesota's last game was at Purdue on Oct. 10, and it went the way a hailstorm goes for a soybean field. Purdue 41, Minnesota 13. The Gophers ran 13 times for 27 yards. They were down 20-3 at the half. And the Boilermakers' leading rusher, Fame Ijeboi, who ran for 195 yards and three touchdowns, used to play for Minnesota. Their rushing offense ranks 129th in FBS, the AP says, at 104.8 yards a game.

So here's the matchup I'll be watching from my chair: a running game that's struggled against a run defense ranked seventh in the nation. I'll bring the good coffee.

One honest note: Hank Brown has led us in passing this year with 832 yards, five touchdowns, and one interception, and he missed the Washington game with an injury. Whoever's under center, I trust the boys up front, and I trust our punter even more.

Who to Watch

Kamari Moulton, running back: 519 yards and four touchdowns on 76 carries, and 208 of those came in Seattle.

Jeremy Hecklinski and Hank Brown, quarterbacks: Hecklinski threw three touchdowns in his start. Brown has the season numbers.

Tony Diaz, receiver: our leader with 28 catches for 329 yards.

Cam Buffington, linebacker: 52 tackles, plus two sacks in Seattle.

Boston Everitt, punter: three punts inside the 20 last time out. Hand-addressed.

Drake Lindsey, Minnesota quarterback: 248 passing yards at Purdue. He can throw it.

Javon Tracy, Minnesota receiver: 32 catches for 375 yards.

Floyd's Family Tree

Minnesota officially leads the series 63-54-2. But we've won nine of the last 10, including 41-3 at Kinnick last year and 31-14 in Minneapolis in 2024, and Floyd has lived in Iowa City since that 2024 game, according to CollegeFootballDigest. He likes it there. We feed him well.

Floyd's been up for grabs since 1935. The original Floyd was a real prize pig from Rosedale Farms near Fort Dodge, Iowa, and he was named for Minnesota's governor, Floyd Olson, according to Wikipedia. His brother, Blue Boy, was in the Will Rogers movie "State Fair." A St. Paul sculptor named Charles Brioschi made the bronze version. So a Minnesota man made the trophy, and Iowa keeps polishing it. I call that teamwork.

The Porch Report: Two Towns

Iowa City. A town of 74,828, according to the 2020 census, and in 2008 UNESCO named it the world's third City of Literature. It's home to the Iowa Writers' Workshop, whose graduates include Flannery O'Connor and John Irving. So we can write you a love letter and a punt.

And then there's the Wave. The University of Iowa's children's hospital overlooks Kinnick Stadium, and after the first quarter of every home game, the whole stadium turns around and wave to the kids and families watching from the windows. I've done it more than I can count, and I get misty every single time. My wife hands me a handkerchief before the quarter ends now. She knows.

Minneapolis. Minneapolis is a fine city of 429,954 that calls itself the City of Lakes, with 13 lakes and a stretch of the Mississippi River. It was once the flour-milling capital of the world. I respect a town that knows its grain.

But I do have to mention the skyways. Minneapolis has 9.5 miles of enclosed pedestrian bridges connecting 80 downtown blocks, so folks can get around without stepping outside, according to Wikipedia. Folks, back home we have something similar. It's called a barn. The difference is, we still go outside to get to it.

And a Gophers fan will tell you how tough they are about the cold. I believe it. But for a town that built nine miles of hallways to avoid the weather, Saturday's forecast had better behave itself.

Closing

Here's what I know. We've got a defense that just held a Big Ten team to minus-3 rushing yards. We've got a running back coming off 208 yards. We've got a punter who writes letters. Minnesota has a solid pass defense, a home crowd, and a running game that managed 27 yards in its last game.

Bring Floyd home. Wave to the kids. Go Hawks.

My call: Iowa Hawkeyes 29, Minnesota Golden Gophers 18.

Jeremy Hecklinski, starting in place of the injured Hank Brown, completed 14 of 19 passes for 202 yards and three touchdowns. He threw two to tight end DJ Vonnahme, from 20 and 24 yards, and one to Reece Vander Zee from eight. Caden Buhr kicked field goals of 51 and 27 yards, and we led 27-0 before Washington scored.
And Boston Everitt punted four times for a 42-yard average, with three of them inside the 20. Three love letters, folks. Washington got each one in the mail.
It was Iowa's first win in the Pacific Time Zone since the 2019 Holiday Bowl, according to the AP. I stayed up late for it. My cows did not appreciate it the next morning.
The Season So Far

We're 5-1, 2-1 in the Big Ten, and No. 15 in the AP poll. We beat Northern Illinois 40-0, Iowa State 16-13, and Northern Iowa 55-0. We won 20-19 at Michigan. Then Ohio State came to Kinnick and beat us, 31-14. I won't sugarcoat it. The Buckeyes were better that day, and we'll learn from it.
Our defense allows 14.5 points per game, eighth in the country, and 84.7 rushing yards a game, seventh, according to the AP. That's the kind of number I'd frame and hang next to the barn door.
Part 2: Up North for Floyd
Saturday, Oct. 24, at 3:30 p.m. Eastern, we visit Minnesota at Huntington Bank Stadium. FS1 has it. And the winner takes home Floyd of Rosedale, the 98-pound bronze pig.

Let me be neighborly first. Minnesota is 4-2 and 2-1 in the Big Ten, and coach P.J. Fleck's team won at Washington, 27-24, and beat Michigan, 20-14, in Minneapolis. The Gophers' pass defense ranks ninth in FBS, allowing 159.7 yards a game, and opponents convert only 30.9 of every 100 third downs against them. Quarterback Drake Lindsey has thrown for 1,335 yards and nine touchdowns. TJ Bush Jr. has four sacks. Maverick Baranowski has 45 tackles. Those are real players, and I respect them.

Now, the less neighborly part. Minnesota's last game was at Purdue on Oct. 10, and it went the way a hailstorm goes for a soybean field. Purdue 41, Minnesota 13. The Gophers ran 13 times for 27 yards. They were down 20-3 at the half. And the Boilermakers' leading rusher, Fame Ijeboi, who ran for 195 yards and three touchdowns, used to play for Minnesota. Their rushing offense ranks 129th in FBS, the AP says, at 104.8 yards a game.
So here's the matchup I'll be watching from my chair: a running game that's struggled against a run defense ranked seventh in the nation. I'll bring the good coffee.

One honest note: Hank Brown has led us in passing this year with 832 yards, five touchdowns, and one interception, and he missed the Washington game with an injury. Whoever's under center, I trust the boys up front, and I trust our punter even more.
Who to Watch
Kamari Moulton, running back: 519 yards and four touchdowns on 76 carries, and 208 of those came in Seattle.
Jeremy Hecklinski and Hank Brown, quarterbacks: Hecklinski threw three touchdowns in his start. Brown has the season numbers.
Tony Diaz, receiver: our leader with 28 catches for 329 yards.
Cam Buffington, linebacker: 52 tackles, plus two sacks in Seattle.
Boston Everitt, punter: three punts inside the 20 last time out. Hand-addressed.
Drake Lindsey, Minnesota quarterback: 248 passing yards at Purdue. He can throw it.
Javon Tracy, Minnesota receiver: 32 catches for 375 yards.
Floyd's Family Tree

Minnesota officially leads the series 63-54-2. But we've won nine of the last 10, including 41-3 at Kinnick last year and 31-14 in Minneapolis in 2024, and Floyd has lived in Iowa City since that 2024 game, according to CollegeFootballDigest. He likes it there. We feed him well.

Floyd's been up for grabs since 1935. The original Floyd was a real prize pig from Rosedale Farms near Fort Dodge, Iowa, and he was named for Minnesota's governor, Floyd Olson, according to Wikipedia. His brother, Blue Boy, was in the Will Rogers movie "State Fair." A St. Paul sculptor named Charles Brioschi made the bronze version. So a Minnesota man made the trophy, and Iowa keeps polishing it. I call that teamwork.
The Porch Report: Two Towns

Iowa City. A town of 74,828, according to the 2020 census, and in 2008 UNESCO named it the world's third City of Literature. It's home to the Iowa Writers' Workshop, whose graduates include Flannery O'Connor and John Irving. So we can write you a love letter and a punt.

And then there's the Wave. The University of Iowa's children's hospital overlooks Kinnick Stadium, and after the first quarter of every home game, the whole stadium turns around and wave to the kids and families watching from the windows. I've done it more than I can count, and I get misty every single time. My wife hands me a handkerchief before the quarter ends now. She knows.

Minneapolis. Minneapolis is a fine city of 429,954 that calls itself the City of Lakes, with 13 lakes and a stretch of the Mississippi River. It was once the flour-milling capital of the world. I respect a town that knows its grain.

But I do have to mention the skyways. Minneapolis has 9.5 miles of enclosed pedestrian bridges connecting 80 downtown blocks, so folks can get around without stepping outside, according to Wikipedia. Folks, back home we have something similar. It's called a barn. The difference is, we still go outside to get to it.
And a Gophers fan will tell you how tough they are about the cold. I believe it. But for a town that built nine miles of hallways to avoid the weather, Saturday's forecast had better behave itself.
Closing

Here's what I know. We've got a defense that just held a Big Ten team to minus-3 rushing yards. We've got a running back coming off 208 yards. We've got a punter who writes letters. Minnesota has a solid pass defense, a home crowd, and a running game that managed 27 yards in its last game.
Bring Floyd home. Wave to the kids. Go Hawks.
My call: Iowa Hawkeyes 29, Minnesota Golden Gophers 18.

articles.title: Crack It Open: The Terps Let a 10-Point Lead Slip Against Rutgers, Take a Week to Regroup, and Get Illinois at Home on Halloween
articles.byline: Abigail 'Abby' Chesapeake, The Maryland Fanatic
articles.matchup: Maryland (2-5): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Illinois (3-3) at Maryland, Sat., Oct. 31, SECU Stadium, College Park
articles.text:
Hello, darlings. Abby Chesapeake, coming to you from a picnic table covered in brown paper, with a wooden mallet in one hand and a stat sheet in the other.

You know my philosophy. Every problem in life has the same answer, and it's Old Bay. Rough Monday? Old Bay. Flat tire on the Beltway? Old Bay, and then call a tow truck. Five-game losing streak?

Well. I've been shaking the can all weekend, and I'll be honest with you: this one may require two cans.

But I'm a Beltway girl. I network, I negotiate, and I never leave a meeting without finding something to build on. So let's crack it open.

Part 1: The Half That Got Away

Rutgers 37, Maryland 30. Saturday, Oct. 17, at SECU Stadium in College Park.

I want to start with the first half, because darlings, the first half was a delight. Damon Hall Jr. scored on a 1-yard run to put us up 7-0. Malik Washington hit Dorian Fleming for a 3-yard touchdown. And then came the kind of play you tell everybody about at the next crab feast: Rutgers scored a touchdown, we blocked the extra point, and Jamare Glasker returned it the other way for two points. Who does that? We do that.

Then Chris Durr Jr. took a handoff 16 yards for a touchdown with 53 seconds left in the half. 23-13, Maryland. I was so happy I put Old Bay on my lemonade. Don't try that.

And then the second half. Darlings, I'm going to say this as diplomatically as a girl from the Washington suburbs can: Rutgers scored the next 24 points. A field goal, a touchdown pass, a touchdown run, another touchdown run. We got one back late, when Washington found DeJuan Williams for a 10-yard score with 2:17 left, but it wasn't enough.

The Good Crabs

Every bushel has some beauties, and this one had a few. Washington threw for 263 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions. Durr caught six passes for 104 yards and ran for that touchdown. Glasker had an interception, a defensive two-point return and six tackles. Messiah Delhomme led us with seven tackles. We didn't turn the ball over once.

The Ones You Throw Back

Rutgers held the ball for 35:52 and converted 9 of 14 third downs. KJ Duff caught nine passes and two touchdowns against us. And we went 0-for-1 on field goals. When the other team keeps the ball for almost 36 minutes, your defense gets tired, and tired crabs don't pinch.

The Season So Far

Here's the honest status report. We're 2-5 and 0-4 in the Big Ten, and we've lost five straight. We started 2-0, beating Hampton and winning at UConn, and then lost to Virginia Tech, UCLA, at Nebraska, at Ohio State and now to Rutgers. That UCLA game was 54-3, and I've asked my staff never to bring it up in my presence. I'm only mentioning it because honesty is a Maryland value.

But here's the thing about crab season: it always comes back around.

Part 2: A Week Off, Then Illinois

Maryland has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. No game. A week to rest, heal and, I hope, practice third-down defense.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, Illinois comes to SECU Stadium. Kickoff time hasn't been announced as I write this. Halloween in College Park, darlings. I'll be dressed as a can of Old Bay. Obviously.

Now, I always open with a compliment. It's good manners and good politics. Illinois is 3-3, and coach Bret Bielema's teams are physical. Receiver Collin Dixon has 47 catches for 608 yards and nine touchdowns. The Illini won 38-37 in overtime at Michigan State two weeks ago, and they host Oregon this Saturday before they come see us.

And now, the negotiation.

Illinois lost at home to Duke and at home to Purdue. Its starting quarterback, Katin Houser, broke his hand against Michigan State, and Bielema said he'd be out for a considerable amount of time. In that game, Illinois led by 16 in the third quarter. Then Bielema went for it on fourth-and-1 at his own 33 with 3:27 left, got stuffed, and Michigan State tied the game. Illinois survived in overtime only because the Spartans' two-point try fell short.

So, darlings: Illinois has a quarterback question, a defense that allows 27.8 points a game, and, before it gets to us, a date with Oregon. That's a team that may arrive in College Park a little bruised. Ours will be rested. I'd call that a favorable negotiating position.

Who to Watch

Malik Washington, quarterback: 1,615 yards, nine touchdowns and six interceptions this season, and none against Rutgers.

Chris Durr Jr., receiver: 52 catches for 580 yards and four touchdowns, our leader. He had 104 yards Saturday.

DeJuan Williams, running back: 281 yards and three touchdowns on 38 carries.

Daniel Wingate: 44 tackles, our leader. Zion Elee: 3.5 sacks.

Jamare Glasker: the man who turned a blocked extra point into two points for us. Watch him on every kick.

Collin Dixon, Illinois receiver: nine touchdown catches. Our secondary will want to shadow him all night.

The History

The series is tied 2-2, according to CollegeFootballDigest. We won the first two meetings, including 63-33 in 2018. Illinois has won the last two, 27-24 in College Park in 2023 and 24-6 last season in Champaign. Tied series, home game, Halloween. Crack it open.

Crab Feast Report: A Tale of Two Towns

College Park. Population 34,740 at the 2020 census, about four miles from the border of Washington, D.C. College Park Airport, established in 1909 so Wilbur Wright himself could teach Army officers to fly, is the world's oldest continuously operated airport. Our mascot, Testudo, is a diamondback terrapin, and since 1994 the diamondback terrapin has been Maryland's official state reptile by act of the General Assembly. Students rub the nose of the Testudo statue outside McKeldin Library for luck, and it shines like a new penny. SECU Stadium has been home since 1950. Maryland claims the 1953 national championship. And of course, Old Bay was created up the road in Baltimore in 1939, and it's named for an old Baltimore steamship company that carried passengers down the bay to Norfolk.

Champaign. Now, Champaign is perfectly lovely. Population 88,302. It's a twin city with Urbana, and it was founded in 1855 when the Illinois Central Railroad laid its tracks two miles west of downtown Urbana. Originally, they called it "West Urbana." Darlings, a town whose first name was just "a little to the left of another town" is not a town with a strong personal brand. I'm in communications. I'd have advised against it.

Illinois football's greatest hero, Red Grange, scored five touchdowns in one game back in 1924, and there's a 12-foot statue of him outside Memorial Stadium. Wonderful. But Illinois hasn't found anyone that exciting lately, and its current quarterback situation could use a Grange or two. I'd send them some Old Bay to liven things up, but darlings, it's Halloween week, and I'm keeping every can for the tailgate.

Final Crack

Here's where I land, and I've run it past my entire focus group, which is my mother. We had a 10-point halftime lead on Saturday. We've had a rough month. But we've got a quarterback who didn't throw an interception, a receiver over 100 yards, a defense that blocks kicks and scores, a week of rest and a home game on Halloween against a team that's banged up at quarterback.

Shake the can. Crack the shell. Fear the Turtle.

articles.title: Framed It, Then Dropped It: The Spartans Lost Another Heartbreaker, and Now They Fly to Pasadena to Face an Unbeaten Team That Plays Home Games 26 Miles From Home
articles.byline: Shay Kowalczyk, The Michigan State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Michigan State (2-5) at No. 9 UCLA (6-0), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. EDT, Rose Bowl, Pasadena (CBS)
articles.text:
Alright, gear on. Mask down. Squat.

I'm Shay Kowalczyk. I caught softball for 11 years around the Lansing area, which means my knees sound like a bowl of cereal and I can tell you exactly what pitch a defense should've called. I've been in the stands for every Spartan home game this year, and most of the road ones, and I'm here to tell you: we've been close, eh. Painfully, ridiculously close.

Every week I frame the game like a pitch-calling sequence. Last week, we had two strikes on Northwestern. Then we blocked the plate, and the runner slid around us.

Part 1: Northwestern, 24-21, Two Seconds Left

On Saturday, Oct. 17, at Spartan Stadium, Northwestern beat us 24-21 on a 34-yard field goal by Jackson Kleather with two seconds left.

Let me walk you through the count.

First pitch: we went for it on fourth-and-1 in the first quarter, and Alessio Milivojevic ran in a 3-yard touchdown. 7-3 Spartans. Called it, framed it.

Second pitch: just before halftime, Milivojevic found Bryson Williams for a 32-yard touchdown, and we led 14-10 at the half. Early in the fourth quarter, Milivojevic hit Chrishon McCray for a 53-yard score. 21-13. Two strikes, baby.

Then the Wildcats' quarterback, Aidan Chiles, who played for us the last two years, ran in a 1-yard touchdown and threw the two-point conversion to tie it at 21 with 7:24 left. Our kicker, Liam Boyd, lined up a 33-yard field goal to retake the lead, and Northwestern's Matthew Smith blocked it. Chiles drove 64 yards in eight plays, and Kleather made the kick.

Foul tip, caught by nobody. Ball game.

Here's what I'm proud of. According to the AP, we were missing our top three inside linebackers and our top three cornerbacks, and we still had five sacks and 10 tackles for loss. We hadn't had a sack in three games. Ben Roberts had two. Dion Crawford made 14 tackles, and Cam Stodghill made 11. Eli Coenen blocked a Northwestern field goal in the first half. Milivojevic went 19 of 30 for 216 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions. Rhys Dakin averaged 48 yards a punt with a 58-yarder. Three penalties all day. That's a clean glove.

And that's two straight weeks we lost by a single point or a single kick. The week before, Illinois beat us 38-37 in overtime when our two-point try fell short. Coach Pat Fitzgerald said afterward that his staff has to coach better to get over the hump, and I respect a catcher who says "my fault" when the ball gets by.

The Season So Far

We're 2-5 and 0-4 in the Big Ten. We beat Toledo 30-20 and Eastern Michigan 35-7. Then came Notre Dame (27-10), Nebraska (31-13), Wisconsin (31-3), Illinois (38-37 in overtime), and Northwestern (24-21). Five straight losses, the last two by a combined four points. My knees hurt, and it's not from squatting.

Part 2: Off to Pasadena

Saturday, Oct. 24, we visit No. 9 UCLA at the Rose Bowl. Kickoff is 3:30 p.m. Eastern, 12:30 p.m. out there, and CBS has it.

Respect first, because a good catcher always shakes the umpire's hand. UCLA is 6-0 and 4-0 in the Big Ten under first-year coach Bob Chesney, who, per the AP, is the first UCLA coach to start his tenure with six straight wins. They won just three games last year. They won at Oregon 17-15. Wayne Knight has 571 rushing yards and 11 touchdowns, with a rushing score in every game. Their defense allows 16.2 points a game and ranks third in FBS on third downs. And last Saturday, backup quarterback Ty Dieffenbach threw for 264 yards in his first start as a Bruin in a 17-7 win over Wisconsin, with Nico Iamaleava out with a leg injury. That's a good ballclub.

Now the scouting report they'd rather keep in the dugout. UCLA averages 83.2 penalty yards a game, which ranks 133rd in FBS, according to the AP. We average 36.3, seventh-best in the country. So if this game comes down to who keeps the yellow flags in somebody's back pocket, I like our glove.

And against Wisconsin, the Bruins scored 17 points. They had the ball for 37 minutes and scored 17 points. In softball we call that leaving the bases loaded.

Who to Watch

Alessio Milivojevic, quarterback: 1,263 yards, seven touchdowns, three interceptions. Zero interceptions against Northwestern. Clean glove.

Jaziun Patterson, running back: 327 yards and five touchdowns, including three at Illinois.

Chrishon McCray and Bryson Williams, receivers: touchdown catches of 53 and 32 yards last Saturday.

Jayden Savoury, receiver: our leader with 27 catches.

Devin Vaught, defensive back: 46 tackles, our leader. Eli Coenen: 3.5 sacks and a blocked kick.

Wayne Knight, UCLA running back: a touchdown in every game this season.

Semaj Morgan, UCLA receiver: 24 catches for 313 yards.

History: The Rose Bowl Knows Us

UCLA leads the series 4-3 and has won four straight, including 38-13 in East Lansing last year, according to CollegeFootballDigest. But here's what I love: three of our seven meetings were in the Rose Bowl Game. We beat UCLA there to cap the 1953 season, 28-20, and again in January 1956, 17-14. UCLA beat our unbeaten, No. 1 1965 team there, 14-12. So we know the way to Pasadena. We've just never visited during the regular season.

Two Towns, Called Like a Ball Game

East Lansing. A town of 47,741, home to Michigan State, the first land-grant college in the United States, designated in 1863. And it's home to the MSU Dairy Store in Anthony Hall, where the university makes its own ice cream and cheese, with milk from university cows. There's a flavor called Spartan Swirl, and it's green, and I'll be eating a pint of it either way on Saturday. Our stadium has been around since 1923 and seats 75,005, though it's held more than 80,000. It's right there on campus. Remember that.

And a reminder, because it's my go-to rule of life: Ann Arbor is just a suburb with a stadium.

Westwood and Pasadena. UCLA's campus is in Westwood, a lovely neighborhood next to Westwood Village and its movie theaters. But the Bruins don't play there. They play at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, and according to Wikipedia, the Bruins travel 26 miles from campus for home games and only 14 miles to play at USC. Ladies and gentlemen, UCLA's road game is closer than its home game. In softball, if you had to drive farther to your home field than to your rival's park, somebody would file a grievance.

The Rose Bowl is a National Historic Landmark, opened in 1922, and seats 89,702. Last Saturday, 36,045 people came to watch an unbeaten team play. That's fine. We'll bring the noise. Plenty of open seats for Spartans.

Closing

Here's my call from behind the plate. We're beat up, and we're 2-5. But our last two games came down to a two-point conversion and a field goal with two seconds left. We protect the football, we don't commit penalties, and our pass rush just woke up.

UCLA's good, and they're undefeated for a reason. But we know the road to Pasadena, and we've won there before.

Framed it. Strike three. Go Green.

My call: UCLA Bruins 32, Michigan State Spartans 17.

blocks.text: Alright, gear on. Mask down. Squat.

I'm Shay Kowalczyk. I caught softball for 11 years around the Lansing area, which means my knees sound like a bowl of cereal and I can tell you exactly what pitch a defense should've called. I've been in the stands for every Spartan home game this year, and most of the road ones, and I'm here to tell you: we've been close, eh. Painfully, ridiculously close.
Every week I frame the game like a pitch-calling sequence. Last week, we had two strikes on Northwestern. Then we blocked the plate, and the runner slid around us.
Part 1: Northwestern, 24-21, Two Seconds Left
On Saturday, Oct. 17, at Spartan Stadium, Northwestern beat us 24-21 on a 34-yard field goal by Jackson Kleather with two seconds left.
Let me walk you through the count.
First pitch: we went for it on fourth-and-1 in the first quarter, and Alessio Milivojevic ran in a 3-yard touchdown. 7-3 Spartans. Called it, framed it.

Second pitch: just before halftime, Milivojevic found Bryson Williams for a 32-yard touchdown, and we led 14-10 at the half. Early in the fourth quarter, Milivojevic hit Chrishon McCray for a 53-yard score. 21-13. Two strikes, baby.

Then the Wildcats' quarterback, Aidan Chiles, who played for us the last two years, ran in a 1-yard touchdown and threw the two-point conversion to tie it at 21 with 7:24 left. Our kicker, Liam Boyd, lined up a 33-yard field goal to retake the lead, and Northwestern's Matthew Smith blocked it. Chiles drove 64 yards in eight plays, and Kleather made the kick.
Foul tip, caught by nobody. Ball game.

Here's what I'm proud of. According to the AP, we were missing our top three inside linebackers and our top three cornerbacks, and we still had five sacks and 10 tackles for loss. We hadn't had a sack in three games. Ben Roberts had two. Dion Crawford made 14 tackles, and Cam Stodghill made 11. Eli Coenen blocked a Northwestern field goal in the first half. Milivojevic went 19 of 30 for 216 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions. Rhys Dakin averaged 48 yards a punt with a 58-yarder. Three penalties all day. That's a clean glove.

And that's two straight weeks we lost by a single point or a single kick. The week before, Illinois beat us 38-37 in overtime when our two-point try fell short. Coach Pat Fitzgerald said afterward that his staff has to coach better to get over the hump, and I respect a catcher who says "my fault" when the ball gets by.
The Season So Far

We're 2-5 and 0-4 in the Big Ten. We beat Toledo 30-20 and Eastern Michigan 35-7. Then came Notre Dame (27-10), Nebraska (31-13), Wisconsin (31-3), Illinois (38-37 in overtime), and Northwestern (24-21). Five straight losses, the last two by a combined four points. My knees hurt, and it's not from squatting.
Part 2: Off to Pasadena
Saturday, Oct. 24, we visit No. 9 UCLA at the Rose Bowl. Kickoff is 3:30 p.m. Eastern, 12:30 p.m. out there, and CBS has it.

Respect first, because a good catcher always shakes the umpire's hand. UCLA is 6-0 and 4-0 in the Big Ten under first-year coach Bob Chesney, who, per the AP, is the first UCLA coach to start his tenure with six straight wins. They won just three games last year. They won at Oregon 17-15. Wayne Knight has 571 rushing yards and 11 touchdowns, with a rushing score in every game. Their defense allows 16.2 points a game and ranks third in FBS on third downs. And last Saturday, backup quarterback Ty Dieffenbach threw for 264 yards in his first start as a Bruin in a 17-7 win over Wisconsin, with Nico Iamaleava out with a leg injury. That's a good ballclub.

Now the scouting report they'd rather keep in the dugout. UCLA averages 83.2 penalty yards a game, which ranks 133rd in FBS, according to the AP. We average 36.3, seventh-best in the country. So if this game comes down to who keeps the yellow flags in somebody's back pocket, I like our glove.
And against Wisconsin, the Bruins scored 17 points. They had the ball for 37 minutes and scored 17 points. In softball we call that leaving the bases loaded.
Who to Watch
Alessio Milivojevic, quarterback: 1,263 yards, seven touchdowns, three interceptions. Zero interceptions against Northwestern. Clean glove.
Jaziun Patterson, running back: 327 yards and five touchdowns, including three at Illinois.
Chrishon McCray and Bryson Williams, receivers: touchdown catches of 53 and 32 yards last Saturday.
Jayden Savoury, receiver: our leader with 27 catches.
Devin Vaught, defensive back: 46 tackles, our leader. Eli Coenen: 3.5 sacks and a blocked kick.
Wayne Knight, UCLA running back: a touchdown in every game this season.
Semaj Morgan, UCLA receiver: 24 catches for 313 yards.
History: The Rose Bowl Knows Us

UCLA leads the series 4-3 and has won four straight, including 38-13 in East Lansing last year, according to CollegeFootballDigest. But here's what I love: three of our seven meetings were in the Rose Bowl Game. We beat UCLA there to cap the 1953 season, 28-20, and again in January 1956, 17-14. UCLA beat our unbeaten, No. 1 1965 team there, 14-12. So we know the way to Pasadena. We've just never visited during the regular season.

East Lansing. A town of 47,741, home to Michigan State, the first land-grant college in the United States, designated in 1863. And it's home to the MSU Dairy Store in Anthony Hall, where the university makes its own ice cream and cheese, with milk from university cows. There's a flavor called Spartan Swirl, and it's green, and I'll be eating a pint of it either way on Saturday. Our stadium has been around since 1923 and seats 75,005, though it's held more than 80,000. It's right there on campus. Remember that.
And a reminder, because it's my go-to rule of life: Ann Arbor is just a suburb with a stadium.

Westwood and Pasadena. UCLA's campus is in Westwood, a lovely neighborhood next to Westwood Village and its movie theaters. But the Bruins don't play there. They play at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, and according to Wikipedia, the Bruins travel 26 miles from campus for home games and only 14 miles to play at USC. Ladies and gentlemen, UCLA's road game is closer than its home game. In softball, if you had to drive farther to your home field than to your rival's park, somebody would file a grievance.

The Rose Bowl is a National Historic Landmark, opened in 1922, and seats 89,702. Last Saturday, 36,045 people came to watch an unbeaten team play. That's fine. We'll bring the noise. Plenty of open seats for Spartans.
Closing

Here's my call from behind the plate. We're beat up, and we're 2-5. But our last two games came down to a two-point conversion and a field goal with two seconds left. We protect the football, we don't commit penalties, and our pass rush just woke up.
UCLA's good, and they're undefeated for a reason. But we know the road to Pasadena, and we've won there before.
Framed it. Strike three. Go Green.

articles.title: Hail to the Stat Sheet: A Carr Came Off the Bench, the Big House Got Loud, and the Defending Champs Are Coming to Ann Arbor
articles.byline: Augustin 'Gus' Hartwell, The Michigan Fanatic
articles.matchup: Michigan (4-2) vs. No. 6 Indiana (6-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. EDT, Michigan Stadium, Ann Arbor (FOX)
articles.text:
I keep a spreadsheet. Of course I do. I'm an engineering student in a maize sweater, and every column on that spreadsheet is labeled with a lyric from "The Victors," because Louis Elbel wrote the greatest fight song in America on a train in 1898, and the least I can do is use it for data management.

Column A is "Hail!" Column B is "the conqu'ring heroes." Column C is "the leaders and best." And on Saturday afternoon, for the first time in a few weeks, I got to fill in Column D: "the champions."

Okay, it was a 21-18 win over a team that's now 0-4 in the Big Ten. But I'm filling it in. Hail to the spreadsheet.

Part 1: The Carr That Came Off the Bench

Michigan 21, Penn State 18, Saturday, Oct. 17, in front of 110,731 at Michigan Stadium.

I'll be honest, because the data demands it. The first half was a lab experiment gone wrong. Penn State led 3-0 at halftime. Bryce Underwood threw two interceptions in the second quarter, his fifth in three games and sixth of the season, one more than his touchdown passes. We needed this game to avoid starting 0-3 in Big Ten play for the first time since 1967, which is the year before Bo Schembechler arrived. Think about that. My spreadsheet doesn't have a column for that, and I don't want one.

So first-year coach Kyle Whittingham benched Underwood at halftime and sent in Tommy Carr. The crowd roared. If you don't know the name, here's the context: Tommy is the grandson of Lloyd Carr, who coached Michigan to the 1997 national championship, and of Tom Curtis, the All-American defensive back who set the school record with 25 career interceptions. The AP noted that Carr jogged onto the same field where his grandfathers made history. I've watched that clip nine times. I'll watch it nine more.

Then the second half happened. Bryson Kuzdzal broke a 43-yard touchdown run. Carr ripped off a 22-yard draw to set up Jordan Marshall's 1-yard touchdown. 14-3.

Penn State scored and added a two-point conversion to make it 14-11 early in the fourth. But then Rocco Becht lost a fumble at the Penn State 16, and Carr ran it in from 12 yards on a third down with 2:58 left. 21-11. Penn State scored with 1:11 to go, and we recovered the onside kick. Ballgame.

Column E: "Hail to the Victors Valiant"

Carr completed five of seven passes for 47 yards and ran four times for 36 yards and the clinching touchdown. Savion Hiter ran 11 times for 78 yards. We ran for 211 yards as a team. On defense, Troy Bowles had 10 tackles, Chris Bracy had a sack and an interception, and Rod Moore Jr. had the other interception. Penn State ran 30 times for 65 yards.

The Season So Far

We're 4-2 and 1-2 in the Big Ten. We beat Western Michigan 13-12 and Oklahoma 17-10, then lost 20-19 to Iowa and 20-14 at Minnesota. Our defense allows 256.5 yards a game, third in FBS, and 16.2 points. Our offense, according to the AP preview, ranks 125th in yards per game. That's not a typo. My spreadsheet highlighted it red on its own.

Part 2: The Defending Champs Come to Ann Arbor

Saturday, Oct. 24, at noon Eastern, No. 6 Indiana comes to Michigan Stadium. FOX has it.

I'll give credit where the data demands it. Indiana is the defending national champion, after a 16-0 season. It's 6-1, and its only loss was 19-15 to Ohio State on Saturday, when Nick Marsh stepped out of bounds on a potential go-ahead touchdown with 1:02 left. Josh Hoover has 18 touchdown passes and zero interceptions. The Hoosiers allow 12.9 points a game, fourth in FBS. That's a very good football team.

But I'm an engineer, and engineers look at the stress points.

Indiana lost two fumbles Saturday after going 1,487 snaps without losing one, according to the AP. Its kicker, Nico Radicic, missed both of his field goals. And the Hoosiers just played the most emotional game in their stadium's history, the first top-five game ever played in Bloomington, and lost it on a toe. Seven days later, they come to the biggest stadium in America, at noon. That's a lot of load on one structure.

And then there's history. Michigan leads the series 62-11, according to CollegeFootballData.com. Indiana won the last meeting, 20-15 in 2024, and the AP says the Hoosiers haven't won two straight against us since 1958 and 1959. Column F: "the champions of the West." We'd like that column back.

Who to Watch

Tommy Carr: Whittingham hasn't named a starter yet. If it's Carr, he has a 90.2 QBR from Saturday and a family tree that reads like the Michigan record book.

Bryce Underwood: 924 yards, five touchdowns, six interceptions. He's a talented young man, and Whittingham said afterward that he couldn't have handled the benching any better. Whatever happens, I'm rooting for him.

Troy Bowles: 50 tackles, our leader. John Henry Daley: four sacks.

JJ Buchanan, receiver: 27 catches, 482 yards, four touchdowns.

Josh Hoover, Indiana quarterback: 1,660 yards, 18 touchdowns, no interceptions. Our pass defense allows 166.8 yards a game, 14th in FBS. Something has to give.

Turbo Richard, Indiana running back: 643 yards and six touchdowns.

The Town Data: A Tale of Two Towns

Ann Arbor. Population 123,851 at the 2020 census. We're "Tree Town," for our name and our forests, and also "A-squared," which is the only city nickname that is also a math problem. The University of Michigan has been here since 1837, it's the oldest university in the state, and Michigan Stadium holds 107,601, the largest stadium in the United States and the Western Hemisphere. Michigan has the most wins in college football history, 1,025 by Wikipedia's count, along with 12 claimed national championships and the winged helmet, which Fritz Crisler brought from Princeton in 1938. When they announce the attendance, the PA announcer thanks the crowd for being part of the largest crowd watching a football game anywhere in America. Every week. Because it's every week.

Bloomington. Bloomington is a lovely college town, and I'll start with the good data. It's the setting of "Breaking Away," the Academy Award-winning 1979 movie about the Little 500 bicycle race. Charming. A town that loves its bicycles.

Now, the complete data. From September 2012 until November 2025, according to Wikipedia, Indiana held the record for the most all-time losses in major college football history. That's right. For 13 years, Indiana and Michigan were in the record book on the exact same page, at opposite ends of it. We had the most wins, and they had the most losses. We were Column A, and they were the footnote.

And Indiana's Memorial Stadium seats 53,524. The Big House seats 107,601. By my math, that's roughly two Indiana stadiums. Saturday, all 107,601 of our fans get to make the noise of two Bloomingtons, and I'm told the Hoosiers are used to bicycles, not jet engines.

The Final Calculation

Here's my honest read. Indiana's the better team on paper, and I'm a man who respects paper. But football isn't played on paper. It's played at noon, in the Big House, in front of 107,601, against a defense that ranks third in the country in yards allowed. If we can get Carr or Underwood to protect the football and keep Hoover from finding Charlie Becker downfield, Column G writes itself.

Hail to the spreadsheet. Go Blue.

My call: Indiana Hoosiers 28, Michigan Wolverines 16.

articles.title: Cold Enough for Ya? Good. The Gophers Got Humbled in West Lafayette, Took a Week to Think It Over, and Now Iowa Has to Come North to Defend a Bronze Pig
articles.byline: Torvald 'Tor' Engebretsen, The Minnesota Fanatic
articles.matchup: Minnesota (4-2) vs. No. 15 Iowa (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. EDT, Huntington Bank Stadium, Minneapolis (FS1)
articles.text:
Well, hi there. Come on in, take your boots off, the rug's new. There's hotdish in the oven and a thermos of coffee by the door, and if you want to talk about rivalry trophies, I'll warn you right now: you'll be here until spring.

I'm Tor Engebretsen. I grew up in Minneapolis ice fishing with my grandpa, who taught me two things. One, never trust ice you haven't checked. Two, the Little Brown Jug is a five-gallon earthenware jug, and anybody who calls it a "pitcher" can see themselves out.

This week, though, it's not the Jug. It's the pig. Ski-U-Mah.

Part 1: The Purdue Game, Which We Will Discuss Politely

I'm a Minnesotan, so I'm going to describe our last game in the most polite way I know how. It was not ideal.

On Oct. 10, at Ross-Ade Stadium, Purdue beat us 41-13. We had last week off, and I spent most of it shoveling a driveway that didn't have any snow on it yet, just to have something to do with my hands.

Here's the honest version. Purdue led 20-3 at halftime and scored on all six of its red-zone trips, according to the AP. We ran the ball 13 times for 27 yards. The Boilermakers ran it 47 times for 305. Their running back, Fame Ijeboi, ran for 195 yards and three touchdowns, and, ope, he used to play for us. That one stung a little, like a January wind off the lake. I wish him well. Mostly.

The bright spots, and there were a few: Drake Lindsey threw for 248 yards, including a 42-yard touchdown to Jalen Smith in the third quarter that cut it to 27-13. Smith had three catches for 89 yards. Javon Tracy caught five for 75. Luke Drzewiecki made field goals from 49 and 37 yards. Maverick Baranowski made 11 tackles, and Tom Weston averaged 45.4 yards on five punts, with a long of 60 and three inside the 20.

Coach P.J. Fleck said afterward that Purdue beat us in every area, which I appreciated, because a fella who tells you the truth about a bad day is a fella you can work with.

The Season So Far

We're 4-2, 2-1 in the Big Ten. We beat Eastern Illinois 59-7 and Akron 41-7. We lost to Mississippi State, 38-13, at home in September, which we don't need to dwell on. Then we won at Washington, 27-24, and beat Michigan, 20-14, right here in Minneapolis, and the Little Brown Jug stayed home where it belongs. That was a good week. My grandpa would've had a second piece of pie.

Part 2: Iowa Comes North, and So Does the Pig

Saturday, Oct. 24, at 3:30 p.m. Eastern, No. 15 Iowa visits Huntington Bank Stadium. FS1 has it. The winner takes home Floyd of Rosedale.

Now, I'm polite, so I'll start with Iowa's good qualities. The Hawkeyes are 5-1. Their defense allows 14.5 points a game, eighth in FBS, and 84.7 rushing yards a game, seventh. Kamari Moulton ran for 208 yards against Washington in their last game. Coach Kirk Ferentz is in his 28th season, the longest-tenured head coach in FBS. Fella has outlasted a lot of snowblowers.

But here's what the Hawkeyes would rather not bring up at the dinner table. Their passing offense ranks 93rd in FBS, according to the AP, at 209.2 yards a game, and Hank Brown, their starting quarterback, missed the Washington game with an injury. They rank 104th in time of possession. Their one-point win at Michigan was nice, but we beat Michigan by six. I'm not saying that's how math works. I'm just saying I wrote it down.

And here's the matchup that matters. Our pass defense ranks ninth in the country, allowing 159.7 yards a game, and opponents convert only 30.9 of every 100 third downs against us. If Iowa can't throw, Iowa has to run into that, and a defense that's had two weeks to think about Purdue is a defense with something on its mind.

Who to Watch

Drake Lindsey, quarterback: 1,335 yards and nine touchdowns. He can throw it to anybody in the stadium, including me if I wave.

Javon Tracy, receiver: our leader with 32 catches for 375 yards.

Jalen Smith, receiver: 89 yards on three catches at Purdue. Fella turns a short pass into a long afternoon for a defense.

TJ Thomas, running back: 317 yards. We need more than 27 rushing yards this time, and he's the guy to fix it.

TJ Bush Jr.: four sacks. Maverick Baranowski: 45 tackles.

Kamari Moulton, Iowa running back: 519 yards. Our biggest job on Saturday is keeping him in front of us.

Tony Diaz, Iowa receiver: 28 catches for 329 yards.

Floyd of Rosedale: A Short Lecture (I Promise Nothing About "Short")

Floyd has been on the table since 1935. The original Floyd was a real prize pig, named for our own Minnesota governor, Floyd Olson, and his brother, Blue Boy, appeared in the Will Rogers movie "State Fair," according to Wikipedia. The bronze trophy was made by a St. Paul sculptor, Charles Brioschi, which means Floyd is, technically, a Minnesotan. We'd simply like him to come home and visit.

Officially, Minnesota leads the series 63-54-2, according to CollegeFootballDigest. Our longest streak against Iowa is 11 straight. In 1960, our No. 3 Gophers beat No. 1 Iowa 27-10 on the way to a national championship, one of seven Minnesota claims.

Now, you know I'm honest, so here's the other side. I rate every town by how it would handle January. Let's begin.

Our downtown has 9.5 miles of skyways connecting 80 blocks, so you can get your groceries in a blizzard without your mittens. Huntington Bank Stadium opened in 2009, has 50,805 seats, and was the first college or pro football stadium to earn LEED certification. January grade: A-plus. We invented being fine in January.

Iowa City. A lovely town of 74,828, the fifth-most populous city in Iowa, and UNESCO named it a City of Literature in 2008, home of the famous Writers' Workshop. I respect that. Since they have so many writers, I'm hoping one of them can help the Hawkeyes' passing game write something longer than 209 yards a game.

Their visiting locker room at Kinnick Stadium is painted pink, a tradition started by coach Hayden Fry to put visitors in a passive mood, according to Wikipedia. Folks, we don't paint your locker room pink here. We just let you sit in the weather. January grade for Iowa City: B. Good people, but they think 20 degrees is cold, and that's sweet.

Closing

Here's where I land. We got humbled at Purdue, and a humble team with an extra week of practice is a dangerous thing. We've got a top-10 pass defense, a quarterback who can throw it, and a home crowd that's been waiting two years to see the pig.

Iowa's good. Iowa's defense is very good. But Floyd's a Minnesotan, and it's about time he came home.

Cold enough for ya? Good. Ski-U-Mah.

My call: Iowa Hawkeyes 29, Minnesota Golden Gophers 18.

blocks.text: Well, hi there. Come on in, take your boots off, the rug's new. There's hotdish in the oven and a thermos of coffee by the door, and if you want to talk about rivalry trophies, I'll warn you right now: you'll be here until spring.

I'm Tor Engebretsen. I grew up in Minneapolis ice fishing with my grandpa, who taught me two things. One, never trust ice you haven't checked. Two, the Little Brown Jug is a five-gallon earthenware jug, and anybody who calls it a "pitcher" can see themselves out.
This week, though, it's not the Jug. It's the pig. Ski-U-Mah.
Part 1: The Purdue Game, Which We Will Discuss Politely
I'm a Minnesotan, so I'm going to describe our last game in the most polite way I know how. It was not ideal.

On Oct. 10, at Ross-Ade Stadium, Purdue beat us 41-13. We had last week off, and I spent most of it shoveling a driveway that didn't have any snow on it yet, just to have something to do with my hands.

Here's the honest version. Purdue led 20-3 at halftime and scored on all six of its red-zone trips, according to the AP. We ran the ball 13 times for 27 yards. The Boilermakers ran it 47 times for 305. Their running back, Fame Ijeboi, ran for 195 yards and three touchdowns, and, ope, he used to play for us. That one stung a little, like a January wind off the lake. I wish him well. Mostly.

The bright spots, and there were a few: Drake Lindsey threw for 248 yards, including a 42-yard touchdown to Jalen Smith in the third quarter that cut it to 27-13. Smith had three catches for 89 yards. Javon Tracy caught five for 75. Luke Drzewiecki made field goals from 49 and 37 yards. Maverick Baranowski made 11 tackles, and Tom Weston averaged 45.4 yards on five punts, with a long of 60 and three inside the 20.
Coach P.J. Fleck said afterward that Purdue beat us in every area, which I appreciated, because a fella who tells you the truth about a bad day is a fella you can work with.

We're 4-2, 2-1 in the Big Ten. We beat Eastern Illinois 59-7 and Akron 41-7. We lost to Mississippi State, 38-13, at home in September, which we don't need to dwell on. Then we won at Washington, 27-24, and beat Michigan, 20-14, right here in Minneapolis, and the Little Brown Jug stayed home where it belongs. That was a good week. My grandpa would've had a second piece of pie.
