articles.title: Go Big Red, and Bring an Umbrella: The Huskers Came Up 28 Seconds Short in Eugene, Rest Up This Week, and Welcome the Other Huskies to a Sold-Out Lincoln
articles.byline: Darla Rasmussen, The Nebraska Fanatic
articles.matchup: Nebraska (5-2): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Washington (4-3) at Nebraska, Sat., Oct. 31, Memorial Stadium, Lincoln
articles.text:
Before we start, I have to mention it. You know I do.

Memorial Stadium has sold out every home game since 1962. It's an NCAA record for any sport, according to Wikipedia. My grandpa saw the early years of it. My daddy saw the middle of it. I've seen the rest, from the student section, from the volleyball bleachers next door and from the cab of a combine with the radio turned all the way up. That streak is the most Nebraska thing in the world: you show up, you fill the seats and you never stop.

Which is exactly what our defense did in Eugene on Saturday night. It just ran out of seconds.

I'm Darla Rasmussen. I grew up on a farm out past Seward, I played volleyball, and I have never once lost an argument at a family reunion. Go Big Red. Let's do this.

Part 1: Twenty-Eight Seconds

Oregon 17, Nebraska 14. Saturday night, Oct. 17, at Autzen Stadium.

Folks, I'm going to tell you about one of the finest defensive games I've seen from a Husker team, and then I'm going to tell you how it ended, and I'd appreciate it if you held my hand for the second part.

For a half, nobody could score. The two teams punted 13 times before the break. Then with four seconds left in the second quarter, Anthony Colandrea found Kwazi Gilmer in the back corner of the end zone for a 17-yard touchdown. 7-0, Huskers.

Oregon kicked two field goals in the third, and then, with seven seconds left in the quarter, Colandrea scrambled six yards and dove for the pylon. 14-6. Oregon's offense had 91 yards, the AP noted, when the Ducks went to the bench for a new quarterback.

That's where the story turns, and I'll tell it straight. Dylan Raiola, who played his first two seasons at Nebraska before transferring to Oregon this year, came in for the fourth quarter. His first drive ended in a field goal. 14-9. One Oregon drive got a boost when our punter took a low snap and accidentally put his knee down. Then, on the final drive, Raiola threw what looked like a touchdown with 33 seconds left, but replay overturned it. Our hearts started beating again. And then, with 28 seconds left, he found Jamari Johnson in the back of the end zone, and the two-point conversion was good. 17-14.

I sat in my truck for a long time after that one. Then I went and checked on the cattle, because the cattle don't care about the score, and sometimes that helps.

The Stat Sheet

Here's what I want everyone to remember. Our defense held Oregon to 242 yards. The Ducks converted 3 of 17 third downs. Owen Chambliss made 15 tackles, Dwayne McDougle III had 13 and an interception, and Caleb Benning had 12 with 2.5 tackles for loss. Coach Matt Rhule called it one of the finest defensive performances he's been around, considering the short fields, and I'd sell out a stadium to watch it again.

Colandrea completed 18 of 33 for 164 yards and the touchdown and ran for another. Gilmer caught six passes for 74 yards.

The hard truth, though: we ran for 78 yards, and this is the second straight week we let a fourth-quarter lead get away. Indiana beat us 20-17 in Lincoln the week before.

The Season So Far

We're 5-2 and 2-2 in the Big Ten. We started 5-0, beating Ohio, Bowling Green and North Dakota, then winning at Michigan State 31-13 and beating Maryland 48-23. Our two losses are by three points each, to the defending national champion and on the road to Oregon. We score 35.6 points a game and allow 15.4. That's a good football team that's a few seconds from 7-0.

Part 2: A Week Off, Then the Other Huskies

Nebraska has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. No game. A week to heal up, get the run game sorted out and let a pretty devastated locker room, in Rhule's words per the AP, breathe for a minute.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, Washington comes to Memorial Stadium in Lincoln. Kickoff time hasn't been announced as I write this. Halloween in Lincoln, and yes, it'll be sold out. I checked. I always check.

Now, Washington's a respectable program, and I'll say so. The Huskies won 38-26 at Purdue on Friday night to snap a three-game losing streak. Elijah Brown threw for 302 yards and three touchdowns in his first start for them, and Trey Cooley broke a 53-yard touchdown run. Jedd Fisch's teams play hard.

But let me sell out this argument.

Washington threw three interceptions and lost two fumbles at Purdue. Five turnovers. Their own coach said you're not usually minus-4 in the turnover battle and win. Folks, you don't usually win that way in Lincoln, either. Ask anybody since 1962.

The Huskies are 4-3 and 1-3 in the Big Ten. They lost at home to Minnesota 27-24 and to Iowa 41-24, and they lost at USC 25-21. They allow 131.1 rushing yards a game. Our defense allows 99.6. They score 27.9 points a game. We score 35.6.

Who to Watch

Anthony Colandrea, quarterback: 1,570 yards, 14 touchdowns and four interceptions this season.

Kwazi Gilmer, receiver: 38 catches for 492 yards and seven touchdowns, our leader.

Jamal Rule, running back: 391 yards and five touchdowns on 60 carries. We need him rolling against a defense that allows 131 yards a game on the ground.

Owen Chambliss: 46 tackles, our leader. Jahsear Whittington: 3.5 sacks.

Demond Williams Jr., Washington quarterback: 1,396 yards and eight touchdowns this season, though Brown made the start Friday.

Dezmen Roebuck, Washington receiver: 48 catches for 484 yards and three touchdowns.

Series History

Nebraska leads the all-time series 5-4-1, according to Washington's athletics site, and we won the last meeting, 51-38 in Lincoln back in 2011. That's 15 years, folks. In that time, we've sold out every single home game. Just saying.

Town Talk: A Tale of Two Towns

Lincoln. The 2020 census counted 291,082 people here, and on a home Saturday, Memorial Stadium fills all 85,458 of its listed seats. The Nebraska State Capitol, finished in 1932, is the second-tallest capitol in the country. Runza started here, too, and if you've never had one, you haven't really been to Nebraska. Since 1994, our team has taken the field with the Tunnel Walk, and the whole stadium does the "Husker Power" chant, half the crowd on each word. When we score our first points, the stands let loose a sky full of red balloons. And the band plays the visiting team's fight song before every home game, and the announcer welcomes "our friends" from the other school. We're polite like that. Right up until kickoff.

Seattle. Seattle is a beautiful city, I'll give it that. The Space Needle, the mountains and Pike Place, where the first Starbucks opened in 1971. But Wikipedia says Seattle has many more rain days than other major American cities and a well-earned reputation for frequent rain. Friends, I'm a farm girl. I pray for rain. Seattle doesn't have to. Seattle has so much rain it opened a coffee shop on every corner just to keep everyone awake through it.

And they're very proud that Husky Stadium is the loudest college football stadium ever recorded, and that fans can sail their boats to the game. That's lovely. But on Oct. 31, the Huskies are coming to Lincoln. No boats. No lake. Just 85,000 people in red, a sky full of balloons and a sellout streak older than most of Washington's coaching staff. Bring an umbrella, Huskies. It's going to be raining red.

Final Word

I'll tell you how I see it. We lost two games by a combined six points to two very good teams. We've got a defense that just held Oregon to 242 yards, a week of rest and a home crowd that has shown up for every game since 1962. Washington turned the ball over five times last week and won. It won't get away with that in Lincoln.

Go Big Red!

articles.title: Footnote: I Was Right. The Wildcats Kicked Their Way Out of East Lansing, and Now the Birthplace of College Football Visits the Newest Stadium in the Big Ten
articles.byline: Ezra Lindqvist, The Northwestern Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 24 Northwestern (5-1) vs. Rutgers (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. EDT, Ryan Field, Evanston (Peacock)
articles.text:
Let me begin with a correction, because I'm a journalist and corrections are a sacred duty.

Last week I wrote, in my notebook, that Northwestern would win at Michigan State by double digits. Northwestern won by three, on a field goal with two seconds left. My prediction was therefore incorrect in its margin but correct in its conclusion, which, as any data journalist will tell you, is the most satisfying kind of wrong.

(Footnote: I was right.)

(Footnote to the footnote: mostly.)

I'm Ezra Lindqvist. I studied the craft a short walk from Lake Michigan, and I fact-check coaches in real time from the stands. My seatmates have asked me to stop. I have declined. Let's report.

Part 1: The Kicker Files

Northwestern 24, Michigan State 21, Saturday, Oct. 17, at Spartan Stadium.

The lede writes itself: Jackson Kleather kicked three field goals, including a 34-yarder with two seconds left, and No. 25 Northwestern rallied from eight points down in the fourth quarter to win on the road.

But the story, as always, is in the details. Kleather opened the scoring with a 39-yarder. Michigan State answered with a 3-yard quarterback run on fourth-and-1. Caleb Komolafe ran 10 yards for a touchdown to give us a 10-7 lead, and then the Spartans blocked a Kleather field goal and scored with 47 seconds left in the half. 14-10. Kleather's 37-yarder in the third made it 14-13, and then Michigan State hit a 53-yard touchdown pass early in the fourth. 21-13.

Here's where our quarterback, Aidan Chiles, took over. Chiles, who started 20 games for Michigan State the previous two seasons before transferring here, ran in from a yard out with 7:24 left, then threw the two-point conversion to Alex Honig. 21-21.

And then the play that deserves its own front page: Matthew Smith blocked a 33-yard Michigan State field goal attempt. Chiles drove us 64 yards in eight plays, and Kleather did the rest.

(Footnote: The AP reports Chiles is one of four former Michigan State quarterbacks starting elsewhere this season and the third to face the Spartans. I have no further comment. I just think it's interesting.)

The Data Desk

Chiles completed 18 of 27 passes for 226 yards with no interceptions and ran for the tying touchdown. Komolafe ran 15 times for 67 yards and caught four passes for 51. Griffin Wilde caught six for 57. We didn't turn the ball over and held it for 34:55.

On defense, Braydon Brus made 15 tackles and Jon Jon Stevens Jr. had 10. The honest note: Michigan State sacked Chiles five times, and we ran for 3.2 yards a carry. A journalist reports the unflattering quotes, too.

Season Coverage

We're 5-1 and 2-1 in the Big Ten, and the AP poll has us at No. 24. We beat South Dakota State and Colorado at our temporary lakefront stadium, lost 29-23 at Indiana, then beat Penn State 34-13 on Oct. 2 in the very first game at our brand-new Ryan Field. We followed that with a 45-14 win over Ball State and Saturday's escape. Chiles has 1,398 passing yards with nine touchdowns and, I'll repeat it, zero interceptions. We score 33.5 points a game and allow 17.

Part 2: Rutgers Comes to Evanston

Saturday, Oct. 24, at noon Eastern, Rutgers visits Ryan Field. Peacock has it.

I'll report fairly, because fairness is the first rule of the newsroom. Rutgers won 37-30 at Maryland last Saturday, coming back from 23-13 down at halftime and scoring 24 straight points. Dylan Lonergan threw for 291 yards and three touchdowns, KJ Duff caught nine passes for 113 yards and two scores, and Clay Thevenin ran for 109 yards. Duff has 741 receiving yards and nine touchdowns this season, and he's the most dangerous player on the field this weekend not wearing purple. Rutgers also commits fewer penalty yards than anyone in FBS, 28.7 a game, according to the AP. That's a disciplined team.

And now, the fact-finding portion.

Rutgers is 2-4. It opened the season with a 37-21 home loss to UMass. (Footnote: I verified this twice. It remains true.) It lost at Boston College, at home to USC and at home to Indiana, 47-15. Per the AP preview, the Scarlet Knights' defense allows 31.8 points a game, 119th in FBS, and 185.2 rushing yards a game, 118th. Their turnover margin is minus-5, 122nd. Ours is plus-7, eighth. And our red-zone offense ranks fourth in FBS, scoring on 96.4 of every 100 trips.

When a newsroom sees numbers like that, it doesn't call them a trend. It calls them a story.

Who to Watch

Aidan Chiles, quarterback: 1,398 yards, nine touchdowns, no interceptions, 70.5 completions for every 100 throws.

Caleb Komolafe, running back: 401 yards and four touchdowns. Rutgers allows 185 rushing yards a game. I expect a feature-length story.

Griffin Wilde, receiver: 30 catches for 482 yards, our leader.

Braydon Brus, linebacker: 52 tackles and three sacks, our leader in both.

Jackson Kleather, kicker: three field goals and the game-winner. Give the young man a byline.

KJ Duff, Rutgers receiver: 42 catches, 741 yards, nine touchdowns. Our pass defense allows 230.5 yards a game, so this is the matchup to watch.

The Archives

Rutgers leads the all-time series 4-2, according to both schools' records and Sports-Reference, and won the last meeting, 24-7 in Piscataway in 2023. The first meeting was on Thanksgiving Day 1919. I like to think somebody fact-checked it.

Dateline: A Tale of Two Towns

Evanston. Population 78,110 at the 2020 census, sitting on Lake Michigan 12 miles north of the Loop. Our campus spans 240 acres on the lakefront, and the Medill School of Journalism, founded in 1921, counts 40 Pulitzer Prizes among its alumni. Our new Ryan Field holds 35,000, the smallest stadium in the Big Ten. (Footnote: We prefer "most exclusive.") It eliminated the nosebleed seats entirely, so every fan in the building is close enough to hear the quarterback's cadence. Its opening was delayed about three weeks by construction, and when it finally opened, we beat Penn State by 21. Worth the wait.

New Brunswick and Piscataway, New Jersey. I'll begin with a sincere compliment. Rutgers played in the first college football game in history, on Nov. 6, 1869, against Princeton, and won 6-4. Every one of us owes them for that.

But, as a journalist, I'm obligated to follow up. That was 157 years ago. Since then, Rutgers has spent a great deal of time telling people about it. (Footnote: In fairness, if I'd invented college football, I'd mention it, too. Constantly. At dinner parties.) The Scarlet Knights invented the sport, then lost to UMass in the 2026 season opener. That's like inventing the printing press and misspelling your own name on the first page.

New Brunswick is known as the Hub City for its medical facilities, which is useful, since its defense allows 185 rushing yards a game. And Rutgers fans give directions by New Jersey Turnpike exit. The famous one, Exit 9, is technically just outside New Brunswick, in East Brunswick, per Wikipedia. (Footnote: Fact-checked. You're welcome, New Jersey.)

The Closing Paragraph

Here's my reporting, and I stand by it. We're 5-1, ranked, at home in a building we've won in by 21 and 31 points, with a quarterback who hasn't thrown an interception all season and a red-zone offense that scores 96 of every 100 times. Rutgers is coming off a nice comeback, but it gives up 31.8 points a game and is minus-5 in turnovers.

(Footnote: I was right.)

Go 'Cats.

My call: Northwestern Wildcats 37, Rutgers Scarlet Knights 19.

articles.title: Out by a Toe: The Buckeyes Survived Bloomington, Are Praying for Their Quarterback, and Now Get a Bye Week Before a Trip to Hollywood
articles.byline: Brecken 'Buck' Holloway, The Ohio State Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 3 Ohio State (6-1): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Ohio State at No. 16 USC (6-1), Sat., Oct. 31, Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum
articles.text:
I want to talk about a left foot.

Not mine. Mine is busy. I'm Buck Holloway, former scout-team receiver, and I still run a deep post down the press box hallway every Saturday because the muscle memory never leaves you. My left foot has run that route a thousand times, and it has never, not once, landed on the white paint.

Nick Marsh's left foot did. With 1:02 left in Bloomington. And that, friends, is why the Buckeyes are 6-1.

Let's go to the film. Real receipts, like always.

Part 1: Survival in Bloomington

Ohio State 19, Indiana 15. Saturday, Oct. 17, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington. The first top-five game ever played there, according to the AP.

Let me give you the stakes. Last December, Indiana beat us in the Big Ten title game, then went on to win the national championship, and we heard about it all offseason. The defending champs came in on a 22-game winning streak overall and 19 straight at home, the two longest active streaks in FBS. And we hadn't beaten a top-10 team in our last three tries.

Connor Hawkins opened the scoring with a 26-yard field goal. Turbo Richard answered with a 7-yard touchdown run, and then, with seven seconds left in the half, Julian Sayin hit Bo Jackson for a 2-yard touchdown pass. Yes, our running back is named Bo Jackson. Yes, I check the roster every week to make sure it's still true. 10-7 at the half. Hawkins added a 29-yarder in the third.

Then early in the fourth, on fourth-and-1, Sayin went deep to Jeremiah Smith for a 38-yard touchdown. Fourth-and-1. Deep shot. That's a Columbus problem for every defense in America. 19-7.

But Indiana's a real team, so here came Josh Hoover, back from his own arm injury, leading a 75-yard drive capped by a 19-yard touchdown pass to Marsh and a two-point conversion. 19-15 with 10:30 left.

And then the drive that took ten years off my life. Hoover got the ball back and moved Indiana into scoring range, and with 1:02 left, Marsh was wide open, sprinting for the front corner of the end zone. He caught it. Fireworks went off. And his left foot was on the white paint.

Out of bounds. We ran out the clock.

The Receipts

Now the honest part, and it's a tough one. Sayin injured his right arm in the fourth quarter, and coach Ryan Day said it looks like he'll miss several weeks. Before he left, Sayin completed 15 of 29 passes for 235 yards with the two touchdowns and two interceptions, the second straight week he threw two. Freshman Luke Fahey finished the game.

Smith caught four passes for 68 yards and that touchdown. Bo Jackson ran 18 times for 56. We only ran for 78 yards as a team, which is not who we are. On defense, Earl Little Jr. led us with eight tackles, and we recovered two Indiana fumbles early in the third quarter. The AP noted Indiana hadn't lost a fumble in 1,487 snaps going back to the 2025 opener. That's a stat I'm framing.

The Season Card

We're 6-1 and 4-0 in the Big Ten. Our only loss was 24-23 at Texas in September. We beat Illinois 42-19, won at Iowa 31-14 and beat Maryland 45-16. We score 39.3 points a game and allow 13.4. The AP poll has us at No. 3.

Part 2: The Bye, Then Hollywood

Ohio State has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. Day called it a bye week to put our heads together and figure things out at quarterback, and I've never been happier to see a blank Saturday on a calendar.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, we go to the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum to play No. 16 USC. Kickoff time hasn't been announced as I write this.

I'll be respectful first, because USC has earned it. The Trojans are 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big Ten. Jayden Maiava has thrown for 2,045 yards with 18 touchdowns and three interceptions. They score 36.4 a game. They won at Penn State 31-23 their last time out, and they're coming off their own bye before playing at Wisconsin this Saturday.

Now the film, because I bring receipts. USC allows 25.1 points a game. We allow 13.4. USC gives up 350 yards a game. We give up 264.3. The Trojans lost 41-27 at home to Oregon, and they've won games against Washington and Rutgers by four and by seven. And they get Wisconsin on the road the week before they see us, while we get a week of rest. I'm not saying that's an advantage. I'm saying I'd take it.

Who to Watch

Jeremiah Smith, receiver: 52 catches, 984 yards and 12 touchdowns in seven games. Whoever's throwing to him, the plan is the same. Throw it up. He'll go get it.

Luke Fahey, freshman quarterback: if Sayin is out, this is his moment. He'll have two weeks of practice and the best receiver in the country. Run your routes, young man.

Bo Jackson: 516 rushing yards and four touchdowns. Best name in the sport.

Earl Little Jr.: our leading tackler, with 38. Kenyatta Jackson Jr.: three sacks, our leader.

Jayden Maiava, USC quarterback: 18 touchdowns, three interceptions. Our secondary has two weeks to prepare for him.

King Miller, USC running back: 595 yards and four touchdowns. Our defense allows 92.9 rushing yards a game.

Series History

Honest receipts: CollegeFootballData.com has USC ahead in the series, 13-10-1. The last meeting was the Cotton Bowl after the 2017 season, which we won 24-7. Somebody tell the Coliseum it's been a while.

Town Report: Cowtown vs. Tinseltown

Columbus. The 2020 census counted 905,748 people here, making Columbus the 14th-most populous city in the country and the second-biggest in the Midwest, behind only Chicago. Our nicknames include "Arch City," for the wooden arches that once spanned High Street, and "The Biggest Small Town in America," which is exactly right. Ohio Stadium opened in 1922, and folks call it the Horseshoe, the Shoe, or the House That Harley Built. Since Oct. 10, 1936, our band has performed Script Ohio, and the moment a fourth- or fifth-year sousaphone player high-steps to the top and dots the "i" is the greatest 15 seconds in college sports. Ohio State claims nine national championships and has had seven Heisman winners, including Archie Griffin, the only two-time winner ever.

Los Angeles. Now, I like Los Angeles. Nice weather. Beaches. But here's a film receipt from Wikipedia: Los Angeles drivers spend an extra 92 hours a year in traffic, according to TomTom, and the area's roads were once ranked the most congested in the country. Friends, 92 hours. That's longer than our bye week. That's longer than a full season of game film. Our team bus will need a GPS, a snack bag and a prayer to make kickoff.

The Coliseum is gorgeous, I'll give them that. It hosted the 1932 and 1984 Olympics, and in 2028 it'll be the first stadium to host the Summer Games three times. Three Olympics. Lots of gold medals handed out in that building. On Oct. 31, it's hosting one more event where somebody from Ohio takes home the hardware.

And their mascot, Traveler, a white horse, has been galloping around the Coliseum since 1961. Traveler's a beautiful animal. But friends, I've watched LA traffic numbers, and that horse is the only thing in Los Angeles that gets anywhere on time.

Final Route

Here's the final word. We survived a top-five road game by a toe. We lost our starting quarterback, but we've got two weeks, the best receiver in the country, a defense allowing 13.4 points a game and a backup who just got his first taste of a big stage. Hollywood loves a story about the young understudy who gets the lead role. I've seen that movie. I like the ending.

That's a Columbus problem. O-H!

articles.title: Uniform of the Week? Ten Out of Ten. Offense of the Week? Let's Talk. The Ducks Stole One From Nebraska With 28 Seconds Left, and Now It's Off to the Prairie
articles.byline: Phoenix 'Nix' Wyatt-Aldana, The Oregon Fanatic
articles.matchup: Oregon (4-2) at Illinois (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3 p.m. EDT, Gies Memorial Stadium, Champaign (BTN)
articles.text:
Hi, hello, welcome to the runway.

I'm Nix Wyatt-Aldana. I design sneakers and uniforms here in Eugene, and I review jerseys and route trees with exactly the same ferocity. I've followed the Ducks to every game this season from the stands, and before I say one word about football, I rate the uniforms. It's the law. My law. In my house.

So, let's start with the scoreboard, because that's the one accessory that always matches: Oregon 17, Nebraska 14. We're 4-2. And, darling, we earned every stitch of it.

Part 1: Nebraska, a Thriller in Three Acts

Saturday night, Oct. 17, at Autzen Stadium. Oregon 17, Nebraska 14.

I'm going to be honest with you, because honesty is the foundation of good tailoring. For three quarters, our offense was a sweater with one sleeve. The Ducks had 91 yards, according to the AP, when coach Dan Lanning made a change at quarterback. Brock Thomas, our third-stringer, made the start, and he gave it everything. Dante Moore, our starter, is still out with a concussion from the USC game on Sept. 26. Healing vibes, always.

Nebraska led 7-0 at halftime on a touchdown pass with four seconds left in the half. Gage Hurych kicked field goals of 36 and 36 yards in the third quarter, and it was 7-6. Then Nebraska's quarterback scrambled six yards and dove for the pylon with seven seconds left in the quarter. 14-6. I set down my sketchbook. I picked it back up. I'm a professional.

Then: costume change. Dylan Raiola came off the bench in the fourth quarter. His first drive ended in a 37-yard field goal from Hurych. 14-9. His last drive was couture. He found Dakorien Moore for what looked like a 4-yard touchdown with 33 seconds left, and it was overturned on review. So he threw another one, to Jamari Johnson, in the back of the end zone, from four yards out, with 28 seconds left. Then Raiola threw the two-point conversion to Hudson Lewis. 17-14.

Raiola, by the way, played two seasons for Nebraska before he came to Eugene. You can't write that. Well, you can. I just did.

The Look Book

Raiola completed 11 of 18 for 59 yards and the winning touchdown in the fourth quarter. Moore caught seven passes. Dierre Hill Jr. ran for 67 yards on 14 carries. Hurych made all three field goals. And our defense held Nebraska to 78 rushing yards, 2.4 a carry, and 242 yards overall. We went 3 for 3 on fourth down, and we committed four penalties for 35 yards. Very tailored.

The Season So Far

We're 4-2 and 2-1 in the Big Ten. We beat Boise State 34-27, Portland State 84-0, and won 41-27 at USC. We lost at Oklahoma State, 39-31, and lost 17-15 to UCLA at home, which I've moved to the clearance rack and don't wish to discuss. Our defense allows 20.7 points a game, and it ranks third in FBS on third down, holding opponents to 25.9 conversions for every 100 tries, per the AP.

Part 2: Off to Champaign

Saturday, Oct. 24, at 3 p.m. Eastern, which is noon back home, the Ducks visit Illinois at Gies Memorial Stadium. BTN has it.

First, the respect, because a good designer always credits the inspiration. Illinois is 3-3, 1-2 in the Big Ten, and won 38-37 in overtime at Michigan State two weeks ago. Receiver Collin Dixon has 47 catches for 608 yards and nine touchdowns, and that's a stat sheet worth framing. Coach Bret Bielema's teams play hard, and the Illini commit just 38.8 penalty yards a game, ninth-best in FBS. Their starting quarterback, Katin Houser, broke a bone in his hand in that Michigan State game, and I hope he's back soon.

Now, the honest fit check. Illinois' red-zone defense ranks 137th in FBS, according to the AP. Opponents have scored on every single trip inside the 20. Every one. And Illinois' pass defense ranks 114th, allowing 248.3 yards a game. Meanwhile, our red-zone offense ranks 20th, scoring 92.9 of every 100 times, and Matayo Uiagalelei has six sacks.

So the plan is simple, darling. Get to the red zone. Accessorize.

Who to Watch

Dylan Raiola, quarterback: the fourth-quarter comeback against his old team. Main character energy.

Jordon Davison, running back: 330 yards and six touchdowns.

Evan Stewart, receiver: our leader with 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns.

Dakorien Moore and Jamari Johnson, receivers: seven catches for Moore, the game-winner for Johnson.

Matayo Uiagalelei, defensive end: six sacks. Stylish and disruptive.

Koi Perich, defensive back: 40 tackles, our leader.

Collin Dixon, Illinois receiver: nine touchdowns. Guard him like a garment bag in the rain.

Archive Collection

Oregon leads the series 3-1 and has won three straight, according to CollegeFootballDigest. The last meeting was 38-9 at Autzen in 2024, when the Ducks were No. 1. Illinois' only win came in Champaign in 1970, 20-16. The Ducks also won the other trip to Champaign, 13-7, in 1993.

The Runway: Two Towns

Eugene. Population 176,654, and the town calls itself "Track Town, USA." Nike got its start here, founded by Oregon runner Phil Knight and his coach, Bill Bowerman, and Nike has outfitted the Ducks since 1995. That's why our uniforms change practically every week, with new looks coordinated by Tinker Hatfield, an Oregon alum and a Nike executive, according to Wikipedia. Hayward Field, rebuilt from 2018 to 2020, hosted the 2022 World Athletics Championships, the first ever held in the United States. And Autzen Stadium, opened in 1967, seats 54,000 and plays "Shout" at the end of the third quarter while everyone dances. Uniform of the week? Ten out of ten. Every week.

Champaign. Champaign is a lovely city of 88,302 in the middle of the prairie, and Memorial Stadium, completed in 1923, is gorgeous: 200 columns, 183 of them carrying the name of an Illinois alum who died in World War I. That's architecture with a soul. Serious respect. There's also a 12-foot statue of Red Grange outside, dedicated in 2009, honoring the man who once scored five touchdowns in a single game there. A statue is the ultimate permanent collection, and I'd love to see one of a Duck someday, ideally in a reflective finish.

But I have a fashion note. On the Illinois campus, the undergraduate library was built underground so it wouldn't cast shadows on the Morrow Plots, the oldest continuously used experimental cornfields in the country, according to Wikipedia. Darling, they built the library in the basement for the corn. I love that for the corn. In Eugene, we'd have designed the corn a capsule collection.

And the Illini's colors are orange and blue. Classic. Timeless. You know what else is timeless? Wearing the same thing every Saturday. In Eugene, we call that a rough week. A tip of my hat to Illinois for owning its look, though. Consistency is a choice.

Closing

Here's my final fit. Our defense is elite on third down. Our quarterback just led a comeback against his old school. Illinois has a terrific receiver and a red-zone defense that hasn't kept anyone out. We'll need a cleaner first half than last week, and the offense knows it.

Pack the good jacket, Ducks. It's the prairie in late October.

Uniform of the week? Ten out of ten. Go Ducks.

My call: Oregon Ducks 34, Illinois Fighting Illini 24.

articles.title: One Scoop at a Time: The Lions Fell Short in the Big House, Get a Week to Regroup, and Then the Boilermakers Come to Happy Valley
articles.byline: Luann Kessler, The Penn State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Penn State (3-4): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Purdue (3-4) at Penn State, Sat., Oct. 31, Beaver Stadium, University Park
articles.text:
Hi, friends. Luann here.

I grew up on a dairy farm in Centre County, I set for the volleyball team back in the day, and I love exactly two things with my whole heart: Creamery ice cream and Penn State linebackers. Sometimes in that order. Sometimes not.

So here's where we are. My Lions are 3-4 and 0-4 in the Big Ten, and we've lost four in a row. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Sugarcoating is for ice cream, and even then the Creamery doesn't need it. But I'm also not going to sulk, because my mama raised me to milk the cows whether it's sunny or sleeting. You show up.

We Are... correct. Let's go.

Part 1: So Close in Ann Arbor

Michigan 21, Penn State 18, Saturday, Oct. 17, at Michigan Stadium, in front of 110,731 people.

Let me start with the good news, because there was plenty. For a half, our defense had Michigan's offense stuck in the mud like a tractor in April. We led 3-0 at halftime on Ryan Barker's 24-yard field goal, and Josiah Zayas and Zion Tracy each intercepted Bryce Underwood in the second quarter. Michigan was so frustrated that it benched its quarterback at halftime.

That's where the story turned. Tommy Carr came in, and Michigan scored twice in the third quarter: a 43-yard touchdown run by Bryson Kuzdzal and a 1-yard run by Jordan Marshall, set up by Carr's 22-yard draw. 14-3.

But we came back, friends. Early in the fourth, Carson Hansen scored from 2 yards, and Rocco Becht threw the two-point conversion to Benjamin Brahmer. 14-11. We had the ball with a chance to tie or take the lead, and then Becht lost a fumble at our own 16, and Carr scored from 12 yards out three plays later. Becht came right back and threw a 24-yard touchdown to Chase Sowell with 1:11 left, but Michigan recovered the onside kick.

Three points. Again.

The Good Stuff

Chase Sowell was spectacular: 11 catches for 151 yards and that touchdown. Becht completed 28 of 44 passes for 267 yards. Tony Rojas, a true Linebacker U linebacker, made 12 tackles with a sack and two tackles for loss. Michigan threw for just 90 yards all day.

The hard stuff: we ran 30 times for 65 yards, and we turned it over three times. Becht said afterward that the game is super humbling, per the AP. Spoken like a young man raised right.

The Ice Cream Rankings

I rank every defense by Creamery flavor. Our defense this year? It's Peachy Paterno. Sweet, steady, and a little underrated. We allow 18.9 points a game, and opponents throw for just 141.3 yards a game against us. The trouble is the other side of the menu. We've lost to Wisconsin 24-20, at Northwestern 34-13, to USC 31-23 and at Michigan 21-18. Three of those four were one-score games. That's not a bad team, friends. That's a team one scoop short.

Part 2: A Week Off, Then Purdue

Penn State has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. No game. The boys get a week to heal, regroup and remember who they are, and coach Matt Campbell, in his first year here after coming over from Iowa State, gets a week to fix the run game. Campbell said after Saturday that he believes this group is pounding away, and I believe him.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, Purdue comes to Beaver Stadium. Kickoff time hasn't been announced. Halloween in Happy Valley, friends. I'll be dressed as a cone of Death by Chocolate. Fitting for the Boilermakers' afternoon, I hope.

Now, Purdue deserves respect. It's 3-4 and 2-2 in the Big Ten, and it's won at Illinois 24-17 and beaten Minnesota 41-13. Ryan Browne has thrown for 1,822 yards. Fame Ijeboi has 568 rushing yards and nine touchdowns. Purdue scores 31.3 points a game. Barry Odom is a good coach.

But let me tell you about Purdue's Friday night against Washington. Purdue forced five turnovers, three interceptions and two fumbles, and the Huskies' quarterback was making his first start. Washington's own coach, Jedd Fisch, said you're not usually minus-4 in the turnover battle and win. Well, Washington won 38-26. Friends, if a farmer gets five free cows and still ends up with fewer cows, somebody has to look at the fence.

And Purdue's defense allows 32.3 points a game and 161.6 rushing yards a game. Ijeboi ran for 19 yards on 13 carries against Washington. Odom himself said Washington's defensive front won the day. Well, we've got Tony Rojas and a week of rest.

Purdue's Ice Cream Flavor

Purdue's defense, in the Luann Kessler Creamery Rankings, is Vanilla With a Hole in the Bottom of the Cone. It looks fine, it tastes fine, and then it's all over your shoes.

Who to Watch

Chase Sowell, receiver: 34 catches, 510 yards, three touchdowns, and coming off his best day.

Rocco Becht, quarterback: 1,664 yards, 12 touchdowns, five interceptions.

Tony Rojas, linebacker: 55 tackles and five sacks, our leader in both. Linebacker U, friends.

Carson Hansen, running back: 278 yards and four touchdowns.

Fame Ijeboi, Purdue running back: 568 yards, nine touchdowns, and our run defense needs to tighten up, because we allow 172.3 rushing yards a game.

Asaad Waseem, Purdue receiver: 38 catches for 588 yards, and nine for 116 against Washington.

The History

Penn State leads the series 17-3-1, according to CollegeFootballData.com, and has won the last six meetings, including 49-10 in 2024. I won't call it a streak. I'll call it a family tradition.

Town Report: A Tale of Two Towns

State College. The largest borough in Pennsylvania, with 40,501 people at the 2020 census, and the heart of Happy Valley. The name goes back to the Great Depression, when the area held up so well economically that folks started calling it happy. Beaver Stadium seats 106,572, the second-largest stadium in the Western Hemisphere. And then there's the Berkey Creamery, founded in 1865 and the largest university creamery in the country, making more than 100 flavors and selling about 750,000 hand-dipped cones a year. Creamery ice cream has been part of football weekends since 1896. There's one rule: no mixing flavors in one cone. I'm told a former president once got an exception, and then didn't the next time. That's the Creamery for you. Rules are rules, even for presidents.

West Lafayette. Now, West Lafayette is a sweet little town of 44,595 on the Wabash River. And Purdue has a wonderful claim to fame. Twenty-seven of its graduates have become astronauts, including Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and Eugene Cernan, the last. They call it the Cradle of Astronauts.

Friends, I love that for them. I do. But I'd point out that 27 Purdue graduates have left the planet, and on Saturday, Purdue's defense let a first-time starting quarterback leave West Lafayette with 302 passing yards. Purdue seems to be very good at helping folks go places.

Their mascot is a train, the Boilermaker Special, and their marching band has the "World's Largest Drum," built back in 1921. That's a big drum, and it makes a big noise. But on Halloween, in a stadium with 106,572 people in it, I'm not sure anyone in Beaver Stadium will hear it.

Final Scoop

Here's how I see it. Our team has lost four straight, but three of those losses came by a single score, our pass defense is one of the best in the country, and we get a week of rest at home before Purdue comes in. Purdue just lost a game where it won the turnover battle by four.

One scoop at a time, friends. We Are... correct. And Penn State!

articles.title: Engineer It: Five Takeaways Weren't Enough Against Washington, so the Boilermakers Head Back to the Drafting Table Before a Halloween Trip to Happy Valley
articles.byline: Barnaby Wolcott-Reese, The Purdue Fanatic
articles.matchup: Purdue (3-4): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Purdue at Penn State (3-4), Sat., Oct. 31, Beaver Stadium, University Park
articles.text:
Ding-ding.

That's my tiny train bell. I ring it every time Purdue scores, and on Friday night against Washington, I rang it for three touchdowns, plus a couple of happy dings for field goals. I also rang it once by accident when I knocked it off my desk reaching for an eraser, which is how you know it was a long night.

I'm Barnaby Wolcott-Reese. I studied mechanical engineering, I draw every Purdue play on graph paper, and I keep the sheets in a binder labeled by week. Week 7 is now a very thick binder. It's thick because I drew the same play over and over, trying to figure out how you force five turnovers and lose by 12.

Engineer it. Let's open the binder.

Part 1: The Stress Test

Washington 38, Purdue 26, Friday night, Oct. 16, at Ross-Ade Stadium.

Here's the design brief. Washington came in on a three-game losing streak, with Elijah Brown making his first start for the Huskies after transferring from Stanford. And on the very first play from scrimmage, we intercepted him. Ding. Okay, no ding, that's not a score. But it felt like one.

We intercepted Brown three times in all, Hudauri Hines, Jojo Hayden and Smiley Bradford, and recovered two Washington fumbles. Washington coach Jedd Fisch said afterward that you're not usually minus-4 in the turnover battle and win the game. He's correct, as a matter of engineering. Usually you don't.

Here's how it went. Jacobo Echeverria Lozano kicked a 24-yard field goal. Antonio Harris ran 1 yard for a touchdown to tie it 10-10. And then came the best bounce of the year: a Washington punt bounced off the back of a Huskies player's foot, we recovered at the Washington 10, and on the next play Ryan Browne hit Fame Ijeboi for a 10-yard touchdown. 17-17. Ding-ding. Physics, friends. Angular momentum works for everybody.

But then a roughing-the-passer penalty on a third-and-10 incompletion kept a Washington drive alive, and Brian Bonner Jr. scored with 27 seconds left in the half. 24-17. Echeverria Lozano hit a 48-yarder in the third, Browne scored on an 8-yard run early in the fourth, and we were down 31-26. Then Trey Cooley broke a 53-yard touchdown run with 10:30 left, and the structure didn't hold.

The Load Analysis

The design flaws, honestly: Brown threw for 302 yards and three touchdowns on 21-of-27 passing despite the three interceptions. Washington outgained us 488 to 371. We ran for 98 yards, most of them on Harris's 59-yarder, and Ijeboi, who'd run for 195 yards against Minnesota the week before, managed 19 on 13 carries. Coach Barry Odom said Washington won at the point of scrimmage, and he's right. That's a load-bearing wall, friends, and it buckled.

The good components: Asaad Waseem caught nine passes for 116 yards. Hayden made nine tackles to go with his interception. Echeverria Lozano made both field goals. Browne threw for 273 yards. And our takeaways, five of them, tell me the defense has the right parts. It just needs better assembly instructions.

The Season Blueprint

We're 3-4 and 2-2 in the Big Ten. We lost a close one to Wake Forest, 38-36, then lost at UCLA, 52-38, and Notre Dame beat us 49-10. Then we won at Illinois 24-17 and beat Minnesota 41-13. The AP noted that we need to win three of our last five games to become bowl eligible. That's a design spec, friends. I like a clear spec.

Part 2: A Week at the Drafting Table, Then Happy Valley

Purdue has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. No game. A week to heal, sharpen the pencils and redraw the run fits.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, we go to Beaver Stadium to play Penn State. Kickoff time hasn't been announced. Halloween in State College.

I'll start with respect, because engineers respect a well-built structure. Penn State's pass defense is excellent, allowing just 141.3 yards a game. Tony Rojas, the linebacker, has 55 tackles and five sacks. Chase Sowell had 11 catches for 151 yards at Michigan on Saturday. Penn State leads our series 17-3-1, according to CollegeFootballData.com, and has won the last six meetings. I'm not hiding from that number. I'm writing it at the top of the page.

Now, the stress analysis.

Penn State is 3-4 and 0-4 in the Big Ten, and it has lost four straight. On Saturday at Michigan, the Nittany Lions ran 30 times for 65 yards, turned the ball over three times and lost a fumble at their own 16 with a chance to tie or take the lead. They allow 172.3 rushing yards a game. Ours, by comparison, allows 161.6, which is not something I'd normally brag about, but on graph paper, smaller numbers are smaller.

And there's a pattern I've charted. Penn State lost to Wisconsin by four, to USC by eight and to Michigan by three. Close games, all of them, and all losses. Purdue's football team has a nickname for this kind of game: the "Spoilermakers." It goes back to 1950, when Purdue broke Notre Dame's 39-game winning streak. We've got a long tradition of showing up where we're not expected and leaving with the win.

Who to Watch

Ryan Browne, quarterback: 1,822 yards, 10 touchdowns and three interceptions this season. Purdue is the Cradle of Quarterbacks, the school of Len Dawson, Bob Griese and Drew Brees, and Browne's got the arm for the family photo.

Fame Ijeboi, running back: 568 yards and nine touchdowns. If he gets going, ding-ding.

Asaad Waseem, receiver: 38 catches for 588 yards.

Jojo Hayden: 48 tackles, our leader. Keyshawn Burgos: 1.5 sacks, our team lead.

Rocco Becht, Penn State quarterback: 12 touchdowns and five interceptions, plus a lost fumble Saturday. Our defense has proven it can take the ball away. Now it has to finish the job.

Carson Hansen, Penn State running back: 278 yards and four touchdowns.

Field Notes: A Tale of Two Towns

West Lafayette. Population 44,595 at the 2020 census, perched on a bluff above the Wabash River. Purdue is the Cradle of Astronauts: 27 graduates have become astronauts, including Gus Grissom of the Mercury Seven, Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and Eugene Cernan, the last. Ross-Ade Stadium opened in 1924 with a homecoming win over Indiana. Our mascot is a train, the Boilermaker Special, named for the trains that carried Purdue teams and fans to road games. And our band carries the World's Largest Drum, built in 1921. We put people on the moon and built the world's biggest drum. That's engineering.

State College. State College is a fine town. It's the largest borough in Pennsylvania, with 40,501 people, and the heart of what locals call Happy Valley. According to Wikipedia, the nickname came from the area's economic resilience during the Great Depression. Friends, I respect that. But by my calculations, Happy Valley is currently 0-4 in conference play. I'd suggest an engineering review of the name.

They're also very proud of the Berkey Creamery, which makes more than 100 flavors of ice cream and has a firm rule against mixing flavors in one cone. More than 100 options, and they still won't let you combine two. I've seen that kind of design philosophy before, friends. It's called Penn State's offense: plenty of parts, and none of them working together.

And Beaver Stadium is enormous, 106,572 seats. When they added the upper deck on the south end, it blocked the view of neighboring Mount Nittany, which, Wikipedia notes, had sentimental value for some fans. Engineers call that an unintended consequence. On Halloween, I'd like to deliver one more.

The Final Draft

Here's my final blueprint. We have two weeks to fix the run game. We have a defense that forces turnovers, a quarterback from the Cradle of Quarterbacks and a nickname, the Spoilermakers, built for exactly this kind of trip. Penn State has lost four straight and can't run the ball.

Engineer it. Boiler up! Ding-ding.

articles.title: Exit 9 Never Lies: Rutgers Rallied From 10 Down in College Park, and Now It's Off to Evanston to See the Smallest Stadium in the Big Ten
articles.byline: Vinny Scolari, The Rutgers Fanatic
articles.matchup: Rutgers (2-4) at No. 24 Northwestern (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. EDT, Ryan Field, Evanston (Peacock)
articles.text:
Yo. Vinny here.

You want directions to how I'm feeling this week? Easy. Get on the Turnpike, go past Exit 8A, where the anxiety lives, and keep going till you hit Exit 9, which is right next to New Brunswick and is where I keep my joy. That's where I am right now. Exit 9. Windows down. Rutgers won.

I'm Vinny Scolari, born and raised off Exit 9, and I grade every Big Ten trench battle like an arm-wrestle on the boardwalk in Seaside. Some weeks we get pinned. This week, friends, we flipped the table.

Exit 9 never lies. Let's go.

Part 1: The Comeback in College Park

Rutgers 37, Maryland 30. Saturday, Oct. 17, at SECU Stadium.

I'm gonna tell you the first half honestly, because Jersey people tell it straight. It was rough. Maryland took a 7-0 lead on a 1-yard run. Dylan Lonergan answered with a 15-yard touchdown pass to KJ Duff. Then Maryland went up 14-7, and Lonergan hit Duff again, this time from nine yards. Good, right? Wrong. Maryland blocked the extra point, and Jamare Glasker returned it for two points the other way. So instead of 14-14, it was 16-13. Then Maryland scored again with 53 seconds left in the half. 23-13 at halftime.

I'll tell you where I was emotionally at halftime: Exit 7A. Somewhere around Great Adventure, and not on a fun ride.

And then the second half. Fuhgeddaboudit.

Dane Pizzaro kicked a 25-yard field goal. Lonergan threw a 19-yard touchdown pass to Clay Thevenin. 23-23. Early in the fourth, Thevenin ran it in from seven yards out. Then Antwan Raymond punched one in from two with 4:03 left. Twenty-four straight points, friends. That's not a comeback. That's a full Jersey Shore summer packed into 30 minutes.

Maryland scored late, but we held on. 37-30.

The Arm-Wrestle Grades

Lonergan: 23 of 35 for 291 yards, three touchdowns, one interception. Grade: pinned 'em.

KJ Duff: nine catches, 113 yards, two touchdowns. Grade: arm-wrestled two guys at once and won both.

Clay Thevenin: 17 carries, 109 yards, a rushing touchdown and a receiving touchdown. Grade: he's the kind of guy who wins at the boardwalk and then wins the stuffed animal for your little cousin, too.

Dyzier Carter caught six passes for 88 yards. Sean Allison led us with eight tackles. We converted 9 of 14 third downs, outgained Maryland 442 to 378 and held the ball for 35:52. Up front, where the big fellas live, we won the arm-wrestle. Pinned it flat.

The Season So Far

Real talk: we're 2-4 and 1-2 in the Big Ten. We lost the opener to UMass, which I don't discuss in public, and then lost at Boston College by seven and to USC by seven. Indiana beat us 47-15. But we beat Howard and now Maryland, and Lonergan has 10 touchdown passes. KJ Duff has 741 receiving yards and nine touchdowns, which puts him on a very short list of the best receivers in the conference. This team's got fight. Ask Maryland. And coach Greg Schiano, who came back to Rutgers in 2020 for his second run here, has these guys playing like they've got somewhere to be. I like a team that's got somewhere to be. It's very Jersey.

Part 2: Off to Evanston

Saturday, Oct. 24, at noon Eastern, we go to Ryan Field to play No. 24 Northwestern. It's on Peacock.

I'll be respectful, 'cause my mother raised me right. Northwestern is 5-1 and ranked. Its quarterback, Aidan Chiles, has nine touchdown passes and no interceptions. Its red-zone offense scores 96.4 of every 100 times, fourth in FBS. Its turnover margin is plus-7, eighth. That's a well-coached football team.

Now let me tell you about their Saturday.

Northwestern played Michigan State, which was 2-5 and 0-4 in the Big Ten coming into the week, and needed a blocked field goal and a 34-yard kick with two seconds left to win. The Spartans sacked Chiles five times. Northwestern's pass defense allows 230.5 yards a game, 100th in FBS. And we've got a quarterback who just threw for 291 and a receiver who's caught nine touchdown passes.

Also, and I say this with love, Northwestern's new stadium holds 35,000 people, the smallest in the Big Ten, and it opened three weeks late because of construction delays. Friends, I've sat in traffic on the Parkway longer than that. I'm from New Jersey. We don't do small. We do eight lanes and a toll.

Who to Watch

KJ Duff, receiver: 42 catches, 741 yards, nine touchdowns. Exit 9 never lies, and neither do this guy's numbers.

Dylan Lonergan, quarterback: 1,066 yards, 10 touchdowns, six interceptions. Needs to keep it clean against a defense that takes the ball away.

Antwan Raymond, running back: 498 yards and five touchdowns. Clay Thevenin: coming off 109 yards.

Chris Joines: 30 tackles, our leader. Sekou Kromah: two sacks.

Aidan Chiles, Northwestern quarterback: 1,398 yards, nine touchdowns, zero interceptions. We need to get one. Just one.

Griffin Wilde, Northwestern receiver: 30 catches, 482 yards.

The History

We lead the all-time series 4-2, according to our athletics site, and we won the last meeting, 24-7 at SHI Stadium in 2023. We held Northwestern to 12 rushing yards that day. Twelve. I'm still bringing it up at barbecues.

Turnpike Report: A Tale of Two Towns

New Brunswick and Piscataway. First, the big one. On Nov. 6, 1869, Rutgers beat Princeton 6-4 in the first college football game ever played. The first one. Every Saturday in America, every band, every tailgate, every fight song: that all starts here. Rutgers is the eighth-oldest college in the country, chartered in 1766 as Queen's College, and New Brunswick is called the Hub City for all its hospitals and medical schools. Johnson & Johnson's headquarters sits right where Rutgers held its first classes, at a spot called the Sign of the Red Lion. SHI Stadium, over in Piscataway, seats 52,454. That's more than 17,000 more seats than Northwestern's place, but who's counting? Me. I'm counting.

Evanston. Now, Evanston's a nice town. Right on Lake Michigan, 12 miles north of Chicago's Loop. Very smart people. Big journalism school. Very proud of all their Pulitzers.

But I gotta give you directions to Northwestern football history, Jersey-style. Get on the record book, go past the wins, keep going past the bowl games, and take the exit marked "most all-time losses in major college football history." According to Wikipedia, Northwestern reclaimed that record from Indiana in November 2025. Reclaimed. Like it was a family heirloom.

And the stadium. Thirty-five thousand seats. That's the smallest in the conference, and they did it on purpose, according to Wikipedia, to get rid of the nosebleed seats. Friends, at the Meadowlands, the nosebleeds are where the real fans live. That's where my uncle Sal sits. You take away Sal's seat, you're gonna hear about it, and you're gonna hear about it all the way from Exit 16W.

Final Exit

Here's my read. We're coming off our best half of football all year. We've got the best receiver on the field, a quarterback who's starting to cook and a 24-point second half on tape. Northwestern needed a last-second field goal to beat a team that's winless in the conference. Nobody expects us to go into Evanston and win. That's fine. Nobody expected Rutgers to invent college football, either.

Exit 9 never lies. Go RU!

My call: Northwestern Wildcats 37, Rutgers Scarlet Knights 19.

Its red-zone offense scores 96.4 of every 100 times, fourth in FBS. Its turnover margin is plus-7, eighth. That's a well-coached football team.
Now let me tell you about their Saturday.

Northwestern played Michigan State, which was 2-5 and 0-4 in the Big Ten coming into the week, and needed a blocked field goal and a 34-yard kick with two seconds left to win. The Spartans sacked Chiles five times. Northwestern's pass defense allows 230.5 yards a game, 100th in FBS. And we've got a quarterback who just threw for 291 and a receiver who's caught nine touchdown passes.

Also, and I say this with love, Northwestern's new stadium holds 35,000 people, the smallest in the Big Ten, and it opened three weeks late because of construction delays. Friends, I've sat in traffic on the Parkway longer than that. I'm from New Jersey. We don't do small. We do eight lanes and a toll.
Who to Watch
KJ Duff, receiver: 42 catches, 741 yards, nine touchdowns. Exit 9 never lies, and neither do this guy's numbers.
Dylan Lonergan, quarterback: 1,066 yards, 10 touchdowns, six interceptions. Needs to keep it clean against a defense that takes the ball away.
Antwan Raymond, running back: 498 yards and five touchdowns. Clay Thevenin: coming off 109 yards.
Chris Joines: 30 tackles, our leader. Sekou Kromah: two sacks.
Aidan Chiles, Northwestern quarterback: 1,398 yards, nine touchdowns, zero interceptions. We need to get one. Just one.
Griffin Wilde, Northwestern receiver: 30 catches, 482 yards.
The History

We lead the all-time series 4-2, according to our athletics site, and we won the last meeting, 24-7 at SHI Stadium in 2023. We held Northwestern to 12 rushing yards that day. Twelve. I'm still bringing it up at barbecues.
Turnpike Report: A Tale of Two Towns

New Brunswick and Piscataway. First, the big one. On Nov. 6, 1869, Rutgers beat Princeton 6-4 in the first college football game ever played. The first one. Every Saturday in America, every band, every tailgate, every fight song: that all starts here. Rutgers is the eighth-oldest college in the country, chartered in 1766 as Queen's College, and New Brunswick is called the Hub City for all its hospitals and medical schools. Johnson & Johnson's headquarters sits right where Rutgers held its first classes, at a spot called the Sign of the Red Lion. SHI Stadium, over in Piscataway, seats 52,454. That's more than 17,000 more seats than Northwestern's place, but who's counting? Me. I'm counting.
Evanston. Now, Evanston's a nice town. Right on Lake Michigan, 12 miles north of Chicago's Loop. Very smart people. Big journalism school. Very proud of all their Pulitzers.

But I gotta give you directions to Northwestern football history, Jersey-style. Get on the record book, go past the wins, keep going past the bowl games, and take the exit marked "most all-time losses in major college football history." According to Wikipedia, Northwestern reclaimed that record from Indiana in November 2025. Reclaimed. Like it was a family heirloom.

And the stadium. Thirty-five thousand seats. That's the smallest in the conference, and they did it on purpose, according to Wikipedia, to get rid of the nosebleed seats. Friends, at the Meadowlands, the nosebleeds are where the real fans live. That's where my uncle Sal sits. You take away Sal's seat, you're gonna hear about it, and you're gonna hear about it all the way from Exit 16W.
Final Exit

Here's my read. We're coming off our best half of football all year. We've got the best receiver on the field, a quarterback who's starting to cook and a 24-point second half on tape. Northwestern needed a last-second field goal to beat a team that's winless in the conference. Nobody expects us to go into Evanston and win. That's fine. Nobody expected Rutgers to invent college football, either.
Exit 9 never lies. Go RU!
My call: Northwestern Wildcats 37, Rutgers Scarlet Knights 19.

articles.title: The Understudy Steals the Show: A Backup Quarterback Kept the Bruins Perfect, and Now Michigan State Gets a Studio Tour of the Rose Bowl
articles.byline: Kensington 'Kenzie' Rhee, The UCLA Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 9 UCLA (6-0) vs. Michigan State (2-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. EDT, Rose Bowl, Pasadena (CBS)
articles.text:
Okay, everybody, settle in, phones on silent. Thank you for taking this meeting.

I'm Kenzie Rhee. I produce short films in Westwood, I storyboard every UCLA drive on index cards, and I have a corkboard in my apartment that my landlord has described as "a lot." This season, that corkboard has six cards on it, and every one of them says W.

Here's the pitch. Picture it: a program that won three games last year. A first-year head coach. Then the star gets hurt, and the understudy steps in on opening night and doesn't miss a cue. Six and oh. Roll credits? No, darling. We're only in the second act.

Part 1: Opening Night for the Understudy

Saturday, Oct. 17, at the Rose Bowl. UCLA 17, Wisconsin 7.

Our starting quarterback, Nico Iamaleava, hurt his leg the week before at Oregon, and he sat this one out. Wishing him a speedy recovery. So in stepped Ty Dieffenbach, who spent two seasons at Pitt and then Cal Poly before coming to Westwood, for his first start as a Bruin. He completed 22 of 33 passes for 264 yards. Our opening drive went 16 plays and took 8 minutes, 42 seconds, both season highs, according to the AP. Dieffenbach completed six of eight passes to five different receivers on that drive, and Mateen Bhaghani kicked a 24-yard field goal. Opening shot, establishing the mood.

In the second quarter, Wayne Knight scored from the 1, giving him a rushing touchdown in all six games this season. 10-0 at the half.

Wisconsin made it 10-7 in the third quarter on a Colton Joseph run, because every good movie needs a little tension. Then, in the fourth, Anthony Woods ran it in from the 3, and the touchdown held up under review after he appeared to bobble the ball. Very dramatic. Very on-brand. 17-7.

And the defense, darlings. Wisconsin passed for 66 yards. Sixty-six, on 6-of-16 throwing. Sammy Omosigho stuffed a fourth-quarter run just short of the first-down marker, and the replay booth agreed, which gave us the ball with 8:43 to go. Jalen Woods made nine tackles and a sack. We had the ball for 37 minutes. Wisconsin was 3 of 10 on third down.

I'll be honest, because honesty is good storytelling: we committed eight penalties for 78 yards and threw two interceptions, one by Semaj Morgan on a trick play that I'm choosing to call experimental cinema. A lot got left on the cutting-room floor. But the box office says 6-0, for the first time since 2022.

The Season So Far

We beat Cal 45-24, San Diego State 28-10, and Purdue 52-38. We won 54-3 at Maryland. We won 17-15 at Oregon. And now Wisconsin. Coach Bob Chesney is the first UCLA coach to begin a tenure with six straight wins, per the AP. We're the only unbeaten team left in the Big Ten or the SEC, and we're No. 9 in the AP poll. Remember: three wins all of last season.

Part 2: Michigan State Comes to the Rose Bowl

Saturday, Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, which is 12:30 p.m. in Pasadena, Michigan State visits the Rose Bowl. CBS has it.

The polite part of the meeting: Michigan State plays hard. The Spartans lost to Illinois 38-37 in overtime and to Northwestern 24-21 on a field goal with two seconds left. Their quarterback, Alessio Milivojevic, has 1,263 yards and seven touchdowns with only three interceptions. Missing several starters on defense, they still had five sacks against Northwestern. And the Spartans commit 36.3 penalty yards a game, seventh-best in FBS. That's a disciplined film crew.

The less polite part: Michigan State is 2-5, 0-4 in the Big Ten, and has lost five straight. Its offense ranks 128th in FBS in yards per game and 113th in scoring, according to the AP. Its rushing offense is 119th. Meanwhile, our run game averages 231 yards a game, 12th in the country, and our defense holds opponents to 25.9 of every 100 third downs, third-best in FBS.

So the plot of this one writes itself: we run the ball, we win on third down, and we, please, darlings, watch the penalties. We're 133rd in penalty yards. I've given the boys a note.

Who to Watch

Wayne Knight, running back: 571 yards and 11 touchdowns, with a rushing score in every game. That's what we call a franchise.

Ty Dieffenbach, quarterback: 264 yards in his first start. A breakout performance.

Semaj Morgan, receiver: 24 catches for 313 yards, plus 84 more against Wisconsin.

Anthony Woods, running back: the bobble-proof touchdown.

Jalen Woods, linebacker: 50 tackles, our leader. Sammy Omosigho: three sacks and the fourth-down stop.

Alessio Milivojevic, Michigan State quarterback: 216 yards and two touchdowns against Northwestern.

Eli Coenen, Michigan State defender: 3.5 sacks and a blocked field goal last week.

The Backstory

UCLA leads the series 4-3 and has won four straight, including 38-13 in East Lansing last season, according to CollegeFootballDigest. Three of the seven meetings came in the Rose Bowl Game. Michigan State won two of them, after the 1953 season and in January 1956. But the sequel was ours: on Jan. 1, 1966, the Bruins beat the unbeaten, top-ranked Spartans 14-12 in Pasadena. Classic. They should remaster it.

Location Scouting: Two Towns

Westwood and Pasadena. UCLA opened in Westwood in 1929, and Westwood Village, right next to campus, was the second planned shopping and entertainment district of its kind in the nation, movie theaters included. And our home stage, the Rose Bowl, opened in 1922, is a National Historic Landmark, and seats 89,702. It's 10 miles from downtown Los Angeles, and I've seen sunsets there that made grown production designers weep. UCLA has claimed one national championship, in 1954, and the 1954 Bruins went 9-0. That one's in the vault.

Now, people love to point out that our home stadium is 26 miles from campus and USC's is only 14. I say every great production shoots on location.

East Lansing. East Lansing is a charming college town of 47,741, home to the first land-grant college in the country, which is a lovely detail for a pitch deck. They have a campus Dairy Store that makes its own ice cream, and I respect a school with in-house catering.

But here's my note on East Lansing. The Spartans' official colors are green and white, and you know what that palette is called in the film business? A placeholder. Spartans, I'd love to do a color pass on that whole thing. We'd keep the green. We'd add a little gold. Call me.

And Sparty, their mascot, is a Spartan warrior, which is a very serious look for a team flying across the country for a 12:30 kickoff in Southern California. Pack the sunscreen, Sparty. The helmet won't block it all.

Closing

Here's the logline. An unbeaten team with an understudy at quarterback, a running back who scores every week, and a third-down defense that ranks third in the country, at home, in the most famous stadium in college football. Michigan State is scrappy and well coached, but it has lost five in a row, and its offense has struggled all year.

Final cut: we keep the streak alive. And... scene.

My call: UCLA Bruins 32, Michigan State Spartans 17.

articles.title: In a World Where 114,419 People Wore White: The Trojans Silenced Beaver Stadium, Rested Up, and Now Head to Madison to Find Out Whether Anyone Can Jump Around in a Parka
articles.byline: Sterling Ashworth-Vance, The USC Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 16 USC (6-1) at Wisconsin (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. EDT, Camp Randall Stadium, Madison (NBC)
articles.text:
In a world... where 114,419 people dressed in white... one team dared to wear cardinal and gold.

Good evening, and welcome to the premiere. I'm Sterling Ashworth-Vance. I grew up a few blocks from the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, I went to film school, and I rate every play on a scale of one to five clapperboards. I've been known to narrate replays in a trailer voice at family dinners. My mother has asked me to stop. I have not stopped.

This week's feature: a Trojan team that went into the loudest building in college football and came out with the reviews. Fight On.

Part 1: The White Out, Silenced

Our last game was Saturday, Oct. 10, at Beaver Stadium. USC 31, Penn State 23. We had last week off, which I spent rewatching it, frame by frame, with a director's commentary only I could love.

Set the scene. The announced crowd of 114,419 was the largest in Beaver Stadium history, according to the AP, and nearly all of them wore white for Penn State's annual White Out. Ladies and gentlemen, that's a stadium-sized wedding, and we were the uninvited guests who caught the bouquet.

Opening shot: Jayden Maiava was perfect on the first drive, finishing it with a 19-yard touchdown pass to Trent Mosley. Five clapperboards. Penn State answered every punch in the first half, and it was 17-17 at the break. We tried an onside kick to open the second half, Penn State recovered, and the Nittany Lions took their only lead on a field goal. A twist in the second act. Every great film has one.

Then King Miller ran in a 13-yard touchdown to put us back in front for good. Kayden Dixon-Wyatt caught a 10-yard touchdown early in the fourth quarter to make it 31-23. And with 3:59 left, Christian Pierce punched the ball loose from a Penn State runner, we recovered, and our offense ran out the clock. Penn State never touched the ball again. Roll credits.

The Reviews

Maiava completed 21 of 33 passes for 301 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. Mosley caught nine passes for 111 yards. Tanook Hines added an 11-yard touchdown catch and 82 receiving yards. Miller ran for 102 yards on 19 carries. And our defense held Penn State to 68 rushing yards on 31 carries, 2.2 yards a carry. Luke Wafle had a sack, and Desman Stephens II made nine tackles. We committed three penalties all night. Coach Lincoln Riley ranked it among the best wins of his head-coaching career, and, darling, it's near the top of my list as a fan, too.

The Season So Far

We're 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big Ten, and No. 16 in the AP poll. We beat San José State, Fresno State 39-0, and Louisiana. We won at Rutgers 42-35. Oregon beat us 41-27 at the Coliseum, which I've filed under "deleted scenes." Then we beat Washington 25-21 and won at Penn State.

Part 2: The Sequel Is Set in Madison

Saturday, Oct. 24, at 7:30 p.m. Eastern, 6:30 p.m. local, we visit Wisconsin at Camp Randall Stadium. NBC has it. Prime time. As it should be.

First, a tip of the cap, because good manners make good cinema. Wisconsin is 4-2, 2-1 in the Big Ten, and won 24-20 at Penn State and 31-3 over Michigan State. The Badgers' defense allows 16.7 points a game, 24th in FBS, and its pass defense ranks 20th, according to the AP. Colton Joseph has thrown for 1,198 yards and 10 touchdowns and leads the team in rushing, too. Tyrell Henry has 27 catches for 343 yards. Cooper Catalano has 50 tackles. Coach Luke Fickell's teams are tough. That's a real co-star.

Now, the plot points Wisconsin would rather leave on the cutting-room floor. Last Saturday at the Rose Bowl, the Badgers passed for 66 yards against UCLA, lost 17-7, and committed 10 penalties for 108 yards, according to the box score. Their passing offense ranks 100th in FBS. Ours ranks seventh, at 310.1 yards a game, and we convert 51.2 of every 100 third downs, 14th in the country.

Our honest weakness: our pass defense ranks 109th, allowing 239 yards a game. Wisconsin's passing game hasn't been explosive, but in a sequel, the villain always gets one big scene. We have to keep it to one.

Who to Watch

Jayden Maiava, quarterback: 2,045 yards, 18 touchdowns, three interceptions. Leading man.

King Miller, running back: 595 yards and four touchdowns, plus 102 at Penn State.

Trent Mosley, receiver: nine catches for 111 yards last time out. A breakout role.

Kayden Dixon-Wyatt, receiver: our leader with 400 yards and four touchdowns.

Christian Pierce: 39 tackles and the forced fumble that ended the White Out. Kennedy Urlacher: three sacks.

Colton Joseph, Wisconsin quarterback: leads the Badgers in passing and rushing.

Sebastian Cheeks, Wisconsin defender: 2.5 sacks.

History: We've Done This Before

USC leads the series 7-1, according to CollegeFootballDigest, and won the last meeting, 38-21 at the Coliseum in 2024. Two of our wins came in the Rose Bowl Game, including the classic on Jan. 1, 1963: top-ranked USC 42, No. 2 Wisconsin 37, after the Badgers nearly came all the way back. Five clapperboards for the drama. Wisconsin's lone win was the 2015 Holiday Bowl, 23-21. And we're 2-0 at Camp Randall, in 1956 and 1965.

Location Scouting: Two Towns

Los Angeles. Our home, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, opened in 1923 as a memorial to the city's World War I veterans. It hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984, it became a National Historic Landmark the day before the 1984 opening ceremony, and in 2028 it will become the first stadium to host the Summer Olympics three times. USC claims 11 national championships. Our mascot, Traveler, has galloped at the Coliseum since 1961, and he's a white horse. Well, technically, most Travelers have been gray horses whose coats turned completely white, according to Wikipedia. In Hollywood, we call that aging gracefully.

Madison, Wisconsin. Madison is a beautiful city of 269,840, built on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona. The city's own trademark is "Lake, City, Lake," which is wonderful, darling, but as a title it needs work. Camp Randall stands on the grounds of a Union Army training camp from the Civil War, and its students do the "Jump Around" before the fourth quarter. After every home game, the marching band plays the Fifth Quarter, a tradition that started during a 24-game losing streak in 1969 and has outlasted it by a few decades.

Now, I adore Madison. But in the land of the cheese curd, I have notes. Wikipedia reports that fresh curds squeak against your teeth and lose that squeak within 12 hours, even when refrigerated. Folks, in Hollywood we call that a short shelf life. In Madison, they call it Saturday.

And their mascot, Bucky Badger, wears a striped varsity sweater. Here's my go-to plot twist: the classic Bucky drawing was created in 1940 by a California commercial artist named Art Evans. So the Badgers' signature look came from our side of the map. You're welcome, Madison. And Bucky, about that sweater in late October in Wisconsin: I understand completely. I'm packing two coats, a scarf, and the kind of gloves that make it impossible to hold popcorn. I'll be jumping around too, mostly to stay warm. Still, a tip of the cap to Camp Randall. It's one of the great sets in the sport.

Closing

Here's the trailer for Saturday night. A Trojan offense with the seventh-best passing attack in the country, a running back coming off 100 yards, and a defense that just shut down the White Out's ground game. Against a Wisconsin defense that's very good, in one of the loudest night environments in America.

It'll be close. Sequels usually are. Fight On, and roll credits.

My call: USC Trojans 26, Wisconsin Badgers 25.

And with 3:59 left, Christian Pierce punched the ball loose from a Penn State runner, we recovered, and our offense ran out the clock. Penn State never touched the ball again. Roll credits.
The Reviews

Maiava completed 21 of 33 passes for 301 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. Mosley caught nine passes for 111 yards. Tanook Hines added an 11-yard touchdown catch and 82 receiving yards. Miller ran for 102 yards on 19 carries. And our defense held Penn State to 68 rushing yards on 31 carries, 2.2 yards a carry. Luke Wafle had a sack, and Desman Stephens II made nine tackles. We committed three penalties all night. Coach Lincoln Riley ranked it among the best wins of his head-coaching career, and, darling, it's near the top of my list as a fan, too.
The Season So Far

We're 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big Ten, and No. 16 in the AP poll. We beat San José State, Fresno State 39-0, and Louisiana. We won at Rutgers 42-35. Oregon beat us 41-27 at the Coliseum, which I've filed under "deleted scenes." Then we beat Washington 25-21 and won at Penn State.
Part 2: The Sequel Is Set in Madison
Saturday, Oct. 24, at 7:30 p.m. Eastern, 6:30 p.m. local, we visit Wisconsin at Camp Randall Stadium. NBC has it. Prime time. As it should be.

First, a tip of the cap, because good manners make good cinema. Wisconsin is 4-2, 2-1 in the Big Ten, and won 24-20 at Penn State and 31-3 over Michigan State. The Badgers' defense allows 16.7 points a game, 24th in FBS, and its pass defense ranks 20th, according to the AP. Colton Joseph has thrown for 1,198 yards and 10 touchdowns and leads the team in rushing, too. Tyrell Henry has 27 catches for 343 yards. Cooper Catalano has 50 tackles. Coach Luke Fickell's teams are tough. That's a real co-star.

Now, the plot points Wisconsin would rather leave on the cutting-room floor. Last Saturday at the Rose Bowl, the Badgers passed for 66 yards against UCLA, lost 17-7, and committed 10 penalties for 108 yards, according to the box score. Their passing offense ranks 100th in FBS. Ours ranks seventh, at 310.1 yards a game, and we convert 51.2 of every 100 third downs, 14th in the country.

Our honest weakness: our pass defense ranks 109th, allowing 239 yards a game. Wisconsin's passing game hasn't been explosive, but in a sequel, the villain always gets one big scene. We have to keep it to one.
Who to Watch
Jayden Maiava, quarterback: 2,045 yards, 18 touchdowns, three interceptions. Leading man.
King Miller, running back: 595 yards and four touchdowns, plus 102 at Penn State.
Trent Mosley, receiver: nine catches for 111 yards last time out. A breakout role.
Kayden Dixon-Wyatt, receiver: our leader with 400 yards and four touchdowns.
Christian Pierce: 39 tackles and the forced fumble that ended the White Out. Kennedy Urlacher: three sacks.
Colton Joseph, Wisconsin quarterback: leads the Badgers in passing and rushing.
Sebastian Cheeks, Wisconsin defender: 2.5 sacks.
History: We've Done This Before

USC leads the series 7-1, according to CollegeFootballDigest, and won the last meeting, 38-21 at the Coliseum in 2024. Two of our wins came in the Rose Bowl Game, including the classic on Jan. 1, 1963: top-ranked USC 42, No. 2 Wisconsin 37, after the Badgers nearly came all the way back. Five clapperboards for the drama. Wisconsin's lone win was the 2015 Holiday Bowl, 23-21. And we're 2-0 at Camp Randall, in 1956 and 1965.
Location Scouting: Two Towns

Los Angeles. Our home, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, opened in 1923 as a memorial to the city's World War I veterans. It hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984, it became a National Historic Landmark the day before the 1984 opening ceremony, and in 2028 it will become the first stadium to host the Summer Olympics three times. USC claims 11 national championships. Our mascot, Traveler, has galloped at the Coliseum since 1961, and he's a white horse. Well, technically, most Travelers have been gray horses whose coats turned completely white, according to Wikipedia. In Hollywood, we call that aging gracefully.

Madison, Wisconsin. Madison is a beautiful city of 269,840, built on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona. The city's own trademark is "Lake, City, Lake," which is wonderful, darling, but as a title it needs work. Camp Randall stands on the grounds of a Union Army training camp from the Civil War, and its students do the "Jump Around" before the fourth quarter. After every home game, the marching band plays the Fifth Quarter, a tradition that started during a 24-game losing streak in 1969 and has outlasted it by a few decades.

Now, I adore Madison. But in the land of the cheese curd, I have notes. Wikipedia reports that fresh curds squeak against your teeth and lose that squeak within 12 hours, even when refrigerated. Folks, in Hollywood we call that a short shelf life. In Madison, they call it Saturday.

And their mascot, Bucky Badger, wears a striped varsity sweater. Here's my go-to plot twist: the classic Bucky drawing was created in 1940 by a California commercial artist named Art Evans. So the Badgers' signature look came from our side of the map. You're welcome, Madison. And Bucky, about that sweater in late October in Wisconsin: I understand completely. I'm packing two coats, a scarf, and the kind of gloves that make it impossible to hold popcorn. I'll be jumping around too, mostly to stay warm. Still, a tip of the cap to Camp Randall. It's one of the great sets in the sport.
Closing

Here's the trailer for Saturday night. A Trojan offense with the seventh-best passing attack in the country, a running back coming off 100 yards, and a defense that just shut down the White Out's ground game. Against a Wisconsin defense that's very good, in one of the loudest night environments in America.
It'll be close. Sequels usually are. Fight On, and roll credits.
My call: USC Trojans 26, Wisconsin Badgers 25.
