articles.title: Rain Is a Home-Field Advantage, and So Is a Win: The Dawgs Snapped Their Skid in West Lafayette, Rest Up, and Head to Lincoln for Halloween
articles.byline: Evangeline 'Vangie' Tollefsrud, The Washington Fanatic
articles.matchup: Washington (4-3): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Washington at Nebraska (5-2), Sat., Oct. 31, Memorial Stadium, Lincoln
articles.text:
Good morning from Union Bay, where it is drizzling, I'm in a kayak, and my coffee is still hot because I've learned to drink it fast.

I'm Vangie Tollefsrud. I'm a Seattle native, I row crew, and I boat to every home game, because when your stadium sits on the water, you'd be silly not to. My friends say I rate every opponent's rain gear. They're right. I do. More on that later.

But first, the news: the Huskies won. Three straight losses, and then a Friday night in Indiana, and we're back. Bow Down to Washington.

Part 1: Five Turnovers and a Win

Washington 38, Purdue 26, Friday night, Oct. 16, at Ross-Ade Stadium in West Lafayette.

I'm going to be honest about this one, because Pacific Northwest people are honest to a fault. It wasn't pretty. Elijah Brown, making his first start for us after transferring from Stanford, threw an interception on the very first play from scrimmage. He threw two more later. We lost two fumbles. Five turnovers. Coach Jedd Fisch said afterward that you're not usually minus-4 in the turnover battle and win.

And yet. Brown completed 21 of 27 passes for 302 yards and three touchdowns, and he never let it rattle him. His first touchdown went to Decker DeGraaf from two yards out. After Purdue tied it, he hit Brian Bonner Jr. for a 25-yard score. Purdue tied it again after a punt bounced off one of our guys and the Boilermakers recovered at our 10, and then, with 27 seconds left in the half, Bonner ran in from one yard to put us ahead for good. 24-17.

Early in the fourth quarter, Brown found Dezmen Roebuck for a 4-yard touchdown. Purdue got within 31-26. And then Trey Cooley took a handoff and went 53 yards for a touchdown with 10:30 left. I stood up in my living room and spilled an entire Americano. Worth it.

The Box Score, With Coffee

Cooley ran eight times for 113 yards, which is 14.1 yards a carry, which is faster than the ferry. Chris Lawson caught six passes for 103 yards. Roebuck caught five for 97 and the touchdown. We outgained Purdue 488 to 371.

And the defense, oh, the defense. Purdue ran for 98 yards, most of them on a single 59-yard run. Fame Ijeboi, who'd run for 195 yards against Minnesota the week before, ran 13 times for 19 yards. Purdue coach Barry Odom said our defensive front won at the point of scrimmage. Rylon Dillard-Allen had an interception and seven tackles, Jeron Jones had another interception, and Alex McLaughlin made seven tackles with 1.5 for loss.

The Season So Far

We're 4-3 and 1-3 in the Big Ten. We started 3-0, beating Washington State, Utah State and Eastern Washington. Then came the rough stretch: 27-24 to Minnesota, 25-21 at USC, and 41-24 to Iowa. Two of those three were one-score games. Now we've got a win, a breath and a fresh pot of coffee.

Part 2: A Week Off, Then Lincoln

Washington has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. That's the honest schedule note. No game. A week to clean up the turnovers and maybe hold a team meeting about ball security. I'll bring muffins.

Then on Saturday, Oct. 31, we go to Memorial Stadium in Lincoln to play Nebraska. Kickoff time hasn't been announced.

Nebraska deserves respect. The Huskers are 5-2, they score 35.6 points a game, allow 15.4, and their defense just held Oregon to 242 yards. Anthony Colandrea has thrown for 1,570 yards and 14 touchdowns. Kwazi Gilmer has seven touchdown catches. Their fans have sold out every home game since 1962, which, I'll admit, is impressive. That's a crowd that shows up.

But here's my rain-gear rating for Nebraska: a nice-looking red jacket with a broken zipper. It looks great until the fourth quarter.

Because, friends, Nebraska has led in the fourth quarter in each of its last two games and lost both. Indiana beat the Huskers 20-17 in Lincoln, and on Saturday night, Oregon came back from 14-6 down in the fourth quarter to win 17-14, on a touchdown pass with 28 seconds left. And the quarterback who threw it, Dylan Raiola, played his first two seasons at Nebraska. Ouch. One Oregon field goal drive even got going after Nebraska's punter took a low snap and accidentally put his knee down.

And the Huskers ran for 78 yards in Eugene. Our defense just held Purdue to 98. I like that matchup.

Who to Watch

Elijah Brown, quarterback: 302 yards and three touchdowns in his first Washington start.

Demond Williams Jr., quarterback: 1,396 yards and eight touchdowns this season.

Dezmen Roebuck, receiver: 48 catches, 484 yards, three touchdowns, our leader.

Trey Cooley, running back: 113 yards on eight carries Friday. Feed him.

Alex McLaughlin: 47 tackles, our leader. Jacob Manu: 2.5 sacks.

Kwazi Gilmer, Nebraska receiver: 38 catches for 492 yards and seven touchdowns. Owen Chambliss, Nebraska linebacker: 15 tackles against Oregon.

The History

Nebraska leads the all-time series 5-4-1, according to Washington's athletics site, and won the last meeting, 51-38 in Lincoln in 2011. That's a long time between visits. We'll knock.

Dockside Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Seattle. The Emerald City, officially since 1982. Home of the Space Needle, built for the 1962 World's Fair, and of Pike Place, where the very first Starbucks opened on March 30, 1971. Yes, we have frequent rain. Wikipedia calls it a well-earned reputation, and we earned it. Husky Stadium seats 72,132 on the shore of Union Bay, and it holds the record as the loudest college football stadium ever recorded. Fans boat to the game, a tradition called sailgating, and our crew team runs shuttles from the boats to the docks. And we claim two national championships, including 1991, when Don James's Huskies went 12-0. Bow Down to Washington, the fight song says, and we mean it politely. Mostly.

Lincoln. Now, Lincoln is a fine town, and very proud of itself. Its state capitol, finished in 1932, is the second-tallest capitol in the country. Second-tallest. Friends, Nebraska's two losses were by three points each. Lincoln seems very comfortable in second place.

And Lincoln is about as far from a lake as I've ever been asked to travel. No water. No boats. I'll have to leave my kayak at home, which is a hardship I'll endure for the team. Their famous local food is the Runza, which started in Lincoln. I'm told it's a sandwich. I'm also told it's best eaten indoors, because it's late October in Nebraska and the wind can be serious.

One more thing. Nebraska's band plays the visiting team's fight song before every home game, and the announcer welcomes "our friends" from the other school. That's very kind. So I'd like to make sure the Cornhuskers know the words. It goes: Bow down to Washington. They'll be hearing it again at the end.

Final Stroke

Here's how I see it. We snapped a three-game skid on the road. We found a quarterback who can shake off mistakes, a running back who runs faster than the ferry and a defense that just shut down Purdue's run game. Nebraska has a great crowd, a stingy defense and a habit of letting fourth quarters get away. We have a week of rest and a whole lot of coffee.

Rain is a home-field advantage. On Halloween, we'll bring our own.

Bow Down to Washington.

articles.title: Polka Break, Then Business: The Badgers Left Pasadena With Two Interceptions and No Win, and Now Hollywood Has to Come to Camp Randall at Night
articles.byline: Lars 'Brat' Ellefson, The Wisconsin Fanatic
articles.matchup: Wisconsin (4-2) vs. No. 16 USC (6-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. EDT, Camp Randall Stadium, Madison (NBC)
articles.text:
Oom-pah, oom-pah, oom-pah-pah!

That's the polka break, folks. I do one before every big stat. It clears the mind and loosens the knees.

I'm Lars Ellefson, but everybody calls me Brat, after the sausage, not the attitude. I played fullback a long time ago, back when my knees still bent in both directions, and I bring a foam cheese wedge to every game. Home, road, the dentist. It's been to more places than my passport.

This week, the cheese wedge stays home, because the Trojans are coming to Camp Randall. Under the lights. In late October. In Wisconsin. Let's talk about it.

Part 1: A Long Way From Home, a Short Way From a Win

Saturday, Oct. 17, at the Rose Bowl. UCLA 17, Wisconsin 7.

I'll be straight with you, because that's the Wisconsin way. We didn't play clean. Oom-pah. Ten penalties for 108 yards, including four on our second drive, according to the AP. Coach Luke Fickell said afterward that we were undisciplined, and when the coach says it first, there's not much for a fella in a foam hat to add.

We went 1 for 6 on third down in the first half and had the ball for only about 11 1/2 minutes before halftime. Gavin Lahm missed his first field goal of the season, a 46-yarder, and we trailed 10-0 at the half.

Then the third quarter happened, and boy, did the Badgers show up. Colton Joseph ran it in from the 3 to make it 10-7, and our defense was flat-out nasty. UCLA ran 37 times for 120 yards, just 3.2 a carry. And Marvin Burks Jr. intercepted two passes. Two! Oom-pah-pah! Sean West punted five times, and four of them landed inside the 20. I'd like to shake that young man's hand, but I'm told that's not how it works, so I'll just clap really hard.

UCLA scored a touchdown in the fourth quarter to make it 17-7. On our next drive, Darrion Dupree was ruled short of a first down by a hair on a review, and that was about the ball game.

Joseph ran for 71 yards on 18 carries, but he completed only six of 16 passes for 66 yards. We'll need more than that. Everybody in the state knows it, including my cousin who thinks a forward pass is a type of curling shot.

The Season So Far

We're 4-2, 2-1 in the Big Ten. We lost to Notre Dame at Lambeau Field to open the year, 41-13. Then we beat Western Illinois 36-9 and Eastern Michigan 54-10. We won 24-20 at Penn State, then ranked 13th, and beat Michigan State 31-3. Then came Pasadena. Our defense allows 16.7 points a game, 24th in the country, and our pass defense ranks 20th, per the AP.

Part 2: Hollywood Comes to Madison

Saturday, Oct. 24, at 6:30 p.m. Central, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, No. 16 USC visits Camp Randall Stadium. NBC has it, and the lights will be on.

Fair is fair, so let's start with what USC does well. Oom-pah. The Trojans are 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big Ten, and they just beat Penn State 31-23 in front of 114,419 people in Happy Valley. Jayden Maiava has thrown for 2,045 yards, 18 touchdowns, and only three interceptions. Their passing offense ranks seventh in FBS at 310.1 yards a game, and they convert 51.2 of every 100 third downs. King Miller has 595 rushing yards. Kayden Dixon-Wyatt has 400 receiving yards. That's a good football team, and I'll shake their hands, too, if anyone lets me.

But here's what the scouting report says on the back page. USC's pass defense ranks 109th in FBS, allowing 239 yards a game, according to the AP, and its scoring defense ranks 80th. And Oregon beat the Trojans 41-27 at their own Coliseum last month.

So the recipe is simple, like a good brat. Our pass defense, 20th in the country, against their big-time passing game. And our quarterback, who can run, against a defense that gives up yards through the air. If Joseph can find Tyrell Henry a few times, this one gets interesting.

Who to Watch

Colton Joseph, quarterback: 1,198 passing yards and 10 touchdowns, plus a team-high 333 rushing yards.

Tyrell Henry, receiver: our leader with 27 catches for 343 yards.

Cooper Catalano, linebacker: 50 tackles.

Marvin Burks Jr., defensive back: two interceptions at the Rose Bowl.

Sebastian Cheeks: 2.5 sacks. Sean West, punter: four inside the 20 last week. A man after my own heart.

Jayden Maiava, USC quarterback: 301 yards and three touchdowns at Penn State.

Trent Mosley, USC receiver: nine catches for 111 yards against Penn State.

History, With Cheese

USC leads the series 7-1, according to CollegeFootballDigest, and won the last meeting, 38-21 in Los Angeles in 2024. The most famous game was the 1963 Rose Bowl, where the No. 2 Badgers rallied in the fourth quarter and fell to No. 1 USC, 42-37. Our lone win came in the 2015 Holiday Bowl, 23-21. Now, the Trojans have won twice at Camp Randall, in 1956 and 1965. That was a long time ago. I wasn't born yet. Neither was my cheese wedge.

And for the record, Wisconsin has its own championship history. The 1942 Badgers were named national champions by the Helms Athletic Foundation, the program's lone national title from a major selector, according to Wikipedia, and that team beat Ohio State along the way. We've won Rose Bowls over UCLA and Stanford, too. So we know a thing or two about beating teams from California. We just prefer to do it at home, where the brats are hot and the air is crisp.

Two Towns: One Has Lakes, One Has Traffic

Madison. Population 269,840 at the 2020 census, Wisconsin's second-largest city, sitting on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona. Camp Randall Stadium sits on the grounds of a Civil War Union Army training camp and has been the Badgers' full-time home since 1917. Before the fourth quarter, the whole place does the "Jump Around." After every home game, the band plays the Fifth Quarter, a tradition that started in 1969. And cheese curds, when fresh, squeak against your teeth. That's the sound of Wisconsin, folks. Somebody pass the curds.

Los Angeles. USC plays at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, opened in 1923 and a National Historic Landmark. It's hosted two Summer Olympics. Very impressive. Their mascot, Traveler, is a white horse, though Wikipedia says most of the horses who've served as Traveler were actually grays whose coats turned completely white. Folks, in Wisconsin we call that a good winter.

And here's my weather report for our guests. The Trojans are coming from Southern California to Madison, at night, in late October. Bring a coat, fellas. Bring two. When the "Jump Around" starts in the fourth quarter, you'll be grateful for the exercise. And if anybody from Los Angeles needs a cheese wedge to keep their head warm, I'll lend you mine. That's Midwest hospitality.

Closing

Here's the deal. We lost a game in Pasadena we could've won if we'd kept the flags in the referees' pockets. Our defense is legit, our punter is a poet, and we're home, under the lights, with 75,822 seats full of people who know how to jump. USC is talented, and their quarterback is excellent. But Camp Randall at night is a different movie.

Oom-pah, oom-pah. On, Wisconsin.

My call: USC Trojans 26, Wisconsin Badgers 25.

blocks.text: Oom-pah, oom-pah, oom-pah-pah!
That's the polka break, folks. I do one before every big stat. It clears the mind and loosens the knees.

I'm Lars Ellefson, but everybody calls me Brat, after the sausage, not the attitude. I played fullback a long time ago, back when my knees still bent in both directions, and I bring a foam cheese wedge to every game. Home, road, the dentist. It's been to more places than my passport.
This week, the cheese wedge stays home, because the Trojans are coming to Camp Randall. Under the lights. In late October. In Wisconsin. Let's talk about it.
Part 1: A Long Way From Home, a Short Way From a Win
Saturday, Oct. 17, at the Rose Bowl. UCLA 17, Wisconsin 7.

I'll be straight with you, because that's the Wisconsin way. We didn't play clean. Oom-pah. Ten penalties for 108 yards, including four on our second drive, according to the AP. Coach Luke Fickell said afterward that we were undisciplined, and when the coach says it first, there's not much for a fella in a foam hat to add.

We went 1 for 6 on third down in the first half and had the ball for only about 11 1/2 minutes before halftime. Gavin Lahm missed his first field goal of the season, a 46-yarder, and we trailed 10-0 at the half.

Then the third quarter happened, and boy, did the Badgers show up. Colton Joseph ran it in from the 3 to make it 10-7, and our defense was flat-out nasty. UCLA ran 37 times for 120 yards, just 3.2 a carry. And Marvin Burks Jr. intercepted two passes. Two! Oom-pah-pah! Sean West punted five times, and four of them landed inside the 20. I'd like to shake that young man's hand, but I'm told that's not how it works, so I'll just clap really hard.
UCLA scored a touchdown in the fourth quarter to make it 17-7. On our next drive, Darrion Dupree was ruled short of a first down by a hair on a review, and that was about the ball game.

Joseph ran for 71 yards on 18 carries, but he completed only six of 16 passes for 66 yards. We'll need more than that. Everybody in the state knows it, including my cousin who thinks a forward pass is a type of curling shot.
The Season So Far

We're 4-2, 2-1 in the Big Ten. We lost to Notre Dame at Lambeau Field to open the year, 41-13. Then we beat Western Illinois 36-9 and Eastern Michigan 54-10. We won 24-20 at Penn State, then ranked 13th, and beat Michigan State 31-3. Then came Pasadena. Our defense allows 16.7 points a game, 24th in the country, and our pass defense ranks 20th, per the AP.
Part 2: Hollywood Comes to Madison
Saturday, Oct. 24, at 6:30 p.m. Central, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, No. 16 USC visits Camp Randall Stadium. NBC has it, and the lights will be on.

Fair is fair, so let's start with what USC does well. Oom-pah. The Trojans are 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big Ten, and they just beat Penn State 31-23 in front of 114,419 people in Happy Valley. Jayden Maiava has thrown for 2,045 yards, 18 touchdowns, and only three interceptions. Their passing offense ranks seventh in FBS at 310.1 yards a game, and they convert 51.2 of every 100 third downs. King Miller has 595 rushing yards. Kayden Dixon-Wyatt has 400 receiving yards. That's a good football team, and I'll shake their hands, too, if anyone lets me.

But here's what the scouting report says on the back page. USC's pass defense ranks 109th in FBS, allowing 239 yards a game, according to the AP, and its scoring defense ranks 80th. And Oregon beat the Trojans 41-27 at their own Coliseum last month.

So the recipe is simple, like a good brat. Our pass defense, 20th in the country, against their big-time passing game. And our quarterback, who can run, against a defense that gives up yards through the air. If Joseph can find Tyrell Henry a few times, this one gets interesting.
Who to Watch
Colton Joseph, quarterback: 1,198 passing yards and 10 touchdowns, plus a team-high 333 rushing yards.
Tyrell Henry, receiver: our leader with 27 catches for 343 yards.
Cooper Catalano, linebacker: 50 tackles.
Marvin Burks Jr., defensive back: two interceptions at the Rose Bowl.
Sebastian Cheeks: 2.5 sacks. Sean West, punter: four inside the 20 last week. A man after my own heart.
Jayden Maiava, USC quarterback: 301 yards and three touchdowns at Penn State.
Trent Mosley, USC receiver: nine catches for 111 yards against Penn State.
History, With Cheese

USC leads the series 7-1, according to CollegeFootballDigest, and won the last meeting, 38-21 in Los Angeles in 2024. The most famous game was the 1963 Rose Bowl, where the No. 2 Badgers rallied in the fourth quarter and fell to No. 1 USC, 42-37. Our lone win came in the 2015 Holiday Bowl, 23-21. Now, the Trojans have won twice at Camp Randall, in 1956 and 1965. That was a long time ago. I wasn't born yet. Neither was my cheese wedge.

And for the record, Wisconsin has its own championship history. The 1942 Badgers were named national champions by the Helms Athletic Foundation, the program's lone national title from a major selector, according to Wikipedia, and that team beat Ohio State along the way. We've won Rose Bowls over UCLA and Stanford, too. So we know a thing or two about beating teams from California. We just prefer to do it at home, where the brats are hot and the air is crisp.
Two Towns: One Has Lakes, One Has Traffic

Madison. Population 269,840 at the 2020 census, Wisconsin's second-largest city, sitting on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona. Camp Randall Stadium sits on the grounds of a Civil War Union Army training camp and has been the Badgers' full-time home since 1917. Before the fourth quarter, the whole place does the "Jump Around." After every home game, the band plays the Fifth Quarter, a tradition that started in 1969. And cheese curds, when fresh, squeak against your teeth. That's the sound of Wisconsin, folks. Somebody pass the curds.

Los Angeles. USC plays at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, opened in 1923 and a National Historic Landmark. It's hosted two Summer Olympics. Very impressive. Their mascot, Traveler, is a white horse, though Wikipedia says most of the horses who've served as Traveler were actually grays whose coats turned completely white. Folks, in Wisconsin we call that a good winter.

And here's my weather report for our guests. The Trojans are coming from Southern California to Madison, at night, in late October. Bring a coat, fellas. Bring two. When the "Jump Around" starts in the fourth quarter, you'll be grateful for the exercise. And if anybody from Los Angeles needs a cheese wedge to keep their head warm, I'll lend you mine. That's Midwest hospitality.
Closing

Here's the deal. We lost a game in Pasadena we could've won if we'd kept the flags in the referees' pockets. Our defense is legit, our punter is a poet, and we're home, under the lights, with 75,822 seats full of people who know how to jump. USC is talented, and their quarterback is excellent. But Camp Randall at night is a different movie.
Oom-pah, oom-pah. On, Wisconsin.
My call: USC Trojans 26, Wisconsin Badgers 25.

articles.title: Hydrate and Dominate: Kansas State Visits Tempe From a Town That Only Exists Because Its Boat Got Stuck
articles.byline: Skylar Vanterpool, The Arizona State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Kansas State (4-2) at Arizona State (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:45 p.m. ET, Mountain America Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Hi, Sun Devils! Skylar Vanterpool here, reporting live from a pool float on Tempe Town Lake in spirit, with a sports-science master's degree in my heart and a 40-ounce water bottle in my hand. Before we start: take a sip. I'm serious. Hydrate and dominate. I'll remind you again in 90 seconds.

This week is a two-part workout. Part one is the cooldown nobody wanted after a rough Saturday in Lubbock. Part two is the warmup for Kansas State, who are flying from the Little Apple into a desert afternoon. I hope they packed electrolytes.

Part 1: The Lubbock Cooldown

Let's be honest, because honesty is good for your heart rate. Texas Tech beat us 53-25 on Saturday in Lubbock. We're 3-3 and 1-2 in the Big 12. AP billed it as a matchup of the past two Big 12 champions, and I'll take the reminder: we won the league in 2024, and nobody can take that banner down.

But the first half was a tough set. Texas Tech scored on its last seven drives of the half and led 43-10 at the break. It started with a 24-yard interception return for a touchdown by Ben Roberts, three plays after we had recovered a fumble at our own 2. J'Koby Williams ran for 165 yards on just 11 carries, including touchdown runs of 62 and 38 yards. That's not a running back, babe. That's a sprinter who wandered onto the wrong field.

Now the bright spots, because every workout has a personal best. Cutter Boley hit Raiden Vines-Bright for a 74-yard touchdown in the first quarter. Boley went 5 of 10 for 124 yards with two interceptions before halftime. Then Mikey Keene came in and was smooth as a lap swim: 25 of 34 for 256 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. He threw a 2-yard touchdown to Reed Harris, his Big 12-leading eighth touchdown catch. Then he hit Cardae Mack for a 12-yarder and passed to Kyson Brown for the two-point conversion. Derek Eusebio caught seven passes for 89 yards.

Coach Kenny Dillingham said he would assess all personnel after watching the tape, and he praised Keene's leadership and veteran presence. So we'll see who starts. I trust the process. I also trust my water bottle.

The hard truth: two weeks ago, Baylor beat us 55-19 at home. We need this defense to recover, rebuild and come back stronger, like a good leg day.

Part 2: Kansas State Comes to the Desert

Saturday, 3:45 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2, at Mountain America Stadium in Tempe. Kansas State (4-2) at Arizona State (3-3). Arizona State leads the all-time series 6-1. We won the last meeting, 24-14 in Manhattan in 2024. The Wildcats' only win in the series came the last time they visited Tempe, in 2002. That was 24 years ago. Some of our students weren't even a sparkle in anybody's eye.

What the Wildcats Bring

I'll be a good host first. Kansas State is legit on the ground. The Wildcats rush for 239.8 yards a game, sixth in FBS, and they convert 59.3 of every 100 third downs, second in the country. Quarterback Avery Johnson has 1,301 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and three interceptions, and he leads the team with 462 rushing yards on 51 carries. Their pass defense allows 136.3 yards a game, third in FBS. Respect. Hydrate.

Last Saturday they beat Kansas 35-24 for their 18th straight win in that rivalry. Joe Jackson ran for 159 yards and Johnson ran for 132.

What the Wildcats Also Bring

But, babe, let's look at the film. Against Kansas, Kansas State fell behind 17-7 at home. AP described a "rash of mistakes." The Wildcats lost a fumble. They failed on two fourth downs inside the Kansas 12. And early in the third quarter, they ran four straight times from first-and-goal at the Kansas 5 and didn't score. Four tries from 5 yards. I can swim 5 yards underwater. Twice.

Two weeks earlier, Houston came to Manhattan and beat Kansas State 35-16. And in September they lost 31-26 at Cincinnati. So the Wildcats are 1-2 in conference play, exactly like us. Same record, very different sunscreen needs.

Their run defense is the soft spot: 160 yards allowed a game, 96th in FBS. Kyson Brown, who has 329 rushing yards this season, should have some room to stretch.

What We Bring

Our passing game ranks 23rd in FBS at 276.7 yards a game. Harris has 41 catches for 653 yards and eight touchdowns. Owen Long leads us with 53 tackles, and Julian Hugo has three sacks. Our defense allows 32 points a game, 120th in FBS, and I won't pretend that number is a personal record. But it's a home game in the desert, against a team built to grind the clock. Kansas State holds the ball for 32:44 a game. That's a lot of time standing in Arizona sunshine. Hydrate, Wildcats. I mean it kindly. Mostly.

Pool Deck Postcards: A Tale of Two Towns

Tempe. Let me show you around. Tempe has 180,587 people, per the 2020 census, and it's built around a real lake. Tempe Town Lake was made by damming the Salt River, and it hosts Ironman Arizona and the Rock 'n' Roll Marathon. Next to our stadium is Hayden Butte, widely known as A-Mountain, with our big "A" on its south face. Even our name is fancy. A pioneer named Darrell Duppa looked at the Salt River valley by the butte and compared it to the Vale of Tempe near Mount Olympus in Greece. We were named after a place near the home of the gods. Just saying.

And our mascot, Sparky, was designed by a Disney illustrator named Berk Anthony after students voted 819 to 196 in 1946 to become the Sun Devils. A Disney artist, babe. Sparky has a trident and a fancier animation pedigree than most cartoon characters.

Manhattan, Kansas. Now. I love a cute college town, and Manhattan is cute. It calls itself the "Little Apple." Which, okay, but you named yourself after New York and then called yourself little. That's like naming your pool "the Pacific, Jr."

And here's my most beloved town fact of the whole season. In June 1855, a steamboat called the Hartford, carrying settlers from Ohio, ran aground in the Kansas River. They had been headed 20 miles farther upstream. They got stuck, joined the local settlement, and insisted it be renamed Manhattan. Before that, the town had been named Boston. So Manhattan, Kansas, was named Boston first, and it only exists because a boat got stuck. Babe, that's not a founding. That's a towing problem.

Manhattan had 54,100 people at the 2020 census. Tempe has more than three Manhattans. The Konza Prairie south of town is a beautiful tallgrass preserve, and Aggieville is a six-block district of restaurants and shops. But when the Wildcats want water recreation, they drive 5 miles to Tuttle Creek Reservoir. We just walk to the lake. And our lake has an Ironman.

To be fair, Manhattan has very nice fall weather. We have late-October sun in the desert. Bring a hat. Bring two. Bring a water bottle. Okay, I'll bring you one.

The Final Rep

Here's how I see it. Kansas State runs the ball as well as anybody, but it stumbles near the goal and it gives up yards on the ground. Arizona State has a top-25 passing game, the Big 12's leading touchdown receiver and a home crowd that knows how to handle an afternoon in the sun. If we stay patient, tackle well and keep our heads cool, this one is ours to take.

Wear gold. Wear sunscreen. Drink water every 90 seconds. Hydrate and dominate, Sun Devils.

My call: Kansas State Wildcats 32, Arizona State Sun Devils 27.

articles.title: A Cardinal Dressed as a Tornado Walks Into Tucson: Iowa State Brings 200 Yards of Offense to the Desert
articles.byline: Inez Paloverde, The Arizona Fanatic
articles.matchup: Iowa State (3-3) at No. 25 Arizona (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, Casino Del Sol Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Hi, hi, hi, Wildcat family! Inez Paloverde here, prickly-pear lemonade in one hand, my old piccolo in the other, and a sunset over the Catalinas that I would rate a perfect ten if I didn't have to save some points for the road. Before you say it: yes, it's still warm in Tucson. It's a dry hype.

We had a bye last Saturday, so this is an honest two-week report. First, the last real game we played, which was gorgeous. Then the week off. Then a very warm desert welcome for Iowa State, a program whose mascot is a bird because, and I am not making this up, a tornado was too hard to sew.

Part 1: The Bye, and the Game Before It

Let me be clear so nobody writes in: Arizona did not play on Oct. 17. Our last game was Oct. 10 at West Virginia, and we won 52-31 in Morgantown. We're 5-1 and No. 25 in the AP poll, and AP noted it's our best six-game start since 2014.

And we did it without our top three wide receivers. Tre Spivey, Giovanni Richardson and Chris Hunter III were all out after getting hurt the week before against Cincinnati. We wish all three a full and speedy recovery, and that's all I'll say about it. Then a sophomore named Isaiah Mizell walked onto that field like the band had just started his song.

Mizell had entered the game with 176 receiving yards for the season. He left it with six catches for 183 yards and two touchdowns, both career highs. The first was a 14-yarder in the first quarter. The second was a short throw over the middle that he turned into a 72-yard touchdown with 13 seconds left in the third quarter. In marching-band terms, that's a soloist stepping out of the formation and hitting every note. Even AP sounded impressed.

Noah Fifita was surgical: 16 of 23 for a season-high 341 yards, three touchdowns and one interception. The third touchdown came on a trick play, a 42-yard toss to Brandon Phelps. Quincy Craig ran 40 yards for a score, Kedrick Reescano punched one in from 8, and Antwan Roberts Jr. added a 30-yard touchdown run to finish it. Lee Molette III scooped up a fumble on a pitch that went behind the runner and took it 32 yards for a touchdown. Cam Chapa made 15 tackles.

Honesty time, because I love you. West Virginia outgained us 522 to 482 and held the ball for 35:50. We won because we made fewer mistakes and took our chances. That's the cactus defense in a nutshell: it doesn't look like much from across the yard, and then you try to grab it.

Then came the bye. A week to heal, rest the legs and let Mizell's highlight reel play on a loop in my kitchen. We've now won four straight: Northern Illinois, Washington State, Cincinnati 34-7 and West Virginia. Our only loss was 28-17 at BYU, and BYU is currently the No. 2 team in the country, so I'm choosing to call that a scheduling compliment.

Part 2: Iowa State Comes to Tucson

Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2, Iowa State (3-3) visits No. 25 Arizona. It's the Cyclones' first trip to Tucson since 1966. The last time they were here, Arizona won 27-24. Welcome back, Cyclones. We kept the porch light on for 60 years.

The series is Arizona 4, Iowa State 2, with one tie. I will be gracious: Iowa State won last year's meeting 39-14 in Ames, and I have not forgotten one single yard of it. My piccolo remembers. My piccolo holds a grudge.

The Forecast in Ames Has Been Cloudy

Iowa State also had a bye last week, and its last game was Oct. 9 at BYU. It lost 24-10. The Cyclones finished with 200 yards of offense, which AP said was their lowest single-game output since 2018. They had 49 yards before halftime, their fewest since 2017. They went three-and-out on three straight second-quarter drives, and in that quarter BYU allowed them six yards. Six. I've marched farther than that during a halftime show while playing "Bear Down, Arizona."

Jaylen Raynor threw for 98 yards that night. On the season, Iowa State ranks 118th in FBS in passing yards (178.2 a game) and 127th in third-down conversions, at 31 of every 100 tries. When your weather-loving friends in Ames talk about a "Cyclone warning," friends, that warning appears to be for third and seven.

Now, to be fair, because Mama Paloverde raised a polite piccolo player: Aiden Flora is a real runner. He has 680 yards and six touchdowns on 90 carries, and Iowa State runs for 181.5 yards a game. And the Cyclones have scored on every single red zone trip this season, which leads FBS. So the plan is simple: don't let them get there. Make them throw it on third down. Repeat until sunset.

Arizona's Offense Is a Fireworks Show

Fifita has 1,756 yards, 16 touchdowns and four interceptions, and he's completing 73.3 of every 100 passes. Arizona throws for 306.7 yards a game, 10th in FBS, and scores 35.7 a game. Mizell leads us with 19 catches for 359 yards and four touchdowns, and remember, 183 of those came in one afternoon. Reescano leads the ground game with 262 yards and four scores.

blocks.text: Hi, hi, hi, Wildcat family! Inez Paloverde here, prickly-pear lemonade in one hand, my old piccolo in the other, and a sunset over the Catalinas that I would rate a perfect ten if I didn't have to save some points for the road. Before you say it: yes, it's still warm in Tucson. It's a dry hype.

We had a bye last Saturday, so this is an honest two-week report. First, the last real game we played, which was gorgeous. Then the week off. Then a very warm desert welcome for Iowa State, a program whose mascot is a bird because, and I am not making this up, a tornado was too hard to sew.
Part 1: The Bye, and the Game Before It

Let me be clear so nobody writes in: Arizona did not play on Oct. 17. Our last game was Oct. 10 at West Virginia, and we won 52-31 in Morgantown. We're 5-1 and No. 25 in the AP poll, and AP noted it's our best six-game start since 2014.

And we did it without our top three wide receivers. Tre Spivey, Giovanni Richardson and Chris Hunter III were all out after getting hurt the week before against Cincinnati. We wish all three a full and speedy recovery, and that's all I'll say about it. Then a sophomore named Isaiah Mizell walked onto that field like the band had just started his song.

Mizell had entered the game with 176 receiving yards for the season. He left it with six catches for 183 yards and two touchdowns, both career highs. The first was a 14-yarder in the first quarter. The second was a short throw over the middle that he turned into a 72-yard touchdown with 13 seconds left in the third quarter. In marching-band terms, that's a soloist stepping out of the formation and hitting every note. Even AP sounded impressed.

Noah Fifita was surgical: 16 of 23 for a season-high 341 yards, three touchdowns and one interception. The third touchdown came on a trick play, a 42-yard toss to Brandon Phelps. Quincy Craig ran 40 yards for a score, Kedrick Reescano punched one in from 8, and Antwan Roberts Jr. added a 30-yard touchdown run to finish it. Lee Molette III scooped up a fumble on a pitch that went behind the runner and took it 32 yards for a touchdown. Cam Chapa made 15 tackles.

Honesty time, because I love you. West Virginia outgained us 522 to 482 and held the ball for 35:50. We won because we made fewer mistakes and took our chances. That's the cactus defense in a nutshell: it doesn't look like much from across the yard, and then you try to grab it.

Then came the bye. A week to heal, rest the legs and let Mizell's highlight reel play on a loop in my kitchen. We've now won four straight: Northern Illinois, Washington State, Cincinnati 34-7 and West Virginia. Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2, Iowa State (3-3) visits No. 25 Arizona. It's the Cyclones' first trip to Tucson since 1966. The last time they were here, Arizona won 27-24. Welcome back, Cyclones. We kept the porch light on for 60 years.

The series is Arizona 4, Iowa State 2, with one tie. I will be gracious: Iowa State won last year's meeting 39-14 in Ames, and I have not forgotten one single yard of it. My piccolo remembers. My piccolo holds a grudge.

articles.title: Let's Renovate That Offense: Baylor Brings Its Toolbox to Lawrence, Where Even the Stadium Is Still a Construction Site
articles.byline: Maggie Whitlock, The Baylor Fanatic
articles.matchup: Baylor (4-2) at Kansas (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET, David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium, TNT
articles.text:
Hey, y'all! Maggie Whitlock here, coming to you from my design studio in Waco with a tape measure on my hip, paint swatches all over the counter and a green-and-gold throw pillow that says "Sic 'Em" in cross-stitch. I'm an interior designer by trade, which means when I watch football, I see the room. I see what's working, what's peeling, and what needs to come down to the studs.

And last Saturday, friends, we found some water damage.

Part 1: The Walkthrough Nobody Wanted

TCU beat us 17-6 on Saturday night at McLane Stadium. We're 4-2, 2-1 in the Big 12, and our four-game winning streak is over. I'm going to walk you through it like a home inspection, because an honest report is the only kind worth having.

The foundation is solid. Our defense held TCU to 17 points and 33 rushing yards on 30 carries. AP noted Baylor hasn't allowed more than 19 points in any game this season. Six straight games under 20 to start a season is our longest such run since 1966. That defense is load-bearing, y'all. You don't touch it. You just put a nice rug on it.

Safety Micah Gifford was everywhere. He forced a fumble at the end of a 31-yard catch, TCU recovered, and then on the very next play he intercepted Jaden Craig. That's a two-for-one, and I love a two-for-one.

The kitchen needs work. We moved the ball and then stalled. In the first half we had field goal attempts on three straight drives, and every one of them lasted at least 12 plays. Rhett Armstrong missed from 47, then made kicks of 39 and 32. Those were our only points. Three long drives, six points. That's spending all weekend on the backsplash and forgetting to hook up the sink.

DJ Lagway went 22 of 53 for 256 yards with an interception. We ran for 54 yards on 34 carries, and TCU defensive end Koron Hayward had three sacks. We went 6 for 21 on third down. Gavin Freeman caught seven passes for 76 yards and Louis Brown IV had five for 74.

And this is the same offense that hung 564 yards and 55 points on Arizona State two weeks earlier, with four Lagway touchdown passes. So the bones are good. The wiring just flickered. We don't tear down a house over one flickering light. We call the electrician.

Part 2: The Lawrence Project

Saturday, 1 p.m. Eastern, on TNT. Baylor (4-2) at Kansas (2-4), at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium in Lawrence.

Here's the paperwork, y'all. Baylor leads the series 19-4. We've won the last 15 meetings, every one since 2010. The last time Kansas beat Baylor was 2007. Our last trip to Lawrence, in 2021, ended 45-7. When you've been in a house that many times, you stop knocking.

Their Floor Plan

I'll start with the nice features, because every listing has some. Kansas runs the ball well, at 207.2 yards a game, 23rd in FBS. Quarterback Isaiah Marshall ran for 117 yards against Kansas State last week and has 1,294 passing yards this season. Dylan Edwards leads them with 375 rushing yards and four touchdowns, and Nik McMillan has 400 receiving yards on just 23 catches. Bryson Hayes returned a kickoff 95 yards for a touchdown last week. That's a lovely accent wall.

Now the inspection. Kansas is 0-3 in the Big 12 and has lost four of its last five games. Last week against Kansas State, the Jayhawks fumbled a punt snap for a safety. Marshall threw an interception in the end zone while they were trying to tie the game. Then a facemask penalty wiped out his 45-yard touchdown run. Y'all, that's a house where you fix the faucet and the ceiling falls in.

Their run defense allows 174.3 yards a game, 106th in FBS. Their passing game completes 52.7 of every 100 throws. Kansas State ran for 359 yards on them last week. We have the No. 9 run defense in FBS, allowing 86.7 yards a game. If their offense is a two-story house, we're about to take out the stairs.

Our Renovation Plan

This week's project is simple: open up the passing game. Baylor throws for 286 yards a game, 16th in FBS, and Freeman leads us with 49 catches for 555 yards. Kansas's pass defense is solid, at 174.3 yards a game, so we'll need to be smart. Dawson Pendergrass leads our runners with 327 yards. And we have to finish. We rank 119th in FBS in red zone scoring, coming away with points on three of every four trips. That's like building a gorgeous mudroom and forgetting the front door.

On defense, Daniel Cobbs has three sacks and Travion Barnes leads us with 36 tackles. Keep doing what you're doing, gentlemen. Don't let anyone touch the foundation.

Open House: A Tale of Two Towns

Waco. Let me give you the tour. Waco sits on the Brazos River, halfway from Dallas to Austin, and it had 138,486 people in the 2020 census. Dr Pepper was invented right here in 1885 at Morrison's Old Corner Drug Store. The Waco Suspension Bridge opened in 1870, the first bridge across the wide Brazos, where cowboys on the Chisholm Trail drove their cattle over the river. Downtown, Magnolia Market at the Silos fills two city blocks under a pair of 120-foot silos built in 1950. It's owned by Chip and Joanna Gaines of HGTV's Fixer Upper. I'm just saying: Waco knows renovation. My name is literally Magnolia.

And McLane Stadium sits on the north bank of the Brazos. It's one of a handful of major college stadiums where you can show up by boat, and fans "sailgate" in the Baylor Basin. We also have two live bear mascots, Judge Indy and Judge Belle. Real bears. You can't sew those.

Lawrence. Lawrence is a charming old town. But let's read the listing. Lawrence was named for Amos A. Lawrence, a man from Massachusetts. Even back in the 1850s, the folks over in Missouri called it "Yankee Town." Y'all have been decorated in New England style for 170 years. I respect a theme.

Then there's the mascot. By KU's own tradition, the Jayhawk is a combination of two birds: a blue jay, described as "a noisy, quarrelsome thing known to rob other nests," and a sparrow hawk. Friends, I've designed a lot of logos. I have never once had a client ask me to include "robs other nests" in the brand story.

And their stadium? Memorial Stadium opened in 1921, and it's one of the oldest college football stadiums in the country. Phase one of the rebuild, on the west side, finished in 2025. Phase two is still under construction and won't be at full capacity until the 2027 season. Bless them. Kansas is living through a renovation, and I'd know. Pro tip from a designer: never invite company over during a remodel.

Kansas is also, let's be honest, a basketball school. James Naismith founded the program there in 1898, and Allen Fieldhouse is famous. Lawrence had 94,934 people in 2020, and I'd guess most of them would rather be watching a jump shot. That's okay. We'll make it quick so they can get to practice.

The Final Walkthrough

Here's how I see it. Baylor has a top-10 run defense, a defense that hasn't allowed 20 points all season and a passing game that can light up a room when the wiring holds. Kansas runs the ball, has a dangerous return man, and has made a lot of costly mistakes. We've won 15 straight in this series. If we fix the red zone and protect Lagway, we'll leave Lawrence the way we leave every job site: cleaner than we found it.

Sic 'em, Bears. Let's renovate that offense.

My call: Baylor Bears 27, Kansas Jayhawks 26.

articles.title: Oh My Heck, We Beat Notre Dame! Now No. 2 BYU Visits the Bounce House, Home of a Team That Hasn't Won on the Road in 12 Tries
articles.byline: Bryce Halvorsen-Tuilagi, The BYU Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 2 BYU (6-0) at UCF (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Acrisure Bounce House, FOX
articles.text:
Oh my heck, Cougar Nation. Bryce Halvorsen-Tuilagi here, and I'm writing this from the trail up Y Mountain, which is where I chart every play, because the view is fantastic and the Wi-Fi is not. I'm a mountain-bike guide by trade, so I know a thing or two about steep climbs, tight switchbacks and finishing strong. And Saturday night, friends, we finished strong.

Why did the Notre Dame fan bring a ladder to Provo? He heard BYU was No. 2 now and wanted to see the view. Okay, that's a dad joke. But it's also true, so it counts double.

Part 1: The Night We Beat the Irish

BYU 28, Notre Dame 24. At LaVell Edwards Stadium, in front of 65,179 people, against a Notre Dame team that came in ranked No. 2 and riding a 16-game winning streak. It's our first win over Notre Dame since 2004 and our first win over a top-10 team since 2018. We're 6-0 for the third straight season, and AP voters moved us up to No. 2. Oh. My. Heck.

And Bear Bachmeier? That young man did everything except sell the concessions. He ran for two touchdowns, a 5-yarder on the opening drive and a 1-yard dive late in the second quarter. Sandwiched in the middle, he caught a 15-yard touchdown pass from Kyler Kasper. AP said he became the only FBS quarterback in the last 30 seasons to score both a rushing and a receiving touchdown against an AP Top 25 opponent. Then he threw for one too. Passing, rushing and receiving touchdowns in one game. That's a trail-guide hat trick: he led the hike, carried the gear and took the group photo.

He finished 23 of 36 for 224 yards. We led 21-10 at halftime, helped by Isaiah Glasker pouncing on a fumble when Notre Dame tried to spike the ball at our 5 in the final seconds of the half.

Now, I'll be honest, because honesty is the best switchback. The third quarter was a rough descent. A penalty on Kasper wiped out a 39-yard touchdown catch by JoJo Phillips that would have made it 28-10. Then we had a muffed punt return and a failed fake punt, and the Irish turned both into field goals. Jonaz Walton scored and ran in the two-point try to put Notre Dame up 24-21 with 9:31 left. Then Jayden Sanders intercepted Bear at the Notre Dame 15.

But the defense forced a three-and-out, and Bachmeier drove us 55 yards in 10 plays. He found Walker Lyons for a 6-yard touchdown with 1:47 left. Cade Uluave made nine tackles. Notre Dame drove to our 9, and the last pass fell incomplete in the end zone.

One more honest note. The next day, the Big 12 said its review found that time remained on the clock when that last pass hit the ground, and that the replay crew cleared the play incorrectly. The league said it would conduct a complete review. The final score stands, and I'll say this: our defense still had to make one more stop either way, and that defense has been doing it all year. We play the game in front of us, then we keep riding.

Part 2: Into the Bounce House

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, on FOX. No. 2 BYU (6-0) at UCF (3-3), at the Acrisure Bounce House in Orlando. BYU leads the series 4-1, and we've won the last three meetings, including 37-24 in Orlando in 2024 and 41-21 in Provo last season.

The Knights' Trail Map

First, kind words, because my mom reads these. UCF quarterback Keyone Jenkins is completing 70.3 of every 100 passes, with 806 yards, eight touchdowns and three interceptions. In his last game he threw four touchdowns at Oklahoma State. Duke Watson has 483 rushing yards. UCF scores on 95.5 of every 100 red zone trips, eighth in FBS, and it's plus-4 in turnover margin. And the Knights had a bye last week, so they're rested.

Now let's check the trail conditions. UCF lost that game at Oklahoma State 42-28. The Knights were driving for a possible go-ahead touchdown early in the fourth quarter when Jenkins's backward pass was knocked down and returned 28 yards for a touchdown. AP noted that UCF had lost a lead for the second straight week and had dropped 12 straight road games. Twelve! I've led hikes with fewer wrong turns than that.

Good news for the Knights: this one's at home. Bad news: their passing game ranks 106th in FBS, at 192.7 yards a game, and their pass defense ranks 105th. And UCF holds the ball for just 27:56 a game, 117th in the country. Our defense would love to send them right back to the sideline benches.

Our Gear Check

BYU's defense is the best gear in the pack. We allow 15.2 points a game (14th in FBS) and 86.2 rushing yards (eighth). Tausili Akana has 3.5 sacks and Uluave leads us with 35 tackles. On offense we convert 56.5 of every 100 third downs, third in the country, and we run for 206.7 yards a game. Bachmeier has 1,257 passing yards, nine touchdowns and just two interceptions this season, and Legend Glasker leads our receivers with 444 yards. LJ Martin has 344 rushing yards on just 44 carries.

We also have to clean up the little stuff. Two special teams mistakes almost cost us against Notre Dame. A good trail guide checks the brakes before every ride.

About That Name

UCF opened in 1968 as Florida Technological University. It kept that name until 1978, when the state changed it to the University of Central Florida. So the Knights already went through one rebrand. I respect a school that knows how to pivot. It's like me switching from road bikes to mountain bikes: same legs, much cooler stories.

Trailhead Talk: A Tale of Two Towns

Provo. Let me give you the view from the top. Provo had 115,162 people at the 2020 census. It sits on the east bank of Utah Lake at 4,549 feet, about 40 miles south of Salt Lake City, with the Wasatch Range rising right behind it. Y Mountain towers over the city, and the big block Y was first built on it in 1906 out of rock and lime. The trail to the Y climbs 1,074 feet, and it's one of the most hiked trails in Utah Valley. Provo was even nicknamed the Garden City for all its orchards.

And our home field, LaVell Edwards Stadium, seats 62,073, the largest in the Big 12, at an elevation of 4,649 feet. When visitors say they're out of breath, we just smile and offer them a water bottle.

Orlando. Orlando is a fun town with a lot of rides. It has more theme parks and attractions than anywhere else in the world. But here's my most beloved fact about it. The most famous one, Walt Disney World, isn't in Orlando at all. It's about 21 miles southwest, in a place called Bay Lake. The only theme park inside Orlando city limits is Universal. So Orlando's most famous landmark lives in a different town. That's like me telling you I live on Y Mountain when I actually live in a cul-de-sac near the Provo River. Close-ish. Not really.

And the Bounce House got its nickname because the stands shake when the crowd jumps in unison. Friends, out here we have actual mountains that don't move. That's the difference between a mountain and a bounce house. One is a geological formation. The other is a birthday party.

Orlando is also flat. The lakes are nice, but there's no Y on any hill, because there aren't any hills. I'll bring my mountain bike anyway, just in case. I'll ride it around the parking lot and pretend.

Coming Down the Mountain

Here's how I see it. BYU is 6-0, ranked No. 2, with a top-15 defense and a quarterback who can beat you three different ways. UCF is rested, scores in the red zone and will have the home crowd bouncing. But the Knights struggle to throw the ball, struggle to defend the pass and keep their offense on the field for less time than almost anybody. If our defense keeps doing its thing and we clean up special teams, we'll leave Orlando 7-0 and still smiling.

Why did the Cougar refuse to play hide-and-seek in Orlando? Because nobody can hide at No. 2. Oh my heck, I'm sorry. Go Cougs.

My call: BYU Cougars 28, UCF Knights 21.

articles.title: That's a Five-Way Take: Cincinnati's 100th Homecoming Welcomes Texas Tech and the 134th-Ranked Pass Defense in America
articles.byline: Lionel 'Skyline' Abernathy, The Cincinnati Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 8 Texas Tech (6-0) at Cincinnati (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Nippert Stadium, FS1
articles.text:
Bearcats, it's Skyline. Lionel Abernathy on my diploma, Skyline to everybody who has ever seen me order. I'm an engineering co-op kid, which means I chart everything, and I chart it in Cincinnati chili ways. A two-way is spaghetti and chili. A three-way adds cheese. Four-way adds onions or beans. A five-way has it all. Every play, every coach's haircut and every opponent gets a rating on that scale. It's science. Delicious science.

This week is huge. It's the University of Cincinnati's 100th Homecoming. One hundred! The parade goes down Clifton Avenue at 8 a.m., we're wearing red, and No. 8 Texas Tech is coming to Nippert for a noon kickoff. But first, an honest postgame report from Morgantown, because a good engineer reviews the failure before the next build.

Part 1: The Morgantown Heartbreaker (a Two-Way, No Cheese)

West Virginia beat us 45-42 on Saturday when Jack Cassidy kicked a 35-yard field goal as time ran out. We're 4-2 and 1-2 in the Big 12, and we've lost two straight, around our bye week.

Here's what kills me. AP said West Virginia never led until that final kick. Not once. The Cincinnati Enquirer counted six different times we were ahead. We outgained them 622 to 598. We didn't turn the ball over. And we lost.

JC French IV was outstanding. He went 22 of 30 for a career-high 389 yards and three touchdowns, and he ran for another. He still hasn't thrown an interception all season. Cole Tabb ran for 118 yards and two touchdowns on 15 carries and caught an 11-yard touchdown pass, too. JV Gibson caught seven passes and opened the scoring on a 4-yard touchdown. Isaiah Johnson had a 51-yard touchdown catch, and Malachi Henry caught just two balls for 128 yards. That's a 64-yard average, folks. That's not a reception. That's a delivery.

Tabb's 6-yard touchdown run put us up 42-35 with 5:35 left. Then the defense let it slip. West Virginia answered in five plays with a 40-yard touchdown pass to Cam Cook. We punted and pinned them at their own 1 with 2:05 left, which is a beautiful punt, a true five-way punt. Then Mike Hawkins Jr. hit Prince Strachan for 41 yards on third down and 40 more two plays later. Hawkins finished with a career-high 464 passing yards.

So the offense was a five-way. The defense? That was a plain bowl of spaghetti. No chili. No cheese. Just noodles. We've got to tackle better, and we all know it.

Part 2: The 100th Homecoming

Saturday, noon Eastern, FS1, at Nippert Stadium. No. 8 Texas Tech (6-0) at Cincinnati (4-2). It's the 100th Homecoming at UC, and the school will honor the 50th the school's Athletics Hall of Fame class, which includes former Bearcat football star Connor Barwin. The parade starts at 8 a.m. on Clifton Avenue. Wear red. Bring your appetite.

The series is Texas Tech 1, Cincinnati 0, with one tie. We tied 10-10 at Nippert in 1968, and the Red Raiders won 44-41 in Lubbock in 2024. So the last two meetings were decided by a combined three points. This one will be close. I can feel it in my spoon.

Texas Tech, Rated in Chili Ways

The run defense: five-way. I'll be honest. Texas Tech allows 82 rushing yards a game, fifth in FBS. That's elite. That's every topping.

The offense: four-way. The Red Raiders score 37.8 points a game. J'Koby Williams ran for 165 yards on 11 carries against Arizona State, with touchdowns of 62 and 38 yards, and leads them with 538 yards. Will Hammond completed 18 of 26 for 232 yards. They're good. Onions, but no beans.

The pass defense: two-way. Now, friends, look at this. Texas Tech allows 281.8 passing yards a game. That ranks 134th in FBS. One hundred thirty-fourth! There are barely more teams than that in the whole division. That's a pass defense that shows up to the chili parlor and orders spaghetti, plain.

And remember who just threw for 389 yards. French is completing 70.6 of every 100 passes with nine touchdowns and zero interceptions. Against a pass defense ranked 134th, I'm ordering the five-way and asking for extra cheese.

The history: a sad one-way. Texas Tech won the Big 12 last year and made the College Football Playoff. Congratulations. Then, in the Orange Bowl quarterfinal, Oregon beat the Red Raiders 23-0. Zero points. In a playoff game. In South Florida. That's a bowl of plain chili with no spaghetti under it, and you dropped the spoon. Also, the Red Raiders needed a two-point game to beat Houston, 28-26, earlier this year.

Our Recipe

Cincinnati runs for 231.2 yards a game, 11th in FBS. Tabb has 448 yards and eight touchdowns on just 49 carries. We're plus-5 in turnover margin, 15th in the country. Jonathan Thompson leads the defense with 52 tackles, and Josh Hough has three sacks.

And yes, our pass defense has had trouble too. It allows 294 yards a game, 136th, and opponents convert 49.4 of every 100 third downs. Texas Tech's passing game ranks 72nd, so this is a chance to steady things up. Tackle the catch. Get off the field. Make it a three-way at least.

The Parlor Board: A Tale of Two Towns

Cincinnati. We're the Queen City. We're the City of Seven Hills, named after the seven hills of Rome. For a while we were "Porkopolis," and honestly I wish we'd kept it. We had 309,317 people in the 2020 census, and that census showed our first population growth since 1950. We're the home of Cincinnati chili, born in 1922 at a little stand called the Empress. And the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings were baseball's first all-professional team. We invented professional baseball, folks. You're welcome, America.

Nippert Stadium has been home to the Bearcats in some form since 1901, and in concrete since 1915. That makes it the fourth-oldest playing site in college football. On Saturday, it gets its 100th Homecoming. Five-way. Every topping. Extra crackers.

Lubbock. Lubbock is a proud town of 257,141 people out on the Llano Estacado, which is a fancy way of saying "very flat." Its nickname is "Hub City." That's a fine name for a bicycle wheel. The town is also, per the encyclopedia, the 10th-windiest city in the United States. You know what you need in a windy town? Something heavy to hold down your lunch. Like a five-way.

And Lubbock's most famous story is the "Lubbock Lights," a series of sightings that became one of the first big UFO cases in America. Friends, if I lived in a town that flat, I'd be looking at the sky a lot, too. There's nothing else to look at.

Even their stadium can't settle on a name. ESPN now lists it as Galaxy Stadium. Fitting for the UFO town. But "The Jones" opened in 1947. Nippert was already 32 years old in concrete by then. We were hosting football before Lubbock's stadium was a sketch.

To be fair, Lubbock gave us Buddy Holly, and he's a legend. I'll play "That'll Be the Day" in the parking lot. Then I'll play it again at about 3 p.m., as a message to our guests.

The Final Recipe

Here's how I see it. Texas Tech has a great run defense, an explosive running back and a perfect record. Cincinnati has a quarterback who hasn't thrown an interception all season, a top-15 running game, a plus turnover margin and a 100th Homecoming crowd. And Tech's pass defense ranks 134th. If we tackle in the back end and let French cook, this one's a five-way.

That's a five-way take, Bearcats. See you on Clifton.

My call: Texas Tech Red Raiders 34, Cincinnati Bearcats 23.

Cincinnati. We're the Queen City. We're the City of Seven Hills, named after the seven hills of Rome. For a while we were "Porkopolis," and honestly I wish we'd kept it. We had 309,317 people in the 2020 census, and that census showed our first population growth since 1950. We're the home of Cincinnati chili, born in 1922 at a little stand called the Empress. And the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings were baseball's first all-professional team. We invented professional baseball, folks. You're welcome, America.

Nippert Stadium has been home to the Bearcats in some form since 1901, and in concrete since 1915. That makes it the fourth-oldest playing site in college football. On Saturday, it gets its 100th Homecoming. Five-way. Every topping. Extra crackers.

Lubbock. Lubbock is a proud town of 257,141 people out on the Llano Estacado, which is a fancy way of saying "very flat." Its nickname is "Hub City." That's a fine name for a bicycle wheel. The town is also, per the encyclopedia, the 10th-windiest city in the United States. You know what you need in a windy town? Something heavy to hold down your lunch. Like a five-way.

And Lubbock's most famous story is the "Lubbock Lights," a series of sightings that became one of the first big UFO cases in America. Friends, if I lived in a town that flat, I'd be looking at the sky a lot, too. There's nothing else to look at.

Even their stadium can't settle on a name. ESPN now lists it as Galaxy Stadium. Fitting for the UFO town. But "The Jones" opened in 1947. Nippert was already 32 years old in concrete by then. We were hosting football before Lubbock's stadium was a sketch.
To be fair, Lubbock gave us Buddy Holly, and he's a legend. I'll play "That'll Be the Day" in the parking lot. Then I'll play it again at about 3 p.m., as a message to our guests.
The Final Recipe

Here's how I see it. Texas Tech has a great run defense, an explosive running back and a perfect record. Cincinnati has a quarterback who hasn't thrown an interception all season, a top-15 running game, a plus turnover margin and a 100th Homecoming crowd. And Tech's pass defense ranks 134th. If we tackle in the back end and let French cook, this one's a five-way.
That's a five-way take, Bearcats. See you on Clifton.
My call: Texas Tech Red Raiders 34, Cincinnati Bearcats 23.

articles.title: Statistically, That's Rad: Colorado Crashes Oklahoma State's Self-Proclaimed 'Greatest Homecoming,' Two Years After a 52-0 Night in Boulder
articles.byline: Moss Feldstein, The Colorado Fanatic
articles.matchup: Colorado (2-4) at Oklahoma State (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7 p.m. ET, Boone Pickens Stadium, FS1
articles.text:
Hey, Buffs. Moss Feldstein here, swinging gently in my hammock under the Flatirons with a kombucha in one hand and a laptop full of regression models in the other. I'm a physicist, I play a mean game of hacky sack, and I run a quant model of this team that I update every Sunday at sunrise. This Sunday, the model and I had a long, honest talk. It was mostly the model talking. I mostly sipped.

Let's go through it together, man. Then let's talk about Stillwater, where they're throwing what they call America's Greatest Homecoming, and we're the guests. Statistically, that's rad.

Part 1: The Late-Night Rally That Almost Was

Utah beat us 27-24 at Folsom Field in a game that ended after midnight. We're 2-4 and 0-3 in the Big 12, and we've lost four straight. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Sugar's bad for you anyway.

The first half was a tough data set. AP pointed out that we had more penalty yards (82) than yards of offense (70) at halftime. My model doesn't even have a variable for that. Utah led 13-0 at the break. We finished with 10 penalties for 93 yards. Penalties, friends, are the one stat you can fix by just chilling out.

But the second half? Pure energy. Isaac Wilson, starting against his old team, hit JaQuail Smith on a 68-yard touchdown pass on our first drive of the half. DeKalon Taylor ran 18 yards for another score. Elliott Arnold kicked a 32-yard field goal, and suddenly we led 17-13. We gained 324 of our 394 yards after halftime. That's not a regression to the mean. That's a progression to the rad.

Utah answered with two Devon Dampier touchdown passes to Braden Pegan. Wilson found DeAndre Moore Jr. for a 2-yard touchdown with 1:21 left to cut it to three. Utah recovered the onside kick, but we got the ball back. Then Wilson found an opening in the middle of the field and pitched to Quanell Farrakhan Jr., who ran to the Utah 38. A review ruled it an illegal forward pass. We tried one last throw, and it didn't connect.

Wilson finished with 256 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions. Naeten Mitchell and Dylan Manuel each intercepted Dampier. And Utah now owns the longest active winning streak in FBS, 12 straight. We had them sweating at midnight. The model calls that a "moral victory coefficient," which isn't a real thing, but it should be.

Part 2: Crashing the Homecoming

Saturday, 7 p.m. Eastern, FS1, at Boone Pickens Stadium. Colorado (2-4) at Oklahoma State (4-2). It's Oklahoma State's homecoming, billed by the university as "America's Greatest Homecoming Celebration." The game is listed as sold out.

Colorado leads the all-time series 27-20-1. And the last time these teams met, Nov. 29, 2024, in Boulder, the final score was Colorado 52, Oklahoma State 0. Fifty-two to zero. I've run that number through every model I own. They all just print a little smiley face.

Oklahoma State, by the Numbers

I'll be fair first, because good science is honest. Oklahoma State's offense is legit. It gains 517.7 yards a game, fifth in FBS, and passes for 329.5 yards a game, fourth. Drew Mestemaker has 1,940 yards, 16 touchdowns and six interceptions. Wyatt Young has 561 receiving yards, and Caleb Hawkins has 592 rushing yards. The Cowboys beat Oregon 39-31 in September. Respect.

Now the rest of the data.

Last Saturday they lost 35-32 at Houston. They trailed 14-3 at halftime, and AP said they never got closer than three points after that. Their coach talked openly about the team's slow starts after the game. So, man, the model has a suggestion: show up to the first half. It's half the game. That's just math.

Oklahoma State converts 34.3 of every 100 third downs, 112th in FBS, and it's minus-4 in turnover margin, 113th. Its run defense allows 151.2 yards a game, 87th. And it opened this season with a 24-10 loss at Tulsa. Last season, per CollegeFootballData, the Cowboys went 1-11.

Honest Buffs Data

We have issues too, and I'll own them. Colorado ranks 136th in FBS in penalty yards, at 84.3 a game. We score on 70.6 of every 100 red zone trips, 130th. We're minus-6 in turnover margin, 126th. So this is a game between two teams that like to hand the ball to the other team. The model calls it "chaos football." I call it "Saturday."

The bright spots: Joseph Williams has 37 catches for 508 yards and five touchdowns. Lamont Lester Jr. has four sacks, and Randon Fontenette leads us with 49 tackles. Our passing game is 46th in FBS. And Oklahoma State's pass defense ranks 66th, so there's room to throw.

The equation for Saturday is simple. Fewer flags plus more red zone touchdowns equals a happy bus ride home. Clean it up, play the whole first half, and good things happen.

The Hammock Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Boulder. We sit at the base of the Rocky Mountain foothills at 5,430 feet. The Flatirons, giant tilted slabs of sedimentary stone, rise west of town and are the symbol of Boulder. In 1967, Boulder voters approved a dedicated tax to buy open space around the city, and in 1972 the city limited building heights to protect the views of the mountains. Think about that, man: Boulder passed a law so nobody could block the view. That's my kind of government.

And at Folsom Field, which opened in 1924 and sits 5,360 feet above sea level, Ralphie the Buffalo runs a horseshoe around the field before each half. She can hit 25 miles per hour, and it takes five handlers to guide her. A real bison. Running. At altitude. Statistically, that's the most rad thing in college football.

Stillwater. Stillwater is a friendly college town of 48,394. Boulder has more than two Stillwaters. And the name? Nobody's totally sure. The town's history, as the encyclopedia tells it, lists three legends. One says the creek water was always still. One says cattlemen always found the water "still there." The third says a man walked up to the creek and announced, "This town should be named Still Water." So the official origin story of Stillwater is, essentially, "Somebody looked at a creek." I've looked at a lot of creeks, man. I didn't name a single one.

Oklahoma State's colors are fun too. The school's original mascot was a tiger copied from Princeton, which is why the Cowboys wear orange and black. So the Cowboys are dressed like a tiger from New Jersey. I'm not judging. I wear socks with sandals. But I know what I'm doing.

To be fair, Stillwater has Eskimo Joe's and the Strip, where Garth Brooks got his start, and Boone Pickens Stadium has the oldest field in the Big 12. And I'll admit the homecoming week sounds charming, with a parade and a fountain they dye for the occasion. We'll try not to spoil it. We'll mostly try.

The Model's Final Output

Here's what my numbers say. Oklahoma State has the better offense this year, no question. But it starts slow, it struggles on third down, it gives the ball away and its run defense is soft. Colorado has to stop the flags, finish in the red zone and play all 60 minutes the way it played the second half against Utah. Do that, and the guests could get the last laugh at somebody else's party.

Grab a kombucha. Swing in a hammock. Believe in variance. Statistically, that's rad.

My call: Oklahoma State Cowboys 30, Colorado Buffaloes 21.

articles.title: Houston, We Have Liftoff: No. 14 Houston Climbs 4,600 Feet to Face No. 10 Utah in a City That Got Demoted From 'Great' in 1868
articles.byline: Yolanda 'Yo' Pacheco, The Houston Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 14 Houston (6-1) at No. 10 Utah (6-0), Sat., Oct. 24, 10:15 p.m. ET, Rice-Eccles Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Mission Control to Coog Nation, do you copy? Yo Pacheco here. By day I'm an engineer who thinks about rockets. By night I'm a film grinder with a remote control, a legal pad and a habit of pausing every Houston snap to admire it. And this week, my friends, the flight plan goes straight up. Houston plays at Utah, and the field at Rice-Eccles Stadium sits 4,637 feet above sea level. Downtown Houston sits at about 50 feet. That's not a road trip. That's a launch.

Houston, we have liftoff... I mean, a story.

Part 1: Five Touchdowns and a Clean Landing

No. 20 Houston beat No. 18 Oklahoma State 35-32 at TDECU Stadium on Saturday night. That's four straight wins, and AP noted it was our first win over a ranked team this season. We're 6-1 and 3-1 in the Big 12, and this week the AP poll moved us up to No. 14.

Conner Weigman was the whole mission crew. He went 24 of 33 for 343 yards and tied his career high with five touchdown passes, of 2, 7, 2, 21 and 48 yards. He also ran for 52 yards. Amare Thomas caught seven passes for 126 yards and two touchdowns. Trent Walker had seven catches for 104 yards and a score. Patrick Overmyer and Koby Young caught touchdowns too, and Koby's 48-yarder in the fourth quarter put us up 35-25.

We led 14-3 at halftime. Then the second half turned into a fireworks show, with the two teams combining for 50 points and more than 650 yards. Oklahoma State got within three on an 8-yard touchdown with 4:54 left. And then came my most beloved part of any mission: the landing.

On third-and-7 with about two and a half minutes left, Weigman hit Walker for 18 yards. Then Weigman ran for another first down with two minutes left, and we took knees. Houston held the ball for 35:12 and went 3 for 3 on fourth down. Will James had an interception, and Kentrell Webb had nine tackles. We gained 505 yards.

Coach Willie Fritz had nothing but praise for his quarterback afterward, and honestly, same, Coach. Same.

Part 2: Mission Control, Salt Lake City

Saturday, 10:15 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. No. 14 Houston (6-1) at No. 10 Utah (6-0) at Rice-Eccles Stadium. Late-night college football from the mountains. Grab a snack and a blanket, Houston. Night launches are the prettiest ones.

The Flight Data

These teams are almost mirror images, and I love a good symmetry problem. Utah gains 486.5 yards a game, ninth in FBS. We gain 485.1, 10th. Utah runs for 220.2 a game. We run for 220.3. Both teams hold the ball for about 33 and a half minutes a game, eighth and ninth in FBS.

But here's where my calculator starts beeping. Houston converts 61.4 of every 100 third downs, and that ranks first in all of FBS. First! Utah went 8 for 17 on third down at Colorado last week. Our run defense allows 82.6 yards a game, sixth in the country, and we're plus-5 in turnover margin, 15th.

Weigman has 1,771 yards, 20 touchdowns and just two interceptions this season. Makhi Hughes has 464 rushing yards, Thomas has 36 catches for 487 yards and six scores, Webb leads us with 43 tackles and Javion White has 2.5 sacks.

The Utah Readout

I respect Utah. It's 6-0 for the first time since 2015, and it's won 12 straight dating to last season, which AP says is now the longest active winning streak in FBS. Its defense allows 14.8 points a game, 12th in FBS. AP says the Utes have scored a touchdown on their opening drive in every game and outscored opponents 75-3 in the first quarter. Devon Dampier has 1,412 passing yards and 15 touchdowns, and Wayshawn Parker has 597 rushing yards.

Now the rest of the readout.

Last week Utah went to Boulder and beat a Colorado team that's now 2-4 by three points. The Utes led 13-0 at halftime and then trailed 17-13 in the third quarter. Dampier threw two interceptions. Colorado had the ball near the Utah 38 in the final minute before a review wiped out the play. That's not a smooth orbit. That's a capsule wobbling on reentry.

And let's look at Utah's schedule so far: Idaho, Arkansas, Utah State, Iowa State, Kansas and Colorado. Respectfully, Houston is the first team on the docket ranked in this week's AP top 25. Utah's pass defense allows 214.5 yards a game, 75th, and Weigman has been throwing like a man with a guidance system.

Oh, and the series? Houston leads it 5-0, according to CollegeFootballData. The last meeting, in 2024, went Houston 17, Utah 14.

The Honest Pre-Flight Checklist

I promised myself I'd never fudge the data. Our pass defense allows 265 yards a game, 129th in FBS. We need to tighten that up against Dampier. We also lost at Texas Tech 28-26 back in September. And this kickoff is 8:15 p.m. Mountain time, in thin air, in front of a loud crowd. The fix is the same as always: win third down, run the ball, protect it and keep that Utah offense standing on the sideline watching.

Space City vs. Salt Lake City

Houston. We're the fourth-most populous city in the United States and the biggest in Texas. Houston became the official "Space City" in 1967, and NASA's Johnson Space Center has run Mission Control for every NASA human spaceflight since Gemini 4. Its radio call sign is "Houston." Think about that. When astronauts need help, they call our town by name. We're also home to the Texas Medical Center, the world's largest concentration of healthcare and research institutions. And in 1965, Houston opened the Astrodome, the world's first indoor domed sports stadium. We invented putting a roof on football. You're welcome, everybody.

Salt Lake City. Salt Lake City is beautiful, with mountains all around it and a stadium that hosted the opening ceremonies of the 2002 Winter Olympics. I'll give them that. But here's a fun bit of history. The city was originally called Great Salt Lake City. In 1868, they dropped the word "Great." On purpose. Houston would never voluntarily give up an adjective. We'd add three.

Then there's the lake itself. The Great Salt Lake is far saltier than seawater, and it's been called "America's Dead Sea." It has no outlet except evaporation. So the most famous body of water in town is a lake that never goes anywhere. Houston has bayous that flow to the Gulf. Salt Lake has a lake that's just stuck in its seat, like a kid at the end of a long school day.

And the addresses there run on a compass grid measured from a single point downtown, so directions sound like a math worksheet. As an engineer, I actually love that. As a visitor, I'll be using my phone.

Final Countdown

Here's the flight plan. Utah has the streak, the altitude and a late-night crowd. Houston has the best third-down offense in the country, a top-10 run defense, a quarterback with 20 touchdowns and two interceptions, and five wins in five meetings with Utah. If we stay on the field and keep their offense off it, this rocket clears the mountains. I believe in my crew.

Houston, we have liftoff.

My call: Utah Utes 34, Houston Cougars 25.
