Saturday, 10:15 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. No. 14 Houston (6-1) at No. 10 Utah (6-0) at Rice-Eccles Stadium. Late-night college football from the mountains. Grab a snack and a blanket, Houston. Night launches are the prettiest ones.
The Flight Data

These teams are almost mirror images, and I love a good symmetry problem. Utah gains 486.5 yards a game, ninth in FBS. We gain 485.1, 10th. Utah runs for 220.2 a game. We run for 220.3. Both teams hold the ball for about 33 and a half minutes a game, eighth and ninth in FBS.

But here's where my calculator starts beeping. Houston converts 61.4 of every 100 third downs, and that ranks first in all of FBS. First! Utah went 8 for 17 on third down at Colorado last week. Our run defense allows 82.6 yards a game, sixth in the country, and we're plus-5 in turnover margin, 15th.

Weigman has 1,771 yards, 20 touchdowns and just two interceptions this season. Makhi Hughes has 464 rushing yards, Thomas has 36 catches for 487 yards and six scores, Webb leads us with 43 tackles and Javion White has 2.5 sacks.
The Utah Readout

I respect Utah. It's 6-0 for the first time since 2015, and it's won 12 straight dating to last season, which AP says is now the longest active winning streak in FBS. Its defense allows 14.8 points a game, 12th in FBS. AP says the Utes have scored a touchdown on their opening drive in every game and outscored opponents 75-3 in the first quarter. Devon Dampier has 1,412 passing yards and 15 touchdowns, and Wayshawn Parker has 597 rushing yards.
Now the rest of the readout.

Last week Utah went to Boulder and beat a Colorado team that's now 2-4 by three points. The Utes led 13-0 at halftime and then trailed 17-13 in the third quarter. Dampier threw two interceptions. Colorado had the ball near the Utah 38 in the final minute before a review wiped out the play. That's not a smooth orbit. That's a capsule wobbling on reentry.

And let's look at Utah's schedule so far: Idaho, Arkansas, Utah State, Iowa State, Kansas and Colorado. Respectfully, Houston is the first team on the docket ranked in this week's AP top 25. Utah's pass defense allows 214.5 yards a game, 75th, and Weigman has been throwing like a man with a guidance system.
Oh, and the series? Houston leads it 5-0, according to CollegeFootballData. The last meeting, in 2024, went Houston 17, Utah 14.
The Honest Pre-Flight Checklist

I promised myself I'd never fudge the data. Our pass defense allows 265 yards a game, 129th in FBS. We need to tighten that up against Dampier. We also lost at Texas Tech 28-26 back in September. And this kickoff is 8:15 p.m. Mountain time, in thin air, in front of a loud crowd. The fix is the same as always: win third down, run the ball, protect it and keep that Utah offense standing on the sideline watching.
Space City vs. Salt Lake City

Houston. We're the fourth-most populous city in the United States and the biggest in Texas. Houston became the official "Space City" in 1967, and NASA's Johnson Space Center has run Mission Control for every NASA human spaceflight since Gemini 4. Its radio call sign is "Houston." Think about that. When astronauts need help, they call our town by name. We're also home to the Texas Medical Center, the world's largest concentration of healthcare and research institutions. And in 1965, Houston opened the Astrodome, the world's first indoor domed sports stadium. We invented putting a roof on football. You're welcome, everybody.

Salt Lake City. Salt Lake City is beautiful, with mountains all around it and a stadium that hosted the opening ceremonies of the 2002 Winter Olympics. I'll give them that. But here's a fun bit of history. The city was originally called Great Salt Lake City. In 1868, they dropped the word "Great." On purpose. Houston would never voluntarily give up an adjective. We'd add three.

Then there's the lake itself. The Great Salt Lake is far saltier than seawater, and it's been called "America's Dead Sea." It has no outlet except evaporation. So the most famous body of water in town is a lake that never goes anywhere. Houston has bayous that flow to the Gulf. Salt Lake has a lake that's just stuck in its seat, like a kid at the end of a long school day.

And the addresses there run on a compass grid measured from a single point downtown, so directions sound like a math worksheet. As an engineer, I actually love that. As a visitor, I'll be using my phone.
Final Countdown

Here's the flight plan. Utah has the streak, the altitude and a late-night crowd. Houston has the best third-down offense in the country, a top-10 run defense, a quarterback with 20 touchdowns and two interceptions, and five wins in five meetings with Utah. If we stay on the field and keep their offense off it, this rocket clears the mountains. I believe in my crew.
Houston, we have liftoff.
My call: Utah Utes 34, Houston Cougars 25.

articles.title: Cyclone Warning for the Desert: Iowa State Heads to a Town With 158 Days a Year Over 90 Degrees and a Wildcat Team That Can't Hold the Football
articles.byline: Twyla Hemmingsen, The Iowa State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Iowa State (3-3) at No. 25 Arizona (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, Casino Del Sol Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Good morning, Cyclone Nation, and welcome to the Ames weather center. Here's your forecast. Today in central Iowa: crisp, golden and gorgeous, with cornfields finished and the Campanile looking like a postcard. Saturday night in Tucson, Arizona: warm, dry and a strong chance of loud, mostly from the visiting section. A Cyclone warning is in effect for the entire Sonoran Desert.

I'm Twyla Hemmingsen. I studied meteorology, I chase storms in the off-season, and I keep a tiny anemometer on my desk for emotional support. This week I owe you an honest two-week report, because we had a bye on Oct. 17, and then a full storm-spotter's briefing on our trip to the desert.

Part 1: The Fog in Provo, and a Week to Clear It

I'll start with the weather nobody wanted. Our last game was Friday, Oct. 9, at BYU, and we lost 24-10. I won't sugarcoat it, because a forecaster who lies is just a person with a map.

We finished with 200 yards of offense. AP said that was our lowest single-game output since 2018. We had 49 yards before halftime, our fewest since 2017, and we went three-and-out on three straight second-quarter drives. That's not a storm, friends. That's a dead calm. My anemometer didn't spin once.

Jaylen Raynor went 16 of 29 for 98 yards and a touchdown. Aiden Flora ran 17 times for 86 yards, though only 11 of those came before halftime. Linebacker Sullivan Schlimgen made 10 tackles, and he leads the team with 56 this season. Bless that young man. He was out there all night like a storm siren that never gets a break.

Now here's the bright spot on the radar. In the fourth quarter, Tiger Bachmeier fumbled a BYU punt, Torrence Sanders recovered at the BYU 49, and we drove for our only touchdown, a 1-yard pass from Raynor to Christian Greenlaw. We put up 131 yards and seven first downs on our three fourth-quarter drives. And our defense, give it credit, stopped BYU on fourth down three times, twice inside our 5. BYU, I'll note, is now the No. 2 team in the country.

Three and three is where we are, friends, not where we have to stay. That's a forecast I can get behind. Then came the bye: two weeks to fix the pass game, rest up and let the clouds clear.

Part 2: Into the Desert

Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2. Iowa State (3-3) at No. 25 Arizona (5-1). It's our first trip to Tucson since 1966. Arizona leads the series 4-2-1, but I'd like to remind everyone, gently, that the most recent meeting was last season in Ames, and Iowa State won it 39-14. That was a 25-point storm system. Arizona is still sweeping up.

What's Rolling In From Ames

Our forecast starts on the ground. Iowa State runs for 181.5 yards a game, and Aiden Flora has 680 yards and six touchdowns on just 90 carries. That's 7.6 yards a carry, friends. That's not a running back. That's a gust front.

And here's my most beloved stat in the whole Cyclone almanac: Iowa State leads FBS in red zone offense. We've scored on every single trip inside the 20 this season. Every one. When we get close, the barometer drops and something happens.

Now the honest part. Our passing game ranks 118th in FBS at 178.2 yards a game, and we convert just 31 of every 100 third downs, 127th. Raynor has 1,001 yards, seven touchdowns and four interceptions. We need the passing game to show up the way the wind shows up in Ames in March, which is to say all at once and with a lot of attitude.

On defense, defensive end Isaac Terrell leads us with three sacks. We allow 21.7 points a game, and we're plus-3 in turnover margin, 34th in the country.

What Tucson Is Bringing

I'll be fair first, because my grandma watches every forecast. Noah Fifita is very good. He has 1,756 yards, 16 touchdowns and four interceptions, and he's completing 73.3 of every 100 throws. Arizona throws for 306.7 yards a game, 10th in FBS. Two weeks ago Isaiah Mizell caught six passes for 183 yards and two touchdowns in a 52-31 win at West Virginia.

Now let's look at the rest of the radar. In that same game, West Virginia outgained Arizona 522 to 482 and held the ball for 35:50. AP noted that West Virginia's defense had allowed an average of 593 yards in its two games before that. And Arizona still got outgained. Hmm. My barometer is raising an eyebrow.

Arizona is minus-3 in turnover margin, 99th in FBS. We're plus-3. So the Wildcats have a habit of letting the football slip away, and the Cyclones have a habit of catching whatever falls out of the sky. That's just science, friends. I took a whole class on precipitation.

And Arizona's pass defense allows 214.2 yards a game, 74th. If our passing game is ever going to find some sunshine, a desert seems like the right place to look.

A History Lesson From the Weather Center

Arizona's 5-1 start is its best since 2014. That's lovely. Truly. But think about what that sentence says: the Wildcats have been waiting 12 years for a nice start. In Ames, we get excited about a nice start every fall, and then we get excited about the next thing, too. We're optimists. It's the weather.

The Five-Day Town Forecast

Ames. Let me tell you about home. Ames sits about 30 miles north of Des Moines, and it's a college town in the best way. Our Campanile went up in 1897 and 1898 as a memorial to Margaret MacDonald Stanton, our first dean of women. It stands 110 feet tall, and it's the symbol of the whole university. Reiman Gardens fills 17 acres with an indoor butterfly wing. And on game days we gather at Jack Trice Stadium, which seats 61,500. It's named for Jack Trice, Iowa State's first African American athlete, who died in 1923 from injuries he suffered in a game against Minnesota. It is the only FBS stadium named for an African American. We say his name with pride every Saturday.

And the name? Iowa State became the Cyclones after a run of tornadoes, then called cyclones, tore through the area in 1898. We named ourselves after the most powerful weather on the plains. That's my kind of branding.

Tucson. Now, Tucson is a pretty place, and I won't pretend otherwise. Saguaros, mountains, very nice sunsets. But I'm a meteorologist, so I looked at the climate data. Tucson averages 158 days a year with a high of 90 degrees or more. A hundred and fifty-eight! That isn't a climate. That's an oven with a zip code.

Tucson also calls itself the "Old Pueblo." And it's the second-largest city in Arizona, behind Phoenix. So every day, Tucson wakes up in second place in its own state. I feel for it. It's like being the backup forecaster who only gets the 4 a.m. slot.

And Arizona plays in a stadium it renamed in 2025. I prefer stadium names that tell you a story. Ours tells you about Jack Trice. Our cardinal mascot, Cy, came about because a cyclone was too hard to put in a costume, which I think is charming. Arizona's mascots are Wildcats named Wilbur and Wilma. In Ames we'd call that a partly cloudy level of creativity.

One more thing. Bring water. I'm serious. It's the desert. Fall in Tucson is, per the record books, sunny and dry, with hot days. Out in Iowa we call that "July."

The Final Forecast

Here's your extended outlook. Arizona has the stronger passing game, and I'll admit that. Iowa State has the hottest running back on the field, a perfect red zone record, a plus turnover margin and two weeks of rest after an ugly night in Provo. If Flora gets going and Raynor hits a couple of passes on third down, this storm has a real chance to make landfall in the desert.

Pack a sweater for the flight home and sunscreen for kickoff. Strong chance of loud, fair chance of louder. Cyclone warning in effect.

My call: Arizona Wildcats 30, Iowa State Cyclones 22.

articles.title: Eighteen Straight Harvests: Kansas State Heads to Tempe, Where They Built a Desert Stadium and Forgot It Might Rain
articles.byline: Hattie Brandvold, The Kansas State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Kansas State (4-2) at Arizona State (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:45 p.m. ET, Mountain America Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Well, howdy, Wildcat neighbors. Hattie Brandvold here, writing from the porch with a cup of coffee, a soil probe and a view of the Flint Hills going gold for fall. I studied agronomy at K-State, so I see football the way I see a field: you prepare the ground, you rotate your crops, you trust the weather, and you never, ever rush a harvest.

Last Saturday we brought in the 18th straight harvest against Kansas. This week we load up the truck and head to Tempe, Arizona, where I'm told the soil is mostly sun.

Part 1: The Eighteenth Harvest

Kansas State beat Kansas 35-24 on Saturday at Bill Snyder Family Stadium. That's 18 straight wins over the Jayhawks. AP pointed out that the last time we lost to them was 2008, the year Collin Klein arrived on campus to play quarterback. Now he's our head coach, and the streak he started as a player is still growing. That's a perennial, friends. It comes back every year.

But I'll be honest, because farmers don't lie about the weather. The first quarter was a hailstorm. Rodney Fields Jr. scored on a 4-yard run to open the game, and then Bryson Hayes took the kickoff back 95 yards for Kansas. The Jayhawks drove 88 yards for another touchdown, a tight end fumble gave them a field goal, and we were down 17-7. My coffee went cold.

Then we did what Kansas State does. We planted. Luis Rodriguez made field goals of 22, 51 and 28 yards before halftime, and along the way, Kansas fumbled the snap on a punt for a safety. We led 18-17 at the break. Rodriguez went 4 for 4 on the day. That young man doesn't kick a football; he sows it.

Joe Jackson ran 27 times for 159 yards and an 8-yard touchdown. Avery Johnson threw for 209 yards and ran for 132 more, and Fields added 66. We ran for 359 yards and held the ball for 36:13. That's a sorghum drive, a wheat drive and a soybean drive, one after another.

I won't hide the weeds. We lost a fumble, failed on two fourth downs inside the Kansas 12, and couldn't punch it in on four straight runs from the Kansas 5. But Logan Bartley intercepted Isaiah Marshall in the end zone in the fourth quarter. On the very next play, Jackson ran for 64 yards. Then Johnson threw a 9-yard touchdown to Jaron Tibbs, our bumper harvest of the day. Rodriguez's 34-yarder with 1:56 left closed the barn door.

Part 2: Into the Desert

Saturday, 3:45 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2, at Mountain America Stadium in Tempe. Kansas State (4-2) at Arizona State (3-3). Both teams are 1-2 in Big 12 play. I'll tell you straight: Arizona State leads the series 6-1, and it beat us 24-14 in Manhattan in 2024. Our only win in the series came the last time we visited Tempe, in 2002, 34-27. So history says we know the way to that field. We just have to find it again.

Our Crop Rotation

Kansas State runs for 239.8 yards a game, sixth in FBS. We convert 59.3 of every 100 third downs, second in the nation. Johnson has 1,301 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and only three interceptions, and he leads us with 462 rushing yards. Tibbs leads the receivers with 25 catches for 268 yards and three scores.

And the defense? Our pass defense allows 136.3 yards a game, third in FBS. Bartley leads us with 34 tackles, and Wendell Gregory has 2.5 sacks. We hold the ball for 32:44 a game, 23rd in the country. We like long drives the way a farmer likes long rows: straight, steady, and finished by sundown.

Their Field Conditions

Now, I'm a guest, so I'll be kind first. Arizona State won the Big 12 in 2024, and Reed Harris leads the league with eight touchdown catches. Their passing game ranks 23rd in FBS. Those are good seeds.

But let's look at the soil report. The Sun Devils allow 32 points a game, 120th in FBS. Two weeks ago, Baylor came to Tempe and won 55-19. AP said the Sun Devils gave up 564 yards that day. Then last Saturday, Texas Tech led them 43-10 at halftime and won 53-25. J'Koby Williams ran for 165 yards on 11 carries. Friends, if Texas Tech can grow 165 yards on 11 carries out there, imagine what a real farm team can do with 50.

Arizona State's run defense allows 156.8 yards a game, 93rd. Our running game is sixth. In agronomy we call that "favorable growing conditions."

And they don't know who's starting at quarterback. Cutter Boley started last week, and Mikey Keene came in after halftime and played well. Coach Kenny Dillingham said he'd assess all personnel after watching the tape. In Kansas we call that "deciding which field to plant in October." Usually you've figured that out by spring.

Field Notes: A Tale of Two Towns

Manhattan. We're the Little Apple, and we wear the name proudly. Our town has 54,100 people and a big heart. South of town is the Konza Prairie, 8,616 acres of native tallgrass prairie in the Flint Hills, the largest remaining unplowed stretch of tallgrass prairie in North America. Some of that grass grows taller than me. Not hard, but still. Five miles north is Tuttle Creek Reservoir. And Aggieville, six square blocks of restaurants and shops, has been the heart of student life for generations.

Bill Snyder Family Stadium opened as KSU Stadium in 1968. Its first game was a 21-0 shutout of Colorado State. That's how you break ground on a stadium. And our Powercat logo has been on the helmets since 1989.

Tempe. Tempe is a perfectly nice place. But I did some reading. Arizona State's stadium was built in 1958, and according to its own history, the designers failed to waterproof it because they assumed a stadium in the desert wouldn't need it. Friends, I am a farmer. I can tell you that it rains in the desert. Not much. But it does. Ask any cactus.

Tempe also has a lake, and they're very proud of it. Tempe Town Lake was made by damming the Salt River in two places. So their lake is a river that got held up. In Kansas we call that "a pond with a press release."

And Sparky? He was drawn by a Disney illustrator. Rumor has it his face was based on Walt Disney himself. Our Willie the Wildcat was not drawn by anyone in Hollywood. He was raised in Manhattan, like a good crop.

Also, the city is named after the Vale of Tempe in Greece, near Mount Olympus. Bless their hearts. We named our town after the Big Apple, I admit. But at least we stayed on the same continent.

The Harvest Report

Here's how I see it. Kansas State runs the ball like a combine through ripe wheat, defends the pass as well as almost anybody in the country and controls the clock. Arizona State can throw it, but it has struggled to stop the run and hasn't decided on a quarterback. If we keep the ball, stay patient and finish drives in the end zone this time instead of near it, we'll come home with a full truck.

You can't rush a harvest. But you can bring one home from the desert.

My call: Kansas State Wildcats 32, Arizona State Sun Devils 27.

blocks.text: Well, howdy, Wildcat neighbors. Hattie Brandvold here, writing from the porch with a cup of coffee, a soil probe and a view of the Flint Hills going gold for fall. I studied agronomy at K-State, so I see football the way I see a field: you prepare the ground, you rotate your crops, you trust the weather, and you never, ever rush a harvest.
Last Saturday we brought in the 18th straight harvest against Kansas. This week we load up the truck and head to Tempe, Arizona, where I'm told the soil is mostly sun.
Part 1: The Eighteenth Harvest

Kansas State beat Kansas 35-24 on Saturday at Bill Snyder Family Stadium. That's 18 straight wins over the Jayhawks. AP pointed out that the last time we lost to them was 2008, the year Collin Klein arrived on campus to play quarterback. Now he's our head coach, and the streak he started as a player is still growing. That's a perennial, friends. It comes back every year.

But I'll be honest, because farmers don't lie about the weather. The first quarter was a hailstorm. Rodney Fields Jr. scored on a 4-yard run to open the game, and then Bryson Hayes took the kickoff back 95 yards for Kansas. The Jayhawks drove 88 yards for another touchdown, a tight end fumble gave them a field goal, and we were down 17-7. My coffee went cold.

Then we did what Kansas State does. We planted. Luis Rodriguez made field goals of 22, 51 and 28 yards before halftime, and along the way, Kansas fumbled the snap on a punt for a safety. We led 18-17 at the break. Rodriguez went 4 for 4 on the day. That young man doesn't kick a football; he sows it.

Joe Jackson ran 27 times for 159 yards and an 8-yard touchdown. Avery Johnson threw for 209 yards and ran for 132 more, and Fields added 66. We ran for 359 yards and held the ball for 36:13. That's a sorghum drive, a wheat drive and a soybean drive, one after another.

I won't hide the weeds. We lost a fumble, failed on two fourth downs inside the Kansas 12, and couldn't punch it in on four straight runs from the Kansas 5. But Logan Bartley intercepted Isaiah Marshall in the end zone in the fourth quarter. On the very next play, Jackson ran for 64 yards. Then Johnson threw a 9-yard touchdown to Jaron Tibbs, our bumper harvest of the day. Rodriguez's 34-yarder with 1:56 left closed the barn door.
Part 2: Into the Desert

Saturday, 3:45 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2, at Mountain America Stadium in Tempe. Kansas State (4-2) at Arizona State (3-3). Both teams are 1-2 in Big 12 play. I'll tell you straight: Arizona State leads the series 6-1, and it beat us 24-14 in Manhattan in 2024. Our only win in the series came the last time we visited Tempe, in 2002, 34-27. So history says we know the way to that field. We just have to find it again.
Our Crop Rotation

Kansas State runs for 239.8 yards a game, sixth in FBS. We convert 59.3 of every 100 third downs, second in the nation. Johnson has 1,301 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and only three interceptions, and he leads us with 462 rushing yards. Tibbs leads the receivers with 25 catches for 268 yards and three scores.

And the defense? Our pass defense allows 136.3 yards a game, third in FBS. Bartley leads us with 34 tackles, and Wendell Gregory has 2.5 sacks. We hold the ball for 32:44 a game, 23rd in the country. We like long drives the way a farmer likes long rows: straight, steady, and finished by sundown.
Their Field Conditions

Now, I'm a guest, so I'll be kind first. Arizona State won the Big 12 in 2024, and Reed Harris leads the league with eight touchdown catches. Their passing game ranks 23rd in FBS. Those are good seeds.

But let's look at the soil report. The Sun Devils allow 32 points a game, 120th in FBS. Two weeks ago, Baylor came to Tempe and won 55-19. AP said the Sun Devils gave up 564 yards that day. Then last Saturday, Texas Tech led them 43-10 at halftime and won 53-25. J'Koby Williams ran for 165 yards on 11 carries. Friends, if Texas Tech can grow 165 yards on 11 carries out there, imagine what a real farm team can do with 50.
Arizona State's run defense allows 156.8 yards a game, 93rd. Our running game is sixth. In agronomy we call that "favorable growing conditions."

And they don't know who's starting at quarterback. Cutter Boley started last week, and Mikey Keene came in after halftime and played well. Coach Kenny Dillingham said he'd assess all personnel after watching the tape. In Kansas we call that "deciding which field to plant in October." Usually you've figured that out by spring.

Manhattan. We're the Little Apple, and we wear the name proudly. Our town has 54,100 people and a big heart. South of town is the Konza Prairie, 8,616 acres of native tallgrass prairie in the Flint Hills, the largest remaining unplowed stretch of tallgrass prairie in North America. Some of that grass grows taller than me. Not hard, but still. Five miles north is Tuttle Creek Reservoir. And Aggieville, six square blocks of restaurants and shops, has been the heart of student life for generations.

Bill Snyder Family Stadium opened as KSU Stadium in 1968. Its first game was a 21-0 shutout of Colorado State. That's how you break ground on a stadium. And our Powercat logo has been on the helmets since 1989.

Friends, I am a farmer. I can tell you that it rains in the desert. Not much. But it does. Ask any cactus.

Tempe also has a lake, and they're very proud of it. Tempe Town Lake was made by damming the Salt River in two places. So their lake is a river that got held up. In Kansas we call that "a pond with a press release."

And Sparky? He was drawn by a Disney illustrator. Rumor has it his face was based on Walt Disney himself. Our Willie the Wildcat was not drawn by anyone in Hollywood. He was raised in Manhattan, like a good crop.
Also, the city is named after the Vale of Tempe in Greece, near Mount Olympus. Bless their hearts. We named our town after the Big Apple, I admit. But at least we stayed on the same continent.

Here's how I see it. Kansas State runs the ball like a combine through ripe wheat, defends the pass as well as almost anybody in the country and controls the clock. Arizona State can throw it, but it has struggled to stop the run and hasn't decided on a quarterback. If we keep the ball, stay patient and finish drives in the end zone this time instead of near it, we'll come home with a full truck.
You can't rush a harvest. But you can bring one home from the desert.
My call: Kansas State Wildcats 32, Arizona State Sun Devils 27.

articles.title: Spite and the Stats: Kansas Hosts Baylor, Whose Offense Took Three 12-Play Drives to Score Six Points
articles.byline: Fitz Calloway, The Kansas Fanatic
articles.matchup: Baylor (4-2) at Kansas (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET, David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium, TNT
articles.text:
Rock Chalk, everybody. Fitz Calloway here. I grew up in Lawrence as a basketball person, and I'll admit I came to football analytics out of pure spite. Somebody told me Kansas football was hopeless, so I started keeping a spreadsheet to prove them wrong. That spreadsheet now has a lot of tabs. Some of them are sad. I'm only here because of spite and the stats.

Fair warning: I convert every football number into basketball. I can't stop. I've tried.

This week: an honest look at a painful Saturday in Manhattan, and then a very warm Lawrence welcome for Baylor, a team that has beaten us 15 straight times. I'm aware. I have it in a spreadsheet.

Part 1: Manhattan, Again

Kansas State beat us 35-24 on Saturday. That's 18 straight losses to them, dating to 2008. I don't have a basketball conversion for that one. In basketball, we'd have beaten them twice in the same month by now.

And here's what hurts. We led 17-7 after the first quarter in their building. Bryson Hayes took a kickoff back 95 yards for a touchdown right after their opening score. Isaiah Marshall threw a 12-yard touchdown to Nik McMillan to cap an 88-yard drive, and Martin Connington added a 31-yard field goal. I was doing math on my napkin. I was converting it to points per possession. It looked like a top-10 offense in the Big 12 Tournament.

Then the second quarter happened. Kansas State kicked three field goals, and we fumbled the snap on a punt for a safety. The Wildcats led 18-17 at the half. Dylan Edwards scored on a 3-yard run against his former team to put us back up 24-18, and the defense even stopped them on four straight runs from first-and-goal at our 5. That was a stand at the goal, a blocked shot at the rim and a charge, all on one possession.

Then the fourth quarter. Marshall threw an interception in the end zone while we were trying to tie it. We got the ball back, and Marshall broke a 45-yard touchdown run that a facemask penalty wiped out. We punted. They kicked a field goal with 1:56 left. Marshall finished with 151 passing yards and 117 rushing yards, which is a heck of a box score. Trey Lathan and Bam Crouch each made eight tackles.

Kansas State outgained us 568 to 319 and ran for 359 yards. AP said the Wildcats dominated everywhere but the scoreboard. I'll take "everywhere but the scoreboard" as a compliment, because the scoreboard was close, and the scoreboard is my most beloved part.

Part 2: Baylor Comes to Lawrence

Saturday, 1 p.m. Eastern, TNT. Baylor (4-2) at Kansas (2-4). I'll do the honest thing and give you the bad number first: Baylor leads the series 19-4 and has won the last 15. The last time Kansas won was 2007, 58-10, right here in Lawrence. That was the 12-1 season that ended with an Orange Bowl win. I remember it like a Final Four.

The Bears' Shot Chart

Baylor's defense is legit, and I won't insult your intelligence. The Bears haven't allowed more than 19 points in a game this season, and they're ninth in FBS in run defense, at 86.7 yards a game. They allow 14.7 points a game, also ninth.

But look at the offense from last Saturday. TCU beat Baylor 17-6 in Waco. Baylor's quarterback, DJ Lagway, went 22 of 53. In basketball terms, that's shooting 22-for-53 from the field, which would get you benched in a church league. The Bears ran 34 times for 54 yards. And in the first half they put together three straight drives of at least 12 plays each. Their reward? A missed 47-yard field goal and two short ones. Six points.

Think about that. Thirty-six-plus plays for six points. In basketball, that's three straight possessions with every offensive rebound you could ask for, and you go 2 for 3 at the free-throw stripe. That's not an offense, friends. That's a shot clock violation with extra steps.

Baylor scores on 75 of every 100 red zone trips, 119th in FBS. And it has field goal issues. I'm told this is what happens when you go to Waco: everything stops halfway. Waco's own Wikipedia page introduces the town as being halfway from Dallas to Austin. It's a rest stop with a stadium.

To be fair, Baylor's passing game is 16th in FBS at 286 yards a game, and Gavin Freeman has 49 catches for 555 yards. Two weeks ago Lagway threw four touchdowns in a 55-19 win at Arizona State. When it's on, it's on. But Baylor's pass defense ranks 110th, allowing 240 yards a game. Marshall has 1,294 passing yards this season and McMillan averages more than 17 yards a catch. That's a fast break waiting to happen.

Our Game Plan, Per the Spreadsheet

We run for 207 yards a game, 23rd in FBS. We score 32 points a game. Edwards has 375 rushing yards and four touchdowns. Leroy Harris III has three sacks, and Lathan leads us with 41 tackles. Our pass defense is 26th in FBS. And we have Hayes back there on kickoffs, which is like having a guy who can hit a half-court shot whenever he wants.

What we need: clean football. No facemasks, no fumbled snaps, no turnovers in the end zone. Last week we beat ourselves. This week, let's let the other team try.

Mass Street Report: A Tale of Two Towns

Lawrence. Let me show you home. Massachusetts Street runs right where the original settlers started building the town in 1854, and it's still the heart of downtown. Up on the hill, Allen Fieldhouse was dedicated on March 1, 1955, with a win over Kansas State, and the Jayhawks have gone undefeated at home 20 times since it opened. James Naismith, the man who invented basketball, founded the KU program in 1898. And our football home, Memorial Stadium, opened in 1921. It's one of the oldest college football stadiums in the country and is widely recognized as the oldest west of the Mississippi. The new west side opened in 2025. Come see it. Bring a friend. Bring everybody you know, honestly.

And when you hear the "Rock Chalk, Jayhawk" chant roll through the stands, you'll understand why we never leave early, even when the spreadsheet says we should.

Waco. Waco is a perfectly nice town of about 138,000. Dr Pepper was invented there in 1885, which I appreciate, because I need a lot of caffeine to watch Baylor's offense. They have a suspension bridge from 1870. And the big tourist draw is Magnolia Market at the Silos, a shopping complex built around two old cotton-oil silos. So the top attraction in town is a pair of old silos that somebody put on TV. I respect the hustle.

They also have live bears. Fine. Real live bears. Our mascot is a mythical bird, and frankly that's a flex, because you can't run out of something that doesn't exist.

And Baylor's stadium, McLane, has 45,140 seats on the Brazos River, where fans can arrive by boat. I'll grant you that's charming. But Lawrence had 94,934 people at the 2020 census, and our football stadium has been here since 1921. Theirs opened in 2014. We have sneakers older than McLane Stadium. Okay, not literally. But spiritually.

The Final Possession

Here's my spreadsheet's honest read. Baylor has the stronger defense and a 15-game streak against us. We have the stronger running game, a return man who can flip the field and a home crowd that's been waiting since 2007. If Baylor's offense keeps stalling in the red zone and we play one clean game, this is the Saturday the streak ends. I've done the math. I've also done the spite.

Rock Chalk. Let's go win one for the spreadsheet.

My call: Baylor Bears 27, Kansas Jayhawks 26.

articles.title: Ride 'Em, Pokes: Colorado Brings One of the Nation's Most-Penalized Teams to America's Greatest Homecoming
articles.byline: Dusty Lockridge, The Oklahoma State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Colorado (2-4) at Oklahoma State (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7 p.m. ET, Boone Pickens Stadium, FS1
articles.text:
Howdy, Cowboy family. Dusty Lockridge here, boots on, hat tipped, coming to you from a lawn chair on the Strip with a basket from Eskimo Joe's in my lap. I grew up around rodeo arenas, and I still explain football with rodeo timing. A good offense is like a good tie-down run: you break the barrier clean, you rope fast, and you're off that horse before the crowd sits back down.

It's homecoming week in Stillwater. That means America's Greatest Homecoming Celebration, the Walkaround, the Sea of Orange Parade and a sold-out Boone Pickens Stadium on Saturday night. But first, we've got to talk about Houston.

Part 1: A Slow Break From the Box

Houston beat us 35-32 on Saturday night. We're 4-2 and 2-1 in the Big 12, and our four-game winning streak is over. I'll give it to you straight, because a cowboy who fibs about his time gets found out at the scoreboard.

We broke the barrier late. Houston led 14-3 at halftime. In rodeo terms, that's a roper who sits in the box admiring his rope while the calf is already halfway to Tulsa. The coaches know it, too. AP noted the staff's frustration with how differently we play in the first and second halves.

Then the second half came, and those two teams combined for 50 points and more than 650 yards. Drew Mestemaker went 22 of 34 for 365 yards and three touchdowns. Caleb Hawkins caught seven passes for 125 yards, including a 66-yard touchdown, and ran for 68 more. Wyatt Young caught five balls for 99 yards and a score, and Justin Bowick's 8-yard touchdown catch got us within 35-32 with 4:54 to go. We had 499 yards. LaDainian Fields intercepted Conner Weigman and brought it back 20 yards. That's what I call a clean catch out of the chute.

But Weigman threw five touchdown passes, and Houston held the ball for 35:12. On third-and-7 with about two and a half minutes left, he hit Trent Walker for 18 yards, then ran for one more first down to finish it. We never got the ball back.

That's a loss. It stings like a fence post on a cold morning. But here's the thing about this team: we went 1-11 last season. We're 4-2 now, and we beat Oregon 39-31 in September. This horse has been bucking all year in the right direction.

Part 2: Homecoming Against the Buffs

Saturday, 6 p.m. Central, 7 Eastern, on FS1. Colorado (2-4) at Oklahoma State (4-2). It's America's Greatest Homecoming, and the athletics department lists the game as sold out.

The series: Colorado leads 27-20-1. And I'll be honest about the last one, because honesty is the cowboy way. On Nov. 29, 2024, in Boulder, Colorado beat us 52-0. I'm aware. I was there in spirit, and my spirit has been sore ever since. This is the first chance to answer it.

What the Buffaloes Bring to the Arena

Colorado has lost four straight. The Buffs are 0-3 in the Big 12 and score 19.5 points a game, 123rd in FBS. They score on 70.6 of every 100 red zone trips, 130th. And they're minus-6 in turnover margin, 126th.

But here's the stat I can't stop reading. Colorado averages 84.3 penalty yards a game. That ranks 136th of 138 FBS teams. Against Utah last week, AP said the Buffs had more penalty yards at halftime (82) than yards of offense (70). Friends, in rodeo that's called breaking the barrier. You get a 10-second penalty for leaving the box early. Colorado leaves the box early about 10 times a game.

They did rally in the second half against Utah, and I'll give them credit for heart. Isaac Wilson threw for 256 yards and two touchdowns against his former team, and JaQuail Smith turned a catch into a 68-yard score. Joseph Williams has 508 receiving yards this season, and Lamont Lester Jr. has four sacks. But they still lost.

What the Cowboys Bring

Our offense gains 517.7 yards a game, fifth in FBS. We throw for 329.5 a game, fourth in the country. Mestemaker has 1,940 yards, 16 touchdowns and six interceptions. Hawkins has 592 rushing yards, and Young has 32 catches for 561 yards and five touchdowns. Linebacker Ethan Wesloski leads us with 62 tackles, and Malik Charles has 2.5 sacks.

And Colorado's defense against the throw allows 226 yards a game, 93rd. That's a calf with a head start and a limp.

Honest note from the chute: we've got to fix our own slow starts, and we've got to hold onto the ball. We're minus-4 in turnovers and 112th on third down. Rodeo rule: the clock doesn't care how pretty your loop was. Break clean, rope fast, tie it off.

The Rodeo Grounds: A Tale of Two Towns

Stillwater. Stillwater was part of the first Oklahoma Land Run, on April 22, 1889, when the cannons fired and settlers raced to claim land. That's my kind of start: everybody breaking the barrier at once, on purpose. Today we're a college town of 48,394. Eskimo Joe's and George's Stables are institutions, and Garth Brooks got his start on the Strip when he was discovered at Willie's Saloon.

And homecoming? Oklahoma State has been celebrating since 1913. The university says it draws more than 40,000 alumni and over 70,000 participants each year. There's the Walkaround, the decorated halls, the Sea of Orange Parade and the Dyeing of the Fountain, more than a dozen events in all. Folks prepare for months. This year's theme is "The Code Calls Us Home," and I'll be honest, I teared up a little reading it. That's why we call it America's Greatest Homecoming. Our mascot, Pistol Pete, has led us since 1923, and he's modeled on Frank Eaton, a real Old West figure students spotted leading Stillwater's Armistice Day Parade. And Boone Pickens Stadium has the oldest field in the Big 12, home to Cowboy football as a complete stadium since 1920.

Boulder. Boulder is pretty. I'll admit it. Mountains, big rocks, a lot of people in fleece vests. But in 1972, Boulder passed a law limiting building heights so nobody could block the view of the mountains. Friends, that's a whole town that made it illegal to get in the way of a nap. And their stadium, Folsom Field, opened in 1924. Ours has been here since 1920. We were playing football in Stillwater when Folsom was still a sketch.

Now, their mascot. Ralphie is a live bison, and that's impressive. But according to her own history, they've always chosen a female bison because they're smaller and less aggressive. So the Buffaloes chose their mascot for being the calmest buffalo available. I respect a calm animal. I've been thrown by the other kind.

Here's how I see it. Oklahoma State has a top-five offense, a tough quarterback, a sold-out homecoming crowd and a two-year-old scoreboard to set right. Colorado has heart, a quarterback who played well last week and more penalty yards than almost anybody in the country. If we break the barrier clean for once and play a full 60 minutes, those buffalo will be headed back up the mountain before the fountain dries.

Ride 'em, Pokes. Go Pokes.

My call: Oklahoma State Cowboys 30, Colorado Buffaloes 21.

articles.title: Yeehaw, That's a Defense: TCU Hosts West Virginia, Whose Beloved Song Was Written on a Road in Maryland and Whose Defense Ranks 137th
articles.byline: Ryder Galloway, The TCU Fanatic
articles.matchup: West Virginia (4-3) at TCU (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Amon G. Carter Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Howdy from the Fort Worth Stockyards, Frog fans. Ryder Galloway here, leaning on a fence rail, boots dusty, pressed shirt still somehow perfect. I grew up around cattle and ended up in an office tower downtown, and I still explain defense the old way. A great defense is a great cattle drive. Everybody rides their lane, nobody lets a steer slip through the gap, and the whole herd ends up exactly where you wanted it.

And on Saturday night in Waco, friends, TCU's defense ran the cleanest drive in Texas.

Yeehaw, that's a turnover. Several of them, actually.

Part 1: Seventeen Points and a Fence That Wouldn't Break

TCU beat Baylor 17-6 at McLane Stadium. We're 3-3 and 1-2 in the Big 12, and we snapped Baylor's four-game winning streak in its own house. I'll admit, the first half of this season was rough. We started 0-2 in the Big 12 for the first time since 2013. If you want to know who's to blame for that, I've got a theory, and it starts with a D and ends with "allas."

But this one felt good. Jaden Craig threw for 294 yards and two touchdowns. He put us ahead to stay with a 25-yard touchdown pass to Ed Small in the first quarter. Then, in the opening minute of the second half, Craig hit Jordan Dwyer on a 67-yard catch-and-run. On the very next snap, he threw an 8-yard touchdown to Ka'Morreun Pimpton, and we led 14-6. Nate McCashland added a 25-yard field goal. Dwyer finished with six catches for 150 yards, and Small had seven for 91.

Now let's talk about the herd. Baylor's quarterback completed 22 of 53 passes. The Bears put together three straight first-half drives of at least 12 plays each and came away with two field goals and a miss. That's a cattle drive where the steers walk 12 miles and end up right back in the pen. Koron Hayward had three of our four sacks. Jamel Johnson intercepted a pass. Kylin Jackson stripped the ball loose late in the first half to get it right back after a turnover of our own. Baylor finished with a season-low 310 yards.

According to AP, it was our highest-scoring game against a Power Four opponent this season. I'll be honest about that too. The offense has some catching up to do.

Part 2: The Mountaineers Ride Into Cowtown

Saturday, noon Eastern, 11 a.m. here in Cowtown, on ESPN2. West Virginia (4-3) at TCU (3-3) at Amon G. Carter Stadium.

What the Mountaineers Bring

I'll tip my hat first. West Virginia can move the ball. It gains 497.1 yards a game, eighth in FBS, and it runs for 272.4 a game, fifth. Cam Cook has 833 rushing yards and seven touchdowns. Last week Mike Hawkins Jr. threw for a career-high 464 yards, three touchdowns and ran for two more in a 45-42 win over Cincinnati. Jack Cassidy kicked a 35-yard field goal as time ran out.

Now, the rest of the herd report.

West Virginia never led that game until the final kick. The Mountaineers give up 483.9 yards a game, 137th in FBS. They give up 310.1 passing yards a game, 138th. Folks, I've seen gates on a ranch hold better than that. AP noted that West Virginia's last four games have all topped 1,000 combined yards. Cincinnati outgained them 622-598 and still lost. They give up 34 points a game, 130th. And before beating Cincinnati, they'd lost three straight.

Last season, per CollegeFootballData, West Virginia went 4-8. We went 9-4.

What the Frogs Bring

Our defense allows 12.2 points a game, third in FBS. It allows 264.2 yards a game, seventh. Opponents convert only 30.2 of every 100 third downs against us, 13th in FBS. Our red zone defense ranks third. And here's my most beloved stat in the whole state of Texas: TCU has held every opponent this season to 21 points or fewer.

Hayward has 4.5 sacks. Hudson Hooper leads us with 32 tackles. Craig has 1,694 yards and 10 touchdowns. Ed Small has 35 catches for 494 yards. Our passing game ranks 20th in FBS, and West Virginia's pass defense ranks 138th. You don't need a finance degree to see that one adds up.

The Honest Brand on the Hide

I don't fib. Our running game averages 110 yards a game, 125th in FBS, and we score 24 points a game, 95th. We're 98th in penalty yards. And the history isn't all ours. West Virginia leads the series 8-6, according to CollegeFootballData, and it won its last three trips to Amon G. Carter, in 2019, 2021 and 2023. We did win the last meeting, 23-17 in Morgantown last season. So keep the herd tight, keep the flags down and make Hawkins throw against the best defense he'll see all year.

Cowtown vs. Morgantown

Fort Worth. Fort Worth started in 1849 as an army outpost on a bluff over the Trinity River, and it's been known ever since as "where the West begins." We're Cowtown, a historic center of the Texas Longhorn cattle trade, and down at the Stockyards, they still run cattle drives through the streets twice a day, weather permitting. Today Fort Worth is the 10th-most populous city in the United States, with an estimated 1,028,117 people, and one of the fastest-growing cities in the country.

And our stadium has history. Amon G. Carter Stadium hosted its first game on Oct. 11, 1930, and TCU beat Arkansas. The Frogs won national championships in 1935 and 1938 under Dutch Meyer. Even our mascot is tough. The Texas horned lizard can squirt an aimed stream of blood from the corners of its eyes as far as 5 feet to confuse predators. Try to top that, Mountaineers.

Morgantown. Morgantown is a pretty town on the Monongahela River with 30,347 people, according to the 2020 census. Fort Worth has more than 30 Morgantowns. And the town has a driverless people-mover system that opened in 1975, three years behind schedule. Friends, in Fort Worth we move people the old-fashioned way: on a horse, on time.

Now, West Virginia's beloved song, "Take Me Home, Country Roads." It's been played at every West Virginia home pregame since 1972, and it's one of the state's official anthems. But according to the songwriters' own story, the idea for that title came while they were driving along Clopper Road in Montgomery County, Maryland. So the official song of West Virginia was dreamed up in Maryland. In Fort Worth, we write our cowboy songs in Texas.

When their stadium opened in 1980, John Denver landed on the field in a helicopter, sang "Country Roads" and then immediately flew away. I respect the efficiency. Even John Denver didn't stick around Morgantown for the second verse. And the stadium design? It was inspired by Jack Trice Stadium at Iowa State. So the Mountaineers play in a building inspired by Iowa, singing a song inspired by Maryland. Somehow I'm sure this is Dallas's fault.

The Last Roundup

Here's the drive. West Virginia has a big-play offense and a defense that ranks near the bottom of FBS. TCU has a top-three scoring defense, a quarterback who just threw for 294 yards and a home crowd that's ready to make some noise. Keep every steer in its lane, make the Mountaineers earn every yard and send them back up the country road a little earlier than they planned.

Yeehaw, that's a turnover. Go Frogs.

My call: TCU Horned Frogs 34, West Virginia Mountaineers 21.

articles.title: Guns Up, Wind's Up: Unbeaten Texas Tech Rides Into Cincinnati, Where They Put Chili on Spaghetti and Blew a Lead With 5:35 Left
articles.byline: Bodie Ratliff, The Texas Tech Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 8 Texas Tech (6-0) at Cincinnati (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Nippert Stadium, FS1
articles.text:
Bodie Ratliff. Lubbock.

That's the whole introduction, mostly. I ride bareback broncs on weekends and chart Air Raid concepts during tumbleweed season, which out here is most seasons. I'm not much for long speeches. But my editor says I need 1,200 words, so I'll make an exception. For the Red Raiders, I'll talk all day.

Guns up. Wind's up. Let's ride.

Part 1: Saturday in Lubbock

Texas Tech 53, Arizona State 25.

One word: thorough.

AP billed it as a meeting of the past two Big 12 champions. We're the reigning one. We're 6-0, 3-0 in the league, and we moved up to No. 8 in this week's AP poll. With that win we set a school record with our eighth straight regular-season conference victory, and we've won 12 straight at home. AP said that's one short of the longest home streak in school history, from 1942. We're 18-2 since the start of last season.

The start was rough for about four minutes. J'Koby Williams fumbled at the Arizona State 2 on our opening drive, the 13th play of it. Three plays later, linebacker Ben Roberts picked off Cutter Boley and returned it 24 yards for a touchdown. AP said that's the fourth time in three games one of our linebackers has returned an interception for a touchdown. Fourth. Our linebackers score more than some offenses.

Then the first half turned into a stampede. We scored on our last seven drives of the half: four touchdowns and three Stone Harrington field goals, from 31, 42 and 37 yards. It was 43-10 at the break, and we already had 404 yards. Will Hammond went 18 of 26 for 232 yards, threw an 11-yard touchdown to Coy Eakin and ran one in from 9. Kenny Johnson caught seven passes for 120 yards.

And Williams? He bounced back from that fumble with 165 yards on 11 carries. His touchdown runs went 62 and 38 yards. On the 38, he went through a gap, got by one defender and spun past another. I've seen broncos with less wiggle. Terrance Carter Jr. added a 1-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter.

We were without Cameron Dickey, who has a high ankle sprain. We hope he's back on his feet soon. Williams carried the load for both of them.

Arizona State scored 15 points after halftime. Fine. We'd already roped the calf.

One more thing. AP pointed out that 17 of the Red Raiders' 18 wins since the start of last season have come by double digits. Coach Joey McGuire is 41-18 in five seasons, with a 26-5 mark at home. In rodeo terms, that's a cowboy who stays on for eight seconds just about every time he climbs into the chute. Steady. That's the word.

Part 2: Riding East

Saturday, noon Eastern, FS1, at Nippert Stadium. No. 8 Texas Tech (6-0) at Cincinnati (4-2). It's Cincinnati's 100th Homecoming, so they'll have a parade and a big crowd in red. Funny. We wear red too.

Series: Texas Tech 1, Cincinnati 0, one tie. We tied 10-10 in Cincinnati in 1968 and won 44-41 at home in 2024.

What Cincinnati Brings

Respect where it's due. JC French IV hasn't thrown an interception all season. Nine touchdowns, 70.6 completions for every 100 throws. Last week he threw for a career-high 389 yards. Cole Tabb has eight touchdowns on 49 carries. The Bearcats run for 231.2 yards a game, 11th in FBS, and they're plus-5 in turnovers.

Now the other side of the ledger.

They lost at West Virginia 45-42 last week. AP said West Virginia never led until the final kick. Cincinnati was up 42-35 with 5:35 left and lost. They punted West Virginia back to its own 1 with 2:05 to go, and West Virginia still went the length of the field for a game-winning field goal.

One word: leaky.

The Bearcats' defense allows 434.3 yards a game, 128th in FBS. Its pass defense is 136th, at 294 yards a game. Opponents convert 49.4 of every 100 third downs, 126th. Two weeks before that, Arizona beat them 34-7. They've lost two straight.

West Virginia's Mike Hawkins Jr. threw for 464 yards on them, a career high, and DJ Epps caught eight balls for 163. That's not a secondary. That's an open gate.

One word: spin. We have a back who spins.

What We Bring

Our run defense allows 82 yards a game, fifth in FBS. A.J. Holmes Jr. has four sacks, and Austin Romaine leads us with 42 tackles. That's the matchup: their run game, 11th, against our run defense, fifth. Somebody gets bucked off.

Two Towns, Few Words

Lubbock. Population 257,141 at the 2020 census. Tenth-most populous city in Texas. We sit on the Llano Estacado, the high, flat plains of West Texas, and our nickname is Hub City, because we're the center of everything for a long way around. We're the 10th-windiest city in America. We don't mind. Wind's up.

Buddy Holly came from here. There's a West Texas Walk of Fame in the Buddy and Maria Elena Holly Plaza downtown. And our Masked Rider is Texas Tech's oldest mascot and was the first official mounted mascot in the country. Black horse, red cape, galloping onto the field since 1954. Your mascot can't do that, Cincinnati. It's a Bearcat. I'm still not sure what that is.

Our stadium, "The Jones," opened in 1947. ESPN lists it as Galaxy Stadium now. It's where we've won 12 straight.

Cincinnati. Nice river town. Big old buildings. They call themselves the Queen City. They also call themselves the City of Seven Hills, after the seven hills of Rome. Borrowed hills. In Lubbock, we don't borrow hills. We don't have any. We're honest about it.

For a while, Cincinnati also went by "Porkopolis." That one's earned.

And their famous dish, Cincinnati chili, is a Mediterranean-spiced meat sauce served over spaghetti. Over spaghetti. They call a five-way "chili" when it's got noodles, cheese, onions and beans in it. Out in West Texas we call that "lunch, confused." I respect the commitment. I'll eat two.

The 2020 census showed Cincinnati growing for the first time since 1950. Seventy years to grow. That's a long wait between harvests. Cincinnati football fans know about long waits, too: their team just waited 60 minutes against West Virginia and still didn't get to the finish.

To be fair, the Queen City did give the world the first all-professional baseball team, in 1869. Good for them. We'll play football.

The Last Word

Here's how I see it. Texas Tech has a top-five run defense, a back who breaks long runs, a quarterback getting more comfortable every week and a 12-game home streak that says we know how to finish. Cincinnati can run, and its quarterback takes care of the ball. But its defense ranks 128th, and it just gave away a seven-point lead in the last five minutes. Homecoming crowds get loud. Then they get quiet.

One word: ride.

Guns up. Wind's up.

My call: Texas Tech Red Raiders 34, Cincinnati Bearcats 23.

articles.title: Keep Your Hands Inside the Bounce House: No. 2 BYU Arrives With a Win the Big 12 Says Ended a Few Seconds Early
articles.byline: Knox Brevard-Stiles, The UCF Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 2 BYU (6-0) at UCF (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Acrisure Bounce House, FOX
articles.text:
Welcome to the Bounce House, everybody! Knox Brevard-Stiles here. I grew up in Orlando, and I design theme-park rides for a living, which means I spend my days making sure people scream safely. I bring a ride-safety gauge to every UCF home game to measure the crowd noise, and I swear on my engineering license that the stands really do move. Please keep your hands, arms and expectations inside the stadium at all times.

We had a bye last week, so this is a two-week ride. First, the honest replay of our last game. Then the main attraction: No. 2 BYU, coming to Orlando straight from a very famous ending.

Part 1: The Stillwater Drop, and a Week in the Maintenance Bay

Our last game was Oct. 10 at Oklahoma State, and we lost 42-28. I'll walk you through it like a ride inspection, because safety first and honesty second, and honestly they're tied.

The launch was perfect. Keyone Jenkins was nearly flawless in the first half: 15 of 18 for 118 yards and three touchdowns. Isaiah Nixon punched the ball loose from an Oklahoma State running back on the Cowboys' second play, a running back who had never fumbled in 314 college carries. Nixon fell on it, and nine plays later Jenkins hit tight end Grayson Brousseau for a 1-yard touchdown. Then he found Josh Derry from 12 yards out, and with 13 seconds left in the half he hit Tyren Hornes for a 3-yard score to tie it at 21. That's a launch coaster, folks. Zero to 21 in one half.

The middle section stalled. In the third quarter, Oklahoma State held us to 65 yards. Sam Keltner kicked two field goals, and the Cowboys led 27-21.

Then the drop. Early in the fourth quarter, we were driving for the go-ahead score when a Jenkins backward pass was knocked down, and Evan Jackson scooped it and returned it 28 yards for a touchdown. That's the moment the ride went down the big hill without us. Jenkins still finished 30 of 42 for 265 yards and four touchdowns, and Derry caught 11 passes. Jahleel Culbreath made 11 tackles. We held the ball for 35:15. We just didn't finish.

Then came the bye. A week in the maintenance bay to tighten the bolts, rest the legs and get ready for the biggest guest of the year.

Part 2: Now Boarding, No. 2 BYU

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, on FOX, at the Acrisure Bounce House. No. 2 BYU (6-0) at UCF (3-3). BYU leads the series 4-1, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I'll remind everybody that the one UCF win came at home, 31-24, in 2014. This building remembers.

The Cougars' Safety Inspection

BYU is unbeaten, and I respect that. The Cougars allow 15.2 points a game, 14th in FBS, and 86.2 rushing yards a game, eighth. They convert 56.5 of every 100 third downs, third in the country. Bear Bachmeier has 1,257 passing yards, nine touchdowns and two interceptions.

Last Saturday they beat Notre Dame 28-24. Bachmeier ran for two touchdowns, caught one and threw the game-winner with 1:47 left. Impressive. Truly. Now let's read the full inspection report.

The day after the game, the Big 12 said its review found that time remained on the clock when Notre Dame's last pass hit the ground, and that the replay crew incorrectly cleared the play. In ride-engineering terms, the ride stopped a few seconds early and the operator admitted it the next morning. The score stands. I'm just saying the Cougars rolled into the station with one wheel still spinning.

And look at the rest of that night. BYU muffed a punt return. It ran a fake punt that failed. A penalty wiped out a 39-yard touchdown catch. The Irish turned the special teams mistakes into two field goals, and Notre Dame led 24-21 with 9:31 left. BYU's passing game ranks 88th in FBS, at 214.5 yards a game. That's a smooth ride with some loose bolts, and loose bolts are my whole profession.

Our Ride Specs

Jenkins is completing 70.3 of every 100 passes, with 806 yards, eight touchdowns and three interceptions. Duke Watson leads our runners with 483 yards and three scores, and Derry leads the receivers with 28 catches. We score on 95.5 of every 100 red zone trips, eighth in FBS. We're plus-4 in turnover margin, 22nd in the country. Tackett Curtis leads the defense with 39 tackles, and Nixon has 2.5 sacks.

Honest maintenance note: our passing game ranks 106th and our pass defense ranks 105th, and we've lost leads in each of our last two games. BYU's run defense is excellent, so we'll need Jenkins to keep the chains moving through the air. And yes, AP noted we've dropped 12 straight road games. Good thing this one isn't on the road. In the Bounce House, we have home-track advantage.

Welcome to the Bounce House

Our stadium earned the nickname "Bounce House" because the stands shake when the crowd jumps in unison. I'm a ride engineer. I'm not supposed to say this. But it's my most beloved structural fact in all of college football. This season the Roth Tower expansion raised capacity to 45,906, which means more people jumping. I've run the numbers. They're very bouncy numbers.

The Park Map: A Tale of Two Towns

Orlando. Orlando has more theme parks and attractions than anywhere else in the world. That's not my opinion. That's the encyclopedia. The city had 307,573 people at the 2020 census, and downtown has Lake Eola and brick streets under century-old oaks. And UCF itself was founded in 1963 to train scientists and engineers for the space program around Kennedy Space Center. We were literally built for the space age. Our rides go to the moon.

UCF also has 70,674 students, the second-largest on-campus student body of any public university in America. And in 2017, the Knights went 13-0 and beat No. 7 Auburn 34-27 to finish unbeaten. Charge On.

Provo. Provo is a lovely mountain town of about 115,000 people, with a big Y on the mountain. I'm told the view is great. But let's look at the sign at the entrance. Provo was named in 1850 for Étienne Provost, a French-Canadian trapper who arrived in the region in 1825. So the town is named after a guy who was just passing through with a trap. That's like naming a ride after the guy who tested the seat belts once.

And Provo is the fourth-largest city in Utah. Fourth! Orlando is a destination for the whole world. Provo is a destination for people who missed the exit for Salt Lake City, which is about 40 miles north.

They'll also tell you about the elevation. Their stadium sits at 4,649 feet. Our stadium sits at sea level, give or take a lake. You know what we have instead of altitude? Humidity, and a stadium that bounces. We'll see how those mountain lungs handle a Florida afternoon. I'll have cold water ready for our guests, because I'm a nice host and a licensed safety professional.

And BYU's mascot is a cougar. Fine. Ours is a Knight. Cougars climb mountains. Knights storm castles, and Orlando knows a thing or two about castles.

Final Safety Check

Here's how I see it. BYU is very good. It has a top-15 defense, a quarterback who can score three different ways, and a 6-0 record. But the Cougars made a lot of special teams mistakes last week, they don't throw it well, and they're walking into the loudest, bounciest building they'll see all season. We're rested, we finish in the red zone and we protect the football. If we hold onto our leads this time, the Knights can shake this place to its foundation.

Please remain seated until the ride comes to a complete stop. Then jump. Charge On!

My call: BYU Cougars 28, UCF Knights 21.

articles.title: Send It, No Fear: Unbeaten No. 10 Utah Welcomes No. 14 Houston From the Flattest Big City in America to an Olympic Stadium at 4,637 Feet
articles.byline: Aspen Mortensen, The Utah Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 14 Houston (6-1) at No. 10 Utah (6-0), Sat., Oct. 24, 10:15 p.m. ET, Rice-Eccles Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Hey, Utes. Aspen Mortensen here, boots clicked into my old race skis even though there's no snow yet, because it helps me think. I spent years racing gates down the Wasatch, and I still break down football the same way. Every defensive player is a slalom racer. Clean through the gate, you win. Hook a tip, you're tumbling into the fence. And right now, this Utah team is 6-0 and still standing at the bottom of the hill.

Send it, no fear.

Part 1: A Run With a Couple of Bobbles

No. 11 Utah won 27-24 at Colorado on Saturday night, in a game that ended early Sunday. I'll be honest, because honesty is what keeps you upright on an icy course. It wasn't our cleanest run. Our coach said as much afterward, and I agree.

The top of the course was perfect. Devon Dampier hit tight end Hunter Andrews for an 8-yard touchdown on our opening drive. AP says we've now scored a touchdown on our opening drive in every game this season, and we've outscored opponents 75-3 in the first quarter. Dillon Curtis added field goals of 27 and 29 yards, the second one as time ran out in the first half, and we led 13-0 at the break. Colorado had more penalty yards (82) than yards of offense (70) by halftime.

Then we hooked a tip. Colorado scored 17 straight points in the third quarter, including a 68-yard touchdown pass, and led 17-13. That's when you find out who can recover on a steep pitch. Dampier found Braden Pegan for a 16-yard touchdown with 1:06 left in the third quarter, then again for 6 yards with 3:43 to go. That made it 27-17.

Colorado scored with 1:21 left, and we recovered the onside kick. In the final minute, the Buffs completed a long play to our 38, but a review ruled it an illegal forward pass. Our defense knocked down one last throw, and that was the race.

Dampier threw for 278 yards and three touchdowns, with two interceptions. Pegan caught eight passes for 86 yards and two scores. Wayshawn Parker ran 23 times for 98 yards. Creed Whittemore had three catches for 88 yards. James Chenault Jr. and Rabbit Evans each had an interception. And we're 6-0 for the first time since 2015.

Even better: Utah has won 12 straight games dating to last season, and AP says that's now the longest active winning streak in FBS.

Part 2: The Cougars Come to the Mountains

Saturday, 10:15 p.m. Eastern on ESPN, which is 8:15 p.m. here. No. 14 Houston (6-1) at No. 10 Utah (6-0) at Rice-Eccles Stadium. A Saturday night under the lights at altitude. My most beloved kind of course: steep, fast and a little cold.

Gate-by-Gate: What Houston Brings

I'm going to tip my helmet first. Houston is good. The Cougars have won four straight, including a 35-32 win over then-No. 18 Oklahoma State last week. Conner Weigman threw for 343 yards and five touchdowns in that one. He has 20 touchdown passes and just two interceptions this season. Houston converts 61.4 of every 100 third downs, first in FBS, and its run defense allows only 82.6 yards a game, sixth.

Now the rest of the course report.

Houston's pass defense allows 265 yards a game. That ranks 129th in FBS. In ski terms, that's a gate somebody forgot to plant. Oklahoma State threw for 365 yards against the Cougars last week and gained 499 yards. Houston also lost at Texas Tech, 28-26, in September.

And Houston gives up 21 points a game, 45th. We give up 14.8, 12th. Our run defense allows 88.7 yards a game, 12th. Houston will want to run, and our front will be waiting at the gate like a course worker with a clipboard.

Gate-by-Gate: What Utah Brings

Our offense gains 486.5 yards a game, ninth in FBS, and scores 40.2 points a game, eighth. We run for 220.2 yards a game. Dampier has 1,412 passing yards, 15 touchdowns and four interceptions. Parker has 597 rushing yards and seven touchdowns. Pegan has 32 catches for 422 yards and six touchdowns. Linebacker Trey Reynolds leads us with 35 tackles, and Karson Kaufusi has two sacks.

We convert 53.2 of every 100 third downs, eighth in FBS. We're plus-4 in turnover margin. And our red zone defense ranks 15th, while Houston's red zone offense is 75th.

The Honest Avalanche Report

Every good skier checks conditions. Here's mine. We threw two interceptions last week and let Colorado back into it. Houston leads the all-time series 5-0, according to CollegeFootballData, and the last meeting, in 2024, went to the Cougars 17-14 in Houston. Weigman can throw it, and the Cougars hold the ball about as long as we do.

But that 2024 game was in Houston, at about 50 feet above sea level. Saturday's field sits at 4,637 feet. Let's see how those Cougar lungs feel in the fourth quarter.

Red Rocks Report: Salt Lake City vs. Houston

Salt Lake City. We're the capital and most populous city in Utah, tucked under the Wasatch. Rice-Eccles Stadium was built to host the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2002 Winter Olympics, and Salt Lake City is set to host the Winter Games again in 2034. The stadium is expected to play that role again. The playing field sits 4,637 feet above sea level, and 400 feet above downtown. Our stadium is literally above the city. And just west of town is the Great Salt Lake, the largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere. It's so salty that swimming in it feels like floating. Even our lake refuses to let you go under.

Houston. Houston is big. Fourth-most populous city in America. Big airports, big highways, big everything. But it's also flat. Really flat. Downtown sits about 50 feet above sea level, and the highest point in the whole city is about 150 feet. Our field is higher than Houston's highest point by roughly 4,487 feet. I've seen bunny hills with more personality.

Houston is also the largest city in the United States without formal zoning regulations. So in Houston, you can build pretty much anything, pretty much anywhere. Up here, the mountains decide where things go. In Houston, there are no mountains to argue with.

And here's my most beloved bit of Houston history. The city was founded in 1836 by land investors, and they ran newspaper advertisements for a town that, at that point, was still mostly an idea. Houston was marketed before it was built. It's the most Houston thing ever, and honestly, I respect the hustle. I just don't respect the elevation.

The Bottom of the Hill

Here's my course report. Houston has a great third-down offense, a strong run defense and a quarterback who's playing as well as anyone in the conference. Utah has the longest active winning streak in FBS, a top-10 offense, a stingy defense and a crowd that's ready to stay up late. If our defense hits every gate and Dampier keeps the ball safe, we're 7-0 by the time the snow cats start their engines.

Drop in, Utes. Send it, no fear.

My call: Utah Utes 34, Houston Cougars 25.

articles.title: Load Up, I Don't Miss: West Virginia Rides a Walk-Off Kick to Fort Worth, Where the Offense Scored 10 Points in Ireland
articles.byline: Jolene Buckhannon, The West Virginia Fanatic
articles.matchup: West Virginia (4-3) at TCU (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Amon G. Carter Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Morning, Mountaineers. Jolene Buckhannon here. Former rifle team captain. I count possessions like rounds in a magazine, I keep a pepperoni-roll tally of every opponent fumble, and I don't do long sentences.

Saturday, we didn't either. We just kept firing.

Load up. I don't miss.

Part 1: Pinned at the 1, and Then the Kick

West Virginia 45, Cincinnati 42. At Milan Puskar Stadium. Jack Cassidy kicked a 35-yard field goal as time ran out. Country Roads, everybody. Sing it loud.

We broke a three-game losing streak. We're 4-3 and 1-3 in the Big 12. And I'll be honest, because a shooter who lies about her score gets caught at the target. We never led that game until the final kick.

Cincinnati scored first. Then we answered. Every time. Mike Hawkins Jr. ran in from 12 yards and from 2 yards in the second quarter. He hit Josh Sapp for a 4-yard touchdown in the third. He found DJ Epps for 37 yards early in the fourth to tie it 28-28. Amari Latimer ran 3 yards to tie it again at 35. Cincinnati went back up 42-35 with 5:35 left. Five plays later, Hawkins hit Cam Cook for a 40-yard touchdown. Tied, 42-42.

Then the hard part. Cincinnati punted and pinned us at our own 1 with 2:05 left. Ninety-nine yards to go. On third down, Hawkins found Prince Strachan for 41 yards. Two plays later, Strachan again, for 40. That put us inside the Cincinnati 20. Cassidy did the rest.

Hawkins finished 25 of 33 for a career-high 464 yards and three touchdowns, with no interceptions. He also ran 26 times for 77 yards and two scores. AP noted he hadn't completed half his passes in any of the previous three games. Saturday he completed 75.8 of every 100 throws. Target acquired.

And Cassidy? AP says he grew up playing Gaelic football in Northern Ireland, and he'd had a rough day before that last kick. Then he split the uprights, and his teammates carried him off on their shoulders. That's what I call a bullseye after a couple of practice rounds.

We had zero turnovers and only four penalties. Clean shooting.

Part 2: The Frogs in Fort Worth

Saturday, noon Eastern on ESPN2. West Virginia (4-3) at TCU (3-3) at Amon G. Carter Stadium.

Scouting the Target

I respect the Frogs' defense. I'll say that first. TCU allows 12.2 points a game, third in FBS. It allows 264.2 yards a game, seventh. It ranks third in red zone defense and 13th on third down. TCU has held every opponent to 21 points or fewer this season. That's a real wall.

Now the offense. Oh, the offense.

TCU runs for 110 yards a game. That's 125th in FBS. It scores 24 points a game, 95th. Last week at Baylor, the Frogs ran 30 times for 33 yards. That's 1.1 yards a carry. I've seen a deer move farther in a standing position. And AP says that before beating Baylor, TCU lost all three of its games against Power Four teams and scored 33 points in those three games combined. Eleven a game.

Here's my most beloved fact. TCU opened its season against North Carolina in Dublin, Ireland, at Aviva Stadium. The Frogs lost 15-10. They flew across an ocean to score 10 points. Our kicker grew up in Ireland and just won a game with his foot. Theirs went to Ireland and left the points there.

TCU also ranks 98th in FBS in penalty yards, at 64.3 a game. We rank 35th. And TCU started 0-2 in Big 12 play for the first time since 2013.

Counting My Rounds

Our offense gains 497.1 yards a game, eighth in FBS. We run for 272.4 a game, fifth. Cam Cook has 833 rushing yards and seven touchdowns. Hawkins has 1,519 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and one interception. One. DJ Epps has 556 yards on just 22 catches. That's more than 25 yards every time he touches it. Linebacker Isaiah Patterson leads us with 44 tackles.

The Honest Range Report

I don't fudge a scorecard. Our defense allows 483.9 yards a game, 137th in FBS, and 310.1 passing yards a game, 138th. Our last four games have all gone over 1,000 combined yards. Fun to watch. Not fun for my blood pressure. TCU's Jaden Craig just threw for 294 yards, and his receivers Jordan Dwyer and Ed Small can run. We have to tackle. And we have to protect Hawkins, because TCU's Koron Hayward has 4.5 sacks this season and got three of them at Baylor alone. Keep him out of the backfield and the rest of this matchup looks a lot friendlier.

Series check: West Virginia leads 8-6, according to CollegeFootballData. We won our last three games in Fort Worth, in 2019, 2021 and 2023. TCU won the last meeting, 23-17 in Morgantown last season. And we went 4-8 last year. This team is already at four wins with five games left. Progress. And here's one more number for the scorecard: Craig has thrown five interceptions this season. We don't need many chances. One clean shot can change a game.

Morgantown vs. Fort Worth

Morgantown. Zackquill Morgan founded our town in 1785, on the Monongahela River near the Pennsylvania border. In 1975, Morgantown opened a driverless people-mover system, one of the few in the United States, and it went its first 42 years without a reported injury. Driverless cars? We were testing the future while the rest of the country was still circling the parking lot.

The pepperoni roll was first sold in 1927 by Giuseppe "Joseph" Argiro at the Country Club Bakery in Fairmont, just down the road. It was made for coal miners, because it didn't need refrigeration. The state tourism bureau calls it the state food of West Virginia. And "Take Me Home, Country Roads" has been played at every home pregame since 1972. When our stadium opened in 1980, John Denver himself landed on the field in a helicopter and sang it. Top that.

Fort Worth. Fort Worth calls itself "where the West begins." Fair enough. But it's the second-largest city in its own metro area, behind Dallas, and Dallas has held the population majority there for as long as records have been kept. Fort Worth has been the little brother in its own neighborhood since before anyone owned a calculator.

And they still run a cattle drive through the Stockyards twice a day, weather permitting. Twice a day. Those cows have a better commute schedule than a city bus.

Then there's the mascot. The Texas horned lizard defends itself by squirting blood from the corners of its eyes, up to 5 feet. I've been on a lot of ranges. I've seen a lot of defenses. That's the first one I've seen that cries at you.

Final Count

Here's my scorecard. TCU has a strong defense and an offense that can't run. West Virginia has a quarterback who just threw for 464 yards, a top-five rushing attack, a kicker with ice in his veins and a defense that needs to show up. If we hold the ball, run Cook downhill and tackle in space, we're singing Country Roads on the bus ride home.

Pepperoni roll tally for TCU's fumbles is at zero. For now. Load up. I don't miss.

My call: TCU Horned Frogs 34, West Virginia Mountaineers 21.
