articles.title: Objection: Sustained. Boston College Takes Its Case to Atlanta, a City With 71 Streets Named Peachtree and a Defense That Ranks 110th
articles.byline: Siobhan Dunleavy, The Boston College Fanatic
articles.matchup: Boston College (3-3) at Georgia Tech (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Bobby Dodd Stadium, ACC Network
articles.text:
All rise. The Court of Siobhan Dunleavy is now in session, and the Honorable Siobhan Dunleavy presiding. Yes, I'm also the prosecutor, the defense attorney and the jury. I was a debate champion, and I've never once met an argument I couldn't win, mostly because I keep appointing myself the judge.

Today's docket: one wicked good comeback, one trip to Atlanta and one very strong opinion about street names.

Objection: sustained.

Part 1: The People vs. a Terrible First Two Minutes

Boston College beat Pittsburgh 27-21 at Alumni Stadium on Saturday. We're 3-3 and 1-2 in the ACC. But let the record show that the first two minutes of this game were, to use the technical legal term, a disaster.

Exhibit A: Pitt scored on the very first play from scrimmage, a 75-yard touchdown pass. Exhibit B: After we went three-and-out, Pitt blocked our punt, and the ball got knocked out of the end zone for a safety. Exhibit C: a Pitt field goal. Twelve to nothing. I nearly called a mistrial.

But the defense rested, and then it didn't. Bo MacCormack III ran in from 1 yard. Mason McKenzie hit Javarius Green for an 11-yard touchdown with 51 seconds left in the half, and we led 14-12. On our first drive of the second half, McKenzie hit Landon Wright for a 69-yard touchdown. Later, McKenzie found Wright again for 53 yards, and Evan Dickens punched it in from 1 yard on the next play. That made it 27-18.

McKenzie went 17 of 28 for 295 yards and two touchdowns, with two interceptions. Wright caught just two passes, for 122 yards. That's a wicked efficient witness. KP Price had an interception, and when Pitt got the ball at our 8 with just over two minutes left, Charlie Comella intercepted another one to end it. Case closed.

The court also notes, for the record, that Pitt was flagged 13 times for 133 yards, including five penalties for 63 yards on a single drive. I didn't have to make that argument. The officials made it for me.

Part 2: Boston College v. Georgia Tech

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern on ACC Network. Boston College (3-3) at Georgia Tech (2-4) at Bobby Dodd Stadium.

Opening Statement for the Prosecution

Members of the jury, I'll be fair. Georgia Tech went 9-4 last season. Its quarterback, Alberto Mendoza, completes 71.2 of every 100 passes and just threw for a career-high 335 yards. Jordan Allen has 38 catches. And the Yellow Jackets beat a previously unbeaten Duke team two weeks ago. Noted.

Now, the evidence.

Georgia Tech is 2-4. It opened the season with a 14-13 home loss to Colorado, a team that's currently 2-4 and has lost four straight. Georgia Tech also lost at Stanford, 34-27. Last week at Virginia Tech, it trailed 24-3 at halftime. On its very first possession, a Georgia Tech runner fumbled the ball through the end zone on his way to a touchdown, and it became a touchback. AP says Georgia Tech's two turnovers led to 10 Virginia Tech points.

The defense? Georgia Tech allows 392.2 yards a game, 110th in FBS, and 179 rushing yards a game, also 110th. It allows 27.2 points a game, 102nd. Opponents convert 43.2 of every 100 third downs, 112th. Georgia Tech is minus-4 in turnover margin, 113th. And it averages 70.5 penalty yards a game, 117th. I rest my case. I rest it very comfortably.

Opening Statement for the Defense (Of My Own Team)

The court is honest. Boston College scores 20.3 points a game, 118th in FBS. We score on just 60 of every 100 red zone trips, 135th. McKenzie has thrown seven interceptions. And let the record reflect that last season, per CollegeFootballData, we went 2-10. Painful testimony. But this team already has three wins.

Our evidence: our pass defense allows 169.3 yards a game, 18th in FBS. We're plus-1 in turnover margin. Demetrius Ballard has 3.5 sacks. Anthony Palano leads us with 52 tackles. McKenzie is also our leading rusher, with 444 yards. And against a Georgia Tech run defense ranked 110th, I'd like to call a few running plays to the stand.

Cross-Examination

The key witness for Georgia Tech is Mendoza. He went 29 of 38 at Virginia Tech, and Allen caught 10 passes for 120 yards. That's the matchup. Our pass defense against their passing game, which ranks 44th. If our secondary keeps everything in front of it, Georgia Tech's offense has to march the length of the field, one completion at a time, against a defense that doesn't give up much through the air. Make them earn it. Make them prove it beyond a reasonable doubt.

Precedent

Georgia Tech leads the series 8-5, according to CollegeFootballData, and it won last season 36-34 in Chestnut Hill. I don't love that precedent. But Boston College won its last two trips to Bobby Dodd Stadium, 41-30 in 2021 and 38-23 in 2023. Precedent, your honor. Precedent.

Change of Venue: Boston vs. Atlanta

Boston. Boston was founded in 1630, and it has a list of firsts that would make any opposing counsel sit down quietly. The nation's first public park, Boston Common, in 1634. The first public school, Boston Latin School, in 1635. The first subway system in America, the Tremont Street subway, in 1897. When the rest of the country needed to learn how to do something, it checked what Boston did first.

Boston College sits in Chestnut Hill, a village six miles west of downtown Boston. It's best known for being home to BC and a section of the Boston Marathon route. Alumni Stadium opened on Sept. 21, 1957. And yes, Chestnut Hill is technically split among Boston, Brookline and Newton. We don't belong to one town. We belong to three. That's called a strong coalition.

Atlanta. Exhibit D: Atlanta has 71 streets with some version of "Peachtree" in their names. Seventy-one! Locals joke that half of Atlanta's streets are named Peachtree and the other half have five names to make up for it. Objection, your honor, the city is leading the witness, and the witness is lost on Peachtree Something.

Exhibit E: Atlanta couldn't settle on a name, either. It was founded as the end point of a railroad, renamed Marthasville in 1842, and then renamed Atlanta. Three names. Boston has had one name since 1630. Consistency, people.

Exhibit F: Georgia Tech's mascot is the Ramblin' Wreck, a 1930 Ford Model A Sport Coupe. It's leading the team out of the tunnel at 96 years old. I respect it deeply. I also have questions about its air bags.

And Bobby Dodd Stadium, I'll concede, is the oldest stadium in FBS, complete since 1913. Charming. Historic. But Boston had a public school for 278 years before Georgia Tech built those stands. Objection: sustained.

Closing Argument

Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, the evidence is clear. Georgia Tech has a talented quarterback, a struggling defense, a turnover problem and a penalty problem. Boston College has a top-20 pass defense, a quarterback who can run it and a team that just proved it can come back from 12 down. If the Eagles win the turnover battle and finish in the red zone, the verdict comes back in our favor.

The court will now adjourn for a lobster roll. Go Eagles.

My call: Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets 28, Boston College Eagles 21.

articles.title: Power to the Play-Call! Cal Marches on Dallas, a City Founded by a Man Who Planted a Stake and Left, to Face No. 23 SMU
articles.byline: Quentin Oyelaran-Fitch, The California Fanatic
articles.matchup: Cal (3-4) at No. 23 SMU (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Gerald J. Ford Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Comrades in blue and gold, greetings. Quentin Oyelaran-Fitch here, philosophy PhD, lifelong Golden Bear and owner of more hand-lettered picket signs than any man in Alameda County. When the play-call is wrong, I protest. When the play-call is right, I protest in favor of it. I believe in the dignity of every snap.

This week I needed a lot of poster board.

Power to the play-call!

Part 1: A Philosophical Crisis in Strawberry Canyon

Wake Forest beat us 41-7 at California Memorial Stadium on Saturday night. We're 3-4 and 2-2 in the ACC. I'm a philosopher, so I'll approach this with Socratic honesty: I know that I know nothing, except that this one hurt.

The first sign went up early. It read "WHY?" Wake's first possession was a five-play, 99-yard touchdown drive. Then we went for it on fourth-and-1 at our own 34 and didn't get it, and Wake scored right away on a 29-yard pass. My second sign read "WHY, PART TWO." Wake scored touchdowns on five of its six first-half possessions and averaged 12.3 yards per play. We trailed 34-0 at halftime. AP says that was our biggest halftime deficit since 2013.

Wake's quarterback threw four touchdown passes, three to the same tight end. Wake outgained us 394-142 in the first half. Existentially speaking, the first half did not exist for us.

Now, the honest silver lining, because philosophy demands balance. We didn't turn the ball over. We had only five penalties. And in the fourth quarter, Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele threw a 28-yard touchdown pass to Mason Mini, and he finished 15 of 18. That's a sign I can hold up proudly: "15 OF 18. RESPECT THE PROCESS."

And remember, one week earlier, we beat Virginia Tech 25-20. This team has a pulse. It just took a night off.

Part 2: The March on Dallas

Saturday, noon Eastern, 11 a.m. in Texas, on The CW. Cal (3-4) at No. 23 SMU (5-1) at Gerald J. Ford Stadium.

The Manifesto on SMU

In fairness, and I'm always fair, SMU is good. It's 5-1 and ranked 23rd. AP says the Mustangs are 10-0 at home in ACC games since joining the conference in 2024. Kevin Jennings completes 72.9 of every 100 passes, and SMU's passing offense ranks fifth in FBS. Its pass defense ranks 11th. Kendrick Raphael ran for 124 yards against Virginia last week. Marques White has 4.5 sacks.

Now, the rest of the manifesto.

SMU beat Virginia 23-13, but its coach said afterward that the offense didn't finish enough drives. AP noted SMU's offense gained just 218 yards against Boston College two weeks earlier. SMU's kicking game was 3 of 7 on field goals this season before last week. Its new kicker is a former SMU soccer player who'd missed his only previous attempt. He made all three on Saturday, and I sincerely applaud him. But one of those field goals came on an untimed down after a roughing-the-passer penalty when time had already expired. The universe gifted SMU three points, and I have a sign about that: "THE COSMOS IS NOT NEUTRAL."

SMU is 114th in FBS in penalty yards, 95th in red zone offense and 93rd in rushing. And it lost at Louisville 41-31 in September.

The Most Important Fact in This Article

Last season, Cal beat SMU 38-35 in Berkeley. That's the most recent meeting, according to CollegeFootballData. SMU leads the series 2-1, but the last word belongs to us. And I'm a philosopher. The last word is all I ever want.

Honest Self-Critique

Every good protester critiques his own movement. Our running game averages 90.3 yards a game, 137th in FBS. Our defense allows 181.4 rushing yards a game, 111th. We're 131st in penalty yards. Those signs read "FIX IT" in very large letters.

But our passing game ranks 15th in FBS. Sagapolutele has 1,290 yards and nine touchdowns. Chase Hendricks has 47 catches. AJ Tuitele has three sacks, and Isaiah Crosby leads us with 40 tackles. If we protect the passer and slow down Raphael, we can make this a game.

Our List of Demands

Every movement needs demands. Here are mine, written in marker on the back of last week's signs.

Demand one: Protect the quarterback. SMU's pass defense ranks 11th in FBS, and White will be hunting. Quick throws to Hendricks. Get the ball out.

Demand two: Run the ball enough to keep SMU honest. Even 3 or 4 yards a carry on early downs changes everything about third down.

Demand three: No fourth-and-1 at our own 34 in the first quarter. I'm a philosopher, not a coach, but some questions answer themselves.

Demand four: Keep the ball safe again. We didn't turn it over against Wake Forest. Do it again, and make SMU drive the whole field against a red zone defense that ranks 24th.

Town Hall: Berkeley vs. Dallas

Berkeley. The University of California was founded in 1868 as the state's first land-grant university, and Berkeley is its founding campus. Our alumni, faculty and researchers include 65 Nobel laureates. Researchers here discovered 16 chemical elements, more than any other university in the world. One of them is named berkelium, after our city. Our town is literally on the periodic table. Show me Dallas on the periodic table. I'll wait. I'm very patient. I have a doctorate.

Our stadium, California Memorial Stadium, opened in 1923, with seating for around 63,000. The hill above it is known as Tightwad Hill, where fans have long tried to watch games for free. That's not stinginess. That's a philosophy of resource allocation.

Dallas. Dallas is big. Ninth-most populous city in the country. I respect scale. But here's the founding story, straight from the history books. In 1839, a man named John Neely Bryan planted a stake in the ground on a bluff near the Trinity River. Then he left. He came back two years later and founded Dallas. So Dallas began with a man making a commitment and immediately walking away from it. Philosophically, that's fascinating.

Dallas is also the largest inland metro area in the United States that lacks any navigable link to the sea. Berkeley has a whole bay. Dallas has highways and confidence.

And here's something I learned while researching. SMU isn't technically in the city of Dallas. Its home, University Park, is a separate town of about 25,000, surrounded by Dallas and Highland Park. So SMU is a Dallas team that lives in its own little enclave. In Berkeley, we'd call that a commune.

The mascot is Peruna, a black Shetland pony that's been at nearly every SMU home game since 1932. Lovely animal. But he was named after a popular patent medicine. A pony named after a tonic. I have no further questions, your honor. Wrong profession, but you get the idea.

Closing Argument

SMU has a strong quarterback, a stout pass defense and a nice home streak. Cal has a talented young quarterback, a strong passing game and the most recent win in this series. If we protect the ball like we did against Wake and finally find a running game, the people's march ends in a victory parade all the way back to Strawberry Canyon.

Power to the play-call! Go Bears!

My call: SMU Mustangs 35, California Golden Bears 18.

articles.title: Orange You Glad I Said It? Clemson Hosts Virginia Tech, Whose Mascot Is a Turkey and Who Lost to a Cal Team That Just Lost by 34
articles.byline: Dixie-Lynn Pruitt, The Clemson Fanatic
articles.matchup: Virginia Tech (5-2) at Clemson (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7 p.m. ET, Memorial Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Well, hey there, y'all! Dixie-Lynn Pruitt here, former Tiger Band flag captain, sitting on my porch in an orange rocking chair named Darlene, sipping sweet tea from an orange cup named Beauregard. I own 43 orange items, and every one of them has a name. I read defensive rotations like halftime choreography: everybody's got a spot, everybody's got a count, and if one person misses a step, the whole formation looks like a kitchen drawer.

On Saturday, sugar, every Tiger hit every count.

Orange you glad I said it?

Part 1: A Shutout in the Valley

Clemson beat Charleston Southern 37-0 at Death Valley on Saturday. We're 4-2. And it was Clemson's first shutout in five seasons, the first since we beat South Carolina 30-0 in 2021.

We scored on our first five possessions. Nolan Hauser opened with a 41-yard field goal. Chris Johnson Jr. ran in from 6 yards. Gideon Davidson ran in from 7. Johnson scored again from 2 yards out. Then, on the very next kickoff, we forced a fumble and safety Kylon Griffin scooped it up and ran 17 yards for a touchdown. That's what I call a flag routine with a surprise toss at the end.

And then, y'all, Hauser. With 47 seconds left before halftime, he kicked a 59-yard field goal that just inched over the crossbar. It's his career long. It beat his famous 56-yarder, the walk-off kick that won Clemson the 2024 ACC title over SMU. My orange throw pillow, Lula Mae, went flying clear across the den. He added a 44-yarder in the fourth quarter for the only points of the second half.

The defense? Choreography, darling. Charleston Southern finished with 76 yards. It went 0 for 11 on third down and 0 for 2 on fourth down. We ran for 231 yards, two weeks after Miami held us to 55. Clemson is now 41-0 all-time against FCS teams.

I'll be honest, because my mama raised me right. Charleston Southern is an FCS team, and we threw two interceptions late. It's one step in the routine, not the whole show. But it was the best we've looked all year, and our coach said the same thing afterward.

And here's my most beloved part of the whole day. It was Military Appreciation Day, and an offensive lineman whose parents both served in the Army carried the American flag down the hill during our entrance. Bless that young man. I cried into an orange hanky named Myrtle.

Part 2: The Gobblers Come to the Valley

Saturday, 7 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. Virginia Tech (5-2) at Clemson (4-2) at Memorial Stadium. A Saturday night in Death Valley. Mercy, I can already hear the cannon.

Grading the Hokies' Routine

Let me be sweet first. Virginia Tech can throw it. Ethan Grunkemeyer completes 72.6 of every 100 passes, with 1,984 yards, 15 touchdowns and just two interceptions. Que'Sean Brown just caught six passes for 182 yards against Georgia Tech. Aycen Stevens has eight sacks, and their run defense allows only 87.4 yards a game, 10th in FBS. That's a real dance company.

Now, honey, the critique.

Virginia Tech lost at home to Pittsburgh, 35-33. Then it lost at Cal, 25-20. And that Cal team just lost 41-7 at home to Wake Forest last Saturday. Bless their hearts. The Hokies' pass defense allows 227.3 yards a game, 95th in FBS. And they're minus-4 in turnover margin, 113th.

Their best wins? VMI, 73-3. Old Dominion. Maryland. Boston College by a touchdown. Georgia Tech, which is 2-4. Sugar, that's a lovely recital. But this is the Valley on a Saturday night.

Grading Our Own Routine

I don't fib, so here's the honest scorecard. Our offense gains 340.7 yards a game, 110th in FBS. Our passing game is 112th. We convert 33.3 of every 100 third downs, 116th. We're minus-4 in turnovers too. We lost 51-10 at LSU to open the season, and Miami beat us 41-13 at home. And last season we went 7-6, per CollegeFootballData. That's not the Clemson I know.

But our defense allows 21.5 points a game, 49th in FBS, and its pass defense ranks 39th. Will Heldt has four sacks, and Corey Myrick leads us with 44 tackles. Davidson has 430 rushing yards and five touchdowns. If we can keep the ball moving on the ground the way we did Saturday, we can keep Grunkemeyer on the sideline.

The Choreography Chart

Here's my flag-captain blocking for Saturday night. Count one: run the ball with Davidson and Johnson and let Death Valley get loud. Count two: keep Tait Reynolds out of third-and-long, because that's where we've struggled all year. Count three: Heldt and the front have to get to Grunkemeyer before he finds Brown deep. Count four: no turnovers. Both teams are minus-4 this year, so whoever cleans that up first probably wins the routine. Hit all four counts, and it's a standing ovation.

History in the Valley

Clemson leads the series 23-11-1, according to CollegeFootballData, and we've won the last six meetings, dating to 2011. That includes a 42-35 win in Orlando in 2016. The last time the Hokies played in Death Valley, in 2012, Clemson won 38-17.

Postcards: Clemson vs. Blacksburg

Clemson. Clemson is a sweet little city of 17,681, and on game days, Memorial Stadium holds 81,500. You read that right. Our stadium holds more than four times our town. It opened on Sept. 19, 1942, with a 32-13 win over Presbyterian College. And in 2007, against Boston College, Death Valley set a record as the loudest stadium in college football at 133 decibels.

Then there's Howard's Rock. In the early 1960s, a friend gave coach Frank Howard a rock from Death Valley, California, saying it was from Death Valley to Death Valley. The Tigers have rubbed it since 1967. Our mascot is a tiger, and our good luck charm is a rock. Neither one has ever gobbled.

Blacksburg. Blacksburg is a charming mountain town. I'll give them that. But I did some reading, and their mascot, the HokieBird, is officially a large, anthropomorphic turkey. The team used to be called the Fighting Gobblers. Darling, we come out to a cannon. They come out to Thanksgiving dinner.

And the word "Hokie"? It comes from a spirit yell written for a contest in 1896, and whatever it originally meant is still a matter of debate. So Virginia Tech's nickname is a word from a cheer contest that nobody can define. My orange dictionary, Ophelia, has no entry for it.

Lane Stadium's first game, in 1965, ended Virginia Tech 9, William & Mary 7. Sixteen points combined. That's not a football game, honey. That's a quiet afternoon on the porch.

Final Formation

Here's how I see the routine. Virginia Tech has a sharp quarterback, a tough run defense and a pass defense that ranks 95th. Clemson has the Valley, the Rock, a defense that just pitched a shutout and a running game that finally found its rhythm. If we protect the ball and make Grunkemeyer throw into a loud Saturday night crowd, the Hokies will be gobbling all the way home. That's not a guarantee, friends. It's a forecast from somebody who has watched this team grow up all season long. Bring your loudest voice, your brightest orange and your best manners for the visitors, because a Saturday night in the Valley is a family affair.

Orange you glad I said it? Go Tigers!

My call: Clemson Tigers 27, Virginia Tech Hokies 24.

articles.title: I Also Passed That Exam: Duke Visits Charlottesville, Where They Call Campus 'the Grounds' and the Offense Ranks 120th on Third Down
articles.byline: Harrison Wexley-Moore IV, The Duke Fanatic
articles.matchup: Duke (4-2) at Virginia (4-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 7 p.m. ET, Scott Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Good evening, Blue Devil faithful. Harrison Wexley-Moore IV here, pre-law, pre-med, pre-MBA, pre-architecture and, as of this morning, pre-astronaut. I've read the playbook, the LSAT prep book and the complete works of Shakespeare, usually in that order. I also passed that exam. Whichever exam you're thinking of. I passed it.

But this week, friends, I need to grade my own team. And as any good academic will tell you, an honest grade is the only grade worth having.

Part 1: The Bell Tolls for Someone Else

North Carolina beat us 24-20 at Wallace Wade Stadium on Saturday. We're 4-2 and 1-2 in the ACC. The Tar Heels ran across the field afterward and took back the Victory Bell. That's a painful sound, friends. I have three music degrees, and that was the worst note I've ever heard.

UNC led 17-0 early in the second quarter after a field goal, a 5-yard touchdown pass and a 4-yard run. Then our defense took over the lecture hall. Safety Andrew Pellicciotta returned a fumble 9 yards for a touchdown. Gavin Strange kicked field goals of 22 and 21 yards. AP says UNC managed only about 100 yards between its first 17 points and its final drive. North Carolina went more than 41 minutes without scoring.

And then, with 4:39 left, Walker Eget hit Nate Sheppard with a short pass, and Sheppard reached the end zone from 7 yards out. Duke led 20-17. My thesis was nearly complete.

But on fourth-and-4 from their own 28 with 3:48 left, UNC completed a pass to keep the drive alive. With 1:53 left, Jaylen McGill ran 24 yards for the winning touchdown.

Sheppard, the nation's leader in rushing yards per game, ran for 77 yards on 20 carries and caught 11 passes for 98 yards. Eget went 24 of 38 for 249 yards. And for the second straight week, AP noted, we took a late lead and gave up the winning touchdown inside the final two minutes. A week earlier, it was 28-25 at Georgia Tech. Duke had also won eight straight games against in-state opponents. Our coach called it two very tough results for a good football team. I concur, with honors.

Part 2: Friday Night in Charlottesville

Friday, 7 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. Duke (4-2) at Virginia (4-3) at Scott Stadium.

And let's be clear about the most recent meeting. Last December, in the ACC Championship Game in Charlotte, Duke beat Virginia 27-20 in overtime. It was Duke's first outright ACC championship since 1962. I wrote three dissertations about it. Virginia did beat us 34-17 in Durham during the regular season, and I respect that. But the championship is the final exam, friends. The final exam counts more.

Peer Review: Virginia

In the spirit of fair academic review, Virginia does several things well. Its pass defense allows 173.9 yards a game, 25th in FBS. It's plus-5 in turnover margin, 15th. Beau Pribula has thrown 13 touchdowns and just one interception. And Virginia went 11-3 last season.

Now the critique, in footnotes.

Virginia has been held under 300 yards in three straight games, according to AP. It finished with 258 yards in a 23-13 loss at SMU last Saturday. Its offense ranks 90th in yards and 96th in passing. It converts 33.0 of every 100 third downs, 120th in FBS. It scores on 74.1 of every 100 red zone trips, 124th. And earlier this month, Virginia lost 38-7 at Florida State. That's not a passing grade. That's a request for an extension.

Here's my most beloved footnote. Duke's defense allows opponents to convert just 29.2 of every 100 third downs, ninth in FBS. Virginia's offense converts 33.0 of every 100, 120th. Those two numbers walked into the same seminar, and one of them is going to leave early.

Self-Assessment: Duke

Our defense allows 16.0 points a game, 19th in FBS, and 92.5 rushing yards a game, 18th. Our running game averages 209.5 yards a game, 22nd. Sheppard has 820 rushing yards and eight touchdowns, and he leads us in receiving too. Kevin O'Connor has three sacks, and Nick Morris Jr. leads us with 33 tackles. We control the clock, too, averaging 33:17 of possession a game, 13th in FBS.

Honest Grade

Here's my B-minus moment. Duke averages 73.8 penalty yards a game, 123rd in FBS. We need to finish games. Two late leads, two late losses. In academic terms, we keep writing brilliant papers and forgetting to put our names on them. Fix the flags, close the fourth quarter and this is an A.

The Syllabus for Friday Night

Week-by-week reading list, condensed into four lessons. Lesson one: feed Sheppard. Virginia's run defense ranks 88th, allowing 152.7 yards a game, and our running game is built for exactly that. Lesson two: win third down on defense. Virginia struggles there more than almost anyone in FBS, and our defense is among the best in the country at getting off the field. Lesson three: don't give the ball away. Virginia is plus-5 in turnovers, and it lives on mistakes. Lesson four, and this is the one that will be on the final: when we have the lead in the fourth quarter, keep it. Two straight weeks, we've learned that one the hard way. Third time's the lesson.

Campus Tour: Durham vs. Charlottesville

Durham. Durham is the fourth-most populous city in North Carolina, with 283,506 people at the 2020 census, and it anchors one corner of the Research Triangle. Duke Chapel, finished in 1935, stands 210 feet tall and is one of the tallest buildings in Durham County. And Wallace Wade Stadium, opened in 1929, hosted the 1942 Rose Bowl. That's right. During World War II, the Rose Bowl came to Durham. Pasadena needed a substitute teacher, and Durham was ready.

Our nickname even has a story. "Blue Devils" comes from "les Diables Bleus," the World War I nickname of the Chasseurs Alpins, the French Alpine light infantry. I also speak French. Naturally.

Charlottesville. Charlottesville is a pleasant city of 46,553. Durham has about six Charlottesvilles. And at Virginia, they don't call it a campus. They call it "the Grounds." Friends, I have a landscaping certificate too, and I can confirm "the Grounds" is what you call the area around a nice house. The University of Virginia has a lovely Rotunda, a famous Lawn and a word for campus that sounds like a coffee order.

Their nickname, "Wahoos," comes from the school's rallying cry, "Wah-hoo-wah!" I've studied linguistics extensively, and I can tell you that's not a word. It's the sound I make when I stub my toe on a Duke textbook.

And Scott Stadium, built in 1931, offers grass hill seating. Charming. At Duke, we sit in chairs. I have an ergonomics degree.

Final Exam

Here's my thesis. Virginia has a sharp passing defense and a quarterback who protects the ball, but an offense that has stalled for three straight weeks. Duke has a top-20 scoring defense, a top-10 third-down defense, a powerful running game led by Sheppard and the memory of a championship won against this exact opponent. If Duke protects a fourth-quarter lead this time, we'll be ringing our own bell on Friday night.

I also passed that exam. Go Duke.

My call: Virginia Cavaliers 25, Duke Blue Devils 23.

articles.title: Motion to Reconsider: Denied. Florida State Takes Its Double-Overtime Heartbreak Into a Bye Week, Then Hosts Clemson, Whose Stadium Nickname Came From California
articles.byline: Gianna Ravello, The Florida State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Florida State (3-4): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Clemson at Florida State, Sat., Oct. 31, Doak Campbell Stadium
articles.text:
The chamber will come to order. Gianna Ravello here, the Florida State Fanatic, a capital-city operator who networks like a lobbyist and reads game coverage like pending legislation. I follow the Seminoles to every game from the stands, and every take I have becomes a bill on the floor.

Today's docket has two items. First, a heartbreaker in Miami Gardens that deserves a full hearing. Second, a bye week, followed by Clemson's visit to Tallahassee. Let the record show I'm ready.

Part 1: Last Week, a Filibuster That Ran Two Overtimes

Florida State lost 43-35 in double overtime at Miami on Saturday night. We're 3-4 and 1-3 in the ACC. Miami came in ranked No. 3 and is now No. 1 in the AP poll. The AP called it a back-and-forth classic, and, colleagues, I'd like that entered into the record.

The first half was a fair debate. Miami scored first on a 7-yard run. Ashton Daniels answered with a 23-yard touchdown pass to Desirrio Riles. Miami scored on a 14-yard pass, and Daniels tied it with a 2-yard touchdown run with 1:40 left in the half. 14-14.

In the third quarter, Ashlynd Barker intercepted a pass in the end zone with the game tied 14-14. Per the AP, that ended a streak of 153 passes to start Miami's quarterback's career without an interception. Then Daniels hit Quintrevion Wisner for a 28-yard touchdown, and we led 21-14. Early in the fourth, our defense stopped Miami on fourth-and-2 inside the red zone. The bill was on the governor's desk.

Then the opposition rallied. Miami tied it with 9:33 left and took a 28-21 lead on a 3-yard touchdown catch with 2:49 left. And 10 seconds later, Daniels found Duce Robinson for a 75-yard touchdown. 28-28. Colleagues, that's what we in the Capitol call a late amendment.

In the first overtime, Daniels hit Robinson again from 20 yards out. Miami answered with a 25-yard touchdown run. In the second overtime, Miami scored on a 3-yard pass and added a two-point conversion to lead 43-35. Then Daniels connected on a 36-yard completion on fourth-and-21 that would have set up a score, but it was called back for holding. On the final play, Miami intercepted a pass in the end zone. It was reviewed and upheld.

Motion to reconsider: denied. I don't like it, but I respect the process.

Here's the vote count. Daniels threw for 298 yards and four touchdowns, with one interception, on 15 of 28 passing. Robinson caught five passes for 113 yards and two touchdowns. Wisner ran for 63 yards and caught four passes for 56 yards and a score. Barker made 13 tackles and the interception. That's a bipartisan effort. On the other side of the aisle, Miami's quarterback threw for 326 yards and three touchdowns, and its top receiver caught 11 passes for 154 yards. Credit where it's due. I always shake hands across the aisle after the vote.

The Minority Report

A good legislator reads the opposition's brief too, so here's my honest one. Florida State went 0-for-3 on fourth down at Miami, including two failed tries from inside the Miami 5. Per the AP, a fourth-and-2 stop near the goal also hurt us in our 44-20 loss at Louisville the week before. And the AP notes we've now lost 14 straight games away from Tallahassee. Miami held the ball for 37:20 and outgained us 583 yards to 443.

We went 5-7 last season. We lost 27-24 to SMU at home and 50-36 at Alabama this year. That's the full record, and the record matters.

Part 2: The Bye, Then Clemson

Florida State doesn't play this Saturday, Oct. 24. It's our open date. The committee is in recess, and I recommend everyone use it wisely: rest, heal, and review the film until it's memorized like the state constitution.

On Saturday, Oct. 31, Clemson visits Doak Campbell Stadium. Kickoff time and TV are still to be announced.

The Opposition's Brief

I'll be gracious to the visiting delegation, because that's how deals get done. Clemson is 4-2. It beat North Carolina 28-20 and won at Cal 24-10. Its kicker, Nolan Hauser, made a 59-yard field goal in its 37-0 win over Charleston Southern last week. Defensive end Will Heldt has four sacks. And last season, Clemson beat us 24-10 in Clemson. That's on the record.

But here's the rest of the file. Clemson lost 51-10 at LSU in its opener. Then it lost 41-13 at home to Miami, the same Miami team that needed two overtimes to beat us. Two of Clemson's four wins came against Georgia Southern and Charleston Southern, an FCS team. And last season, Clemson went 7-6 and lost the Pinstripe Bowl 22-10 to Penn State.

Clemson also hosts Virginia Tech this Saturday, while we rest. So when the Tigers arrive in Tallahassee, they'll be coming off a game, and we'll be coming off two weeks of preparation. Advantage: the incumbent.

Our Legislative Agenda

1. Feed the veto-proof majority. Daniels has proven he can make every throw. Robinson's 75-yard touchdown showed it. Keep taking shots.
2. Finish in the red zone. We had two fourth-down failures inside the Miami 5. Convert those, and that game is a different bill entirely.
3. Make the stops count. Our defense made two big fourth-down stops in the second half at Miami. Bring that energy home.

The Capital vs. the Valley

Tallahassee. Tallahassee has been the capital of Florida since 1824, back when Florida was still a territory. It's the only incorporated municipality in Leon County, so we don't share. Its estimated 2024 population was 205,089, and its student population tops 70,000. We're hilly by Florida standards, with elevation reaching just over 200 feet, and the state capitol sits on one of the highest hills in town. We're also known for our canopy roads.

Doak Campbell Stadium opened in 1950, and the Seminoles won its first game 40-7 over Randolph-Macon. In 2004, the Florida Legislature added Bobby Bowden's name to the field. Colleagues, our stadium was literally named by an act of the legislature. And before home games, Osceola and Renegade ride to midfield and plant a burning spear in the turf, a tradition since 1978 that's supported by leaders of the Seminole Tribe of Florida.

Clemson. Clemson is a charming city of 17,681. Tallahassee has about 12 Clemsons. And here's an item for the record. The nickname "Death Valley" comes partly from Death Valley National Park, in California. The famous Howard's Rock came from Death Valley, California, too. So Clemson's stadium nickname and its lucky rock were both imported from out of state. Colleagues, that's not a tradition. That's an interstate commerce issue.

Closing Arguments

Here's the summary for the committee. Florida State took the No. 1 team in the country to two overtimes on its home field, with a quarterback who threw four touchdown passes. Clemson has a strong kicker and a solid pass rush but has struggled against its best opponents. We have a bye to rest and prepare, and Clemson has to play Virginia Tech first. If we finish in the red zone and keep making explosive plays, the vote on Oct. 31 goes our way.

Motion to reconsider: denied. The bye week is in session.

articles.title: Graph Paper Doesn't Lie: Georgia Tech Hosts Boston College, Whose Hometown Isn't Technically a Town and Whose Red Zone Offense Ranks 135th
articles.byline: Wendell Quist, The Georgia Tech Fanatic
articles.matchup: Boston College (3-3) at Georgia Tech (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Bobby Dodd Stadium, ACC Network
articles.text:
Greetings, Jackets. Wendell Quist reporting, aerospace engineering degree on the wall, mechanical pencil behind my ear and a fresh pad of graph paper on the desk. I model the trajectory of every Georgia Tech punt. I chart every drive as a vector. I believe everything in this world is physics, and football is just physics wearing a helmet.

This week's experiment produced mixed results. That's okay. That's science. You record the data honestly, adjust the variables and run it again.

Graph paper doesn't lie.

Part 1: A Steep Initial Slope

Virginia Tech beat us 34-24 in Blacksburg on Saturday. We're 2-4 and 1-2 in the ACC. I'll present the data exactly as it happened, because an engineer who fudges data builds bridges that fall down.

The first half was a negative-slope graph. Virginia Tech scored a 60-yard touchdown on the game's third play and scored on four of its first five possessions. On our first possession, we fumbled the ball through the end zone on the way to a touchdown, and it became a touchback. That's a perfect trajectory with a catastrophic landing. Aidan Birr kicked a 31-yard field goal, but we trailed 24-3 at halftime.

Then the curve bent upward. Trelain Maddox ran 42 yards for a touchdown to open the third quarter. Two minutes later, Alberto Mendoza hit Dalen Penson for a 33-yard touchdown. Suddenly it was 24-17. In engineering terms, that's a rapid rate of change.

Virginia Tech answered with a touchdown and a field goal, and Mendoza found Jaiven Plummer for a 6-yard score late. But it wasn't enough.

Here's the data point I'll be framing: Mendoza completed 29 of 38 passes for a career-high 335 yards and two touchdowns. Jordan Allen caught 10 passes for 120 yards. And Georgia Tech outgained Virginia Tech 428-409. More yards, fewer points. AP noted our two turnovers led to 10 Virginia Tech points. That's the whole equation. Coach Brent Key talked afterward about consistency and the improvement he saw, and the graph agrees with him on both.

Part 2: The Eagles Land in Atlanta

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern on ACC Network. Boston College (3-3) at Georgia Tech (2-4) at Bobby Dodd Stadium.

Boston College: The Data Set

Let me tip my hard hat first. Boston College just came back from a 12-0 hole to beat Pittsburgh 27-21. Its pass defense allows 169.3 yards a game, 18th in FBS. Mason McKenzie threw for 295 yards and two touchdowns in that game, and he's also BC's leading rusher with 444 yards. Respect.

Now let's graph the rest.

Boston College scores 20.3 points a game, 118th in FBS. It scores on only 60 of every 100 red zone trips, 135th. Visualize that. Picture a rocket that clears the atmosphere and then forgets how to land. McKenzie has thrown seven touchdowns and seven interceptions, and I'm an engineer, so I can tell you that ratio has a slope of exactly 1.

Boston College's season includes a 34-15 loss at Cincinnati and a 22-16 win over Maine, an FCS team. Against Pitt, it trailed 12-0 in the first quarter after giving up a touchdown on the first play from scrimmage and a blocked punt that went for a safety. Its run defense allows 159.5 yards a game, 95th. And last season, per CollegeFootballData, Boston College went 2-10.

Georgia Tech: The Data Set

Mendoza completes 71.2 of every 100 passes, with 1,528 yards, nine touchdowns and four interceptions. Justice Haynes has 462 rushing yards. Allen has 38 catches for 432 yards. Tae Harris leads us with 38 tackles, and Noah Carter has three sacks. Our passing game ranks 44th in FBS. And two weeks ago, we beat a previously unbeaten Duke team, 28-25.

Error Bars

Honesty section. Our defense allows 392.2 yards a game, 110th in FBS, and 179 rushing yards a game, also 110th. We're minus-4 in turnover margin and 117th in penalty yards. We also lost our opener 14-13 to Colorado. Those numbers need to move. The fix is simple physics: an object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by an outside force. Be the outside force, defense.

The series: Georgia Tech leads 8-5, according to CollegeFootballData, and we won last season 36-34 in Chestnut Hill. But BC won its last two trips to Bobby Dodd, in 2021 and 2023. Time to correct that trend.

The Experiment Design

Here's my hypothesis for Saturday. Boston College's run defense ranks 95th. Ours has to be better than it was in Blacksburg, but our offense should get to lean on Haynes and Maddox, who ran for a 42-yard touchdown last week. That pulls defenders toward the ball and opens the air for Mendoza and Allen against a pass defense that's been good all year. Variable two: ball security. We had two turnovers last week and they cost us 10 points. Remove that variable, and the curve changes shape. Variable three: the crowd. This is a 3:30 home kickoff in late October in Atlanta, at the oldest stadium in FBS. Control group, meet home field.

Field Notes: Atlanta vs. Chestnut Hill

Atlanta. Atlanta sits in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains at just over 1,000 feet above sea level, and it has the densest urban tree coverage of any major city in the United States. Hartsfield-Jackson has been the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic since 1998, except for 2020. Atlanta hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics, the first time every one of the invited national Olympic committees sent athletes, a record 197 of them.

And our stadium? Bobby Dodd Stadium has been home to Georgia Tech football in some form since 1905 and as a complete stadium since 1913. It's the oldest stadium in FBS, and it's been the site of more home wins than any other FBS stadium. Our mascot, the Ramblin' Wreck, is a 1930 Ford Model A Sport Coupe that's led the team onto the field since 1961. An engineering school whose mascot is a working machine. That's not a mascot. That's a thesis.

Chestnut Hill. Boston College plays in Chestnut Hill, a village six miles west of downtown Boston. Here's my most beloved fact about it: Chestnut Hill is not an incorporated municipality. It's split among three different places: Brookline, Boston and Newton. So Boston College's hometown is, technically, a shared rounding error between three other towns. As an engineer, I find that wonderful. As a mapmaker, I find it stressful.

Also, the name. Chestnut Hill isn't named after one hill. It refers to several small hills overlooking a reservoir. So it's not "Chestnut Hill." It's "Chestnut Hills, Approximately." And Boston itself, measured at its airport, sits about 19 feet above sea level. Our city is more than 50 times higher. On graph paper, that's not even close. Those Eagles are going to need a longer runway.

Final Calculation

Here's my model. Georgia Tech has the better passing game and a quarterback who's completing better than 70 of every 100 throws. Boston College has a good pass defense, but an offense that struggles to finish drives. If our defense wins third down and we keep the ball off the ground, the Wreck gets to take a victory lap.

Graph paper doesn't lie. Go Jackets!

My call: Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets 28, Boston College Eagles 21.

Boston College has a good pass defense, but an offense that struggles to finish drives. If our defense wins third down and we keep the ball off the ground, the Wreck gets to take a victory lap.
Graph paper doesn't lie. Go Jackets!

articles.title: Hold Your Hats: Louisville Wins in Syracuse, Takes a Bye, Then Welcomes Stanford, a Cardinal With No Actual Bird
articles.byline: Bianca Thornberry, The Louisville Fanatic
articles.matchup: Louisville (4-3): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Stanford at Louisville, Sat., Oct. 31, L&N Federal Credit Union Stadium
articles.text:
Well, hello, darlings, and welcome to the party. Bianca Thornberry here, the Louisville Fanatic, Derby-party hostess, keeper of the sweet tea pitcher, and a woman who knows tempo stats as well as she knows millinery. I follow the Cardinals to every game from the stands, and I rate every game by its hat-worthiness. A one-hat game is a nice afternoon. A five-hat game requires a fascinator, a sun hat and a backup hat for the backup hat.

So pour yourself a sweet tea, and let me tell you about our trip to Syracuse.

Part 1: Last Week, a Two-Hat Win in the Dome

Louisville beat Syracuse 34-26 on Saturday. We're 4-3 and 3-2 in the ACC, and we've won two straight.

Now, the first half was a full-on Derby day. Per the AP, the two teams combined for 669 yards before halftime, the most in the ACC since 2022. Syracuse led 10-0 early, but Keyjuan Brown scored from 5 yards out, and then Lincoln Kienholz ran a quarterback counter 82 yards for a touchdown to give us a 14-10 lead late in the first quarter. Eighty-two yards, darlings. That man ran like he had a garland of roses waiting at the finish.

Syracuse kept answering. Kienholz plowed in from a yard out to put us up 21-16, and Syracuse scored again to lead 23-21. Then, with 28 seconds left in the half, Kienholz hit Isaac Brown for a 46-yard touchdown, and we led 28-23 at the break. Louisville gained 367 yards in the first half alone. Hat-worthiness rating: four hats and a boutonniere.

The second half was a different party. We gained just 58 yards after halftime, and Coach Jeff Brohm called it a tale of two halves. But our defense saved the evening. The Cardinals intercepted Syracuse's quarterback twice in the second half and forced a fumble. Syracuse kicked a field goal to make it 28-26 early in the fourth quarter. Then Cameron White intercepted a pass, and Keyjuan Brown scored from 5 yards out with 7:34 left. 34-26. Hold your hats.

Kienholz completed 14 of 26 passes for 310 yards and a touchdown, with two interceptions, and ran for 53 yards and two scores. Per the AP, his 10 rushing touchdowns this season are second only to Florida State quarterback Ashton Daniels. Lawayne McCoy caught five passes for 93 yards. Keyjuan Brown ran for two touchdowns. And Isaac Brown, who ran for 235 yards the week before against Florida State, was held to 22 yards, but he still found a way to score on that 46-yard catch. That's a man who changes hats mid-party.

And here's a stat I adore. Per the AP, Louisville has scored at least 28 points in every game this season. Every single one. That's consistent hosting, darlings. In my world, that's like serving the same perfect sweet tea at every party for seven straight weeks. Guests notice, and they come back.

The Honest Seating Chart

Every good hostess knows where the trouble sits. Our three losses came by a combined nine points: 41-38 to Ole Miss in Nashville, 30-27 at home to Wake Forest and 31-28 at NC State. Three points, three points, three points. Darlings, we're one hat pin away from 7-0. That's maddening, but it's also encouraging.

And our defense gave up a lot of easy plays in the first half against Syracuse. Coach Brohm said as much afterward. So we've got some tidying up before guests arrive.

Part 2: The Bye, Then Stanford

Louisville doesn't play this Saturday, Oct. 24. It's our open date. The party planners are taking a week off. Rest those legs, ice those shoulders and press those suits.

Then, on Saturday, Oct. 31, Stanford visits L&N Federal Credit Union Stadium. Kickoff time and TV are still to be announced. It's Halloween, darlings, so I'm planning a costume hat.

The Guest List: Stanford

I'll be gracious, because that's the Louisville way. Stanford's running back, Micah Ford, just ran for four touchdowns against Elon, tying the school's single-game record. And I must be honest: the last time we played Stanford, in 2024, Stanford beat us 38-35 in California. We remember. We've got the RSVP.

Now, the rest of the guest list. Stanford is 3-4, and that win over Elon came against an FCS team. It lost 45-6 at home to Miami, 35-7 at Duke, 57-3 at Wake Forest and 58-7 at Notre Dame. Its defense allows 452 yards a game, 134th in FBS, and 36.6 points a game, 133rd. And its red zone defense ranks 136th, allowing opponents to score on 96.4 of every 100 trips. Darlings, that's not a defense. That's a garden party with no guest list. Everybody walks right in.

Stanford also has to play NC State on Friday, while we rest. So we'll have two weeks to prepare, and they'll have a short week coming off a game.

Party Prep

1. Keep the scoring streak alive. We've scored at least 28 points every game. Against Stanford's defense, that streak shouldn't be in danger.
2. Fix the second half. We gained 58 yards after halftime in Syracuse. Two weeks of rest should help us finish the party with energy.
3. Contain Ford. He's their best guest. Tackle well, and don't let him break one.

Louisville vs. the Farm

Louisville. Louisville was founded in 1778 by George Rogers Clark and named after King Louis XVI of France, making it one of the oldest cities west of the Appalachians. It grew up as a portage site around the Falls of the Ohio, the only major obstruction to river traffic between the upper Ohio and the Gulf of Mexico. We're home to the Kentucky Derby, first run in 1875 and known as "The Most Exciting Two Minutes in Sports." We're also home to Muhammad Ali, Kentucky Fried Chicken and the Louisville Slugger. Darlings, we've got the fastest horses, the best fried chicken and the most famous bat in America. What more could a girl want?

Stanford. Now, here's a fun fact. Stanford and Louisville are both "Cardinals." But Stanford's team name refers to the color, not the bird, and the university doesn't have an official mascot. The unofficial one is the Stanford Tree, a sequoia that belongs to the marching band and regularly shows up on internet "worst mascot" lists. Darlings, we're the Cardinals with an actual bird. They're the Cardinal with an actual tree.

And Stanford, California, isn't technically a city. It's an unincorporated census-designated place of 21,150 people, mostly living in campus housing. Louisville's consolidated population was 782,969 at the 2020 census. I've hosted Derby parties with more guests than Stanford has neighbors. All right, not quite, but you see my point.

The Last Toast

Here's the honest wrap-up. Louisville has a quarterback who can beat you with his arm or his legs, a 28-point scoring streak and three losses by a combined nine points. Stanford has a talented running back and a defense ranked near the bottom of FBS. We get a bye to rest, and they play on a short week. If we finish games better and keep Ford in check, Halloween at the L&N will be a treat, not a trick. Until then, enjoy the off week, Cardinals fans. Rest up, rewatch the highlights, and save your voices for a Halloween night that I expect to remember for a long time.

Hold your hats.

articles.title: It's All About the U, Baby: No. 1 Miami Survives Double Overtime and Welcomes Pitt From the City of 446 Bridges
articles.byline: Javi 'The Breeze' Castillo, The Miami Fanatic
articles.matchup: Pittsburgh (5-2) at No. 1 Miami (6-0), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Hard Rock Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
¡Wepa, familia! Javi "The Breeze" Castillo here, linen shirt pressed, sunglasses on, café cubano steaming on the balcony. I used to play defensive back, so I still scout every game like I'm backpedaling against a slot receiver: eyes up, hips loose, never panic. And I talk in rhymes, because life's too short for one-liners that don't land.

Saturday night, my hips were loose and my heart was not. Two overtimes, baby. Two!

It's all about the U, baby.

Part 1: Double Overtime, Double the Drama

No. 3 Miami beat Florida State 43-35 in double overtime at Hard Rock Stadium. We're 6-0 and 4-0 in the ACC, and this week the AP poll moved us up to No. 1. Uno. Número uno, ¿y qué? Rhyme number one: "Down in Miami Gardens, the 'Noles came to play; we sent 'em home in overtime, that's the 305 way."

Darian Mensah threw for 326 yards and three touchdowns, going 23 of 34. Malachi Toney caught 11 passes for 154 yards and two touchdowns, and then he threw the two-point conversion to Cooper Barkate after his overtime score. A receiver throwing the clincher? That's flavor, familia. Javian Mallory ran for 108 yards and two touchdowns, including a 25-yarder in the first overtime. Mark Fletcher Jr. added a 7-yard touchdown run.

Now, I'll be honest, because The Breeze doesn't blow smoke. This one got scary. Elija Lofton caught a 3-yard touchdown pass with 2:49 left to put us up 28-21, and Florida State tied it on a 75-yard touchdown pass 10 seconds later. In the first overtime, they scored first. Mallory answered. In the second overtime, Mensah hit Toney from 3 yards out, and Toney threw the two-pointer.

Then Florida State completed a 36-yard pass on fourth-and-21 that would've made it a two-point game, but it was called back for holding. On the next play, a final heave into the end zone, Bryce Fitzgerald came down with the interception. After a review, the call stood, and the Hurricanes stormed the field. ¡Qué noche!

Miami gained 583 yards, ran for 257 and held the ball for 37:20. Florida State went 0 for 3 on fourth down, including two stops inside our 5. AP says Miami has now won seven of its last 10 against the Seminoles. And here's a stat for the defensive backs out there: Mensah had thrown 153 passes as a Hurricane before his first interception. One-fifty-three. That's not a quarterback. That's a vault.

Part 2: Pitt Comes to the 305

Saturday, noon Eastern on ESPN. Pittsburgh (5-2) at No. 1 Miami (6-0) at Hard Rock Stadium. Rhyme number two: "Pitt's flying south, sun's shining bright; we'll be done by lunch, you'll be home by night."

Scouting the Panthers

Respect first, always. Pitt's run defense allows 57.3 yards a game. That's first in FBS. Its scoring defense is 23rd. Cataurus Hicks has 500 receiving yards on just 26 catches, and he caught a 75-yard touchdown on the very first play last week. Damon Ferguson Jr. ran for 119 yards. That's a real team.

Now, the scouting report.

Pitt has lost two straight, 21-17 at home to North Carolina and 27-21 at Boston College. AP noted the Panthers had a brief stay in the AP Top 25 before those losses. Against BC, Pitt was flagged 13 times for 133 yards, including five penalties for 63 yards on a single drive. Pitt averages 81.7 penalty yards a game, 132nd in FBS. Its pass defense allows 249 yards a game, 115th. AP also pointed to numerous breakdowns in the secondary against BC.

Familia, you know what Miami does? Miami throws for 333 yards a game, third in FBS. Mensah completes 80.8 of every 100 passes, with 18 touchdowns and one interception. Toney has 50 catches for 758 yards and eight touchdowns. Rhyme number three: "Pitt's secondary, I don't mean to be rude, but Toney's coming through, and he's bringing the U."

And the last time we met, on Nov. 29, 2025, Miami won 38-7 in Pittsburgh.

The Honest Breeze

The Breeze keeps it real. Our pass defense allows 223.3 yards a game, 91st in FBS, and Florida State threw for 305 on us last week. We gave up 35 points. The secondary needs to tighten up, and as a former DB, it hurts my soul to say it. But our run defense allows only 58.5 yards a game, second in FBS. We score 48.5 points a game, first in the country. Marquise Lightfoot has five sacks. And last season, we went 13-3 and played for the national championship, falling 27-21 to Indiana. That still stings. This team is playing like it remembers.

Postcards: The 305 vs. the Steel City

Miami. Miami is the only major city in the United States founded by a woman. Julia Tuttle owned the land, convinced Henry Flagler to bring his railroad south and became known as "the mother of Miami." The city was incorporated on July 28, 1896, with just over 300 people. Today it's 442,241 strong, and they call it the Magic City, The 305 and the Gateway to the Americas. The University of Miami sits in Coral Gables, a planned city incorporated in 1925 and built on the City Beautiful Movement.

And Hard Rock Stadium? Six Super Bowls, two World Series, four BCS title games and two College Football Playoff championships. Our program has five national championships, in 1983, 1987, 1989, 1991 and 2001. Our mascot, Sebastian the Ibis, has represented the U since 1926. Rhyme number four: "Sunshine and titles, palm trees and swagger; Miami's the city, the rest are the laggers." Okay, that one needs work.

Pittsburgh. Pittsburgh sits where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet to form the Ohio. Beautiful spot. But they call it the City of Bridges because it has 446 of them. Four hundred forty-six! Familia, in Miami we have one bridge we care about, and it takes us to the beach. In Pittsburgh, you need a bridge to get to the bridge.

And the hills? Pittsburgh's Monongahela Incline, a cable car up the side of a hill, opened in 1870 and is the oldest continuously operating funicular in the country. A whole city that needs a 156-year-old cable car to go up the street. In Miami, the land averages about 6 feet above sea level. You know what we call that? Walking.

Pitt also claims nine national championships, and only two of them, 1937 and 1976, came from the major wire-service polls. Nine claimed. We'll stick with our five. I'll let the rhyme speak: "Nine on the banner, but who's counting, bro? We counted ours twice, and it's still five, though." Okay, that's another one that needs work. But give me credit: I'm honest even when I rhyme.

Final Whistle

Here's the scouting report. Pitt has the best run defense in the country and a dangerous deep threat. Miami has the No. 1 ranking, the top scoring offense in FBS, a quarterback who almost never throws it to the other team and a home crowd that's ready to party at noon. Throw it early, throw it often and let the 305 do the rest.

Rhyme number five: "Panthers in the sunshine, here's my last clue: when it's all said and done, it's all about the U."

My call: Miami Hurricanes 37, Pittsburgh Panthers 19.

Miami. Miami is the only major city in the United States founded by a woman. Julia Tuttle owned the land, convinced Henry Flagler to bring his railroad south and became known as "the mother of Miami." The city was incorporated on July 28, 1896, with just over 300 people. Today it's 442,241 strong, and they call it the Magic City, The 305 and the Gateway to the Americas. The University of Miami sits in Coral Gables, a planned city incorporated in 1925 and built on the City Beautiful Movement.

And Hard Rock Stadium? Six Super Bowls, two World Series, four BCS title games and two College Football Playoff championships. Our program has five national championships, in 1983, 1987, 1989, 1991 and 2001. Our mascot, Sebastian the Ibis, has represented the U since 1926. Rhyme number four: "Sunshine and titles, palm trees and swagger; Miami's the city, the rest are the laggers." Okay, that one needs work.

Pittsburgh. Pittsburgh sits where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet to form the Ohio. Beautiful spot. But they call it the City of Bridges because it has 446 of them. Four hundred forty-six! Familia, in Miami we have one bridge we care about, and it takes us to the beach. In Pittsburgh, you need a bridge to get to the bridge.

And the hills? Pittsburgh's Monongahela Incline, a cable car up the side of a hill, opened in 1870 and is the oldest continuously operating funicular in the country. Throw it early, throw it often and let the 305 do the rest.
Rhyme number five: "Panthers in the sunshine, here's my last clue: when it's all said and done, it's all about the U."

articles.title: Wolfpack, Howl! NC State Comes Off Its Bye and Flies West to Stanford, a Town That Isn't Technically a Town, Guarded by a Tree
articles.byline: Rutherford 'Ruff' Pegram, The NC State Fanatic
articles.matchup: NC State (3-3) at Stanford (3-4), Fri., Oct. 23, 10:30 p.m. ET, Stanford Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Well, howdy, Pack. Rutherford "Ruff" Pegram here, Wake County born and raised, engineer by trade, and keeper of the finest charcoal grill in the Carter-Finley lot. I explain every scheme with a grill thermometer, because football and barbecue are the same science: control the heat, watch the clock, don't flip it too early. And I howl exactly once per segment. No more, no less. It's a discipline.

This week, the grill stayed cold. NC State had a bye. But don't worry, Pack, I spent the off week cleaning the grates and studying film. Let's get to it.

Part 1: The Bye, and the Week Before It

NC State didn't play on Oct. 17. It was our open date. So let's look honestly at the last game we did play, and I'll warn you now, it was a burnt brisket.

Wake Forest beat us 38-14 at Carter-Finley Stadium on Oct. 10. We're 3-3 and 1-2 in the ACC. The first half was fine, honestly. Wake scored first, then CJ Bailey hit Chance Robinson for a 24-yard touchdown to tie it. In the second quarter, Will Wilson threw a 2-yard touchdown pass to Hunter Provience, and we led 14-7. Wake kicked a field goal on the final play of the half, and we led 14-10 at the break. Grill temp: a perfect 225.

Then the second half caught fire, and not the good kind. Wake scored 28 straight points, three in the third quarter alone. Its quarterback threw for 303 yards and three touchdowns, and Jack Foley caught eight passes for 156 yards. That's when the thermometer jumped to 500, and somebody forgot to close the lid.

Here's the honest number that hurt most. NC State ran 24 times for 15 yards. Fifteen. That's 0.6 yards a carry. My grill tongs move farther than that when I flip a burger.

Bailey completed 28 of 39 passes for 241 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions. Keenan Jackson caught five passes for 61 yards. Linebacker Popo Aguirre made 12 tackles and recorded a sack. The effort was there. The heat control wasn't.

But here's the good news: we went 8-5 last season and won the Gasparilla Bowl 31-7 over Memphis. And this season, we beat Louisville 31-28 just two weeks before Wake. This team can cook.

Part 2: A Late-Night Cookout in California

Friday, 10:30 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. NC State (3-3) at Stanford (3-4) at Stanford Stadium. That's a 7:30 p.m. kickoff out there. Pack, put on a pot of coffee.

Reading Stanford's Thermometer

I'll be fair first. Stanford just beat Elon 34-7, and running back Micah Ford had four touchdowns, tying Stanford's single-game record, including an 81-yard run. Ford has 529 rushing yards and eight touchdowns this season. Stanford also beat Georgia Tech 34-27. Respect.

Now let's read the gauge.

Stanford is 3-4, and Elon is an FCS team. Against Miami, Stanford lost 45-6 at home. At Duke, it lost 35-7. At Wake Forest, 57-3. At Notre Dame, 58-7. Stanford's defense gives up 452 yards a game, 134th in FBS, and 36.6 points a game, 133rd. Opponents convert 47.8 of every 100 third downs against it, 131st. And here's the one that made my thermometer pop out of the meat: Stanford's red zone defense allows opponents to score on 96.4 of every 100 trips. That ranks 136th in FBS. Pack, that's not a defense. That's a welcome mat.

Stanford's offense scores 18.3 points a game, 127th, and runs for 103.4 yards a game, 131st. Last season, per CollegeFootballData, Stanford went 4-8.

Reading Our Thermometer

NC State converts 51.1 of every 100 third downs, 15th in FBS. We average 32:52 of possession a game, 20th. We score 33 points a game. Bailey has 1,507 yards and nine touchdowns. Jayden Scott has 358 rushing yards and four touchdowns, and Jackson has 27 catches for 400 yards and five touchdowns. Aguirre leads us with 54 tackles, and Elijah Satchell has three sacks.

And the last time we met, on Nov. 2, 2024, in Raleigh, NC State won 59-28.

Three Keys From the Grill Thermometer

1. Low and slow. Stanford averages 28:19 of possession a game, 108th in FBS. We average 32:52. Long, patient drives keep their offense on the sideline and let the coals do the work.
2. Finish the cook. Our red zone offense scores on 85.2 of every 100 trips, 71st in FBS. Against a red zone defense ranked 136th, every trip inside the 20 should end with a plate on the table.
3. Mind the flare-ups. Ford can break one at any moment, like that 81-yard run last week. Tackle in groups. The Pack travels in packs.

The Honest Grill Report

I've burned a few briskets in my day, and I don't hide them. Our defense allows 27.7 points a game, 104th in FBS. Our pass defense allows 230.3 yards a game, 99th. We lost our opener 34-8 at Virginia and lost 35-31 at Vanderbilt. And after 15 rushing yards against Wake, we have to find the run game again. Stanford's run defense allows 196.6 yards a game, 125th. So, Pack, this is the week to fire up the smoker and run the ball.

Wolfpack, howl! (That's my one for this segment.)

Postcards: Raleigh vs. Stanford

Raleigh. Raleigh is the capital of North Carolina. The site was chosen in 1788, and the city was incorporated in 1792, making it an early example of a planned city in the United States. We're known as the "City of Oaks" for our oak-lined streets, and with 467,665 people at the 2020 census, we're the second-most populous city in the state and the largest city in the Research Triangle. Carter-Finley Stadium has been home to the Pack since 1966, and it seats 56,919. And our team name? It came from an unsigned letter to the NC State Alumni News in 1921 suggesting "Wolf Pack." The fans named the team. That's the people's Pack.

Stanford. Here's the thing about Stanford, California. It's not technically a city. It's a census-designated place, and it remains unincorporated. Its population is 21,150, and those residents mostly live in on-campus housing. Raleigh has about 22 Stanfords. Stanford's football team plays in a place that's basically a very large dorm with a ZIP code.

Then there's the mascot. Stanford's team name, Cardinal, refers to the color, not the bird, and the university doesn't have an official mascot. The unofficial one is the Stanford Tree, a sequoia that belongs to the marching band. It regularly shows up on internet "worst mascot" lists. Pack, our mascot is a wolf. Their mascot is something you'd grill on. Well, not a sequoia. But you get it. Run with the Pack, and the tree gets chopped.

And the stadium? Stanford Stadium was built in five months in 1921. Then it was demolished and rebuilt after the 2005 season. Even their stadium needed a do-over.

Final Temperature

Here's the read. Stanford has a talented running back and a defense ranked near the bottom of FBS in nearly every category. NC State has a top-15 third-down offense, a quarterback who protects the ball and a whole bye week of film study. If we get the run game going, finish drives in the red zone and keep Ford in check, the Pack eats well on Friday night.

Run with the Pack.

My call: NC State Wolfpack 33, Stanford Cardinal 25.

articles.title: Carolina Blue, Through and Through: The Victory Bell Comes Home, and Syracuse Visits Kenan From a City That Got 143.1 Inches of Snow and Still Plays Indoors
articles.byline: Ainsley Pemberton, The North Carolina Fanatic
articles.matchup: Syracuse (2-4) at North Carolina (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, Kenan Stadium, ACC Network
articles.text:
Well, hello, darlings. Ainsley Pemberton here, Carolina-blue debutante, holder of a PhD in kinesiology and owner of more pearls than any one woman needs. I watch every Tar Heels game from the stands, and I analyze it the way I was trained: biomechanically, lovingly and with a gentle word or two about Duke.

And oh, this week I have more than a word or two about Duke. Because, sugar, the Victory Bell is coming home to Chapel Hill.

Part 1: Last Week, We Rang the Bell

North Carolina beat Duke 24-20 on Saturday in Durham. We're 4-2 and 2-1 in the ACC, and we've won two straight road games.

It started like a debutante ball. Rece Verhoff kicked a 28-yard field goal. Billy Edwards Jr. hit Jordan Shipp for a 5-yard touchdown. On the third play of the second quarter, Demon June ran in from 4 yards out, and we led 17-0. I was so composed. I took one sip of sweet tea and smoothed my skirt.

Then the punch bowl tipped over. Duke's safety returned a fumble 9 yards for a touchdown in the second quarter. Duke kicked two field goals in the second half. We went more than 41 minutes without scoring, and with 4:39 left, Duke took its first lead, 20-17, on a 7-yard touchdown catch. My kinesiology training tells me a sustained elevated heart rate is good cardio. That was a full workout.

But Carolina girls don't faint. Our final drive went 78 yards. With 3:48 left and facing fourth-and-4 from our own 28, we went for it, and Edwards found Jelani Thurman over the middle for 12 yards. Coach Bill Belichick made it clear afterward that he was done punting and wanted to take his best shot. Darling, I love a man with conviction.

Then, with 1:53 left, Jaylen McGill burst through for a 24-yard touchdown run. 24-20, Tar Heels. Kenton Dopson III had an interception in the game, and at the end the players rushed across the field to reclaim the Victory Bell. The bell, by the way, is an old railway bell from the Southern Railway, and the trophy dates to 1948. Duke will have to visit us to see it now, and we'll paint it blue for them. We're good hosts.

Edwards completed 15 of 25 passes for 191 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions. McGill ran for 75 yards on 12 carries. Shipp caught seven passes for 75 yards. Linebacker Peyton Seelmann made 16 tackles. And Duke's Nate Sheppard, the nation's leading rusher in yards per game, was held to 77 yards on 20 carries. Our defense played like it had studied the anatomy chart.

And Duke? Bless its heart. It had won eight straight games against in-state opponents. That streak is now in the history books, right next to Duke's hopes of keeping the bell.

Part 2: Syracuse Comes to Kenan

Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern on ACC Network. Syracuse (2-4, 0-4 ACC) at North Carolina (4-2) at Kenan Stadium, in the pines.

Respect Where It's Due

Every lady compliments her guests first. Syracuse receiver Umari Hatcher is the real thing. He has 50 catches for 784 yards and seven touchdowns, and last week against Louisville he set career highs with 13 catches for 224 yards. Syracuse's passing offense ranks 12th in FBS at 291.0 yards a game, and its time of possession ranks fifth at 33:59. Ahmad Miller ran for 123 yards last week. Linebacker Chris D'Appolonia made 12 tackles, and Davien Kerr intercepted two passes. That's real talent.

Now, the Diagnosis

Syracuse lost 34-26 to Louisville last week, and it trailed 28-23 at halftime. According to the AP, Syracuse has now lost 11 straight ACC games and 12 straight against Power 4 opponents, and it has been outscored 78-36 in the second half this season. Darling, from a kinesiology standpoint, that's a stamina issue.

Syracuse also leads the country in penalties. It averages 98.0 penalty yards a game, 138th in FBS. Last week, it had three unsportsmanlike penalties in the first half alone. North Carolina, meanwhile, averages 33.7 penalty yards a game, fifth-fewest in FBS. Manners matter, sugar. My mother taught me that, and apparently our football team listened.

Syracuse's red zone offense scores on 78.1 of every 100 trips, 111th in FBS. Our red zone defense ranks 22nd, allowing scores on 73.7 of every 100 trips. And our scoring defense allows 19.2 points a game, 34th.

My Honest Self-Exam

A good doctor checks herself first. Our offense averages 329.7 yards a game, 117th in FBS, and our run game averages 116.2 yards, 120th. Our time of possession ranks 130th at 27:00. Our third-down defense allows conversions on 43.3 of every 100 tries, 113th, and against Duke we fumbled twice. We went 4-8 last season. So I'm not handing out bouquets yet.

But last year, on Oct. 31, 2025, we beat Syracuse 27-10 in its own dome. And Edwards has nine touchdown passes this season, with Shipp leading us in receiving at 441 yards.

My Three Prescriptions

1. Stay disciplined. Syracuse gives away yards with penalties. Let them. We keep our composure and take every free yard they offer.
2. Finish strong. Syracuse has been outscored 78-36 in second halves. Our conditioning should show late.
3. Shadow Hatcher. He's elite. Bracket him, rotate safeties and make the Orange beat us another way.

A Tale of Two Towns: Chapel Hill vs. Syracuse

Chapel Hill. The University of North Carolina was chartered on Dec. 11, 1789, and began enrolling students in 1795. It's one of three universities that claim to be the oldest public university in America, and it's the only one that conferred degrees as a public institution in the 18th century. Darling, we were handing out diplomas while George Washington was president. Our town is named for New Hope Chapel, a small chapel of ease built on the crest of the hill in 1752, and our main street, Franklin Street, was named in memory of Benjamin Franklin. Kenan Stadium opened in 1927, and its first game was a 27-0 win over Davidson. And our live mascot, Rameses, is a Dorset Horn sheep who attends games with his horns painted Carolina blue. Even the livestock has a signature color.

Syracuse. Syracuse is a charming city, and it's honest about its weather. A normal season brings about 127.8 inches of snow, and it won the Golden Snowball Award for 2025-26 with 143.1 inches, its second straight title. Its record season was 192.1 inches in 1992-93. So what does a city that gets 143 inches of snow do with its football team? It puts the team indoors. The JMA Wireless Dome is the largest domed stadium on any college campus. Sugar, they built a giant snow globe and climbed inside. Saturday night in Chapel Hill, they'll get to see football under an actual sky.

And Syracuse is named after an ancient Greek city in Sicily. It borrowed its name from a sunny Mediterranean island and then got 143 inches of snow. That's like naming your goldfish "Shark." Its mascot is Otto the Orange, a fruit, and the team name comes from a color. Our mascot is a ram. Fruit doesn't fare well against horns, darling.

The Benediction

Here's my final diagnosis. North Carolina has a top-35 scoring defense, one of the most disciplined teams in America and the Victory Bell. Syracuse has a terrific receiver, a passing offense to respect and a penalty problem that ranks dead last in FBS. If we stay disciplined, finish strong and keep Hatcher in front of us, Kenan will be singing on Saturday night.

Carolina blue, through and through.

My call: North Carolina Tar Heels 29, Syracuse Orange 20.
