Linebacker Peyton Seelmann made 16 tackles. And Duke's Nate Sheppard, the nation's leading rusher in yards per game, was held to 77 yards on 20 carries. Our defense played like it had studied the anatomy chart.
And Duke? Bless its heart. It had won eight straight games against in-state opponents. That streak is now in the history books, right next to Duke's hopes of keeping the bell.
Part 2: Syracuse Comes to Kenan
Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern on ACC Network. Syracuse (2-4, 0-4 ACC) at North Carolina (4-2) at Kenan Stadium, in the pines.
Respect Where It's Due

Every lady compliments her guests first. Syracuse receiver Umari Hatcher is the real thing. He has 50 catches for 784 yards and seven touchdowns, and last week against Louisville he set career highs with 13 catches for 224 yards. Syracuse's passing offense ranks 12th in FBS at 291.0 yards a game, and its time of possession ranks fifth at 33:59. Ahmad Miller ran for 123 yards last week. Linebacker Chris D'Appolonia made 12 tackles, and Davien Kerr intercepted two passes. That's real talent.
Now, the Diagnosis

Syracuse lost 34-26 to Louisville last week, and it trailed 28-23 at halftime. According to the AP, Syracuse has now lost 11 straight ACC games and 12 straight against Power 4 opponents, and it has been outscored 78-36 in the second half this season. Darling, from a kinesiology standpoint, that's a stamina issue.

Syracuse also leads the country in penalties. It averages 98.0 penalty yards a game, 138th in FBS. Last week, it had three unsportsmanlike penalties in the first half alone. North Carolina, meanwhile, averages 33.7 penalty yards a game, fifth-fewest in FBS. Manners matter, sugar. My mother taught me that, and apparently our football team listened.

Syracuse's red zone offense scores on 78.1 of every 100 trips, 111th in FBS. Our red zone defense ranks 22nd, allowing scores on 73.7 of every 100 trips. And our scoring defense allows 19.2 points a game, 34th.
My Honest Self-Exam

A good doctor checks herself first. Our offense averages 329.7 yards a game, 117th in FBS, and our run game averages 116.2 yards, 120th. Our time of possession ranks 130th at 27:00. Our third-down defense allows conversions on 43.3 of every 100 tries, 113th, and against Duke we fumbled twice. We went 4-8 last season. So I'm not handing out bouquets yet.
But last year, on Oct. 31, 2025, we beat Syracuse 27-10 in its own dome. And Edwards has nine touchdown passes this season, with Shipp leading us in receiving at 441 yards.
My Three Prescriptions

1. Stay disciplined. Syracuse gives away yards with penalties. Let them. We keep our composure and take every free yard they offer. 2. Finish strong. Syracuse has been outscored 78-36 in second halves. Our conditioning should show late. 3. Shadow Hatcher. He's elite. Bracket him, rotate safeties and make the Orange beat us another way.
A Tale of Two Towns: Chapel Hill vs. Syracuse

Chapel Hill. The University of North Carolina was chartered on Dec. 11, 1789, and began enrolling students in 1795. It's one of three universities that claim to be the oldest public university in America, and it's the only one that conferred degrees as a public institution in the 18th century. Darling, we were handing out diplomas while George Washington was president. Our town is named for New Hope Chapel, a small chapel of ease built on the crest of the hill in 1752, and our main street, Franklin Street, was named in memory of Benjamin Franklin. Kenan Stadium opened in 1927, and its first game was a 27-0 win over Davidson. And our live mascot, Rameses, is a Dorset Horn sheep who attends games with his horns painted Carolina blue. Even the livestock has a signature color.

Syracuse. Syracuse is a charming city, and it's honest about its weather. A normal season brings about 127.8 inches of snow, and it won the Golden Snowball Award for 2025-26 with 143.1 inches, its second straight title. Its record season was 192.1 inches in 1992-93. So what does a city that gets 143 inches of snow do with its football team? It puts the team indoors. The JMA Wireless Dome is the largest domed stadium on any college campus. Sugar, they built a giant snow globe and climbed inside. Saturday night in Chapel Hill, they'll get to see football under an actual sky.

And Syracuse is named after an ancient Greek city in Sicily. It borrowed its name from a sunny Mediterranean island and then got 143 inches of snow. That's like naming your goldfish "Shark." Its mascot is Otto the Orange, a fruit, and the team name comes from a color. Our mascot is a ram. Fruit doesn't fare well against horns, darling.
The Benediction

Here's my final diagnosis. North Carolina has a top-35 scoring defense, one of the most disciplined teams in America and the Victory Bell. Syracuse has a terrific receiver, a passing offense to respect and a penalty problem that ranks dead last in FBS. If we stay disciplined, finish strong and keep Hatcher in front of us, Kenan will be singing on Saturday night.
Carolina blue, through and through.
My call: North Carolina Tar Heels 29, Syracuse Orange 20.

articles.title: Dat's a Yinz Problem: Pitt Heads to No. 1 Miami, Whose Pass Defense Ranks 91st and Whose Stadium Has Worn Eight Different Names
articles.byline: Dominic 'Yinz' Bertolucci, The Pittsburgh Fanatic
articles.matchup: Pittsburgh (5-2) at No. 1 Miami (6-0), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Hard Rock Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
How's it goin', yinz? Dominic "Yinz" Bertolucci here, coming at you from a stool down the Strip District with a homemade whistle around my neck. I played linebacker back in a mill town, and I still grade every tackle on my own personal scale. A great hit's a "yinz." A whiff's a "yikes." Somewhere in between is a "n'at."

This week, I blew that whistle a lot. Some yinz. Some yikes. A lot of yellow flags.

Dat's a yinz problem, not a yikes problem. Mostly.

Part 1: The Fastest Start in Chestnut Hill

Boston College beat Pitt 27-21 on Saturday. We're 5-2 and 2-2 in the ACC, and we've lost two straight. I'll level with yinz, because a linebacker who lies about a missed tackle gets caught on film.

But first, a moment for the start. On the very first play from scrimmage, true freshman Corey Dailey, making his first career start, threw a 75-yard touchdown pass to Cataurus Hicks. First play! Yinz! After BC went three-and-out, Kanye Thompson blocked a punt, and the ball got knocked out of the end zone for a safety. Then Antonio Chadha kicked a 28-yard field goal. Pitt led 12-0 in a little over seven minutes. My whistle was singing.

Then the flags came. Pitt was penalized 10 times for 103 yards in the first half alone, including five penalties for 63 yards on a single BC drive early in the second quarter. That's a yikes, yikes, yikes, yikes and a yikes. We finished with 13 penalties for 133 yards. BC scored the next 14 points and hit a 69-yard touchdown on the first drive of the second half.

Chadha kicked field goals of 29, 42 and 38 yards to keep it close. Damon Ferguson Jr. ran 17 times for 119 yards. Hicks caught five passes for 135 yards. And Raion Strader intercepted two passes, the second one giving us the ball at the BC 8 with just over two minutes left. We couldn't finish. BC intercepted a pass to end it.

Here's the honest truth. Dailey stepped in after Mason Heintschel was lost for the season with a knee injury two weeks ago, and our whole city is pulling for Mason's recovery. Dailey's a true freshman, and he made plays. The flags weren't on him. They were on all of us.

Part 2: Down to the Sunshine

Saturday, noon Eastern on ESPN. Pittsburgh (5-2) at No. 1 Miami (6-0) at Hard Rock Stadium.

Grading the Hurricanes

I'll give Miami its due. It's No. 1 in the country, it scores 48.5 points a game, first in FBS, and Darian Mensah completes 80.8 of every 100 passes with 18 touchdowns and one interception. Malachi Toney has 758 receiving yards. Their run defense is second in the country. That's a "yinz" on my scale, with a little extra whistle.

Now, the film.

Miami needed two overtimes to beat Florida State last week, and Florida State is 3-4. The Seminoles threw for 305 yards on the Hurricanes and scored 35 points. With 2:49 left, Miami took a 28-21 lead, and Florida State tied it 10 seconds later with a 75-yard touchdown pass. In the second overtime, Florida State completed a 36-yard pass on fourth-and-21 that would have made it a two-point game, but a holding penalty wiped it out. Miami survived on an interception that went to review.

Miami's pass defense allows 223.3 yards a game. That ranks 91st in FBS. That's a "yikes" in a stadium full of sunshine. And Hicks has 500 receiving yards on just 26 catches. That's 19.2 yards every time he touches it.

Grading the Panthers

Our run defense allows 57.3 yards a game. First in FBS. First! Miami runs for 226.5 yards a game, and something's got to give. Our scoring defense allows 16.4 points a game, 23rd, and our red zone defense is 13th. Cruce Brookins leads us with 46 tackles, and Jaeden Moore has 2.5 sacks. Our passing game ranks 17th. We're plus-4 in turnover margin.

And the honest part: we average 81.7 penalty yards a game, 132nd in FBS. Our pass defense allows 249 yards a game, 115th, and AP noted breakdowns in our secondary at BC. Miami beat us 38-7 the last time we met, in Pittsburgh, on Nov. 29, 2025. That's the film. Yinz gotta watch it, learn from it and go play.

The Whistle Plan

Here's how I'd draw it up on a napkin at the diner. One: keep stuffing the run. Miami likes balance, and if our front takes away Javian Mallory, Mensah has to do it all. Two: get Dailey comfortable early with Ferguson, because a true freshman on the road at noon in the sunshine needs a friendly first few plays. Three: take a shot to Hicks. He's already done it once on a first play this season. Four, and I'm gonna blow this whistle till it squeaks: no more flags. Thirteen penalties won't beat Boston College, and it sure won't beat the No. 1 team in the country.

Postcards: The Steel City vs. Miami Gardens

Pittsburgh. Pittsburgh sits right where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet to form the Ohio River. They call us the Steel City, and they call us the City of Bridges, because we have 446 of them. Yinz can get anywhere in Pittsburgh, and yinz can do it over water. The Monongahela Incline opened in 1870 and is the oldest continuously operating funicular in the United States. We don't just climb hills. We built a ride for it.

And Pitt's campus has the Cathedral of Learning, a 42-story, 535-foot Gothic tower that's the tallest educational building in the Western Hemisphere. Our program claims nine national championships, including 1937 and 1976 from the major wire-service polls. And Acrisure Stadium, our home since 2001, rose up after the old Three Rivers Stadium came down.

Miami Gardens. Miami's games are at Hard Rock Stadium, which is in Miami Gardens. The University of Miami itself is in Coral Gables. So the Miami Hurricanes play in a stadium that's not in Miami, for a university that's not in Miami either. That's a "yikes" on my map scale.

And the stadium's name? Hard Rock Stadium opened in 1987 as Joe Robbie Stadium. Since then, it's also been Pro Player Park, Pro Player Stadium, Dolphins Stadium, Dolphin Stadium, Land Shark Stadium and Sun Life Stadium. That's eight names, n'at. Yinz have had more names for one stadium than I've had whistles, and I go through a lot of whistles.

Miami's elevation averages about 6 feet above sea level. Our Cathedral of Learning alone is 535 feet tall. Yinz could stack Miami on top of itself about 89 times before you reached our classroom ceiling.

Final Whistle

Here's my grade. Miami is No. 1, has a great quarterback and runs a top-two run defense. Pitt has the No. 1 run defense in the country, a deep threat who averages 19 yards a catch and a lot of fight. If we cut the penalties in half, slow down Toney and take our shots to Hicks against that 91st-ranked pass defense, this could be a whole lot closer than folks think.

Dat's a yinz problem, not a yikes problem. Hail to Pitt!

My call: Miami Hurricanes 37, Pittsburgh Panthers 19.

articles.title: Pony Up or Sit Down, Sugar: No. 23 SMU Welcomes Cal, Whose Stadium Sits on a Fault and Whose First Half Last Week Didn't Exist
articles.byline: Tatum Delacroix-Price, The SMU Fanatic
articles.matchup: Cal (3-4) at No. 23 SMU (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Gerald J. Ford Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Well, hello, darlings. Tatum Delacroix-Price here, coming to you from the back of my boutique in University Park, steamer in one hand, red-and-blue scarf in the other. I treat every SMU tailgate on the Boulevard like it's fashion week, I treat every game like a runway show, and I grade every performance. I am never wrong. I'm occasionally early, but never wrong.

Last Saturday's look? Classic, tailored and a little understated. Not every outfit needs sequins, sugar. Sometimes a crisp navy blazer wins the room.

Pony up or sit down.

Part 1: The Little Black Dress of Football Games

No. 24 SMU beat Virginia 23-13 at Gerald J. Ford Stadium. We're 5-1 and 3-1 in the ACC. It wasn't flashy. It was the little black dress of football games: simple, elegant and it always works.

Kevin Jennings went 23 of 36 for 246 yards and two touchdowns, with no interceptions. He hit Randy Pittman Jr. for a 6-yard touchdown on fourth-and-1 in the second quarter, after Yannick Smith's 59-yard catch set it up. Then, early in the fourth quarter, Jennings found Jalen Hale on a 37-yard catch-and-run score. Kendrick Raphael ran 22 times for 124 yards. We went 4 for 5 on fourth down. And before that touchdown, Jennings got hit as he threw on fourth-and-3, and Yamir Knight still caught the fluttering ball past the marker. Darling, that's what we call effortless.

And can we please talk about Brendan Baird? AP says he's a former SMU soccer player, and he'd missed his only previous kick. On Saturday he made field goals of 23, 45 and 26 yards. The 45-yarder came on an untimed down at the end of the first half and gave us a 13-10 lead. A soccer player walking onto the football field and draining three kicks? That's a wardrobe change worthy of an award show.

The defense was couture. Virginia came in with the ACC's top pass defense and left with 258 yards. That's the third straight game Virginia has been held under 300. We didn't turn it over once. And the weather finally cooperated: 57 degrees at kickoff, per AP. Sweater weather, darling. My most beloved season.

AP also noted SMU is now 10-0 at home in ACC games since rejoining a power conference in 2024, and 17-3 in the ACC overall. Ten and oh at home. In my business, that's called a sold-out collection.

Part 2: The Bears Walk Our Runway

Saturday, noon Eastern, 11 a.m. here, on The CW. Cal (3-4) at No. 23 SMU (5-1) at Gerald J. Ford Stadium. It's the last of four straight home games for us, and the final fitting of the season.

Cal's Look, Graded

Let me be sweet first, because I'm a Southern host. Cal can throw it. Its passing game ranks 15th in FBS, and Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele went 15 of 18 last week. Chase Hendricks has 47 catches. And yes, Cal beat us 38-35 in Berkeley last season. I remember. I wore black for a week.

Now, sugar, the critique.

Last Saturday, Wake Forest beat Cal 41-7 in Berkeley. Wake scored touchdowns on five of six first-half possessions and led 34-0 at halftime. AP says it was Cal's biggest halftime deficit since 2013. Wake opened with a 99-yard drive. Darling, I've seen runway models take longer to walk 99 feet.

Cal runs for 90.3 yards a game. That's 137th in FBS. Its defense gives up 181.4 rushing yards a game, 111th, and 27.7 points a game, 104th. Cal also averages 81.4 penalty yards a game, 131st. And earlier this season, Cal lost at UNLV, 39-31. Grade? Incomplete, sweetheart. Come back after alterations.

SMU's Look, Graded

Jennings completes 72.9 of every 100 passes and has 16 touchdowns. Our passing offense ranks fifth in FBS. Our pass defense allows 164.8 yards a game, 11th. Raphael has 542 rushing yards and six touchdowns, and Knight has 35 catches. Marques White has 4.5 sacks, and Alexander Kilgore leads us with 35 tackles.

Against a run defense ranked 111th, Raphael should be strutting.

Here's my styling plan, darlings. Start with Raphael, the statement piece. Once Cal's defense commits to him, accessorize with Jennings on play-action to Knight and Smith. Keep the pass defense buttoned up against Sagapolutele and Hendricks, because Cal's offense lives through the air. And whatever you do, keep Baird's confidence high. A soccer player who just made three kicks in his first big night is the hottest new designer in town.

Honest Fitting Notes

I'm honest with every client. We're 114th in penalty yards and 95th in red zone offense, and our coach said himself that we didn't finish enough drives against Virginia. We lost at Louisville in September. And until last week, our kicking game was 3 of 7 on field goals. A good tailor fixes the hem before the show. Let's fix ours.

The series: SMU leads 2-1, according to CollegeFootballData, but Cal won the last one. Time for a return engagement, darling.

Postcards: University Park vs. Berkeley

University Park and Dallas. SMU was founded in 1911 and sits in University Park, a charming town of 25,278 that, with Highland Park, makes up the Park Cities. Dallas surrounds us, and Dallas is the ninth-most populous city in America, the anchor of an 8.5-million-person metro. Jack Kilby invented the integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in 1958, and TI is headquartered in Dallas. So every phone in every pocket owes a little thank-you note to our city. And the State Fair of Texas, held at Fair Park and run nearly every year since 1886, claims more than 2 million visitors a year, with Big Tex, a 55-foot cowboy, presiding since 1952.

Our mascot, Peruna, is a black Shetland pony who's been at every SMU home game but one since 1932. SMU won a national championship in 1935. And Doak Walker is the only Mustang to win the Heisman Trophy. Gerald J. Ford Stadium opened on Sept. 2, 2000. Polished, modern and always camera-ready.

Berkeley. Berkeley is lovely, and it's very smart. I'll give it that. But I've been reading. California Memorial Stadium was built in 1923 directly on top of the Hayward Fault. So they built the stadium in two halves. Darling, that's not a stadium. That's a two-piece outfit held together by geology.

Then there's the name. Berkeley is named after George Berkeley, a philosopher who argued that familiar objects like tables and chairs can't exist without being perceived. That actually explains a lot. Against Wake Forest, Cal's first half simply wasn't perceived. Therefore it didn't exist. Philosophy, sugar.

And the hill above Cal's stadium is nicknamed Tightwad Hill, where fans have long gathered to watch for free. I run a boutique. I can't even look at a word like that.

The Final Look

Here's my grade for Saturday. SMU has a top-five passing game, a top-15 pass defense, a powerful running back and a perfect home record in ACC play. Cal has a strong arm and a lot of alterations to make. If we finish drives and keep the flags off the field, the Mustangs walk off the runway at 6-1 and looking fabulous.

Pony up or sit down, sugar.

My call: SMU Mustangs 35, California Golden Bears 18.

Part 1: The Little Black Dress of Football Games
No. 24 SMU beat Virginia 23-13 at Gerald J. Ford Stadium. We're 5-1 and 3-1 in the ACC. It wasn't flashy. It was the little black dress of football games: simple, elegant and it always works.

Kevin Jennings went 23 of 36 for 246 yards and two touchdowns, with no interceptions. He hit Randy Pittman Jr. for a 6-yard touchdown on fourth-and-1 in the second quarter, after Yannick Smith's 59-yard catch set it up. Then, early in the fourth quarter, Jennings found Jalen Hale on a 37-yard catch-and-run score. Kendrick Raphael ran 22 times for 124 yards. We went 4 for 5 on fourth down. And before that touchdown, Jennings got hit as he threw on fourth-and-3, and Yamir Knight still caught the fluttering ball past the marker. Darling, that's what we call effortless.

And can we please talk about Brendan Baird? AP says he's a former SMU soccer player, and he'd missed his only previous kick. On Saturday he made field goals of 23, 45 and 26 yards. The 45-yarder came on an untimed down at the end of the first half and gave us a 13-10 lead. A soccer player walking onto the football field and draining three kicks? That's a wardrobe change worthy of an award show.

The defense was couture. Virginia came in with the ACC's top pass defense and left with 258 yards. That's the third straight game Virginia has been held under 300. We didn't turn it over once. And the weather finally cooperated: 57 degrees at kickoff, per AP. Sweater weather, darling. My most beloved season.
AP also noted SMU is now 10-0 at home in ACC games since rejoining a power conference in 2024, and 17-3 in the ACC overall. Ten and oh at home. In my business, that's called a sold-out collection.
Part 2: The Bears Walk Our Runway
Saturday, noon Eastern, 11 a.m. here, on The CW. Cal (3-4) at No. 23 SMU (5-1) at Gerald J. Ford Stadium. It's the last of four straight home games for us, and the final fitting of the season.
Cal's Look, Graded

Let me be sweet first, because I'm a Southern host. Cal can throw it. Its passing game ranks 15th in FBS, and Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele went 15 of 18 last week. Chase Hendricks has 47 catches. And yes, Cal beat us 38-35 in Berkeley last season. I remember. I wore black for a week.
Now, sugar, the critique.

Last Saturday, Wake Forest beat Cal 41-7 in Berkeley. Wake scored touchdowns on five of six first-half possessions and led 34-0 at halftime. AP says it was Cal's biggest halftime deficit since 2013. Wake opened with a 99-yard drive. Darling, I've seen runway models take longer to walk 99 feet.

Cal runs for 90.3 yards a game. That's 137th in FBS. Its defense gives up 181.4 rushing yards a game, 111th, and 27.7 points a game, 104th. Cal also averages 81.4 penalty yards a game, 131st. And earlier this season, Cal lost at UNLV, 39-31. Grade? Incomplete, sweetheart. Come back after alterations.
SMU's Look, Graded

Jennings completes 72.9 of every 100 passes and has 16 touchdowns. Our passing offense ranks fifth in FBS. Our pass defense allows 164.8 yards a game, 11th. Raphael has 542 rushing yards and six touchdowns, and Knight has 35 catches. Marques White has 4.5 sacks, and Alexander Kilgore leads us with 35 tackles.
Against a run defense ranked 111th, Raphael should be strutting.

Here's my styling plan, darlings. Start with Raphael, the statement piece. Once Cal's defense commits to him, accessorize with Jennings on play-action to Knight and Smith. Keep the pass defense buttoned up against Sagapolutele and Hendricks, because Cal's offense lives through the air. And whatever you do, keep Baird's confidence high. A soccer player who just made three kicks in his first big night is the hottest new designer in town.
Honest Fitting Notes

I'm honest with every client. We're 114th in penalty yards and 95th in red zone offense, and our coach said himself that we didn't finish enough drives against Virginia. We lost at Louisville in September. And until last week, our kicking game was 3 of 7 on field goals. A good tailor fixes the hem before the show. Let's fix ours.
The series: SMU leads 2-1, according to CollegeFootballData, but Cal won the last one. Time for a return engagement, darling.
Postcards: University Park vs. Berkeley

University Park and Dallas. SMU was founded in 1911 and sits in University Park, a charming town of 25,278 that, with Highland Park, makes up the Park Cities. Dallas surrounds us, and Dallas is the ninth-most populous city in America, the anchor of an 8.5-million-person metro. Jack Kilby invented the integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in 1958, and TI is headquartered in Dallas. So every phone in every pocket owes a little thank-you note to our city. And the State Fair of Texas, held at Fair Park and run nearly every year since 1886, claims more than 2 million visitors a year, with Big Tex, a 55-foot cowboy, presiding since 1952.

Our mascot, Peruna, is a black Shetland pony who's been at every SMU home game but one since 1932. SMU won a national championship in 1935. And Doak Walker is the only Mustang to win the Heisman Trophy. Gerald J. Ford Stadium opened on Sept. 2, 2000. Polished, modern and always camera-ready.

Berkeley. Berkeley is lovely, and it's very smart. I'll give it that. But I've been reading. California Memorial Stadium was built in 1923 directly on top of the Hayward Fault. So they built the stadium in two halves. Darling, that's not a stadium. That's a two-piece outfit held together by geology.

Then there's the name. Berkeley is named after George Berkeley, a philosopher who argued that familiar objects like tables and chairs can't exist without being perceived. That actually explains a lot. Against Wake Forest, Cal's first half simply wasn't perceived. Therefore it didn't exist. Philosophy, sugar.
And the hill above Cal's stadium is nicknamed Tightwad Hill, where fans have long gathered to watch for free. I run a boutique. I can't even look at a word like that.
The Final Look

Here's my grade for Saturday. SMU has a top-five passing game, a top-15 pass defense, a powerful running back and a perfect home record in ACC play. Cal has a strong arm and a lot of alterations to make. If we finish drives and keep the flags off the field, the Mustangs walk off the runway at 6-1 and looking fabulous.
Pony up or sit down, sugar.
My call: SMU Mustangs 35, California Golden Bears 18.

articles.title: Let's Pivot to the Run Game: Stanford Rides Micah Ford's Record-Tying Day Into a Friday Night Launch Against NC State, Whose Ground Game Gained 15 Yards
articles.byline: Ignatius 'Iggy' Yamamoto-Ross, The Stanford Fanatic
articles.matchup: NC State (3-3) at Stanford (3-4), Fri., Oct. 23, 10:30 p.m. ET, Stanford Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Greetings, stakeholders. Ignatius "Iggy" Yamamoto-Ross here, founder of three failed apps and one great Cardinal model. The apps were a social network for houseplants, a ride-share for scooters and a subscription service for socks that only came in pairs of one. The Cardinal model, though? Strong product-market fit. I follow this team from the stands, every game, with a laptop full of slide decks nobody asked for.

This week's deck has a title slide in bright Cardinal red: Let's pivot to the run game.

Part 1: Last Week, a Successful Relaunch

Stanford beat Elon 34-7 on Saturday at Stanford Stadium. We're 3-4. Elon is an FCS team, and I'll say that up front, because honest metrics are the foundation of any healthy organization.

Here's the honest arc. The first quarter was scoreless. Both teams missed field goals. My investor presentation slide for that quarter just says "pre-revenue."

Then the second quarter started, and Micah Ford launched. He opened the scoring with a 1-yard run 4 seconds into the quarter. Two drives later, he broke several tackles on a 7-yard touchdown run. Stanford led 14-0 at halftime. Our coach, Tavita Pritchard, said afterward that he challenged the team at halftime because the energy and focus in the first half weren't where they needed to be. That's what I call a mid-cycle performance review.

The second half was a hockey-stick growth chart. Davis Warren hit Sedrick Irvin for a 27-yard touchdown in the third quarter. On the next drive, Ford bobbled the snap, secured it and scooted 5 yards for his third score. Then, on his first touch of the fourth quarter, Ford broke free for an 81-yard touchdown run.

Four touchdowns. That tied Stanford's single-game record. Ford finished with 179 rushing yards on 19 carries, plus five catches for 52 yards. And let's not forget he scored three touchdowns against Hawaii in the season opener. Investors, that's what we call a unicorn.

Warren completed 27 of 39 passes for 279 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions. JonAnthony Hall caught five passes for 70 yards. Stanford gained 515 yards. The defense held Elon to 52 passing yards on 8-of-27 throwing and allowed points on just one of Elon's 12 drives.

And now the honest part of the earnings call. This was a bounce-back after two lopsided road losses, 57-3 at Wake Forest and 58-7 at Notre Dame. We also lost 45-6 to Miami and 35-7 at Duke. Every startup has a rough quarter. Ours had several. But we also beat Hawaii 37-27 and Georgia Tech 34-27, and now we have momentum.

Part 2: Friday Night Launch Event vs. NC State

Friday, 10:30 p.m. Eastern on ESPN, which is a civilized 7:30 p.m. here on the Farm. NC State (3-3) visits Stanford (3-4). NC State's fans will be watching at what is, for them, a very late hour. Somebody brew them a cold brew.

Competitive Analysis

I'll give the Wolfpack their due, because every good pitch deck respects the competition. NC State converts 51.1 of every 100 third downs, 15th in FBS. It averages 32:52 of possession a game, 20th. Quarterback CJ Bailey has 1,507 passing yards, nine touchdowns and just four interceptions. Keenan Jackson has 27 catches for 400 yards and five touchdowns. NC State beat Louisville 31-28 and went 8-5 last season. And the last time we met, in 2024, NC State won 59-28 in Raleigh. Painful? Yes. A data point? Also yes.

Now, let's look at the vulnerabilities in their roadmap.

Two weeks ago, NC State led Wake Forest 14-10 at halftime at home. Then Wake scored 28 straight points and won 38-14. In that game, NC State ran the ball 24 times for 15 yards. That's 0.6 yards per carry. My scooter ride-share app moved people farther than that, and it went out of business.

NC State's defense allows 27.7 points a game, 104th in FBS, and 230.3 passing yards a game, 99th. It opened the season with a 34-8 loss at Virginia and later lost 35-31 at Vanderbilt. Friends, that's a pass defense in beta testing.

Our Product Roadmap

I'm not hiding our numbers. Our defense allows 452 yards a game, 134th in FBS, and 36.6 points a game, 133rd. Our red zone defense ranks 136th. Our offense scores 18.3 points a game, 127th. Those numbers need a serious pivot.

But here's the vision. Ford has 529 rushing yards and eight touchdowns. Warren has 1,630 passing yards with only two interceptions. Caden High has 337 receiving yards and three touchdowns. And Jay Green leads us with 43 tackles.

Four Deliverables for Friday

1. Pivot to the run game. Ford just ran for 179 yards. NC State's run defense allows 133.5 yards a game. Give him the ball, then give it to him again. That's not a strategy. That's a scalable business model.
2. Protect the asset. Warren has thrown two interceptions all season. Keep that number low, and we keep possession of the football and of the narrative.
3. Win third down. NC State is great at converting third downs. Our defense allows opponents to convert 47.8 of every 100 times, 131st. If we get stops on third down, NC State's best metric becomes a slide we get to delete.

4. Own the clock. We average 28:19 of possession a game, 108th in FBS, while NC State averages 32:52. Long Ford-powered drives flip that metric and keep Bailey on the sideline, which is where I like my competitors' best features: unused, like the "share" button on my houseplant app.

Town Hall: The Farm vs. Raleigh

The Farm. Stanford University was founded in 1885 by Leland Stanford and his wife, Jane, in memory of their only child, and it admitted its first students in 1891. After World War II, provost Frederick Terman inspired an entrepreneurial culture that gave rise to what's now known as Silicon Valley. So yes, my three failed apps were basically a local tradition. Stanford Stadium was built in five months in 1921, then demolished and rebuilt after the 2005 season. That's what we call a full platform migration. And our team name, Cardinal, refers to the color, not the bird. We're not a mascot. We're a brand.

Raleigh. Raleigh is a lovely state capital, the "City of Oaks." But it's named after Sir Walter Raleigh, who founded the Roanoke Colony, which is famous for getting lost. Naming your city after the founder of the lost colony is a bold branding choice. I'd never ship that.

And the Wolfpack name? It came from an unsigned letter to the NC State Alumni News in 1921. The brand identity was created by an anonymous source. As a founder, I respect crowdsourcing, but I'd at least get the guy to sign an NDA.

The Closing Pitch

Here's the summary slide. Stanford has a record-tying running back, a quarterback who protects the football and a fresh win. NC State has a strong third-down offense and a quarterback who has thrown nine touchdowns, but it also has a run game that went missing against Wake and a pass defense ranked 99th. If we pivot to the run game and get key stops on third down, this product could ship on time.

Friday night. Let's pivot to the run game.

My call: NC State Wolfpack 33, Stanford Cardinal 25.

articles.title: That's a Foot of Snow of a Take: Syracuse Brings Umari Hatcher to Chapel Hill, Where the Offense Ranks 117th and Once Went 41 Minutes Without Scoring
articles.byline: Nico Calabrese, The Syracuse Fanatic
articles.matchup: Syracuse (2-4) at North Carolina (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7:30 p.m. ET, Kenan Stadium, ACC Network
articles.text:
Hey there, Orange Nation. Nico Calabrese here, Central New York born, lake-effect tested and shovel certified. I follow the Orange to every game from the stands, and I rate every play in feet of snow. One foot is a nice play. Three feet is a highlight. Six feet means school's canceled, and we're all at the Dome.

This week, the forecast is mixed. Let me give you the honest weather report.

Part 1: Last Week, a Snow Squall That Wouldn't Quit

Syracuse lost 34-26 to Louisville on Saturday at the Dome. We're 2-4 and 0-4 in the ACC. I'll be straight with you. It stung like a January wind off Onondaga Lake.

But the start? Oh, the start was a five-foot blizzard. Shay Barker kicked a 26-yard field goal. Then Malachi Nelson threw a 41-yard touchdown pass to Umari Hatcher, and we led 10-0. Louisville answered twice, but early in the second quarter, Nelson found freshman Calvin Russell III for a 24-yard touchdown, and we led 16-14. Later, Ahmad Miller ran 20 yards for a touchdown to make it 23-21. Louisville hit a 46-yard touchdown pass with 28 seconds left in the half, and we went to the locker room down 28-23.

The two teams combined for 669 yards in the first half, the most in the ACC since 2022, according to the AP. That's a whiteout. Nobody could see the defense.

Then our defense showed up like a city plow at 5 a.m. Louisville gained just 58 yards after halftime. Davien Kerr intercepted two passes. Linebacker Chris D'Appolonia made 12 tackles, including a sack and 3.5 tackles for loss. And Isaac Brown, who ran for 235 yards the week before, gained just 22 yards on nine carries against us. That's a three-foot defensive performance. I'm shoveling it with pride.

Barker's 24-yard field goal early in the fourth cut it to 28-26. But Louisville intercepted a pass to set up a 5-yard touchdown run with 7:34 left, and that was the final margin.

Now, the highlights. Hatcher caught 13 passes for 224 yards, both career highs. It was his fourth 100-yard game this season, and his touchdown was his ACC-leading seventh. That's an eight-foot performance, folks. Pack your boots. Nelson, in his second start, completed 26 of 39 passes for 315 yards and two touchdowns. Miller ran for 123 yards on 18 carries. Russell caught six passes for 53 yards and his first touchdown.

Coach Fran Brown said afterward he wasn't happy with the loss and there's plenty to clean up with a young team, but he was proud of how hard the guys fought at the end. That's the Syracuse way. We dig out.

Part 2: Saturday Night in Chapel Hill

Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern on ACC Network. Syracuse (2-4) at North Carolina (4-2, 2-1 ACC) at Kenan Stadium. Forecast for Chapel Hill: no snow. I'll pack a light jacket anyway, because I'm from Syracuse, and we never trust a forecast.

The Honest Forecast for Us

Let me shovel the walkway first. Syracuse has lost 11 straight ACC games and 12 straight against Power 4 teams, according to the AP. We've been outscored 78-36 in the second half this season. We lead the country in penalties, at 98.0 penalty yards a game, 138th in FBS, and we had three unsportsmanlike penalties in the first half last week. Our red zone offense scores on 78.1 of every 100 trips, 111th. We went 3-9 last season, and last year North Carolina beat us 27-10 at the Dome. Those are snow days I'd rather forget.

But here's the sunshine. Our passing offense averages 291.0 yards a game, 12th in FBS. Our offense averages 449.7 yards a game overall, 29th. We hold the ball for 33:59 a game, fifth in FBS. And our pass defense allows 191.8 yards a game, 43rd.

The Forecast for Carolina

Now let me tell you about the folks in the pines. North Carolina beat Duke 24-20 last week, and I respect that. They reclaimed the Victory Bell with a 24-yard touchdown run with 1:53 left. Their defense allows 19.2 points a game, 34th in FBS, and they commit the fifth-fewest penalty yards in FBS. Billy Edwards Jr. has nine touchdown passes, and Jordan Shipp has 441 receiving yards. Credit where it's due.

But after jumping out to a 17-0 lead over Duke, UNC managed only about 100 yards until its final drive, according to the AP, and went more than 41 minutes without scoring. That's a flurry that melted on the driveway.

North Carolina's offense averages 329.7 yards a game, 117th in FBS. Its rushing offense averages 116.2 yards, 120th. It holds the ball for 27:00 a game, 130th. And its third-down defense allows opponents to convert 43.3 of every 100 times, 113th. They also went 4-8 last season. That's a half-inch dusting, Carolina. In Syracuse, we wouldn't even close the schools for that.

Three Shovels for Saturday

1. Feed Hatcher. He has 50 catches for 784 yards and seven touchdowns. Carolina will try to bracket him, so move him around and let him work.
2. Clean it up. No more unsportsmanlike penalties. Every flag is a snowdrift we have to dig out of.
3. Own the clock. We rank fifth in time of possession, and they rank 130th. Long drives keep their offense in the cold.

Weather Report: Syracuse vs. Chapel Hill

Syracuse. Let me tell you about the Salt City. Syracuse grew up around brine springs that made it the nation's leading salt producer in the 19th century. The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, ran right through the center of town, and the city became a crossroads of commerce and a center of the abolitionist movement and the Underground Railroad. On Tipperary Hill, a traffic light has hung green above red since 1928. And the snow? A normal season brings about 127.8 inches. We won the Golden Snowball Award for 2025-26 with 143.1 inches, our second straight title. We don't complain about it. We win trophies for it.

And our home, the JMA Wireless Dome, is the largest domed stadium on any college campus. Our football program won the 1959 national championship, and its alumni include Jim Brown and Ernie Davis, the first Black winner of the Heisman Trophy. Respect the Orange.

Chapel Hill. Chapel Hill is a pretty town, folks. But it's named after a chapel. On a hill. That's not a name. That's a set of directions. The town was founded to serve the university, so even the town is a student. And Kenan Stadium's first game in 1927 drew 9,000 spectators. In Syracuse, we get more people than that shoveling out a single block after a storm.

Then there's the mascot. Rameses is a live sheep who attends games with his horns painted Carolina blue. A sheep, Carolina. We have an orange. At least ours doesn't need a haircut every spring.

The Final Forecast

Here's the honest outlook. North Carolina has a strong scoring defense, great discipline and a fresh rivalry win. Syracuse has an elite receiver, a top-15 passing offense and a defense that just held Louisville to 58 second-half yards. If we cut the penalties and keep feeding Hatcher, this game could get snowy late, even in North Carolina.

That's a foot of snow of a take.

My call: North Carolina Tar Heels 29, Syracuse Orange 20.

blocks.text: Hey there, Orange Nation. Nico Calabrese here, Central New York born, lake-effect tested and shovel certified. I follow the Orange to every game from the stands, and I rate every play in feet of snow. One foot is a nice play. Three feet is a highlight. Six feet means school's canceled, and we're all at the Dome.
This week, the forecast is mixed. Let me give you the honest weather report.
Part 1: Last Week, a Snow Squall That Wouldn't Quit
Syracuse lost 34-26 to Louisville on Saturday at the Dome. We're 2-4 and 0-4 in the ACC. I'll be straight with you. It stung like a January wind off Onondaga Lake.

But the start? Oh, the start was a five-foot blizzard. Shay Barker kicked a 26-yard field goal. Then Malachi Nelson threw a 41-yard touchdown pass to Umari Hatcher, and we led 10-0. Louisville answered twice, but early in the second quarter, Nelson found freshman Calvin Russell III for a 24-yard touchdown, and we led 16-14. Later, Ahmad Miller ran 20 yards for a touchdown to make it 23-21. Louisville hit a 46-yard touchdown pass with 28 seconds left in the half, and we went to the locker room down 28-23.
The two teams combined for 669 yards in the first half, the most in the ACC since 2022, according to the AP. That's a whiteout. Nobody could see the defense.

Then our defense showed up like a city plow at 5 a.m. Louisville gained just 58 yards after halftime. Davien Kerr intercepted two passes. Linebacker Chris D'Appolonia made 12 tackles, including a sack and 3.5 tackles for loss. And Isaac Brown, who ran for 235 yards the week before, gained just 22 yards on nine carries against us. That's a three-foot defensive performance. I'm shoveling it with pride.
Barker's 24-yard field goal early in the fourth cut it to 28-26. But Louisville intercepted a pass to set up a 5-yard touchdown run with 7:34 left, and that was the final margin.

Now, the highlights. Hatcher caught 13 passes for 224 yards, both career highs. It was his fourth 100-yard game this season, and his touchdown was his ACC-leading seventh. That's an eight-foot performance, folks. Pack your boots. Nelson, in his second start, completed 26 of 39 passes for 315 yards and two touchdowns. Miller ran for 123 yards on 18 carries. Russell caught six passes for 53 yards and his first touchdown.

Coach Fran Brown said afterward he wasn't happy with the loss and there's plenty to clean up with a young team, but he was proud of how hard the guys fought at the end. That's the Syracuse way. We dig out.
Part 2: Saturday Night in Chapel Hill

Saturday, 7:30 p.m. Eastern on ACC Network. Syracuse (2-4) at North Carolina (4-2, 2-1 ACC) at Kenan Stadium. Forecast for Chapel Hill: no snow. I'll pack a light jacket anyway, because I'm from Syracuse, and we never trust a forecast.
The Honest Forecast for Us

Let me shovel the walkway first. Syracuse has lost 11 straight ACC games and 12 straight against Power 4 teams, according to the AP. We've been outscored 78-36 in the second half this season. We lead the country in penalties, at 98.0 penalty yards a game, 138th in FBS, and we had three unsportsmanlike penalties in the first half last week. Our red zone offense scores on 78.1 of every 100 trips, 111th. We went 3-9 last season, and last year North Carolina beat us 27-10 at the Dome. Those are snow days I'd rather forget.

But here's the sunshine. Our passing offense averages 291.0 yards a game, 12th in FBS. Our offense averages 449.7 yards a game overall, 29th. We hold the ball for 33:59 a game, fifth in FBS. And our pass defense allows 191.8 yards a game, 43rd.
The Forecast for Carolina

Now let me tell you about the folks in the pines. North Carolina beat Duke 24-20 last week, and I respect that. They reclaimed the Victory Bell with a 24-yard touchdown run with 1:53 left. Their defense allows 19.2 points a game, 34th in FBS, and they commit the fifth-fewest penalty yards in FBS. Billy Edwards Jr. has nine touchdown passes, and Jordan Shipp has 441 receiving yards. Credit where it's due.

But after jumping out to a 17-0 lead over Duke, UNC managed only about 100 yards until its final drive, according to the AP, and went more than 41 minutes without scoring. That's a flurry that melted on the driveway.

North Carolina's offense averages 329.7 yards a game, 117th in FBS. Its rushing offense averages 116.2 yards, 120th. It holds the ball for 27:00 a game, 130th. And its third-down defense allows opponents to convert 43.3 of every 100 times, 113th. They also went 4-8 last season. That's a half-inch dusting, Carolina. In Syracuse, we wouldn't even close the schools for that.
Three Shovels for Saturday

1. Feed Hatcher. He has 50 catches for 784 yards and seven touchdowns. Carolina will try to bracket him, so move him around and let him work. 2. Clean it up. No more unsportsmanlike penalties. Every flag is a snowdrift we have to dig out of. 3. Own the clock. We rank fifth in time of possession, and they rank 130th. Long drives keep their offense in the cold.
Weather Report: Syracuse vs. Chapel Hill

Syracuse. Let me tell you about the Salt City. Syracuse grew up around brine springs that made it the nation's leading salt producer in the 19th century. The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, ran right through the center of town, and the city became a crossroads of commerce and a center of the abolitionist movement and the Underground Railroad. On Tipperary Hill, a traffic light has hung green above red since 1928. And the snow? A normal season brings about 127.8 inches. We won the Golden Snowball Award for 2025-26 with 143.1 inches, our second straight title. We don't complain about it. We win trophies for it.

And our home, the JMA Wireless Dome, is the largest domed stadium on any college campus. Our football program won the 1959 national championship, and its alumni include Jim Brown and Ernie Davis, the first Black winner of the Heisman Trophy. Respect the Orange.

Chapel Hill. Chapel Hill is a pretty town, folks. But it's named after a chapel. On a hill. That's not a name. That's a set of directions. The town was founded to serve the university, so even the town is a student. And Kenan Stadium's first game in 1927 drew 9,000 spectators. In Syracuse, we get more people than that shoveling out a single block after a storm.
Then there's the mascot. Rameses is a live sheep who attends games with his horns painted Carolina blue. A sheep, Carolina. We have an orange. At least ours doesn't need a haircut every spring.
The Final Forecast

Here's the honest outlook. North Carolina has a strong scoring defense, great discipline and a fresh rivalry win. Syracuse has an elite receiver, a top-15 passing offense and a defense that just held Louisville to 58 second-half yards. If we cut the penalties and keep feeding Hatcher, this game could get snowy late, even in North Carolina.
That's a foot of snow of a take.
My call: North Carolina Tar Heels 29, Syracuse Orange 20.

articles.title: Exit Light, Enter Stats: Virginia Tech Marches Into Death Valley, Where Even the Nickname and the Lucky Rock Came From California
articles.byline: Ruthanne Dellinger, The Virginia Tech Fanatic
articles.matchup: Virginia Tech (5-2) at Clemson (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 7 p.m. ET, Memorial Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Attention, Hokie Nation! Ruthanne Dellinger reporting, former Corps of Cadets drum major, mace in hand, posture perfect. I break down defense the Lunch Pail way: no names on the backs, just goals in a battered metal pail and 11 people carrying them out. And I jump. Every time our defense makes a stop, I jump, out loud, with a little "hup!" My neighbors in Blacksburg have learned to live with it.

On Saturday, I jumped a lot.

Exit light, enter stats.

Part 1: Four of the First Five

Virginia Tech beat Georgia Tech 34-24 at Lane Stadium on Saturday. We're 5-2 and 2-2 in the ACC, and we snapped a two-game losing streak. Our previous two games, both losses, had come down to the final play. This one didn't. Hup!

It took three plays. Ethan Grunkemeyer found Que'Sean Brown for a 60-yard touchdown on the game's third snap. Then Grunkemeyer ran 20 yards for another score. He hit Ja'Ricous Hairston for a 5-yard touchdown, and John Love added a 39-yard field goal. We scored on four of our first five possessions and led 24-3 at halftime. That's a parade formation, people. Everybody in step.

Georgia Tech came back in the third quarter and got within 24-17. That's when a drum major raises the mace and calls for the next song. Grunkemeyer threw a 26-yard touchdown to Jeffrey Overton Jr. with 5:41 left in the third. Then Brown returned a punt 63 yards to set up Love's 24-yard field goal, and it was 34-17.

Grunkemeyer finished 15 of 22 for 250 yards and three touchdowns, with no interceptions. And Brown? Six catches, 182 yards. AP says that's a career high for him and the sixth-most receiving yards in a game in Virginia Tech history. Quentin Reddish had an interception, and on Georgia Tech's very first possession, the ball came loose at the goal and rolled through the end zone for a touchback. AP says Georgia Tech's two turnovers led to 10 of our points. Hup, hup, hup!

Honest note from the drum major: Georgia Tech outgained us 428-409, and its quarterback had a career day. We've got cleanup to do on defense. But we won, and our coach was pleased with how all three phases contributed. So am I.

Part 2: Marching Into the Valley

Saturday, 7 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. Virginia Tech (5-2) at Clemson (4-2) at Memorial Stadium. This starts the hardest stretch of our season, with three of our next four on the road, at Clemson, SMU and Miami.

Inspecting the Tigers

Respect first, always. Clemson just beat Charleston Southern 37-0. Its kicker, Nolan Hauser, made a 59-yard field goal. Will Heldt has four sacks. And Death Valley on a Saturday night is a loud place. I'll bring earplugs and my best posture.

Now, the inspection.

Charleston Southern is an FCS team. Against FBS teams, Clemson lost 51-10 at LSU to open the season and 41-13 at home to Miami two weeks ago. Miami held the Tigers to 55 rushing yards. Clemson's offense gains 340.7 yards a game, 110th in FBS. Its passing game averages 187.5 yards a game, 112th. It scores 22.3 points a game, 106th. And Clemson converts 33.3 of every 100 third downs, 116th.

Clemson's passing game ranks 112th, and ours ranks 11th, at 301.6 yards a game. That's a gap of 101 spots. In marching band terms, that's the difference between the drum major and the kid who forgot his shoes. And last season, per CollegeFootballData, Clemson went 7-6.

Inspecting the Hokies

Grunkemeyer completes 72.6 of every 100 passes, with 1,984 yards, 15 touchdowns and two interceptions. Brown has 46 catches for 616 yards. Overton has 613 rushing yards. We score 37.1 points a game, 23rd in FBS. And Aycen Stevens has eight sacks. Eight! That man owns real estate in the backfield.

Lunch Pail report: our run defense allows 87.4 yards a game, 10th in FBS. Opponents convert only 32.6 of every 100 third downs, 29th. Clemson's offense lives on the ground, and our front is built to say no.

Honest Inspection Notes

The drum major doesn't hide a wrong note. Our pass defense allows 227.3 yards a game, 95th. We're minus-4 in turnover margin, 113th. We lost at Cal 25-20 and lost at home to Pitt 35-33. And Clemson leads the series 23-11-1, according to CollegeFootballData, and has won the last six meetings, dating to 2011. The last time we played in Death Valley, in 2012, Clemson won 38-17. Streaks end, people. Somebody has to end them.

The Drum Major's Game Plan

Every parade needs a plan, so here's mine, in four counts. Count one: stop the run. Clemson ran for 231 yards last week, but it was held to 55 by Miami, and our run defense ranks 10th. Make Clemson throw. Count two: let Stevens loose. Eight sacks in seven games is a man who knows the route to the quarterback by heart. Count three: take the shots to Brown. Clemson's pass defense is solid, but Brown just showed he can win any matchup. Count four: protect the ball. Both teams are minus-4, and the first team to turn it over in Death Valley at night is going to hear about it from 81,500 people.

Hit all four counts, and we march out of the Valley in step.

Postcards: Blacksburg vs. Clemson

Blacksburg. Blacksburg was officially established on Jan. 13, 1798, and today it's a mountain town of 44,826, according to the 2020 census. Lane Stadium played its first game in 1965. And for about 25 years, our team has entered to Metallica's "Enter Sandman," with the whole stadium jumping. Jumping! You see where I get it from.

Our traditions are humble and tough. The Lunch Pail started as a symbol of a no-name, blue-collar defense, and every week, a list of goals goes inside and a player earns the honor of carrying it to the sideline. There's even a Lunch Pail Defense Foundation that funds academic scholarships for students near Blacksburg. That's a tradition that feeds people's futures. And yes, our HokieBird is a big, proud turkey, the successor to the old Fighting Gobblers, created in 1981. Laugh all you want, Clemson. Turkeys are tough, they travel in flocks and they've got the best seat at every family table in America.

Clemson. Clemson is a lovely little city of 17,681. Blacksburg is more than twice its size. And here's what I learned. The nickname "Death Valley" comes partly from Death Valley National Park, in California. And the famous Howard's Rock? It came from Death Valley, California, too. So Clemson's stadium nickname and its lucky rock were both borrowed from California. Even the scenery is a transfer.

Clemson's tigers rub that rock before the game. In Blacksburg, we carry a lunch pail full of goals. One tradition is about a rock. The other is about work. Hup!

Dismissed

Here's my final inspection. Clemson has a loud stadium, a strong kicker and an offense that's struggled all season against FBS teams. Virginia Tech has a quarterback with 15 touchdown passes, a top-10 run defense, an eight-sack pass rusher and a wide receiver coming off a historic day. If the Lunch Pail stops the run and Grunkemeyer protects the ball, Death Valley gets very quiet. And I'll be jumping.

Exit light, enter stats. Go Hokies!

My call: Clemson Tigers 27, Virginia Tech Hokies 24.

articles.title: As Mr. Jefferson Would've Charted It: Virginia Hosts Duke, From a City That Exists Because a Steam Engine Needed a Drink of Water
articles.byline: Prescott Ashby-Lowell, The Virginia Fanatic
articles.matchup: Duke (4-2) at Virginia (4-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 7 p.m. ET, Scott Stadium, ESPN
articles.text:
Good evening, and welcome to the Grounds. I am Prescott Ashby-Lowell, fourth-generation Wahoo, and you'll notice I said "Grounds." Not campus. Never campus. At the University of Virginia, we have the Lawn, the Rotunda and the Grounds, and if you say "campus" within earshot, I will clear my throat in a very disappointed manner.

I keep a leather-bound ledger of every Virginia game, charted in fountain pen, much as Mr. Jefferson charted the weather at Monticello. And this week's entry requires both honesty and a fresh nib.

As Mr. Jefferson would've charted it.

Part 1: A Close Contest in Dallas

SMU beat Virginia 23-13 at Gerald J. Ford Stadium on Saturday. We're 4-3 and 2-2 in the ACC. Allow me to record the facts faithfully, for a gentleman's ledger contains no embellishment.

It was a respectable contest for long stretches. Beau Pribula scored our touchdown on a 1-yard run on fourth down in the second quarter, and we led 7-3. Will Bettridge kicked a 47-yard field goal to tie it 10-10 with 25 seconds left before halftime. AP noted that Virginia controlled SMU for long stretches.

But a few large plays changed the afternoon. A 59-yard catch set up an SMU touchdown on fourth-and-1. And at the end of the first half, after time had expired, a roughing-the-passer penalty gave SMU an untimed down. SMU kicked a 45-yard field goal for a 13-10 halftime lead. Bettridge answered with a 43-yarder in the third quarter, making it 16-13, but a 37-yard catch-and-run early in the fourth sealed it.

Pribula went 13 of 22 for 137 yards. We finished with 258 yards. Our defense came in with the ACC's top pass defense and faced the third-best passing offense in the country, and it held SMU to 246 passing yards. It was 57 degrees at kickoff, according to AP, on Virginia's first visit to Texas in 14 years. Delightful weather. Disappointing result.

I'll be candid. AP noted we've been held under 300 yards for three straight games. That's a column in my ledger that needs attention.

Part 2: Friday Evening on the Grounds

Friday, 7 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. Duke (4-2) at Virginia (4-3) at Scott Stadium. A Friday night under the lights in Charlottesville. The bow ties are pressed. It's a nationally televised Friday night game on ESPN, the whole country watching Mr. Jefferson's university, and I intend for every one of us in the stands to be wearing orange and blue and our very best manners. This is also our last home game before a trip to Wake Forest, so the Grounds will want to send the Cavaliers off properly.

A Recent History Lesson

Last season, we met Duke twice. In November, Virginia won 34-17 in Durham. Then in December, Duke beat us 27-20 in overtime in the ACC Championship Game in Charlotte. I won't pretend that second one didn't sting. I put down my fountain pen for a week. But Virginia went 11-3 last season and finished first in the ACC regular-season standings. A gentleman remembers both chapters.

An Assessment of the Blue Devils

Duke's defense is excellent, and I'll say so plainly. It allows 16.0 points a game, 19th in FBS, and opponents convert only 29.2 of every 100 third downs. Nate Sheppard leads the nation in rushing yards per game and has 820 yards and eight touchdowns.

Now, the critique, delivered with impeccable manners.

Duke has lost two straight. A week ago at Georgia Tech, it took a late lead and lost 28-25. Last Saturday at home against North Carolina, it took a 20-17 lead with 4:39 left and lost 24-20. Duke had led, and then Duke had not. Two weeks in a row. And North Carolina's players carried the Victory Bell off the field in Durham.

Duke averages 73.8 penalty yards a game, 123rd in FBS. Virginia averages 49.3, 38th. Mr. Jefferson valued order and discipline. Duke values... flags, apparently.

And Duke's passing game ranks 66th in FBS. Our pass defense ranks 25th.

Our Own Ledger

Pribula has thrown 13 touchdowns and just one interception all season. We're plus-5 in turnover margin, 15th in FBS. Matthew Fobbs-White has four sacks. Jacobie Henderson leads us with 38 tackles. Da'Shawn Martin has five touchdown catches on just 15 receptions.

Our honest entries: we convert 33.0 of every 100 third downs, 120th in FBS. We score on 74.1 of every 100 red zone trips, 124th. Our run defense allows 152.7 yards a game, 88th, and Sheppard will test it. We also lost 38-7 at Florida State. The ledger is frank, because a ledger that flatters is worthless.

The Evening's Itinerary

As Mr. Jefferson would've charted it, here is the plan for Friday, in four tidy entries. First: contain Sheppard. He's a dual threat, and he caught 11 passes last week, so our linebackers must account for him on every snap. Second: make Duke throw. Its passing game ranks 66th, and our secondary has been the pride of the conference. Third: win the hidden yardage. Duke's penalties have handed opponents field position all season, and we must be disciplined enough to take advantage. Fourth: Pribula must be Pribula. Thirteen touchdowns and one interception is an elegant ratio by any standard, and on a Friday night at Scott Stadium, elegance is precisely what's called for.

A Tour of Two Cities

Charlottesville. Charlottesville was established by an act of the Albemarle County assembly in 1762, and it was home to two U.S. presidents, Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe. Monticello, Jefferson's home, sits three miles southeast of town, and it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with the University's Academical Village. Mr. Jefferson founded the University in 1819, and three presidents, Jefferson, Madison and Monroe, played a part in its founding. He designed the original buildings and the course of study himself. And the Grounds were planned around a library, the Rotunda.

Scott Stadium, built in 1931, is the oldest active FBS football stadium in Virginia. With the hillside seating, it's the most gracious place in the Commonwealth to watch a game.

Durham. Durham is a much larger city, with 283,506 people at the 2020 census. Larger, certainly. But here is how Durham began. In the 19th century, wood-burning steam locomotives had to stop frequently for wood and water, and the new North Carolina Railroad needed a depot between Raleigh and Hillsborough. So, a railway depot was established in 1849. Durham, my friends, exists because a train needed a drink of water. Charlottesville exists because the Commonwealth decided it should. Mr. Jefferson would have charted the difference.

And the name Blue Devils comes from the French Alpine light infantry of World War I, "les Diables Bleus." So Duke is named for French mountain soldiers. Durham, I'll note, sits nowhere near the Alps. I admire the ambition.

The Final Entry

Here is my assessment, in fountain pen. Duke has a superb defense and a powerful running back, but a habit of losing late leads and an excess of penalties. Virginia has a quarterback who protects the ball, a top-25 pass defense, a turnover margin that ranks 15th and a home crowd on a Friday night. If our offense finally finds its footing on third down, the final entry in tonight's ledger will be written in orange and blue.

Wahoowa, and good evening.

My call: Virginia Cavaliers 25, Duke Blue Devils 23.

At the University of Virginia, we have the Lawn, the Rotunda and the Grounds, and if you say "campus" within earshot, I will clear my throat in a very disappointed manner.
I keep a leather-bound ledger of every Virginia game, charted in fountain pen, much as Mr. Jefferson charted the weather at Monticello. And this week's entry requires both honesty and a fresh nib.

articles.title: Roll the Quad! No. 17 Wake Forest Rolls Past Cal 41-7, Takes a Well-Earned Bye, Then Welcomes Virginia, Who Still Calls Its Campus 'the Grounds'
articles.byline: Eloise Brightman-Rowe, The Wake Forest Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 17 Wake Forest (6-1): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Virginia at Wake Forest, Sat., Oct. 31, Allegacy Federal Credit Union Stadium
articles.text:
Resolved: Wake Forest is having a marvelous season. I'll argue the affirmative. Eloise Brightman-Rowe here, the Wake Forest Fanatic, Wake grad, debate-team darling and a woman who keeps a roll of celebratory toilet paper in her handbag at all times, just in case. I follow the Demon Deacons to every game from the stands, and I roast bad tackling the way I used to roast weak rebuttals: politely, thoroughly and with footnotes.

This week's opening statement is short. Roll the Quad!

Part 1: Last Week, an Opening Argument That Ended the Debate

Wake Forest beat Cal 41-7 on Saturday night in Berkeley. We're 6-1 and 4-1 in the ACC. We came in ranked No. 21 in the AP poll, our first AP ranking in four years, and we've now climbed to No. 17.

Here's my evidence, and it's overwhelming. On our first possession, Gio Lopez led a five-play, 99-yard drive and finished it with a 39-yard touchdown pass to tight end Dominick Barry. Ninety-nine yards in five plays. Judges, I rest my case. But I'll keep going anyway.

On Cal's second possession, our defense stopped them on fourth-and-1 at their own 34. One play later, Lopez hit Jack Foley for a 29-yard touchdown. Then Jamar Searcy capped a 78-yard drive with a 1-yard run. Ty Clark III ran 31 yards for another touchdown. And with nine seconds left in the half, Lopez found Barry again from 30 yards out. Wake Forest led 34-0 at halftime.

Per the AP, we scored touchdowns on five of our six first-half possessions, averaged 12.3 yards per play and outgained Cal 394-142 before halftime. Barry added a 2-yard touchdown catch in the third quarter to make it 41-0, and Cal scored in the fourth to avoid the shutout.

Lopez completed 16 of 23 passes for 267 yards and four touchdowns, with no interceptions. Per the AP, he now has 23 touchdowns this season, passing and running. Barry caught four passes for 102 yards and three touchdowns. Kam Shanks caught five for 79. Searcy ran for 61 yards on five carries. Linebacker Myles Turpin made 10 tackles, with 1.5 for loss. And per the AP, it was our fourth road win over a power conference team this season. Counterargument? There is none.

Points of Information Against Myself

A good debater concedes what's true. We committed 11 penalties for 110 yards in Berkeley. That's a lot of flags, Deacs, and against a stronger opponent, it'll cost us. Our only loss came 33-20 at home to Miami, the team that's now No. 1. And yes, I watched one or two tackles in the fourth quarter that I'd grade as "needs a stronger thesis." We'll fix it.

Part 2: The Bye, Then Virginia

Wake Forest doesn't play this Saturday, Oct. 24. It's our open date, and I'll call it what it is: a well-earned recess. Rest, recover and review the tape. Even champion debaters need a weekend off between tournaments.

Then, on Saturday, Oct. 31, Virginia visits Allegacy Federal Credit Union Stadium. Kickoff time and TV are still to be announced.

The Opposition's Case

Let me fairly state Virginia's case. Virginia is 4-3. It opened the season with a 34-8 win over NC State, a team we beat 38-14, and it beat Syracuse 28-25. Virginia went 11-3 last season. That's a strong résumé, and I respect it.

And now, my rebuttal. Virginia lost 38-7 at Florida State, 38-27 to West Virginia and 23-13 at SMU last week. Two of its four wins came against FCS teams, Norfolk State and Delaware. And last season, Wake Forest beat Virginia 16-9 in Charlottesville, during the same 11-3 season Virginia likes to bring up. Points of information, judges.

Virginia also hosts Duke on Friday, while we rest. So we'll have two weeks to prepare, and Virginia will be coming off a game on a short week.

Cross-Examination: The Numbers

Let's enter some statistics into evidence, courtesy of the AP's preview of Virginia's game against Duke. Virginia quarterback Beau Pribula has thrown 13 touchdown passes and just one interception, and Virginia is plus-5 in turnover margin, 15th in FBS. Its pass defense ranks 25th. Those are strong exhibits, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But the cross-examination continues. Virginia converts only 33.0 of every 100 third downs, 120th in FBS. It scores on 74.1 of every 100 red zone trips, 124th. And its run defense allows 152.7 yards a game, 88th. Judges, a team that can't finish drives and can't stop the run is a team with a hole in its argument. And Wake Forest has Searcy and Clark, who combined for two rushing touchdowns and 114 yards in Berkeley on just 13 carries. I'd like the record to reflect that.

We went 9-4 last season, and this team looks even sharper. Six wins in seven games, four of them on the road against power conference teams, per the AP. That's not a fluke. That's a well-researched case.

Our Debate Prep

1. Keep Lopez upright. He has four touchdown passes in a game and 23 touchdowns this season. Protect the asset, and the case makes itself.
2. Clean up the flags. Eleven penalties are 10 too many for a debate champion. Discipline wins tournaments.
3. Tackle with conviction. Every missed tackle is a weak rebuttal. Wrap up, finish and win the round.

Winston-Salem vs. Charlottesville: A Formal Debate

Winston-Salem. I'll argue for my hometown. Winston-Salem was created in 1913 when two neighboring towns, Salem, a Moravian settlement established in 1766, and Winston, established in 1849, merged into one. We're a city with two names and one heart. We had an estimated 249,545 residents at the 2020 census, making us the fifth-most populous city in North Carolina. We grew into a major center of tobacco, textile manufacturing and banking, with companies including R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company, Hanes and Wachovia.

Wake Forest was founded by Baptist Christians in 1834 and moved to Winston-Salem in 1956. And our nickname? In 1923, after a big win over Trinity College, the school that became Duke, a reporter wrote that the Deacons "fought like Demons." That's how we became the Demon Deacons. Our stadium, which opened in 1968, holds 31,500 people, the smallest permanent capacity in the Power Four. I call that intimate. Every seat is a front-row seat to excellence.

Charlottesville. Charlottesville is a lovely city, named after Queen Charlotte, with 46,553 residents at the 2020 census. Winston-Salem has more than five Charlottesvilles. And at Virginia, they don't call it a campus. They call it "the Grounds." Judges, I'd argue "the Grounds" sounds less like a university and more like what's left at the bottom of your coffee cup. We roll the Quad. They tend the Grounds.

Closing Statement

Here's my summation. Wake Forest has a quarterback with 23 touchdowns, a tight end who just caught three touchdown passes, a defense that held Cal scoreless for three quarters and a No. 17 ranking. Virginia has a solid résumé but three losses, including two on the road. We get two weeks to prepare, and Virginia doesn't. If we clean up the penalties and tackle with conviction, the judges will find for the affirmative on Oct. 31. Until then, the Deacons get to rest, study film and enjoy a quiet Saturday. I'll be drafting my opening argument, polishing my old gold and black, and reminding anyone who will listen that two weeks of preparation is a gift, and gifts are meant to be used wisely.

Resolved: Roll the Quad!

articles.title: Seven Drives, Seven Touchdowns, Two Passes: Army Ships Its Ground Game to Tulsa, Where the 'Golden Hurricane' Lives Hundreds of Miles From Any Ocean
articles.byline: Capt. (Ret.) Thaddeus Rourke, The Army Fanatic
articles.matchup: Army (4-2) at Tulsa (4-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 8:30 p.m. ET, Skelly Field at H. A. Chapman Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Attention on deck. Capt. Thaddeus Rourke, retired, reporting from the stands above the Hudson, where my boots are shined, my clipboard is laminated and my coffee is exactly the temperature the regulations recommend. I spent a career moving the right item to the right place at the right time. Then I retired, and I discovered that Army football does the same thing, except the item is a football and the place is the end zone.

This week's operations order has two phases. Phase one: an after-action review of the most efficient supply run I have ever witnessed. Phase two: a Friday night deployment to Tulsa, Oklahoma, home of a hurricane that has never once seen the sea. Copy that, and beat Navy.

Part 1: After-Action Review, Army 56, Florida Atlantic 24

Let the record show that on Saturday, Oct. 17, in front of 28,537 at Michie Stadium, Army beat Florida Atlantic 56-24, and the Black Knights reached the end zone on their first seven possessions. Seven for seven. In logistics, we call that a perfect delivery record. In football, I believe the technical term is "please stop."

The mission started before the coffee cooled. On the very first snap, Elijah Walton intercepted FAU quarterback Caden Veltkamp. On the very next snap, Samari Howard ran 30 yards for a touchdown. Two plays, one takeaway, one score. I have seen slower service at the mess hall.

Then quarterback Cale Hellums took over the convoy. He ran 58 yards for a touchdown on Army's next possession, then added three short scoring runs in the second quarter for a 35-14 halftime lead. He added another one early in the fourth. His final report: 25 carries, 195 yards and five rushing touchdowns. Five. That is not a stat sheet, troops. That is a shipping manifest.

The relief drivers were sharp, too. On the third play of the second half, Jake Rendina burrowed up the middle and broke free for a 61-yard score. On Army's last possession, Bryson Luter went 69 yards for the final touchdown. Rendina finished with 86 yards on seven carries, and Luter had 78 on three. When the third-string convoy averages 26 yards a trip, the depot is in good order.

Now the numbers, filed properly. Army ran 60 times for 479 yards, eight yards a carry. Army threw two passes. Two. Hellums completed one of them for two yards to Howard, which is still a completion on half his throws, and I will hear no criticism of it. The Black Knights went 4-for-4 on fourth down, committed zero turnovers, drew only two penalties for 20 yards, and did not punt until midway through the fourth quarter. The punter showed up, filled out his paperwork and went home with clean cleats.

To be fair to our guests, Veltkamp threw for 318 yards and three touchdowns, and Easton Messer caught 14 passes. FAU matched Army's first two touchdowns. After that, the Owls ran into the supply chain, and the supply chain does not negotiate.

Part 2: Deployment Orders, Army at Tulsa

Friday night, 8:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2, Army (4-2, 3-1 American) visits Tulsa (4-3) at Skelly Field at H. A. Chapman Stadium. It is a short week, a road trip and a night game. I have packed three clipboards.

The Inventory

My call: Army Black Knights 28, Tulsa Golden Hurricane 24.
