articles.title: Checkered Flag at Last: Charlotte Took Its First Win in Philadelphia, Takes an Open Week to Refuel, Then Welcomes a Tulane Offense That's Last in FBS at Holding the Ball
articles.byline: Priya Halloran, The Charlotte Fanatic
articles.matchup: Charlotte (1-6): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Tulane (3-3) at Charlotte, Fri., Oct. 30, 7 p.m. ET, Jerry Richardson Stadium, Charlotte
articles.text:
Hi, friends. Priya Halloran here, color-coded spreadsheet open, pit-crew headset on, writing from the Queen City. I track Charlotte football the way a NASCAR crew chief tracks a race: lap by lap, tire by tire, with a stopwatch in one hand and a highlighter in the other. And for six weeks this fall, every row in my spreadsheet had the same word in the last column.

Not anymore. Saturday in Philadelphia, the 49ers took the checkered flag. Let's review the race, honestly. Then let's talk about the open week, because Charlotte does not play this Saturday, and about the next race on the schedule: Tulane, at home, on a Friday night.

Part 1: Charlotte 38, Temple 31, and the First Checkered Flag

On Oct. 17 at Lincoln Financial Field, Conner Harrell threw for two touchdowns and ran for two more, and Charlotte beat Temple 38-31 for its first win of the season.

It was a door-to-door race. Khamani Alexander scored from a yard out in the first quarter. Temple answered on a 21-yard Keveun Mason run, and Ajani Sheppard's 7-yard run put the Owls up 14-7 at halftime. Then Harrell took over the third quarter: a 24-yard touchdown pass to Derrick Eley and an 8-yard touchdown run. Sheppard broke a 44-yarder to tie it 21-21 heading to the fourth.

The fourth quarter was pure short-track racing. Harrell hit Gus McGee for a 9-yard touchdown, Temple tied it on a 4-yard pass to Peter Clarke, and Harrell ran in from 10 yards to make it 35-28 with 8:40 left. Then Aiden Bui hit a career-long 47-yard field goal with 1:48 to play for a 38-28 lead. Temple kicked a short field goal with 48 seconds left, and the onside kick didn't come back to the Owls. Checkered flag.

My lap chart. Harrell completed 23 of 31 passes for 281 yards with no interceptions. Henry Rutledge ran 17 times for 123 yards, including a 48-yard burst. Eley caught six passes for 96 yards. Charlotte gained 449 yards, held the ball for 32:49, and went 6-for-10 on third down. And the 49ers committed just three penalties for 11 yards. That's a clean pit stop, friends.

Now, honest data: Temple gained 455 yards and ran for 206 at 6.1 per carry. Sheppard ran for 70 yards and two scores on seven carries and threw for 236. The defense still has work to do.

The Open Week, and the Season So Far

Charlotte has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. A refuel, and the 49ers have earned it.

I'll be straight about the season. Charlotte is 1-6 and 1-2 in the American. The first six races were rough: a 43-41 loss to The Citadel, a 41-9 loss at Ole Miss, a 26-21 loss at App State, a 34-7 loss to Louisiana, a 59-8 loss to Memphis and a 50-10 loss at North Texas. Charlotte allows 40.6 points per game and scores 19.1. Those numbers don't hide. But in the last race, Harrell produced 38 points. A crew chief notices a lap time like that.

Part 2: Tulane at Charlotte, Friday, Oct. 30

Next up: Tulane (3-3, 1-1 American) at Jerry Richardson Stadium, Friday, Oct. 30, at 7 p.m. Eastern, per ESPN. A Friday night race under the lights.

Tulane's Car

Tulane just beat Memphis 31-17 by forcing six turnovers, and I'll give the Green Wave defense full credit. Its red zone defense ranks fifth in FBS, allowing scores on 65.4 of every 100 trips, and it holds opponents to 21.7 points per game, 50th.

Where Tulane Runs Out of Fuel

Now look under the hood. Per the AP's preview of Tulane's game this week, the Green Wave are last in FBS in time of possession, at 26:20 per game. Tulane's offense averages 332.0 yards per game, 116th, and 20.5 points per game, 117th. Against Memphis, it went three-and-out on its first three drives, with freshman Trace Johnson making his first start, and converted 4 of 16 third downs.

And the Tulane defense allows 212.5 rushing yards per game, 133rd in FBS, with opponents converting 45.6 of every 100 third downs, 124th. Rutledge just ran for 123 yards. My highlighter is ready.

Tulane does have a big game before ours: UTSA on Saturday. Then a short week and a trip to Charlotte on Friday. Friends, a pit crew loves a car that just ran a hard race and is coming in on short rest.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists Tulane ahead 2-0: 34-3 in Charlotte in 2024 and 27-0 in New Orleans last season. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. It's the reason my spreadsheet has a whole tab called "Payback."

Town Report: Charlotte vs. New Orleans

Charlotte. The Queen City had 874,579 people at the 2020 census and is named for Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, queen consort of Great Britain and Ireland from 1761. Charlotte is home to the NASCAR Hall of Fame, and Wikipedia says about three of every four of the NASCAR industry's race teams, employees and drivers are based nearby. Charlotte Motor Speedway is just up the road in Concord. We also have the Billy Graham Library, the U.S. National Whitewater Center, the Mint Museum, the Carolina Panthers and the Charlotte Hornets.

And here's my go-to piece of local history. In 1799, in nearby Cabarrus County, 12-year-old Conrad Reed found a 17-pound rock that his family used as a doorstop. It turned out to be nearly solid gold. Per Wikipedia, it was the first documented gold find of any consequence in the United States, and it set off the nation's first gold rush. So when you call our team the 49ers, friends, remember that this area had a gold rush half a century before California did. Many more veins of gold turned up around here through the 19th century, and in 1837 the federal government opened the Charlotte Mint. Gold country, friends. Gold country.

Our stadium, Jerry Richardson Stadium, is a 15,314-seat horseshoe on campus. It hosted its first game on Aug. 31, 2013, a Charlotte win over Campbell, in the program's very first season.

New Orleans. New Orleans is a wonderful city with beautiful music and the beignets at Café du Monde. But consider the nicknames. Wikipedia says "the Big Easy" may "possibly" refer to musicians finding work easily there. Possibly. A city that's not sure where its own nickname came from.

And Tulane football spent nearly 40 seasons playing indoors at the Superdome before moving back to campus in 2014. Four decades with a roof. Friends, we race outdoors in the Carolinas, rain or shine. And Tulane's old wave mascot, per Wikipedia, was nicknamed "Gumby" by fans. I have no further questions.

The Pit Stop

Here's the plan for the open week: refuel, heal up, study the Tulane film. Here's the plan for Friday: run Rutledge at the 133rd-ranked run defense, keep Harrell clean and turnover-free, and make Tulane's offense, the shortest-possession offense in FBS, try to keep up.

And one more note for the crew: Charlotte has scored 48 points in its last two games combined, 38 of them last Saturday. The arrow on my spreadsheet finally points up. A race team doesn't need to win every lap. It needs to keep getting faster.

One checkered flag down. Let's go get another.

articles.title: Hoist the Colors, Pack the Tricorn: ECU Sails Into Memphis Seeking a Fourth Straight Win Over a Tiger That Commutes in an Air-Conditioned Trailer
articles.byline: Bartholomew 'Bart' Quidley, The East Carolina Fanatic
articles.matchup: East Carolina (3-3) at Memphis (5-2), Thu., Oct. 22, 7:30 p.m. ET, Simmons Bank Liberty Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Ahoy from Pitt County, mateys. Bart Quidley here, reporting from the same tailgate spot my family has held since before I could walk, with a purple tricorn hat on the seat beside me. I only wear it for big games. I have been staring at it all week. It's coming to Memphis.

East Carolina fans are, arrr-guably, the best fans anywhere. We needed every one of them last Thursday. So let's do this the honest way: first the storm we sailed through in Birmingham, then the voyage to the Mississippi River. Hoist the colors.

Part 1: Lost at Sea in Overtime, UAB 30, East Carolina 17

For three quarters and change, it was a pirate's dream. The Pirates opened the game on Oct. 15 with a 14-play, 75-yard drive, and Emory Williams flipped a 3-yard touchdown to Ray Ray Joseph Jr. for a 7-0 lead. Forty-seven seconds into the second quarter, Williams hit Ismael Smith Flores on a 16-yard pass, the ball came loose at the goal, and Dawson Quarterman fell on it in the end zone. Touchdown, ECU, 14-0. I'll take a treasure chest however it washes ashore.

UAB answered only with Jonah Delange field goals, from 41, 26 and 50 yards, and Noah Perez hit a career-long 43-yarder with 9:24 left to make it 17-9. The Blazers had not scored a touchdown all night. I had the tricorn halfway onto my head.

Then the wind turned. UAB quarterback Ryder Burton drove the Blazers 93 yards in 10 plays without a timeout and hit Bam McReynolds for a 17-yard touchdown with 35 seconds left. Burton ran in the two-point try. Seventeen all. In overtime, Burton threw a 6-yard touchdown to Rod Robinson II, and on our possession Delvon Gulley intercepted Williams and went 80 yards the other way. Final: UAB 30, East Carolina 17.

There is no hiding the box score, and Bart doesn't hide things. Williams finished 18 of 27 for 126 yards, two touchdowns and the interception. TJ Engleman Jr. carried 26 times for 104 yards, a real workhorse night, and Ashton Levells-Mitchell led the defense with six tackles. The defense held UAB without a touchdown for 59 minutes and 25 seconds. That deserves a cheer from the crow's nest. It just needed 35 more seconds.

We're 3-3 and 1-1 in the American. The season has had squalls, a 48-10 loss at Alabama and a 27-24 loss to App State, and fair winds, too: a 20-17 win at Old Dominion, a 42-9 win over North Carolina Central and a 28-12 win over Rice. A short week and a road game. Pirates were built for this.

Part 2: Sailing for the Bluff City

Thursday night, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2, East Carolina (3-3) visits Memphis (5-2, 2-1 American) at Simmons Bank Liberty Stadium.

Respect for the Tigers' Big Guns

I'll be gracious, because pirates have a code. The Memphis offense is a man-of-war. It averages 512.6 yards per game, sixth in FBS, with 237.7 rushing yards (eighth) and 274.9 passing yards (25th). Marcus Stokes has thrown for 1,841 yards and 18 touchdowns, Jaylin Carter has 780 rushing yards and eight scores, and Hunter Tipton has 380 receiving yards and five touchdowns. That is a lot of cannon.

But Have You Seen the Hull?

Now look at what happened last Friday night in New Orleans. Tulane forced six turnovers in a 31-17 win over Memphis. Six. TJ Smith returned an interception 76 yards for a touchdown on the last play of the first half, and Kevin Adams III picked off another late to seal it. AP noted Tulane had forced one turnover in its first five games combined. Then Memphis handed over a half-dozen in one night. Mateys, that's not a ship. That's a treasure chest with the lid propped open.

The Memphis defense allows 372.4 yards per game (89th) and 172.9 rushing yards per game (104th). That's a happy port for Engleman. If ECU can run the ball the way it did in Birmingham, the Pirates can keep the Tigers' man-of-war anchored on the sideline.

Our Own Repairs, Logged Honestly

I won't pretend our ship is seaworthy everywhere. ECU converts 31.3 of every 100 third downs, 125th in FBS, and scores on 73.7 of every 100 red zone trips, also 125th. We average 26:57 of possession, 132nd. Memphis's red zone defense ranks sixth. Those numbers have to change on Thursday, or the Tigers will play keep-away.

But here's the good news from the lookout. Our defense allows 326.5 yards per game, 38th in FBS, and 187.5 passing yards per game, 34th. For 59 minutes and 25 seconds last week, it didn't allow a touchdown. That defense is the keel of this ship.

The Treasure Map

CollegeFootballData.com lists East Carolina ahead 18-8 in this series. ECU won 30-29 at Memphis in 2021, 47-45 in Greenville in 2022 and 31-27 in Greenville last season. That's three straight, mateys. Our colors have been flying over this matchup since 2021, and I intend to fly them again.

Mascot Costume Review

I grade every opposing mascot's costume, and fairness is the pirate's code. Memphis has Pouncer, a costumed tiger, and a solid effort: good stripes, nice posture, a B-plus. Memphis also has TOM, a live Bengal tiger tradition that dates to 1972. Wikipedia reports that TOM attended home games in a special soundproof, air-conditioned trailer. A soundproof, air-conditioned trailer, mateys! Our PeeDee the Pirate walks into Dowdy-Ficklen on his own two boots, in the North Carolina heat, and he's never once asked for a climate-controlled carriage.

Port Report: Greenville vs. Memphis

Greenville. Our home port sits on the Tar River, 87,521 strong at the 2020 census and growing. It's the health, entertainment and educational hub of North Carolina's Coastal Plain. Dowdy-Ficklen Stadium holds 51,000, and on Sept. 3, 2022, 51,711 of us packed it for NC State. The field is Bagwell Field. The stadium opened in 1963 with a win over Wake Forest, with 10,000 seats. We've been adding seats ever since because the crew keeps growing.

And here's my go-to bit of local history. For more than a century, Greenville was known for its tobacco market and "a small state-supported college," founded as East Carolina Teacher's Training School. The athletic teams were once called the Teachers. Then they changed it to the Pirates. Mateys, we went from grading papers to raiding ships. That's the greatest glow-up in college sports.

Memphis. Memphis is a big, proud river city, 633,104 strong at the 2020 census, with Beale Street, Sun Studio and the Stax Museum of American Soul Music. It hosts the World Championship Barbecue Cooking Contest, which Guinness lists as the largest pork barbecue contest in the world. I respect a city that cooks.

But I have a few questions for the harbormaster. Memphis has a pyramid. A pyramid, mateys, on the Mississippi River in Tennessee. It's one of the city's listed landmarks. I've sailed a lot of rivers in my imagination, and I've never seen a pharaoh come up one.

And the Tigers' stadium was built in 1965 on the old Mid-South Fairgrounds, next to an amusement park called Libertyland that has since been demolished. So the Tigers play next to a former amusement park, which explains last Friday. Six turnovers. That was a roller coaster.

Weigh Anchor

Here's the voyage plan. Run Engleman. Win third down. Protect the ball, because the Memphis defense needs gifts, and Tulane proved it will take them. Make Stokes earn every yard against a pass defense that ranks 34th. The Tigers have the bigger cannons. We have the streak, the hat and a crew that never quits.

Hoist the colors, mateys. The tricorn is packed.

My call: Memphis Tigers 33, East Carolina Pirates 21.

articles.title: Owls vs. Owls, and Only One Flock Can Throw: FAU Paddles Back Out After an Army Wipeout to Host a Rice Offense Averaging 79.7 Passing Yards
articles.byline: Kaia Brightwater, The Florida Atlantic Fanatic
articles.matchup: Rice (1-6) at Florida Atlantic (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Flagler Credit Union Stadium, ESPNU
articles.text:
Hey, babe. Kaia Brightwater here, sunglasses on, wax on the board, coming to you from Boca Raton, where the sand is soft, the sun is loyal and the Owls' passing game is the cleanest set of waves on the Atlantic coast. I read offenses like swell reports. Clean, choppy or closeout. And last Saturday, at West Point, the surf report was not great.

So this week we're doing two things. First, an honest wipeout review, because a surfer who won't watch her own tape stays a beginner forever. Then we paddle back out at home against the other Owls. Yes, babe. It's Owls vs. Owls. Only one flock gets to fly.

Part 1: The Wipeout Review, Army 56, Florida Atlantic 24

Let's be real. Army beat FAU 56-24 on Oct. 17 at Michie Stadium, and the Black Knights scored touchdowns on their first seven possessions. Seven. I've seen gentler sets during hurricane season.

It started with a closeout. On the very first snap, Army's Elijah Walton intercepted Caden Veltkamp. On the next snap, Samari Howard ran 30 yards for a touchdown. Then Cale Hellums went 58 yards for another. Army ran 60 times for 479 yards, and Hellums alone had 25 carries, 195 yards and five touchdowns. The Black Knights threw two passes. Two. That's not an offense, babe. That's a riptide. You just get pulled out.

But here's the thing about surfers: we find the good waves even on a bad day. Veltkamp answered both early Army scores. He hit Easton Messer for a 24-yard touchdown and Kelby Valsin for a 34-yarder, and it was 14-14 in the first quarter. Veltkamp finished 33 of 48 for 318 yards and three touchdowns, with a late 19-yard score to Tucker Holloway. Messer caught 14 passes for 102 yards. Valsin had seven for 89. Collin Rogers hit a 41-yard field goal. FAU went 10-for-14 on third down and 2-for-2 on fourth.

The honest part: three turnovers, two lost fumbles and that first-snap interception, against a team that doesn't give you the ball back. And Army ran for eight yards a carry. That's the stuff we fix before we paddle out, not the stuff we cry about on the beach.

FAU is 4-2 and 1-1 in the American. The season so far: a 66-21 loss at Florida, then wins over Navy 38-30, Florida International 16-10, at UL Monroe 45-17 and over Texas Southern 66-10. Then the Army wave. Paddle back out.

Part 2: Rice at Florida Atlantic

Saturday at noon Eastern on ESPNU, at Flagler Credit Union Stadium. Owls (1-6, 0-3 American) at Owls (4-2, 1-1). Bring sunscreen. It's a noon kickoff in Boca in October, and I don't make the rules.

Our Swell Report

The FAU passing game is clean, glassy and well-formed. FAU throws for 307.3 yards per game, ninth in FBS, and scores 35.0 points per game. On third down, the Owls convert 53.1 of every 100, ninth in the country. Veltkamp has 1,743 yards, 15 touchdowns and three interceptions, and he completes 72.1 of every 100 throws. Valsin leads the receivers with 47 catches for 601 yards and six touchdowns, and Ethan Ervin leads the run game with 361 yards.

My honest notes, because I don't post filtered photos of my stats. The FAU defense allows 416.5 yards per game, 120th in FBS, and 218.2 rushing yards per game, 134th. Army found that out. Rice will try to find it, too.

The Other Owls' Swell Report

Rice runs the ball. A lot. The Rice offense averages 238.9 rushing yards per game, seventh in FBS, and Jacurri Brown is the whole break: 668 rushing yards and six touchdowns. Last week at home against Tulsa he ran for 154 yards, with touchdown runs of 50 and 78 yards. That's a real wave, babe. Respect.

Now look at the rest of the forecast. Rice throws for 79.7 yards per game, 136th in FBS. Brown completed two of six passes against Tulsa for 47 yards, and for the season he completes 48.2 of every 100 throws. Rice scores 17.0 points per game, 131st, and 318.6 yards per game, 124th. After its two long touchdown runs last week, Rice did not score for the final 40 minutes and 59 seconds. That's not a swell. That's flat water. You can't surf flat water, babe. You can only float.

And the Rice turnover margin is minus-6, 126th in FBS. FAU is plus-2.

The Matchup in Surf Terms

This game is about one thing: can our run defense stand up on Rice's one big wave? If FAU stops Brown, Rice has to throw, and Rice throwing is a closeout at low tide. If Brown breaks contain, it gets choppy.

On the other side, Rice's pass defense is decent, allowing 188.7 yards per game, 36th, but it gives up 42.6 of every 100 third downs, 108th. Veltkamp on third down has been our best set all year. Keep the chains moving, babe.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has this one even at 3-3. FAU won 17-14 at home in 2022, Rice won 24-21 in Houston in 2023, and FAU won 27-21 at Rice last year. Even series. Home water. Our tide.

Postcard From Paradise: Boca Raton vs. Houston

Boca Raton. We're a beach city of 97,422 at the 2020 census, 45 miles north of Miami. Boca is, in its present form, mostly the creation of architect Addison Mizner, who started in the 1920s and gave the city its Mediterranean Revival and Spanish Colonial Revival look. In 1925 he announced Boca would be "the foremost resort city on the North American continent." Big talk. We've been living up to it ever since. Boca is also the birthplace of IBM's first personal computer, back in the 1980s, so yes, babe, the beach town invented your laptop's great-grandpa.

The name comes from old maritime language: "boca" meant mouth, as in an inlet on a sailor's map. Our stadium, Flagler Credit Union Stadium, opened in 2011 and hosts the Boca Raton Bowl every December. The playing surface is Howard Schnellenberger Field, named for the founding coach who built FAU football from scratch starting in 2001.

Houston. Houston is huge, babe. It's the fourth-most populous city in the country, 2.3 million at the 2020 census, and the city sprawls over 640.4 square miles. That's not a city. That's a weather system. It's also the largest city in America without formal zoning, which explains a lot about the drive from the airport.

Its climate is humid subtropical, and Wikipedia says summer mornings average a relative humidity above 90 on a scale that tops out at 100. Babe, in Boca we call humidity "the ocean breeze." In Houston, they call it the air.

And the other Owls' band, the Marching Owl Band, also known as the MOB, is a scatter band. Wikipedia says its members do not march. A marching band that doesn't march. That's a surfer who doesn't get wet, and I love them for it, but it's a choice.

Dropping In

Here's the plan. Stop Brown, and the Rice offense goes flat. Keep Veltkamp upright, keep the ball out of the other Owls' talons and let Valsin and Messer ride the clean water on third down. Home crowd. Noon sun. One flock flies.

Surf's up on tempo, babe.

My call: Florida Atlantic Owls 33, Rice Owls 24.

The playing surface is Howard Schnellenberger Field, named for the founding coach who built FAU football from scratch starting in 2001.

Houston. Houston is huge, babe. It's the fourth-most populous city in the country, 2.3 million at the 2020 census, and the city sprawls over 640.4 square miles. That's not a city. That's a weather system. It's also the largest city in America without formal zoning, which explains a lot about the drive from the airport.

Its climate is humid subtropical, and Wikipedia says summer mornings average a relative humidity above 90 on a scale that tops out at 100. Babe, in Boca we call humidity "the ocean breeze." In Houston, they call it the air.

And the other Owls' band, the Marching Owl Band, also known as the MOB, is a scatter band. Wikipedia says its members do not march. A marching band that doesn't march. That's a surfer who doesn't get wet, and I love them for it, but it's a choice.
Dropping In

Here's the plan. Stop Brown, and the Rice offense goes flat. Keep Veltkamp upright, keep the ball out of the other Owls' talons and let Valsin and Messer ride the clean water on third down. Home crowd. Noon sun. One flock flies.
Surf's up on tempo, babe.
My call: Florida Atlantic Owls 33, Rice Owls 24.

articles.title: Six Turnovers Was the Wrong Song: Memphis Gets Its Groove Back Thursday Against a Pirate Crew That Docks on the Tar River
articles.byline: Otis Delaney-Crum, The Memphis Fanatic
articles.matchup: East Carolina (3-3) at Memphis (5-2), Thu., Oct. 22, 7:30 p.m. ET, Simmons Bank Liberty Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Well, good evening, Bluff City. Otis Delaney-Crum here, guitar on my knee, a plate of dry-rub ribs at my elbow and a bassline in my chest that has not been right since Friday night. Football and music are the same thing to me. A good drive has a backbeat. A good defense keeps time. And last Friday in New Orleans, friends, the whole band dropped its instruments.

So here's the set list. First, the blues, because Memphis invented the blues and we know how to sing them honest. Then, the comeback number: Thursday night at the Liberty Bowl against East Carolina. Go Tigers Go.

Part 1: The Blues in B-Flat, Tulane 31, Memphis 17

Let me play it straight. Memphis turned the ball over six times at Tulane on Oct. 16 and lost 31-17. Six. AP pointed out that the Green Wave had forced one turnover in its first five games combined. Then we gave them six in one night. That's not a slump, friends. That's a donation.

And it started with a groove. Philippe Laforge hit a 44-yard field goal on our first possession, and early in the second quarter Marcus Stokes threw a short pass to Stonka Burnside, who turned it into a 76-yard touchdown. Memphis led 10-3. I hummed my riff. My neighbor asked me to stop. I did not stop.

Then the record skipped. Tulane's Cooper Helmke kicked field goals from 56, 40 and 29 yards, and the Green Wave recovered a fumble at midfield that set up Trace Johnson's 38-yard touchdown to Destyn Hill. On the final play of the first half, TJ Smith returned an interception 76 yards for a touchdown. Tulane led 23-10 at halftime.

To their credit, the Tigers kept playing. Stokes found Jemyri Davis for a 6-yard touchdown with 3:34 left to cut it to 23-17, and the defense got the ball back. But Kevin Adams III intercepted Stokes again, and Johnnie Daniels ran 48 yards on fourth-and-1 to put it away.

The box score has some good notes in it. Stokes threw for 306 yards and two touchdowns. Burnside caught seven passes for 151 yards. Jaylin Carter ran 23 times for 135 yards. Mike Montgomery made 10 tackles. When you out-gain a team and lose by 14, the song isn't wrong. The tempo is. Hold the ball, and this band plays the hits.

We're 5-2 and 2-1 in the American, with wins at UNLV, over Arkansas State and UT Martin, a 59-8 win at Charlotte and a 38-13 win over UAB. The only other loss came 38-20 at Boise State, the No. 21 team in the country. Nobody's canceling the tour.

Part 2: The Comeback Number, East Carolina at Memphis

Thursday night, 7:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2, at Simmons Bank Liberty Stadium. Short week. Home crowd. Friends, that's a revival meeting.

The Memphis Rhythm Section

When it holds the ball, this offense swings. Memphis averages 512.6 yards per game, sixth in FBS. It runs for 237.7 (eighth) and throws for 274.9 (25th). That's a full band, horns and drums. Stokes has 1,841 passing yards, 18 touchdowns and six interceptions. Carter has 780 rushing yards and eight touchdowns. Hunter Tipton has 22 catches for 380 yards and five touchdowns.

And the defense does its best work when it matters. Opponents convert only 31.5 of every 100 third downs against Memphis, 20th in FBS, and our red zone defense ranks sixth, allowing scores on 66.7 of every 100 trips. The Tigers are disciplined, too, at 44.3 penalty yards a game, 22nd.

The Pirates' Sheet Music

I'll be fair to the visitors, because the blues teaches respect. East Carolina's defense is legit. It allows 326.5 yards per game (38th) and 187.5 passing yards per game (34th). Last Thursday it held UAB without a touchdown until 35 seconds were left in regulation.

But listen to the Pirate offense, and the tempo drags. ECU averages 339.5 yards per game, 112th in FBS, and 183.7 passing yards, 114th. It converts 31.3 of every 100 third downs, 125th, and scores on 73.7 of every 100 red zone trips, also 125th. It holds the ball 26:57 a game, 132nd. Friends, that's a band that shows up, plays two verses and goes home before the chorus.

And last week? ECU led UAB 17-9 with under 10 minutes to go, gave up a 93-yard drive in the final minute, then lost in overtime when Delvon Gulley returned an interception 80 yards. TJ Engleman Jr. is a real back, with 490 rushing yards on the season, and our run defense has to tighten its strings. But Emory Williams threw for 126 yards. On the soul scale, that's a hum, not a holler.

The Fight Song Soul Scale

I rank everything the visitors sing on my soul scale, one to ten. I'm told Pirate fans like to greet each other with "Arrr." That's not a song. That's the sound a man makes when he lifts a cooler. I'll give it a four for enthusiasm. Our "Go Tigers Go" has a backbeat you can feel in your shoes.

The Honest Verse

CollegeFootballData.com has East Carolina ahead 18-8 in this series, and the Pirates have won the last three: 30-29 here in 2021, 47-45 in Greenville in 2022 and 31-27 in Greenville last year. I don't hide a sour note. I play through it. Thursday, it's time to change the key.

Two Towns, One Jukebox: Memphis vs. Greenville

Memphis. We sit on the Chickasaw Bluffs above the Mississippi River, 633,104 strong at the 2020 census. Beale Street is a national historic landmark and the heart of the Memphis blues. Sam Phillips's Sun Studio still stands and is open for tours. Stax Records built a 1960s soul sound that Wikipedia calls much grittier and more horn-based than Detroit's Motown. Graceland is here. And every May we host the World Championship Barbecue Cooking Contest, which Guinness lists as the largest pork barbecue contest on the planet. Friends, when Memphis cooks, the whole world brings a plate.

Our stadium opened in 1965 as Memphis Memorial Stadium, dedicated to Memphians who served their country. It hosts the Liberty Bowl and the Southern Heritage Classic. That's a stage with history.

Greenville. Now, Greenville, North Carolina, is a pleasant town of 87,521, on the Tar River. Wikipedia says that for more than a century it was known as "an important tobacco market and the home of a small state-supported college." That's the whole album, friends. One single and a B-side.

And that small college started as a teacher training school, and the teams were called the Teachers. Then they changed it to the Pirates. I respect a reinvention; Memphis musicians do it every decade. But I have never in my life seen a pirate ship on the Tar River. I've seen plenty of steamboats on the Mississippi. On the Tar River, I believe the pirates take a canoe.

The Last Verse

Here's the arrangement. Hold the football. That's the whole song. If Memphis protects the ball, its offense ranks sixth in the country, and ECU's offense can't keep up with a full band. Run Carter, find Burnside and Tipton, and let the defense handle third down the way it has all year.

Get to the Liberty Bowl early, fire up the smoker and bring your loudest Go Tigers Go. That drive is going to have a backbeat.

My call: Memphis Tigers 33, East Carolina Pirates 21.

articles.title: Steady as She Goes, Then Hard to Port: Navy Lost a Four-Point Shootout in the Alamodome and Now Hosts a Mean Green Air Show That Ranks Second in the Nation in Passing
articles.byline: Cmdr. (Ret.) Annabel Merriweather, The Navy Fanatic
articles.matchup: North Texas (4-2) at Navy (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium, CBS Sports Network
articles.text:
Good morning, shipmates. Commander Annabel Merriweather, retired, reporting from the seawall in Annapolis with a thermos of coffee, a pair of binoculars and a logbook that has recorded every Navy kickoff for longer than I'll admit in print. I write my game notes like a ship's log: time, heading, sea state, and an honest account of anything that went over the side.

This week's log has two entries. First, a hard-fought loss in San Antonio that I'll record truthfully, because a log that hides the bad watches isn't a log, it's a brochure. Then a homecoming of sorts: North Texas sails up the Chesapeake on Saturday, and I have some thoughts about the Mean Green, their passing game and their hometown.

Part 1: Log Entry, UTSA 38, Navy 34

Sea state on Oct. 17 at the Alamodome: rough, with waves of points from both sides.

Navy came out at full speed. Jackson Gutierrez ran in from 2 yards in the first quarter and from 5 yards early in the second, and Navy led 14-0. Then UTSA's Owen McCown found the range: a 46-yard touchdown to Mekhi Anderson, a 14-yarder to Brandon Young Jr., and A'Marion Peterson's 1-yard run put the Roadrunners ahead 21-14. Gutierrez answered with a 25-yard touchdown pass to Jordan Collins just before halftime.

Early in the fourth quarter came the moment I'll keep in the log for years. Gutierrez found Collins for a 92-yard touchdown, and Navy led 27-24. UTSA answered with Will Henderson III's 31-yard run. Navy answered right back, and Braxton Woodson scored from 7 yards to make it 34-31 with 4:50 left. Then McCown drove UTSA 75 yards in six plays and hit Peterson for a 41-yard touchdown with 2:24 to go. Navy's last series ended on downs.

The honest accounting. Navy ran for 294 yards on 48 carries, 6.1 per carry. Gutierrez ran 21 times for 139 yards and two touchdowns and threw for 120 yards and two more on just three completions. Collins caught two passes for 117 yards. Woodson ran five times for 73 yards and even threw a 63-yard completion. And Navy did not turn the ball over.

The bad watch: McCown completed 28 of 38 for 359 yards and three touchdowns, and Navy allowed UTSA to convert twice on fourth down. That's how you lose a four-point game. It was also, per the AP, the first time the two programs had ever met, and I'd like a rematch at a time and place of my choosing.

Navy is 2-4, 1-3 in the American. The losses: 38-30 at Florida Atlantic, 24-20 at UAB, 14-9 at Air Force and this one. Four road losses by a combined 21 points. Not one of them a blowout. The wins: Towson 42-15 and Tulsa 34-26, both at home. Which brings me to the good news. We're coming home.

Part 2: North Texas at Navy

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium in Annapolis, on CBS Sports Network. North Texas (4-2, 2-0 American) at Navy (2-4, 1-3).

Our Heading

Navy runs the ball. Navy averages 297.8 rushing yards per game, fourth in FBS. Gutierrez has more than 640 rushing yards and nine touchdowns on 123 carries, and he has thrown for 559 yards and six touchdowns with just one interception. Collins has five catches all season for 189 yards and three touchdowns. That's nearly 38 yards a catch. When Navy throws, it throws to win the watch.

The defense has a strength, too. Navy allows 98.8 rushing yards per game, 21st in FBS. And Navy commits only 45 penalty yards per game, 24th. Discipline, shipmates. It's in the uniform.

The Weather Report

Here's the storm coming over the horizon. North Texas averages 533.8 yards per game, third in FBS, 347 passing yards per game, second, and 42.2 points per game, fifth. Tayven Jackson has thrown for 1,868 yards, 15 touchdowns and four interceptions, completing 72.2 of every 100 passes. Jahiem White has run for 687 yards and nine touchdowns. Justin Stevenson has 33 catches for 453 yards and five scores.

I'll log the honest concern. Navy allows 247.7 passing yards per game, 113th, and opponents convert 44.6 of every 100 third downs, 121st. And Navy's turnover margin is minus-6, 126th.

Where the Mean Green Takes On Water

Every ship has a leak. North Texas allows 29.2 points per game, 113th in FBS, and 355.8 yards per game, 70th. Its rush defense allows 142.7 per game, 73rd. Navy runs the ball for nearly 300 a game. Do the navigation, shipmates. That's a heading.

North Texas also commits 70.2 penalty yards per game, 115th in FBS. Navy commits 45. I've seen tidier decks on a fishing trawler.

And the Mean Green's resume has a few soft ports. They beat Houston Christian 63-14 and UNLV 44-6, and they beat Charlotte 50-10 on Oct. 10, a team that was winless at the time. Against Indiana, they lost 52-16. At Texas State, they lost 49-35. North Texas took last weekend off. Navy took the weekend to play a four-point thriller on the road. Ask yourself which crew is sea-tested.

The Chart: Series History

CollegeFootballData.com lists Navy ahead 2-1. Navy won 74-62 in Denton in 2007, a game that produced 136 points and, I assume, a severe shortage of scoreboard light bulbs. Navy won 27-24 in Annapolis in 2023. North Texas won 31-17 in Denton last year. Navy is 1-0 against North Texas in Annapolis, and I intend to keep that record spotless.

Port Report: Annapolis vs. Denton

Annapolis. Annapolis is the capital of Maryland, a city of 40,812 at the 2020 census, sitting on the Chesapeake Bay at the mouth of the Severn River. It was the temporary capital of the United States in 1783 and 1784, and it was in the Maryland State House, the oldest state house in continuous legislative use in the country, that George Washington resigned his commission as commander of the Continental Army. That State House is topped by the largest wooden dome built without nails in the country. They knew how to build things here.

Annapolis is known as "America's Sailing Capital" and hosts the Annapolis Sailboat Show, the largest in-water sailboat show in the world. The Naval Academy, established in 1845, sits right next to the city limits. Our stadium, Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium, opened in 1959 with a 29-2 win over William & Mary, and it is a memorial to everyone who has served in the Navy and Marine Corps, with thousands of memorial plaques. You do not walk into that place casually. You walk in grateful.

Denton. Denton is a fine college town of 139,869 people at the 2020 census. Wikipedia lists it as the 10th-most populous city in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex. Tenth. In its own metro. Annapolis is first in all of Maryland at being the capital, and we didn't need a population count to do it.

Denton is proud of its music scene and its University of North Texas College of Music, the first school to offer a degree in jazz studies. I respect that. But I note that Denton also claims the largest community garden in the nation, the 14.5-acre Shiloh Field Community Garden. Shipmates, we have the Chesapeake Bay. They have a very large vegetable patch. Lovely tomatoes, I'm sure.

Final Entry

The orders are simple. Run the ball at a defense ranked 73rd against the run. Keep Jackson on the sideline by holding the ball. Win third down on defense, which hasn't happened often enough this year, and protect the football. Do that at home, in front of the Brigade, and this log gets a happy entry.

I'll be honest, as always: the forecast doesn't favor us. But a forecast is just a forecast. The sea decides.

Steady as she goes.

My call: North Texas Mean Green 34, Navy Midshipmen 30.

And the Mean Green's resume has a few soft ports. They beat Houston Christian 63-14 and UNLV 44-6, and they beat Charlotte 50-10 on Oct. 10, a team that was winless at the time. Against Indiana, they lost 52-16. At Texas State, they lost 49-35. North Texas took last weekend off. Navy took the weekend to play a four-point thriller on the road. Ask yourself which crew is sea-tested.
The Chart: Series History

CollegeFootballData.com lists Navy ahead 2-1. Navy won 74-62 in Denton in 2007, a game that produced 136 points and, I assume, a severe shortage of scoreboard light bulbs. Navy won 27-24 in Annapolis in 2023. North Texas won 31-17 in Denton last year. Navy is 1-0 against North Texas in Annapolis, and I intend to keep that record spotless.
Port Report: Annapolis vs. Denton

Annapolis. Annapolis is the capital of Maryland, a city of 40,812 at the 2020 census, sitting on the Chesapeake Bay at the mouth of the Severn River. It was the temporary capital of the United States in 1783 and 1784, and it was in the Maryland State House, the oldest state house in continuous legislative use in the country, that George Washington resigned his commission as commander of the Continental Army. Annapolis is known as "America's Sailing Capital" and hosts the Annapolis Sailboat Show, the largest in-water sailboat show in the world. The Naval Academy, established in 1845, sits right next to the city limits. Our stadium, Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium, opened in 1959 with a 29-2 win over William & Mary, and it is a memorial to everyone who has served in the Navy and Marine Corps, with thousands of memorial plaques. You do not walk into that place casually. You walk in grateful.

Denton. Denton is a fine college town of 139,869 people at the 2020 census. Wikipedia lists it as the 10th-most populous city in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex. Tenth. In its own metro. Annapolis is first in all of Maryland at being the capital, and we didn't need a population count to do it.

Denton is proud of its music scene and its University of North Texas College of Music, the first school to offer a degree in jazz studies. I respect that. But I note that Denton also claims the largest community garden in the nation, the 14.5-acre Shiloh Field Community Garden. Shipmates, we have the Chesapeake Bay. They have a very large vegetable patch. Lovely tomatoes, I'm sure.
Final Entry

The orders are simple. Run the ball at a defense ranked 73rd against the run. Keep Jackson on the sideline by holding the ball. Win third down on defense, which hasn't happened often enough this year, and protect the football. Do that at home, in front of the Brigade, and this log gets a happy entry.
I'll be honest, as always: the forecast doesn't favor us. But a forecast is just a forecast. The sea decides.
Steady as she goes.
My call: North Texas Mean Green 34, Navy Midshipmen 30.

articles.title: An Open Week, Then a Drum Solo on the Chesapeake: North Texas Brings the Nation's Second-Best Passing Attack to Annapolis, a Capital the Country Moved Out of in Nine Months
articles.byline: Grady Mayhew-Ochoa, The North Texas Fanatic
articles.matchup: North Texas (4-2) at Navy (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium, CBS Sports Network
articles.text:
Mean Green, baby. Grady Mayhew-Ochoa here, sticks in my back pocket, brushes on the snare, coming to you from a back booth on the Denton Square. I'm a jazz drummer. I hear football in time signatures. Most offenses play in four-four: run, run, pass, punt. The North Texas offense plays in seven-eight, the kind of time that makes defensive coordinators count on their fingers and still come in a beat late.

Two notes before the downbeat. First, North Texas did not play last Saturday. It was an open week, honest and simple, so my game review is the last time the band was on stage, Oct. 10 against Charlotte. Second, the next gig is on the road, in Annapolis, against a Navy team that plays in a very different key.

Part 1: The Last Set, North Texas 50, Charlotte 10

The open week came after a rout. On Oct. 10 at DATCU Stadium, Tayven Jackson threw five touchdown passes, a personal best for the second straight game, and North Texas beat Charlotte 50-10.

Listen to the arrangement. Dominic De Freitas opened with a 26-yard field goal. Then Jackson hit Justin Stevenson for a 5-yard touchdown. In the second quarter it turned into a solo: a 12-yard touchdown to Kyle Koch, a 75-yard bomb to Baron Tipton, a safety, a 61-yard Jahiem White touchdown run and a 20-yard touchdown to Max Reese with 20 seconds left in the half. The halftime score was 40-10. Jackson's fifth touchdown, 34 yards to Stevenson, made it 47-10 in the third quarter, and he sat for the fourth.

Jackson finished 24 of 31 for 349 yards, five touchdowns and no interceptions. White ran 12 times for 105 yards. Stevenson, a senior transfer from Wyoming, caught nine passes for 122 yards and two scores, his second straight two-touchdown game. North Texas gained 580 yards and didn't turn the ball over. On defense, Davion Rhodes had two sacks, and CJ Coombes and Tyson Wilson each made an interception.

Honest critique from the drum chair: Charlotte hit a 75-yard touchdown pass on the play right after we scored. That's a dropped beat. And North Texas went 5-for-14 on third down. The band was loud but not always tight.

So far the season reads like a setlist. A 52-16 loss at Indiana. A 44-6 win over UNLV. A 49-35 loss at Texas State. A 63-14 win over Houston Christian. A 45-44 overtime win at Tulsa on Oct. 2. Then Charlotte. North Texas is 4-2 and 2-0 in the American.

Part 2: North Texas at Navy

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, on CBS Sports Network, at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium in Annapolis. North Texas (4-2, 2-0) at Navy (2-4, 1-3).

Our Band

North Texas averages 533.8 yards per game, third in FBS. It throws for 347 yards per game, second in the nation, and scores 42.2 points per game, fifth. Jackson has thrown for 1,868 yards, 15 touchdowns and four interceptions, completing 72.2 of every 100 passes. White has 687 rushing yards and nine touchdowns on 96 carries. Stevenson leads the receivers with 33 catches for 453 yards and five touchdowns.

The band converts 48.8 of every 100 third downs, 21st, and scores on 93.9 of every 100 red zone trips, 16th. It holds the ball for 33:00 per game, 17th. The Mean Green don't just play fast. They hold the stage.

Navy's Key Signature

Navy plays the ballad. One note, played forever, with feeling. The Midshipmen run for 297.8 yards per game, fourth in FBS, and throw for 115.5, 134th. Jackson Gutierrez has more than 640 rushing yards and nine touchdowns. That's a real groove, and their defense stops the run, too, allowing just 98.8 yards per game, 21st.

But the pass defense? Navy allows 247.7 passing yards per game, 113th in FBS. Opponents convert 44.6 of every 100 third downs, 121st. And opponents score on 87.5 of every 100 red zone trips, 95th. Against the second-best passing offense in the country, that's a drummer who forgot his sticks.

Navy's turnover margin is minus-6, 126th. North Texas is plus-2, 47th.

The Honest Part of the Chart

My music teacher said honest players get more gigs, so here's the note. North Texas allows 29.2 points per game, 113th in FBS, and 142.7 rushing yards per game, 73rd. Navy will run, and run, and run. And North Texas commits 70.2 penalty yards per game, 115th. Rushing the tempo is how you lose a song. Stay in the pocket, fellas.

Navy has also been close in every loss. It lost by four last week at UTSA. It lost by five at Air Force, four at UAB and eight at Florida Atlantic. Navy plays a long, slow song, and it's still on its feet at the final note.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists Navy ahead 2-1 in the series. Navy won 74-62 in Denton in 2007, a game with 136 points, which is basically free jazz. Navy won 27-24 in Annapolis in 2023. North Texas won 31-17 in Denton last season. Time to even the record.

Tour Notes: Denton vs. Annapolis

Denton. Denton is a city of 139,869 at the 2020 census, at the north end of the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex on Interstate 35, and Wikipedia says it's known for its active music scene. Wikipedia says its big annual events, including the North Texas State Fair and Rodeo and the Denton Arts and Jazz Festival, draw more than 300,000 people to town every year. The University of North Texas College of Music was the first school to offer a degree in jazz studies. Yes, baby. Jazz studies as a college degree started right here. This is my kind of town. Since 1976, the Denton Community Band and Jazz Ensemble has been playing local concerts and holiday festivals, too.

Our stadium has its own sound, too. DATCU Stadium opened in 2011 and was the first newly built stadium to achieve LEED Platinum certification. It has a giant eagle wing in the end zone facing the freeway, and a scale-replica cannon named "Boomer" that fires every time the team scores. Against Charlotte, Boomer got a workout. And the school shares its nickname with the most famous Mean Green of all, Pro Football Hall of Famer "Mean" Joe Greene.

Annapolis. Annapolis is the capital of Maryland and a very handsome harbor town of 40,812. It was also the capital of the United States for a while. Congress was in session in the Maryland State House from Nov. 26, 1783, to Aug. 19, 1784. Less than nine months. Baby, I've had gigs with a longer run than that. The whole country came to Annapolis, looked around and moved out before the end of the next summer.

Annapolis calls itself "America's Sailing Capital" and hosts the world's largest in-water sailboat show. That's beautiful. But a sailboat only goes where the wind sends it. North Texas brings its own wind.

The Closing Number

Here's the arrangement. Throw early. Let Jackson attack a pass defense ranked 113th. Make Navy chase the score so it can't play the slow song. Tackle Gutierrez, cut the penalties, and don't hand the Midshipmen the extra possessions they need.

Count it off. Seven-eight time, baby.

My call: North Texas Mean Green 34, Navy Midshipmen 30.

articles.title: N Equals Six, and Six Says Even: Rice's Clinical-Trial Ground Game Visits a Boca Defense Ranked 134th Against the Run
articles.byline: Odalys Chen-Moreau, The Rice Fanatic
articles.matchup: Rice (1-6) at Florida Atlantic (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 12 p.m. ET, Flagler Credit Union Stadium, ESPNU
articles.text:
Good morning from the Rice campus, where the live oaks are shady, the lab coffee is strong and I'm wearing my stats-cop badge on my lanyard. Odalys Chen-Moreau, bioengineering Ph.D., reporting for duty. I model football like a clinical trial. I want a hypothesis, a control group and a sample size large enough to mean something. And whenever someone on the internet declares a team "finished" after one bad quarter, I say the same thing: N equals too small.

This week's protocol has two phases. Phase one: the results from our 38-17 loss to Tulsa, reported honestly, because suppressing negative data is a crime against science. Phase two: an Owls-on-Owls road trial in Boca Raton, where the defense has a very interesting weakness.

Part 1: Trial Results, Tulsa 38, Rice 17

Let me start with the positive findings, because they were spectacular. Jacurri Brown ran 50 yards for a touchdown in the first quarter on Oct. 17. Tommy Bauchiero added a 32-yard field goal. Then, after Tulsa scored, Brown went 78 yards for another touchdown. Rice led 17-7 early in the second quarter. Brown finished with 154 rushing yards on 11 carries, tying a career high. That's 14 yards a carry. In my field, a result that large gets you the front page of a journal.

Rice ran for 289 yards on 54 carries. Defensive data, also encouraging: Austin Harnetiaux and Stone Combs each made 10 tackles, and Harnetiaux added a sack.

Now the negative findings, which I will not bury in a supplementary appendix. Tulsa scored 21 points in the second quarter, two of the touchdowns on short throws from Baylor Hayes, and led 21-17 at halftime. Rice was shut out for the final 40 minutes and 59 seconds. Brown completed two of six passes for 47 yards. Tulsa out-gained us 401-351, and Hayes went 20 of 27 for 249 yards and three touchdowns without a turnover.

So, the conclusion. The run game works. The passing game is, statistically speaking, a pilot study. We are 1-6 and 0-3 in the American. That record includes a 52-0 loss at Notre Dame, which is a perfectly valid data point that I acknowledge exists. It also includes a 16-14 loss to UTSA and a 28-21 loss to Western Michigan. Two of our losses were by one score, and N is still too small to write the obituary. Seven games is a pilot study, not a peer-reviewed conclusion, and I will not let anyone publish early.

Part 2: The Road Trial, Rice at Florida Atlantic

Saturday at noon Eastern on ESPNU, Rice (1-6) visits Florida Atlantic (4-2, 1-1) at Flagler Credit Union Stadium in Boca Raton. Owls vs. Owls. I've prepared a control group: it's also Owls.

The Hypothesis

Here is my hypothesis, and it's a strong one. Rice runs for 238.9 yards per game, seventh in FBS. Florida Atlantic allows 218.2 rushing yards per game, 134th in FBS. FAU also allows 416.5 yards per game overall, 120th, and 31.5 points per game, 118th. Last week, Army ran for 479 yards against it. I'm not saying we'll do that. Army has a much larger sample of running plays than anyone. But the trend is not subtle.

Brown leads Rice with 668 rushing yards and six touchdowns on 118 carries, and he has 478 passing yards with three touchdowns. Tyvonn Byars and D'Andre Hardeman Jr. give the run game depth.

The Confounding Variables

A good scientist lists her confounders. The FAU passing game is real. FAU throws for 307.3 yards per game, ninth in FBS, and converts 53.1 of every 100 third downs, also ninth. Caden Veltkamp has 1,743 passing yards, 15 touchdowns and only three interceptions. Kelby Valsin has 47 catches for 601 yards. Our pass defense is respectable, 188.7 yards allowed per game, 36th, but our third-down defense allows 42.6 conversions for every 100 tries, 108th.

And our turnover margin is minus-6, 126th. That's a variable I'd like to control.

The Control I Like

Here's the part nobody talks about. FAU holds the ball 27:28 per game, 125th in FBS. Rice holds it 29:51. If we run the ball like the data says we can, Veltkamp spends long stretches of a hot Boca noon sitting on a bench. You cannot complete 72 of every 100 passes from a bench. I checked the literature.

FAU's red zone offense also ranks 91st, scoring on 82.6 of every 100 trips, while our red zone defense ranks 29th. When the field gets small, our defense gets smart.

Prior Studies

CollegeFootballData.com lists this series at 3-3, a perfectly balanced trial. FAU won 17-14 in 2022, Rice won 24-21 at home in 2023, and FAU won 27-21 in Houston last season. Six games, three each. A coin would be proud.

A Note on Small Samples

FAU fans will tell you their team is "back" after beating Texas Southern 66-10. Respectfully, N equals too small. That same FAU team lost 66-21 at Florida in the opener and 56-24 at Army last week. Sixty-six and 56. That's not a defense, that's a placebo.

Field Notes: Houston vs. Boca Raton

Houston. Our home is the fourth-most populous city in America, 2.3 million at the 2020 census, nicknamed the Bayou City and Space City. It's home to the Texas Medical Center, the world's largest concentration of healthcare and research institutions, which is where people like me get our coffee. NASA's Johnson Space Center, home of Mission Control, is here. And on Sept. 12, 1962, President John F. Kennedy stood in Rice Stadium, now First Community Stadium, built in 1950, and gave the "We choose to go to the Moon" speech. Our football stadium launched the most famous sentence of the space race. Name another stadium that can say that. I'll wait, and I'll time it.

We also have the Marching Owl Band, the MOB. Members do not march. They wear pinstriped suits and fedoras and play violins, a cello and occasionally a harp. It is the most well-designed experiment in college football.

Boca Raton. Boca is a beach city of 97,422 people at the 2020 census. In 1925, architect Addison Mizner announced it would be "the foremost resort city on the North American continent." Mizner also planned a main street called El Camino Real that would be 20 lanes wide. Twenty lanes. In a beach town. As a bioengineer, I have studied blood vessels with smarter traffic planning.

The name is a delight, too. Wikipedia says "boca" meant a mouth, as in an inlet on a sailor's map. And the meaning of "ratones," it says, "is less certain." A city that isn't sure what half its own name means. Please, Boca, run the study.

And Boca, Wikipedia notes, is "still centered around luxury beach culture" and "dotted by many malls." We have Mission Control. They have a mall. Both are excellent places to go when you need to buy something, but only one of them landed on the Moon.

Conclusion and Discussion

The data say Rice should run the ball, run it again and then run it once more for statistical significance. Control the clock, keep Veltkamp on the bench, finish drives, and don't hand the other Owls the ball. If the hypothesis holds, this is a much closer trial than the record suggests. If it doesn't, I'll report it honestly next Monday, with error bars.

Go Owls. The real ones.

My call: Florida Atlantic Owls 33, Rice Owls 24.

Our pass defense is respectable, 188.7 yards allowed per game, 36th, but our third-down defense allows 42.6 conversions for every 100 tries, 108th.
And our turnover margin is minus-6, 126th. That's a variable I'd like to control.
The Control I Like

Here's the part nobody talks about. FAU holds the ball 27:28 per game, 125th in FBS. Rice holds it 29:51. If we run the ball like the data says we can, Veltkamp spends long stretches of a hot Boca noon sitting on a bench. You cannot complete 72 of every 100 passes from a bench. I checked the literature.
FAU's red zone offense also ranks 91st, scoring on 82.6 of every 100 trips, while our red zone defense ranks 29th. When the field gets small, our defense gets smart.
Prior Studies

CollegeFootballData.com lists this series at 3-3, a perfectly balanced trial. FAU won 17-14 in 2022, Rice won 24-21 at home in 2023, and FAU won 27-21 in Houston last season. Six games, three each. A coin would be proud.
A Note on Small Samples

FAU fans will tell you their team is "back" after beating Texas Southern 66-10. Respectfully, N equals too small. That same FAU team lost 66-21 at Florida in the opener and 56-24 at Army last week. Sixty-six and 56. That's not a defense, that's a placebo.
Field Notes: Houston vs. Boca Raton

Houston. Our home is the fourth-most populous city in America, 2.3 million at the 2020 census, nicknamed the Bayou City and Space City. It's home to the Texas Medical Center, the world's largest concentration of healthcare and research institutions, which is where people like me get our coffee. NASA's Johnson Space Center, home of Mission Control, is here. And on Sept. 12, 1962, President John F. Kennedy stood in Rice Stadium, now First Community Stadium, built in 1950, and gave the "We choose to go to the Moon" speech. Our football stadium launched the most famous sentence of the space race. Name another stadium that can say that. I'll wait, and I'll time it.

We also have the Marching Owl Band, the MOB. Members do not march. They wear pinstriped suits and fedoras and play violins, a cello and occasionally a harp. It is the most well-designed experiment in college football.

Boca Raton. Boca is a beach city of 97,422 people at the 2020 census. In 1925, architect Addison Mizner announced it would be "the foremost resort city on the North American continent." Mizner also planned a main street called El Camino Real that would be 20 lanes wide. Twenty lanes. In a beach town. As a bioengineer, I have studied blood vessels with smarter traffic planning.

The name is a delight, too. Wikipedia says "boca" meant a mouth, as in an inlet on a sailor's map. And the meaning of "ratones," it says, "is less certain." A city that isn't sure what half its own name means. Please, Boca, run the study.

And Boca, Wikipedia notes, is "still centered around luxury beach culture" and "dotted by many malls." We have Mission Control. They have a mall. Both are excellent places to go when you need to buy something, but only one of them landed on the Moon.
Conclusion and Discussion

The data say Rice should run the ball, run it again and then run it once more for statistical significance. Control the clock, keep Veltkamp on the bench, finish drives, and don't hand the other Owls the ball. If the hypothesis holds, this is a much closer trial than the record suggests. If it doesn't, I'll report it honestly next Monday, with error bars.
Go Owls. The real ones.
My call: Florida Atlantic Owls 33, Rice Owls 24.

articles.title: Ninety-Six Yards to the Treasure: USF's Defense Plundered Kent State on Homecoming, the Bulls Drop Anchor for an Open Week, and UAB Sails Into Tampa on Halloween
articles.byline: Reina Valdés-Kowalski, The South Florida Fanatic
articles.matchup: South Florida (5-2): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: UAB (4-3) at South Florida, Sat., Oct. 31, time TBA, Raymond James Stadium, Tampa
articles.text:
Ahoy from Tampa Bay! Reina Valdés-Kowalski here, writing from a bench on Bayshore Boulevard with my Gasparilla beads still on from last January, because a true Tampa pirate never fully takes them off. I grade every USF game on one scale. Is it Pirate-approved, or does it walk the plank?

This week: a homecoming win that was half treasure and half shipwreck, an honest open week, and a Halloween visit from UAB. Hoist the colors.

Part 1: South Florida 29, Kent State 2

On Oct. 17 at Raymond James Stadium, USF beat Kent State 29-2 in front of an announced homecoming crowd of 31,384, and it snapped a two-game losing streak. The defense? Pirate-approved. The first-half offense? Let's talk.

Here's the treasure. Late in the first quarter, Kent State drove 77 yards in 14 plays, got stopped on downs at the 3, and then tackled D.J. Crowther in the end zone for a safety. So the Golden Flashes led 2-0. Then, in the second quarter, Kent State drove inside our 1 and tried a quarterback sneak on third-and-goal. Dru DeShields mishandled the snap, and defensive end C.J. Hicks scooped it up and ran 96 yards for a touchdown. Per WUSF, that was a school-record fumble return. Ninety-six yards, mateys. That's not a play. That's a voyage.

Nico Gramatica hit a 49-yard field goal with five seconds left in the half for a 10-2 lead. In the third quarter, backup quarterback Luke Kromenhoek capped a 15-play, 73-yard drive with a 1-yard touchdown. In the fourth, Michael Van Buren Jr. hit Cameron Seldon for a 36-yard touchdown. Gramatica added a 33-yarder, and the defense got a safety of its own with 11 seconds left.

The defense held Kent State to 228 yards and 1.8 yards per carry, and the Golden Flashes failed on all four of their fourth-down tries. Per WUSF, they had 31 yards of offense in the second half. Michael Williams II had a sack and a half. Van Buren went 22 of 27 for 193 yards.

Now the shipwreck part, and I'll be honest, because pirates keep a true log. Per WUSF, USF had only 107 yards of offense in the first half, and for the fourth straight game, the Bulls didn't score an offensive touchdown before halftime. USF finished with 271 yards and 78 rushing yards on 32 carries, against a Kent State defense that, WUSF noted, came in allowing 379 yards per game. That's not Pirate-approved. That walks the plank.

Overall, USF is 5-2 and 1-2 in the American. The Bulls beat Florida International 19-9, won 28-24 at Army, beat Delaware State 59-17, won 14-6 at Bowling Green, then lost 17-13 to Temple and 31-24 at UTSA before the Kent State win.

The Open Week

USF does not play this Saturday, Oct. 24. It's an open week. Drop anchor, mend the sails and find a first-half offense somewhere in the hold.

And honestly, the timing is good. USF has played seven straight weeks, including a Thursday road trip to UTSA on Oct. 8. A two-week gap gives this crew time to heal up and to look hard at why the offense keeps waking up only after halftime. Four straight games without a first-half offensive touchdown isn't bad luck, mateys. It's a pattern, and patterns can be fixed.

Part 2: UAB at South Florida, Saturday, Oct. 31

Next up: UAB (4-3, 2-1 American) at Raymond James Stadium on Halloween. ESPN lists the kickoff time as to be announced, so I won't guess.

Our Crew

Per ESPN's season numbers, the USF defense allows just 15.1 points per game. That's the treasure chest of this team. Van Buren has thrown for 1,266 yards and six touchdowns, completing 64.2 of every 100 passes. Crowther leads the run game with 518 yards and seven touchdowns. Bryson Rodgers has 30 catches for 334 yards. USF scores 26.6 points per game.

Their Crew

UAB is coming off a 30-17 overtime win over East Carolina on Oct. 15, a comeback after trailing 14-0. Ryder Burton led a 93-yard drive in the final minutes to tie it, then threw the overtime touchdown, and Delvon Gulley sealed it with an 80-yard interception return. Credit where it's due.

Burton has 1,184 passing yards, six touchdowns and five interceptions, completing 54.5 of every 100 passes. Rod Robinson II has 436 rushing yards, and CJ Smith has 19 catches for 350 yards. UAB's pass defense is stingy, allowing 126.0 yards per game, so this will be a ground war. And there, UAB is vulnerable: it allows 190.6 rushing yards per game. Crowther, sharpen your cutlass.

UAB's record has some barnacles, too. It lost 42-23 at Illinois, 21-14 at Louisiana and 38-13 at Memphis, and its wins came against UL Monroe, Navy, Samford and ECU, the Samford one being an FCS team. Five interceptions from the starting quarterback. Our defense will be waiting, matey.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists USF ahead 3-2. UAB won 22-19 in Tampa in 2003, USF won 45-20 at Legion Field in 2004, UAB won 56-35 in Birmingham in 2023, USF won 35-25 in Tampa in 2024, and USF won 48-18 at Protective Stadium last season. Two in a row. Let's make it three.

Town Report: Tampa vs. Birmingham

Tampa. Tampa had 403,364 people at the 2020 census, and the Tampa Bay metro area is the second-largest in Florida. Every year since 1904, with a few exceptions, Tampa has held the Gasparilla Pirate Festival, a friendly "invasion" by the crew of the mythical pirate José Gaspar. The crew sails across Tampa Bay on the Jose Gasparilla II, a 137-foot replica pirate ship, with hundreds of boats and a barrage of mini-cannons, and then there's a parade. A whole city that dresses like pirates on purpose. Pirate-approved.

Bayshore Boulevard has a six-mile continuous sidewalk, which Wikipedia calls the longest in the world. Ybor City is a National Historic Landmark district, built around the cigar factories that jump-started Tampa's growth in the 1880s. And our stadium, Raymond James, opened in 1998 with a replica pirate ship in the north end zone. We play college football next to a pirate ship. Beat that.

And the area has earned a nickname lately. After the Buccaneers won a Super Bowl at home and the Lightning won the 2021 Stanley Cup, Wikipedia says the region got called "Champa Bay." Champions, pirates and the world's longest sidewalk. Not bad for one bay.

Birmingham. Birmingham is a historic city, nicknamed "The Magic City" for its rapid industrial growth from 1881 to 1920, and it's home to the Vulcan statue, the largest cast iron statue in the world. I respect a city with a giant iron god on a hill. Truly.

But per Wikipedia, after the 2020 census, Birmingham lost its long-standing status as Alabama's largest city. Huntsville passed it. Huntsville! The Magic City got out-magicked by Huntsville. In Tampa, we didn't lose anything. We just keep adding pirates.

Final Plank

Here's the treasure map for Halloween. Score in the first half, for once. Run Crowther at a run defense that allows 190 yards per game. Let the defense hunt Burton, who's thrown five interceptions. And don't let UAB hang around, because the Blazers proved against ECU that they can come back.

Hoist the colors, Bulls. Pirate-approved.

articles.title: Yo, We Gotta Talk: Temple Lost a Fourth-Quarter Shootout to Charlotte, Takes the Week Off, Then Heads to Greenville, a Town That Moved Itself Three Miles Before It Settled Down
articles.byline: Teddy Fiorella, The Temple Fanatic
articles.matchup: Temple (2-5): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Temple at East Carolina, Sat., Oct. 31, time TBA, Dowdy-Ficklen Stadium, Greenville, N.C.
articles.text:
Yo. Teddy Fiorella here, writing from a corner booth in South Philly with a cheesesteak in one hand and my Temple scarf in the other. Cherry and white, born and raised. And I'm gonna be honest with you, because that's how we do it in this city. We don't sugarcoat. We don't spin. We tell you what happened, and then we tell you why next week is gonna be different.

What happened was Charlotte. Charlotte came into the Linc without a win, and Charlotte left with one. That's on us. So this week, we review it straight, we take our open week like grown-ups, and then we look at the next one: a trip to Greenville, N.C., on Halloween.

Part 1: Charlotte 38, Temple 31

On Oct. 17 at Lincoln Financial Field, Conner Harrell threw for two touchdowns and ran for two more, and Charlotte beat Temple 38-31 for its first win of the season. I'll say it once and I'll mean it: credit to the 49ers. They earned it.

Here's the good part, and there was plenty. Ajani Sheppard was electric. He threw for 236 yards and a touchdown and ran seven times for 70 yards and two touchdowns, including a 44-yard run that tied it 21-21 late in the third quarter. Peter Clarke caught five passes for 127 yards and a 4-yard touchdown that tied it again, 28-28, early in the fourth. Keveun Mason ran 13 times for 64 yards and a 21-yard touchdown in the first quarter. Temple led 14-7 at halftime, gained 455 yards, ran for 206 at 6.1 a carry and didn't turn the ball over.

Now the part that keeps me up. Harrell went 23 of 31 for 281 yards with no interceptions, and he scored on runs of 8 and 10 yards. Henry Rutledge ran for 123 yards. Charlotte held the ball for 32:49 and converted 6 of 10 third downs, and Temple went 0-for-2 on fourth down. Aiden Bui's career-long 47-yard field goal with 1:48 left made it 38-28. Carl Hardin's 28-yard field goal with 48 seconds left brought us within seven, but the onside kick didn't come back. Ballgame.

So here's the season, straight. Temple is 2-5 and 1-2 in the American. It beat Rhode Island 38-14 and won 17-13 at South Florida. It lost to Penn State 27-9, at Toledo 49-48, to Army 21-17, to UConn 34-20 and to Charlotte. That's three losses by one score, including one by a single point at Toledo. Yo, that's a lot of heartbreak in one sandwich.

And the defense? Curly Ordonez made eight tackles and a sack against Charlotte, and Avery Powell added six tackles. Those guys played hard. But this defense gave up 449 yards to a team that came in winless, and that can't happen again. The guys up front have to win on early downs so we're not chasing third-and-short all afternoon. I watched the third quarter through my fingers, and I'm a grown man.

The Open Week

Temple has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. Honest. Use it. Rest the legs, fix the run defense, and watch some East Carolina film. In Philly, we don't call it a week off. We call it a week of homework. And Temple has a lot of homework.

Part 2: Temple at East Carolina, Saturday, Oct. 31

Next up is a Halloween Saturday at Dowdy-Ficklen Stadium in Greenville, N.C. ESPN lists the kickoff time as to be announced, so I'm not gonna pretend to know it.

Our Guys

Per ESPN's season numbers, Temple averages 25.7 points per game and 385.7 yards per game, with 202.1 of those on the ground. Sheppard has thrown for 1,127 yards and eight touchdowns, and Mason leads the run game with 513 yards and three touchdowns on 94 carries. When this offense runs the ball, it moves.

The honest concern: the defense allows 28.0 points per game and 404.6 yards per game, including 238.7 through the air. That's gotta tighten up.

Their Guys

East Carolina is 3-3 and 1-1 in the American. It plays at Memphis on Thursday night, Oct. 22, then comes home to face us nine days later. ECU scores 23.5 points per game and gains 339.2 yards per game, both less than Temple. Emory Williams has thrown for 655 yards with seven touchdowns and two interceptions. TJ Engleman Jr. has 490 rushing yards. Ray Ray Joseph Jr. has 29 catches for 272 yards.

Their defense is solid, I'll admit it: 23.8 points and 326.3 yards allowed per game. But look at their last game. On Oct. 15 at UAB, the Pirates led 14-0 in the second quarter. Then UAB's Ryder Burton drove 93 yards in 10 plays and tied it with 35 seconds left, and the Blazers won 30-17 in overtime, the last points coming on an 80-yard interception return. That's a team that knows how to hold a lead about as well as I know how to hold a diet. And they'll have just played Memphis. Temple will have had two full weeks. Rested legs on Halloween, baby.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has East Carolina ahead 12-10 overall. And yeah, I know the recent history. ECU has won the last five, including 45-14 at the Linc last season. But before that, Temple won five straight, from 2015 through 2019, and three of those wins came in Greenville. We've done it down there before. We'll do it again.

Town Report: Philadelphia vs. Greenville

Philadelphia. Yo, where do I even start? Philadelphia is the sixth-most populous city in the country, with 1.60 million people at the 2020 census. The Declaration of Independence was adopted here on July 4, 1776. Philly served as the nation's first capital starting in 1775, and as the capital again on several more occasions until 1800. We have 67 National Historic Landmarks, including Independence Hall.

We have more murals than any other American city, thanks to the Mural Arts Program, which has funded more than 2,800 of them. The Philadelphia Museum of Art is one of the largest art museums in the world, and its front steps got kind of famous after a movie called Rocky in 1976. And the food? Hoagies, soft pretzels, water ice, Tastykakes, roast pork and the cheesesteak. Our home field, Lincoln Financial Field, opened in 2003 and seats 67,594. That's a real stadium in a real city.

Greenville. Greenville, N.C., is a nice college town of 87,521 people at the 2020 census, the 12th-most populous city in North Carolina. Twelfth. In its own state. Philadelphia is first in Pennsylvania and sixth in America.

And here's my go-to Greenville fact. The town was founded in 1771 as "Martinsborough," named after a royal governor. Then, in 1774, the whole town moved three miles west to the south bank of the Tar River. Then it changed its name to "Greenesville." Then it shortened that to Greenville. Yo, Greenville, choose a spot and a name and stick with it. We've been Philadelphia since the 1600s.

Final Word

So here's the deal. Take the open week. Get healthy. Run the ball with Mason and Sheppard, because this offense goes when the ground game goes. Make Williams beat us through the air. And on Halloween, go into Greenville and take one back.

Yo, that's Temple Made.

And the defense? Curly Ordonez made eight tackles and a sack against Charlotte, and Avery Powell added six tackles. Those guys played hard. But this defense gave up 449 yards to a team that came in winless, and that can't happen again. The guys up front have to win on early downs so we're not chasing third-and-short all afternoon. I watched the third quarter through my fingers, and I'm a grown man.
The Open Week

Temple has an open date this Saturday, Oct. 24. No game. Honest. Use it. Rest the legs, fix the run defense, and watch some East Carolina film. In Philly, we don't call it a week off. We call it a week of homework. And Temple has a lot of homework.
Part 2: Temple at East Carolina, Saturday, Oct. 31
Next up is a Halloween Saturday at Dowdy-Ficklen Stadium in Greenville, N.C. ESPN lists the kickoff time as to be announced, so I'm not gonna pretend to know it.
Our Guys

Per ESPN's season numbers, Temple averages 25.7 points per game and 385.7 yards per game, with 202.1 of those on the ground. Sheppard has thrown for 1,127 yards and eight touchdowns, and Mason leads the run game with 513 yards and three touchdowns on 94 carries. When this offense runs the ball, it moves.
The honest concern: the defense allows 28.0 points per game and 404.6 yards per game, including 238.7 through the air. That's gotta tighten up.
Their Guys

East Carolina is 3-3 and 1-1 in the American. It plays at Memphis on Thursday night, Oct. 22, then comes home to face us nine days later. ECU scores 23.5 points per game and gains 339.2 yards per game, both less than Temple. Emory Williams has thrown for 655 yards with seven touchdowns and two interceptions. TJ Engleman Jr. has 490 rushing yards. Ray Ray Joseph Jr. has 29 catches for 272 yards.

Their defense is solid, I'll admit it: 23.8 points and 326.3 yards allowed per game. But look at their last game. On Oct. 15 at UAB, the Pirates led 14-0 in the second quarter. Then UAB's Ryder Burton drove 93 yards in 10 plays and tied it with 35 seconds left, and the Blazers won 30-17 in overtime, the last points coming on an 80-yard interception return. That's a team that knows how to hold a lead about as well as I know how to hold a diet. And they'll have just played Memphis. Temple will have had two full weeks. Rested legs on Halloween, baby.
The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has East Carolina ahead 12-10 overall. And yeah, I know the recent history. ECU has won the last five, including 45-14 at the Linc last season. But before that, Temple won five straight, from 2015 through 2019, and three of those wins came in Greenville. We've done it down there before. We'll do it again.
Town Report: Philadelphia vs. Greenville

Philadelphia. Yo, where do I even start? Philadelphia is the sixth-most populous city in the country, with 1.60 million people at the 2020 census. The Declaration of Independence was adopted here on July 4, 1776. Philly served as the nation's first capital starting in 1775, and as the capital again on several more occasions until 1800. We have 67 National Historic Landmarks, including Independence Hall.

We have more murals than any other American city, thanks to the Mural Arts Program, which has funded more than 2,800 of them. The Philadelphia Museum of Art is one of the largest art museums in the world, and its front steps got kind of famous after a movie called Rocky in 1976. And the food? Hoagies, soft pretzels, water ice, Tastykakes, roast pork and the cheesesteak. Our home field, Lincoln Financial Field, opened in 2003 and seats 67,594. That's a real stadium in a real city.

Greenville. Greenville, N.C., is a nice college town of 87,521 people at the 2020 census, the 12th-most populous city in North Carolina. Twelfth. In its own state. Philadelphia is first in Pennsylvania and sixth in America.

And here's my go-to Greenville fact. The town was founded in 1771 as "Martinsborough," named after a royal governor. Then, in 1774, the whole town moved three miles west to the south bank of the Tar River. Then it changed its name to "Greenesville." Then it shortened that to Greenville. Yo, Greenville, choose a spot and a name and stick with it. We've been Philadelphia since the 1600s.
Final Word

So here's the deal. Take the open week. Get healthy. Run the ball with Mason and Sheppard, because this offense goes when the ground game goes. Make Williams beat us through the air. And on Halloween, go into Greenville and take one back.
Yo, that's Temple Made.
