articles.title: Six Takeaways and a Freshman Debut: Tulane Rolls Into a Saturday Night at Yulman Against a Roadrunner Defense Ranked 128th Against the Run, From a City That Keeps Its River in the Basement
articles.byline: Antoine 'Twan' Ducros-Labat, The Tulane Fanatic
articles.matchup: UTSA (6-1) at Tulane (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 8 p.m. ET, Yulman Stadium, ESPNU
articles.text:
Roll Wave! Antoine Ducros-Labat here, but everybody Uptown calls me Twan. I play trumpet in a brass band on the weekends, I keep powdered sugar on my good shirt from Café du Monde, and I rate every Tulane win like a bowl of gumbo. Some wins are thin. Some wins are a dark roux that took all afternoon. Friday night against Memphis? That was a roux you could stand a spoon in.

Here's the setlist for this week. First, the Memphis game, which I'll tell straight, warts and all. Then a Saturday night at Yulman against UTSA, a 6-1 team that I respect and that I would like to send back to San Antonio with a little humility and a box of pralines.

Part 1: Tulane 31, Memphis 17, and Six Takeaways

On Oct. 16 at Yulman Stadium, the Green Wave forced six turnovers. Six. Per the AP, Tulane had forced one turnover in its first five games combined. Then it got six in one night. That's not a gumbo. That's a whole crawfish boil.

And it came with a freshman quarterback, Trace Johnson, making his first collegiate start. I'll say it plainly: the offense went three-and-out on its first three drives. But redshirt freshman kicker Cooper Helmke made a 56-yard field goal to tie it 3-3 early in the second quarter. Memphis went ahead 10-3 on a short pass that Stonka Burnside turned into a 76-yard touchdown. Helmke answered from 40.

Then the Wave started taking the ball. After Tulane's third fumble recovery of the night set up a drive at midfield, Johnson threw a 38-yard touchdown to Destyn Hill for a 13-10 lead. Helmke added a 29-yarder. And on the final play of the first half, TJ Smith intercepted Marcus Stokes and ran it back 76 yards for a touchdown. Tulane led 23-10 at the break, and I hit a high note on the trumpet that I haven't hit since my cousin's wedding.

Memphis cut it to 23-17 with 3:34 left on a 6-yard touchdown pass to Jemyri Davis. Then, on fourth-and-1, Johnnie Daniels ran 48 yards for the touchdown with 1:34 left, and Johnson hit Hill on the two-point try. Kevin Adams III made two interceptions, the second one sealing it. Per the AP, it was Tulane's first six-turnover game since a 2013 win over Jackson State.

Now the honest part, because a gumbo critic has to taste everything. Memphis out-gained Tulane 488 to 325 and piled up 27 first downs to our 12. Tulane converted 4 of 16 third downs and had nine penalties for 80 yards. Johnson completed 11 of 21 passes for 165 yards with a touchdown and an interception. The defense and special teams carried that night. The offense brought the napkins.

Tulane is 3-3 and 1-1 in the American: losses at Duke 17-3, at Kansas State 31-20 and at Army 20-17, and wins over South Alabama 28-24, Southern Miss 24-21 and now Memphis. All three wins came at home. Hold that thought.

Part 2: UTSA at Tulane

Saturday, 8 p.m. Eastern, on ESPNU, at Yulman Stadium in Uptown New Orleans. UTSA (6-1, 3-0 American) at Tulane (3-3, 1-1).

The Roadrunners' Recipe

I'll give UTSA its flowers. Owen McCown completed 28 of 38 passes for 359 yards and three touchdowns last week against Navy, including the game-winner with 2:24 left. For the season he has 1,578 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and two interceptions, and UTSA's turnover margin is plus-4, 22nd in FBS. Will Henderson III leads the run game with 562 yards. UTSA scores 32.3 points per game, 49th.

Where the Roux Breaks

Now taste the defense. UTSA allows 199.9 rushing yards per game, 128th in FBS, and 400.0 yards per game overall, 112th. It allows 27.0 points per game, 100th. Navy ran for 294 yards on it last week. That's an open kitchen for Johnnie Daniels and Maurice Turner, who has 315 rushing yards on just 37 carries this season.

And UTSA averages 83.9 penalty yards per game, 134th in FBS. One hundred thirty-fourth. Out of 138 teams, cher. I've seen Mardi Gras parades hold formation with more discipline than that.

Our Honest Ingredients

Here's what Tulane has to fix. The Green Wave are last in FBS in time of possession, at 26:20 per game. The offense ranks 116th in yards, 332.0 per game, and 117th in scoring, 20.5 per game. The run defense allows 212.5 yards per game, 133rd, and opponents convert 45.6 of every 100 third downs, 124th. That's a pot that needs stirring.

But here's the spice. Tulane allows 21.7 points per game, 50th in FBS, despite all those yards, and its red zone defense ranks fifth in the country, allowing scores on only 65.4 of every 100 trips. Bend all you like, Roadrunners. The Wave doesn't break near the goal.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists UTSA ahead 2-1. UTSA won 10-7 in the Alamodome in 2013, Tulane won 29-16 at Yulman in 2023, and UTSA won 48-26 in San Antonio last season. Tulane is 1-0 against UTSA at Yulman. Let's keep the home kitchen clean.

Town Report: New Orleans vs. San Antonio

New Orleans. We are the Crescent City, named for the bend of the Mississippi River through town, and the Big Easy, a nickname Wikipedia says may come from early 20th-century musicians who found work easy to find here. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by French colonists, and it is known for its music, its Creole cuisine and Mardi Gras. The French Quarter holds Jackson Square, St. Louis Cathedral, Preservation Hall and the French Market, including Café du Monde, famous for café au lait and beignets. I'm a regular. The powdered sugar is a lifestyle.

Our stadium, Yulman, opened on Sept. 6, 2014, with a home opener against Georgia Tech, bringing Tulane football back to campus after nearly 40 seasons in the Superdome. And Tulane's first bowl win came in the very first Sugar Bowl, played in Tulane's own stadium. Sugar Bowl history started on our campus.

San Antonio. San Antonio is a big, lovely city, seventh-most populous in the country, with 1.43 million people at the 2020 census. Its Spanish mission was founded in 1718. Same year as New Orleans. Twins, cher. But one twin got the beignets.

The famous San Antonio River Walk, per Wikipedia, sits "one level down from the automobile street." San Antonio is so proud of its river that it put it in the basement. In New Orleans, the river is right there, wide as a parish, and we built the whole city around its curve.

And the Alamodome? It opened in 1993, and Wikipedia says the building was intended to attract a professional football franchise. Intended. That's a beignet stand with no powdered sugar, cher. Nice setup. Something's missing.

The Last Spoonful

The recipe Saturday is simple. Run the ball at the 128th-ranked run defense in the country, hold onto it, and shorten the game. Make McCown throw into a defense that just found its taste for takeaways. Get Helmke in range. Win at home, where all three wins came this year.

It'll be close. UTSA has won six of seven, and the Roadrunners have earned their record. But they haven't played in our kitchen this year, and a good roux always takes its time.

Roll Wave!

My call: Tulane Green Wave 27, UTSA Roadrunners 24.

articles.title: Gusher in Houston, Now Drill Army: Tulsa Hosts a Team That Threw Two Passes Last Week and a Town That Isn't Technically a Town
articles.byline: Wiley Pettibone, The Tulsa Fanatic
articles.matchup: Army (4-2) at Tulsa (4-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 8:30 p.m. ET, Skelly Field at H. A. Chapman Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Howdy from the Oil Capital of the World. Wiley Pettibone here, petroleum geology grad, Golden Hurricane lifer and the only man in Tulsa who reads a box score like a well log. Every good drive is a gusher. Every bad one is a dry well. And last Saturday in Houston, friends, the second quarter came in like Spindletop.

This week we've got two jobs on the rig. First, the core sample from our 38-17 win at Rice. Second, a Friday night date at Chapman Stadium with Army, a team that treats the forward pass the way I treat a dry hole: politely, and from a distance.

Part 1: The Core Sample, Tulsa 38, Rice 17

I'll be honest with you, because a geologist who fudges the readings gets people hurt. The first 19 minutes in Houston were a dry well. Rice quarterback Jacurri Brown ran 50 yards for a touchdown in the first quarter, Tommy Bauchiero kicked a field goal, and then Brown ran 78 yards for another score. Tulsa trailed 17-7 early in the second quarter, and I started checking the drilling permits.

Then the pressure built, the way it does. Damari Alston had already punched in a 4-yard run. Baylor Hayes hit Javon Ross for an 11-yard touchdown with 2:48 left in the half, then found Oran Singleton Jr. from 8 yards out with 33 seconds left. Twenty-one points in the second quarter, and a 21-17 halftime lead. That's not a drive, friends. That's a field coming in.

After that, the Rice offense never struck oil again. The Owls were shut out over the final 40 minutes and 59 seconds. Owen Carey hit a 35-yard field goal in the third, Hayes threw a 6-yard touchdown to Sevion Morrison early in the fourth, and Trequan Jones ran 45 yards for a score, with Hayes running in the two-point try, to make it 38-17.

The readings, filed properly: Hayes completed 20 of 27 passes for 249 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Singleton caught seven balls for 87 yards. Jones ran 12 times for 77 yards, and Alston added 52 and a touchdown. Tulsa had zero turnovers and out-gained Rice 401-351. Tyson Williams led the defense with 12 tackles. Brown ran for 154 yards, a career-high-tying day, and I'll tip my hard hat to him. But a quarterback who completes two of six passes is a one-pump operation, and our defense eventually capped the well.

Tulsa is 4-3, 1-2 in the American, and the season has had some real geology to it. We opened by beating Oklahoma State 24-10, which I will mention at every family reunion until the Lord calls me home. We lost a 45-44 heartbreaker to North Texas and dropped a 34-26 game at Navy. Now we've won two of three, and we get the other service academy at home.

Part 2: Army Comes to Chapman

Friday night, 8:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2. Army (4-2, 3-1 American) at Tulsa. Lights on, Route 66 out front, and a crowd that remembers last November.

What We Know About the Black Knights

I'll give the visitors their due, because Mama raised me to respect a hard worker. Army beat Florida Atlantic 56-24 last Saturday. Cale Hellums ran for 195 yards and five touchdowns. The Black Knights scored on their first seven possessions, ran for 479 yards and threw exactly two passes. Two. I have seen more forward passes at a church picnic.

Army leads FBS at 357.5 rushing yards per game and holds the ball 34:42 a game, third in the country. Hellums has 719 rushing yards and 13 rushing touchdowns. It's a slow, steady, deep-well operation, and it works.

Now let me tell you what the survey shows underneath. Army's defense allows 368.0 yards per game, 84th in FBS, and opponents convert 52.1 of every 100 third downs on it. That's 124th in the country. Friends, that's not a defense. That's a porous rock formation. Oil flows right through it.

The Matchup, Explained With Rocks

Our honest problem: Tulsa allows 191.6 rushing yards per game, 121st in FBS, and Army runs the ball more than anybody in the country. If the Black Knights get their convoy rolling, it'll be a long night of watching the clock drain like a tank with a leak.

Our honest advantage: Tulsa is plus-11 in turnover margin, third in FBS. This defense takes the ball away. When you play a team that runs 60 times a game, every carry is another chance for somebody in gold to rip it loose. One fumble against an option team is a gusher. Two is a boom town.

On offense, Hayes has 1,081 passing yards, eight touchdowns and one interception this year, and Singleton leads the team with 38 catches for 474 yards. Army's pass defense allows 220.0 yards per game, 87th. I like Hayes throwing into that formation.

The thing that has to change is third down. Tulsa converts 31.3 of every 100, 125th in FBS. Against a defense that lets opponents convert 52.1 of every 100, Friday is a chance to fix that reading for good. Stay on the field, keep Army's offense on the sideline, and make the cadets watch.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has Tulsa ahead 2-1 all-time. Tulsa won 49-39 at West Point in 2007. Army won 49-7 here in 2024, and I don't want to talk about it. And last November, Tulsa went to West Point and won 26-25. One point, on the road, against the academy. That one goes in the core library, labeled and sealed.

Town Report: Tulsa vs. "West Point"

Tulsa. We are a city of 413,066 people as of the 2020 census, and for most of the 20th century the whole world called us the Oil Capital of the World. That boom built a skyline full of Art Deco. We call ourselves the Birthplace of Route 66, and Chapman Stadium, which opened in 1930 as Skelly Field, sits right on it. Cain's Ballroom, built in 1924, is where Bob Wills popularized Western swing. The Gathering Place is a 66-acre park on the river with a boathouse, a skate park and trails. The Philbrook Museum of Art sits in an oil pioneer's old villa.

And we have the Golden Driller, a 76-foot, 43,500-pound statue of an oil worker in front of the Expo Center. The inscription at his base dedicates him to the men of the petroleum industry and credits what they built to "God's abundance." Amen to that. He has been the official state monument since 1979. You don't get a monument like that by throwing two passes a game.

West Point. Now, I love our troops, and I thank God for every one of them. But somebody has to read the survey on their hometown, and I've got the clipboard. West Point, New York, is not technically a town. It's a census-designated place inside the town of Highlands. The 2020 census counted 7,341 people. The Black Knights' entire hometown would fill about a quarter of Chapman Stadium, with room left over for the band.

West Point was picked because of an S-curve in the Hudson River, and during the Revolution they strung a great chain across that river to stop ships. Friends, that's a whole town built around a traffic jam. It's also where Benedict Arnold tried to hand the place to the British, which is the most famous thing to happen there that didn't involve a parade.

And the mascot. Army brings mules, a tradition that dates to 1899, chosen because mules hauled Army gear. A pack animal. We have a hurricane. I understand the hurricane is a little far from the ocean, and I've heard the jokes. But I'll take a storm over a cargo animal any Friday night.

Closing the Well

Here's my reading. Army is going to run the ball, and run it, and run it. We need to hit the rock hard, take the ball away when the chance comes, and let Hayes find Singleton when Army's defense creeps up. Win the turnovers. Win third down. Drill a gusher or two before halftime and make the cadets throw a third pass.

Come early, grab a seat on Route 66, and wave at the Golden Driller on the way in. He's been waiting since 1966. He can wait one more night for a win.

My call: Army Black Knights 28, Tulsa Golden Hurricane 24.

Then the pressure built, the way it does. Damari Alston had already punched in a 4-yard run. Baylor Hayes hit Javon Ross for an 11-yard touchdown with 2:48 left in the half, then found Oran Singleton Jr. from 8 yards out with 33 seconds left. Twenty-one points in the second quarter, and a 21-17 halftime lead. That's not a drive, friends. That's a field coming in.

After that, the Rice offense never struck oil again. The Owls were shut out over the final 40 minutes and 59 seconds. Owen Carey hit a 35-yard field goal in the third, Hayes threw a 6-yard touchdown to Sevion Morrison early in the fourth, and Trequan Jones ran 45 yards for a score, with Hayes running in the two-point try, to make it 38-17.

The readings, filed properly: Hayes completed 20 of 27 passes for 249 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Singleton caught seven balls for 87 yards. Jones ran 12 times for 77 yards, and Alston added 52 and a touchdown. Tulsa had zero turnovers and out-gained Rice 401-351. Tyson Williams led the defense with 12 tackles. Brown ran for 154 yards, a career-high-tying day, and I'll tip my hard hat to him. But a quarterback who completes two of six passes is a one-pump operation, and our defense eventually capped the well.

Tulsa is 4-3, 1-2 in the American, and the season has had some real geology to it. We opened by beating Oklahoma State 24-10, which I will mention at every family reunion until the Lord calls me home. We lost a 45-44 heartbreaker to North Texas and dropped a 34-26 game at Navy. Now we've won two of three, and we get the other service academy at home.
Part 2: Army Comes to Chapman
Friday night, 8:30 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN2. Army (4-2, 3-1 American) at Tulsa. Lights on, Route 66 out front, and a crowd that remembers last November.
What We Know About the Black Knights

I'll give the visitors their due, because Mama raised me to respect a hard worker. Army beat Florida Atlantic 56-24 last Saturday. Cale Hellums ran for 195 yards and five touchdowns. The Black Knights scored on their first seven possessions, ran for 479 yards and threw exactly two passes. Two. I have seen more forward passes at a church picnic.

Army leads FBS at 357.5 rushing yards per game and holds the ball 34:42 a game, third in the country. Hellums has 719 rushing yards and 13 rushing touchdowns. It's a slow, steady, deep-well operation, and it works.

Now let me tell you what the survey shows underneath. Army's defense allows 368.0 yards per game, 84th in FBS, and opponents convert 52.1 of every 100 third downs on it. That's 124th in the country. Friends, that's not a defense. That's a porous rock formation. Oil flows right through it.
The Matchup, Explained With Rocks

Our honest problem: Tulsa allows 191.6 rushing yards per game, 121st in FBS, and Army runs the ball more than anybody in the country. If the Black Knights get their convoy rolling, it'll be a long night of watching the clock drain like a tank with a leak.

Our honest advantage: Tulsa is plus-11 in turnover margin, third in FBS. This defense takes the ball away. When you play a team that runs 60 times a game, every carry is another chance for somebody in gold to rip it loose. One fumble against an option team is a gusher. Two is a boom town.

On offense, Hayes has 1,081 passing yards, eight touchdowns and one interception this year, and Singleton leads the team with 38 catches for 474 yards. Army's pass defense allows 220.0 yards per game, 87th. I like Hayes throwing into that formation.

The thing that has to change is third down. Tulsa converts 31.3 of every 100, 125th in FBS. Against a defense that lets opponents convert 52.1 of every 100, Friday is a chance to fix that reading for good. Stay on the field, keep Army's offense on the sideline, and make the cadets watch.
The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has Tulsa ahead 2-1 all-time. Tulsa won 49-39 at West Point in 2007. Army won 49-7 here in 2024, and I don't want to talk about it. And last November, Tulsa went to West Point and won 26-25. One point, on the road, against the academy. That one goes in the core library, labeled and sealed.
Town Report: Tulsa vs. "West Point"

Tulsa. We are a city of 413,066 people as of the 2020 census, and for most of the 20th century the whole world called us the Oil Capital of the World. That boom built a skyline full of Art Deco. We call ourselves the Birthplace of Route 66, and Chapman Stadium, which opened in 1930 as Skelly Field, sits right on it. Cain's Ballroom, built in 1924, is where Bob Wills popularized Western swing. The Gathering Place is a 66-acre park on the river with a boathouse, a skate park and trails. The Philbrook Museum of Art sits in an oil pioneer's old villa.

And we have the Golden Driller, a 76-foot, 43,500-pound statue of an oil worker in front of the Expo Center. The inscription at his base dedicates him to the men of the petroleum industry and credits what they built to "God's abundance." Amen to that. He has been the official state monument since 1979. You don't get a monument like that by throwing two passes a game.

West Point. Now, I love our troops, and I thank God for every one of them. But somebody has to read the survey on their hometown, and I've got the clipboard. West Point, New York, is not technically a town. It's a census-designated place inside the town of Highlands. The 2020 census counted 7,341 people. The Black Knights' entire hometown would fill about a quarter of Chapman Stadium, with room left over for the band.

West Point was picked because of an S-curve in the Hudson River, and during the Revolution they strung a great chain across that river to stop ships. Friends, that's a whole town built around a traffic jam. It's also where Benedict Arnold tried to hand the place to the British, which is the most famous thing to happen there that didn't involve a parade.

And the mascot. Army brings mules, a tradition that dates to 1899, chosen because mules hauled Army gear. A pack animal. We have a hurricane. I understand the hurricane is a little far from the ocean, and I've heard the jokes. But I'll take a storm over a cargo animal any Friday night.
Closing the Well

Here's my reading. Army is going to run the ball, and run it, and run it. We need to hit the rock hard, take the ball away when the chance comes, and let Hayes find Singleton when Army's defense creeps up. Win the turnovers. Win third down. Drill a gusher or two before halftime and make the cadets throw a third pass.
Come early, grab a seat on Route 66, and wave at the Golden Driller on the way in. He's been waiting since 1966. He can wait one more night for a win.
My call: Army Black Knights 28, Tulsa Golden Hurricane 24.

articles.title: Forged in the Fourth Quarter: UAB Came Back From 14-0 to Beat ECU in Overtime, Cools the Iron on an Open Week, Then Sails to Tampa to Face a Pirate Who Doesn't Technically Exist
articles.byline: Ozella Birchfield, The UAB Fanatic
articles.matchup: UAB (4-3): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: UAB at South Florida, Sat., Oct. 31, time TBA, Raymond James Stadium, Tampa
articles.text:
Good morrow, Blazers. Ozella Birchfield here, writing from a bench in the shadow of Vulcan himself, with a forge apron in my lap and a dog-eared copy of Shakespeare on the seat next to me. I believe in two things about football. One: a great team is forged, not given. Iron has to go through the fire before it becomes steel. Two: every season deserves a little drama, preferably in five acts.

Last Thursday night, UAB gave me all five acts in one game. Let me tell it honestly, from the opening scene to the curtain. Then we'll talk about this week, which is an open week, and the next act: a Halloween trip to Tampa.

Part 1: UAB 30, East Carolina 17 (OT)

Act One, Oct. 15 at Protective Stadium: the Pirates take the stage. East Carolina marched 75 yards in 14 plays on the opening drive, and Emory Williams threw a 3-yard touchdown to Ray Ray Joseph Jr. Early in the second quarter, Dawson Quarterman recovered a fumble in the end zone, and ECU led 14-0. I'll be honest. The iron was cold.

Act Two: the fire is lit. Jonah Delange kicked a 41-yard field goal before halftime, a 26-yarder in the third quarter and a 50-yarder with 1:26 left in the third. Three for three. ECU led just 14-9 heading into the fourth.

Act Three: the Pirates strike back. Noah Perez kicked a career-long 43-yard field goal with 9:24 left, and ECU led 17-9.

Act Four: the hammer falls. Ryder Burton took over at his own 7 and drove UAB 93 yards in 10 plays, without a timeout, and hit Bam McReynolds for a 17-yard touchdown with 35 seconds left. Then Burton ran in the two-point try himself. Seventeen all. Overtime. "Once more unto the breach, dear friends."

Act Five: the curtain. In overtime, Burton threw a 6-yard touchdown to Rod Robinson II. On ECU's possession, Delvon Gulley intercepted Williams and ran it back 80 yards for a touchdown. UAB 30, East Carolina 17. Forged, not given.

The stage notes. Burton finished 19 of 37 for 262 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions. CJ Smith caught eight passes for 119 yards. Jo'Tavion Pierce made 16 tackles and Muaaz Byard made 15, and UAB didn't turn the ball over.

Now the honest review, because a critic who only praises is no critic. UAB ran for just 99 yards on 32 carries. ECU held the ball for 34:11 and ran 50 times. UAB went 6-for-16 on third down and committed nine penalties for 76 yards. That's a lot of sparks flying in the wrong directions.

The Open Week

UAB does not play this Saturday, Oct. 24. After a Thursday game on Oct. 15, the Blazers get more than two weeks before their next kickoff. In the forge, we call this letting the steel temper. You heat it, you hammer it, and then you let it cool so it holds its shape.

UAB is 4-3 and 2-1 in the American. The Blazers lost 42-23 at Illinois, beat UL Monroe 26-20, lost 21-14 at Louisiana, beat Navy 24-20, beat Samford 33-14, lost 38-13 at Memphis and beat ECU. All four wins came at Protective Stadium. Now we take the fire on the road.

Part 2: UAB at South Florida, Saturday, Oct. 31

Next up is a Halloween Saturday at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa. ESPN lists the time as to be announced.

Our Blacksmiths

Per ESPN's season numbers, UAB allows only 126.0 passing yards per game, and 24.6 points per game overall. Burton has thrown for 1,184 yards and six touchdowns. Robinson leads the run game with 436 yards, and Smith has 19 catches for 350 yards, more than 18 yards a catch.

The honest concern: UAB allows 190.6 rushing yards per game, and Burton has thrown five interceptions. Those need fixing during the open week. The forge is hot, and there's time to hammer them out.

Their Pirates

South Florida is 5-2 and 1-2 in the American, and it's coming off a 29-2 homecoming win over Kent State. I'll grant the Bulls their defense, which allows 15.1 points per game per ESPN, and their defensive end C.J. Hicks, whose 96-yard fumble return set a school record, per WUSF.

But listen to the Bulls' own local reporters. Per WUSF, USF had only 107 yards of offense in the first half against Kent State, and it was the fourth straight game in which the Bulls failed to score an offensive touchdown in the first half. Four straight! "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark," and also in the first half in Tampa. USF also lost two straight before that, 17-13 at home to Temple and 31-24 at UTSA.

Michael Van Buren Jr. has 1,266 passing yards and six touchdowns, and D.J. Crowther has 518 rushing yards and seven touchdowns.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists South Florida ahead 3-2. UAB won 22-19 in Tampa in 2003 and 56-35 in Birmingham in 2023. USF won 45-20 at Legion Field in 2004, 35-25 in Tampa in 2024 and 48-18 in Birmingham last season. Revenge is a dish best served on Halloween.

Town Report: Birmingham vs. Tampa

Birmingham. They call us the Magic City, for the rapid industrial growth that built Birmingham from 1881 to 1920, and also the Pittsburgh of the South. Per Wikipedia, the Birmingham District is the only place in the world where significant amounts of iron ore, coal and limestone, the three main raw materials of steel, are all found close together. We were built to forge.

On Red Mountain stands Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and the forge, 56 feet tall and the largest cast iron statue in the world. He was Birmingham's entry for the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis, and today he stands on a 126-foot sandstone pedestal at the top of Red Mountain, looking out over the whole city like a coach watching practice. Sloss Furnaces is a National Historic Landmark. And Birmingham's history includes the Civil Rights Movement, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s Letter from Birmingham Jail and protests that helped lead to the Civil Rights Act of 1964. That's a city with a soul of iron. Our home field, Protective Stadium, opened downtown in 2021 and seats about 47,100.

Tampa. Tampa is a sunny city of 403,364, and I hear the beaches are pleasant. But consider its most famous party. Every year since 1904, give or take, Tampa holds the Gasparilla Pirate Festival, a "friendly invasion" by the crew of the pirate José Gaspar. And Wikipedia calls him a mythical pirate. Mythical! The whole city dresses up to celebrate a buccaneer who, per Wikipedia, was the stuff of legend. In Birmingham, our symbol is a 56-foot iron god, and you can go visit him.

And USF plays its home games in an NFL stadium with a replica pirate ship in the end zone. Ahoy. "All the world's a stage," and Tampa built a boat on it.

The Final Act

Here's the script for Halloween. Cool the iron this week, fix the run defense and protect the football. Then go to Tampa, make USF's first-half offense prove it exists, and let Burton and Smith work. UAB just showed it can come from 14 down. Let's not need to.

Forged, not given.

articles.title: Birds Up, Medals On: 6-1 UTSA Flies to New Orleans After a 2:24 Comeback, to Face a Green Wave That's Dead Last in FBS at Holding the Ball
articles.byline: Marisol Ybarra, The UTSA Fanatic
articles.matchup: UTSA (6-1) at Tulane (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 8 p.m. ET, Yulman Stadium, ESPNU
articles.text:
Birds up! Marisol Ybarra here, writing from a patio off the River Walk with a sash so loaded with Fiesta medals it jingles when I type. Every big UTSA win earns a medal on my sash. I had to sew on a second ribbon this season, and it's only October.

Let's do this the right way. First, Saturday night's 38-34 win over Navy, which had more twists than a Fiesta parade route. Then the trip to New Orleans, where a 3-3 Tulane team is waiting with a defense that just forced six turnovers and an offense that, frankly, can't keep the ball.

Part 1: UTSA 38, Navy 34, and a Medal Earned at 2:24

It did not start pretty. On Oct. 17 at the Alamodome, Navy's Jackson Gutierrez ran for touchdowns of 2 and 5 yards, and the Midshipmen led 14-0 early in the second quarter. I set my sash down. I did not take it off.

Then Owen McCown went to work. He hit Mekhi Anderson for a 46-yard touchdown, then Brandon Young Jr. for a 14-yarder, and A'Marion Peterson punched in a 1-yard run. UTSA scored 21 straight points and led 21-14. Navy got a touchdown back before halftime, and Michael Petro's 36-yard field goal made it 24-20 in the third.

The fourth quarter was a Battle of Flowers. Gutierrez threw a 92-yard touchdown to Jordan Collins, and Navy led 27-24. Will Henderson III answered with a 31-yard touchdown run. Navy answered back, with Braxton Woodson scoring from 7 yards to make it 34-31 with 4:50 to play.

And then, medal time. McCown led a six-play, 75-yard drive and hit Peterson for a 41-yard touchdown with 2:24 left. Navy's final series ended on downs. UTSA 38, Navy 34.

McCown finished 28 of 38 for 359 yards and three touchdowns, without an interception. David Amador II caught seven passes for 71 yards. Henderson ran for 78 yards. UTSA didn't turn it over and went 2-for-3 on fourth down. Per the AP, it was the first-ever game in the series. Navy, thank you for coming. Come back anytime.

The honest part, since a medal means nothing if you didn't earn it. Navy ran for 294 yards on 48 carries, 6.1 per carry, and UTSA committed seven penalties for 60 yards. You don't get to give up nearly 300 rushing yards every week and still wear the sash.

UTSA is 6-1 and 3-0 in the American. The wins: UT Rio Grande Valley 45-16, at Texas State 31-26, Colorado State 59-45, at Rice 16-14, South Florida 31-24 and Navy. The lone loss was 30-6 at Texas. Six medals. One week I'd rather forget.

Part 2: UTSA at Tulane

Saturday, 8 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, at Yulman Stadium in New Orleans. UTSA (6-1, 3-0) at Tulane (3-3, 1-1).

Our Parade

McCown has 1,578 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and just two interceptions, completing 69.5 of every 100 passes. Henderson leads the run game with 562 yards on 94 carries. DJ Allen Jr. has 24 catches for 325 yards. UTSA scores 32.3 points per game and gains 411.1 yards per game. And UTSA's turnover margin is plus-4, 22nd in FBS.

Tulane's Float

Let me be gracious first: Tulane's defense just forced six turnovers against Memphis, and it ranks fifth in FBS in red zone defense, allowing scores on 65.4 of every 100 trips. Kevin Adams III had two interceptions Friday. TJ Smith returned an interception 76 yards for a touchdown. Respect.

Now the parade route. Tulane's offense averages 332.0 yards per game, 116th in FBS, and 20.5 points per game, 117th. It throws for 179.7 yards per game, 116th. Against Memphis, it went three-and-out on its first three drives and converted 4 of 16 third downs, with freshman Trace Johnson making his first start.

And Tulane is last in FBS in time of possession. Last. 26:20 per game. That's not a parade, that's a drive-by. The Green Wave hold the ball like it's a hot tamale fresh off the comal. Drop it, blow on your fingers, pass it along.

Its run defense allows 212.5 yards per game, 133rd, and opponents convert 45.6 of every 100 third downs, 124th. Henderson and Peterson, put your dancing shoes on.

The Honest Part

Our defense gives up yards, too. UTSA allows 199.9 rushing yards per game, 128th, and 400.0 yards overall, 112th. And UTSA averages 83.9 penalty yards per game, 134th in FBS. I love a big parade, but even a parade has to stay on the route. Tighten it up, Birds.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists UTSA ahead 2-1. UTSA won 10-7 in the Alamodome in 2013, Tulane won 29-16 in New Orleans in 2023, and UTSA won 48-26 in San Antonio last season. That 2023 loss at Yulman is the one medal missing from my sash. Time to sew it on.

Town Report: San Antonio vs. New Orleans

San Antonio. San Antonio is the seventh-most populous city in America and the second-most in Texas, with 1.43 million people at the 2020 census. A Spanish mission and outpost was founded here in 1718, and in 1731 San Antonio became the first chartered civil settlement in present-day Texas. The city is home to five 18th-century Spanish frontier missions, including the Alamo, and together they were named UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2015.

Our River Walk winds one level below the streets, lined with restaurants and shops, and crucial funding came in 1939 from the Works Progress Administration, which built some 17,000 feet of walkways and about 20 bridges. And every April we throw Fiesta San Antonio, an annual festival since 1891 with more than 100 events and more than three million people taking part. That's where I get my medals.

Even our stadium story has a parade in it. The Alamodome opened in 1993, and when UTSA football played its first-ever game on Sept. 3, 2011, against Northeastern State, it drew 56,743 people, a record for a start-up FBS program, per Wikipedia. UTSA's first season averaged 35,521 at home, a record for a new program.

New Orleans. New Orleans is a beautiful city, and I mean that. But let's look at its nicknames. Wikipedia says "the Big Easy" is "possibly" a reference to how easy it was for musicians to find work. Possibly. A city that's not even sure where its own nickname came from. We know exactly where "Remember the Alamo" came from.

And Tulane's own mascot history is a delight. Riptide the Pelican debuted in 1998, but before that the school used an angry wave, which, per Wikipedia, fans nicknamed "Gumby." A wave. Named Gumby. The Roadrunner salutes you, Gumby, and then runs right past you.

The Final Float

The plan writes itself. Make Tulane's young quarterback throw. Run Henderson at a defense ranked 133rd against the run. Hold the ball, because the Green Wave can't. Don't hand Tulane's defense the takeaways it lives on, and stay out of the penalty-flag parade.

It'll be close in New Orleans. Both of our road wins this year, at Texas State and at Rice, came by five points or fewer, so this team knows how to win a tight one away from home. And I brought an extra ribbon, just in case.

Birds up!

My call: Tulane Green Wave 27, UTSA Roadrunners 24.

blocks.text: Birds up! Marisol Ybarra here, writing from a patio off the River Walk with a sash so loaded with Fiesta medals it jingles when I type. Every big UTSA win earns a medal on my sash. I had to sew on a second ribbon this season, and it's only October.

Let's do this the right way. First, Saturday night's 38-34 win over Navy, which had more twists than a Fiesta parade route. Then the trip to New Orleans, where a 3-3 Tulane team is waiting with a defense that just forced six turnovers and an offense that, frankly, can't keep the ball.
Part 1: UTSA 38, Navy 34, and a Medal Earned at 2:24

It did not start pretty. On Oct. 17 at the Alamodome, Navy's Jackson Gutierrez ran for touchdowns of 2 and 5 yards, and the Midshipmen led 14-0 early in the second quarter. I set my sash down. I did not take it off.

Then Owen McCown went to work. He hit Mekhi Anderson for a 46-yard touchdown, then Brandon Young Jr. for a 14-yarder, and A'Marion Peterson punched in a 1-yard run. UTSA scored 21 straight points and led 21-14. Navy got a touchdown back before halftime, and Michael Petro's 36-yard field goal made it 24-20 in the third.

The fourth quarter was a Battle of Flowers. Gutierrez threw a 92-yard touchdown to Jordan Collins, and Navy led 27-24. Will Henderson III answered with a 31-yard touchdown run. Navy answered back, with Braxton Woodson scoring from 7 yards to make it 34-31 with 4:50 to play.
And then, medal time. McCown led a six-play, 75-yard drive and hit Peterson for a 41-yard touchdown with 2:24 left. Navy's final series ended on downs. UTSA 38, Navy 34.

McCown finished 28 of 38 for 359 yards and three touchdowns, without an interception. David Amador II caught seven passes for 71 yards. Henderson ran for 78 yards. UTSA didn't turn it over and went 2-for-3 on fourth down. Per the AP, it was the first-ever game in the series. Navy, thank you for coming. Come back anytime.

The honest part, since a medal means nothing if you didn't earn it. Navy ran for 294 yards on 48 carries, 6.1 per carry, and UTSA committed seven penalties for 60 yards. You don't get to give up nearly 300 rushing yards every week and still wear the sash.

UTSA is 6-1 and 3-0 in the American. The wins: UT Rio Grande Valley 45-16, at Texas State 31-26, Colorado State 59-45, at Rice 16-14, South Florida 31-24 and Navy. The lone loss was 30-6 at Texas. Six medals. One week I'd rather forget.
Part 2: UTSA at Tulane
Saturday, 8 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, at Yulman Stadium in New Orleans. UTSA (6-1, 3-0) at Tulane (3-3, 1-1).
Our Parade

McCown has 1,578 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and just two interceptions, completing 69.5 of every 100 passes. Henderson leads the run game with 562 yards on 94 carries. DJ Allen Jr. has 24 catches for 325 yards. UTSA scores 32.3 points per game and gains 411.1 yards per game. And UTSA's turnover margin is plus-4, 22nd in FBS.
Tulane's Float

Let me be gracious first: Tulane's defense just forced six turnovers against Memphis, and it ranks fifth in FBS in red zone defense, allowing scores on 65.4 of every 100 trips. Kevin Adams III had two interceptions Friday. TJ Smith returned an interception 76 yards for a touchdown. Respect.

Now the parade route. Tulane's offense averages 332.0 yards per game, 116th in FBS, and 20.5 points per game, 117th. It throws for 179.7 yards per game, 116th. Against Memphis, it went three-and-out on its first three drives and converted 4 of 16 third downs, with freshman Trace Johnson making his first start.

And Tulane is last in FBS in time of possession. Last. 26:20 per game. That's not a parade, that's a drive-by. The Green Wave hold the ball like it's a hot tamale fresh off the comal. Drop it, blow on your fingers, pass it along.
Its run defense allows 212.5 yards per game, 133rd, and opponents convert 45.6 of every 100 third downs, 124th. Henderson and Peterson, put your dancing shoes on.

San Antonio. San Antonio is the seventh-most populous city in America and the second-most in Texas, with 1.43 million people at the 2020 census. A Spanish mission and outpost was founded here in 1718, and in 1731 San Antonio became the first chartered civil settlement in present-day Texas. The city is home to five 18th-century Spanish frontier missions, including the Alamo, and together they were named UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2015.

Possibly. A city that's not even sure where its own nickname came from. We know exactly where "Remember the Alamo" came from.

And Tulane's own mascot history is a delight. Riptide the Pelican debuted in 1998, but before that the school used an angry wave, which, per Wikipedia, fans nicknamed "Gumby." A wave. Named Gumby. The Roadrunner salutes you, Gumby, and then runs right past you.

It'll be close in New Orleans. Both of our road wins this year, at Texas State and at Rice, came by five points or fewer, so this team knows how to win a tight one away from home. And I brought an extra ribbon, just in case.
Birds up!
My call: Tulane Green Wave 27, UTSA Roadrunners 24.

articles.title: Call Sign: No Fumbles: Air Force Ran for 430 Yards Past UNLV and Now Climbs 600 Feet Higher to Laramie, Where the Cowboys Throw for 146 a Game
articles.byline: Lt. Col. (Ret.) Marissa Okonkwo-Hale, The Air Force Fanatic
articles.matchup: Air Force (5-1) at Wyoming (4-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 9 p.m. ET, War Memorial Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Good morning, wingmen. Lieutenant Colonel Marissa Okonkwo-Hale, retired, reporting from a lawn chair in the Falcon Stadium parking lot with a thermos of coffee and a clipboard. I give every opponent a call sign before kickoff. I give every Air Force win a mission rating. And I don't hand out "mission accomplished" lightly, because in my experience the people who say it too early are usually the ones who have to say "never mind" later.

This week's brief: the debrief on Saturday's 41-31 win over UNLV, then the flight plan for a Friday night in Laramie, where the air is even thinner than ours. Call sign for the opponent this week: "Tumbleweed." It'll make sense later.

Part 1: Debrief, Air Force 41, UNLV 31

On Oct. 17 at Falcon Stadium, Evan Medders ran for 152 yards and three touchdowns, and Air Force pulled away in the fourth quarter to beat UNLV 41-31.

It was not a clean flight for three quarters. UNLV's Jackson Arnold hit Kayden McGee for a 60-yard touchdown early in the second quarter, and the Rebels led 17-13 at halftime after Ethan Schwartz hit a 60-yard field goal on the final play of the half. Sixty yards! I salute the kicker. I do not salute the coverage. Arnold found McGee again for an 8-yard touchdown late in the third, and UNLV led 24-20.

Then Air Force did what Air Force does. Six seconds into the fourth quarter, Medders finished a four-play, 75-yard drive with a 32-yard touchdown run for a 27-24 lead. About four and a half minutes later, he crashed in from the 1 for a 34-24 lead. Owen Allen's 2-yard run with 3:53 left made it 41-24. Mission accomplished, and I waited until 3:53 to say so.

The flight data: Air Force ran 62 times for 430 yards, 6.9 a carry. Medders had 152 yards on 18 carries, Rocco Conti had 103 on 12, including a 50-yarder, and Allen had 96. Air Force threw three passes and completed two for 18 yards. It held the ball for 35:13, converted 2 of 2 on fourth down and committed just three penalties. Carter Cremascoli kicked two field goals.

And here's my go-to stat of the season. Per the AP, Air Force has not fumbled the ball this season, through 431 plays. The Falcons haven't fumbled since the second quarter against New Mexico in 2025, a streak of 549 plays. Call sign for the offense: "Velcro."

The honest debrief. UNLV converted 9 of 13 third downs. Arnold threw for 246 yards and two touchdowns and McGee caught five passes for 99 yards. A defense that lets an opponent go 9-for-13 on third down needs a long talk in the hangar.

Air Force is 5-1 and 3-1 in the Mountain West. It beat Duquesne 34-0, lost 38-32 to North Dakota State, won 36-33 at Nevada, beat Navy 14-9, won 28-7 at Northern Illinois and beat UNLV. Five wins in a row. The only blemish is a six-point home loss to North Dakota State in September, and the Bison are 6-1 and very good. I'll accept that one on the record and move on.

Part 2: Air Force at Wyoming

Friday, Oct. 23, 9 p.m. Eastern, on The CW, at War Memorial Stadium in Laramie. Air Force (5-1, 3-1) at Wyoming (4-3, 3-1).

Our Formation

Air Force runs for 343.0 yards per game, second in FBS, and converts 52.9 of every 100 third downs, 10th. It holds the ball for 36:22 per game, second in the country. And it commits just 43.2 penalty yards per game, 20th. Liam Szarka leads the team with 391 rushing yards and seven touchdowns, and he has 296 passing yards.

The defense is the quiet hero: 295.7 yards allowed per game, 23rd in FBS, and 19.7 points per game, 38th. The pass defense ranks 24th at 172.3 per game. Air Force's turnover margin is plus-3, 34th.

Call Sign "Tumbleweed"

Wyoming throws for 146.4 yards per game, 133rd in FBS, and scores 18.3 points per game, 127th. Its offense averages 333.1 yards per game, 115th. And the turnover margin is minus-7, 131st. A tumbleweed rolls wherever the wind sends it, and lately the wind has been sending Wyoming's footballs to the other team. Tyler Hughes has thrown seven interceptions to go with three touchdown passes.

And Wyoming's red zone offense ranks 104th, scoring on 80.8 of every 100 trips. Our red zone defense ranks 30th, allowing scores on 76.5 of every 100 trips.

Threat Assessment

I don't underestimate anyone. Hughes is a dangerous runner. Against Northern Illinois on Saturday he completed 16 of 19 passes for 196 yards and ran for a career-high 183 yards and four touchdowns, including a 53-yarder, in a 41-23 win. Wyoming ran for 314 yards that day. The Cowboys' defense also allows only 20.9 points per game, 43rd.

But Wyoming's run defense allows 172.1 yards per game, 101st in FBS. And the Air Force run game does not ask permission.

Series History

CollegeFootballData.com has Air Force ahead 32-28-3 all time. Wyoming won 31-19 in 2024. Air Force won 24-21 last season. This is a real rivalry, two high-altitude programs that have been trading punches for decades, and I respect it. Sixty-three games and only four wins apart. That's a close formation.

Base Report: Colorado Springs vs. Laramie

Colorado Springs. Our town had 478,961 people at the 2020 census and is the second-most populous city in Colorado. It sits at 6,035 feet, more than a mile high, near the base of Pikes Peak, which rises to 14,115 feet. Colorado Springs is nicknamed Olympic City USA and is home to the U.S. Olympic & Paralympic Training Center and the headquarters of the U.S. Olympic & Paralympic Committee. NORAD was set up inside the Cheyenne Mountain Complex during the Cold War. And there's Garden of the Gods, which is exactly as beautiful as it sounds.

Falcon Stadium opened in 1962 with a 34-0 win over Colorado State, and its field sits at 6,621 feet, second-highest in FBS.

Laramie. Laramie is a historic town, 31,407 at the 2020 census, and it deserves real credit: in 1870, five Laramie residents became the first women in the world to serve on a jury, and Louisa Swain of Laramie became the first woman in the United States to cast a legal vote in a general election. That's a proud town.

But consider the weather report. Per Wikipedia, Laramie's average window for freezing temperatures runs from Sept. 14 through June 6, and the window for accumulating snow runs from Oct. 5 through May 12. Wingmen, that's not a winter. That's a nine-month deployment. Laramie's summer is so short it needs a permission slip. Call sign for the town: "Frostbite." I'll be packing the cold-weather gear and the good gloves.

And War Memorial Stadium is the highest stadium in FBS, at 7,222 feet. Six hundred feet higher than ours. Wyoming fans love to brag about the thin air. Wingmen, we breathe thin air for a living. We're a flight school.

Flight Plan

Run the ball, hold the ball, and protect the ball, which this team has done perfectly all year. Make Hughes throw, because the passing game is where Tumbleweed blows off course. Fix the third-down defense. And bring a jacket. It's Laramie in late October.

Call sign: correct.

My call: Air Force Falcons 26, Wyoming Cowboys 19.

articles.title: A 9:30 a.m. Kickoff, Island Time: Hawai'i Flies to DeKalb to Face a Winless Huskie Defense That Lets Opponents Convert 61.6 of Every 100 Third Downs
articles.byline: Kainoa Akana-Baird, The Hawai'i Fanatic
articles.matchup: Hawai'i (1-6) at Northern Illinois (0-6), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Huskie Stadium, MW+
articles.text:
Aloha kakou. Kainoa Akana-Baird here, coming to you from a lanai in Mānoa with a plate lunch, a cold can of guava nectar and a whiteboard covered in time-zone math. Being a Hawai'i football fan means doing arithmetic every Saturday. When the Rainbow Warriors play on the mainland, I'm converting Eastern, Central and Mountain to Hawai'i time before the coin toss. And this Saturday's game in DeKalb kicks off at 3:30 p.m. Eastern. That's 2:30 Central. And it's 9:30 in the morning here in Honolulu.

Breakfast football. Island time, but on schedule.

I've done this math my whole life. A noon Eastern kickoff is 6 a.m. here. A 7 p.m. Eastern kickoff is 1 p.m. here, which is perfect. A 10:30 p.m. Eastern kickoff on the mainland is 4:30 p.m. here, which is the best time slot in America, and I'll fight anyone about that. But 9:30 in the morning? That's a pancakes-and-play-calling Saturday. I'm making the coffee strong.

This week, I'll walk through Saturday's 21-10 loss to New Mexico, honestly, because nobody learns anything from a highlight reel. Then the trip to Northern Illinois, where two teams that badly need a win will meet in the middle of the Midwest.

Part 1: New Mexico 21, Hawai'i 10

On Oct. 17 at the Clarence T.C. Ching Athletics Complex, Hawai'i led 10-0 at halftime and lost 21-10.

The first half was beautiful. Sean Olvera-Harle hit a 27-yard field goal in the first quarter. With six seconds left in the half, Micah Alejado threw a 1-yard touchdown to Titan Lacaden. The defense held New Mexico scoreless for 30 minutes. Wynden Ho'ohuli and Jamih Otis each made 10 tackles, and Ho'ohuli and Noah Wily each had a sack. New Mexico committed 16 penalties for 145 yards and turned the ball over three times. Sixteen penalties! The Lobos were practically handing out gifts.

Then the second half happened. Scottre Humphrey scored from a yard out to open the third quarter, capping a nine-play, 75-yard drive that took 5:17. With 6:57 left, Toa Fa'avae ran 21 yards for the go-ahead touchdown. With 3:24 left, Humphrey ran 49 yards up the middle for the final points. New Mexico ran for 243 yards on 48 carries.

The honest part, from the whiteboard. Hawai'i ran 27 times for 48 yards, 1.8 per carry, and went 3-for-13 on third down. Alejado threw for 250 yards, completing 23 of 40, with a touchdown and an interception. Devin Alves caught five passes for 76 yards. But when a team gets three turnovers and 145 penalty yards from its opponent and still loses, it has to look in the mirror.

Hawai'i is 1-6 and 0-4 in the Mountain West. The season: a 37-27 loss at Stanford, a 21-6 loss to UNLV, a 29-19 win over New Mexico State, a 27-10 loss at Wyoming, a 20-16 loss to San José State, a 30-12 loss at Arizona State and Saturday's loss. Three of those losses came by 11 points or fewer. This team is closer than its record looks, and the record looks rough.

Part 2: Hawai'i at Northern Illinois

Saturday at 3:30 p.m. Eastern at Huskie Stadium in DeKalb, Ill., streaming on MW+. That's 9:30 a.m. in Honolulu. Hawai'i (1-6, 0-4) at Northern Illinois (0-6, 0-2).

Our Passing Game

Hawai'i throws for 268 yards per game, 32nd in FBS. Alejado has 1,862 passing yards, six touchdowns and five interceptions. Kainoa Carvalho has 32 catches for 384 yards. Yes, they share my first name. No, we're not related. Yes, I'm proud anyway.

The honest note: Hawai'i runs for 77.4 yards per game, 138th in FBS, and scores 15.7 points per game, 133rd. DeVon Rice leads the run game with 314 yards. If we can't run, we can't close.

The Huskies

Now, Northern Illinois. I want to be gracious. The Huskies just joined the Mountain West this season as a football-only member, so welcome to the conference, neighbors. Well, sort of neighbors.

But look at the third-down numbers. NIU's defense allows opponents to convert 61.6 of every 100 third downs, 138th in FBS. Sixty-one point six. That's not a defense. That's a revolving door. On third down, opponents keep the ball more often than not.

NIU's red zone offense ranks 138th, scoring on just 46.7 of every 100 trips. The Huskies score 14.2 points per game, 137th, and gain 307.7 yards per game, 131st. Their run defense allows 228.5 yards per game, 135th. And they've been shut out once, 40-0 at Iowa in the opener.

They have weapons. Telly Johnson Jr. ran for 139 yards against Wyoming last week and has 439 for the season. Taron Dickens has thrown for 1,193 yards. DeAree Rogers has 49 catches. NIU's pass defense ranks 33rd, allowing 187 yards per game, so Alejado won't have it easy through the air.

The Math on the Whiteboard

Here's my equation. Hawai'i's run game ranks 138th in FBS, and NIU's run defense ranks 135th. Something has to give. If Rice and Cam Barfield can run even a little, Alejado can throw on second-and-short instead of third-and-long. And on third down, against a defense that allows 61.6 of every 100, Hawai'i should be able to stay on the field.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has no previous meeting on record for Hawai'i and Northern Illinois. A first date. Let's make a good impression.

Town Report: Honolulu vs. DeKalb

blocks.text: Aloha kakou. Kainoa Akana-Baird here, coming to you from a lanai in Mānoa with a plate lunch, a cold can of guava nectar and a whiteboard covered in time-zone math. Being a Hawai'i football fan means doing arithmetic every Saturday. When the Rainbow Warriors play on the mainland, I'm converting Eastern, Central and Mountain to Hawai'i time before the coin toss. And this Saturday's game in DeKalb kicks off at 3:30 p.m. Eastern. That's 2:30 Central. And it's 9:30 in the morning here in Honolulu.
Breakfast football. Island time, but on schedule.

I've done this math my whole life. A noon Eastern kickoff is 6 a.m. here. A 7 p.m. Eastern kickoff is 1 p.m. here, which is perfect. A 10:30 p.m. Eastern kickoff on the mainland is 4:30 p.m. here, which is the best time slot in America, and I'll fight anyone about that. But 9:30 in the morning? That's a pancakes-and-play-calling Saturday. I'm making the coffee strong.

This week, I'll walk through Saturday's 21-10 loss to New Mexico, honestly, because nobody learns anything from a highlight reel. Then the trip to Northern Illinois, where two teams that badly need a win will meet in the middle of the Midwest.
Part 1: New Mexico 21, Hawai'i 10
On Oct. 17 at the Clarence T.C. Ching Athletics Complex, Hawai'i led 10-0 at halftime and lost 21-10.

The first half was beautiful. Sean Olvera-Harle hit a 27-yard field goal in the first quarter. With six seconds left in the half, Micah Alejado threw a 1-yard touchdown to Titan Lacaden. The defense held New Mexico scoreless for 30 minutes. Wynden Ho'ohuli and Jamih Otis each made 10 tackles, and Ho'ohuli and Noah Wily each had a sack. New Mexico committed 16 penalties for 145 yards and turned the ball over three times. Sixteen penalties! The Lobos were practically handing out gifts.

Then the second half happened. Scottre Humphrey scored from a yard out to open the third quarter, capping a nine-play, 75-yard drive that took 5:17. Saturday at 3:30 p.m. Eastern at Huskie Stadium in DeKalb, Ill., streaming on MW+. That's 9:30 a.m. in Honolulu. Hawai'i (1-6, 0-4) at Northern Illinois (0-6, 0-2).

Hawai'i throws for 268 yards per game, 32nd in FBS. Alejado has 1,862 passing yards, six touchdowns and five interceptions. Kainoa Carvalho has 32 catches for 384 yards. Yes, they share my first name. No, we're not related. Yes, I'm proud anyway.

Now, Northern Illinois. I want to be gracious. The Huskies just joined the Mountain West this season as a football-only member, so welcome to the conference, neighbors. Well, sort of neighbors.

NIU's red zone offense ranks 138th, scoring on just 46.7 of every 100 trips. The Huskies score 14.2 points per game, 137th, and gain 307.7 yards per game, 131st. Their run defense allows 228.5 yards per game, 135th. And they've been shut out once, 40-0 at Iowa in the opener.

They have weapons. Telly Johnson Jr. ran for 139 yards against Wyoming last week and has 439 for the season. Taron Dickens has thrown for 1,193 yards. DeAree Rogers has 49 catches. NIU's pass defense ranks 33rd, allowing 187 yards per game, so Alejado won't have it easy through the air.
The Math on the Whiteboard

If Rice and Cam Barfield can run even a little, Alejado can throw on second-and-short instead of third-and-long. And on third down, against a defense that allows 61.6 of every 100, Hawai'i should be able to stay on the field.

articles.title: Send It on Your 130th Birthday: Nevada Shakes Off a Fargo Wipeout and Hosts an SJSU Offense That Ranks 111th on Third Down, From a Town That Gave Itself a Nickname
articles.byline: Ridge Corbell, The Nevada Fanatic
articles.matchup: San José State (4-3) at Nevada (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 5 p.m. ET, Mackay Stadium, MW+
articles.text:
Yo, Pack nation. Ridge Corbell here, writing from the back of my truck outside Reno with my board waxed and the first snow of the season somewhere in the forecast. I rate football games like runs down a mountain. Some are fresh powder. Some are sheet ice. And some, like last Saturday in Fargo, start out as a perfect run and end with you face-first in a tree well.

Here's the trail map for this week. First, an honest look at the 31-17 loss at North Dakota State. Then a home game against San José State on a very big day: per the program's own history, Nevada football was founded on Oct. 24, 1896, as the Sagebrushers. Saturday is the Wolf Pack's 130th birthday. Let's send it.

Part 1: North Dakota State 31, Nevada 17

On Oct. 17 at the Fargodome, the run started perfect. AJ Bianco ran 15 yards for a touchdown early in the second quarter, Trace Estes ran in the two-point try, and Joe McFadden added a 39-yard field goal. Nevada led 11-0. Fresh powder, baby.

Then the tree well. NDSU's Nathan Hayes ran for a 5-yard touchdown, then threw a 21-yard touchdown to Mekhi Collins with 21 seconds left in the half. On the final play of the half, McFadden's long field goal try came up short, and Jackson Williams caught it and returned it 100 yards for a touchdown. NDSU led 19-11 at the break.

Nevada fought back. In the third quarter, Bianco threw a 19-yard touchdown to Gary Givens III. But the two-point try was returned the other way by Matthew Stenbroten for two NDSU points. Drew Klein kicked a 39-yard field goal, and Hayes threw a 12-yard touchdown to Reis Kessel early in the fourth.

The honest trail report. Bianco went 17 of 34 for 190 yards with a touchdown and two interceptions, and ran for a score. Dominic Kelley ran 11 times for 60 yards and caught five passes. Jeremy Naborne-Owens made 13 tackles and EJ Smith made 12. NDSU committed 11 penalties for 98 yards, and Nevada still lost, mostly because it held the ball for just 21:51 to NDSU's 38:09 and gave up points in the kicking game. McFadden went 1-for-3 on field goals. That's hooking a toe on a blue run.

Nevada is 2-4 and 1-2 in the Mountain West. The Pack beat Western Kentucky 49-14, lost 20-7 to Montana State, lost 27-20 at Middle Tennessee, lost 36-33 to Air Force, won 30-13 at UTEP and lost at NDSU. The three-point loss to 5-1 Air Force still stings.

Here's the thing, though. Look at the losses. Seven points at Middle Tennessee. Three points to Air Force, which hasn't lost since. And Nevada led NDSU, a 6-1 team, 11-0 on the road before a last-second touchdown and a 100-yard return flipped it in about 21 seconds of game clock. That's not a team that can't ride. That's a team that keeps catching one bad patch of ice. Fix the kicking, fix the turnovers, and this board starts carving.

Part 2: San José State at Nevada

Saturday at 5 p.m. Eastern, 2 p.m. in Reno, at Mackay Stadium, streaming on MW+. San José State (4-3, 2-1) at Nevada (2-4, 1-2).

Our Gear

Nevada's pass defense is a legit black diamond, allowing just 155.3 passing yards per game, seventh in FBS. Opponents convert 32.6 of every 100 third downs, 29th. The defense did its job against NDSU's offense for long stretches, too, until the kicking game and the clock got away from it. The run game is solid as well: 192.8 yards per game, 37th. Kelley leads it with 500 yards and four touchdowns on 87 carries. Givens leads the receivers with 15 catches for 260 yards.

Their Gear

SJSU throws for 246 yards per game, and Luke Weaver has 1,529 passing yards, 11 touchdowns and six interceptions. But against our seventh-ranked pass defense, that's a skier trying to carve on sheet ice.

Look at the rest of the SJSU trail map. The Spartans convert 34.4 of every 100 third downs, 111th in FBS. They score 21.4 points per game, 111th. They run for 138.7 yards per game, 98th. Their pass defense allows 240.9 yards per game, 111th. And they hold the ball for 26:41 per game, 135th. That's a lot of bunny-hill numbers, dude.

I will tip my helmet to Viliami Teu, who ran for 156 yards and two touchdowns at UTEP last week, including a 67-yarder. Respect.

The Honest Part

We've got to fix stuff. Nevada's turnover margin is minus-8, 134th. Its red zone defense ranks 127th, allowing opponents to score on 94.4 of every 100 trips. The run defense allows 184.3 yards per game, 116th. And Nevada holds the ball for 26:55, 133rd. If Teu runs like he did in El Paso, this gets icy fast.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists Nevada ahead 21-8. SJSU won 35-31 in 2024. Nevada won 55-10 last season. Fifty-five. That was a powder day.

Town Report: Reno vs. San Jose

Reno. "The Biggest Little City in the World." Reno had 264,165 people at the 2020 census and sits at about 4,400 feet in the Truckee River valley, on the eastern side of the Sierra Nevada, about 23 miles northeast of Lake Tahoe. Dude, Tahoe is 23 miles away. I can be on a chairlift before San Jose finishes its commute.

The first Reno Arch went up downtown on Oct. 23, 1926, and the slogan first appeared on it in 1929. The city is named for Union Gen. Jesse L. Reno. Every year we host the Great Reno Balloon Race, Hot August Nights and the Reno Air Races. And Mackay Stadium, opened Oct. 1, 1966, sits at 4,610 feet. That's high enough to feel it, dude. Bring your lungs.

And when the Pack gets rolling, there's nothing like Mackay on a cool fall afternoon with the hills behind it. Saturday is a 2 p.m. local kickoff in late October. I'll be there in a hoodie, yelling for the defense on every third down. San José State comes from sea level on the bay. We'll see how their legs feel in the second half at 4,610 feet.

San Jose. San Jose is a big city, more than a million people at the 2020 census, and it's proud of its tech. In 1988, Mayor Tom McEnery adopted the motto "Capital of Silicon Valley." Adopted. They gave themselves the title. Dude, that's like giving yourself a trophy at the end of a run. In Reno, our slogan came from a contest.

San Jose was also founded in 1777, and in 1791, Wikipedia says, severe flooding moved the settlement about a mile south. A whole town that had to relocate because it got wet. Bro, we live near Lake Tahoe. We're not afraid of water.

Drop In

Here's the run I'd take Saturday. Make SJSU throw into our seventh-ranked pass defense. Run Kelley. Hold the ball, because a 21:51 time of possession is how you end up in a tree well. Make the kicks. And please, protect the football. A minus-8 turnover margin is a lot of yard sales.

It's the Pack's 130th birthday. Nobody wants to lose at their own party. Light the candles. Send it.

My call: Nevada Wolf Pack 26, San José State Spartans 20.

articles.title: Red or Green? Both: New Mexico Leads the Nation in Takeaways and Scoring Defense, and Now the Bison Climb 4,200 Feet From a Domed Stadium to Face Them Under the Sandias
articles.byline: Paloma Begaye-Ortiz, The New Mexico Fanatic
articles.matchup: North Dakota State (6-1) at New Mexico (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 10 p.m. ET, University Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Buenos días, Lobo nation. Paloma Begaye-Ortiz here, writing from the tailgate of my chase truck with a breakfast burrito in my hand. Red or green? Both. Always both. I'm a hot air balloon pilot, which means I read the wind for a living, and I read football the same way. You check the conditions, you trust your instruments, and you don't panic when you drift.

Saturday in Honolulu, the Lobos drifted. For a whole half, we drifted. And then the burner kicked on. Let's review it, and then let's talk about the biggest home game of the season: North Dakota State, under the lights, at University Stadium.

Part 1: New Mexico 21, Hawai'i 10

On Oct. 17 at the Clarence T.C. Ching Athletics Complex, New Mexico trailed 10-0 at halftime and came back to beat Hawai'i 21-10.

The first half was low clouds. Hawai'i kicked a 27-yard field goal in the first quarter and scored on a 1-yard touchdown pass with six seconds left in the half. New Mexico hadn't scored.

Then the burner. To open the third quarter, the Lobos went 75 yards in nine plays and 5:17, and Scottre Humphrey crashed in from the 1 to make it 10-7. With 6:57 left, Toa Fa'avae ran 21 yards for the go-ahead touchdown. And with 3:24 left, Humphrey ran 49 yards right up the middle to seal it. Liftoff.

The flight log: New Mexico ran 48 times for 243 yards. Humphrey had 90 yards and two touchdowns on 15 carries, Kiefer Sibley had 87 on 17, and Fa'avae had 77 on 10. The Lobos converted all three of their fourth-down tries. The defense held Hawai'i to 48 rushing yards on 27 carries, 1.8 per carry, and 3-of-13 on third down. Darren Agu had 3.5 tackles for loss and a sack. And the defense forced two turnovers.

Now the honest pilot's report, because you don't lie in a flight log. New Mexico committed 16 penalties for 145 yards. Sixteen. Fa'avae completed 5 of 10 passes for 59 yards with two interceptions, and the Lobos lost a fumble. Three turnovers and 145 penalty yards on the road, and we still won by 11. Imagine the flight with clean air.

And here's what I love about that comeback. A balloon doesn't fight the wind. It finds the right layer and rides it. In the second half, the Lobos stopped fighting and found their layer: run the ball, run it again, and trust the defense. Twenty-one unanswered points. That's a pilot who knows her instruments.

The Lobos are 5-1 and 2-0 in the Mountain West. They beat Central Michigan 38-7 and Mercyhurst 70-7, lost 14-6 at Oklahoma, won 42-18 at New Mexico State, beat UTEP 61-7 and won at Hawai'i.

Part 2: North Dakota State at New Mexico

Saturday, 10 p.m. Eastern, 8 p.m. here, at University Stadium, on The CW. North Dakota State (6-1, 3-1 Mountain West) at New Mexico (5-1, 2-0).

Our Instruments

New Mexico leads FBS with a plus-17 turnover margin. Plus seventeen! The Lobos allow 10.5 points per game, first in the nation. Their red zone defense ranks first, allowing scores on 62.5 of every 100 trips. They allow 262.7 yards per game, sixth, 92 rushing yards per game, 15th, and 170.7 passing yards, 19th. Opponents convert just 30.8 of every 100 third downs, 15th.

The offense scores 39.7 points per game, 10th. It runs for 214.5 yards per game, 21st, and it holds the ball for 33:46, seventh. Humphrey has 422 yards and eight touchdowns. Fa'avae has 698 passing yards, five touchdowns and three interceptions. Bailen George has 12 catches for 240 yards and three touchdowns, 20 yards a catch.

The honest note: New Mexico throws for 163.5 yards per game, 127th, and Fa'avae completes 56.2 of every 100 throws.

The Bison

North Dakota State has a great defense, and I won't pretend otherwise. It allows 246 yards per game, second in FBS, 133.9 passing yards per game, second, and 11.3 points per game, second. articles.title: Oh, for Cute: A Hundred-Yard Hotdish Delivery Beat Nevada, and Now the Bison Take the Nation's Second-Ranked Defense to Albuquerque, a City That Spells Its Own Namesake Wrong
articles.byline: Ingeborg 'Inga' Halvorsen, The North Dakota State Fanatic
articles.matchup: North Dakota State (6-1) at New Mexico (5-1), Sat., Oct. 24, 10 p.m. ET, University Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Well, hi there! Inga Halvorsen here, writing from my kitchen in south Fargo with a tater tot hotdish in the oven and my green-and-yellow apron on. I've been following the Bison since before some of these boys were born, and I rate every game like a church potluck. Some games are a nice Jell-O salad. Some are a lefse with butter and sugar. And some, like Saturday night, are a big ol' pan of hotdish that somebody brought late and everybody went back for seconds.

This week we'll talk about the 31-17 win over Nevada, honestly, because Mother always said, "Ingeborg, don't fib." Then we'll look at a big one: the Bison's first trip to Albuquerque to play a New Mexico team that leads the whole country in turnover margin.

Part 1: North Dakota State 31, Nevada 17

On Oct. 17 at the Fargodome, Nathan Hayes accounted for three touchdowns, Jackson Williams returned a missed field goal 100 yards for a touchdown, and the Bison beat Nevada 31-17. Uff da, what a night.

Now, I'll be honest. It didn't start nice. Nevada's AJ Bianco ran 15 yards for a touchdown early in the second quarter, the Wolf Pack ran in the two-point try, and Joe McFadden kicked a 39-yard field goal. Nevada led 11-0, and I set down my coffee.

Then the Bison got going. Hayes ran in from 5 yards. With 21 seconds left in the half, he threw a 21-yard touchdown to Mekhi Collins. And on the last play of the half, Nevada tried a 57-yard field goal, and Jackson Williams caught it in the end zone, broke a couple of tackles and ran along the sideline all 100 yards for a touchdown. Bison 19, Nevada 11 at halftime. Oh, for cute! That's a hotdish delivered piping hot, straight from the oven to the table.

In the third quarter, Nevada scored on a 19-yard pass to pull within two, then tried a trick play on the two-point try, fumbled, and Matthew Stenbroten picked it up and ran it back for two Bison points. That was dessert. Drew Klein kicked a 39-yard field goal, and Hayes threw a 12-yard touchdown to Reis Kessel early in the fourth.

Hayes went 19 of 25 for 153 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions, and ran for another score. Williams caught five passes for 58 yards. NDSU ran 45 times for 192 yards, held the ball for 38:09 and didn't turn it over. The defense made two interceptions.

Now the part I won't fib about. The Bison committed 11 penalties for 98 yards. Ninety-eight! That's like burning the bars at a bake sale. And the passing game managed 153 yards. Mother would say, "That's fine, dear, but you can do more," and she'd be right. I'm saying it nicer.

NDSU is 6-1 and 3-1 in its first Mountain West season, after the Bison joined the conference and moved to FBS on July 1. They beat Jacksonville State 33-7 and Fordham 38-0, won 38-32 at Air Force and 31-10 at Sacramento State, beat Wyoming 28-0, lost 13-7 at UNLV and beat Nevada. The UNLV loss still gives me heartburn.

Part 2: North Dakota State at New Mexico

Saturday at 10 p.m. Eastern, which is 9 p.m. in Fargo and 8 p.m. in Albuquerque, at University Stadium, on The CW. North Dakota State (6-1, 3-1) at New Mexico (5-1, 2-0).

Our Casserole

The Bison defense is the best dish on the table. It allows 246 yards per game, second in FBS, 133.9 passing yards per game, also second, and 11.3 points per game, second again. Second, second, second. And the Bison turnover margin is plus-7, eighth in FBS.

Hayes has 1,272 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and five interceptions, completing 65 of every 100 passes. Myles Mitchell leads the run game with 354 yards. Williams leads the receivers with 28 catches for 432 yards.

The honest note: NDSU's passing game ranks 113th at 187.3 yards per game, and the offense ranks 92nd at 362 yards per game.

Their Casserole

I'll be gracious, because I was raised right. New Mexico is good. The Lobos lead FBS with a plus-17 turnover margin. They allow 10.5 points per game, first in FBS. Their red zone defense ranks first. They score 39.7 points per game, 10th, and they run for 214.5 per game, 21st. Scottre Humphrey has 422 rushing yards and eight touchdowns.

But here's the recipe card. New Mexico throws for 163.5 yards per game, 127th in FBS. Toa Fa'avae has completed 56.2 of every 100 passes, and against Hawai'i last week, he went 5 of 10 for 59 yards with two interceptions. The Lobos committed 16 penalties for 145 yards in that game. Sixteen! Oh, my. And they trailed Hawai'i, a team that's now 1-6, 10-0 at halftime.

Against the second-ranked pass defense in the country, a passing game that ranks 127th is a casserole without the cream of mushroom soup. It just doesn't hold together.

And a big part of that 10.5 points per game came from the schedule: Central Michigan, Mercyhurst, New Mexico State, UTEP and Hawai'i. The Lobos did lose 14-6 at Oklahoma, and I'll give them credit for that fight. But the Bison are a different dish.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has no previous meeting on record for these two. First time at the table. Let's bring the good bars.

Town Report: Fargo vs. Albuquerque

Fargo. Fargo is the most populous city in North Dakota, with 125,990 people at the 2020 census. It was founded in 1871 on the Red River of the North, and it has a twin city, Moorhead, right across the river in Minnesota. When the Northern Pacific Railroad arrived, Fargo became known as the "Gateway to the West." The Fargo Theatre is a restored 1926 Art Deco movie house, and I've been going there since I was a girl.

And the Fargodome, which opened in 1992, holds 18,700 for football. Per Wikipedia, the Bison won 10 NCAA FCS national championships from 2011 to 2024. Ten! You don't get those by accident, dear.

Fargo winters are, per Wikipedia, among the coldest in the contiguous United States. That's why we play indoors. We're not soft. We're smart.

Albuquerque. Albuquerque is a lovely, sunny city of 564,559 people, with the Sandia Mountains on the east side and the Rio Grande running right through. Wikipedia says the city averages 278 days of sunshine a year. Well, aren't they lucky.

But here's the thing that made me set down my rolling pin. Albuquerque was founded in 1706 as La Villa de Alburquerque, named in honor of the Duke of Alburquerque. With an extra "r." Somewhere along the way, the city dropped a letter from the name of the man it was named after. In Fargo, we'd never. We'd at least bring the Duke a hotdish and apologize.

And the famous Sandia Mountains? Per Wikipedia, "sandía" is Spanish for "watermelon." Their mountains are named after fruit. Our river is the Red River of the North. One of those sounds like a Viking saga, and one sounds like a picnic.

Last Bite

Here's the plan. Make Fa'avae throw into the second-ranked pass defense. Hold onto the football against a team that lives on takeaways. Clean up those penalties, because 98 yards is too many in any kitchen. And bring a jacket for an 8 p.m. kickoff in the high desert.

Oh, for cute. Go Bison.

My call: New Mexico Lobos 27, North Dakota State Bison 19.

articles.title: Knee-High by the Fourth of July, Winless by Late October: NIU Hosts a Hawai'i Offense That Ranks 138th in Rushing, and This Is the Week the Harvest Comes In
articles.byline: Nola Brandvik, The Northern Illinois Fanatic
articles.matchup: Hawai'i (1-6) at Northern Illinois (0-6), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Huskie Stadium, MW+
articles.text:
Hi there, Huskie fans. Nola Brandvik here, writing from the tailgate of my pickup on a gravel road outside DeKalb, with the combines working the fields on both sides of me. It's harvest season in northern Illinois. And I'll be honest with you: the Huskies' harvest has been thin this year.

I measure football like a crop. Knee-high by the Fourth of July is the old saying, and by October you find out what you've really got in the bin. Right now, the Huskies have zero wins in the bin. That's the truth, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But I've seen a lot of falls, and I've seen late rain save a field.

This week: an honest review of a 41-23 loss at Wyoming, then the best chance of the season to get a win in the bin. Hawai'i is coming to Huskie Stadium.

Part 1: Wyoming 41, Northern Illinois 23

On Oct. 17 at War Memorial Stadium in Laramie, Wyoming's Tyler Hughes ran for a career-high 183 yards and four touchdowns, threw for 196 more, and the Cowboys beat NIU 41-23.

Hughes did most of the damage himself. He scored on runs of 53, 24, 6 and 11 yards, and completed 16 of 19 passes. Wyoming ran for 314 yards and led 20-6 at halftime.

But there were green shoots, and I'm going to point them out. Telly Johnson Jr. ran 16 times for 139 yards, 8.7 per carry, and scored on a 13-yard run in the third quarter, and George Dimopoulos ran in the two-point try to make it 27-17. JJ Schlenhardt made field goals of 44, 22 and 46 yards. Taron Dickens threw for 216 yards and hit La'Don Bryant for a 34-yard touchdown. DeAree Rogers caught 11 passes for 89 yards. NIU ran for 176 yards on 29 carries, 6.1 per carry, and didn't turn the ball over. Brady Kerperin made 11 tackles.

The weeds. NIU went 4-for-14 on third down and committed eight penalties for 90 yards. Dickens completed 24 of 44 passes, and NIU kicked three field goals in a game it lost by 18. You can't win a yield contest with field goals when the other farm is bringing in touchdowns.

NIU is 0-6 and 0-2 in its first season in the Mountain West, where it joined as a football-only member this year. The season: 40-0 at Iowa, 28-24 to Illinois State, 42-17 at Arizona, 35-14 at Georgia State, 28-7 to Air Force and 41-23 at Wyoming. That four-point loss to Illinois State hurt. I'm still not over it.

But here's something a farmer knows. You don't judge a field by the worst rows. Iowa and Arizona are Big Ten and Big 12 programs, both on the road, and Air Force is 5-1. The Huskies have played four of six games away from DeKalb. Now they get to come home, sleep in their own beds and play in front of their own folks. Home field matters, especially in late October in northern Illinois.
