articles.title: Ship It to Prod: SJSU's Ground Game Pushed a 156-Yard Release in El Paso, and Now the Spartans Head to Reno, a City Whose Famous Slogan Was Written by a Californian
articles.byline: Tessa Nakagawa-Ruiz, The San José State Fanatic
articles.matchup: San José State (4-3) at Nevada (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 5 p.m. ET, Mackay Stadium, MW+
articles.text:
Hey, team. Tessa Nakagawa-Ruiz here, product manager by day, Spartan superfan by every other hour, writing from a standing desk in downtown San Jose with a whiteboard of sprint tickets behind me. I treat every SJSU season like a product launch. Every game is a release. Every release gets a retro. And when something works, we ship it to prod.

This week's sprint review looks at Saturday's 24-11 win at UTEP, which shipped clean, and the next release: a trip to Reno to play a Nevada team that, per its own program history, was founded on Oct. 24, 1896. Happy birthday, Wolf Pack. We brought you a present. It's a loss. (Respectfully. One hundred thirty years is a great run, and that's per Nevada's own program history: it started as the Sagebrushers.)

Part 1: Release Notes, San José State 24, UTEP 11

On Oct. 17 at the Sun Bowl in El Paso, Viliami Teu ran for 156 yards and two touchdowns, and SJSU beat UTEP 24-11.

The first feature shipped early. Daniel Rolovich capped a nine-play, 80-yard drive with an 11-yard touchdown pass to Carson Clark with 7:59 left in the first quarter. Then the second half opened with a five-play, 75-yard drive, and Teu scored from 2 yards. About eight minutes later, Teu broke a 67-yard touchdown run, and SJSU led 21-0. Trajan Sinatra added a 26-yard field goal early in the fourth.

Release notes. Teu: 20 carries, 156 yards, 7.8 per carry, two touchdowns. Rolovich: 12 of 23 for 193 yards and a touchdown, no interceptions, plus 39 rushing yards. Clark: five catches for 104 yards. SJSU ran for 233 yards at 6.7 per carry and had zero turnovers. Dylan Lee made 12 tackles with two sacks. Brian Dukes Jr. and Naseri Danielson each made 10 tackles.

Now the bug report, because a retro that only lists wins isn't a retro. UTEP outgained SJSU 462 to 426 and held the ball for 35:17. The Miners piled up 27 first downs to our 17 and completed 25 of 34 passes. UTEP missed two field goals and went 5-for-16 on third down, which helped us a lot. The defense bent hard. It didn't break, which is the definition of a passing build, but not a clean one.

SJSU is 4-3 and 2-1 in the Mountain West. The release log: a 42-26 loss at USC, a 27-21 win at Eastern Michigan, a 30-20 win over Cal Poly, a 26-10 loss to Fresno State, a 20-16 win at Hawai'i, a 16-13 loss to Wyoming and the UTEP win.

Part 2: San José State at Nevada

Saturday at 5 p.m. Eastern, which is 2 p.m. Pacific for both towns, at Mackay Stadium in Reno, streaming on MW+. San José State (4-3, 2-1) at Nevada (2-4, 1-2).

Our Feature Set

Luke Weaver has thrown for 1,529 yards, 11 touchdowns and six interceptions this season. Jabari Bates leads the run game with 556 yards. Clark leads the receivers with 42 catches for 509 yards and five touchdowns. SJSU throws for 246 yards per game, 53rd, and averages 47.3 penalty yards per game, 31st. And SJSU's turnover margin is even, 68th, which beats Nevada's by a lot.

Their Known Issues

Nevada's turnover margin is minus-8, 134th in FBS. Nevada's red zone defense ranks 127th, allowing opponents to score on 94.4 of every 100 trips. Ninety-four point four! That's not a firewall. That's an open port. Its run defense allows 184.3 yards per game, 116th, and Teu just ran for 156.

And last week at North Dakota State, Nevada led 11-0 in the second quarter and then gave up a touchdown pass with 21 seconds left in the half and, on the final play of the half, a 100-yard return of a missed field goal. Nevada's offense threw two interceptions and held the ball for just 21:51. Its passing game ranks 122nd at 171.8 yards per game.

Their Strengths, Honestly

Nevada's pass defense is legitimately good, allowing just 155.3 yards per game, seventh in FBS. And opponents convert only 32.6 of every 100 third downs against it, 29th. Dominic Kelley is a real runner, with 500 yards on 87 carries, and Nevada runs for 192.8 per game, 37th.

Our honest bug: SJSU converts only 34.4 of every 100 third downs, 111th, and scores 21.4 points per game, 111th. Our pass defense allows 240.9 per game, 111th. Both teams rank near the bottom in time of possession: Nevada is 133rd at 26:55, and SJSU is 135th at 26:41. Expect a fast build.

Version History

CollegeFootballData.com lists Nevada ahead 21-8. SJSU won 35-31 in 2024. Nevada won 55-10 last season, which I have filed as a critical bug and assigned to this Saturday for a fix.

Town Report: San Jose vs. Reno

San Jose. San Jose was founded on Nov. 29, 1777, as the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, the first city founded in the Californias. After statehood, San Jose served as California's first state capital. The 1990 census showed San Jose had passed San Francisco in population, and in 2020 the city counted 1,013,240 people. In 1988, Mayor Tom McEnery adopted the motto "Capital of Silicon Valley." We have the Tech Interactive, the Children's Discovery Museum and the Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum.

And SJSU football has sent 139 players to the NFL, including Pro Football Hall of Famers Bill Walsh and Dick Vermeil. Our home field, CEFCU Stadium, opened in 1933 as Spartan Stadium.

Reno. Reno had 264,165 people at the 2020 census, sits about 23 miles northeast of Lake Tahoe and is named for Union Gen. Jesse L. Reno. I respect all of that. But here's the bug I found in the code. Reno's famous slogan, "The Biggest Little City in the World," came from a city contest after the first Reno Arch went up in 1926. And per Wikipedia, the winner was G. A. Burns of Sacramento. Sacramento, California! Reno's whole brand was written by a Californian. Team, that's outsourcing.

And "Biggest Little City" is a contradiction in terms. If my engineers shipped a spec that said "biggest little," I'd send it back for clarification. Then again, Reno is also home to the National Bowling Stadium. A national stadium. For bowling. San Jose has the Capital of Silicon Valley. Reno has lanes.

Ship Notes

The plan for Saturday's release: Run Teu and Bates at a run defense that ranks 116th, because Nevada's pass defense is the toughest code in the repo. Finish drives, because Nevada's red zone defense lets opponents score 94 of every 100 times. Protect the football against a team that's been giving it away. And the defense has to get off the field on third down, which it didn't do enough of in El Paso.

Clean build. Zero turnovers. Let's go.

One more product note. SJSU has played four of its seven games on the road and won three of them, at Eastern Michigan, at Hawai'i and at UTEP. The only road loss came at USC. This team knows how to travel, and Saturday makes back-to-back road trips. Pack the laptop, pack the charger, and pack a jacket, because Reno sits at about 4,400 feet.

Ship it to prod.

My call: Nevada Wolf Pack 26, San José State Spartans 20.

articles.title: Intermission, Darling: UNLV Took a Fourth-Act Hit in Colorado Springs, Takes an Open Week Backstage, Then Raises the Curtain on Halloween Night Against a Winless Northern Illinois From the Town That Invented the Fence
articles.byline: Vegas Monroe-Kalani, The UNLV Fanatic
articles.matchup: UNLV (4-3): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Northern Illinois at UNLV, Sat., Oct. 31, 10:30 p.m. ET, Allegiant Stadium, Las Vegas
articles.text:
Ladies, gentlemen and Rebels of all ages, welcome back to the show. Vegas Monroe-Kalani here, your host, your hype machine and your humble usher, writing from a dressing room mirror lined with light bulbs. Yes, I named myself after the town. No, I will not be taking questions about that.

This week, the Rebels go dark. An open date on Saturday, Oct. 24. No game, no stage, no curtain. The cast rests, the crew resets, and I get exactly one Saturday to steam my sequined jacket.

So let's do the review of the last show, a thriller in Colorado Springs that ended in the wrong key, and then let's talk about opening night, Halloween edition: Northern Illinois at Allegiant Stadium.

Part 1: Air Force 41, UNLV 31

On Oct. 17 at Falcon Stadium, Air Force beat UNLV 41-31. And for three acts, darling, we were the headliner.

Act One was a quick change. Air Force kicked a 37-yard field goal late in the first quarter. Then, eight seconds into the second quarter, Jackson Arnold hit Kayden McGee for a 60-yard touchdown. Seven-three, Rebels. Air Force answered with Evan Medders' 24-yard run, and Jai'Den Thomas punched in from the 3 to put UNLV back on top 14-10.

Then came the showstopper. Air Force kicked a 34-yard field goal with 49 seconds left in the half to cut it to 14-13, and on the last play of the half, Ethan Schwartz drilled a 60-yard field goal. Sixty yards! At the buzzer! I stood on my seat. I may have dropped my opera glasses. UNLV led 17-13 at intermission.

In Act Three, Rocco Conti ran 6 yards to give Air Force a 20-17 lead, and Arnold found McGee again from 8 yards out with 1:41 left in the third. That made it 24-20 Rebels.

And then the fourth act, which I'd like to rewrite. Medders ran 32 yards for a touchdown six seconds into the quarter, then scored from the 1, and Owen Allen added a 2-yard run with 3:53 left. Arnold ran in from the 3 with 38 seconds left to make it 41-31.

articles.title: Outgained and Out of Luck: UTEP Piled Up 462 Yards and Lost to San Jose State, Takes an Open Week, Then Trades 302 Days of Sun for a Dome in a Town Where January Averages 9.2 Degrees
articles.byline: Ernesto 'Neto' Galindo, The UTEP Fanatic
articles.matchup: UTEP (1-6): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: UTEP at North Dakota State, Sat., Oct. 31, 3:30 p.m. ET, Fargodome, Fargo
articles.text:
¿Qué onda, Miner nation? Neto Galindo here, writing from my abuela's kitchen table on the west side, with a stack of flour tortillas, a jar of roasted green chile and a view of the Franklin Mountains out the window. If something's great, I call it Hatch-hot. If something's not great, I call it a learning experience. Last Saturday night at the Sun Bowl was a learning experience with a few Hatch-hot moments.

This week, UTEP has an open date. No game Saturday, Oct. 24. The Miners rest up, heal up and get ready for the longest trip on the schedule: Fargo, N.D., on Halloween. So let's look back at San Jose State, and then let's look ahead to the Bison.

Part 1: San Jose State 24, UTEP 11

On Oct. 17 at the Sun Bowl, San Jose State beat UTEP 24-11. And here's the strange part, amigos. The Miners outgained the Spartans 462 yards to 426. They had 27 first downs to San Jose State's 17. They held the ball for 35:17. They didn't turn it over once. And they still lost by 13.

How? The Spartans hit big plays, and UTEP didn't finish drives.

San Jose State scored first on an 80-yard drive, capped by Daniel Rolovich's 11-yard touchdown pass to Carson Clark with 7:59 left in the first quarter. It stayed 7-0 into the third. Then Viliami Teu ran in from the 2 to open the second half, and later broke a 67-yard touchdown run to make it 21-0. Teu finished with 156 yards and two touchdowns.

The Miners finally got on the board when Carlos Arreola hit a 47-yard field goal with 2:07 left in the third. And in the fourth, Nik Henry ran 8 yards for a touchdown, and Jaden Smith threw the two-point conversion to Cash Cheeks. A trick play on a two-pointer? Hatch-hot.

Now the good stuff, because there was good stuff. Raymond Moore III completed 19 of 28 passes for 195 yards. EJ Colson Jr. came in and completed all six of his passes for 87 yards. Six for six! Jaden Smith caught 12 passes for 90 yards. Kam Thomas caught four for 96, including a 64-yarder. And the Miners went 3-of-4 on fourth down.

The learning experience: UTEP converted 5 of 16 third downs, and Arreola made one of three field goals. You can't move the ball 462 yards and come away with 11 points. In the kitchen, that's like roasting a whole sack of chile and forgetting to bring any home.

The Miners are 1-6 and 0-3 in the Mountain West. They opened at Oklahoma and lost 51-0, beat Texas Southern 51-10, lost 52-17 at Michigan, lost 33-7 to Oregon State, lost 61-7 at New Mexico, and lost 30-13 to Nevada before San Jose State. That's a tough road, with Oklahoma and Michigan on it. I'm not hiding the record. I'm just telling you the last game was the closest the Miners have looked to turning a corner in a while.

Part 2: Next Up, UTEP at North Dakota State

After the open week, UTEP travels to the Fargodome to face North Dakota State on Saturday, Oct. 31, at 3:30 p.m. Eastern. That's 1:30 p.m. here in El Paso. It's on MW+.

The Bison

North Dakota State is 6-1 and 3-1 in the Mountain West in its first season in FBS, and it plays at New Mexico this Saturday. The Bison won 10 FCS national titles from 2011 to 2024, per Wikipedia. That's a lot of trophies. I hope they have a big shelf.

Their defense is the real deal. It allows 246 yards per game and 11.3 points per game, both second in FBS, per ESPN. Nathan Hayes has thrown for 1,272 yards, 10 touchdowns and five interceptions. Myles Mitchell leads them with 354 rushing yards. Jackson Williams has 28 catches for 432 yards.

But here's the thing, Bison. Your offense ranks 92nd in FBS at 362 yards per game, and your passing attack is 113th. Hayes has thrown five interceptions, and two weeks ago UNLV picked him off three times in a 13-7 Bison loss. Seven points! In Las Vegas! That's a learning experience.

Our Miners

Moore has 414 rushing yards and two touchdowns, and Colson has thrown for 628 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions, per ESPN. Kam Thomas has 16 catches for 270 yards. UTEP scores 15.1 points per game and runs for 134.4 yards per game.

The honest note: UTEP allows 37.3 points per game. The defense has to get off the field. But if the offense moves the ball the way it did against San Jose State and finishes in the red zone, this team can make the Bison sweat. Well, maybe not sweat. It's Fargo in late October.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has no previous meeting on record. First time ever. Let's make it memorable.

Town Report: El Paso vs. Fargo

El Paso. El Paso had 678,815 people at the 2020 census, per Wikipedia, the sixth-most populous city in Texas and the biggest in West Texas. We sit on the Rio Grande, right across the border from Ciudad Juárez, in the Chihuahuan Desert. The Franklin Mountains run right through the middle of town, and Franklin Mountains State Park, at 24,000 acres, is one of the largest urban parks in the United States. You can ride the Wyler Aerial Tramway up the mountain or drive Scenic Drive and look out over two countries at once.

The Ysleta Mission dates to 1682, and it's still a working church. The Plaza Theatre, built in 1930, still hosts Broadway shows. And the city hosts the Sun Bowl, the second-oldest bowl game in the country, in a stadium built into a natural bowl at the foot of the mountains.

And the sun, amigos. Per the National Weather Service, as cited on Wikipedia, the sun shines 302 days a year here. That's why we're called the Sun City.

Fargo. Fargo is a fine city on the Red River of the North, founded in 1871, with a lovely 1926 Art Deco movie house called the Fargo Theatre. But Wikipedia says its winters are among the coldest in the contiguous United States. January has a normal mean temperature of 9.2 degrees. Fargo averages 43 days a year at or below zero, and 51.4 inches of snow a season.

We have 302 days of sun. Fargo has 51 inches of snow. No wonder the Bison play indoors. If I lived in Fargo, I'd put a roof on the stadium too. And on the car. And on myself.

So here's my plan for the trip. I'm packing two jackets, three hoodies, a beanie my tía knitted and a thermos of green chile stew. If the Fargodome gets chilly, I'll pass it around. It's Hatch-hot. It'll thaw anybody out.

The Road Ahead

Here's the deal. UTEP outgained a winning Mountain West team last week. It didn't turn the ball over. Colson went six for six. Jaden Smith caught 12 balls. The pieces are there. Use the open week to fix the red zone and the kicking, and go to Fargo ready to make some history.

And on Halloween, I'll be wearing orange. Not as a costume. That's just what Miners wear.

articles.title: Yep: Tyler Hughes Ran for 183 and Threw for 196, and Now Air Force Rides Up to the Highest Stadium in FBS, Where a Team That Throws for 65 Yards a Game Learns What Thin Air Means
articles.byline: Colter Sprague, The Wyoming Fanatic
articles.matchup: Air Force (5-1) at Wyoming (4-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 9 p.m. ET, War Memorial Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Colter Sprague. Laramie. I don't say much. My wife says I say "yep" about 40 times a day, and I said, "Yep." But my editor tells me a column needs more than one word, so I'll stretch it out. Pull up a hay bale.

Two things to talk about. Saturday, the Cowboys beat Northern Illinois. Friday, Air Force comes to town. Both are worth some words. Not too many. But some.

Part 1: Wyoming 41, Northern Illinois 23

On Oct. 17 at War Memorial Stadium, Tyler Hughes ran for a career-high 183 yards and four touchdowns and threw for 196 more, and Wyoming beat Northern Illinois 41-23.

Did he play well? Yep.

Erik Sandvik opened with a 37-yard field goal. Then Hughes took off on a 53-yard touchdown run in the first quarter. He went 24 yards for another score in the second quarter, and Sandvik added a 24-yarder at the half to make it 20-6. In the third quarter, Hughes scored from 6 yards. In the fourth, he scored from 11. Landon Sims added an 11-yard touchdown run, the fifth rushing touchdown of the day.

The defense did make some plays. Jones Thomas broke up three passes. Gary Rutherford and Kevin Sjogren each had a sack. NIU's Taron Dickens completed 24 of 44 passes, and the Huskies went 4-for-14 on third down. That's a defense that gets off the field when it has to. It'll have to a lot on Friday.

Part 2: Air Force at Wyoming

Friday, Oct. 23, 9 p.m. Eastern, on The CW, at War Memorial Stadium. Air Force (5-1, 3-1 Mountain West) at Wyoming (4-3, 3-1).

Who's Coming

Air Force runs the ball. Then it runs the ball. Then, for variety, it runs the ball. The Falcons run for 343.0 yards per game, second in FBS. They hold it for 36:22 a game, second. They convert 52.9 of every 100 third downs, 10th. Per the AP, they haven't fumbled once this season, through 431 plays. That's respectable. I'll tip my hat.

Then I'll put it back on and look at the other column. A team that doesn't fumble is a team that doesn't give you free possessions, and that means we have to earn every one of ours. Air Force throws for 65.0 yards per game, 138th in FBS. Sixty-five. I've thrown a calf farther than that in a day. Their leading passer, Liam Szarka, has 296 yards for the season, one touchdown and four interceptions, completing half his passes. Their leading receiver, Simon Kibbee, has seven catches. All year. Yep.

What We've Got

Hughes runs for 470 yards and five touchdowns and has thrown for 1,018. Kyle Frendt has 11 catches for 216 yards, almost 20 a catch. Wyoming runs for 186.7 yards per game, 42nd. Honest Part

The run defense allows 172.1 per game, 101st. Against the second-best rushing offense in the country, that's a fence with a hole in it, and the cattle know where the hole is.

So the plan's simple. Hold the ball. Score in the red zone, where we rank 104th. Don't give the ball away. Make Air Force throw.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has Air Force ahead 32-28-3. Wyoming won 31-19 in 2024. Air Force won 24-21 last year. Close series, close games. Yep.

Town Report: Laramie vs. Colorado Springs

Laramie. Population 31,407 at the 2020 census. Elevation 7,200 feet. Laramie came to life in 1868 when the Union Pacific Railroad reached the Laramie River, and it sits in the Laramie Valley, with the Snowy Range on one side and the Laramie Range on the other. Wikipedia says the city draws outdoor enthusiasts with its abundance of outdoor activities. I'd say that's an understatement. Twenty-one sites in Laramie are on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Wyoming Territorial Penitentiary, which now shows off a frontier community of the late 1800s. You can tour the old prison. Everybody gets out by suppertime.

Here's the history I'm proudest of. In March 1870, five Laramie residents became the first women in the world to serve on a jury. On Sept. 6, 1870, Laramie's Louisa Swain became the first woman in the United States to cast a legal vote in a general election. Before anybody else did it, Laramie did it. Yep.

War Memorial Stadium went up in the spring and summer of 1950, and at 7,222 feet it's the highest stadium in FBS. Falcon Stadium in Colorado Springs is second, at 6,621. Six hundred feet lower. The Falcons fly, sure. But they fly lower than we sit.

Colorado Springs. Colorado Springs is a big, pretty place. 478,961 people at the 2020 census, and Wikipedia says the city "stands over 1 mile above sea level." They're real proud of that mile. They put it right up top in their description. Laramie's at 7,200 feet. We don't brag about the mile. We passed it a while back and kept climbing.

Colorado Springs is also, per Wikipedia, the most extensive city by area in Colorado. That's a polite way to say it takes a while to drive across. In Laramie, you can get from one end of town to the other before your coffee cools. In Colorado Springs, you need a second thermos.

And the city's nickname is "Olympic City USA." Fine. In Laramie, we just call it home.

Last Word

Friday night. Late October. 7,222 feet. Maybe cold, maybe windy. Hold the ball, protect it, and make the Falcons throw. If they won't throw, stuff the run. If they do throw, catch it.

That's about all I've got. Yep.

My call: Air Force Falcons 26, Wyoming Cowboys 19.

articles.title: Pack a Jacket, Dukes: Unbeaten JMU Climbs 3,333 Feet Into Boone After App State's Four-Touchdown Friday at the Beach
articles.byline: Zebulon 'Zeb' Coldiron, The App State Fanatic
articles.matchup: James Madison (7-0) at App State (4-2), Thu., Oct. 22, 7 p.m. ET, Kidd Brewer Stadium, ESPNU
articles.text:
Mornin' from the porch. Zeb Coldiron here, notebook in my lap, black and gold twine around it, and a cup of coffee going cold because I keep getting up to look at the ridgeline. The leaves are turning in Watauga County, the wind has a bite to it, and Thursday night a team with a zero in the loss column is driving up our mountain. Slow down, the view's worth the wait. Let's take this hike one switchback at a time.

Part 1: Friday Night at the Beach

Last Friday, Oct. 16, App State went down to Conway, S.C., and beat Coastal Carolina 35-32 at Brooks Stadium in front of 19,485 people. It was not a stroll on the boardwalk. It was a climb with loose gravel.

Coastal hit us first. Deuce Bailey threw a 21-yard touchdown pass to Tristian Gardner to open the game, and I wrote "steady" in my notebook, because that's what you write when you're nervous. Then Jaquari Lewis went to work. He scored from 12 yards out to tie it, and then Malachi Singleton drove us 88 yards in eight plays, capped by Lewis's 1-yard plunge for a 14-7 lead after one quarter.

The second quarter was the foggy part of the trail. Bailey hit Robby Washington for 71 yards, then found Ben Verges for 8 yards with 1:53 left before the half. A fumble with 12 seconds left set up a 58-yard field goal by Nico Cavanillas Alti, a career long, and Coastal led 24-14 at the break. Credit to that young man. That kick would have cleared most of the hills in South Carolina, which, to be fair, is not a long list.

Then the view opened up. Lewis ran in from 12 yards midway through the third. Devin Henderson picked off Bailey, and 10 plays later Lewis scored from 3 yards out for a 28-24 lead. Four rushing touchdowns for Jaquari Lewis: 12, 1, 12 and 3 yards. That's a man who knows the way home.

And here's the part of the story I'll be telling at the general store all winter. Henry Hasselbeck, a junior backup, came in and ran 21 times for 125 yards. He also completed 9 of 12 passes for 112 yards, and his first career touchdown pass was a 31-yarder to Sam Pickett III for a 35-24 lead with 6:41 left. Singleton had been sharp before that, 12 of 14 for 151 yards. Two quarterbacks, 21 of 26 together, 516 yards as a team, 253 on the ground.

Coastal scored with 3:11 left, added the two-pointer to make it 35-32, and then our boys ran out the clock. That's mountain football: you hold the ball until the other fella's legs give out. We had it for 33:17. App State is 4-2 and 1-1 in the Sun Belt, and we're back on the trail after that 10-3 home loss to Old Dominion on Oct. 10.

Part 2: The Dukes Come Up the Mountain

Thursday night, 7 o'clock Eastern, on ESPNU, James Madison comes to Kidd Brewer Stadium. Let me be honest, because I'm a porch-honest man: this is the best team in the Sun Belt right now, and the numbers aren't shy about it.

JMU is 7-0 and 4-0 in league play. Last Saturday it beat Georgia State 49-22 in Harrisonburg. Camden Coleman threw two touchdown passes, and George Pettaway ran for 119 yards, his fourth straight 100-yard game. AP reports the Dukes have won 12 straight Sun Belt regular-season games and 11 straight at home. ESPN has them scoring 42.9 points a game and allowing 16.0. Earlier this year they beat Wagner 87-3, which is less a football score and more a ZIP code.

Pettaway has 767 rushing yards and seven touchdowns. Coleman has 13 touchdown passes against one interception. Nakian Jackson leads them with 50 tackles. Respect where it's due. They're a good team. Now pack a jacket, Dukes, because here's what you're walking into.

Our Side of the Trail

Jaquari Lewis has eight rushing touchdowns this season, and four of them came last Friday. Singleton has 1,429 passing yards with seven touchdowns and two interceptions. Sam Pickett III has 411 receiving yards and four touchdowns. Caleb Sandstrom has five sacks, and Colton Phares leads us with 38 tackles. We average 421.7 yards a game. That's a lot of trail for a road team to defend in the dark.

The key is the run game. JMU allows 114.3 rushing yards a game. We just ran for 253 at Coastal, and we did it with two quarterbacks and a running back who kept falling into the end zone like it was the only warm room in the house. If we hold the ball like we did Friday, the Dukes' 42.9-point offense spends a lot of the night on the sideline, zipping up its coat.

A Little History, Kindly Told

I won't pretend last year went our way. CollegeFootballData.com has it at JMU 58, App State 10 in Harrisonburg in 2025. I wrote that one in pencil, and I've been erasing it ever since. But in 2024, the Dukes came to Boone and we won 34-20. The mountain remembers.

And while we're opening the scrapbook: App State won three straight FCS national championships, from 2005 to 2007, the first FCS team to do that since the playoffs began in 1978. On Sept. 1, 2007, we went to Michigan Stadium and beat the fifth-ranked Wolverines 34-32 in front of more than 109,000 people. JMU has two FCS titles, 2004 and 2016, and I tip my cap to both. But it's a little like bringing two jars of apple butter to a church supper where somebody already brought three pies and a Big House.

The Dukes joined the Sun Belt for the 2023 football season. We hosted the very first Sun Belt Championship Game, right here in Boone, on Dec. 1, 2018, and won it. Welcome to the league, neighbors. Mind the stairs.

About That Duke

Here's a piece of history I found on JMU's own centennial website, and I love it. The Dukes aren't named for a duke at all. In 1947, the school's first men's basketball players chose the name in honor of Madison College President Samuel P. Duke. JMU says the players told him they'd name the team after him if he'd provide them with towels and equipment. Now that is a mountain-level deal. Some programs get a nickname from a legend. The Dukes got theirs for a stack of towels.

And then, JMU explains, there wasn't really any way to turn a "Duke" into a mascot, so the school went with an English bulldog, the pet of British royalty. Today the Duke Dog is eight feet tall with a crown and cape. We have Yosef, a mountaineer who dresses for the weather. A bulldog in a cape is a fine thing. But it's going to be windy up here Thursday, and capes catch wind.

Porch Talk: Boone vs. Harrisonburg

Boone. We sit at 3,333 feet above sea level. Wikipedia says an older survey had it at 3,332, and somebody went back and found the extra foot. That's how serious we are about up. Boone has the highest elevation of any town of its size east of the Mississippi River, and we average nearly 25 inches of snow a year, far more than the lowlands in the rest of North Carolina. The town is named for Daniel Boone, who camped here more than once, and every summer since 1952, except 2020, folks have watched "Horn in the West," the outdoor drama about the early settlers, in an amphitheater near town. Our 2020 census population was 19,092, and on a Thursday night in October it feels like every one of them is wearing a jacket and yelling at the same time. Yosef will be there. Yosef is always there.

Harrisonburg. Now, I like Harrisonburg. It's a pretty little independent city in the Shenandoah Valley, and Wikipedia says downtown was named Virginia's first culinary district in 2014. Good for them. A valley is a fine place to eat a meal, and it's a fine place to look up at the mountains from. That's what valleys are for.

But I want to point out how most folks reach it: Interstate 81, the main north-south highway in western Virginia, where you can spend a whole afternoon admiring the back of a tractor-trailer. Our roads to Boone have switchbacks. Theirs have tailgates, and I don't mean the fun kind. I'd rate the drive from Harrisonburg to Boone at about 11 switchbacks once you leave the interstate, and every one of them is a little reminder that the Dukes are heading uphill.

Harrisonburg's 2020 population was 51,814, nearly three Boones. Bridgeforth Stadium seats about 24,877, according to Wikipedia. It was built so it can someday expand past 40,000. That's a valley for you: always planning to grow up. We already did. We just did it vertically.

Steady, Then a View

Here's how I see the hike. JMU is unbeaten, scores a bushel of points and hasn't lost at home since last season. But Thursday isn't at home. Thursday is on a mountain, at night, in late October, in front of a crowd that knows how to make a 7-0 team feel like it's 3-0 and lost. We have a back with eight touchdowns, a quarterback room that just went 21 of 26, and a run game that held the ball for more than 33 minutes on Friday.

Bring a jacket, Dukes. Bring two. And slow down when you come over the ridge. The view's worth it.

My call: James Madison Dukes 35, App State Mountaineers 20.

Good for them. A valley is a fine place to eat a meal, and it's a fine place to look up at the mountains from. That's what valleys are for.

But I want to point out how most folks reach it: Interstate 81, the main north-south highway in western Virginia, where you can spend a whole afternoon admiring the back of a tractor-trailer. Our roads to Boone have switchbacks. Theirs have tailgates, and I don't mean the fun kind. I'd rate the drive from Harrisonburg to Boone at about 11 switchbacks once you leave the interstate, and every one of them is a little reminder that the Dukes are heading uphill.

Steady, Then a View

Here's how I see the hike. JMU is unbeaten, scores a bushel of points and hasn't lost at home since last season. But Thursday isn't at home. Thursday is on a mountain, at night, in late October, in front of a crowd that knows how to make a 7-0 team feel like it's 3-0 and lost. We have a back with eight touchdowns, a quarterback room that just went 21 of 26, and a run game that held the ball for more than 33 minutes on Friday.
Bring a jacket, Dukes. Bring two. And slow down when you come over the ridge. The view's worth it.
My call: James Madison Dukes 35, App State Mountaineers 20.

Coastal's 58-yard field goal was a beauty, and it still cleared more hills than most of South Carolina has to offer.
Backup Henry Hasselbeck ran for 125 yards and threw his first touchdown pass, a 31-yarder to Sam Pickett III that put App State up 35-24 with 6:41 left.
JMU's own history says its players took the Dukes name in 1947 in exchange for towels and equipment. Boone traded for nothing; we just climbed.
James Madison is 7-0 after a 49-22 win over Georgia State, and AP reports 12 straight Sun Belt regular-season wins and 11 straight home wins.

articles.title: Quack-Quack, Wrong Pond: Georgia State Flies From a Converted Baseball Park Into Jonesboro, and the Red Wolves Just Held the Ball for 40 Minutes
articles.byline: Ty Doucet-Harmon, The Arkansas State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Georgia State (4-2) at Arkansas State (3-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 7 p.m. ET, Centennial Bank Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Quaaack. That's the sound of a mallard settling into the decoys, and it's the sound of me settling into my seat at Centennial Bank Stadium. Ty Doucet-Harmon here, Delta duck guide, Red Wolves lifer, and the only man in Craighead County who brings a duck call to a football game and uses it for every first down. Pull up a bucket. Let's talk scouting. And if you hear a little quack in the middle of a paragraph, that's not a typo. That's tradition.

Part 1: Forty Minutes in the Blind

Duck hunting is mostly waiting. You get up before dawn, you sit very still, and you outlast the birds. Last Saturday night in Hattiesburg, the Red Wolves went duck hunting. Arkansas State beat Southern Miss 23-13 at Renasant Stadium, in front of 22,585, and we held the ball for 40 minutes and 8 seconds. Southern Miss had it for 19:52. Quack. That's patience, friends.

It wasn't pretty, and I won't pretend it was. AP counted five punts, four of them after three-and-outs. We went 4-for-17 on third down. But every time we did score, we built a real drive: AP says all five scoring drives ran from seven to 13 plays. And we went 3-for-3 on fourth down, which in duck terms means we didn't flinch when the birds circled.

Clune Van Andel was the man in the blind. He made field goals of 29, 40 and 44 yards and both extra points, 3-for-3 and 11 points. Kenyon Clay ran in from 2 yards to make it 13-0 in the second quarter, and Timothy Carter added a 2-yard touchdown early in the fourth for a 23-7 lead. Trey Owens completed 17 of 25 passes for 170 yards with no interceptions, and we didn't turn it over once.

The defense picked off Landry Lyddy twice. AG McGhee had one of those and led the team with seven tackles, and Dontrae Henderson had the other. Southern Miss also turned it over on downs three times. Then, to finish it, the Red Wolves ran the last 7:21 off the clock with a 14-play drive to the Southern Miss 11. That's not football, friends. That's a man sitting in a cold blind until the sun comes up, smiling.

We're 3-4 and 1-2 in the Sun Belt, and this was our first road win of the season. Our other two wins came at home, over West Georgia and Kennesaw State. A week earlier, on Oct. 8, we lost a 56-49 shootout at home to South Alabama, so this was a happy change of pace. Quack-quack.

Part 2: Panthers, Meet the Ridge

Saturday, 7 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN+, Georgia State comes to Jonesboro. And I'll be fair first, because my granddaddy said you compliment the bird before you call it in.

The Panthers can play. AP's preview has them 23rd in FBS in yards at 452.7 a game, 26th in scoring at 36.5 points a game, and 26th on third down, converting 47.5 of every 100. Cameran Brown has 1,291 passing yards and 13 touchdown passes. Rodshaun Dorsey has seven touchdown catches, and Xavier Esqillion has seven sacks. Seven! That fella hunts.

Now let me tell you what I see from the blind.

The Last Flight Didn't Land

Georgia State just flew to Harrisonburg and got plucked, 49-22, by James Madison. JMU led 35-10 at halftime. The Panthers went 4-for-13 on third down and turned it over twice. And according to AP, Georgia State's turnover margin is minus-4 this season, 113th in FBS. Arkansas State's is plus-3, 34th. That's a duck that drops its own feathers, friends. We scoop them up.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com has Arkansas State 7-2 against Georgia State in their meetings. The last one, in 2024, was a 27-20 Red Wolves win in Atlanta. Seven and two. That's not a rivalry. That's a migration pattern.

Where It Gets Real

I won't hide our own soft spots, because honest guides bring home more ducks. AP's preview has our defense 124th in FBS against the run, giving up 195.4 yards a game, and 129th on third down. The Panthers run for 206 yards a game. That's the whole hunt right there: if the Red Wolves stop the run, Georgia State's 32:34 average time of possession, 25th in FBS, turns into a lot of punting.

On our side, Owens has 1,631 passing yards and nine touchdowns. Hunter Summers leads us with 31 catches for 422 yards. Joe Drew leads the team with 64 tackles, and he's been in on everything all year. And our pass defense is 31st in FBS. Georgia State, you can throw it, but bring a retriever.

The Mascot Report

In 2008 Arkansas State became the Red Wolves. The red wolf is a real North American animal,, and it never needed a name change since. Georgia State's Panthers have only played football since 2010. Their whole program is younger than some of the decoys in my truck. I respect a young program. I just like mine aged, like a good cast-iron skillet.

Ty's Blind Report: Jonesboro vs. Atlanta

Jonesboro. We live on top of a ridge, folks. Wikipedia says Jonesboro sits atop Crowley's Ridge in northeast Arkansas, a rare bit of high ground rising out of the flat Delta. Everybody else in the Delta looks up at us. Craighead Forest Park, owned by the city, sits right on the ridge with a 60-acre fishing lake, camping, hiking and biking trails. The Delta Symphony Orchestra, the only professional symphony in northeast Arkansas, has been playing here for more than four decades. So yes, I have a duck call in one pocket and a symphony ticket in the other.

Our population in 2020 was 78,576, and on a Saturday night at Centennial Bank Stadium, which seats 30,406 since 2015, it sounds like all of them brought calls. The stadium opened in 1974. It's been ours from day one.

Atlanta. Now, Atlanta. It's a big city, 498,715 people in 2020, and it's got a lot going for it. The Coca-Cola Company has its headquarters there, and Hartsfield-Jackson is the world's busiest airport. Friends, when your proudest landmark is the place where everybody's trying to leave, I have questions.

And Georgia State's football stadium? Wikipedia says Center Parc Stadium was built for the 1996 Summer Olympics, then turned into Turner Field for the Braves. Then the Braves packed up after 2016 and moved to Truist Park in Cobb County. So the Panthers play in a ballpark that the baseball team left. That's like setting up your decoys on a pond after the ducks already flew to the next county. Quack-quack, wrong pond.

I'll grant Atlanta this: it has big skyscrapers along Peachtree. Jonesboro has a ridge. Theirs was built by people. Ours was built by God, and nobody's ever had to repaint it.

The Final Call

Here's my scouting report. Georgia State scores a lot, holds the ball, and brings a pass rusher with seven sacks. Arkansas State just held the ball for 40 minutes, didn't turn it over, picked off two passes, and owns a 7-2 record against the Panthers. The question is our run defense. If the Red Wolves tighten up, this one comes down to the fourth quarter, and a fourth quarter in Jonesboro is a cold blind at dawn. We're used to waiting. The Panthers are city cats.

Get in the blind early, keep your voice low until it counts, and when it counts, let it rip. Quaaack.

My call: Arkansas State Red Wolves 30, Georgia State Panthers 29.

articles.title: Low Tide, Then High Tide: Coastal Takes a Bye After a Three-Point Loss to App State, and Next Up Is a Halloween Trip to Atlanta, Where the Chants Are 4-0
articles.byline: Marigold 'Goldie' Seabrook, The Coastal Carolina Fanatic
articles.matchup: Bye week for Coastal Carolina (2-5) on Oct. 24. Next: Coastal Carolina at Georgia State (4-2), Sat., Oct. 31, Center Parc Stadium, Atlanta (kickoff time and TV to be announced)
articles.text:
Hey, y'all. Goldie Seabrook here, sandals on, because it is not November yet and I have principles. This week's Low Tide Notes come to you from a quiet dock on the Waccamaw, because Coastal Carolina has no game on Saturday, Oct. 24. It's a bye week. That's the honest truth, and I'm going to use it the way the tide uses the moon: to pull back, regroup and come in strong.

So, two things today. First, we look back at Friday night's 35-32 loss to App State. Then we look ahead to Halloween in Atlanta, where the Chanticleers have a little history I'd like to tell you about, kindly and at length.

Part 1: The Friday Night Tide Chart

App State beat Coastal 35-32 at Brooks Stadium on Friday, Oct. 16, in front of 19,485 people. We're 2-5 and 1-2 in the Sun Belt. That stings like stepping on a shell barefoot. But I want you to see the whole beach, not just the shell.

The first half was high tide. Deuce Bailey threw a 21-yard touchdown pass to Tristian Gardner on our first drive. After App State went up 14-7, Bailey found Robby Washington for 71 yards to tie it. Then Bailey put together a 13-play, 78-yard drive and hit Ben Verges for an 8-yard touchdown with 1:53 left in the half. And then, my friends, the moment I'll be telling my grandchildren about. Reggie Jean recovered a fumble with 12 seconds left. Bailey hit Colton Hinton for 24 yards. And Nico Cavanillas Alti kicked a career-long 58-yard field goal as the half ended. 24-14, Chants. Teal deal, y'all.

Then the tide went out. App State scored 21 straight points. Jaquari Lewis finished with four touchdown runs, and the Mountaineers' backup, Henry Hasselbeck, ran 21 times for 125 yards and threw a 31-yard touchdown pass for a 35-24 lead with 6:41 left. Devin Henderson picked off Bailey in the third quarter to set up one of those scores.

But here's the part I love. Our kids came back. Jaden Allen-Hendrix ran it in from 2 yards out with 3:11 left, and Bailey hit Dominic Lee-Knicely for the two-point conversion. 35-32. App State ran out the clock from there, but the Chants made them earn every second.

Bailey threw for 298 yards and three touchdowns. Washington caught five passes for 118 yards. Lee-Knicely ran for 90. Marcellius Pulliam made 12 tackles, and he leads the team with 67 this season. And we had only one turnover and five penalties.

Here's my sunburn, though. App State ran for 253 yards and converted 8 of 14 third downs. We'll need to fix that during this off week. Our run defense is giving up 198.7 yards a game, per ESPN.

Before Friday, we won 27-21 at Marshall on Oct. 10. So the season isn't a shipwreck. It's a boat that needs one good week in the dry dock.

The Bye Week, Honestly

Nobody plays Coastal this Saturday. I'll spend it on the Conway Riverwalk, the stretch of restaurants along the Waccamaw River that anchors the downtown renovation, according to Wikipedia. I'll eat something fried, watch the river and arrange seashells into formations on the table until the waiter asks me to stop. A bye week is just low tide, y'all. Low tide is when you find the good shells.

Part 2: Halloween in the City Named Terminus

Our next game is Saturday, Oct. 31, at Georgia State, at Center Parc Stadium in Atlanta. ESPN has the kickoff time and TV as not yet announced, so I'll tell you when I know.

Let me tip my sun hat to the Panthers first. Georgia State is 4-2, and ESPN has them scoring 36.5 points a game while allowing 24.0. Cameran Brown has thrown for 1,291 yards and 13 touchdowns. Rodshaun Dorsey has seven touchdown catches. Lanear McCrary Jr. has 385 rushing yards. Xavier Esqillion has seven sacks, which is a lot of sacks, and I will be explaining him to you with a very large seashell. They also have their own business on Saturday, at Arkansas State, so they'll come into our game off a road trip while we come in rested. Tide's coming in.

Now. The history. According to CollegeFootballData.com, Coastal Carolina has played at Center Parc Stadium four times: 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Coastal won all four. And on Oct. 31, 2020, which was Halloween, Coastal beat Georgia State 51-0 in that stadium. Fifty-one to nothing, on Halloween, in Atlanta. Y'all, that's a spooky little stat for somebody, and it isn't us.

The overall series is close. CFBD has Coastal up 5-4, and we won 40-27 in Conway last November. Georgia State also beat us 30-17 in Conway in 2023. So I respect the Panthers. But in their building, in four tries, our rooster has never lost.

And about that building. Wikipedia says Center Parc was built for the 1996 Olympics, then converted into Turner Field, the home of the Atlanta Braves, and then converted again for football. It's had more makeovers than my beach bag. We, meanwhile, play on the teal turf at Brooks Stadium, which The Sun News reports was the idea of former Chants punt returner Zach Silverberg and debuted Sept. 19, 2015. The school believes it was the first teal field in the world. Their stadium was built for the Olympics, then baseball, then football. Ours was built for us, and then we painted the grass the color of the sea.

Let's talk mascots, kindly. A Panther is a fine animal. But the Sun News explains that our Chanticleer comes from Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales, a rooster who rules the barnyard with cunning and wit. It's pronounced SHON-ti-cleer. Georgia State's mascot is a big cat. Ours has a literary pedigree going back more than 600 years. One of us was assigned reading.

Tales From Two Towns

Conway. My hometown sits on a bluff overlooking the Waccamaw River. Wikipedia says it was founded in 1732 as part of Royal Governor Robert Johnson's township plan, and the early colonists called it Kings Town and then Kingston. Today it has 24,849 people, up from 17,103 in 2010, and it's part of the Myrtle Beach metro area, which means the ocean is a short drive from my front porch. We've got the Riverwalk, the river, the beach down the road and a teal football field. If you want a better way to spend a fall Saturday, I don't know where you'd find it.

Atlanta. Atlanta is a big, busy city of 498,715, and I hope its folks have a lovely Halloween. But Wikipedia tells me the place was first named Terminus, because it was the end point of a railroad. Then Thrasherville. Then Marthasville, when it had six buildings and 30 residents in 1842. Conway was already more than a hundred years old by then. Atlanta also has the world's busiest airport, per Wikipedia, which tells me a whole lot of people are trying very hard to get somewhere else, like the beach. And the city was literally named Terminus, meaning the end. For Georgia State on Halloween, in four tries, it has been.

Low Tide Notes

1. Run defense. App State ran for 253 yards. The bye week is for the big guys up front.
2. Keep Bailey cooking. He's thrown 16 touchdowns with four interceptions this season, per ESPN.
3. Remember Halloween 2020. The tide can come all the way in.

Rest up, Chants. Teal deal, y'all.

Xavier Esqillion has seven sacks, which is a lot of sacks, and I will be explaining him to you with a very large seashell. They also have their own business on Saturday, at Arkansas State, so they'll come into our game off a road trip while we come in rested. Tide's coming in.

Now. The history. According to CollegeFootballData.com, Coastal Carolina has played at Center Parc Stadium four times: 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Coastal won all four. And on Oct. 31, 2020, which was Halloween, Coastal beat Georgia State 51-0 in that stadium. Fifty-one to nothing, on Halloween, in Atlanta. Y'all, that's a spooky little stat for somebody, and it isn't us.

The overall series is close. CFBD has Coastal up 5-4, and we won 40-27 in Conway last November. Georgia State also beat us 30-17 in Conway in 2023. So I respect the Panthers. But in their building, in four tries, our rooster has never lost.

And about that building. Wikipedia says Center Parc was built for the 1996 Olympics, then converted into Turner Field, the home of the Atlanta Braves, and then converted again for football. It's had more makeovers than my beach bag. We, meanwhile, play on the teal turf at Brooks Stadium, which The Sun News reports was the idea of former Chants punt returner Zach Silverberg and debuted Sept. 19, 2015. The school believes it was the first teal field in the world. Their stadium was built for the Olympics, then baseball, then football. Ours was built for us, and then we painted the grass the color of the sea.

Let's talk mascots, kindly. A Panther is a fine animal. But the Sun News explains that our Chanticleer comes from Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales, a rooster who rules the barnyard with cunning and wit. It's pronounced SHON-ti-cleer. Georgia State's mascot is a big cat. Ours has a literary pedigree going back more than 600 years. One of us was assigned reading.
Tales From Two Towns

Conway. My hometown sits on a bluff overlooking the Waccamaw River. Wikipedia says it was founded in 1732 as part of Royal Governor Robert Johnson's township plan, and the early colonists called it Kings Town and then Kingston. Today it has 24,849 people, up from 17,103 in 2010, and it's part of the Myrtle Beach metro area, which means the ocean is a short drive from my front porch. We've got the Riverwalk, the river, the beach down the road and a teal football field. If you want a better way to spend a fall Saturday, I don't know where you'd find it.

Atlanta. Atlanta is a big, busy city of 498,715, and I hope its folks have a lovely Halloween. But Wikipedia tells me the place was first named Terminus, because it was the end point of a railroad. Then Thrasherville. Then Marthasville, when it had six buildings and 30 residents in 1842. Conway was already more than a hundred years old by then. Atlanta also has the world's busiest airport, per Wikipedia, which tells me a whole lot of people are trying very hard to get somewhere else, like the beach. And the city was literally named Terminus, meaning the end. For Georgia State on Halloween, in four tries, it has been.
Low Tide Notes

1. Run defense. App State ran for 253 yards. The bye week is for the big guys up front. 2. Keep Bailey cooking. He's thrown 16 touchdowns with four interceptions this season, per ESPN. 3. Remember Halloween 2020. The tide can come all the way in.
Rest up, Chants. Teal deal, y'all.

articles.title: Granddad's Binder Says Rest Up: Georgia Southern Takes a Bye After Winning in Norfolk, Then App State Comes to the Prettiest Little Stadium in America on Halloween
articles.byline: Royce Ogeechee, The Georgia Southern Fanatic
articles.matchup: Bye week for Georgia Southern (3-4) on Oct. 24. Next: App State (4-2) at Georgia Southern, Sat., Oct. 31, Allen E. Paulson Stadium, Statesboro (kickoff time and TV to be announced)
articles.text:
Pull up a lawn chair, friends. Royce Ogeechee here, sweet tea in one hand and my granddad's old wooden playbook binder in the other. Welcome to this week's Creek Side Chat. Hail Southern.

First, the honest news: Georgia Southern doesn't play this Saturday, Oct. 24. It's an open date. That works out fine for this old farm kid, because the Eagles already did their work for the week. They went to Norfolk on Thursday night and brought home a win. And when the bye is over, the next game is the one that circles itself on every Bulloch County calendar. App State is coming to Statesboro on Halloween.

Part 1: A Thursday Night Win in Norfolk

Georgia Southern beat Old Dominion 23-15 on Thursday, Oct. 15, at S.B. Ballard Stadium, in front of 17,912 people. That makes us 3-4 overall and 2-1 in the Sun Belt. I'll take it, and I'll take it with extra ice.

It didn't start pretty. Old Dominion opened the game with an 11-play, 75-yard drive and a 20-yard touchdown pass to tight end Leon Haughton Jr. But the Eagles answered right back with a 12-play, 75-yard drive of their own, and Terrance Gibbs ran it in from 11 yards out. Tied 7-7.

Then the defense took over. Aaron Sears recovered a fumble, and Tripp Bryant kicked a 33-yard field goal. Bryant added a 43-yarder and then a 31-yarder in the final minute of the half. Three field goals in one quarter, folks. My granddad used to say a field goal is a touchdown that wore its church clothes. We were dressed up for Sunday by halftime, 16-7.

Turner Helton hit Gibbs for an 11-yard touchdown at the end of an 11-play drive in the third quarter, and it was 23-7. Gibbs scored on the ground and through the air, and that's the kind of night that gets you a sweet tea rating of five full glasses. ODU did hit a 71-yard touchdown pass and a two-point conversion with about 10 minutes left. But it got no closer.

Helton went 23 of 30 for 205 yards. Alex Taylor caught seven passes for 75 yards. Tyrese Woodgett ran for 77. Anthony Bynum had two sacks. And look at this, from AP: Old Dominion managed only 65 rushing yards on 32 carries. That's 2.0 a carry. We had the ball for 36:26.

Now, the binder has notes in the margin, and they're honest notes. We were flagged 13 times for 120 yards. We went 3-for-12 on third down. Those are bye-week chores, like fixing the fence before the cows get out.

The Bye Week

So nobody plays Georgia Southern this Saturday. Here's how I'll spend it. I'll rate a couple of tailgates I'm not even going to, just for practice. And I'll keep one eye on Thursday night, because App State hosts unbeaten James Madison in Boone on Oct. 22. Whatever happens there, the Mountaineers will have nine days to get ready for us. We'll have had two weeks. Granddad would call that a head start.

Part 2: App State, Halloween, and the Prettiest Little Stadium in America

On Saturday, Oct. 31, App State visits Allen E. Paulson Stadium. ESPN lists the kickoff time and TV as not yet announced.

App State is 4-2 and 1-1 in the league. I'll be respectful, the way Granddad taught me, because this rivalry has earned it. Jaquari Lewis has 346 rushing yards and eight touchdowns, per ESPN, and he just ran for four touchdowns at Coastal. Sam Pickett III has 411 receiving yards. Caleb Sandstrom has five sacks. The Mountaineers average 29.5 points a game. That's a real football team.

But the Mountaineers come in with a few things to answer for. They scored three points in their last home game, a loss to Old Dominion, and that's the same ODU team we just beat in Norfolk. Their run defense gives up 137.8 a game, according to ESPN. And they'll be playing their second Sun Belt game in nine days after hosting a team that's 7-0.

Now, the history, from the binder and from CollegeFootballData.com. Last November, Georgia Southern went up the mountain and won 25-23 in Boone. WTOC reported that Tripp Bryant, then a freshman, made four field goals that night. The year before that, we beat App State 29-20 in Statesboro. And in 2022, at Paulson, we won 51-48. In Statesboro, the last two times App State visited, they went home the long way, with nothing but the leaves to look at.

The rivalry has a name, and it's a good one: Deeper Than Hate. It's a terrible name for a Sunday school class, but it's a perfect name for a football rivalry. Deeper than hate, kinder than you'd think.

Then there's the stadium. Wikipedia says the phrase "Prettiest Little Stadium in America" was coined by Erk Russell, the coach Georgia Southern hired in 1982 to start the new program. Erk's bust now stands along the fence near the Gene Bishop Fieldhouse. And this program has six FCS national championships, per Wikipedia. App State has a lovely stadium on a mountain. We have a pretty stadium, Erk's blessing and six trophies.

Let me open Granddad's binder to the page with the dog-eared corner. Wikipedia says Erk Russell's Eagles won their first national championship in 1985, then went back to Tacoma in 1986 and beat the Arkansas State Indians for another one. Erk won one more in his final game in 1989, and Tim Stowers' Eagles made it four in 1990. The program has also produced two Walter Payton Award winners, which makes it one of only five schools with more than one. Granddad wrote "1985" on the first page in pencil, and I won't let anybody erase it.

Tales From Two Towns

Statesboro. This is home, the 'Boro, the county seat of Bulloch County, with 33,438 people at the 2020 census. Wikipedia says the Georgia legislature created the town of "Statesborough" in December 1803. In 1906, it was picked as home of the First District A&M School, which grew into Georgia Southern. And Statesboro inspired a whole song. Blind Willie McTell wrote "Statesboro Blues" in the 1920s, and the Allman Brothers Band recorded a well-known version. Name me another Sun Belt town with its own blues song, friend. I'll wait right here on the porch.

Boone. Boone is a fine little mountain town of 19,092, Wikipedia says, up in the Blue Ridge, and its folks are kind. But here's the story of how it got its name. Daniel Boone camped there on several occasions. That's it. The man pitched a tent a few times, and they named the whole town after him. Down here, we'd call that a tailgate. Boone also had a little railroad nicknamed "Tweetsie," until the flood of 1940. Statesboro has a song. Boone has a train that tweets.

And one more thing, App State. You're bringing your boys down from the mountain to the flat, warm country of south Georgia on Halloween. Come hungry, bring a light jacket, and leave your snow boots at home. We'll have the sweet tea ready.

Creek Side Checklist

1. Clean up the flags. Thirteen is too many.
2. Keep running the clock. 36:26 of possession is how you keep a good offense on the sideline.
3. Get Bryant in range. The young man has been App State's worry before.

Rest well, Eagles. Hail Southern.

articles.title: Next Stop, Jonesboro: Georgia State Brings the No. 23 Offense in FBS to a Ridge Whose Defense Ranks 124th Against the Run
articles.byline: Malik Overstreet, The Georgia State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Georgia State (4-2) at Arkansas State (3-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 7 p.m. ET, Centennial Bank Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Next stop, third-and-long. Malik Overstreet here, MARTA card in one pocket, third-down chart in the other, typing this from a train car somewhere under downtown Atlanta. If you're new: I rate every opponent by Atlanta traffic. A light opponent is a Sunday-morning Downtown Connector. A tough one is I-285 at 5:15 on a Friday in the rain. Let's ride.

Part 1: The Harrisonburg Detour

I'm a policy-school guy, so we start with the honest report. James Madison beat us 49-22 last Saturday at Bridgeforth Stadium. The Dukes are 7-0, they've won 12 straight Sun Belt regular-season games according to AP, and they played like it. Traffic rating: I-75/85 through Midtown during a Falcons game. Nobody's getting home on time.

It started fine. JMU scored first, and then Lanear McCrary Jr. ran it in from a yard out to tie it 7-7 in the first quarter. That was a nice merge. Then JMU scored four touchdowns in the second quarter alone, and Samer Layous's 33-yard field goal was our only answer before halftime. It was 35-10 at the break.

The second half had some good rides. Cameran Brown hit Rodshaun Dorsey for a 32-yard touchdown in the third quarter. Late in the fourth, Ayden Pereira scored on a 1-yard run. Brown finished 13 of 25 for 134 yards with a touchdown and an interception, and he ran nine times for 71 yards. DJ Murray Jr. added 56 yards on nine carries. As a team we ran for 188 yards at 5.1 a carry against the best defense in the league, and we had the ball for 30:09, a hair more than they did.

The bad news: we went 4-for-13 on third down, and that's my department. We missed both two-point tries. And we turned it over twice. That's how you lose by 27 to an unbeaten team in its own building. We're 4-2 and 1-1 in the Sun Belt. And let's keep the whole route in view: before Harrisonburg, this team beat North Carolina A&T 59-10, won 31-17 at Kennesaw State, beat Northern Illinois 35-14 and handled Old Dominion 42-10, with a loss at UCF in there too. Before last weekend, the Panthers had a week off to rest. One bad trip on the Connector doesn't mean you give up on the car. Next stop, Jonesboro.

Part 2: The Ridge Route

Saturday, 7 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN+, Georgia State visits Arkansas State at Centennial Bank Stadium.

Let me be fair to the Red Wolves first. They won 23-13 at Southern Miss last Saturday, held the ball for 40:08, didn't turn it over and got three field goals from Clune Van Andel. They went 3-for-3 on fourth down. AP's preview has them 34th in FBS in turnover margin at plus-3, and 31st against the pass. Joe Drew leads them with 64 tackles. That's a real defense in the air. I respect it.

Now let's look at the map.

The Run Game Express

AP's preview lists Arkansas State 124th in FBS in run defense, at 195.4 yards a game. It's 129th on third-down defense, letting opponents convert 45.9 of every 100 times, and 113th in red zone defense, letting opponents score on 91.3 of every 100 trips.

Georgia State runs for 206.0 yards a game, 26th in FBS. We convert 47.5 of every 100 third downs, 26th, and we score on 92 of every 100 red zone trips, 24th. We average 452.7 yards a game, 23rd in FBS, and 36.5 points, 26th. McCrary has 385 rushing yards and four touchdowns. Brown has 1,291 passing yards, 13 touchdowns and 65.4 completions for every 100 throws. Dorsey has seven touchdown catches.

Traffic rating for that Red Wolves run defense? Peachtree Street at 6 a.m. on a holiday. Green lights all the way down.

The Pass Rush

Xavier Esqillion has seven sacks this season. Seven. Arkansas State quarterback Trey Owens has thrown six interceptions, and the Red Wolves just ran 51 times for 2.6 yards a carry at Southern Miss. If they have to throw, Esqillion is going to be the Hartsfield-Jackson security checkpoint at Thanksgiving: you're not getting through quickly, and you're going to think about your choices.

Honest Commuter's Note

Arkansas State has had our number. CollegeFootballData.com has the Red Wolves 7-2 against us, and they won 27-20 in Atlanta in 2024. And our turnover margin is minus-4, 113th in FBS, per AP. That's the pothole on this route. Hold onto the football, and the ride's smooth. And yes, the Red Wolves just lost a 56-49 shootout at home to South Alabama on Oct. 8. Fifty-six at home. Traffic rating: no traffic at all, just open road for the other guys.

Big City vs. The Ridge: A Tale of Two Towns

Atlanta. Welcome to my city, population 498,715 in 2020. Atlanta's Latin motto is "Resurgens," rising again, after the phoenix. Our skyline runs north to south along Peachtree through Downtown, Midtown and Buckhead. We have the headquarters of Coca-Cola, Home Depot, Delta and Chick-fil-A, and Hartsfield-Jackson is the world's busiest airport. Georgia State is the largest in-person university by enrollment based in Georgia, per Wikipedia, with 53,144 students.

And our stadium has a story nobody else in the Sun Belt can tell. Center Parc Stadium was built as Centennial Olympic Stadium for the 1996 Summer Olympics. It became Turner Field, home of the Braves, from 1997 to 2016. Now it's ours. Your stadium has hosted football games. Ours hosted the world.

Jonesboro. Now, Jonesboro. Lovely place, 78,576 people in 2020, and I mean that kindly. It sits on top of Crowley's Ridge, which I'm told is the high ground in northeast Arkansas. We have skyscrapers. They have a ridge. The ridge is very proud of itself.

Here's my go-to fact, straight from Wikipedia: the Mall at Turtle Creek, which opened in 2006, was the largest mall in northeast Arkansas and the only enclosed mall built in the whole country that year. The only one! In 2006, every developer in America looked at the map and said, "Not here." Jonesboro said, "Hold my shopping bags."

And traffic? I tried to rate Jonesboro traffic and my scale broke. On my system, an Atlanta Tuesday is a 9. A Jonesboro Saturday is a red light that turns green while you're still finding your sunglasses. Wikipedia lists one parkway through town, the Crowley's Ridge Parkway. We have I-285, which has its own weather.

I'll give Jonesboro this: Centennial Bank Stadium seats 30,406, and those folks bring duck calls. I've been warned. I'm bringing earplugs and a playbook full of run plays. And when it's over, I'm taking the long way home through Memphis, because after a win you want the scenic route, and from Jonesboro, honestly, every route is the scenic route. There's just a lot of scenery and not much else in the way, which, for a commuter like me, is its own kind of paradise.

Last Stop

Here's my route map. Georgia State is a top-30 offense in yards, scoring, rushing and third downs. Arkansas State is in the bottom 10 in FBS against the run and on third-down defense. The Red Wolves will try to hold the ball like they did in Hattiesburg. That works great until you face a team that also likes to hold the ball, 32:34 a game, 25th in FBS. Hold onto it, run it, and let Esqillion hunt.

Next stop, Jonesboro. Mind the gap, and mind the ridge.

My call: Arkansas State Red Wolves 30, Georgia State Panthers 29.

AP's preview lists Arkansas State 124th in FBS in run defense, at 195.4 yards a game. It's 129th on third-down defense, letting opponents convert 45.9 of every 100 times, and 113th in red zone defense, letting opponents score on 91.3 of every 100 trips.

Georgia State runs for 206.0 yards a game, 26th in FBS. We convert 47.5 of every 100 third downs, 26th, and we score on 92 of every 100 red zone trips, 24th. We average 452.7 yards a game, 23rd in FBS, and 36.5 points, 26th. McCrary has 385 rushing yards and four touchdowns. Brown has 1,291 passing yards, 13 touchdowns and 65.4 completions for every 100 throws. Dorsey has seven touchdown catches.
Traffic rating for that Red Wolves run defense? Peachtree Street at 6 a.m. on a holiday. Green lights all the way down.
The Pass Rush

Xavier Esqillion has seven sacks this season. Seven. Arkansas State quarterback Trey Owens has thrown six interceptions, and the Red Wolves just ran 51 times for 2.6 yards a carry at Southern Miss. If they have to throw, Esqillion is going to be the Hartsfield-Jackson security checkpoint at Thanksgiving: you're not getting through quickly, and you're going to think about your choices.
Honest Commuter's Note

Arkansas State has had our number. CollegeFootballData.com has the Red Wolves 7-2 against us, and they won 27-20 in Atlanta in 2024. And our turnover margin is minus-4, 113th in FBS, per AP. That's the pothole on this route. Hold onto the football, and the ride's smooth. And yes, the Red Wolves just lost a 56-49 shootout at home to South Alabama on Oct. 8. Fifty-six at home. Traffic rating: no traffic at all, just open road for the other guys.
Big City vs. The Ridge: A Tale of Two Towns

Atlanta. Welcome to my city, population 498,715 in 2020. Atlanta's Latin motto is "Resurgens," rising again, after the phoenix. Our skyline runs north to south along Peachtree through Downtown, Midtown and Buckhead. We have the headquarters of Coca-Cola, Home Depot, Delta and Chick-fil-A, and Hartsfield-Jackson is the world's busiest airport. Georgia State is the largest in-person university by enrollment based in Georgia, per Wikipedia, with 53,144 students.

And our stadium has a story nobody else in the Sun Belt can tell. Center Parc Stadium was built as Centennial Olympic Stadium for the 1996 Summer Olympics. It became Turner Field, home of the Braves, from 1997 to 2016. Now it's ours. Your stadium has hosted football games. Ours hosted the world.

Jonesboro. Now, Jonesboro. Lovely place, 78,576 people in 2020, and I mean that kindly. It sits on top of Crowley's Ridge, which I'm told is the high ground in northeast Arkansas. We have skyscrapers. They have a ridge. The ridge is very proud of itself.

Here's my go-to fact, straight from Wikipedia: the Mall at Turtle Creek, which opened in 2006, was the largest mall in northeast Arkansas and the only enclosed mall built in the whole country that year. The only one! In 2006, every developer in America looked at the map and said, "Not here." Jonesboro said, "Hold my shopping bags."

And traffic? I tried to rate Jonesboro traffic and my scale broke. On my system, an Atlanta Tuesday is a 9. A Jonesboro Saturday is a red light that turns green while you're still finding your sunglasses. Wikipedia lists one parkway through town, the Crowley's Ridge Parkway. We have I-285, which has its own weather.

I'll give Jonesboro this: Centennial Bank Stadium seats 30,406, and those folks bring duck calls. I've been warned. I'm bringing earplugs and a playbook full of run plays. And when it's over, I'm taking the long way home through Memphis, because after a win you want the scenic route, and from Jonesboro, honestly, every route is the scenic route. There's just a lot of scenery and not much else in the way, which, for a commuter like me, is its own kind of paradise.
Last Stop

Here's my route map. Georgia State is a top-30 offense in yards, scoring, rushing and third downs. Arkansas State is in the bottom 10 in FBS against the run and on third-down defense. The Red Wolves will try to hold the ball like they did in Hattiesburg. That works great until you face a team that also likes to hold the ball, 32:34 a game, 25th in FBS. Hold onto it, run it, and let Esqillion hunt.
Next stop, Jonesboro. Mind the gap, and mind the ridge.
My call: Arkansas State Red Wolves 30, Georgia State Panthers 29.

articles.title: Purple Reign Goes Uphill: 7-0 JMU Brings 42.9 Points a Game to a Boone Team That Scored Three on Its Last Home Saturday
articles.byline: Lila Shenandoah, The James Madison Fanatic
articles.matchup: James Madison (7-0) at App State (4-2), Thu., Oct. 22, 7 p.m. ET, Kidd Brewer Stadium, ESPNU
articles.text:
Purple reign, y'all! Lila Shenandoah here, pom-poms fluffed, glitter in places glitter should never be, and a fresh chant already stuck in my head. Ready? "Seven and oh! Seven and oh! Up the mountain, here we go!" Thank you. I'll be here all week. Well, until Thursday. Then I'll be in Boone, wearing every layer I own.

Part 1: Forty-Nine Reasons to Smile

Last Saturday, the Dukes beat Georgia State 49-22 at Bridgeforth Stadium in front of 25,225 friends, and honey, it was a pep rally with a scoreboard.

JC Evans got us started with a 2-yard touchdown run. Georgia State tied it on a 1-yard run by Lanear McCrary Jr., and I'll give the Panthers that: they had a nice six minutes. Then Camden Coleman hit Michael Scott for 20 yards, Evans scored again from the 1, and Coleman found KD Mosley for 19 yards. Seth Cromwell punched in a 3-yarder, and it was 35-10 at halftime. Cheer break: "Thirty-five! Ten! Do it all again!"

Coleman finished 13 of 19 for 185 yards and two touchdowns. George Pettaway ran 14 times for 119 yards and a 12-yard touchdown, and AP says that's his fourth straight game with at least 100 yards. Then, with a minute left, Evans threw a 22-yard touchdown pass to Miles Halbert, because apparently our backup quarterback also has range. The Dukes ran for 250 yards and threw for 265. That's 515 yards, and I made it rhyme: "Five-fifteen! Purple machine!"

The defense showed up with style, too. JT Hooten made 10 tackles, Ernest Willor Jr. had two sacks, and DJ Kelly picked off Cameran Brown. Georgia State went 4-for-13 on third down.

I'll be honest, because cheer captains don't lie about the scoreboard: Morgan Suarez missed two field goals. He also made all seven extra points, and I've already written him a chant. "Seven for seven! Kicking to heaven!"

AP says JMU has now won 12 straight Sun Belt regular-season games and 11 straight home games, and the Dukes are 6-0 all time against Georgia State. We're 7-0 and 4-0 in league play. Earlier this year we beat Wagner 87-3. I tried to write a chant for that one, but I ran out of numbers.

Part 2: Climbing to Boone

Thursday night, 7 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, Kidd Brewer Stadium. JMU at App State.

First, the nice part, because my mama raised a cheerleader, not a grump. App State won at Coastal Carolina 35-32 on Friday, Oct. 16, and it was a gutsy one. Jaquari Lewis scored four rushing touchdowns, and backup Henry Hasselbeck ran for 125 yards and threw a 31-yard touchdown to Sam Pickett III. The Mountaineers came back from 24-14 down at halftime. Good for them. Truly. Pom-poms up.

Now, the scouting report.

The Last Time Boone Was Home

The last time App State played a home game, on Oct. 10, it lost 10-3 to Old Dominion. Three points. At home. In front of its own mountain. Sweetie, I've seen bake sales score more than three. I'm not saying the Mountaineers can't score in Boone. I'm saying their last home crowd went to bed early.

And App State's defense gave up 437 yards to a 2-5 Coastal team on Friday. Deuce Bailey threw for 298 yards and three touchdowns. Now it gets an offense that averages 461.0 yards and 42.9 points a game, per ESPN. Chant with me: "Four-sixty-one! Mountain, run!"

The Purple Machine, By the Numbers

Pettaway has 767 rushing yards and seven touchdowns this season. Coleman has 1,335 passing yards, 13 touchdown passes and only one interception. Thirteen to one! I can't even get thirteen people to one practice. Corey Scott leads us with 333 receiving yards, and Nakian Jackson leads the defense with 50 tackles and 2.5 sacks.

As a team, JMU allows 16.0 points a game, and opponents run for just 114.3 yards a game. App State likes to run. App State is going to find out what a purple wall looks like at 3,333 feet.

History Says Hello

CollegeFootballData.com has last year's meeting in Harrisonburg as JMU 58, App State 10. Fifty-eight! I made that one into a pyramid. To be fair, App State won 34-20 in Boone in 2024, and I respect a home crowd. But we're a different team now, and we've got a quarterback who throws touchdowns the way I throw glitter: everywhere, constantly, joyfully.

The Mountaineers love to talk about their three straight FCS titles from 2005 to 2007, and about beating Michigan in 2007. Those are wonderful memories, darling. That was 19 years ago. Some of our freshmen were in diapers. Some of our freshmen were not yet a twinkle. Meanwhile, the Dukes have two FCS national titles of their own, in 2004 and 2016, and a 7-0 record this season. We're making memories on Thursday night TV.

Valley vs. Mountain: A Tale of Two Towns

Harrisonburg. Let me roll out the purple carpet. Harrisonburg is an independent city in the Shenandoah Valley, and in 2014 downtown was designated Virginia's first culinary district, according to Wikipedia. It was also named a Great American Main Street by the National Main Street Association that same year, and back in 2001 it became Virginia's first Arts and Cultural District. We are the first at a lot of things. We like being first. It's a theme.

Game day at Bridgeforth means the Marching Royal Dukes, nicknamed "Virginia's Finest," with one of the largest college marching band rosters in the country: 535 members in 2024, per Wikipedia. That's not a band. That's a small town with tubas. And of course there's Duke Dog, eight feet tall, with a crown and a cape, who debuted in his current form on Nov. 28, 1982. JMU's own history says our players picked the name Dukes in 1947 in honor of President Samuel P. Duke, and they asked for towels and equipment in return. That's not a bribe, it's team-building.

Boone. Now, Boone is lovely. I mean that. It sits at 3,333 feet, and Wikipedia says it has the highest elevation of any town its size east of the Mississippi. It averages nearly 25 inches of snow a year. It's named for Daniel Boone, who camped there several times. Sweetie, so do I, every time I drive in. Camping is the polite word for what happens when you leave the interstate and start counting switchbacks.

Boone's 2020 population was 19,092. Harrisonburg's was 51,814, almost three Boones. Our marching band alone is about one-thirty-sixth of Boone. I did that math with a calculator covered in rhinestones, and it held up.

And here's the thing about mountains: they're beautiful to look at and exhausting to climb. JMU has been looking at Boone from the valley for a long time. On Thursday, we climb it, plant a purple flag and come back down for supper on the culinary district.

The Final Chant

Here's the scouting report in one breath. JMU is 7-0, scores 42.9 points a game, allows 16.0, has a quarterback with 13 touchdown passes and one interception, and a running back with four straight 100-yard games. App State is a good, gritty team that scored three points in its last home game and gave up 437 yards in its last road game.

Pack a jacket, Dukes Nation. Pack two. Then pack your loudest voice, because 535 band members can't do all the work.

Ready? Okay! "Purple! Reign! Up the mountain, down again!"

My call: James Madison Dukes 35, App State Mountaineers 20.
