articles.title: Peachy: Louisiana Tech Pitched a 24-0 Shutout in the I-20 Showdown, and Now an Old Dominion Offense Ranked 138th in Yards Comes to Ruston
articles.byline: Booker 'Champ' Tullos, The Louisiana Tech Fanatic
articles.matchup: Old Dominion (2-5) at Louisiana Tech (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 5 p.m. ET, Joe Aillet Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Well, howdy, and welcome to the orchard. Champ Tullos here, former fullback, full-time peach man and the proudest Bulldog in Lincoln Parish. I spent my playing days running into people a yard from the end zone, and I spend my Saturdays now hollering at Joe Aillet Stadium. Life is good, the peaches are in the freezer till next June, and the Bulldogs are 2-0 in their brand-new league. That's what we call peachy.

Part 1: The I-20 Showdown, Picked Clean

Last Saturday night, Louisiana Tech went 35 miles east to Monroe and beat UL Monroe 24-0. A shutout. A goose egg. A peach pit with nothing left on it. It was the first I-20 Showdown since 2000, according to ULM Athletics, and 20,653 folks showed up to watch.

Now, I'll be honest, because a fullback tells you exactly where he's going. The first half was slower than a tractor on a two-lane road. It was 0-0 at the break. ULM sacked Blake Baker on the second play, Armoni Rue picked him off, and the Warhawks blocked one of our field goals. Their defense played hard in that first half, and I tip my cap. We also missed two other kicks. Kaegan Kent went 1-for-3 on field goals and Hunter Rioux missed one. Somebody get those boys a peach cobbler and a hug.

Then the second half came, and the orchard bloomed. Taeden Rogers intercepted Aidan Armenta on ULM's first pass of the half, and Sergio Snider ran it in from the 5 for a 7-0 lead. Then Baker threw a 2-yard touchdown pass to Brayden Bockler at the end of an 11-play, 66-yard drive. Then he did it again early in the fourth, another 2-yarder to Bockler. Same play, same man, same result. As a fullback, I love a short-yardage play so good you run it twice. Kent closed it out with a 21-yard field goal.

Baker finished 15 of 21 for 178 yards and two touchdowns. Marcus Calwise Jr. caught eight passes for 119 yards. Andrew Burnette carried 22 times for 79 yards and just kept leaning on folks. Alonzo Jackson Jr. made eight tackles with two for loss, and Kam Franklin returned an interception 66 yards. ULM finished with 228 yards and went 2-for-11 on third down.

That makes two straight Sun Belt wins. The week before, Oct. 10, we beat Louisiana 32-31 at home. One point, one heartbeat, one very sweet Saturday. We're 4-2 overall and 2-0 in our first season in the Sun Belt, which we joined on July 1, 2026, after 13 years in Conference USA.

Part 2: Hear Ye, Hear Ye, the Monarchs Are Coming

Saturday, 5 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Old Dominion visits Joe Aillet Stadium.

The Monarchs are 2-5 and 1-3 in the Sun Belt, and they lost 23-15 at home to Georgia Southern last Thursday. They went 3-for-10 on third down and ran 32 times for 65 yards. Sixty-five yards on 32 carries. Friends, I used to get more than two yards a carry with three linebackers hanging off my back.

The Peach Ripeness Scale

I grade every offense like a peach. A ripe one gives a little when you squeeze it and smells like summer. A green one is hard as a doorknob.

AP's preview has Old Dominion's offense 138th in FBS in yards, at 266 a game. It's 131st in passing, 122nd in rushing and 130th in scoring at 17.7 points a game. ODU converts just 33 of every 100 third downs, 120th, and holds the ball for 27:30 a game, 123rd. That, my friends, is a green peach. You could knock on it like a front door.

Meanwhile, Louisiana Tech scores 33.3 points a game, 43rd in FBS. Our turnover margin is plus-5, 15th in the country, and ODU's is minus-3, 99th. Baker has nine touchdown passes and only one interception. Jalen Mickens leads us with 32 catches for 476 yards. And Alonzo Jackson Jr. leads the defense with 41 tackles and five sacks. That's a ripe one.

Credit Where It's Due

I'll say it plain: Old Dominion's defense is solid. AP ranks it 47th in FBS in yards allowed. Lucas Struck has 52 tackles and Javen Gibson has five sacks. And here's my honest-fullback confession: according to AP, our red zone offense ranks 118th, scoring on 76 of every 100 trips. That's the part of the field where I used to live! I want those Bulldogs running behind the big guys up front like it's the last peach on the tree.

And the history isn't on our side. CollegeFootballData.com has ODU 2-0 against us, winning 30-27 in 2014 and 23-20 in 2021, both in Norfolk. Two three-point games. Well, the Monarchs have never been to Ruston for this one. Welcome. Wipe your feet.

A Brief History of Royalty

The Monarchs played football from 1930 to 1940, then stopped for 68 years, per Wikipedia, and started back up in 2009. Sixty-eight years! That's not a bye week. That's a peach tree that took a nap through World War II, the moon landing and the invention of the microwave. Louisiana Tech, on the other hand, has been playing since 1901. Our first game was a 57-0 loss to LSU, and we kept showing up anyway. That's Ruston for you.

And speaking of history, Terry Bradshaw played quarterback here. Wikipedia says he started out second on the depth chart behind Phil Robertson, who later invented the Duck Commander duck call. Only in Ruston could the backup become a Hall of Famer and the starter go on to build a duck empire. We grow talent like we grow peaches.

Champ's Porch: Ruston vs. Norfolk

Ruston. Our little city had 22,166 people in the 2020 census, and every June we host the annual Peach Festival. The historic Dixie Theater opened in 1928, and it's still the arts hub of town, home to the community theater, the civic symphony and the Piney Hills Gallery. Grambling is six miles down the road. The railroad helped build this town, and Interstate 20 runs right through it, so you can get here easy. Leaving is the hard part.

Norfolk. Now, Norfolk is home to Naval Station Norfolk, the world's largest naval base, and I salute every sailor stationed there, sincerely. Norfolk also has the Nauticus maritime museum, the battleship USS Wisconsin and the Chrysler Museum of Art. Fine places.

But think about it: a town built around the world's biggest Navy base, and its football team is named for kings. In America! We fought a whole war to get rid of those. The Monarchs show up in Ruston, a town that grew up on land donated by a parish sheriff, not a king, and they want us to bow? Friends, the only royalty in Lincoln Parish is a Peach Festival queen.

Norfolk had 238,005 people in 2020, more than 10 Rustons. But it's a water town. The city's own history is all ships and harbors. When the Monarchs come inland to the Piney Hills, there's no harbor, no ocean breeze and no battleship to hide behind. Just a whole lot of pine trees, a red-and-blue crowd and a stadium we've been playing in since 1968.

Peach Pie Wisdom

Here's my plain fullback math. Louisiana Tech is 2-0 in the Sun Belt, coming off a shutout, with a quarterback who's thrown one interception all year and a defense that just held a team to 228 yards. Old Dominion has the 138th-ranked offense in yards and just ran for 65 yards on 32 carries. If the Bulldogs fix their kicking and finish in the red zone, this one will be peachy by halftime instead of after it.

Come early, bring a lawn chair, and if anybody offers you a peach, say yes ma'am.

My call: Louisiana Tech Bulldogs 31, Old Dominion Monarchs 18.

Last Saturday night, Louisiana Tech went 35 miles east to Monroe and beat UL Monroe 24-0. A shutout. A goose egg. A peach pit with nothing left on it. It was the first I-20 Showdown since 2000, according to ULM Athletics, and 20,653 folks showed up to watch.

Now, I'll be honest, because a fullback tells you exactly where he's going. The first half was slower than a tractor on a two-lane road. It was 0-0 at the break. ULM sacked Blake Baker on the second play, Armoni Rue picked him off, and the Warhawks blocked one of our field goals. Their defense played hard in that first half, and I tip my cap. We also missed two other kicks. Kaegan Kent went 1-for-3 on field goals and Hunter Rioux missed one. Somebody get those boys a peach cobbler and a hug.

Then the second half came, and the orchard bloomed. Taeden Rogers intercepted Aidan Armenta on ULM's first pass of the half, and Sergio Snider ran it in from the 5 for a 7-0 lead. Then Baker threw a 2-yard touchdown pass to Brayden Bockler at the end of an 11-play, 66-yard drive. Then he did it again early in the fourth, another 2-yarder to Bockler. Same play, same man, same result. As a fullback, I love a short-yardage play so good you run it twice. Kent closed it out with a 21-yard field goal.

Baker finished 15 of 21 for 178 yards and two touchdowns. Marcus Calwise Jr. caught eight passes for 119 yards. Andrew Burnette carried 22 times for 79 yards and just kept leaning on folks. Alonzo Jackson Jr. made eight tackles with two for loss, and Kam Franklin returned an interception 66 yards. ULM finished with 228 yards and went 2-for-11 on third down.

That makes two straight Sun Belt wins. The week before, Oct. 10, we beat Louisiana 32-31 at home. One point, one heartbeat, one very sweet Saturday. We're 4-2 overall and 2-0 in our first season in the Sun Belt, which we joined on July 1, 2026, after 13 years in Conference USA.
Part 2: Hear Ye, Hear Ye, the Monarchs Are Coming
Saturday, 5 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Old Dominion visits Joe Aillet Stadium.

The Monarchs are 2-5 and 1-3 in the Sun Belt, and they lost 23-15 at home to Georgia Southern last Thursday. They went 3-for-10 on third down and ran 32 times for 65 yards. Sixty-five yards on 32 carries. Friends, I used to get more than two yards a carry with three linebackers hanging off my back.
The Peach Ripeness Scale
I grade every offense like a peach. A ripe one gives a little when you squeeze it and smells like summer. A green one is hard as a doorknob.

AP's preview has Old Dominion's offense 138th in FBS in yards, at 266 a game. It's 131st in passing, 122nd in rushing and 130th in scoring at 17.7 points a game. ODU converts just 33 of every 100 third downs, 120th, and holds the ball for 27:30 a game, 123rd. That, my friends, is a green peach. You could knock on it like a front door.

Meanwhile, Louisiana Tech scores 33.3 points a game, 43rd in FBS. Our turnover margin is plus-5, 15th in the country, and ODU's is minus-3, 99th. Baker has nine touchdown passes and only one interception. Jalen Mickens leads us with 32 catches for 476 yards. And Alonzo Jackson Jr. leads the defense with 41 tackles and five sacks. That's a ripe one.
Credit Where It's Due

I'll say it plain: Old Dominion's defense is solid. AP ranks it 47th in FBS in yards allowed. Lucas Struck has 52 tackles and Javen Gibson has five sacks. And here's my honest-fullback confession: according to AP, our red zone offense ranks 118th, scoring on 76 of every 100 trips. That's the part of the field where I used to live! I want those Bulldogs running behind the big guys up front like it's the last peach on the tree.

And the history isn't on our side. CollegeFootballData.com has ODU 2-0 against us, winning 30-27 in 2014 and 23-20 in 2021, both in Norfolk. Two three-point games. Well, the Monarchs have never been to Ruston for this one. Welcome. Wipe your feet.
A Brief History of Royalty

The Monarchs played football from 1930 to 1940, then stopped for 68 years, per Wikipedia, and started back up in 2009. Sixty-eight years! That's not a bye week. That's a peach tree that took a nap through World War II, the moon landing and the invention of the microwave. Louisiana Tech, on the other hand, has been playing since 1901. Our first game was a 57-0 loss to LSU, and we kept showing up anyway. That's Ruston for you.

And speaking of history, Terry Bradshaw played quarterback here. Wikipedia says he started out second on the depth chart behind Phil Robertson, who later invented the Duck Commander duck call. Only in Ruston could the backup become a Hall of Famer and the starter go on to build a duck empire. We grow talent like we grow peaches.
Champ's Porch: Ruston vs. Norfolk

Ruston. Our little city had 22,166 people in the 2020 census, and every June we host the annual Peach Festival. The historic Dixie Theater opened in 1928, and it's still the arts hub of town, home to the community theater, the civic symphony and the Piney Hills Gallery. Grambling is six miles down the road. The railroad helped build this town, and Interstate 20 runs right through it, so you can get here easy. Leaving is the hard part.

Norfolk. Now, Norfolk is home to Naval Station Norfolk, the world's largest naval base, and I salute every sailor stationed there, sincerely. Norfolk also has the Nauticus maritime museum, the battleship USS Wisconsin and the Chrysler Museum of Art. Fine places.

But think about it: a town built around the world's biggest Navy base, and its football team is named for kings. In America! We fought a whole war to get rid of those. The Monarchs show up in Ruston, a town that grew up on land donated by a parish sheriff, not a king, and they want us to bow? Friends, the only royalty in Lincoln Parish is a Peach Festival queen.

Norfolk had 238,005 people in 2020, more than 10 Rustons. But it's a water town. The city's own history is all ships and harbors. When the Monarchs come inland to the Piney Hills, there's no harbor, no ocean breeze and no battleship to hide behind. Just a whole lot of pine trees, a red-and-blue crowd and a stadium we've been playing in since 1968.
Peach Pie Wisdom

Here's my plain fullback math. Louisiana Tech is 2-0 in the Sun Belt, coming off a shutout, with a quarterback who's thrown one interception all year and a defense that just held a team to 228 yards. Old Dominion has the 138th-ranked offense in yards and just ran for 65 yards on 32 carries. If the Bulldogs fix their kicking and finish in the red zone, this one will be peachy by halftime instead of after it.
Come early, bring a lawn chair, and if anybody offers you a peach, say yes ma'am.
My call: Louisiana Tech Bulldogs 31, Old Dominion Monarchs 18.

articles.title: Laissez les Bons Stats Rouler: The Cajuns Ran for 243 Yards, and Now They Visit a Southern Miss Defense Allowing 252 on the Ground
articles.byline: Amélie 'Mimi' Fontenot, The Louisiana Fanatic
articles.matchup: Louisiana (5-2) at Southern Miss (1-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 5 p.m. ET, Renasant Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Allons danser, mes amis! Mimi Fontenot here, ledger in one hand, accordion playlist in the other, and my two-step shoes already laced for Hattiesburg. If you're new to my corner: I'm an accountant by trade and a zydeco dancer by calling, and I see football the way I see a good dance floor. It's all rhythm. Who's leading, who's following and who just stepped on whose foot. Last Saturday, the Cajuns led every single dance.

Part 1: La Grande Danse at Our Lady of Lourdes

Louisiana beat Troy 33-6 on Oct. 17 at Our Lady of Lourdes Stadium in Lafayette, in front of 20,623, on Family Weekend and the Hall of Fame Game. Grandmère would have been proud. We ran for 243 yards, held the ball for 36:39 and didn't turn it over once. Zéro. My ledger loves a zero in the right column.

It started with a gift. Troy forced a four-and-out on our first drive, but then the Trojans muffed the punt and Harrison Kidder pounced on it at the Troy 8. Three plays later, Lunch Winfield threw a 3-yard touchdown pass to KeDarius Wade. Merci beaucoup, Troy.

The defense stood tall when Troy put together a 15-play drive to open the second quarter, and the Trojans missed a 42-yard field goal at the end of it. Then JJ Garner broke a 37-yard touchdown run with 2:21 left in the half. Tony Sterner kicked a 42-yard field goal with 1:44 left and a 46-yarder as time ran out. That's 12 points in the last 2:21 of a half, and if you've ever seen a zydeco band hit the final chorus, you know exactly how that felt. It was 19-0 at the break.

Troy scored on a 23-yard Tucker Kilcrease run in the third quarter and missed the extra point. Then came the moment I loved most, a 16-play, 91-yard drive that ate 8:22 and ended with Steven Blanco's 2-yard touchdown run. That is a slow waltz, cher, and Troy was waiting for the song to end. Anthony Reagan Jr. finished the scoring with a 15-yard run early in the fourth.

Winfield led a balanced ground game with 65 yards on 15 carries. Garner had 62 on 10, Reagan had 58 on 11, and Blanco had 50 on 10. Four different backs, four different dance partners, all in step. We went 10-for-17 on third down. Jake St. Andre had eight tackles, Maurion Eleam had a sack, and Brent Gordon Jr. broke up three passes. Troy had 267 yards and went 3-for-12 on third down. I'd like to say a quick, sincere prayer for Troy quarterback Goose Crowder, who left the game in the third quarter with what AL.com reported was a shoulder injury.

The Cajuns are 5-2 and 2-1 in the Sun Belt. A week earlier we lost 32-31 at Louisiana Tech, and I'm still not ready to talk about the last step of that dance. Let's leave it in the old ledger.

Part 2: Two-Step to Hattiesburg

Saturday, 5 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN+, Louisiana visits Southern Miss at Renasant Stadium.

Bless them, the Golden Eagles are 1-5 and 0-2 in the Sun Belt. Last Saturday they lost 23-13 at home to Arkansas State. Arkansas State held the ball for 40:08 against them. Forty minutes! The Southern Miss defense was on the dance floor so long it should have gotten a punch card at the band stand.

The Ledger, Please

Mimi always opens the books. Per ESPN's team numbers, Southern Miss allows 252.0 rushing yards a game and 32.7 points. Louisiana runs for 200.1 yards a game and allows only 104.3 on the ground and 19.3 points. In accounting we call that a favorable variance. In Cajun French, I call it bon appétit.

Winfield is our leading rusher with 463 yards and eight touchdowns, and he has 1,153 passing yards. KeDarius Wade leads us with 226 receiving yards. St. Andre has 48 tackles. As a team, we allow only 298.3 yards a game.

Now, fair is fair. Southern Miss has weapons. Mario Sanders has 492 receiving yards and five touchdowns, Steven Robinson has 432 rushing yards and five scores, and Landry Lyddy has thrown for 1,032 yards. Mathis Haygood has 55 tackles. But against Arkansas State, Southern Miss turned it over on downs three times and threw two interceptions. That's not a two-step. That's tripping over your own boots.

The Honest Entry

Here's the part an honest accountant puts in bold. CollegeFootballData.com has Southern Miss ahead 24-5 in this series, and the Golden Eagles won 22-10 in Lafayette last year. Twenty-four to five. That's not a rivalry, mes amis. That's an audit we keep failing. We did win 23-13 in Hattiesburg in 2024, though, so I know the way to the dance hall. Time to balance the books.

The Name Game

And I have to mention The Rock. For 50 years Southern Miss played at M. M. Roberts Stadium. This August, according to the Hattiesburg American and Southern Miss Athletics, the stadium was renamed Renasant Stadium. I support it. Everybody deserves a new name for a fresh start. But here's my question for the Golden Eagles: how's the fresh start going? We have Our Lady of Lourdes on our stadium. I'd say we've got the stronger patron.

A Tale of Two Hub Cities

Here's a fun fact, and I verified it twice because I'm an accountant: both of these towns are nicknamed "The Hub City."

Lafayette. We've had the nickname as Lafayette grew, connected by roads to all its neighboring settlements, and we're also called the "Heart of Acadiana." Our 2020 population was 121,374, and we sit on the Vermilion River. The town was founded as Vermilionville and renamed in 1884 for General Lafayette, the French aristocrat who helped the Continental Army in the Revolution. So we even named our town after a Frenchman who helped win a war. Très Cajun. Wikipedia notes that Lafayette has been among the leaders in restaurants per capita in Louisiana since 2015 and that we host the Festivals Acadiens et Créoles. Cajun and Creole music, Cajun and Creole food, and on Saturdays, Cajun football.

Hattiesburg. Now, Hattiesburg is a fine Pine Belt town of 48,730 people. Its nickname also happens to be "The Hub City." According to Wikipedia, Hattiesburg got that nickname in 1912 from a contest in the local newspaper. A contest! We earned "Hub City" by growing. Hattiesburg won it in the paper, like a crossword. Ma chère, a nickname from a newspaper contest is like a dance partner you won in a raffle.

I'll be fair: Hattiesburg is home to the Hattiesburg Zoo at Kamper Park, and Camp Shelby to the south is the largest National Guard training base east of the Mississippi. I respect it deeply and I thank everyone who trains there. But for a Saturday night? Lafayette has the festival. Hattiesburg has a very nice zoo, which, honestly, is where the Golden Eagles' run defense has been spending its weekends: watching other animals run by.

And size matters in a ledger. Lafayette has about two and a half Hattiesburgs. Two Hub Cities, one wheel. I know whose spokes are turning.

The Last Dance

Here's the rhythm I see. Louisiana runs for 200 yards a game, and Southern Miss gives up 252. Louisiana didn't turn it over against Troy, and Southern Miss gave the ball away five times against Arkansas State, counting turnovers on downs. The series history isn't on our side, but the ledger this season is. Lace up, Cajuns. Let's two-step through Hattiesburg and dance all the way home on I-59 and I-10.

Laissez les bons stats rouler!

My call: Louisiana Ragin' Cajuns 31, Southern Miss Golden Eagles 22.

articles.title: We Are... Rested: Marshall Outgained Coastal by 197 Yards, Took a Week Off, and Now South Alabama Brings the 131st-Ranked Scoring Defense to The Joan
articles.byline: Mercy Holderby, The Marshall Fanatic
articles.matchup: South Alabama (4-2) at Marshall (3-3), Tue., Oct. 20, 7:30 p.m. ET, Joan C. Edwards Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
How am I? We are. That's what I tell everybody who asks, from the folks at church to the night-shift nurses on my floor. Mercy Holderby here, green ribbon on my microphone, Marshall green in my closet and, I'm told, Marshall green in my baby pictures. I was born in Huntington and raised on the story of this program, and I'll be at Joan C. Edwards Stadium Tuesday night with my voice ready. We are... Marshall!

Part 1: The Week Off, and the Game That Stung

First, the honest news: Marshall did not play last weekend. The Herd had an open date after the Oct. 10 game against Coastal Carolina, and I spent mine the way a nurse spends a rare free Saturday: catching up on sleep, and watching every Sun Belt game with my clipboard.

That Coastal game still stings, so let's lance it and put a bandage on it. Coastal Carolina beat us 27-21 at The Joan in front of 23,029. And here's the strange part. We outgained them 505 yards to 308. We ran for 221 yards and threw for 284. We went 9-for-15 on third down. Coastal threw for just 73 yards.

So how did we lose? Turnovers. AP counted six of them: three interceptions and three lost fumbles. You can outgain a team by almost 200 yards and still lose if you hand them the ball six times. My grandmother would call that "setting the table and then giving the turkey away."

Coastal led 13-0 at halftime, and Dominic Lee-Knicely broke a 70-yard touchdown run on the first play of the second half. It was 27-0. Then the Herd showed its heart. Judah Price ran 50 yards for a touchdown late in the third quarter. Zion Turner hit Price for a 9-yard touchdown with 2:52 left, and 38 seconds later Turner found Owen Sweeney for 19 yards. It was 27-21, and The Joan was rocking. We just ran out of time.

Price finished with 124 rushing yards on 12 carries. Turner completed 18 of 27 for 219 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Adrian Norton caught four passes for 77 yards, Javae Gilmore made 10 tackles, and Caleb Clark-Glover picked off a pass. We're 3-3 and 0-2 in the Sun Belt. But a team that scores 21 points in a quarter and a half is a team with a pulse. Trust a nurse on that.

Part 2: The Jaguars Come North

Tuesday night, 7:30 Eastern, on ESPN2, South Alabama comes to Huntington. A national TV game on a Tuesday night in October, at The Joan. Get there early, friends.

I'll be kind, because kindness is free and I hand it out like ice chips. South Alabama is 4-2 and 2-0 in the league. Keenan Phillips is a terrific back, with 444 rushing yards and five touchdowns, and in the Jaguars' last game, a 56-49 win at Arkansas State on Oct. 8, he returned a kickoff 100 yards for a touchdown. Their run game ranks 16th in FBS, per AP, and their turnover margin is plus-7, eighth. That's a healthy patient.

Now let's read the rest of the chart.

The Vitals on That Defense

AP's preview has South Alabama's defense 126th in FBS in yards allowed, at 429.0 a game. The pass defense ranks 127th, giving up 264.8 yards a game, and the scoring defense ranks 131st, at 34.5 points. Arkansas State's quarterback threw for 418 yards and four touchdowns against them. The Jaguars won that game 56-49, which means they gave up 49 and called it a good night.

Marshall throws for 247.8 yards a game, 50th in FBS. Xayvion Turner-Bradshaw leads us with 22 catches, 324 yards and four touchdowns, and we just threw for 284 yards against Coastal. Diagnosis: South Alabama's secondary is going to need a lot of fluids.

Our Own Chart

I'm a nurse. I don't hide the hard numbers. Marshall's turnover margin is minus-9, 136th in FBS, per AP, and our red zone offense is 129th. Our run defense is 123rd. Take care of the football, and that Coastal game looks very different. On Tuesday, the prescription is simple: hold onto it.

The Only Other Visit

CollegeFootballData.com lists one meeting, in 2023, a 28-0 South Alabama win in Mobile. I remember. I was not happy. But that was on the Bay, and this one is on the Ohio, at The Joan, where Wikipedia says Marshall went 192-45 through the end of the 2024 season. We are a different team at home.

A Young Program, Kindly Noted

And a gentle history note, with love. South Alabama started playing football in 2009, and according to Wikipedia, its first game ever was against Hargrave Military Academy, a prep school. Marshall has two I-AA national championships, in 1992 and 1996. I respect every young program. I just like to remind our guests that we were winning national titles when their first opponent was still doing homework.

Two River Towns, One Bay Town

Huntington. We sit on the Ohio River, and our city was built as the western end of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway, finished in 1873. Wikipedia says the town is named for Collis P. Huntington, the railroad's founder. Before that, this land was known as Holderby's Landing, after a farmer named James Holderby, and his estate included the land gifted in 1837 to found what is now Marshall University. articles.title: Hear Ye, Hear Ye: The Monarchs Who Held App State to 158 Yards Sail Inland to Ruston, Where the Bulldogs Couldn't Score for a Half Against a Winless Team
articles.byline: Winifred 'Winnie' Pocklington, The Old Dominion Fanatic
articles.matchup: Old Dominion (2-5) at Louisiana Tech (4-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 5 p.m. ET, Joe Aillet Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Hear ye, hear ye! The royal court of Old Dominion is now in session. Winnie Pocklington presiding, tiny crown slightly crooked, salt air in my lungs and a harbor-tour microphone that I absolutely did not return at the end of summer. I'm a Norfolk girl from a Navy family, and I treat every Monarch win like a coronation. This week, I'm treating a loss like a royal inquiry. Order in the court.

Part 1: The Thursday Night Inquiry

Georgia Southern beat Old Dominion 23-15 last Thursday at S.B. Ballard Stadium, in front of 17,912 loyal subjects. We're 2-5 and 1-3 in the Sun Belt. The court accepts the verdict, though it filed a strongly worded scroll.

It began like a coronation. On our very first drive, Quinn Henicle marched us 75 yards in 11 plays and threw a 20-yard touchdown pass to tight end Leon Haughton Jr. Hear ye! Seven-nothing, Monarchs.

Then the Eagles tied it, and we lost a fumble that set up the first of three Tripp Bryant field goals. He made all three, from 33, 43 and 31 yards, and Georgia Southern led 16-7 at halftime. Turner Helton hit Terrance Gibbs for an 11-yard touchdown in the third, and it was 23-7.

But the crown doesn't fall that easily. Backup Ryan Huff threw a short pass to TJ Johnson, and Johnson turned it into a 71-yard touchdown with 11:13 left. Huff then hit Haughton for the two-point conversion, and it was a one-score game. That's as close as we came.

The court notes some honors. Lucas Struck made 11 tackles. Daevon Iles and Ja'Mez Drummer had 10 each. Mario Easterly had a sack, and Javen Gibson intercepted Helton. And our defense held Georgia Southern to 3-for-12 on third down. The penalties, though, 12 of them for 100 yards, have been sentenced to extra film study.

And let us remember the week before, because royals keep records. On Oct. 10 we went to Boone and beat App State 10-3. AP reported we held the Mountaineers to 158 yards and forced three turnovers. Devin Roche ran for 101 yards. That was a coronation on a mountain, and I'm still wearing the crown.

Part 2: The Royal Voyage to Ruston

Saturday, 5 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN+, Old Dominion visits Louisiana Tech at Joe Aillet Stadium.

The court is gracious. The Bulldogs are 4-2 and 2-0 in the Sun Belt, and they beat UL Monroe 24-0 last Saturday. Blake Baker threw two touchdown passes to Brayden Bockler, and Marcus Calwise Jr. caught eight passes for 119 yards. Credit to the Bulldogs. A royal always curtsies first.

And then she reads the scroll.

The First Half That Wasn't

It was 0-0 at halftime in Monroe, against a ULM team that is 0-6. ULM sacked Baker on the second play and intercepted him soon after. The Bulldogs went 1-for-3 on field goals, with one blocked, and missed another with a second kicker. Four field goal tries, one make. Hear ye, hear ye: the royal kicking inspector has questions.

AP's preview also lists Louisiana Tech's red zone offense 118th in FBS, scoring on 76 of every 100 trips. My defense would like a word with that red zone.

The Monarch Defense, By Royal Decree

AP ranks our defense 47th in FBS in yards allowed, at 335.7 a game, and 50th against the pass. Struck leads us with 52 tackles. Gibson has five sacks. We held App State to 158 yards in its own house, and that was two weeks ago, not two decades ago.

The court admits, with a sigh, that our offense has struggled. AP has it 138th in yards. But Roche has 373 rushing yards, Johnson has three touchdown catches and Huff just showed what a quick throw can do. Louisiana Tech allows 148.5 rushing yards a game, 84th in FBS. A royal procession runs right down the middle of the road.

The Royal Archives

CollegeFootballData.com reports Old Dominion is 2-0 all time against Louisiana Tech. We won 30-27 in 2014 and 23-20 in 2021. Two meetings, two coronations. The Bulldogs have never beaten the Monarchs. By royal decree, that is the natural order of things.

And while we're in the archives: Louisiana Tech's very first football game, in 1901, was a 57-0 loss to LSU. A difficult debut, darlings. Ours came in 1930. And yes, the Monarchs paused football from 1940 to 2009. Royals take long naps. We woke up and went 9-2 in our first season back.

Also, a gentle reminder that the Bulldogs only joined the Sun Belt on July 1 of this year. Welcome to the kingdom, new subjects. Please mind the protocol, and kindly stop tripping over the long drives of the visiting court.

A Tale of Two Towns: The Harbor and the Orchard

Norfolk. Ladies and gentlemen of the court, behold my kingdom. Norfolk is home to Naval Station Norfolk, established in 1917, which Wikipedia says remains the world's largest naval base. My family has served there, and I salute every sailor who does. Our waterfront has the Nauticus maritime museum and the battleship USS Wisconsin, and the city has the Chrysler Museum of Art and the Virginia Zoo. Waterside, a festival marketplace on the harbor, opened in 1983 and was redeveloped in 2017. Norfolk had 238,005 people in 2020. On a fall Saturday, I can give you a harbor tour in the morning and a Monarch win at night, and I will narrate both.

Ruston. Now, Ruston is a charming little city of 22,166, according to the 2020 census. That's roughly one Ruston for every 10 and a half Norfolks, and I checked with the royal mathematician. It's in the Piney Hills of north Louisiana, and it's famous for its annual Peach Festival. In June. The Peach Festival is in June, darlings, and we're arriving in late October. We've missed the only royal ball on the calendar. I've been told to expect a lot of pine trees.

The Dixie Theater opened in 1928, and I respect a historic theater. But a town where the most famous building is a theater should know drama when it sees it. And their team is named for a bulldog. Ours is named for a monarch. One of us wears a crown. The other one wears a collar.

And travel? From the harbor, the royal fleet would like to sail to Ruston. Sadly, Ruston is a landlocked town in the Piney Hills, a long way from any harbor. The court will travel by land, like peasants, along Interstate 20, and arrive fashionably on time. I've packed a tiara, a rain jacket and a strongly worded letter to whoever schedules Sun Belt road trips. A Monarch should never have to change planes to reach a peach.

The Royal Decree

Here is the ruling of the court. Old Dominion has a top-50 defense, a recent road win in which it held App State to 158 yards and a 2-0 record against Louisiana Tech. The Bulldogs needed a half to find any points against a winless ULM, went 1-for-4 on field goals and rank 118th in the red zone. If the Monarchs protect the ball, keep the penalty flags in their pockets and let the defense rule, this voyage could end in a coronation in the Piney Hills.

Long live the Monarchs. Hear ye, hear ye: the court is adjourned.

My call: Louisiana Tech Bulldogs 31, Old Dominion Monarchs 18.

articles.title: Throw Me a First Down: 4-2 South Alabama Rides a 100-Yard Kickoff Return and the Nation's 8th-Best Turnover Margin Into Huntington, Where the Herd Ranks 136th
articles.byline: Azalea Fairhope-Grice, The South Alabama Fanatic
articles.matchup: South Alabama (4-2) at Marshall (3-3), Tue., Oct. 20, 7:30 p.m. ET, Joan C. Edwards Stadium, ESPN2
articles.text:
Well, hey, y'all! Azalea Fairhope-Grice here, red-white-and-blue beads around my neck, coaching whistle on a ribbon and a glue gun still warm from float-building season prep. I'm a Mobile girl, born and raised on the Bay, and I grade every football play the way I grade a Mardi Gras float: Is it bold? Does it move? Did the crowd scream? South Alabama has been building a very pretty float this fall, and Tuesday night, we're rolling it all the way to West Virginia.

Part 1: An Open Week, and the Parade Before It

Let's be honest first, because my mama raised me honest and my volleyball players feared it. South Alabama did not play last weekend. The Jaguars had an open date after their Thursday game on Oct. 8, so you get two things from me today: a love letter to that last game and a little praise for a smart week of rest.

And honey, that last game was a parade. South Alabama beat Arkansas State 56-49 in Jonesboro, and AP called it the most combined points of any FBS game this season. The two teams scored 62 points in the first half alone, also an FBS high this year, per AP.

Grand marshal of the parade: Keenan Phillips. He ran 19 times for 157 yards and three touchdowns, including a 42-yarder early in the fourth quarter that made it 56-35. And then, because a float needs sparkle, he returned a kickoff 100 yards for a touchdown in the first quarter. One hundred yards! That float didn't just roll down the parade route; it ran the whole route and came back for seconds. Float grade: A-plus, with glitter.

Jared Hollins had a quiet day in the air, 6 of 10 for 76 yards, but he ran in two short touchdowns 21 seconds apart late in the second quarter and threw a 7-yarder to Rod Gibbs. PJ Martin ran for 95 yards and a touchdown. As a team, AP says, the Jaguars ran 50 times for 296 yards. And when Arkansas State got within seven with under seven minutes left, we chewed up the rest of the clock with a 13-play drive. Defense? Cole Blaylock made 10 tackles, and Damyrion Darby and Masey Lewis each picked off a pass.

AP also pointed out that South Alabama had already matched its number of wins from all of 2025, when it went 4-8. We're 4-2 and 2-0 in the Sun Belt. Mardi Gras isn't until February, but y'all, it feels early this year.

Part 2: Rolling to Huntington

Tuesday night, 7:30 Eastern, on ESPN2, South Alabama visits Marshall at Joan C. Edwards Stadium. Prime time on a Tuesday. The whole country is watching, and I've already ironed my beads.

First, the gracious part. Marshall is 3-3 and had a week off, too. It has a real receiver in Xayvion Turner-Bradshaw, with 22 catches for 324 yards and four touchdowns, and Caleb Clark-Glover leads the Herd with 44 tackles. Its passing game ranks 50th in FBS, according to AP. I tip my tiara.

Now, the float inspection.

Turnovers: Throw Me Something, Mister

At a Mobile parade, you yell "Throw me something, mister!" and the krewes toss you beads. Marshall has embraced the spirit. AP's preview lists the Herd's turnover margin at minus-9, 136th in FBS. South Alabama is plus-7, eighth in the nation.

In its last game, a 27-21 home loss to Coastal Carolina, AP says Marshall turned the ball over six times. Six! Honey, that's not a football team. That's a parade float handing out beads to the other side of the street.

The Jaguar Ground Parade

South Alabama runs for 220.3 yards a game, 16th in FBS, and scores 38.8 points a game, 15th. Phillips has 444 rushing yards and five touchdowns. We hold the ball 33:03 a game, 16th in the country.

Marshall's run defense allows 193.8 yards a game, which AP ranks 123rd. Its defense overall is 132nd in yards allowed, and 129th in scoring defense. And the Herd's red zone offense is 129th, scoring on 70.8% of trips. That's a float that gets all the way to the reviewing stand and then stalls in front of the judges.

A Word About Our Own Float

I'm a coach, so I'll tell you where we need to be better. AP ranks South Alabama's defense 126th in yards and 131st in scoring, at 34.5 points allowed a game. We gave up 49 to Arkansas State and 418 passing yards to Trey Owens. That's a float with a beautiful top and loose wheels. Tighten the bolts, girls. Tighten the bolts.

The Last Time

CollegeFootballData.com lists one previous meeting: South Alabama 28, Marshall 0, in Mobile in 2023. A shutout. One parade, zero floats for the visitors. Tuesday is Marshall's first try at evening the books, and I hope the Herd brings a sturdy trailer.

The Parade Route: Mobile vs. Huntington

Mobile. Darlin', we invented this. Wikipedia says Mobile has the oldest organized Carnival celebration in the United States. French colonial settlers first celebrated Carnival here in 1703, at the Old Mobile Site, and in 1830 Mobile became home to the country's first organized Carnival mystic society to parade. New Orleans is our lovely younger sister; we taught her everything she knows. Our official cultural ambassadors are the Azalea Trail Maids, and yes, I took my name very seriously growing up.

Mobile had 187,041 people in 2020, and we sit right on Mobile Bay. Our team has played at Hancock Whitney Stadium since it opened in 2020. Before that, the Jaguars played at Ladd-Peebles Stadium. On a fall Saturday you can catch a sunset over the Bay, a game at the Hancock and, if you're lucky, a mystic society planning next year's float in somebody's garage.

Huntington. Huntington is a river town on the Ohio, and it's a sweet one. Its 2020 population was 46,842, about a quarter of Mobile. But Wikipedia tells me something delightful. Before 1870, the area was known as Holderby's Landing, after a farmer named James Holderby. Then the town was renamed for Collis P. Huntington, founder of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway, who built it as the railroad's western end.

So Huntington is named for a railroad founder, and the farmer whose land it sat on got relegated to history. Honey, in Mobile we name things after flowers and parades. In Huntington they name them after the man who owned the trains. I'll say this: at least you always know which way to go home. Just follow the tracks.

And here's my sincere note, because I'm a Southern lady. Marshall's story, its rebirth after the 1970 plane crash, is one of the most moving in all of sports. I'll be in my seat Tuesday night with a hand over my heart for "We Are... Marshall." Then I'll be on my feet for every Jaguar first down.

The Grand Finale

Here's my float card. South Alabama runs the ball, holds the ball and protects the ball. Marshall is 136th in turnover margin, 129th in the red zone and 123rd against the run. Our defense has to tighten the bolts against a Herd passing game that can move, but if Keenan Phillips gets loose, this parade will have a grand marshal and an encore.

Throw me a first down, Jaguars. Throw me 20.

My call: South Alabama Jaguars 34, Marshall Thundering Herd 32.

South Alabama has been building a very pretty float this fall, and Tuesday night, we're rolling it all the way to West Virginia.

articles.title: To the Top, Sugar: Southern Miss Is 1-5, but It Owns a 24-5 Series Lead Over the Cajuns, and Hattiesburg Was the Hub City First
articles.byline: Delphine 'Dee' Broussard, The Southern Miss Fanatic
articles.matchup: Louisiana (5-2) at Southern Miss (1-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 5 p.m. ET, Renasant Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Well, hey there, sugar. Dee Broussard, coming to you from a rocking chair on a porch in the Pine Belt, with a sweet tea that's sweeter than my disposition this week and a black-and-gold bow big enough to be seen from Camp Shelby. I was a sorority president once, and I learned two things: you smile through the hard weeks, and you always, always know where every page of the record book is filed. Kindly. With a smile. Let's talk.

Part 1: The Night Arkansas State Wouldn't Give the Ball Back

I won't sugarcoat it, and you know I love sugar. Arkansas State beat Southern Miss 23-13 at Renasant Stadium last Saturday night, in front of 22,585 faithful who deserved more. We're 1-5 and 0-2 in the Sun Belt.

The story of the night was the clock. Arkansas State held the ball for 40:08. We had it for 19:52. Bless their hearts, the Red Wolves went 4-for-17 on third down and still found a way to keep it, because they went 3-for-3 on fourth down and then ran the last 7:21 off the clock. That's like a houseguest who says he's leaving and then sits back down for pie.

They kicked three field goals, from 29, 40 and 44 yards, and scored on short runs by Kenyon Clay and Timothy Carter. We got on the board in the second quarter when Landry Lyddy hit Preston Kilgore for a 16-yard touchdown to make it 13-7. Late in the fourth, Steven Robinson ran it in from a yard out, but the two-point try failed.

There were bright spots, and a good hostess points them out. Mathis Haygood made 13 tackles, 2.5 of them for loss. Wesley Edison had 11 tackles and a sack, and JR Stegall had a sack too. Mario Sanders caught six passes for 88 yards. Robinson ran 21 times for 84 yards and caught five passes. The two teams were only 15 yards apart in yards, according to AP. But two interceptions and three turnovers on downs will spoil any party.

It's been that kind of fall. We lost 24-21 at Tulane by a field goal and fell 55-34 at Troy on Oct. 7. The season has been a lot of almost, sugar. But you don't quit a debutante ball because the first song was slow. We opened the year with a 49-3 win over Alcorn State, and we've been in fourth quarters with Tulane and Arkansas State. This team is close. A sorority president knows the look of a chapter that's one good rush week away from turning it around, and I've got that feeling in my pearls.

Part 2: The Cajuns Come Calling

Saturday, 5 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Louisiana at Southern Miss.

The Ragin' Cajuns are 5-2 and beat Troy 33-6 last Saturday. They ran for 243 yards, and Tony Sterner hit two field goals in the last 1:44 of the first half. I'll give them their flowers. A gracious lady always brings flowers.

Then she reads the card.

Their Passing Game, Bless It

Against Troy, Lunch Winfield completed 11 of 21 passes for 70 yards. Seventy. I've thrown farther than that at a bouquet toss. For the season, ESPN lists him at 1,153 passing yards, four touchdown passes and four interceptions. Four and four, honey. That's not a passing game. That's a coin you keep flipping.

And look at how the Cajuns scored their first touchdown: Troy muffed a punt at its own 8, per AP. A sweet gift. I don't expect one from us.

Now, Winfield runs well, 463 yards and eight touchdowns, and Louisiana as a team runs for 200.1 a game. I won't pretend otherwise. Our run defense has had a hard autumn, allowing 252.0 yards a game, per ESPN. That's the whole party on Saturday: stop the run, and Louisiana has to throw.

Our Weapons

Mario Sanders leads us with 34 catches for 492 yards and five touchdowns. Steven Robinson has 432 rushing yards and five touchdowns. Lyddy has thrown for 1,032 yards and seven touchdowns. And Haygood has 55 tackles. That young man is everywhere, like a sorority sister who knows everybody's business.

The Family Album

Here's where I set down my tea. CollegeFootballData.com has Southern Miss leading this series 24-5. Twenty-four to five, sugar. And last year we went to Lafayette and won 22-10. When you've been invited to somebody's house 29 times and won 24 of them, you're not a guest anymore. You're family. You get your own coffee mug.

And Southern Miss Athletics notes we've won conference titles in 1996, 1997, 1999, 2006 and 2011 at The Rock. Louisiana didn't even officially become the Ragin' Cajuns until 1974, according to Wikipedia. Before that, they were the Bulldogs. I love a glow-up, darling. We just had our glow a little earlier.

A Tale of Two Hub Cities

Now, I've heard the Cajuns' Fanatic likes to point out that both of our towns are called "The Hub City." Sugar, let's set the record straight.

Hattiesburg. We earned that name in 1912 in a contest held by the local newspaper, per Wikipedia. The people chose it. That's democracy, honey, in a town born on lumber and railroads, which is exactly what a hub is. We're the anchor of the Pine Belt, 48,730 strong in 2020. We have the Hattiesburg Zoo at Kamper Park, a longtime hit with the little ones. And just south of town is Camp Shelby, the largest National Guard training base east of the Mississippi River, which hosts up to 100,000 Guardsmen and Reservists a year. God bless every one of them.

And our stadium? It's The Rock. It has been since long before anybody painted a new name on the sign. Southern Miss Athletics says it was renovated and expanded before the 1976 season, and this year it became Renasant Stadium. Call it what you want. When those 36,000 seats fill up, it's still The Rock.

Lafayette. Lafayette is a lovely city, 121,374 people in 2020, on the Vermilion River. But let me tell you a little story from Wikipedia. Lafayette used to be called Vermilionville. In 1884, it changed its name to Lafayette, after a French general. Sugar, Hattiesburg kept its name. Lafayette changed its name, changed its team's name from the Bulldogs to the Ragin' Cajuns, and even its university used to compete as Southwestern Louisiana. That is a lot of name tags at one reunion.

They call themselves the "Heart of Acadiana," and I believe them; they've got a big heart. They host the Festivals Acadiens et Créoles, and I hear the food is wonderful. I'll bring a casserole dish to the visitors' section anyway. Southern hospitality never takes a week off, even when the guests are 5-24 in our family album.

Sweet Tea and Truth

Here's the honest picture. Louisiana is 5-2 and runs the ball well. Southern Miss is 1-5 and needs to stop the run. But the Cajuns' passing game threw for 70 yards last week, and the history of this series reads like our family Bible: Southern Miss on nearly every page. We're at home, at The Rock, under the lights of a late-October Saturday. Hold onto the ball, keep their quarterback in the pocket and make them throw.

To the top, sugar. We're just climbing from the bottom step.

My call: Louisiana Ragin' Cajuns 31, Southern Miss Golden Eagles 22.

articles.title: That's Peanuts, Buddy: Troy Comes Home to The Vet, Where It's 3-0, and Welcomes a 0-6 ULM Team Allowing 41.2 Points a Game
articles.byline: Marlo Pickens, The Troy Fanatic
articles.matchup: UL Monroe (0-6) at Troy (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 4 p.m. ET, Veterans Memorial Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Hey there, buddy. Marlo Pickens, former Trojan long snapper, peanut farmer's son and the only man in Pike County who measures a football field in peanut rows. I spent my playing days looking at the world upside down between my legs, so trust me when I tell you this: a bad Saturday looks a whole lot better once you flip it right side up. Let's flip last week over and look at it straight.

Part 1: Shelled in Lafayette

I won't sugar-roast it. Louisiana beat Troy 33-6 last Saturday at Our Lady of Lourdes Stadium. That's peanuts, buddy, and not the good kind. We're 3-3 and 1-1 in the Sun Belt, and AL.com noted we're 0-3 on the road this year.

Troy's own athletics office called it a game of missed opportunities, and I can't top that. Our defense forced a four-and-out on the Cajuns' first drive, and then we muffed the punt. Louisiana recovered at our 8 and scored three plays later. We put together a 15-play drive to open the second quarter that ate nearly seven minutes, and we missed a 42-yard field goal at the end of it. Troy Athletics says we also dropped two interceptions, and both of those drives ended in Louisiana touchdowns. Then the Cajuns kicked two field goals in the last 104 seconds of the half, and it was 19-0.

We came out of the locker room swinging. Our first drive of the second half went 75 yards, and Tucker Kilcrease ran a designed keeper 23 yards for a touchdown, his first of the season. That came right after Goose Crowder left the game with a shoulder injury, according to AL.com. We're praying for a quick recovery, and we'll wait on official word. Kilcrease went 5 of 10 for 76 yards, and Crowder had gone 9 of 16 for 65 before that.

There were peanuts worth saving. Jordan Perry made a career-high 13 tackles. Donnie Smith made a career-best seven tackles, though his streak of nine straight games with a sack came to an end. Jace Petty tied a career high with four catches and set a career best with 69 receiving yards. And Troy Athletics points out that the Trojans held Louisiana to 108 passing yards.

But we turned it over twice inside our own 28, and Troy Athletics says that led to 10 Louisiana points. We went 4-for-16 on third and fourth down. You don't win a peanut festival by dropping the bag on the way to the booth.

Part 2: Back to The Vet

Saturday, 4 p.m. Eastern, on ESPN+, UL Monroe comes to Veterans Memorial Stadium. And buddy, I'm happy to be home. Troy Athletics says the Trojans are 3-0 at The Vet this season. We beat Sam Houston 24-21, Alabama State 34-17 and Southern Miss 55-34 there. Home cooking, boiled peanuts and a full stadium. That's the recipe.

Being Neighborly First

I'll say something kind about the Warhawks, because Mama didn't raise a grump. Their defense played tough in the first half against Louisiana Tech last week. It was 0-0 at halftime, and ULM sacked Blake Baker four times, blocked a field goal and picked off a pass. Noah Flemmings has 51 tackles and Tyrell Brown has 2.5 sacks. That's real effort, and effort deserves respect.

Now, the Peanut Count

But here's the full harvest report, from AP's preview. UL Monroe is 0-6. Its defense ranks 136th in FBS in yards allowed, at 483.2 a game, 136th against the run, at 229.7, and 137th in scoring defense, at 41.2 points a game. Buddy, that's not a defense. That's an unlocked peanut barn with the lights on.

Troy runs for 204.7 yards a game, 27th in FBS, and holds the ball for 32:32 a game, 26th. Gavin Griffin leads us with 359 rushing yards. TK Keyes has 282 receiving yards and three touchdowns, and Donnie Smith still has five sacks. Keno Jones leads us with 40 tackles.

ULM's offense, per AP, ranks 121st in scoring at 20 points a game and 133rd on third down, converting 29.6 of every 100. And here's one I love: Troy's red zone defense ranks ninth in the country, allowing scores on 68.2 of every 100 trips. ULM's red zone offense ranks 116th. That's a peanut that can't get out of the shell.

Clean Up the Mess

We do have to clean up our own field. AP's preview has Troy 125th in FBS in penalty yards, at 75.3 a game. ULM is 37th. A long snapper notices these things, buddy, because a long snapper gets blamed for everything. If the Trojans stop flagging themselves, the field gets a lot shorter.

The History Book

CollegeFootballData.com has Troy 11-8 against ULM. Last year we won 37-14 in Monroe. Now, I'm an honest peanut man, so I'll tell you: in 2024, ULM won 13-9 at our place. That one still sits in my craw like a peanut skin. Time to get it out.

ULM, according to Wikipedia, has played in one FBS bowl game ever, the 2012 Independence Bowl. One. I've got more trophies from the Pike County 4-H than that, and I'm not proud of how many of them are for peanut butter.

Troy. Our little city had 17,727 people in 2020, and it's the seat of Pike County, one of the first counties established in Alabama, back in 1821. There's a 45-acre Pike County Lake on the south end of town, the Pioneer Museum of Alabama hosts Troy Pioneer Days every year, and TroyFest fills the downtown square with art. Our motto, according to Wikipedia, is "A Wonderful Place to Live!" with an exclamation point. That's how you know we mean it.

Monroe. Monroe is a fine river city on the Ouachita, the seat of Ouachita Parish, with 47,702 people in 2020. Then, and I'm quoting Wikipedia here, "as the airline expanded, it moved to Atlanta." Buddy, when your town invents an airline and the airline uses it to fly away, that's a sign. Even the planes didn't stay for the second half.

We've got to protect the ball, cut the penalties, and keep Pike County proud. Do that, and the Trojans will be shelling Warhawks all afternoon.

Come early, buddy. Bring a sack of boiled peanuts. Bring two. I'll bring the puns.

My call: Troy Trojans 36, UL Monroe Warhawks 18.

articles.title: Keep the Faith: 0-6 ULM Held Louisiana Tech Scoreless for a Half, and Now It Visits a Troy Team That Ranks 125th in Penalty Yards and Lost to ULM at Home in 2024
articles.byline: Darnell Vidrine, The UL Monroe Fanatic
articles.matchup: UL Monroe (0-6) at Troy (3-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 4 p.m. ET, Veterans Memorial Stadium, ESPN+
articles.text:
Good evening, night owls, and welcome back to the overnight show. Darnell Vidrine here, Delta-born, coffee-powered and broadcasting from the warm glow of a radio booth where hope never signs off. If you're new, here's how it works: every week I keep an optimism counter. Every week, something tries to knock it down. And every week, I reset it to 100. Friends, I just reset it again. Counter: 100. Let's keep the faith.

Part 1: The Best Half of Football in Monroe This Year

Louisiana Tech beat ULM 24-0 last Saturday at our place, in front of 20,653 people, in the first I-20 Showdown since 2000. We're 0-6 and 0-2 in the Sun Belt. I won't dress it up. But I'm going to tell you about the first half, because you need to hear it, and because I need to say it out loud.

The first half ended 0-0. Zero to zero, against a 4-2 team that was 2-0 in the league. Our defense came to play. Marcus Ross sacked Blake Baker on the second play of the game. Armoni Rue picked off Baker for his first career interception. Jaeden Calender got a sack. Billy Pullen had a sack and two tackles for loss. Then Tyrell Brown blocked a 39-yard field goal, the first blocked field goal by ULM since 2025, according to ULM Athletics. Louisiana Tech also missed from 46 and 41 in that half. By halftime, my counter read 140, and ULM went on to finish with four sacks. I had to recalibrate.

Then the second half happened. Taeden Rogers intercepted our first pass of the half, and Louisiana Tech scored on the drive that followed. Baker threw two 2-yard touchdown passes to Brayden Bockler, and the Bulldogs added a field goal. Counter dipped. Counter recovered. Counter is a professional.

Aidan Armenta went 14 of 24 for 119 yards and ran for 25 more. JP Coulter caught four passes for 42 yards. Kevontay Wells and Noah Flemmings each made eight tackles. And ULM Athletics counted 11 penalties for 118 yards, our most this season. That's the part we fix this week. Counter: holding at 100.

Part 2: Road Trip to The Vet

Saturday, 4 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, ULM visits Troy at Veterans Memorial Stadium.

Let me give the Trojans their due, because the overnight show is a kind show. Troy is 3-3 and 3-0 at home, according to Troy Athletics. It runs for 204.7 yards a game, 27th in FBS, and its red zone defense ranks ninth, per AP. Donnie Smith has five sacks. They've got a good program, with back-to-back Sun Belt titles in 2022 and 2023. Respect.

Now, my callers have some notes.

Caller One: "Darnell, What About Last Week?"

Great question, caller. Last Saturday, Louisiana beat Troy 33-6. Troy Athletics' own recap called it a game of missed opportunities. The Trojans muffed a punt that set up Louisiana's first touchdown. They missed a 42-yard field goal after a 15-play drive. They dropped two interceptions. They turned it over twice inside their own 28. They went a combined 4-for-16 on third and fourth down. Friends, ULM isn't the only team looking for its rhythm.

Caller Two: "What's Our Path?"

Penalties, caller. AP's preview ranks Troy 125th in FBS in penalty yards, at 75.3 a game. ULM ranks 37th, at 49.2. Yes, we had a rough flag night last week, but over a whole season we're one of the more disciplined teams in the country. Troy hands out free yards like a church bake sale hands out free cookies. We'll take a few.

And the Trojans' passing game ranks 102nd in FBS at 198 yards a game, per AP. Our pass rush just got four sacks against a team that's 2-0 in the league. Tyrell Brown leads us with 2.5 sacks, and Noah Flemmings has 51 tackles. If our defense plays like it did in the first half last week for a whole game, the counter goes past 100. I'll need new batteries.

Caller Three: "Have We Ever Done It There?"

Oh, caller. You've made my night. CollegeFootballData.com says that in 2024, ULM went to Troy and won 13-9. At The Vet. In their house. The series is 11-8 Troy, and the Trojans won 37-14 last year, but we know the road to Troy, and we know it ends in a parking lot where the Warhawks once celebrated. Counter: 115.

My Honest Moment

I keep the faith, but I don't fib on the overnight show. AP ranks our defense 136th in yards allowed and 137th in scoring defense, at 41.2 points a game. Our offense ranks 121st in scoring. That's real. But we lost by six at UAB and by three to Southeastern Louisiana. We've been close. Close is a seed, and seeds grow.

Tales From Two Towns

Monroe. Here's what the late-night crowd should know about home. Monroe sits on the Ouachita River, the seat and largest city of Ouachita Parish, with 47,702 people in 2020, and with West Monroe across the river, we're the twin cities of northeast Louisiana. And this, friends, is my go-to piece of trivia: Wikipedia says Biedenharn, the first bottler of Coca-Cola, moved to Monroe, and he and his son helped found Delta Dusters, a crop-dusting company that grew into the airline Delta. That's right. An airline was born here, fighting boll weevils from the sky. His home and gardens are still open to the public as the Biedenharn Museum and Gardens. So when somebody says nothing takes off in Monroe, I tell them: friend, the whole Delta fleet does, in spirit.

Troy. Now, Troy is a sweet little city, 17,727 people in 2020, the seat of Pike County. But Wikipedia tells me a remarkable story. Troy started out as Deer Stand Hill. Then it was Zebulon. Then Centreville. And finally, in 1838, Troy. Four names! Friends, that town changed identities more often than our call-in show changes callers. I'd keep the faith in a town like that, too. It took three tries to get it right, which, as a ULM man, I deeply respect.

Monroe has about two and a half Troys. Troy has a 45-acre Pike County Lake, which is lovely. We have a whole river. Troy's team is named for heroes of an ancient city, and it lives in a town of under 18,000. Monroe helped start an airline that now flies all over the world. One of us thinks big, folks. And on a cool fall night by the Ouachita, with the lights on at our stadium and the river rolling by, I'll take our view over a lake every time.

Sign-Off

Here's the overnight forecast. Troy is the more complete team on paper, and it's at home. ULM is 0-6, and I won't pretend otherwise. But the Warhawks just held a 2-0 Sun Belt team scoreless for a half, Troy commits 75.3 penalty yards a game, and the last time we went to The Vet, we came home happy. Cut the flags, keep the pass rush, protect the football. Do that, and Saturday is the night the counter breaks.

Counter: reset to 100. Keep the faith, Warhawks.

My call: Troy Trojans 36, UL Monroe Warhawks 18.

articles.title: Check the Tread: Akron Drives 'Down the Road' for the Wagon Wheel Against a Kent State Offense That Ranks 138th in Scoring and Went 0-for-4 on Fourth Down in Tampa
articles.byline: Hollister 'Zip' Grubbs, The Akron Fanatic
articles.matchup: Akron (1-6) at Kent State (2-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET, Dix Stadium, Kent, Ohio, ESPN+
articles.text:
Greetings from the lab, Zips fans. Hollister "Zip" Grubbs here, polymer-science grad, tread-depth gauge in my shirt pocket and a little rubber dust on my sleeves. For the uninitiated, here's my whole philosophy: when a season starts to look bald, you don't throw out the car. You check the pressure, rotate the tires and drive to Kent. That's this week.

It's Wagon Wheel week.

Part 1: Bald Spots in Oxford

Miami (Ohio) beat Akron 34-14 on Saturday at Yager Stadium. We're 1-6, 0-3 in the MAC, and AP notes it's five losses in a row. I'm a scientist. I report the data.

But first, the sticky tread. Our first drive was gorgeous. Eleven plays, 97 yards, and Brayden Roggow finished it with a 6-yard touchdown pass to Marcel Williams with 5:18 left in the first quarter. Ninety-seven yards! That's not tread. That's a full set of new radials.

And Miami's offense threw for only 65 yards all day. Caleb Heavner went 8 of 16. Our defense did its job against the pass, and Donelius Johnson made 10 tackles. He has 67 for the season, which is a lot of rubber meeting a lot of road. Cyrus Durham had 1.5 sacks. Brandon Hills returned a kickoff 71 yards in the third quarter to set up Jordan Gant's 10-yard touchdown run. And we had the ball for 32:04, longer than Miami did.

Now the bald spots. Miami ran for 324 yards at 9.3 a carry, and Rodney Nelson had a career-high 142 yards and two touchdowns on just 13 carries, including a 58-yarder. Roggow threw for 234 yards but was intercepted four times, and Blayne Myrick returned one for a touchdown in the third quarter. We went 6-for-17 on third down and ran for just 81 yards. Those are the readings. A good engineer doesn't argue with the gauge.

The season so far has been a long drive on a gravel road. We lost to Wake Forest, Minnesota, UNLV and Central Michigan, beat Robert Morris 45-10, and lost to Eastern Michigan by two, 25-23. Two points, friends. That's one air-pressure check away.

Part 2: The Wagon Wheel, and a Very Muddy Origin Story

Saturday, 1 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Akron visits Kent State at Dix Stadium. The Golden Flashes are 2-5 and 1-2 in the MAC.

This is the Wagon Wheel game, and I need you to hear the legend, as Akron Athletics tells it. In the spring of 1870, John R. Buchtel, an Akron industrialist, rode out to Kent looking for a site for a new college. His wagon got stuck in the mud, right about where Kent State is today. The horses broke away, and pieces of the carriage were scattered, including one wheel that stayed wedged in the mud. Buchtel went home to Akron and founded Buchtel College, which became the University of Akron. In 1902, workers building a pipeline dug up the wheel. And in 1945, a Kent State dean suggested making it a trophy.

Friends, our founder went to Kent, lost a wheel, and decided the whole thing would work better back in Akron. That's the best scouting report in Ohio history. 3. Bring the Wheel home. It was ours first, and it was stuck in Kent's mud.

Check the tread, Zips. That's some sticky tread.

articles.title: Here's a Joke and a Punt Chart: Ball State Won on a Two-Point Try in Overtime for Its First Road Win in Nearly Two Years, and Now First-Year FBS Sac State Comes to Muncie on a Five-Game Skid
articles.byline: Gus Ponder, The Ball State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Sacramento State (1-6) at Ball State (2-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Scheumann Stadium, Muncie, Ind., ESPN+
articles.text:
Gus Ponder here, coming to you from the garage, where the whiteboard is full of arrows, the coffee is lukewarm and the punt chart is up to date. If you're new, here's the deal. I tell one dad joke for every Ball State punt. Saturday in Bowling Green, Cole Stumbaugh punted four times. So you get four jokes, plus a bonus, because I'm in a good mood. Why? Because the Cardinals won on the road. Hold on to your whiteboards.

Part 1: Two Points, One Overtime, Zero Sleep

Ball State beat Bowling Green 32-31 in overtime on Saturday at Doyt L. Perry Stadium, and AP says it was the Cardinals' first road win in nearly two years, a span of 14 games. We're 2-5, 1-2 in the MAC. I'm hoarse. My whiteboard is hoarse.

We led most of the day. Brody Boehm hit a 39-yard field goal in the first quarter. TJ Horton ran in from 8 yards out. Keldric Luster took off for a 28-yard touchdown run in the third quarter, and it was 17-10.

Then the fourth quarter got bananas. Bowling Green tied it with 1:12 left on a 6-yard touchdown pass from Jay Kastantin. On the very next play, Luster scrambled for 10 yards, the ball got knocked loose, and D'kyah Banks returned it 35 yards for a touchdown. Bowling Green led 24-17 with 1:01 left.

Here's where it gets good. Per AP, Luster led a seven-play, 78-yard drive. The ball was snapped with five seconds left, Bowling Green had six defensive backs lined up at the goal, and Luster found Eli Hohlt wide open on the right side of the end zone. 24-24. Overtime.

Bowling Green scored first in overtime on Austyn Dendy's 4-yard run. Horton answered from 1 yard out. And then the Cardinals went for two. Luster found Alex Scherle. Ball State 32, Bowling Green 31. I yelled so loud my neighbor's dog started a podcast.

Luster threw for 195 yards and a touchdown and ran for 125 yards and another one. Horton had two touchdowns. CJ Nelson caught six passes for 59 yards. Will Yates intercepted Kastantin, and Gavin Forsha made eight tackles. Ball State ran for 240 yards and went 2-for-2 on fourth down.

Now, the punt chart. Stumbaugh punted four times for a 41.0 average, with a long of 56. Four punts, four jokes.

Punt one: Why did the football coach go to the bank? To get his quarterback.

Punt two: I asked the punter how he stays so calm. He said he just kicks back.

Punt three: What do you call a cardinal that wins on the road? A redbird with a passport.

Punt four: Why are football stadiums so cool? Because every seat has a fan in it.

Bonus: Why was the two-point conversion so happy? Because it finally got the point. Both of them.

Part 2: Sac State Comes to Muncie

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Sacramento State visits Scheumann Stadium.

Let me be a good host. The Hornets are new to all of this. Sac State joined the MAC as a football-only member on July 1, according to Sac State Athletics, and this is its first FBS season. The school says it brought back only six starters and added 73 new players. And before this, Sac State won Big Sky titles in 2019, 2021 and 2022. So I respect the Hornets. They know how to win.

They just haven't done it much yet up here. Sac State is 1-6 and 0-4 in the MAC, and AP says the Hornets have lost five in a row. Ohio beat them 48-7 on Saturday night in Sacramento. Ohio had 30 first downs and ran for 265 yards. The Hornets were flagged 12 times for 130 yards. ESPN's season numbers say Sac State scores 15.0 points a game and allows 176.1 rushing yards. They lost 35-6 at home to UMass. Their only win came against Mississippi Valley State.

And you know my go-to stat this week? Sac State's defense allows 176.1 rushing yards a game. Ball State just ran for 240. Luster ran for 125. Horton has 392 rushing yards and seven touchdowns this season. If I were drawing it on the whiteboard, I'd just draw a big arrow pointing straight ahead and write "run" next to it.

Now, the honest part, because a punt chart never lies. Our defense allows 37.9 points and 201.6 rushing yards a game, per ESPN. Matt Coleman has 473 receiving yards and four touchdowns for Sac State, and Isaiah Ene averaged 8.4 yards a carry last week. We can't take anybody lightly. We're 2-5. Nobody in this game gets to strut. But I'll say this for the Cardinals: we just learned how to finish. Down a touchdown with 1:01 left on the road, this team didn't fold. It drove 78 yards, scored with no time on the clock and then went for the win in overtime instead of settling. That's the kind of thing that changes a locker room. I'm just a guy with a whiteboard, but I know what a turning point looks like on paper.

But here's the matchup, the way I see it. A Cardinal is a bird. A Hornet is a bug. I'm not a scientist, but I've watched a lot of nature shows from this garage, and I know how that one usually ends.

Tales From Two Towns

Muncie. Muncie is a city of 65,195 on the White River, and it has a story. Wikipedia says the Ball brothers built their glass factory here in 1888, and they bought the old school property and donated it to the state, and that became the forerunner of Ball State in 1918. That's the Ball in Ball State, the same Ball family name you've seen on canning jars. Ball State's David Owsley Museum of Art has more than 11,000 works. The campus has the David Letterman Communication and Media Building. And Jim Davis, the man who created Garfield, studied art and business at Ball State, per Wikipedia. So yes, the world's most famous lasagna-loving cat has Muncie roots. Garfield hates Mondays. We love Saturdays.

Muncie was also the real town behind "Middletown," the famous 1929 study of everyday American life. Some people say that means average. I say that means the researchers came to Muncie and stayed for two books.

Sacramento. Sacramento is the capital of California and a big city of 524,943. It's lovely. But according to Wikipedia, its streets are laid out as a grid of 26 lettered streets and 31 numbered ones. I'd get lost on C Street trying to find 16th. It's not a city, it's a spelling test. And during the Great Flood of 1862, Wikipedia says the new governor, Leland Stanford, traveled to his own inauguration in a rowboat. In Muncie, our governors show up by car.

Here's my last dad joke, for free. Why did the Hornet fly all the way to Muncie? Because it heard the Cardinals were serving canned food.

Garage Whiteboard

1. Run the ball. Then run it again.
2. Clean tackling. Sac State's backs had some long runs on Saturday.
3. Keep Stumbaugh rested. Fewer punts, fewer jokes. I'll make that sacrifice.

My call: Ball State Cardinals 32, Sacramento State Hornets 22.

articles.title: The Save Rate Says No: Bowling Green Lost a 60-Minute Thriller to Ball State in Overtime, Now Heads to Amherst, Where the Falcons Won on Their Last Two Trips
articles.byline: Darcy Fenwick, The Bowling Green Fanatic
articles.matchup: Bowling Green (2-5) at Buffalo (4-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Broadview Stadium, Amherst, N.Y., ESPN+
articles.text:
Darcy Fenwick here, former club goalie, current Falcons fanatic, and the only person in Wood County who grades pass defense by save rate. If you're new: every pass the other team completes is a shot on goal. Every incompletion is a save. Every interception is a glove save. And an interception returned for a touchdown is what I call a shorty. Lace 'em up.

Part 1: The Overtime Loss That Hurt Like a Puck Off the Shin

Ball State beat Bowling Green 32-31 in overtime on Saturday at Doyt L. Perry Stadium, in front of 19,875 people. We're 2-5 and 2-1 in the MAC. That's going to sting for a while.

The first period... I mean quarter... was quiet. Ball State hit a field goal and then scored on an 8-yard run to go up 10-0. Then Jay Kastantin hit Brennan Ridley for a 77-yard touchdown, just 17 seconds later. That's a breakaway goal. Travis Kenner tied it at 10 on a 49-yard field goal before halftime.

Ball State went up 17-10 in the third quarter. Then came the wildest two minutes of the season. With 1:12 left, Kastantin finished an 80-yard drive with a 6-yard touchdown pass to Eli Jacon-Duffy. 17-17. And on the very next play from scrimmage, Keldric Luster scrambled, the ball came loose, and D'kyah Banks scooped it and went 35 yards for a touchdown. 24-17, Falcons, with 1:01 left. That's a short-handed goal in a playoff game, friends.

Then Ball State drove 78 yards in seven plays, and AP says the Cardinals scored on a snap with five seconds left, on a pass to a wide-open Eli Hohlt in the right side of the end zone. We had six defensive backs out there, per AP. That's six skaters back, and the puck still found the net. In overtime, Austyn Dendy scored from 4 yards out to put us up again, but Ball State answered and went for two, and the try was good. 32-31.

Here's the honest scoresheet. Kastantin went 17 of 24 for 215 yards and two touchdowns, 70.8 completions for every 100 throws. Ridley had two catches for 84. Dorian Pringle made 10 tackles, and Will Yates picked off Kastantin for Ball State. Ball State ran for 240 yards on us, and Luster ran for 125 by himself. Our run defense has to tighten up its gap control. That's not a goalie problem. That's a defensemen problem.

But we're 2-1 in the MAC, after beating Miami (Ohio) 24-20 on the road and Sac State 38-10 at home. We're right in the middle of the MAC race. In hockey terms, we're still in playoff position.

And I want to give some love to the special teams. Ryan Kingston punted four times and put three inside the 20. In hockey, that's a penalty kill that keeps the other team pinned in its own zone.
