articles.title: Forecast: Clear Skies Over Amherst. Buffalo Beat UMass in Overtime, and Bowling Green Brings the 136th-Ranked Offense in FBS and a Run Defense Allowing 209.6 a Game
articles.byline: Kendra Woolcott, The Buffalo Fanatic
articles.matchup: Bowling Green (2-5) at Buffalo (4-3), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Broadview Stadium, Amherst, N.Y., ESPN+
articles.text:
Good morning, Western New York. Kendra Woolcott with your Bulls weather report. Current conditions: 4-3, 2-1 in the MAC, two straight wins and a light breeze of optimism off Lake Erie. Wind chill: irrelevant, because we're dressed for it. Extended outlook: Bowling Green rolls in Saturday, and I see a high-pressure system parked over Broadview Stadium. Bring a parka and a pass rush.

Part 1: Storm Warning, Then a Clear Sky in Overtime

Buffalo beat UMass 25-18 in overtime on Saturday at Broadview Stadium. That's the kind of game where the sky changes every 10 minutes, so let me give it to you in weather terms.

First half: scattered special teams with a chance of chaos. Phillip Folmar returned a kickoff 71 yards to set up an Oliver Hautanen field goal. Sedrick Vessah sacked the UMass quarterback for a safety. Joseph Stoever recovered a muffed punt to set up another Hautanen field goal. UMass recovered one of ours, too, and turned it into a short touchdown. UMass led 15-8 at halftime. Cloudy.

Third quarter: clearing. Jason Wright hit Clint Walker for a 2-yard touchdown, and it was 15-15.

Fourth quarter: a sudden front. UMass's Derek Morris, who had missed two field goals earlier, made a 53-yarder with less than two minutes left to put the Minutemen up 18-15. But AP says Buffalo answered with a quick drive, and Hautanen hit a 29-yarder with 2 seconds left to force overtime. That's his third field goal of the day. That kicker is a snowplow. He clears the road.

Overtime: sunshine. Wright found Walker again, from 15 yards, for the 25-18 lead on our first possession. Then UMass's Logan Inagawa threw incomplete into the end zone on fourth down. Game over, roads open, school's back on.

Messiah Burch ran 28 times for a career-high 172 yards, per AP, with a long of 46. He leads the team with 661 rushing yards. Walker caught seven passes and both touchdowns. SaVeon Brown made 10 tackles and has 59 this season. Miles Greer had a sack and seven tackles. Kobi Blackwell intercepted Inagawa. And per AP, Buffalo is now 2-0 in the Flagship Cup against UMass, a series named for each school's standing as the flagship university of its state.

Honest weather note: the passing game was foggy. Wright went 16 of 35 for 134 yards, and we turned it over twice. AP's preview lists our passing offense 128th in FBS. Something to work on while the leaves fall.

The bigger picture, though, is sunny. We beat Toledo 23-8 on the road on Oct. 10. Now we've won two straight, and we're 2-1 in the league.

Part 2: The Falcons Fly In

Saturday, 3:30 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Bowling Green at Buffalo, Broadview Stadium.

Let me be fair to the Falcons first. Bowling Green is 2-1 in the MAC, after wins over Miami (Ohio) and Sacramento State. Myles Bradley has seven sacks, which is a real front moving through. Dorian Pringle has 66 tackles. Jay Kastantin completes 66.5 of every 100 passes. And AP ranks BG's pass defense 28th in FBS. That's a real defense against the throw.

Now for the forecast, and it's looking great for us. All rankings are from AP's preview.

Bowling Green's offense averages 280.4 yards a game, 136th in FBS. It scores 18 points a game, 129th. It runs for 106 yards a game, 127th. That offense moves like traffic on the Thruway in a lake-effect band.

Bowling Green's run defense is giving up 209.6 yards a game, 132nd in FBS. And BG's red zone defense ranks 129th, letting opponents score on 95.2 of every 100 trips. So here's the plan: hand Burch the ball. Then hand him the ball again. Our rushing offense ranks 58th at 165.3 a game, and he just ran for 172.

And then there's last week. Bowling Green tied Ball State with 1:12 left, then scored on a 35-yard fumble return to lead by seven with 1:01 left. And it still lost. Ball State drove 78 yards and scored on the final play of regulation, and then won on a two-point try in overtime. Per AP, Bowling Green had six defensive backs lined up at the goal on that last regulation snap, and the receiver was still wide open. That's a snow day nobody saw coming.

BG also lost at home to Tarleton State in its opener, 20-13. Tarleton State is an FCS team.

Now, the history. According to CollegeFootballData.com, Buffalo won 28-3 at Bowling Green last season, and the Bulls have won four of the last six meetings, including 49-7 in 2019 and 38-7 at BG in 2022. And Wikipedia remembers Nov. 21, 2008, when Buffalo beat Bowling Green 40-34 in double overtime to clinch its first outright MAC East title. Two weeks later, Buffalo beat Ball State 42-24 at Ford Field for the 2008 MAC championship. Buffalo's sky has been clear against the Falcons for a while.

A little more program history for the newcomers, since I'm in a sharing mood. Wikipedia says UB switched its mascot to the Bulls in 1931 to tell the school apart from the city's pro teams. The Bulls moved up to Division I-A in 1999, and in 2019 they won the first bowl game in program history, beating Charlotte 31-9 in the Bahamas Bowl. A Buffalo team playing in the Bahamas in December. That's the best weather report I've ever filed.

Tales From Two Towns

Buffalo. My city of 278,349 sits on the eastern shore of Lake Erie, at the head of the Niagara River on the Canadian border, per Wikipedia. Buffalo was picked as the terminus of the Erie Canal in 1825. It hosted the 1901 Pan-American Exposition, whose centerpiece, the Electric Tower, had more than two million light bulbs. Frank Lloyd Wright designed the Martin House here. And Wikipedia says Buffalo is known for its winter weather, Buffalo wings, the Bills and the Sabres. You come to Buffalo for wings, you stay for the snow, and you leave with a parka you didn't know you needed. UB moved its home to the town of Amherst, just north of the city, in 1985, and Broadview Stadium opened in 1993 to host the World University Games.

Bowling Green. Bowling Green, Ohio, is a nice college town of 30,808, the seat of Wood County. But Wikipedia says the land was once the Great Black Swamp, and it was drained and settled in the 1800s. And here's the best part. Bowling Green was named after Bowling Green, Kentucky, by a retired postal worker who had once delivered mail there. So Bowling Green, Ohio, is named for a different town in a different state that a mailman liked. Buffalo got its name from a creek. Bowling Green got its name forwarded.

To be fair, BG has a fun Black Swamp Arts Festival every September. But it's the only Bowling Green in the MAC, and it's still not the original.

Kendra's Seven-Day Outlook

1. Run Burch until the snow melts.
2. Clear up the passing game. Fog advisory in effect.
3. Keep special teams sharp. Folmar and Hautanen just won a game.

Stay warm, Bulls fans. Bring a thermos, bring a friend, bring the whole family, and bring your loudest voice, because this team has earned a home crowd that sounds like it believes.

My call: Buffalo Bulls 27, Bowling Green Falcons 20.

articles.title: Ope, Sack: Central Michigan Rallied Late Against Western, and Now Miami Brings a Pass Defense Ranked 132nd in FBS to the Oil Capital of Michigan
articles.byline: Brynn Haverkamp, The Central Michigan Fanatic
articles.matchup: Miami (OH) (4-3) at Central Michigan (3-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET, Mount Pleasant, Mich., ESPN+
articles.text:
Hey there, Chippewas. Brynn Haverkamp here, blaze-orange beanie on, snowmobile trailer in the driveway and a fresh stack of sack tags on the kitchen table. If you're new, here's how my season works. Every sack is a tag. You fill a tag, you holler, "Ope, sack!" You go home happy. Some weeks you come back with a full freezer. Some weeks you come back with a story and a sandwich.

Last week was a sandwich week. This week, I've got my eye on a bird.

Part 1: Three Quiet Quarters and a Loud Fourth

Western Michigan beat Central Michigan 21-14 on Saturday in Mount Pleasant, in front of 25,352 people. We're 3-4, 1-2 in the MAC. I'll be honest with you, because I'm always honest in the deer stand: the first three quarters were rough.

Western's Jalen Buckley ran for 150 yards and two touchdowns. Broc Lowry threw for only 48 yards, but he didn't have to, because the Broncos ran for 224. It was 21-0 after three quarters, per AP. Western Michigan now leads the series 55-40-2, according to AP, in the 97th meeting.

But then the fourth quarter showed up wearing its good boots. Angel Flores led a 93-yard drive and finished it with a 32-yard touchdown pass to Jaden Allen. Later, Jadyn Glasser scored from 2 yards out with 44 seconds left. 21-14. We couldn't get the onside kick, but the Chippewas made it a game.

Flores carried it 31 times for 117 yards and went 14 of 25 for 162 yards. That's a quarterback who wants the ball every play, and I respect a grinder. Langston Lewis caught four passes for 74 yards, including a 44-yarder. Xavier White made 11 tackles, Mayson Hitchens made 10 and shared a sack, and Jaion Jackson and JJ Douglas made nine each.

Now, the tag report. One shared sack. Half a tag. Ope. We'll need more of those.

And the honest field notes: we went 4-for-15 on third down and 3-for-7 on fourth, and Caden VanHuis missed a field goal. Western's Scoop Gardner Jr. had two sacks on us. That loss also matters beyond the standings. 3. Finish drives. Red zone scores are the trophy buck.

articles.title: Gray Turf, Bright Future: Eastern Michigan Is Still 3-1 in the MAC After a Tough Day Against Toledo, and Ohio's Passing Game Ranks 126th in FBS
articles.byline: Imogen Tremblay, The Eastern Michigan Fanatic
articles.matchup: Eastern Michigan (4-4) at Ohio (5-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 4 p.m. ET, Peden Stadium, Athens, Ohio, ESPNU
articles.text:
Hi, everybody. Imogen Tremblay here, writing from a corner table in Depot Town with a coffee and the quiet confidence of someone who has spent her whole life explaining that Ypsilanti is not a suburb of Ann Arbor. It's not. Ann Arbor is a suburb of us, if you squint, and I always squint.

We had a rough Saturday. But I'll tell you something before we get into it: Eastern Michigan is 3-1 in the MAC. Write that on the gray turf in chalk. Gray turf, bright future.

Part 1: The Factory Had a Slow Shift

Toledo beat Eastern Michigan 34-14 on Saturday at Rynearson Stadium, the place Wikipedia says folks call "The Factory." We're 4-4 overall and 3-1 in the league.

I won't sugarcoat it. Toledo went up 31-7 by halftime. John Alan Richter threw for 288 yards, Autavius Ison ran for 104, and CJ Miller scored twice from short range. AP says Toledo's defense got six sacks and nine tackles for loss and stopped us on downs four times. We ran for 34 yards on 28 carries, and we lost two fumbles. That was a Saturday for the scrapbook's back pages.

But here's what I'll keep in the front pages. Noah Kim threw two touchdown passes. He hit Joshua Long for 30 yards in the second quarter, and he found Harold Mack for a 12-yard score in the third. Long caught seven passes for 84 yards. Benson Prosper caught two for 39. Bryce Llewellyn made 10 tackles, Juan Salas made eight, and Zach Mowchan added seven. Zach leads the team with 58 for the season.

And this is a team that has learned to win. We beat Sacramento State 28-17 in our opener. We won 38-14 at UMass and 25-23 at Akron. We beat Lindenwood 29-3. Kim has 1,678 passing yards and 11 touchdowns, and Quincy Byas has four sacks. We're one loss into conference play, and the season is very much alive. Toledo was a bad shift at The Factory. It wasn't a plant closure.

Why I Love The Factory

Let me tell you about our home, because a road week makes me homesick. Wikipedia says Rynearson's field went artificial in 1991, became FieldTurf in 2005, and got its gray FieldTurf before the 2014 season. Gray! Everybody else has green. We have the color of a Michigan November sky, and we wear it proudly. The biggest crowd in Rynearson history, 26,188, came on Nov. 28, 2008, when Eastern beat Central Michigan 56-52. Fifty-six to fifty-two! That's the kind of afternoon that keeps a fan coming back for decades.

And our name has a history, too. Wikipedia says Eastern's teams were the Normalites from 1899 to 1928, then the Hurons, and then the Eagles starting in 1991. We grew up. We got wings. That's what a bright future looks like.

Part 2: A Road Trip to Athens

Saturday, 4 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, Eastern Michigan visits Ohio at Peden Stadium.

Let me be gracious first. Ohio is 5-2 and 3-0 in the MAC, and AP says the Bobcats have won four straight. They just beat Sacramento State 48-7. Duncan Brune scored twice on Saturday, Irving Brown ran for 87 on eight carries, and Will Hryszko made a 50-yard field goal. Ohio runs for 207 yards a game, 24th in FBS. And Wikipedia says Ohio won the 2024 MAC championship. That's a real program.

Now let me pull up the Bobcats' stat sheet, from AP's preview, and point out a few things.

Ohio's passing offense ranks 126th in FBS, at 164.3 yards a game. Nick Poulos has thrown for 503 yards all season. Five hundred and three, in seven games. Kim threw for 214 on Saturday alone, in a loss.

And Ohio's defense ranks 106th on third down, letting opponents convert 42.1 of every 100 times. Our offense converts 41.9 of every 100 third downs, 56th in FBS. That's where we win this thing. Keep the chains moving, keep Kim upright, and make Ohio throw it.

Also, I'd like to gently remind Athens about Oct. 3. Ohio beat Kent State 13-10. Kent State, which AP ranks 138th in FBS in scoring at 12.0 points a game. Ohio needed everything it had to get past Kent by three. And South Alabama scored 41 on Ohio in September. This defense can be had.

To be fair to the Bobcats' defense, Michael Molnar leads them with 52 tackles, Ike Ackerman has 4.5 sacks, and Barry Dillon intercepted a pass on Saturday. They allow 22.1 points a game, 57th in FBS. And AP says both of us are among the least penalized teams in FBS: Ohio is 18th in penalty yards and we're 15th. So nobody's going to give this one away with flags. It'll be decided on the field, which is how I like it.

The history isn't in our favor lately, and I won't pretend. CollegeFootballData.com says Ohio has won the last five meetings, including 28-21 in Ypsilanti last year. But the last time we played in Athens before 2024, in 2016, Eastern Michigan won 27-20. We've done it at Peden.

About That Stadium

Wikipedia says Peden Stadium has been home to the Bobcats since 1929 and is the oldest college football venue in the MAC. And here's my go-to Peden fact. It was originally called "Ohio Stadium." Not to be confused, Wikipedia helpfully adds, with Ohio Stadium in Columbus. So Ohio University's stadium was named after Ohio State's stadium. Even the building wanted to be somewhere else.

Tales From Two Towns

Ypsilanti. Ypsi, as we call it, is a city of 20,648 on the Huron River. Wikipedia says it's named for Demetrios Ypsilantis, a hero of the Greek War of Independence, and his bust stands at the base of our Ypsilanti Water Tower, built in 1890 on the highest point in town and 147 feet tall. Eastern Michigan was founded here in 1849 as Michigan's first normal school, a teachers' college. We have historic Depot Town, the old Detroit–Chicago Road, and Ford Lake. And during World War II, Ford's Willow Run Bomber Plant, which Wikipedia says the city is closely associated with, built more than 8,500 B-24 Liberator bombers. Ypsilanti doesn't just make teachers. It made the arsenal of democracy.

Athens. Athens, Ohio, is a pretty town of 23,849 on the Hocking River in Appalachian Ohio. But Wikipedia says it's known as the "World Capital of Halloween," and Athens has been cited as one of the 10 most haunted cities in America. It throws a Halloween Block Party that Wikipedia calls an international spectacle. I'm sure the Bobcats are very brave. But we're coming down the weekend before Halloween, and I'm not saying their defense is a ghost story, but third downs keep disappearing on them.

And notice the names. We named our town after a Greek hero. They named their town after a Greek city. Then they named their school Ohio and their stadium Ohio Stadium. Somebody in Athens really needed a thesaurus.

Imogen's Notes From the Corner Table

1. Protect Kim. Six sacks is too many.
2. Run the ball enough to keep Ohio honest. Thirty-four yards won't do it.
3. Make Ohio throw. 503 passing yards in seven games is a gift.

Gray turf, bright future.

My call: Ohio Bobcats 32, Eastern Michigan Eagles 19.

articles.title: I Expected This: Kent State Scored Two Points in Tampa, but the Wagon Wheel Lives in Kent, and the Zips Bring a Run Defense Ranked 130th and a Five-Game Skid
articles.byline: Ozzie Brannigan, The Kent State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Akron (1-6) at Kent State (2-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET, Dix Stadium, Kent, Ohio, ESPN+
articles.text:
Hello. It's Ozzie Brannigan. I'm sitting on a bench near Brady's Leap, wearing a navy-and-gold scarf I have rated, honestly, a 7 out of 10, and I'm here to tell you about Kent State football. You already know how I feel. I expected this. I always expect this. And I'm right about half the time, which, for a Kent State fan, is a pretty good number.

Part 1: Two Points, a Long Flight and a Fumbled Snap

South Florida beat Kent State 29-2 on Saturday night at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa. We are 2-5. I expected this.

But I want you to know something, because I'm a pessimist, not a liar. For one whole quarter, Kent State led. True freshman defensive end Dion'Dre Taylor stuffed USF's D.J. Crowther in the end zone for a safety with 1:52 left in the first quarter. By The Belt reported that it was Kent's first lead against a non-conference FBS opponent since 2023. I stood up. I sat back down. I knew.

Here's what happened next. Kent State drove to the USF 1-yard... the USF 1. I can't even say it right. On third down, Dru DeShields tried a quarterback sneak, the snap didn't come cleanly, and USF's C.J. Hicks scooped it up and went 96 yards the other way for a touchdown. USF's postgame notes say it tied the longest fumble return in program history. Of course it did. If you're going to break my heart, at least make the record book.

By The Belt also said that Kent State became the first FBS team to score exactly two points since 2020. USF's notes say we drove inside its 30 four times and came away with nothing. We went 0-for-4 on fourth down and missed a field goal. We gave up a safety with 11 seconds left. And the run game managed 63 yards on 35 carries.

Now the part I'll admit through clenched teeth. The defense was good. USF ran for 78 yards, 2.4 a carry, and By The Belt counted four sacks and eight tackles for loss. Hayden Dawahare made nine tackles and a sack. Aiden Burgess had a sack. Rocco Nicholl had a tackle for loss and a pass breakup. DeShields threw for 165 yards without an interception, and Brendyn Smith caught four passes for 56 yards. If you're a defensive player at Kent State, I would like to knit you a nice sweater.

As for my weekly fourth-down rating: 0 out of 4, rated 0 out of 10. As for the uniforms: navy and gold, clean, classic, 8 out of 10. The uniforms are doing fine. The uniforms can't snap the ball.

Part 2: The Wheel Is Ours, So Naturally I'm Worried

Saturday, 1 p.m. Eastern, ESPN+, Akron at Kent State, at Dix Stadium. It's Wagon Wheel week. And something unusual is true, so let me say it slowly. Kent State has the Wheel.

Last November, Kent State beat Akron 42-35 in overtime at InfoCision Stadium, according to Kent State Athletics. That brought the Wheel back to Kent for the first time since 2022. It's been here for almost a year. I keep checking on it, the way you check on a cake in the oven, sure that it's about to fall.

Now, let's look at Akron, and let me tell you, it's helping my mood.

The Zips are 1-6 and 0-3 in the MAC. AP says they've lost five in a row. Last week, Miami (Ohio) ran for 324 yards against them, 9.3 a carry, and Rodney Nelson had a career-high 142 on just 13 carries. Akron's run defense ranks 130th in FBS at 200.4 yards a game. Its scoring defense ranks 124th, at 32.4 points a game. And Akron's turnover margin of minus-7 ranks 131st. Brayden Roggow has thrown eight interceptions this year, including four last week.

I know what you're thinking. "Ozzie, our offense ranks 138th in scoring." It does. AP lists us at 12.0 points a game, and 137th in yards. I'm aware. I'm always aware. But if there was ever a week for Kent State's running game to find itself, it's against a team that just gave up 324 rushing yards. Mason King has 202 yards this season. Wayne Harris has 396 receiving yards. And this defense has some real talent: Nicholl has three sacks and Dawahare leads us with 35 tackles.

Akron has good players, too. I'm a pessimist, so I respect every opponent. Jordan Gant has 456 rushing yards. Donelius Johnson has 67 tackles. Akron opened its game in Oxford with a 97-yard touchdown drive. Then it scored once more all day.

And here's the history, which I memorize so I can worry about it in detail. Akron Athletics says that in the spring of 1870, John R. Buchtel, an Akron industrialist, came to Kent looking for a place to build a college. His wagon got stuck in the mud, roughly where Kent State is today, and he lost a wheel. He went back to Akron and started Buchtel College, the school that became the University of Akron. The wheel turned up in 1902, when workers building a pipeline dug it out, and a Kent State dean, Dr. Raymond Manchester, made it a trophy in 1945.

So let me get this right. Akron's founder came to Kent, couldn't get his wagon through, and went home. Akron has been trying to get back to this exact spot ever since. Some programs have a spirit. Akron has unfinished business with our mud.

Tales From Two Towns

Kent. Kent is a college town of 28,215 on the Cuyahoga River. It was settled in 1805 and was called Franklin Mills for years, until it was renamed Kent in 1864 for Marvin Kent, the businessman who brought the railroad shops to town, per Wikipedia. We're "The Tree City," home of the Davey Tree Expert Company. We've got nearly 20 parks and preserves, festivals for Earth Day and folk music, and Brady's Leap, a city park named for Captain Samuel Brady's 21-foot jump across the river around 1780. And the Kent State University Museum in Rockwell Hall focuses on the history of fashion design from the 18th century to now. I rate everything I see there a 10. Even the hats.

Akron. Akron is a big city, 190,469 people, the "Rubber Capital of the World," and it has nice things, like Stan Hywet Hall and Gardens and the Soap Box Derby. But Wikipedia says its name comes from the Greek word for "summit," because it was built at the high point of a canal. The high point of a canal, friends. That's like being the tallest person in a basement. And the Zips are named after the Zippers, a rubber boot made by B.F. Goodrich. Akron's football team is named after galoshes. You know what you wear galoshes for? Mud. Akron's whole identity has been about getting through Kent's mud since 1870.

Ozzie's Worry List

1. Hold onto the snap. I'm begging.
2. Run the ball against the 130th-ranked run defense, and keep running it.
3. Keep the Wheel. I've gotten used to it. You know I don't get used to things.

Do I think we'll win? I expected you to ask that. Here's the honest answer.

My call: Kent State Golden Flashes 27, Akron Zips 22.

articles.title: One If by Land, Two If by Overtime: UMass Fell to Buffalo in OT, and Now the Minutemen March to an Old Airfield in East Hartford, Where UConn's Pass Defense Ranks 135th
articles.byline: Abner Kettleworth, The Massachusetts Fanatic
articles.matchup: UMass (4-3) at UConn (3-3), Fri., Oct. 23, 7 p.m. ET, Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field, East Hartford, Conn., CBSSN
articles.text:
Hear ye, hear ye, patriots of the Pioneer Valley. Abner Kettleworth here, tricorn hat on, musket-shaped umbrella at the ready, and a pot of strong tea on the hearth. If you're new to my dispatches, I report on the Minutemen the way the old broadsides reported on the Revolution: with great passion, a few puns and an unshakable belief in the cause.

The news from Buffalo was not what we wanted. But a Minuteman doesn't retreat. He reloads.

Part 1: The Skirmish at Broadview

Buffalo beat UMass 25-18 in overtime on Saturday at Broadview Stadium in Amherst, New York. Yes, the other Amherst. We're 4-3, 1-3 in the MAC.

It was a battle of special teams in the first half, and AP gives a full account. Buffalo got a 71-yard kickoff return, a safety and a muffed-punt recovery, and turned them into eight points. But the Minutemen struck first, when Logan Inagawa ran 20 yards for a touchdown in the first quarter. Then TJ Magee recovered a Buffalo muffed punt, and Elijah Faulkner punched it in from 2 yards out. Inagawa hit Jabari Lewis for the two-point conversion, and UMass led 15-8 at halftime. A fine first engagement.

Buffalo tied it in the third quarter. Then, with less than two minutes left, Derek Morris drilled a 53-yard field goal to give UMass an 18-15 lead. Fifty-three yards, friends, after he had missed two earlier. That's what the Founders called perseverance.

Alas, Buffalo drove quickly and kicked a 29-yard field goal with 2 seconds left to force overtime. Buffalo scored a touchdown on its first possession, and on fourth down, Inagawa's throw to the end zone fell incomplete. 25-18.

Inagawa threw for 168 yards and ran 19 times for 66 more. Faulkner ran for 84 yards and a touchdown. Kezion Dia-Johnson caught five passes for 79 yards. Timmy Hinspeter made eight tackles and has 59 this season, and Kendall Bournes made eight too. And our defense held Buffalo's passing game to 134 yards on 16-of-35 throwing.

This campaign has had glorious moments. On Sept. 3, UMass went to Rutgers, a Big Ten school, and won 37-21. We won 35-6 at Sacramento State. We beat Sacred Heart and Stonehill. And our last two losses came by one point to Miami (Ohio) and in overtime to Buffalo. This army is close. It just needs one more volley. And remember how this team is built: Faulkner leads us with 361 rushing yards, Hinspeter and Bournes lead a defense that ranks among the best in FBS, and Morris just proved he can hit from 53 under pressure. Muskets are loaded.

Part 2: The March to East Hartford

Friday, 7 p.m. Eastern, CBS Sports Network, UMass visits UConn at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field. A Friday night skirmish across the border. The redcoats would never.

First, a salute to the Huskies, because a gentleman honors his opponent. UConn is 3-3. AP ranks its offense 24th in FBS in yards and 29th in scoring, at 35.7 points a game. Kalieb Osborne has thrown for 1,421 yards and 10 touchdowns. Cyncir Bowers has six rushing touchdowns. UConn also rested last week, after beating Temple 34-20 on Oct. 10.

Now, the intelligence report, all from AP's preview.

UConn's pass defense ranks 135th in FBS. It allows 290.5 passing yards a game. Its defense overall ranks 115th. It ranks 113th on third-down defense, letting opponents convert 43.3 of every 100 times. And UConn is 130th in FBS in penalty yards, at 79.0 a game. That is a defense that fires before it sees the whites of anybody's eyes.

Meanwhile, the Minutemen's defense ranks 30th in FBS in yards allowed and 30th against the pass. It allows 19.1 points a game, 33rd. And UMass has a turnover margin of plus-7, which ranks 8th in all of FBS. We take the ball like a militia takes a bridge.

William Watson III has completed 74.0 of every 100 passes this season, with seven touchdowns. T.Y. Harding has 28 catches. Against the 135th-ranked pass defense in the country, I'd like to see the Minutemen open up the passing game and see what happens.

And here's a dispatch about UConn's own record. The Huskies lost to Miami (Ohio), 24-21, a team UMass lost to by a single point. They lost 42-41 to Syracuse. They lost 38-14 to Maryland at home. UConn is the more decorated army on paper, but it can be beaten.

The history, per CollegeFootballData.com: UConn leads the series 6-4. But in 2018, UMass went to this very stadium in East Hartford and won 22-17. And in 2021, UMass beat UConn 27-13. We've crossed this river before.

Tales From Two Towns

Amherst. Amherst is in the Connecticut River valley, in the Pioneer Valley of western Massachusetts, a town of 39,263 at the 2020 census and the most populous in Hampshire County, per Wikipedia. It's home to three of the Five Colleges: UMass, Amherst College and Hampshire College. The Emily Dickinson Museum is here, at the house where the poet was born and lived her whole life. "Hope is the thing with feathers," she wrote. She wasn't writing about football, but she could have been. And the Minutemen themselves, per Wikipedia, won the 1998 Division I-AA national championship. We've hoisted the big one. Wikipedia says the program began play in 1879, moved up to the FBS starting in 2011 and rejoined the MAC as a full member on July 1, 2025, after years as an independent. A long march, and a proud one. McGuirk hosted its first game on Sept. 25, 1965, and UMass beat American International College 41-0. A fine way to christen a fort.

East Hartford. East Hartford is a town of 51,045 on the east bank of the Connecticut River, right across from Hartford, and it's the home of the jet-engine maker Pratt & Whitney. But here's the thing. Wikipedia says UConn's main campus is in Storrs, and it played its home games on campus there from 1953 to 2002. Then it moved off campus. UConn's stadium sits on the site of Pratt & Whitney's old company airfield. So the Huskies play home games on a former airport, in a different town from their campus. Now, in the spirit of honesty that built this republic, I'll confess: Wikipedia says our own McGuirk Stadium, home of the Minutemen since 1965, sits just across the town border in Hadley. But it's on our campus, and it holds 17,000 of the loudest patriots in the valley. Our stadium sits just over a town border, still on campus. Theirs left campus entirely. If you've got to fly to your own home game, it's not really a home game.

And let's talk about the mascots, gently. A husky is a fine sled dog. But a sled dog's whole job is to pull somebody else where they want to go. A Minuteman answers the call himself, on a minute's notice. That's the difference between Storrs and Amherst.

Dispatches for the Troops

1. Throw the ball. The 135th-ranked pass defense awaits.
2. Keep taking the ball away. Plus-7 is a winning flag.
3. Finish. Two close losses were enough. Ring the bell this time.

Onward, Minutemen. The British are coming, and so are the Huskies, and we are ready for both.

My call: UConn Huskies 33, Massachusetts Minutemen 21.

articles.title: Four Interceptions and a Little Cradle Talk, Darling: Miami Wins Back-to-Back for the First Time This Season and Heads to Mount Pleasant, Where the Chippewas Throw for 108 Yards a Game
articles.byline: Cordelia Van Doren, The Miami (OH) Fanatic
articles.matchup: Miami (OH) (4-3) at Central Michigan (3-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET, Mount Pleasant, Mich., ESPN+
articles.text:
Hello, darlings. Cordelia Van Doren here, writing from a bench in Uptown Oxford with a cup of tea, a red scarf and a very good feeling about the RedHawks. I've been told I'm a bit much about Miami University. I've been told correctly. When your football program is called the Cradle of Coaches, a little drama comes with the territory.

So let's talk about Saturday, and then let's talk about Mount Pleasant.

Part 1: The Afternoon the Secondary Went Shopping

Miami beat Akron 34-14 on Saturday at Yager Stadium, in front of 18,515 people. We're 4-3, 2-1 in the MAC, and AP says it's the first time this season we've won back-to-back games. Darling, I'll take a streak of two. Streaks have to start somewhere.

Now, the defense. Akron's Brayden Roggow threw four interceptions, and four different RedHawks caught them: Blayne Myrick, Ben Minich, Kaleb Martin and Amariyun Knighten. Myrick returned his for a touchdown in the third quarter that made it 27-7. Four interceptions from four people. That's not a defense. That's a dinner party, and everyone brought a dish.

Grant Lyons had two sacks and two tackles for loss. Malcolm McCain made 10 tackles, and he leads the team with 58 this season.

Much like Central Michigan's passing game, the well looks promising, and then very little comes out.

1. Keep running. 324 yards is the outfit of the season.
2. Stop Flores. He is the whole Central Michigan wardrobe.
3. Keep taking the ball away. Four interceptions is a lovely accessory.

Ta-ta, darlings. Love and Hawks.

My call: Central Michigan Chippewas 24, Miami (OH) RedHawks 23.

articles.title: Brick by Brick: Ohio Has Won Four Straight and Sits at 3-0 in the MAC, and an Eastern Michigan Team That Ran for 34 Yards Last Week Comes to Peden
articles.byline: Penny Trautman, The Ohio Fanatic
articles.matchup: Eastern Michigan (4-4) at Ohio (5-2), Sat., Oct. 24, 4 p.m. ET, Peden Stadium, Athens, Ohio, ESPNU
articles.text:
Well, hello from Court Street! Penny Trautman here, standing on the bricks, where every Bobcat fan should stand at least once a week. If you've never been to Athens, the streets downtown are paved in brick, and so is my philosophy of football: lay one good block at a time, keep it level, and before long you've built a road nobody can wash out. Ohio has laid four good bricks in a row. Let's keep paving.

Part 1: A 48-7 Brick Wall in Sacramento

Ohio beat Sacramento State 48-7 on Saturday night at Hornet Stadium, and AP says it's four straight wins for the Bobcats. We're 5-2 and 3-0 in the MAC. That's a sturdy foundation.

The offense was a masonry crew. Ohio piled up 30 first downs and 468 yards, per ESPN's box score, and ran for 265 yards. Duncan Brune scored on runs of 3 and 14 yards. Victor Rosa ran one in from 16. Irving Brown ran eight times for 87 yards, including a 50-yarder, and scored from 2 yards out late. Levi Davis added a 14-yard touchdown run. Nick Poulos went 11 of 14 for 165 yards, and he hit Preston Bowman on a 67-yard catch-and-run touchdown about two minutes into the third quarter that made it 34-0. Will Hryszko made a 50-yard field goal and a 37-yarder and all six extra points.

The defense held Sac State scoreless for three quarters. Barry Dillon picked off a pass. Michael Molnar had a sack and a pass breakup, and he leads the team with 52 tackles. Darren James-Hamilton made six tackles. Ohio had the ball for 33:11 and committed zero turnovers.

Not bad for a long flight. Bricks travel well, as long as you pack them carefully.

And look at how this streak was built. The Bobcats started 1-2 after losing at Nebraska and at South Alabama, where they scored 36 and still came up short. Then they beat Stonehill 35-7. Then came a 13-10 grinder at Kent State, the kind of game where you have to set every brick by hand. Then a 31-14 win over Central Michigan at home, and then this one. Before all that, in September, the Bobcats beat Jacksonville State 29-27. That's a team that's learned how to win close and how to win big. Riley Neer has 32 catches for 441 yards and five touchdowns this season. Brune has 330 rushing yards. And Poulos hasn't thrown an interception all year, per AP. Not one. I'd call that a well-pointed wall.

Part 2: Eastern Michigan Comes to Peden

Saturday, 4 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, Eastern Michigan visits Peden Stadium.

A word of respect first, because that's how we do it on Court Street. Eastern Michigan is 4-4 and 3-1 in the MAC. It beat Akron, UMass and Sacramento State. Noah Kim has thrown for 1,678 yards and 11 touchdowns, and he threw two touchdown passes against Toledo on Saturday. Joshua Long has 38 catches. Zach Mowchan has 58 tackles, and Quincy Byas has four sacks. And EMU doesn't beat itself: AP ranks it 15th in FBS in penalty yards. That's a good, disciplined team.

Now, the inspection report. All numbers from AP.

Toledo beat Eastern Michigan 34-14 on Saturday in Ypsilanti and led 31-7 at halftime. Toledo's defense got six sacks and nine tackles for loss and stopped the Eagles on downs four times. And Eastern Michigan ran for 34 yards. Thirty-four yards on 28 carries. Friends, I've seen longer walks from my front door to the bricks.

AP's preview ranks EMU's rushing offense 128th in FBS, at 105 yards a game. Its offense overall is 123rd in yards. Its scoring offense is 110th, at 21.5 points a game. And Ohio's rushing offense ranks 24th, at 207 yards a game. One of us builds a road on the ground. The other one is stuck in the mud.

Here's what I'm watching. AP ranks our third-down defense 106th, so I'd like to see the Bobcats get off the field a little faster. Kim converts. But if Eastern can't run, it's playing on one leg, and Ohio's pass rush, led by Ike Ackerman's 4.5 sacks, can go after Kim the way Toledo just did.

The history, from CollegeFootballData.com: Ohio has won the last five meetings with Eastern Michigan, including 35-10 at Peden in 2024 and 28-21 in Ypsilanti last season. Ohio leads the series 22-12-1.

And the Bobcats are the reigning example of how to build something. Wikipedia lists Ohio's 2024 MAC championship, its first since 1968, plus five MAC East titles. That's how a program gets laid down. One brick at a time, with good mortar. And before the MAC, Wikipedia says, Ohio won six Buckeye Athletic Association titles in the 1920s and 1930s. This program has been stacking bricks for a long time.

A Word About Peden

Wikipedia says Peden Stadium has been home to the Bobcats since 1929, sitting on the banks of the Hocking River, and it's the oldest college football venue in the MAC. It seats 24,000 and has been called Frank Solich Field at Peden Stadium since 2022. Old buildings are the best buildings, friends. They're built with bricks. Eastern Michigan's field is famous for being gray. Ours is famous for still standing after nearly a century. Wikipedia says the place was built for $185,000 and finished in 1929, and it was renamed for Don Peden, who coached and ran athletics at Ohio for 27 years, after he retired in 1946. They added the north end zone stands in 1986. That's a building with a family tree.

Tales From Two Towns

Athens. Athens is a town of 23,849 on the Hocking River in Appalachian Ohio, about 65 miles southeast of Columbus, per Wikipedia. Ohio University was chartered here in 1804, the first public institution of higher learning in the Northwest Territory. WOUB, the public media station here, notes our brick tradition goes back to the Athens Block Company, founded in 1891, and folks still feel strongly about keeping the bricks on the streets. Athens also throws the Halloween Block Party, which Wikipedia calls an international spectacle, and the town has a reputation as the "World Capital of Halloween." Our university was the first public one in the whole Northwest Territory. Our streets are made of bricks. And our ghosts have tenure.

Ypsilanti. Ypsilanti is a nice city of 20,648 on the Huron River, and its fans have spent a long time explaining that they're not Ann Arbor. I respect that. But Wikipedia lists a water tower among the things Ypsilanti is best known for. A water tower! It's 147 feet tall and it was built in 1890, and they're very proud of it. We have an entire university district of brick buildings. They have a very tall pipe.

And Eastern Michigan's teams were once called the Normalites, from 1899 to 1928, according to Wikipedia. The Normalites! Ohio's teams are the Bobcats. I'd take a bobcat over a Normalite in any alley in Athens.

Penny's Building Checklist

1. Lay the foundation with the running game. 207 a game is good mortar.
2. Make Eastern run. It ran for 34 yards last week.
3. Get off the field on third down. Close the door and latch it.

Brick by brick, Bobcats.

My call: Ohio Bobcats 32, Eastern Michigan Eagles 19.

articles.title: Plate It Up in Muncie: First-Year FBS Sac State Brings a Farm-to-Fork Appetite to a Ball State Defense Allowing 37.9 Points and 201.6 Rushing Yards a Game
articles.byline: Mateo Villaseñor, The Sacramento State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Sacramento State (1-6) at Ball State (2-5), Sat., Oct. 24, 3:30 p.m. ET, Scheumann Stadium, Muncie, Ind., ESPN+
articles.text:
Welcome to the kitchen, Hornets. Mateo Villaseñor here, apron on, knife sharp, and a cutting board full of Sacramento Valley produce. Every week I narrate the game like a cooking show, because football, like food, is about preparation, timing and heat. Some weeks the soufflé rises. Some weeks it falls. This week, we went into the oven and came out a little crispy. But we're cooking again on Saturday. In Muncie, Indiana. Plate it up.

Part 1: The Kitchen Got Hot

Ohio beat Sacramento State 48-7 on Saturday night at Hornet Stadium, in front of 17,661 people. We're 1-6, 0-4 in the MAC. AP says that's five losses in a row. I'm not going to garnish that. You can't garnish a 48-7.

Here's the honest recipe card. Ohio had 30 first downs. It ran for 265 yards. Muncie got a research paper about being typical.

Muncie is also where the Ball brothers built their glass factory in 1888, which is lovely, and it's the Ball in Ball State. The Ball Brothers made glass jars. Sacramento grows what goes in the jars. I think we know who's the main ingredient and who's the container.

And yes, I know Jim Davis, the man behind Garfield, studied at Ball State, per Wikipedia. Garfield is a fine cat who loves lasagna. But he has never once eaten a farm-to-fork tomato. That's the difference between Muncie and Sacramento.

1. Clean up the penalties. 130 yards is too much salt.
2. Feed the running game. Ball State gives up 201.6 rushing yards a game.
3. Stay patient. A first-year FBS program is a slow braise, not a microwave.

Plate it up, Hornets.

My call: Ball State Cardinals 32, Sacramento State Hornets 22.

articles.title: 400 Horsepower and Six Sacks: Toledo Rolled Through Ypsilanti, and Now an Unbeaten-in-the-MAC Western Michigan Team With the 129th-Ranked Passing Game Rolls Into the Glass Bowl
articles.byline: Rocco Szczepanski, The Toledo Fanatic
articles.matchup: Western Michigan (5-2) at Toledo (5-2), Sat., Oct. 24, noon ET, Glass Bowl, Toledo, Ohio, CBSSN
articles.text:
Rocco Szczepanski here, reporting from a garage on the north side of Toledo with a socket wrench in one hand and a pierogi in the other. I'm a Jeep-town kid, so I grade every offense in horsepower. A sputtering offense is a lawnmower. A good one is a V-6. And a great one, folks, is 400 horsepower of four-wheel-drive fun.

Saturday in Ypsilanti, the Rockets had the engine running hot.

Part 1: Full Throttle at The Factory

Toledo beat Eastern Michigan 34-14 on Saturday at Rynearson Stadium. We're 5-2 and 2-1 in the MAC.

The offense started the engine early. John Alan Richter threw a 28-yard touchdown pass to Adjatay Dabbs midway through the first quarter. Reice Griffith kicked a 30-yard field goal. CJ Miller scored from a yard out. Autavius Ison ran it in from 13 yards. Miller scored again from 3. It was 31-7 at halftime. That's a V-8 with a fresh tune-up.

Richter went 24 of 30 for 288 yards and a touchdown, 80 completions for every 100 throws. Ison ran 18 times for 104 yards, with a long of 42. Bryson Hammer caught five passes for 69 yards, Dabbs caught five for 66, and Cooper Rusk had a 45-yard catch. We piled up 480 yards.

And the defense was a monster truck. AP says the Rockets had six sacks and nine tackles for loss, and stopped Eastern on downs four times. Eastern ran for 34 yards on 28 carries. Andrew Zock had two sacks and, per ESPN's box score, nine quarterback hurries. Nine! Ezra Odinjor had two sacks. Julian Fox made 11 tackles, and Isaac Zay had 2.5 tackles for loss.

Now the honest inspection sticker: we were flagged 14 times for 118 yards. That's a check-engine light, and we have to fix it this week.

Horsepower rating for Saturday: 400. Four-wheel drive engaged.

Let me walk you through the whole season's service record, because this engine's been running for a while. We lost 30-20 at Michigan State in the opener, which is no shame. Then we beat Central Connecticut 63-10, outlasted Temple 49-48 and beat San Diego State 41-16, all at home. We won 39-24 at Ball State. We hit a pothole against Buffalo. And now we're back on the highway after Saturday. The offense has scored 34 or more five times. That's a motor that turns over every morning, even in a Toledo winter.

Part 2: The Broncos Come to the Glass Bowl

Saturday, noon Eastern, CBS Sports Network, Western Michigan at Toledo.

I'll be a gentleman about it. Western Michigan is 5-2 and 3-0 in the MAC. It lost 13-12 at Michigan in its opener. Its defense is good: AP ranks it 25th in FBS in scoring defense, at 16.9 points a game, and 17th in red zone defense. Jalen Buckley ran for 150 yards against Central Michigan. Justyce Betts has 51 tackles. Western is disciplined and takes care of the ball. That's a well-maintained vehicle.

But let's pop the hood on that offense, using AP's preview.

Western Michigan's passing offense ranks 129th in FBS, at 157.6 yards a game. Its offense overall ranks 121st in yards. Its scoring offense ranks 90th. Against Central Michigan, Broc Lowry threw eight passes for 48 yards. Forty-eight yards! That's a riding lawnmower. With a bag on the back.

Meanwhile, Toledo's offense ranks 20th in FBS in yards, 27th passing and 28th in scoring, at 36.3 points a game. Richter has 14 touchdown passes and one interception. Dabbs has 468 receiving yards and five touchdowns. Miller has 426 rushing yards and six touchdowns. And Zock has seven sacks on the season.

So here's the math, Jeep-plant style: Western has to run the ball to move. Our run defense ranks 46th in FBS. If we make Western throw, we're putting a lawnmower on the freeway.

The Broncos also got a little help from the schedule. They lost 32-7 at home to Boise State, a different set of Broncos entirely. Even the Broncos couldn't handle the Broncos.

I'll admit two things. One, Buffalo beat us 23-8 at the Glass Bowl on Oct. 10, and that was a flat tire. Two, Western beat us 14-13 last season, according to CollegeFootballData.com. But Toledo leads the series 39-24. We won 49-31 in 2023 and 34-15 in 2021, both at the Glass Bowl. This is our garage.

And a little Rockets history for the road. Wikipedia says Toledo played its first few years without a nickname, until two long touchdown runs in a 1923 game against Carnegie Tech got the team dubbed the "Rockets." We lost that game. But we came out of it with the best nickname in the conference. That's how Toledo works: even on a bad day, we build something. Wikipedia also lists Toledo with a 12-11 record in bowl games. We've been to the postseason plenty, and we'd like to go again.

Tales From Two Towns

Toledo. Toledo is a city of 270,871 at the western end of Lake Erie, on the Maumee River, per Wikipedia. We're "The Glass City," because glass makers started arriving in the 1880s, and the Toledo Museum of Art has a large glass collection to prove it. Jeep has its headquarters here, with two production plants called the Toledo Complex, and Wikipedia says Toledo's industries built the Willys Jeep for the military in World War II. And our stadium is the Glass Bowl, a Works Progress Administration project finished in 1937 that got its glass touches after the war and its name in 1946. You want horsepower, glass and grit? This is the place. The same New Deal era brought the Toledo Zoo its amphitheater and aquarium, per Wikipedia, and the Toledo Museum of Art got a major expansion. Toledo was building in the 1930s while other towns were waiting.

And a little history for our friends from up north. Wikipedia says Ohio and the Michigan Territory fought the nearly bloodless Toledo War in the 1830s over the strip of land that includes Toledo. Michigan lost. We've been in Ohio ever since. Some folks call it a border dispute. I call it Michigan's first loss in Toledo.

Kalamazoo. Kalamazoo is a nice city of 73,598, and I'll admit the name is fun. Wikipedia says it's become a byword for faraway places, as in "from Timbuktu to Kalamazoo." That's right: Kalamazoo is the place people name when they mean somewhere far away and exotic. Folks, it's in the very next state, right up the road from us. I've driven there in a Wrangler, and I didn't even need four-wheel drive. And its big civic achievement is the Kalamazoo Mall, the first outdoor pedestrian shopping mall in the country, which was built by closing part of Burdick Street to cars. Toledo builds Jeeps. Kalamazoo closed a street so nobody could drive on it. I don't think I need to explain which town has more horsepower.

Rocco's Pre-Drive Checklist

1. Fix the check-engine light. Fourteen flags won't fly against a team this disciplined.
2. Make Western throw. A lawnmower can't win a drag race.
3. Keep Richter clean. One interception all year. Keep it that way.

That's 400 horsepower of run game. Go Rockets.

My call: Toledo Rockets 26, Western Michigan Broncos 22.

articles.title: That's a Full Stack: Western Michigan Is 3-0 in the MAC After Taking the Cannon From Central, and Toledo Brings a Defense That Just Lost 23-8 at Home and Ranks 126th in Penalty Yards
articles.byline: Corwin Dahlquist, The Western Michigan Fanatic
articles.matchup: Western Michigan (5-2) at Toledo (5-2), Sat., Oct. 24, noon ET, Glass Bowl, Toledo, Ohio, CBSSN
articles.text:
Good morning, Broncos. Corwin Dahlquist here, at my usual Kalamazoo diner booth, with a syrup bottle, a pencil and a paper placemat full of pancake diagrams. For the newcomers: I rate every opponent on the pancake scale. A short stack is a team you should handle. A full stack is a real meal. And a tall stack with butter and whipped cream is a team that might ruin your whole Saturday.

Toledo is a tall stack. But so are we.

Part 1: The Rivalry Breakfast in Mount Pleasant

Western Michigan beat Central Michigan 21-14 on Saturday in Mount Pleasant. We're 5-2 and 3-0 in the MAC, per ESPN. And it was the 97th meeting in the series, per AP, with Western now leading 55-40-2. That's a lot of pancakes.

This was a ground game breakfast. Jalen Buckley ran 24 times for 150 yards and two touchdowns, from 9 and 7 yards out. Lolo Mataele added 60 yards on 13 carries. Western Michigan ran for 224 yards as a team. Broc Lowry only needed to throw eight passes, but he made one count, a 10-yard touchdown to Nate Levicki in the second quarter. We led 21-0 after three quarters.

The defense was syrup on the plate. Justyce Betts made 12 tackles, and he has 51 this season. Scoop Gardner Jr. had two sacks. Dillon Moore had a sack and a tackle for loss, and Domanick Moon broke up a pass. Central got two late scores, but our hands team held the onside kick. Full stack.

Wikipedia says this game decides the Cannon Trophy, and it counts toward the Michigan MAC Trophy. So the Cannon stays in Kalamazoo. Row the boat home, friends. Next stop on the trophy tour is Eastern Michigan later this season, and I've already bought extra syrup.

And look at this season's menu. We lost 13-12 at Michigan in the opener, by a single point, to a Big Ten team in the Big House. We won at Rice and at Buffalo, beat Monmouth, crushed Kent State 38-7 and now beat Central on the road. AP ranks our scoring defense 25th in FBS, at 16.9 points a game, and our red zone defense 17th. We're 22nd in turnover margin at plus-4, and 24th in penalty yards. That's a disciplined kitchen.

Part 2: Brunch at the Glass Bowl

Saturday, noon Eastern, CBS Sports Network, Western Michigan at Toledo, at the Glass Bowl.

Let me rate the Rockets fairly. Toledo is 5-2 and 2-1 in the MAC. AP ranks its offense 20th in FBS in yards and 28th in scoring, at 36.3 points a game. John Alan Richter has thrown for 1,853 yards, 14 touchdowns and only one interception, and he went 24 of 30 for 288 yards against Eastern Michigan on Saturday. Adjatay Dabbs has 468 receiving yards. Andrew Zock has seven sacks. Toledo's defense got six sacks against Eastern. That's a tall stack, with extra butter.

But I see some burnt edges.

Two weeks ago, on Oct. 10, Buffalo went to the Glass Bowl and beat Toledo 23-8. Toledo scored eight points at home against a Buffalo defense that AP ranks 85th in scoring. Burnt.

Toledo also ranks 126th in FBS in penalty yards, per AP, at 76.0 a game. It had 14 penalties for 118 yards against Eastern Michigan, according to ESPN's box score. You can't flip a pancake if you keep dropping the spatula. And Toledo had to hang on to beat Temple 49-48 in September.

Meanwhile, Western Michigan is one of the least penalized teams in FBS. We take care of the ball. And our scoring defense allows 16.9 points a game. When a high-scoring offense meets a stingy defense, I like the team with the better table manners.

I'll be honest about our weak spot, because a pancake man doesn't lie about the batter. AP ranks our passing offense 129th in FBS, at 157.6 yards a game. We'll need Buckley and the run game, which ranks 59th, to carry the plate again. He has 542 rushing yards and seven touchdowns.

And the history? Last season, per CollegeFootballData.com, Western Michigan beat Toledo 14-13 in Kalamazoo. By one point. Toledo leads the overall series 39-24, but our boat has rowed past them before: 20-14 in 2022, and 41-38 in 2020. These games are close. Get your syrup ready.

And here's a menu item from the Rockets' own history. Wikipedia says Toledo played without a nickname in its early years and was dubbed the "Rockets" after two long touchdown runs in a 1923 loss to Carnegie Tech. So Toledo got its name from a game it lost. I respect a program that finds the bright side. I'll be happy to help them find it again on Saturday.

Our own history is a stack I'm proud to serve. Wikipedia says Western Michigan has played at Waldo Stadium since 1939. In 2016, the Broncos finished the regular season 13-0 as MAC champions, the best in school history, and became the first MAC team to play in the Cotton Bowl. That was a tall stack with whipped cream, a cherry and a side of bacon. This year's team has the same kind of defense-first ingredients.

Tales From Two Towns

Kalamazoo. Kalamazoo is a city of 73,598, and it's named after the Kalamazoo River, per Wikipedia. The name comes from an Algonquian language and has been explained as meaning "boiling water," "reflecting river," "it smokes" or "otters beneath the surface." Every one of those is a great name for a football team. Kalamazoo is so fun to say that it's become a byword for faraway places, as in "from Timbuktu to Kalamazoo." In 1959, the city created the Kalamazoo Mall, the first outdoor pedestrian shopping mall in the United States, by closing part of Burdick Street to cars. And Gibson guitars got their start here, when Orville Gibson incorporated the company in 1902. Kalamazoo rocks, literally. Fun fact for the diner crowd: Wikipedia says the town was first named Bronson, after its founder, Titus Bronson, who settled there in 1829, and it became Kalamazoo in 1836. Good call. Bronson is a fine name. Kalamazoo is a fine name with otters in it.

Toledo. Toledo is a big city of 270,871 at the western end of Lake Erie, on the Maumee River. It's called "The Glass City" for its long history of glass manufacturing, and Jeep has its headquarters there. Respect. But Wikipedia says Ohio and the Michigan Territory once had a near-bloodless dispute called the Toledo War, over the strip of land that holds Toledo. And Ohio won. So Michigan lost Toledo. And every Michigander I know at this diner considers that the best loss in state history.

And the stadium? Wikipedia says the Glass Bowl was originally called University Stadium, finished in 1937, and was renovated with glass elements after World War II and renamed in 1946. A football stadium made partly of glass, in a town that keeps getting penalized. I'd tiptoe.

Corwin's Pancake Ratings

1. Toledo's offense: tall stack, extra butter.
2. Toledo's discipline: one burnt pancake, 126th in penalty yards.
3. Western's defense: full stack, syrup on the side.

Row the boat, Broncos. That's a full stack.

My call: Toledo Rockets 26, Western Michigan Broncos 22.

articles.title: Shhh, It's Tuesday Night: Delaware Lost a Heartbreaker in Murfreesboro, and Now a Missouri State Defense Ranked 127th in FBS Comes to the First State
articles.byline: Hen Lofland, The Delaware Fanatic
articles.matchup: Missouri State (2-4) at Delaware (2-4), Tue., Oct. 20, 7 p.m. ET, Delaware Stadium, Newark, Del., ESPNU
articles.text:
Good evening, and please lower your voices. This is a library. Kidding. Shout all you like. I'm Hen Lofland, short for Henrietta, and I spend my days at a circulation desk in Newark and my nights thinking about the buck sweep. I believe every good argument needs a footnote, every good season needs a second chapter, and every good Tuesday night needs the Blue Hens on television.

This Tuesday, we get exactly that. But first, I owe you an honest book report on last week.

Part 1: A Page-Turner With a Sad Last Chapter

Delaware lost 33-30 at Middle Tennessee last Tuesday night. I won't pretend otherwise. We're 2-4 and 0-2 in Conference USA.

But oh, what a story it was. Tucker Smack opened the scoring with a 33-yard field goal. Middle Tennessee answered with a field goal and a safety and took a 12-3 lead early in the second quarter. Then Kaderris Roberts ran one in from 11 yards. And with 24 seconds left in the half, George Mullins intercepted Roman Gagliano, per AP. Then Bryson Graves threw a 15-yard touchdown pass to Tyler Bell. Yes, our quarterback caught a touchdown. Shelve that one under "Plot Twists."

Bell played the whole night in place of Nick Minicucci, who AP says missed his second straight game. Bell went 22 of 36 for 306 yards, two touchdowns and one interception. He hit Josh Humes for a 33-yard score in the third quarter, and his 23-yard touchdown pass to Kaderris Roberts gave Delaware a 30-26 lead with 9:57 left. Donovan Lewis caught six passes for 83 yards. Gavin Moul made 10 tackles, with 1.5 tackles for loss.

Then Middle Tennessee went 93 yards in 10 plays, and Gagliano threw a 14-yard touchdown pass to Neo Clifton with 3:06 to go. That was the final chapter.

Here's my librarian's note in the margin. The two teams were nearly even in yards, 396 to 391, per ESPN's box score. But Delaware ran for 70 yards on 30 carries and was flagged 13 times for 101 yards. We lost by three. You can find those three points in the penalty column. We'll fix our citations and try again.

Part 2: The Bears Come to Newark

Tuesday, 7 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, Missouri State at Delaware.

First, a kind word for our guests. Missouri State has some good pages in its book this year. Isaiah Myers has 554 receiving yards and five touchdowns on 27 catches. Henry Belin IV threw for 300 yards and two touchdowns against Kennesaw State last Wednesday, and Myers caught both. Then Yousef Obeid kicked a field goal as time expired to win it 24-21. AP called it the Bears' first win over an FBS team under coach Casey Woods. Congratulations. Truly. I'd put that one on the "New Arrivals" shelf.

Now, the reference desk is open, and I've pulled AP's preview.

Missouri State's defense ranks 127th in FBS, allowing 430.8 yards a game. Its pass defense ranks 120th, at 254.3 yards a game, and its run defense ranks 108th, at 176.5. It allows 30.5 points a game, which ranks 116th. And opponents convert 44.4% of third downs against the Bears, which ranks 120th. That isn't a defense. That's a library with no late fees. Everybody just walks right out with whatever they want.

Meanwhile, Delaware's passing game ranks 29th in FBS, at 271.0 yards a game. Sean Wilson has 25 catches for 339 yards and three touchdowns. Our run game ranks 135th, at 94.0 yards, which my wing-T heart has read with great sorrow. But against a run defense ranked 108th, this may be the week the buck sweep gets checked out again.

And the Bears' road record has some overdue notices. Missouri State lost 50-0 at Texas A&M, 34-24 at SMU and 34-13 at Western Kentucky. It's 0-3 away from Springfield. Its red zone offense ranks 106th in FBS, scoring on 80.0% of trips. Delaware's red zone defense ranks 55th.

I'll be honest about our side, because librarians don't hide books. Our pass defense ranks 125th, allowing 259.2 yards a game, so Myers is the chapter I'm worried about. Blake Matthews has 4.5 sacks, and he'll need to visit whoever plays quarterback for the Bears early and often. AP's preview lists Skyler Locklear as their season passing leader, and Belin threw for 300 last week. Our home record is 2-1, with wins over Merrimack, 42-7, and Coastal Carolina, 22-14.

And this is a first edition. CollegeFootballData.com lists no previous meeting between these programs. So let's write the first page properly.

Tales From Two Towns

Newark. Wikipedia says Newark was founded in 1694 by Scots-Irish and Welsh settlers and got its charter from King George II in 1758. A grammar school moved here in 1765 and became the Newark Academy, and three of its early graduates signed the Declaration of Independence. We had a school turning out founders before there was a country. Tradition holds that the Battle of Cooch's Bridge, just outside town, was the first time the Stars and Stripes flew in battle. The Curtis Paper Mill was the oldest paper mill in the United States until it closed in 1997, which is the most librarian sentence I've ever written. And Newark is a center of figure skating, with national, world and Olympic champions who trained at the University of Delaware's club.

Then there's our name. Wikipedia says one story of the Blue Hen goes back to the Revolutionary War, when Captain Jonathan Caldwell's company, recruited mostly in Kent County, carried blue game chickens with a fearsome reputation. The Blue Hen became Delaware's state bird in 1939, and the university still keeps a small flock. We are, quite literally, the birds of a revolution.

And Delaware Stadium? It opened on Nov. 15, 1952, with a 13-12 win over Lafayette. On a typical home game day, per Wikipedia, the stadium becomes the fourth-largest city in the state. The field was named in 2002 for longtime coach Harold "Tubby" Raymond. Wikipedia says the wing-T, built on the run and deceptive fake handoffs, was the identity of Delaware football for nearly 50 years, and it credits Dave Nelson with bringing it and with bringing the winged helmet, designed by his old coach Fritz Crisler. Six national titles, too: 1946, 1963, 1971, 1972, 1979 and 2003. Rich Gannon and Joe Flacco played here. Check the card catalog, friends. It's full.

Springfield. Springfield, Missouri, is a pleasant city of 169,176 in the Ozarks, per Wikipedia. Its nicknames include "Queen City of the Ozarks" and "The Birthplace of Route 66." That's right: Springfield's claim to fame is a road out of Springfield. It's also the headquarters of Bass Pro Shops, so one of its best-known companies is devoted to helping people go somewhere else and sit quietly in a boat. And Wikipedia notes that Springfield is known for its own local variations of cashew chicken. I'm a Blue Hen, and frankly, I find that a little threatening. Newark had a paper mill making pages for centuries. Springfield made a chicken dish. I rest my case, quietly, because we're in a library.

Hen's Reading List for Tuesday

1. Fewer flags. Thirteen penalties is a whole overdue shelf.
2. Run the ball. A 108th-ranked run defense is an open invitation to the buck sweep.
3. Protect the secondary's homework. Keep a safety over Myers and make the Bears go the long way.
4. Get after the quarterback. Matthews, please pay a visit.

Tuesday night in Newark, under the lights. Bring your library card and your loudest voice. This is the one night I won't shush you.

My call: Delaware Blue Hens 29, Missouri State Bears 24.

articles.title: Cafecito and a Brick Wall: FIU's Defense Ranks Ninth in FBS, and Now a Middle Tennessee Offense Ranked 122nd Comes to Pitbull Stadium on a Tuesday Night
articles.byline: Lourdes Ibarguen-Tate, The Florida International Fanatic
articles.matchup: Middle Tennessee (3-3) at Florida International (3-3), Tue., Oct. 20, 7 p.m. ET, Pitbull Stadium, Miami, CBSSN
articles.text:
¡Hola, Panther people! Lourdes Ibarguen-Tate here, from a kitchen table in Sweetwater, about five minutes from campus. This is where my abuela taught me football with dominoes and sugar packets. The dominoes were the players. The sugar packets were the defense. And let me tell you, this year the sugar packets are winning.

Before we talk about Tuesday, I owe you the truth about last Tuesday. Abuela taught me that too.

Part 1: So Close in Jacksonville

On third-and-15, AP says, he escaped pressure and found Maguire Anderson for a 50-yard touchdown. Then he hit Anderson again from 30 yards out to tie it 17-17 before halftime. Josiah Taylor made his first career interception late in the second quarter. ¡Qué bueno!

In the third quarter, Devonte Lyons scored from 8 yards out to tie it at 24. But the Gamecocks drove 82 yards in 13 plays, and Garrison Rippa kicked a 26-yard field goal with 44 seconds left. Our last try didn't fall. AP says Jacksonville State is 19-3 at home since moving to FBS, so that's a tough house to visit.

Kohl went 24 of 38 for 278 yards and two touchdowns, with no interceptions. Anderson caught eight passes for 133 yards and both scores. Lyons ran 15 times for 73 yards. FIU outgained Jacksonville State 404 to 387, had the ball for 33:44 and committed zero turnovers, per ESPN's box score.

First, cariño for our guests. Middle Tennessee is a gritty team. Roman Gagliano has 11 touchdown passes and just two interceptions, and last week he led a 93-yard drive to beat Delaware 33-30. AP ranks the Blue Raiders 22nd in FBS in turnover margin, at plus-4. Cam'ron Lacy has 35 catches. Korey Smith has 56 tackles. That's a team that doesn't quit, and I respect it. I'd offer them a croqueta.

Middle Tennessee's offense ranks 122nd in FBS, at 321.5 yards a game. Its rushing offense ranks 114th, and its scoring offense ranks 103rd. And who does it meet on Tuesday? DeeJay Holmes Jr. has five sacks. DeAndre Boykins has 37 tackles. We held Long Island and New Mexico State to 3 points apiece, and Buffalo to 20. That's not a defense, mi gente. That's a brick wall with a cafecito in its hand.

And Middle Tennessee's defense? Its run defense ranks 127th, allowing 199.2 yards a game. Its red zone defense ranks 114th, allowing scores on 91.7% of trips. Lyons should be licking his lips. Our offense ranks 29th in third-down conversions, at 46.4%, and 10th in time of possession. Middle Tennessee ranks 119th. We'll hold the ball like abuela holds the TV remote. Nobody else touches it.

Also, the Blue Raiders lost 55-0 at Kansas earlier this month, and 23-13 at Jacksonville State. I say that kindly, because we know that stadium.

I'll be honest about our side. Our scoring offense ranks 122nd. Our three losses came by 10, 6 and 3 points, two of them on the road against Florida neighbors, South Florida and Florida Atlantic. Kohl has seven interceptions on the year, so ball security matters. But this team has a defense, and defense travels, and on Tuesday it doesn't even have to travel.

And history? CollegeFootballData.com says Middle Tennessee leads the series 14-7. But FIU won the last two, 35-24 at home in 2024 and 56-30 in Murfreesboro last year. Fifty-six. I still have the dominoes from that one lined up on the shelf.

Tales From Two Towns

Miami. Wikipedia says Miami is the only major city in the United States founded by a woman, Julia Tuttle, who owned the land it was built on. They call it the Magic City because it grew so fast that winter visitors said it was like magic. We have the third-largest skyline in the country and the Calle Ocho Festival, the largest Latin music festival in the country, running since 1978. Cuban immigrants in the 1960s brought the Cuban sandwich, croquetas and Cuban espresso, and you can still get them at window cafés all over town, including landmarks like Versailles in Little Havana. And my Sweetwater is 12 miles west of downtown, a city of 19,363, informally known as "Little Managua" for its longtime Nicaraguan community. Mi barrio.

And FIU is a Miami story. The university was founded in 1965 and opened to students in 1972. Our football team began play in 2002, with a 27-3 win over Saint Peter's in its very first game. Our stadium opened in 1995 with 7,500 seats and now holds 20,000. In 2007, while the stadium was being rebuilt, FIU played at the Orange Bowl, and Wikipedia says FIU's 38-19 win over North Texas was the last college football game ever played there. When the new stadium opened in 2008, FIU's first win there came on Oct. 11 against, yes, Middle Tennessee, 31-21. And in 2010, FIU won the Sun Belt and the Little Caesars Bowl. Fans held signs that said "¡Sí se puede!"

Murfreesboro. Murfreesboro is a pleasant city of 152,769 southeast of Nashville, per Wikipedia. It was the capital of Tennessee from 1818 to 1826. Then, after eight years, the capital moved to Nashville. So Murfreesboro is a town that had the big job and handed it back. I understand. I've seen their red zone defense. Today Wikipedia calls it the largest suburb of Nashville. And it's the geographic center of Tennessee, marked by a stone monument. The middle of Middle Tennessee. Abuela says that's the part of the pastelito where all the filling ends up, and she means it with love.

Lourdes's Domino Plan for Tuesday

1. Feed Lyons. A 127th-ranked run defense is a buffet.
2. Keep the sugar packets stacked. A ninth-ranked defense against a 122nd-ranked offense is abuela's go-to kind of matchup.
3. Fewer flags. Twelve penalties is a whole box of dominoes on the floor.
4. Finish in the red zone. Their defense lets 91.7% of trips score. Make it touchdowns.

Come to the stadium in blue and gold, bring your colada, and stay loud. ¡Vamos, Panthers!

My call: Florida International Panthers 28, Middle Tennessee Blue Raiders 16.

articles.title: Low and Slow Wins the Fourth Quarter: Unbeaten-in-League Jacksonville State Takes an Open Week After a Late Kick Beat FIU, Then Heads West to Las Cruces
articles.byline: Burl Ashcraft-Neeley, The Jacksonville State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Open week for Jacksonville State (5-2) this week. Next: Jacksonville State at New Mexico State (2-4), Wed., Oct. 28, 8 p.m. ET, Aggie Memorial Stadium, Las Cruces, N.M., ESPN2
articles.text:
Low and slow wins the fourth quarter! Burl Ashcraft-Neeley here, Calhoun County pitmaster, and I've never lived more than 10 miles from campus. I've got hickory in the smoker, a mop bucket of sauce and a lawn chair with my name on it. And this week, friends, the smoker gets a rest, because Jacksonville State doesn't play. It's an open week. I'll be honest about that right up front, just like I'm honest about how long a brisket takes.

So let's look back at the last cook, and then look ahead to the next one.

Part 1: A 13-Play Drive, Smoked to Perfection

Jacksonville State beat FIU 27-24 last Tuesday night at AmFirst Stadium. We're 5-2 and 3-0 in Conference USA, and that's four straight wins.

That's how you do it in this county: low and slow, then finish strong. Caden Creel threw first-quarter touchdown passes of 38 yards to Luke Gilbert and 36 yards to Deondre Johnson, and Garrison Rippa kicked a 47-yard field goal. We led 17-7. FIU came back to tie it at the half, and again at 24 in the third quarter, after Justus Savage scored his first collegiate touchdown on a 4-yard run, per AP.

Then came the good part. Tied at 24 heading into the fourth, the Gamecocks drove 82 yards in 13 plays, and Rippa kicked a 26-yard field goal with 44 seconds left. That's a 13-hour brisket, friends. You don't rush it. You let it go, and you serve it at the very end.

Creel went 16 of 22 for 214 yards and two touchdowns, and he ran 19 times for 95 yards. Johnson caught four passes for 93 yards. We ran for 173 yards, 5.4 a carry, per ESPN's box score. Morven Joseph made nine tackles. And AP says Jacksonville State is 19-3 at home since moving to FBS. You don't come into a man's backyard and steal his ribs.

Now, the honest part. FIU outgained us 404 to 387, and we threw an interception. We got a little lucky at the end of the first half, too, when FIU missed a field goal. That defense has some work to do on the long passes.

And here's a nugget from the league office. Conference USA's Oct. 13 notes said the Gamecocks had rushed for a touchdown in 64 straight games, a streak 24 games longer than any other active streak in FBS or FCS. Then Savage ran one in against FIU. Smoke and fire, friends. Smoke and fire. The same notes said Creel had 405 rushing yards and four rushing touchdowns this season heading into the FIU game, and that his 1,480 rushing yards since the start of last season ranked second among all FBS quarterbacks, behind only Army's Cale Hellums. Then he ran for 95 more. That young man runs like he smells a cookout at the end of the field.

The Open Week, Honestly

Jacksonville State has no game this week. The rest of the league plays Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and we watch. That's fine. A good pitmaster knows when to let the coals settle. I'll spend the week cleaning the grates, restocking the hickory and watching the other teams sweat it out on a school night.

And there's plenty of season left to cook. We lost 33-7 at North Dakota State and 29-27 at Ohio, I won't hide that. But since then? We beat Georgia Southern 31-27, and Middle Tennessee 23-13 at home, won 27-26 at Kennesaw State, and then beat FIU. Four straight. And the league says Jacksonville State is 12-1 in its weekday Conference USA games over four years. The weeknight belongs to us.

Part 2: West to Las Cruces

Next up: Wednesday, Oct. 28, 8 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2, Jacksonville State at New Mexico State, at Aggie Memorial Stadium.

First, a kind word for the Aggies, because my mama raised me right. James Jones has 599 rushing yards on 92 carries. Gabe Peterson has 4.5 sacks. Nick Session has 50 tackles. And the Aggies beat us 20-17 in Las Cruces in 2023, per CollegeFootballData.com. I remember that one. It's still stuck in my teeth.

But let's check the meat thermometer, using AP's latest preview of New Mexico State. The Aggies' turnover margin is minus-5, which ranks 122nd in FBS. Their red zone defense ranks 118th, allowing scores on 92.9 of every 100 trips. They rank 127th in time of possession. And their scoring offense ranks 97th. In their last game, a 22-3 loss at FIU, they turned it over three times. That's a brisket that came off the smoker too early. Gray in the middle, and nobody's asking for seconds.

New Mexico State plays Sam Houston on Wednesday night first, so those numbers will move a little before we get there. I'll be watching from my lawn chair with a plate of pulled pork.

And here's a fun fact from CollegeFootballData.com: the last time New Mexico State came to Jacksonville, in 2024, we won 54-13. Fifty-four. That's a whole-hog cookout.

Tales From Two Towns

Jacksonville. Jacksonville, Alabama, is a city of 14,385, per Wikipedia, and it's added 71.2 residents for every 100 it had in 2000. It sits in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains, in a valley between Choccolocco Mountain and smaller ridges to the west. It was founded on July 20, 1833, first called Drayton, and renamed for President Andrew Jackson in 1834. Jacksonville State University was founded here in 1883, and it's one of the biggest employers around.

And our football history is good smoked meat. Wikipedia says Jacksonville State fielded its first team in 1904, and we've been the Gamecocks since before the 1947 season, when we also switched from blue and gold to red and white. In 1992, we won the Division II national championship, beating Pittsburg State 17-13. We joined FBS and Conference USA in 2023. AmFirst Stadium seats 24,000. And country singer Riley Green played quarterback here. You can't make up a better backyard soundtrack.

Las Cruces. Now, Las Cruces is a nice city in the Mesilla Valley, and I hear they know their chile. But Wikipedia says it's 225 miles from Albuquerque and 42 miles from El Paso, Texas. So the second-biggest city in New Mexico is closer to Texas than to the biggest city in its own state. And Aggie Memorial Stadium sits at 3,980 feet above sea level. That's so high, friends, that a pitmaster's smoke would have to stop and catch its breath. Down here in the foothills, our smoke rolls right across the parking lot, and everybody follows it to the cooker.

One more thing. Wikipedia says New Mexico State was last ranked in the AP poll in 1960. Friends, that's a long cook. Even my slowest pork shoulder doesn't take 66 years.

Burl's Pit Notes for the Open Week

1. Rest the legs. A brisket needs to rest before you slice it, and so does a running game.
2. Tighten up the secondary. FIU threw for 280 yards. Let's not serve that again.
3. Keep the streak smoking. A rushing touchdown every game, low and slow.
4. Get ready to travel. Las Cruces is a long drive with a cooler.

Light the coals, friends. The Gamecocks will be back on a weeknight, which is right where we like it.
