articles.title: Patch Notes, Version 6.0: Kennesaw State Lost Another Close One, but It Has Beaten Liberty Two Years Running, and the Flames Rank 137th in FBS in Penalty Yards
articles.byline: Ximena Holcombe-Reyes, The Kennesaw State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Liberty (5-1) at Kennesaw State (1-5), Thu., Oct. 22, 7 p.m. ET, Fifth Third Stadium, Kennesaw, Ga., CBSSN
articles.text:
Hey, Owl Nation! Ximena Holcombe-Reyes here, logging in from Marietta with a computer science degree and a T-shirt from Kennesaw State's very first football season. I was there for version 1.0. The shirt no longer fits. That's growth.

Here's my operating system: some programs have a hundred years of history, and Kennesaw State gets to write ours live, in front of us. Every number I share is sourced and debugged. When I find a bug, I log it. Then we patch it, and we ship again.

Time for this week's patch notes.

Part 1: Bug Report From Springfield

Kennesaw State lost 24-21 at Missouri State last Wednesday night. We're 1-5 and 0-2 in Conference USA, and it's five straight losses. I won't sugarcoat a stack trace.

But look at how close the build was to compiling. The Bears led 6-0 on two field goals. Then, on the last play of the first half, Rickie Collins threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Dylan Gary, and we went into the locker room up 7-6. After Missouri State scored, Collins ran one in from 9 yards to tie it at 14. After the Bears scored again, Boogie Woods III ran it in from a yard out to tie it 21-21 with 6:06 left. Then Missouri State drove the field and kicked a field goal as time expired.

Collins went 26 of 34 for 260 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions, per ESPN's box score. Gary caught 10 passes for 135 yards, with a long of 51. Javon Rogers caught six for 79. Tywon Christopher made 12 tackles, with two tackles for loss. Tay'vion Lawson intercepted a pass. And we didn't turn the ball over once.

The bug? Eleven penalties for 95 yards. AP's preview ranks us 129th in FBS in penalty yards, at 77.8 a game. That's a memory leak, and it's on the fix list.

And here's the bigger pattern in the logs. We lost 17-14 at Arkansas State, 27-26 at home to Jacksonville State and 24-21 at Missouri State. Three losses by a combined seven points. That's not a broken program. That's a program that's a few good snaps away from 4-2. We opened the year with a 47-0 win over West Georgia, too. The core functions work. We just need the final few functions to return true.

Part 2: Liberty Comes to Fifth Third Stadium

Thursday, 7 p.m. Eastern, CBS Sports Network, Liberty at Kennesaw State.

First, a respectful code review of our guests. Liberty is 5-1 and has won five straight. AP ranks its rushing offense 15th in FBS, at 223.0 yards a game, and its scoring defense 15th, at 15.3 points a game. Kam Davis has 524 rushing yards. Makai Jackson has 515 receiving yards on 22 catches. Deshawn Purdie has eight touchdown passes and no interceptions. Opponents convert just 28.4 of every 100 third downs on the Flames, which ranks eighth. That's clean code, and I respect it.

Now let's run the debugger.

Liberty ranks 137th in FBS in penalty yards, at 85.8 a game, per AP. In its last game, against Sam Houston, Liberty was flagged 15 times for 117 yards, per ESPN. Fifteen! If our 77.8 yards a game is a memory leak, Liberty's is the whole server room on fire. Its passing offense ranks 105th, at 192.8 yards a game. And in September, the Flames beat Gardner-Webb, an FCS team, 24-23. One point. At home. I'm just reading the logs.

And Liberty finished 4-8 last year, per Wikipedia. So, respectfully, the Flames know about rebuilds, too.

Here's my most-starred repository: the head-to-head history. CollegeFootballData.com says Kennesaw State beat Liberty 27-24 at Fifth Third Stadium in 2024, and 48-42 in Lynchburg last year. We lead the all-time series 3-2. Version history matters.

Honest notes on our side. Our red zone defense ranks 132nd, allowing scores on 95.5 of every 100 trips, and Liberty's red zone offense ranks 45th. That's a critical vulnerability. Our scoring offense ranks 106th. We rank 102nd in time of possession, and Liberty ranks 12th. So the patch is simple: hold on to the ball, keep Collins moving, and get Liberty's rushers on the ground before they reach the red zone.

Tales From Two Towns

Kennesaw. Kennesaw is a city of 33,036 northwest of Atlanta, per Wikipedia, and it added 10.9 residents for every 100 over the last decade. It has an important place in railroad history. On April 12, 1862, it was the staging ground for the Great Locomotive Chase, and today the Southern Museum of Civil War and Locomotive History sits across from the old train depot. Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park is just southeast of the city, and the mountain's summit, at 1,808 feet, is the highest point in the Atlanta metro area. And Kennesaw State is the third-largest public university in Georgia.

Yes, the town was called Big Shanty until 1887, after the shanty towns that housed the workers building the Western and Atlantic Railroad. We prefer to think of it as the beta release. The city was renamed for the mountain, and the mountain was the site of major fighting in the Battle of Kennesaw Mountain, part of the Atlanta campaign. We've been a place where things happen for a long time.

And our football program is a startup success story. Wikipedia says the Owls began play in 2015 with a 56-16 win over East Tennessee State under Brian Bohannon, our first coach. We moved to FBS and Conference USA in 2024. Then, in 2025, first-year coach Jerry Mack led us to a 9-3 regular season and the Conference USA championship, with a 19-15 win over defending champion Jacksonville State. From version 1.0 to a conference title in 11 seasons. Ship it. Wikipedia also notes that Bron Breakker played football at Kennesaw State before he became a WWE star, and Travis Bell became the first Kennesaw State player selected in the NFL draft, in 2023, in the seventh round. The alumni network is growing, too, one commit at a time.

Lynchburg. Lynchburg, Virginia, is a pleasant city of 79,009 in the Blue Ridge foothills, per Wikipedia. It's nicknamed the "City of Seven Hills," which, as far as I can tell, means seven separate uphill walks to wherever you were going. It was founded by John Lynch, who ran a ferry across the James River. So the town started as a way to get across the river to somewhere else. And Wikipedia says Thomas Jefferson built his Poplar Forest retreat near Lynchburg "to avoid the many visitors at Monticello." That's right. One of the most famous Americans ever went to Lynchburg to get away from people. I'm a software engineer, and I respect that, but I wouldn't put it on a tourism brochure.

Ximena's Release Checklist for Thursday

1. Fix the penalty bug. Seventy-eight yards a game is too much overhead.
2. Protect the red zone. Ninety-five and a half of every 100 is a vulnerability, not a feature.
3. Make Liberty throw. Its passing offense ranks 105th.
4. Keep Collins and Gary connected. Ten catches and 135 yards last week is a stable build.

Wear your gold on Thursday night, Owl Nation. Bugs happen. We patch them, and we ship again.

My call: Liberty Flames 28, Kennesaw State Owls 18.

articles.title: Praise the Lord and Hand Me a Program: Liberty Rested Up After a 297-Yard Rushing Night, and Now the Flames Visit a Kennesaw State Team That Ranks 132nd in Red Zone Defense
articles.byline: Gideon Fairweather, The Liberty Fanatic
articles.matchup: Liberty (5-1) at Kennesaw State (1-5), Thu., Oct. 22, 7 p.m. ET, Fifth Third Stadium, Kennesaw, Ga., CBSSN
articles.text:
Well, praise the Lord and pass the program! Gideon Fairweather here, coming to you from Lynchburg, where I'm a youth pastor by trade and a middle-school football coach on the side. That means I've given a halftime speech on perseverance to eleven 12-year-olds who mostly wanted to know what flavor the sports drink was. I'm ready for anything, friends, including a Thursday night in Georgia.

Part 1: A Week of Rest After a Night of Running

Let me be honest first, because that's how my mama raised me: Liberty didn't play last week. We had the week off. So let me tell you about the last time the Flames took the field, because it was a good one.

On Oct. 8, Liberty beat Sam Houston 35-3 at Williams Stadium. We're 5-1 and 2-0 in Conference USA, and AP says that made it five straight wins.

The Flames ran the ball like they were late for a church potluck. We piled up 297 rushing yards on 39 carries, 7.6 a carry, per ESPN's box score. Jaylon Coleman ran seven times for 92 yards. Kam Davis ran 10 times for 67 yards and a touchdown. Ethan Vasko scored twice, from 1 and 3 yards out. Terron Kellman added a 9-yard touchdown run. And Deshawn Purdie went 10 of 14 for 114 yards, ran seven times for 57 more, and threw a 15-yard touchdown pass to Bryce Randolph to cap an eight-play, 75-yard drive on the game's opening possession.

The defense was a blessing, too. Sam Houston managed 243 yards and one field goal. AP says the Bearkats turned the ball over on downs three times in the second half. Derrell Farrar made nine tackles, and Markus Clark had a sack.

Now, every sermon needs a confession. We were flagged 15 times for 117 yards. Fifteen! My middle-schoolers would be running laps until Christmas. AP's preview ranks Liberty 137th in FBS in penalty yards, at 85.8 a game. We need to clean that up, and I trust these young men to do it.

And this streak has been earned. We opened with a 20-13 loss at James Madison. Then we squeaked past Gardner-Webb 24-23, beat Ball State 51-15, won 34-17 at Coastal Carolina and won 30-14 at Delaware. Five straight. That's the kind of perseverance I preach about.

Part 2: Thursday Night in Kennesaw

Thursday, 7 p.m. Eastern, CBS Sports Network, Liberty at Kennesaw State.

First, some honest respect, because the Owls have earned it. Wikipedia says Kennesaw State won the 2025 Conference USA championship under first-year coach Jerry Mack, beating Jacksonville State 19-15 in the title game. And they've beaten us two years running, 27-24 at their place in 2024 and 48-42 at ours last year, per CollegeFootballData.com. The Owls lead the series 3-2. Rickie Collins is a dual threat, with five rushing touchdowns. Dylan Gary caught 10 passes for 135 yards last week. These are good young men, somebody's sons, and they play hard.

But brothers and sisters, let's open the AP preview and read the scripture.

Kennesaw State is 1-5 and has lost five straight. Its scoring offense ranks 106th in FBS, at 22.3 points a game. Its pass defense ranks 102nd. And its red zone defense ranks 132nd, allowing opponents to score on 95.5 of every 100 trips. Ninety-five and a half out of every hundred! Friends, that's not a red zone. That's an open church door on Sunday morning. Everybody's welcome, and everybody gets in.

Meanwhile, Liberty's rushing offense ranks 15th in FBS, at 223.0 yards a game. Kam Davis has 524 yards and four touchdowns. Makai Jackson has 515 receiving yards and five touchdowns on just 22 catches. And Purdie has eight touchdown passes and zero interceptions. Zero! That's a young man who listens in Sunday school.

Our defense ranks 19th in FBS in yards allowed and 15th in scoring, at 15.3 points a game. Our pass defense ranks 15th. And opponents convert just 28.4 of every 100 third downs against us, which ranks eighth. We also rank 12th in time of possession. The Owls rank 102nd. So the Flames like to hold the ball, and when the other fellas get it, they don't keep it long.

I'll be honest about the Owls' grit. They lost 17-14 at Arkansas State, 27-26 at home to Jacksonville State and 24-21 at Missouri State on a field goal as time expired. That's three losses by three points or fewer. They're close, and close teams are dangerous. We'll pray for them on Friday morning. On Thursday night, we'll play.

Tales From Two Towns

Lynchburg. Lynchburg is a city of 79,009 in the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, along the James River, per Wikipedia. It's called the "City of Seven Hills" and the "Hill City." It was founded in 1757 by John Lynch, a Quaker ferry operator and abolitionist, who started a ferry across the James when he was about 17. Thomas Jefferson built his retreat, Poplar Forest, nearby in 1806, and Wikipedia quotes him calling Lynchburg "the most interesting spot in the state." Mr. Jefferson knew a thing or two. We've got Point of Honor, the Trails of Blackwater Creek along old railroad beds, and Riverside Park. Wikipedia also says Lynchburg was the only major city in Virginia not recaptured by Union forces before the end of the Civil War, thanks to its strategic importance. And it's a college town several times over, home to Liberty, the University of Lynchburg, Randolph College and more. Lynchburg on game day feels like a family reunion with a marching band.

And Liberty football is a story of faith. Wikipedia says the Flames began play in 1973. Williams Stadium was built in 1989 and seats 25,000. In 2023, Jamey Chadwell's first season, Liberty went undefeated in the regular season, won Conference USA, and played in the Fiesta Bowl, the program's first major bowl. From a brand-new team to a New Year's Six bowl in 50 years. That's what perseverance looks like.

Kennesaw. Now, Kennesaw is a nice city northwest of Atlanta. But Wikipedia says that from the 1830s until 1887, the town was called Big Shanty. Big Shanty! I'm sure it was a lovely shanty. Big, too. And the town is named for Kennesaw Mountain, which is the highest point in the Atlanta area, and which Wikipedia says is located southeast of the city limits. So Kennesaw has one mountain, and it isn't even in town. Lynchburg has seven hills, and we keep every one of them inside the city.

Kennesaw is famous for the Great Locomotive Chase in 1862, when a train left town and folks had to chase it down. I hope the Owls' defense brings its running shoes on Thursday, because our ball carriers are leaving the station, too.

Coach Gideon's Halftime Speech, Delivered Early

1. Run the ball. A 15th-ranked rushing offense is our daily bread.
2. Finish in the red zone. Their defense lets 95.5 of every 100 trips score. Make them all touchdowns.
3. Keep your heads and your hands to yourselves. Fifteen flags is too many for any Thursday.
4. Respect the Owls. They beat us the last two years, and they won the league last season.

Bless these young men on both sidelines. Play hard, play fair, and let's see the joy on their faces.

My call: Liberty Flames 28, Kennesaw State Owls 18.

articles.title: Have a Biscuit, Sugar: Middle Tennessee Went 93 Yards to Beat Delaware, and Now the Blue Raiders Head to Miami to Face an FIU Offense That Ranks 122nd in Scoring
articles.byline: Opal Stonebriar, The Middle Tennessee Fanatic
articles.matchup: Middle Tennessee (3-3) at Florida International (3-3), Tue., Oct. 20, 7 p.m. ET, Pitbull Stadium, Miami, CBSSN
articles.text:
Well, hey there, sugar. Come in, sit down and have a biscuit. I'm Opal Stonebriar, a Rutherford County girl and a church choir director, and folks around Murfreesboro call me the front-row grandma. I'm 34. It's a spiritual title. I'll feed you, I'll love on these Blue Raiders like they're my own, and if you say something untrue about my team, I'll correct you sweetly and with a citation.

And honey, last Tuesday night, my choir would've sung the Hallelujah chorus.

Part 1: Ninety-Three Yards to Glory

Middle Tennessee beat Delaware 33-30 last Tuesday night at Floyd Stadium. We're 3-3 and 1-1 in Conference USA.

It took the whole hymnal. Dominic Bourgeois kicked a 47-yard field goal, and our defense got a safety in the first quarter. Roman Gagliano ran it in from a yard out early in the second quarter for a 12-3 lead. Delaware came back to lead 16-12 at the half. Then, on the very first play of the second half, Gagliano threw an 80-yard touchdown pass to Koraun Perdue. AP says so, and so does my heart.

The teams traded the lead after that, and Delaware went up 30-26 with 9:57 left. And then, sugar, Gagliano took us 93 yards in 10 plays. He found Neo Clifton for a 14-yard touchdown with 3:06 remaining, and we held on. I stood up in the front row and didn't sit back down till Wednesday.

Gagliano went 22 of 32 for 291 yards and three touchdowns, with a rushing touchdown too. Perdue caught four passes for 103 yards. Clifton caught four for 64 yards and two touchdowns. On defense, Korey Smith made 10 tackles and a sack, Ashton Taylor had 1.5 sacks, and Bryce Williams intercepted a pass. And we were flagged just five times for 45 yards, per ESPN's box score. That's a well-behaved choir.

Now, I'll be honest, because I don't fib. Delaware threw for 321 yards against us and kept it close all night. And earlier this month, we lost 55-0 at Kansas. That one I've prayed over. But we beat Murray State and Nevada at home, we lost by two at Marshall, and now we've learned how to finish a fourth quarter. That's growth.

Part 2: The Blue Raiders Go to Miami

Tuesday, 7 p.m. Eastern, CBS Sports Network, Middle Tennessee at FIU.

First, I'll say something sweet about the Panthers, because Mama raised me right. FIU's defense is very, very good. AP ranks it ninth in FBS in yards allowed and ninth in scoring defense, at 14.7 points a game. DeeJay Holmes Jr. has five sacks. FIU's passing offense ranks 37th, and Maguire Anderson caught eight passes for 133 yards and two touchdowns last week. Those are fine young men, and I'd bake them a pie.

Now, bless their hearts. Bless their big guys up front, too.

FIU's scoring offense ranks 122nd in FBS, at 19.7 points a game. Its rushing offense ranks 117th, at 120.0 yards a game. Its red zone offense ranks 93rd. AP has the Panthers 82nd in turnover margin, at minus-1. And JJ Kohl has seven interceptions this season, per AP's preview. Our turnover margin is plus-4, which ranks 22nd. Our quarterback has two interceptions all year. Sugar, those two numbers are a sermon all by themselves.

And last week in Jacksonville, FIU was flagged 12 times for 100 yards and lost by three. The Panthers have lost at South Florida, at Florida Atlantic and at Jacksonville State. Every road they've been down this year has a pothole in it. But we're the ones traveling this time, so let me be careful.

I'll be honest about my own family. Our offense ranks 122nd in yards, and our run defense ranks 127th, allowing 199.2 yards a game. Our red zone defense ranks 114th. So, yes, we've got some chores to do. But Gagliano has 11 touchdown passes, Antonio Martin has 433 rushing yards, and Cam'ron Lacy has 35 catches for 369 yards and four touchdowns. Korey Smith has 56 tackles. That's a choir with some soloists.

And the history book? CollegeFootballData.com says Middle Tennessee leads the all-time series 14-7. We won five straight meetings from 2019 through 2023, including 50-17, 50-10 and 40-6 games at home. FIU has won the last two, I'll admit it, sugar. Every family has a couple of rough holidays.

Tales From Two Towns

Murfreesboro. Wikipedia says Murfreesboro was settled in 1811. It was first named Cannonsburgh, and about a month later it was renamed for Colonel Hardy Murfree, a Revolutionary War hero. It was the capital of Tennessee from 1818 to 1826, and today has 152,769 people. It's the geographic center of Tennessee, with a stone monument about half a mile north of MTSU, and it's the center of population, too. Since the 1990s, it's been Tennessee's fastest-growing major city. We have the Stones River National Battlefield, which preserves the site of a major Civil War battle fought at the turn of 1863, Cannonsburgh Village downtown, the Oaklands Historic House Museum and a Greenway walking trail along the river. And our stadium is Floyd Stadium, which Wikipedia says opened on Oct. 14, 1933, with a scoreless tie against Jacksonville State and now seats 27,303. Our football team started in 1911, and we've been to 14 bowl games. That's a lot of Sunday dinners. Derek Mason was hired as our 15th head coach in December 2023, per Wikipedia, and he follows Rick Stockstill, who led the program from 2006 to 2023 and won a share of the Sun Belt title in his very first season. We know how to build something here, and we know how to be patient while it rises, like a good biscuit dough.

We're the heart of the state, sugar. Literally. Look it up. I did.

Miami. Now, Miami is a big, beautiful city with a skyline full of high-rises, I know. But here's something I learned, and I'll say it gently. Wikipedia says FIU's main campus is in Westchester, and its stadium sits in unincorporated Miami-Dade County with a Miami mailing address. So Miami's team isn't technically in Miami. It just gets the mail there. And FIU plays in a stadium named Pitbull Stadium. Sugar, that sounds like a place with a chain-link fence and a "Beware" sign on the gate. Our stadium is named for a coach. Theirs sounds like it bites.

And Miami calls itself the Magic City. Wikipedia says that's because winter visitors thought the city grew so fast it was like magic. Honey, Murfreesboro has been the fastest-growing major city in Tennessee for three decades, and nobody had to call it magic. We just call it Tuesday. And I've got a little magic too. It's called a 93-yard drive.

Opal's Sunday Dinner Plan for Tuesday

1. Protect the football. Plus-4 got us here. Keep it in the family.
2. Stop the run. Their rushing offense ranks 117th, so make them throw it into the wind.
3. Bless the big guys up front. Keep Gagliano clean, and he'll keep finding Perdue and Clifton.
4. Score touchdowns. A ninth-ranked defense won't hand out many chances, so cash in every one.

Pack a biscuit and come sit with us, even if it's on the TV this time. You'll leave a Blue Raider. I promise.

My call: Florida International Panthers 28, Middle Tennessee Blue Raiders 16.

articles.title: Keep Everybody in the Canoe: Missouri State Won on a Field Goal as Time Expired, and Now the Bears Float East to a Delaware Team Whose Run Game Ranks 135th in FBS
articles.byline: Clementine Bilyeu, The Missouri State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Missouri State (2-4) at Delaware (2-4), Tue., Oct. 20, 7 p.m. ET, Delaware Stadium, Newark, Del., ESPNU
articles.text:
Howdy from the Ozarks! Clementine Bilyeu here, drying off a paddle on the bank of the James River. I guide float trips for a living, so I take a practical view of football. Read the current. Respect the rocks. Keep everybody in the canoe. And when the river gives you a nice long stretch of smooth water at the end, you paddle like crazy.

Last Wednesday night, the Bears paddled like crazy.

Part 1: A Smooth Finish at Plaster Stadium

Missouri State beat Kennesaw State 24-21 last Wednesday at Plaster Stadium. We're 2-4 and 1-1 in Conference USA. And AP says it was the Bears' first win over an FBS team under coach Casey Woods. That's a milestone you carve into the canoe.

It started slow, like the top of any good float. Yousef Obeid kicked two field goals in the second quarter, and we led 6-0 until Kennesaw State scored on the last play of the half. Then Henry Belin IV found Isaiah Myers for a 14-yard touchdown, and Connor Lair ran in the two-point try. Kennesaw tied it. Belin found Myers again, from 12 yards, for a 21-14 lead with 9:20 left. Kennesaw tied it again with 6:06 to go.

Then the Bears got the ball, and the river went smooth. We marched down the field and ran out the clock, and Obeid kicked a field goal as time expired. Three for three on the night. Calm, cool and dry.

Belin went 28 of 39 for 300 yards, which AP calls a career high, with two touchdowns and one interception. Eight different receivers caught passes, per AP. Myers had seven catches for 135 yards and both touchdowns. Jmariyae Robinson caught eight passes for 77 yards and returned two punts for 34 more. Lair ran 14 times for 65 yards. Jared Lloyd made 10 tackles. We outgained the Owls 421 to 337, per ESPN's box score.

Now the honest part, because a good guide tells you about the rapids. We were flagged nine times for 84 yards. We let a 6-0 lead slip right before halftime. And this season's had some white water: a 50-0 loss at Texas A&M to open the year, a 30-24 loss at home to Marshall, a 34-24 loss at SMU and a 34-13 loss at Western Kentucky. But we beat Lindenwood 48-14, and now we've got our first FBS win. The current is turning.

Part 2: The Bears Float East to Newark

Tuesday, 7 p.m. Eastern, ESPNU, Missouri State at Delaware.

First, my respects to the Blue Hens. Delaware can throw it. AP ranks its passing offense 29th in FBS, at 271.0 yards a game. Sean Wilson has 25 catches for 339 yards and three touchdowns. Tyler Bell threw for 306 yards and two touchdowns at Middle Tennessee last week, and he even caught a touchdown pass. Blake Matthews has 4.5 sacks. That's a real crew. I'd let them in my canoe.

But I'd make them sit in the middle and not touch the paddles. Let's read the current from AP's preview.

Delaware's run game ranks 135th in FBS, at 94.0 yards a game. At Middle Tennessee, it ran 30 times for 70 yards, per ESPN. That's not a river. That's a puddle on a gravel bank after a dry August. Paddle all you want, friends. You're not going anywhere.

Delaware's pass defense ranks 125th, allowing 259.2 yards a game. And Myers has 554 receiving yards and five touchdowns. I've seen that kind of matchup before, out on the water. It's called a downstream current, and you just point the canoe and enjoy the ride.

And the Blue Hens have had some leaks in the hull. They lost 42-3 at Virginia. They were flagged 13 times for 101 yards at Middle Tennessee, per ESPN, and they lost by three. They're 0-2 in Conference USA. AP ranks Delaware 112th in FBS in time of possession.

I'll be honest about my own boat. Our defense ranks 127th in FBS in yards allowed, and opponents convert 44.4% of third downs on us. Our red zone offense ranks 106th. Those are rocks, and I see them. But we just learned how to finish, and that's the hardest stroke to teach.

And this one's a brand-new river. CollegeFootballData.com lists no previous meeting between these two programs. First float. Let's make it a good story.

Tales From Two Towns

Springfield. Springfield is the third-most-populous city in Missouri, with 169,176 people, and the largest city in the Ozarks, per Wikipedia. Its nicknames include "Queen City of the Ozarks," since 1878, and "The Birthplace of Route 66." Since 2010, we've thrown the Birthplace of Route 66 Festival downtown, with a parade of vintage cars down the old highway. We're the headquarters of Bass Pro Shops and the Wonders of Wildlife Museum & Aquarium. O'Reilly Auto Parts started here in 1957 as a family business with 13 employees. We have our own local style of cashew chicken, and we're within reach of the James River, Table Rock Lake and the Buffalo National River. That's a float guide's paradise. Wilson's Creek National Battlefield, site of an 1861 Civil War battle, is a few miles southwest of town. History, rivers and good food, all in one place.

And our ballpark has history. Wikipedia says Plaster Stadium was built in 1941, as SMS Stadium, as a Works Progress Administration project costing $60,000. Missouri State's first team took the field in 1909. The school was Southwest Missouri State until 2005. In 1990 the Bears were ranked second in the country for three weeks, the highest ranking in school history. And they've won 10 conference titles. In 1970 the stadium was renamed for Arthur Briggs, the school's all-time winningest coach, and in 1991 it took the Plaster name after a donation paid for an upper deck and luxury suites. Now the Bears are in their first season as full FBS members, after joining Conference USA in 2025. This is a young river, friends, and we're running it for the first time together.

Newark. Newark, Delaware, is a lovely college town of 30,601, per Wikipedia. Springfield's metro area could hold about 16 of it. Newark sits less than a mile from a spot called The Wedge, where Delaware, Maryland and Pennsylvania meet, so it's a town that's always one short walk from being in a different state. Wikipedia says that on a typical home game day, Delaware Stadium becomes the fourth-largest city in the state. In Missouri, we'd call that a busy Saturday at Bass Pro.

Then there's the mascot. Wikipedia says the Blue Hen is not a recognized chicken breed. I'd just like to point out, gently, that our mascot is a bear. Bears don't need a breed registry. Bears also eat chicken. Especially in Springfield, where we put cashews on it.

Clementine's Float Plan for Tuesday

1. Paddle to Myers. A 125th-ranked pass defense is a downstream current.
2. Stack the box. Make the Blue Hens prove they can run.
3. Stop the flags. Nine penalties is too many rocks in one stretch.
4. Finish drives. Field goals got it done last week, but touchdowns float better.

Pack a snack and a dry bag, Bears fans. It's going to be a fun float.

My call: Delaware Blue Hens 29, Missouri State Bears 24.

articles.title: Hatch Hot on a Wednesday: Rested New Mexico State Brings James Jones and 599 Rushing Yards to Huntsville, Where Sam Houston's Run Defense Ranks 129th
articles.byline: Esperanza Lujan-Tafoya, The New Mexico State Fanatic
articles.matchup: New Mexico State (2-4) at Sam Houston (1-5), Wed., Oct. 21, 8 p.m. ET, Bowers Stadium, Huntsville, Texas, ESPN2
articles.text:
¡Buenas noches, Aggies! Esperanza Lujan-Tafoya here, a Las Cruces native, a chile farmer's daughter and an ag-science grad. Everything gets a chile rating from me. A routine first down? Mild. A 40-yard run? Hatch hot. A fourth-down stop? So hot you need a glass of milk and a minute alone.

But I never heat up the facts. So let's start with the honest truth.

Part 1: An Open Week, and a Cool Night in Miami

New Mexico State didn't play last week. We had an open date, and I spent it out in the fields. So let me tell you about our last game, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, in Miami.

FIU beat us 22-3. That one was mild, friends. Very mild. AP says FIU's Robert Czeremcha made five field goals, a career high that tied a program record, from 40, 52, 33, 21 and 48 yards. We turned the ball over three times, and Kyah Francone's 26-yard field goal was our only score. We're 2-4 and 1-1 in Conference USA.

But here's something worth knowing. Our defense allowed one touchdown all night, a 1-yard run in the first quarter. And New Mexico State actually outgained FIU, 230 yards to 220, per ESPN's box score. FIU ran 44 times for 100 yards, 2.3 a carry. Gabe Peterson had two sacks and three tackles for loss. Sone Aupiu had a sack and three tackles for loss. Nick Session made 13 tackles. Javon Gillespie intercepted a pass. That defense was Hatch hot, even on a cool night.

The offense was the bug in the chile patch. We went 3 for 12 on third down and had the ball for just 22:06. James Jones ran 15 times for 89 yards, and he came into that game leading Conference USA at 102.0 rushing yards a game, per AP.

This season's had some heat and some frost. We lost at Florida State, 34-17, and at Hawai'i, 29-19. We lost to New Mexico at home, which I won't discuss, because Mama says if you can't say anything nice about the Lobos, eat a tamale. But we beat Mercyhurst 51-14 and Western Kentucky 34-13. And the Hilltoppers have won their last two since, so that win looks better every week.

Part 2: Wednesday Night in Huntsville

Wednesday, 8 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2, New Mexico State at Sam Houston.

First, my respects to the Bearkats, because they've earned some. AP ranks Sam Houston's pass defense fourth in FBS, at 137.8 yards a game. Fourth! And it ranks 24th in third-down defense, allowing conversions 32.1% of the time. Landyn Locke has 11 touchdown passes. Chris Reed has 289 receiving yards and three touchdowns. Dean Ford has 38 tackles. Those are good young men with real fight.

Now let me get out my chile scale.

Sam Houston's run defense ranks 129th in FBS, allowing 200.3 yards a game. And who do we have? James Jones, with 599 rushing yards on 92 carries. That's 6.5 a carry. Chile rating for that matchup: Hatch hot, roasted, peeled and ready to serve.

Sam Houston's rushing offense ranks 134th, at 95.0 yards a game. Its scoring offense ranks 123rd, at 19.5 points a game. In its last two games, a 35-3 loss at Liberty and a 16-3 loss at home to Western Kentucky, the Bearkats scored six points combined. Against WKU, they gained 177 yards, per AP. Chile rating: bell pepper. No heat at all. And our run defense ranks 47th. So the Bearkats will have to throw, and Peterson has 4.5 sacks. I like our chances.

The Bearkats also rank 108th in FBS in penalty yards, at 67.3 a game. We rank 42nd. And the Bearkats rank 38th in time of possession, while we rank 127th, so we'll need to make every snap count.

I'll be honest about our side, because farmers can't lie about the weather. Our turnover margin is minus-5, which ranks 122nd. Our red zone defense ranks 118th. And Trey Hedden, who started the first four games, has six interceptions. We've got to hold onto the ball.

And history? CollegeFootballData.com says New Mexico State leads the series 2-1. We won 27-13 at home in 2023 and 37-10 at home last year. Sam Houston won 31-11 in Huntsville in 2024. So this is only our second trip to Bowers Stadium. Time to roast something new.

Tales From Two Towns

Las Cruces. Las Cruces is a city of 111,385, the second-largest in New Mexico, per Wikipedia. It's the heart of the Mesilla Valley, the farming country on the floodplain of the Rio Grande, and the Organ Mountains rise just 10 miles east of town. We're home to New Mexico State, the state's only land-grant university. Spaceport America, which has offices in Las Cruces, operates about 55 miles to the north and has completed several successful crewed suborbital flights. Our neighbors launch people into space. We grow the chile they'll want when they get back. Wikipedia says the town was founded in 1849, when the U.S. Army first surveyed it after the Mexican-American War, and the White Sands Missile Range is one of the area's big employers. Science, farming and football, all under the same big sky.

And Aggie Memorial Stadium has a story. Wikipedia says it opened in 1978, seats 28,853 and sits at 3,980 feet above sea level. The original Memorial Stadium was dedicated to New Mexico A&M students who died in World War II, World War I and the Spanish-American War. We remember. And our program has history, too: one of NMSU's earliest games was against New Mexico on Jan. 1, 1894, before New Mexico was even a state. In 2017, we beat Utah State 26-20 in overtime in the Arizona Bowl, our first bowl game in 57 years. In 2022, we beat Bowling Green in the Quick Lane Bowl. In 2023, we beat Auburn 31-10. Hatch hot. And our coach, Tony Sanchez, is one of our own. Wikipedia says the former UNLV head coach played at New Mexico State before he was named head coach in January 2024. He knows what Aggie chile tastes like.

Huntsville. Huntsville, Texas, is a pleasant town of 45,941 in the East Texas Piney Woods, per Wikipedia. It got its start around 1836 as a trading post, and its first postmaster named it after his hometown, Huntsville, Alabama. So even the name was borrowed. Its most famous landmark is a 67-foot statue of Sam Houston that Wikipedia says can be seen from Interstate 45 for 6.5 miles. So most folks see Huntsville's best attraction from the highway, on the way to somewhere else. And the town is named for Huntsville, the stadium is named for a university president, and the university is named for Sam Houston. Las Cruces has the Organ Mountains. You can't borrow a mountain.

Esperanza's Chile Recipe for Wednesday

1. Feed James Jones. A 129th-ranked run defense is a fresh-roasted batch.
2. Hold onto the ball. Minus-5 is too much salt.
3. Make them throw. Sam Houston's rushing offense ranks 134th.
4. Finish in the red zone. Field goals are mild. Touchdowns are hot.

Grab your green chile stew and turn on ESPN2, Aggies. It's going to be a spicy Wednesday.

My call: New Mexico State Aggies 24, Sam Houston Bearkats 23.

articles.title: Pull Up a Stump: Sam Houston's Pass Defense Ranks Fourth in FBS, and a New Mexico State Team With a Minus-5 Turnover Margin Rides Into Big Sam's Town
articles.byline: Lem Coxwell, The Sam Houston Fanatic
articles.matchup: New Mexico State (2-4) at Sam Houston (1-5), Wed., Oct. 21, 8 p.m. ET, Bowers Stadium, Huntsville, Texas, ESPN2
articles.text:
Evenin', folks. Pull up a stump. I'm Lemuel Coxwell, but everybody from here to the Trinity River calls me Lem. I'm a Walker County native and a high school history teacher, and I collect Texas folklore the way some folks collect bottle caps. My students say I can turn a fire drill into a three-part saga. They're not wrong.

A good storyteller never needs to stretch the truth. So let me tell you this week's story plain, starting with the hard chapter.

Part 1: A Long, Quiet Night at Bowers

Sam Houston lost 16-3 to Western Kentucky last Wednesday night at Bowers Stadium. We're 1-5 and 0-2 in Conference USA.

I won't dress it up. The offense struggled. AP says we gained 177 yards and managed 12 first downs. Landyn Locke went 13 of 30 for 112 yards with an interception. MJ Dowdy ran 14 times for 55 yards. Chris Reed caught three passes for 51 yards. Sam Carpenter kicked a 42-yard field goal in the second quarter for our only points. And we were flagged nine times for 100 yards, per ESPN's box score. My students would call that a pop quiz nobody studied for.

But here's the part of the story folks will skip if I don't tell it. Our defense played its heart out. Western Kentucky scored its only touchdown on its first drive, an 11-play, 65-yard march capped by a 23-yard pass. After that, the Hilltoppers had to settle for three field goals. WKU gained 276 yards and threw for just 132. Dean Ford made 12 tackles. Railyn Adams made six. Tokyo Gordon broke up a pass. The defense kept us in it for 60 minutes. That's the kind of grit Sam Houston himself would've tipped his hat to.

And this season's been a long trail. We lost 24-21 at Troy and 23-17 at home to Tulsa, both one-score games. We beat Nicholls 59-0. We lost at Texas Tech and at Liberty. Now we come home to face a team we know.

Part 2: The Aggies Come to Huntsville

Wednesday, 8 p.m. Eastern, ESPN2, New Mexico State at Sam Houston.

Let me start with respect, because that's how my granddaddy told stories. New Mexico State has a fine running back in James Jones, who has 599 yards on 92 carries. Gabe Peterson has 4.5 sacks. Nick Session has 50 tackles. And the Aggies beat us 37-10 last season in Las Cruces, per CollegeFootballData.com. I don't forget, and I don't pretend.

But now let me open the history book to this year's chapter, courtesy of AP's preview.

New Mexico State's turnover margin is minus-5, which ranks 122nd in FBS. Trey Hedden has six interceptions. In their last game, at FIU, the Aggies turned it over three times and scored three points. Their red zone defense ranks 118th, allowing scores on 92.9% of trips. And it ranks 127th in time of possession. Folks, that's a wagon train with a loose wheel, no water barrel and a map drawn upside down.

And the Aggies haven't played since Oct. 7. They had a week off to think about that FIU game. I've had weeks like that. They're long.

Meanwhile, our pass defense ranks fourth in FBS, allowing 137.8 yards a game. Fourth! Our third-down defense ranks 24th, allowing conversions just 32.1% of the time. And Locke has 11 touchdown passes this season, with Reed catching 289 yards' worth and three scores. This team has chapters left to write.

I'll be honest about our side. Our run defense ranks 129th, allowing 200.3 yards a game, so Jones is the outlaw we have to round up. Our rushing offense ranks 134th, and our scoring offense ranks 123rd. And we rank 108th in penalty yards. Those are real problems, and a history teacher doesn't erase the chalkboard before class is over.

But here's a bit of folklore for you: the Aggies have made exactly one trip to Huntsville in this series, per CollegeFootballData.com. That was 2024. We won 31-11. Home cooking agrees with us.

Tales From Two Towns

Huntsville. Huntsville is a town of 45,941 in the East Texas Piney Woods, per Wikipedia, and it's where Sam Houston lived. You know him. He led the Texas Army at the Battle of San Jacinto, the decisive victory of the Texas Revolution. He served as the first and third president of the Republic of Texas, then as a U.S. senator and governor. Near the end of his life, Wikipedia notes, he opposed the Civil War, a very unpopular position in his day. Courage like that deserves a tall statue. Huntsville has two of his homes, his grave and the Sam Houston Memorial Museum. And standing on a 10-foot granite base is a 67-foot statue of him, A Tribute to Courage, by David Adickes, which Wikipedia calls the world's tallest statue of an American hero. It was dedicated to the city on Oct. 22, 1994. Big Sam turns 32 on Thursday. The game's the night before. I'd call that a birthday present.

Our town got its start around 1836, when Pleasant and Ephraim Gray opened a trading post here. Ephraim named it after his hometown, Huntsville, Alabama. Texans have always known a good name when they hear one, and we made it bigger. We've also got Huntsville State Park, a folk and cowboy music festival every April and a university that's been here since 1879. Sam Houston has played football since 1912. We won the FCS national title in the 2020-21 season, beating South Dakota State 23-21, and we claim a 1964 NAIA title, too. We've played at Bowers Stadium, named for former university president Elliott T. Bowers, since 1986. And Phil Longo, the former Wisconsin offensive coordinator, has been our head coach since December 2024.

Las Cruces. Now, Las Cruces is a perfectly nice city in the Mesilla Valley. But I'm a history teacher, so let me give you the lesson. Wikipedia says that in 1860, the leading settlement in the area wasn't Las Cruces. It was Mesilla, with more than twice as many residents. So Las Cruces started out as the little brother in its own valley. And today, Wikipedia notes, Spaceport America, which keeps offices in Las Cruces, operates about 55 miles north of town. Folks in Las Cruces built a whole facility for leaving the planet. Here in Huntsville, we built a 67-foot statue of a man who stayed.

One more history lesson. Wikipedia says New Mexico State has one of the longest droughts of any current FBS team in the AP poll. It was last ranked in 1960. I teach history, friends, but even I don't go back that far.

Lem's Lesson Plan for Wednesday

1. Round up James Jones. A 129th-ranked run defense has to tighten the lasso.
2. Make them throw. A fourth-ranked pass defense is our Alamo... no, our San Jacinto. We win this one.
3. Take the ball away. Minus-5 means the Aggies will give us chances. Catch them.
4. Clean up the flags. One hundred penalty yards is a chapter we don't reread.

Come on out to Bowers on Wednesday night, folks. Bring a lawn chair and a story. I'll bring the history.

My call: New Mexico State Aggies 24, Sam Houston Bearkats 23.

articles.title: A Clean Shave in Huntsville: Western Kentucky Held Sam Houston to 177 Yards, Takes an Open Week, Then Welcomes a Delaware Pass Defense Ranked 125th to the Hill
articles.byline: Thurman 'Tops' Whitsitt, The Western Kentucky Fanatic
articles.matchup: Open week for Western Kentucky (3-4) this week. Next: Delaware (2-4) at Western Kentucky, Tue., Oct. 27, 7 p.m. ET, Houchens Industries-L.T. Smith Stadium, Bowling Green, Ky., CBSSN
articles.text:
Go Tops! Thurman Whitsitt here, but everybody in Warren County calls me Tops. I've been cutting hair in Bowling Green for three decades, and I've told a Hilltopper story with every haircut. Sit down in the chair, friend. I'll give you a trim and the truth, and I won't charge extra for either.

First, the truth: Western Kentucky doesn't play this week. It's an open week. My clippers get a rest, and so do the Tops. So let's talk about last Wednesday, and then about what's coming to the Hill.

Part 1: The Cleanest Shave in Texas

Western Kentucky beat Sam Houston 16-3 last Wednesday night in Huntsville. We're 3-4 and 2-1 in Conference USA, and that's two straight wins.

That was a clean shave, friends. AP says the defense forced a Sam Houston three-and-out in 50 seconds to open the game, and then the offense went 65 yards in 11 plays. Brock Glenn finished it with a 23-yard touchdown pass to Coleson Arends. Karl Campbell made all three of his field goals, from 33, 35 and 39 yards. And that was plenty.

Because our defense gave the Bearkats nothing but a little off the top. Sam Houston gained 177 yards, with 12 first downs, per AP. Its only points came on a field goal in the second quarter. Freshman Westen Ard made a career-high 10 tackles with 1.5 sacks. We committed zero turnovers and just four penalties for 33 yards, per ESPN's box score. That's a tidy cut. Not a hair out of place.

AP also says WKU is 4-1 against Sam Houston and perfect against the Bearkats since they joined Conference USA in 2023.

Now, a barber tells the truth even when the customer doesn't want to hear it. The offense was choppy. Glenn went 14 of 30 for 127 yards, and we went 8 for 20 on third down. And this season's had some rough haircuts. We lost at Nevada, 49-14, at Georgia, 70-20, and at Indiana, 38-0. We lost 34-13 at New Mexico State. But we beat Mercyhurst 52-7, Missouri State 34-13 and Sam Houston. The fade is coming together.

And let me brag on a young man. Jonathan Stafford Jr. caught five passes against Sam Houston, and AP says his 41 receptions are already third on WKU's freshman list. Conference USA's Oct. 13 notes said he became the first player in league history to win three straight Freshman of the Week awards, and that he ranked third among FBS freshmen in catches. Folks in the shop haven't stopped talking about him.

The Open Week, Honestly

There's no WKU game this week. The rest of the league plays Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. We sit in the waiting chairs with a magazine. That's fine by me. Fresh legs and a clean neckline for the stretch run. Five regular-season games remain after this week, and all five are against Conference USA teams. Every one of them matters.

Part 2: Delaware Comes to the Hill

Next up: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 7 p.m. Eastern, CBS Sports Network, Delaware at Western Kentucky.

First, a kind word, because my mama would come back to haunt the shop if I didn't give one. Delaware can throw it. AP's Oct. 18 preview ranks its passing offense 29th in FBS, at 271.0 yards a game. Sean Wilson has 339 receiving yards. Blake Matthews has 4.5 sacks. And they gave us a close one last year: we won 27-24 in Newark, per CollegeFootballData.com.

But let me pull out the mirror and show the Blue Hens the back of their head.

Delaware's pass defense ranks 125th in FBS, allowing 259.2 yards a game. Its rushing offense ranks 135th, at 94.0 yards a game. Its scoring offense ranks 103rd. The Blue Hens are 0-3 on the road this season, and they've lost three straight: at Virginia, at home to Liberty and at Middle Tennessee. At Middle Tennessee, they were flagged 13 times for 101 yards, per ESPN. Friends, that's not a haircut. That's a bowl cut done in the dark.

Delaware plays Missouri State on Tuesday night first, so those numbers will change a bit before they come to town. I'll be watching from the shop with the TV turned up.

And here's my honest worry. Our offense has been a little shaggy. But a defense that just held a team to 177 yards and three points goes a long way, and the Hill is home.

Tales From Two Towns

Bowling Green. Bowling Green is a city of 72,294, the third-most populous in Kentucky, per Wikipedia, behind only Louisville and Lexington. It was founded by pioneers in 1798, and by 1810 it had all of 154 residents. Steamboats on the Barren River helped it grow, and it kept right on growing. And the Bowling Green Assembly Plant has built every Chevrolet Corvette since 1981. Every one! We've got the National Corvette Museum, too, and companies like Spalding and Fruit of the Loom. One story Wikipedia tells about our name says it came from the Bowling Green in New York City, where patriots pulled down a statue of King George III and turned the lead into bullets during the Revolution. Bowling Green: home of the Corvette and named for a little Revolutionary spunk.

And Hilltopper football has a fine haircut, too. Wikipedia says the 2002 team won the FCS national championship. The program has 13 conference titles and seven FBS bowl wins. Our stadium, Houchens Industries-L.T. Smith Stadium at Jimmy Feix Field, opened in 1968 and seats 22,000. It was expanded in 2008 to get ready for the move to FBS, which WKU completed in 2009. Wikipedia calls it one of the smallest stadiums in FBS. I call it cozy, like a two-chair shop where everybody knows your name. Our program goes way back, too: WKU first fielded a team in 1908, and its first sanctioned season, in 1913, was a single 20-0 win over Elizabethtown. Undefeated. Somebody frame that. And our logo? Since 2003, it's been a red towel. That's a logo a barber can respect. Every good shop has a clean towel ready.

Newark. Newark, Delaware, is a fine little college town of 30,601, per Wikipedia. But Wikipedia also has to tell you how to say it: "NEW-ark." So even the town's name comes with a pronunciation guide. Newark's oldest big industry was the Curtis Paper Mill. Bowling Green builds Corvettes. I don't think I need to tell you which town has the shinier paint. And the Blue Hen? Wikipedia says it isn't a recognized chicken breed. Friends, I've been cutting hair for 30 years, and I know when somebody's just made up a style and given it a fancy name.

Tops's Barbershop Checklist for the Open Week

1. Rest up. Every good haircut starts with a clean, sharp pair of clippers.
2. Keep the defense sharp. Three points allowed is a cut worth framing.
3. Throw at that secondary. A 125th-ranked pass defense is a head of hair begging for a trim.
4. Stay clean. Four penalties and zero turnovers is how the Tops win on the road and at home.

The shop's open all week, friends. Come on in, sit down, and we'll talk Hilltoppers until the Blue Hens get here.

articles.title: Paint It Blue: No. 21 Boise State Finally Beat Fresno, Rested Up, and Now Heads to Pullman to Face a Cougar Offense Ranked 130th at a Stadium About 200 Feet Below Downtown Boise
articles.byline: Thatcher Bluestem, The Boise State Fanatic
articles.matchup: No. 21 Boise State (5-1) at Washington State (1-6), Sat., Oct. 24, 6 p.m. ET, Gesa Field at Martin Stadium, USA Network
articles.text:
Morning, Bronco Nation. Thatcher Bluestem here, writing from my back porch in the North End with a cup of coffee, a blue flannel and a blue dog named Turf. He's not actually blue. He's a heeler. But in my heart, he's blue. Everything is, if you squint. My rule for life is simple: if it's worth doing, paint it blue.

The Broncos had an open date on Saturday, Oct. 17, so there's no new game to review this week. That means we get to go back and savor the last one one more time, because it was a sweet one. Then we'll talk about the trip to Pullman.

Part 1: Boise State 38, Fresno State 31 (Oct. 10)

On Oct. 10 at Valley Children's Stadium, the Broncos beat Fresno State 38-31. Per the AP, it ended a three-game losing streak against the Bulldogs. Three in a row! I'd been carrying that one around like a rock in my boot.

Dylan Riley set the tone right away. On Boise State's second play from scrimmage, he ripped off a 72-yard touchdown run. Zeke Martinez ran in the two-point conversion, and the Broncos led 8-7 less than five minutes in. They never trailed again.

Maddux Madsen hit Terrious Favors for a 22-yard touchdown. Sire Gaines, back after missing two games, ran in from the 2. Canaan Moore kicked a 49-yard field goal with two seconds left in the half for a 25-20 lead, then a 38-yarder in the third. And on the first play of the fourth quarter, Madsen found Riley on a 44-yard catch-and-run touchdown for a 35-20 lead. Moore added a 39-yarder with 1:34 left, and that sealed it.

The box score, painted blue: Riley ran 19 times for 150 yards and caught four passes for 64. Gaines ran 20 times for 120. Madsen completed 23 of 34 passes for 238 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Boise State ran for 274 yards at 6.1 per carry, piled up 512 yards of offense, went 4-for-4 on fourth down, didn't turn it over once and held the ball for 38:56. Per the AP, the Broncos scored on seven of their eight real drives.

The honest part. Boise State committed nine penalties for 83 yards, and Fresno State's Jayden Mandal and Ezekiel Avit made some big plays. Avit had six catches for 96 yards and two touchdowns. The Bulldogs kicked a field goal with 36 seconds left to make it a one-score game. Too close for my blood pressure.

That made it five straight wins since a 34-27 loss at Oregon to open the year. The Broncos beat Memphis 38-20 and South Dakota 38-24, won 32-7 at Western Michigan, beat Utah State 37-18 and then won at Fresno. They're 5-1 and 2-0 in the Pac-12, and they're No. 21 in the AP poll, per the AP.

Part 2: Boise State at Washington State

Saturday at 6 p.m. Eastern, which is 4 p.m. here in Mountain time and 3 p.m. in Pullman, at Gesa Field at Martin Stadium. It's on USA Network, per the AP. No. 21 Boise State (5-1, 2-0 Pac-12) at Washington State (1-6, 0-3).

The Broncos

Boise State runs for 234.5 yards per game, ninth in FBS, and scores 35 points per game. It converts 50.6 of every 100 third downs, 16th. And it leads the entire country in time of possession at 36:41 per game. That's not a game plan. That's the football moving in with us and changing its mailing address.

Riley has 835 rushing yards and six touchdowns on 127 carries. Madsen has thrown for 1,296 yards with 13 touchdowns and zero interceptions. Zero! I'd paint that number blue too, but it's already perfect. Rasean Jones leads the receivers with 23 catches for 359 yards.

The honest note: Boise State's pass defense allows 261.3 yards per game, 126th in FBS. That's the one wall in the house that needs a fresh coat.

The Cougars

Washington State is 1-6. Its offense ranks 130th in FBS at 308.3 yards per game, its passing attack is 119th and its scoring offense is 120th at 20.1 points per game. Its turnover margin is minus-7, 131st. And it averages 65.6 penalty yards per game, 102nd.

To be fair, the Cougars made a quarterback change last week, and redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman made his first career start against Oregon State, per the AP. He threw for 289 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 136 yards and a touchdown. That's a real performance, and the Broncos' pass defense needs to take it seriously. Branden Ganashamoorthy caught 11 passes for 147 yards in that game.

But Oregon State still won 48-30. The Beavers led 17-0 after one quarter and 27-10 at the half, and Braden Atkinson threw for 347 yards. And the Broncos have the nation's best clock-eating offense.

The Series

CollegeFootballData.com lists seven previous meetings, and Washington State leads the series 5-2. The Broncos won the last one, 45-24, in 2024. The Cougars won 47-44 in 2017. Time to paint the series blue.

Town Report: Boise vs. Pullman

Boise. Boise had 235,685 people at the 2020 census, per Wikipedia, the capital and largest city in Idaho. The name comes from French trappers, who called the area "la rivière boisée," the wooded river. We're the City of Trees, and the nickname goes back to the 1860s, when Thomas J. Davis planted several thousand fruit trees. The Boise River runs right through town. We have the Idaho State Capitol, the Boise Art Museum, Zoo Boise, the Egyptian Theatre and the Basque Block, where you can learn about Boise's Basque heritage and eat very well while you do it. And every March, the Treefort Music Fest takes over the place.

And Albertsons Stadium? Its blue playing surface went in in 1986, and Wikipedia calls it the first non-green playing surface in football history. People call it Smurf Turf. Players just call it "The Blue." We didn't follow a trend. We painted one.

Pullman. Pullman is a nice little town of 32,901, per the 2020 census, in the rolling wheat hills of the Palouse. It was originally called Three Forks, and in 1881 it was renamed after an industrialist named George Pullman. So the town traded a perfectly good river name for a railroad-car guy's last name. Boise got its name from French trappers admiring trees. Pullman got its name from a man who made sleeping cars.

Pullman is also, per Wikipedia, home to the National Lentil Festival, which has been held since 1989 and includes a lentil cook-off. I like a lentil. Turf likes a lentil. But Boise has a music festival named after a tree, and Pullman has a festival named after a legume.

And here's my go-to stat of the week. Wikipedia says Martin Stadium's field sits at about 2,510 feet, once the highest in the old Pac-10. Downtown Boise sits at 2,704. So the Broncos are actually coming down to Pullman. We're bringing the thin air with us.

Final Brushstroke

Here's the plan. Run Riley and Gaines. Keep the clock. Make the pass defense earn that fresh coat of paint against a talented young quarterback. And don't give the Cougars any turnovers, because they've had a tough enough time creating them.

Wave the flag, Pullman. We'll paint it blue.

My call: Boise State Broncos 31, Washington State Cougars 20.

articles.title: Thin Air, Thick Skin: Colorado State Got Run Over in San Marcos, Comes Home to 5,003 Feet, and Hosts an Aztec Offense Ranked 133rd From a City That Couldn't Keep Its First Name
articles.byline: Ansel Rimrock, The Colorado State Fanatic
articles.matchup: San Diego State (3-4) at Colorado State (2-4), Sat., Oct. 24, 6:30 p.m. ET, Canvas Stadium, The CW
articles.text:
Morning, Rams. Ansel Rimrock here, writing from a trailhead at Horsetooth Mountain with a thermos of coffee, a green-and-gold beanie and a set of boots that have seen a lot of switchbacks. I've got a motto, and I've had it for years: thin air, thick defense. Right now, I'm going to have to be honest with you. The air's still thin. The defense needs work.

But a mountain man doesn't quit on the climb because of one rockslide. Let's look at Thursday night in Texas, and then let's talk about coming home.

Part 1: Texas State 66, Colorado State 27

On Thursday, Oct. 15, at UFCU Stadium in San Marcos, Texas State beat Colorado State 66-27. Per the AP, the Bobcats ran for a school-record 503 yards and piled up a school-record 716 yards of offense.

I'm not going to dress it up. Torrance Burgess Jr. ran for 224 yards and four touchdowns. Brad Jackson ran for 181 and three touchdowns and threw for 213 more. Texas State led 28-0 early in the second quarter and 45-21 at halftime, and it scored touchdowns on six straight possessions, per the AP. That was a rockslide.

Now here's what the Rams did right, because they did some things right. K'saan Farrar completed 26 of 41 passes for 289 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions. Durell Robinson ran for two touchdowns, from 15 yards and 1 yard. Farrar hit Nader Chirchi for a 21-yard score and Terrence Smith Jr. for a 37-yarder. Jackson Harper caught five passes for 91 yards, and Tommy Maher had a 57-yard catch. The Rams gained 437 yards, held the ball for 30:36 and didn't turn it over once.

And from 28-0 down, the Rams scored three touchdowns in the second quarter alone. They didn't fold. That counts for something up here.

Defensively, Tre'Shawn Moore led the Rams with nine tackles, and Oumar Diomande added seven. They kept chasing all night. The effort was there. The tackling angles need a tune-up, and that's what a week of practice at altitude is for.

But you can't win giving up 9.1 yards a carry. Colorado State is 2-4 and 0-2 in the Pac-12. The Rams beat Wyoming 35-13 and Southern Utah 58-24, then lost 41-23 to BYU, 59-45 at UTSA, 56-26 to Oregon State and 66-27 at Texas State. That's a tough stretch of trail.

Part 2: San Diego State at Colorado State

Saturday at 6:30 p.m. Eastern, which is 4:30 here, at Canvas Stadium. It's on The CW, per the AP. San Diego State (3-4, 2-1 Pac-12) at Colorado State (2-4, 0-2).

Our Rams

Let me get the hard truth out of the way. Colorado State's defense ranks 138th in FBS in yards allowed at 530.3 per game, 138th against the run at 274.3 and 138th in scoring at 43.2 points per game. Opponents convert 43.7 of every 100 third downs, 133rd. That's the bottom of the canyon.

But the offense is a different story. The Rams gain 445.3 yards per game, 34th in FBS, and throw for 274.7, 26th. They score 35.7 points per game, 29th. They're plus-8 in turnover margin, sixth in FBS, and they average just 42.3 penalty yards per game, 17th. RJ Vick has 24 catches for 367 yards and four touchdowns. Farrar has five touchdown passes and two interceptions.

The Aztecs

San Diego State won a 26-23 thriller over Fresno State last week on Cooper DiLeva's 53-yard field goal with 57 seconds left. Lucky Sutton ran for 110 yards. Credit where it's due.

But look at the Aztecs' offense. It ranks 133rd in FBS at 292.9 yards per game. Its passing attack is 132nd at 148.4 yards per game. It converts 29.3 of every 100 third downs, 135th. Its red zone offense is 126th. And it holds the ball for 24:47 a game, 138th, dead last.

Its defense isn't stout either. The Aztecs allow 449 yards per game, 133rd, and 276.6 passing yards, 131st. Farrar is licking his chops.

And the Aztecs' starting quarterback, Jayden Denegal, left last week's game with an ankle injury. Per the AP, his X-rays were negative. I hope the young man is healthy. But whoever takes the snaps for San Diego State, the Rams have a chance to make it a long afternoon.

The Altitude

Canvas Stadium's field sits at 5,003 feet, per Wikipedia. San Diego is at sea level, more or less. Thin air, Aztecs. Bring a deep breath and a little extra ambition.

The Series

San Diego State leads the series 23-15, per CollegeFootballData.com, and won 45-24 in 2025. Time to climb.

One more thing about this matchup. Both of these teams know how to light up a scoreboard against a soft defense, and both have soft spots. San Diego State gave up 66 points at Oregon State two weeks ago. We gave up 66 to Texas State last week. Somebody's defense is going to have a good day on Saturday, and I'd like it to be the one wearing green and gold. A mountain man always believes in the next switchback.

Town Report: Fort Collins vs. San Diego

Fort Collins. Fort Collins had 169,810 people at the 2020 census, per Wikipedia, the fourth-most populous city in Colorado. It sits on the Cache la Poudre River, at the base of the Rocky Mountain foothills, about 4,982 feet up. Horsetooth Mountain, named for a tooth-shaped granite rock, watches over the western skyline, and on a clear day you can see Longs Peak to the southwest. Horsetooth Reservoir stretches about 6.5 miles through the foothills just west of town.

Our Old Town sits right next to the original 1864 Army post. And per Wikipedia, Fort Collins is known as one of the towns that inspired Main Street, U.S.A., at Disney's theme parks. That's right. Walt's people looked at a lot of towns, and they took notes on ours.

And CAM the Ram? Per Wikipedia, the live mascot has been played by Rambouillet sheep since 1947, and the name came from a 1946 contest, an acronym for Colorado Agricultural and Mechanical College. Canvas Stadium opened in 2017, right on campus, with 36,500 seats and room for as many as 41,000, per Wikipedia. It replaced Hughes Stadium, the Rams' home since 1968. Sit up high on a fall evening, watch the light fade on the foothills, and tell me there's a prettier view in college football. I'll wait.

San Diego. San Diego is a big, sunny city. Fine. But per Wikipedia, when Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo claimed the bay in 1542, he named it "San Miguel." Then Sebastián Vizcaíno came through in 1602 and renamed it. San Diego couldn't even keep its first name! Fort Collins has been Fort Collins since the 1860s.

And the Aztecs' stadium, Snapdragon, opened in 2022 on a parcel west of the main campus, per Wikipedia. You take the trolley to get there. Our stadium is on campus. You walk.

Oh, and San Diego is known for its mild Mediterranean climate. Mild. That's the word they lead with. Up here, we lead with mountains. Mild is a salsa, my friend. Fort Collins is the main course. You don't come up here for mild. You come up here for the Poudre, the foothills, Old Town and a kickoff nearly a mile up.

Summit Plan

Here's the plan. Let Farrar throw at the 131st-ranked pass defense. Keep protecting the football. Make the 135th-ranked third-down offense earn every inch. And let the thin air do its job in the fourth quarter.

Thin air, thick skin. That's this week's motto. Go Rams.

My call: San Diego State Aztecs 33, Colorado State Rams 32.

articles.title: Not That Valley, Babe: Fresno State Lost on a 53-Yarder in San Diego, Takes an Open Week Under the Ash Trees, Then Hosts Oregon State From a Town Whose Tallest Structure Ever Built Is a Football Stadium
articles.byline: Rosalind 'Roz' Ayala, The Fresno State Fanatic
articles.matchup: Fresno State (4-3): open date Sat., Oct. 24. Next: Oregon State at Fresno State, Sat., Oct. 31, time TBA, Valley Children's Stadium, Fresno
articles.text:
Hi, Red Wave. Roz Ayala here, writing from a picnic table at Woodward Park with a bag of fresh peaches from a fruit stand, a red Bulldog hoodie and my reading glasses on top of my head where I will lose them in about four minutes. When people from out of state hear "the Valley," they think of tech or Hollywood. And I tell them, every time: not that Valley, babe. Ours grows the food.

The Bulldogs have an open date on Saturday, Oct. 24. No game, no tailgate, no Red Wave this week. So let's go back over a painful one in San Diego, and then let's look ahead to Halloween and Oregon State.

Part 1: San Diego State 26, Fresno State 23

On Oct. 17 at Snapdragon Stadium, San Diego State beat Fresno State 26-23 on Cooper DiLeva's 53-yard field goal with 57 seconds left. Per the AP, it was a career long for him. Of course it was. Of course it had to be the longest kick of his life.

It started rough. The Aztecs led 13-0 early in the second quarter after two DiLeva field goals and a 52-yard touchdown pass from Jayden Denegal to Jaylon Hawkins.

Then the Bulldogs came roaring back. Manaki Watanabe hit a 51-yard field goal, and Bryson Donelson ran in from the 4 to make it 13-10. San Diego State kicked a field goal at the end of the half to go up 16-10, but in the third quarter, Julius Gillick ran 7 yards for a touchdown, and Fresno State led 17-16.

San Diego State answered with a trick play, a 7-yard touchdown pass from wide receiver Bert Emanuel Jr., and led 23-17. And with 5:02 left, Gillick punched in from the 2 to tie it at 23. The extra point failed. Then the Aztecs converted a third-and-10 with a 26-yard pass, and DiLeva won it.

The box score: Fresno State held the ball for 31:34 and ran 40 times for 135 yards. Donelson ran for 62 yards and a touchdown, and Gillick scored twice. Jayden Mandal completed 13 of 25 passes for 141 yards. Josiah Freeman had three catches for 49 yards. K'vion Thunderbird led the defense with nine tackles.

The honest Valley report: Fresno State gained 276 yards, went 4-of-13 on third down and lost a fumble. And one missed extra point turned into a three-point loss. That one stung like a peach-fuzz rash.

But I'll tell you what I saw. I saw a team that fell behind 13-0 on the road and didn't flinch. I saw Gillick run hard every time he touched it. I saw a defense that held San Diego State to 384 yards and kept the Bulldogs in it until the last minute. That's a team that's going to win a lot of close ones before this season's over.

The Bulldogs are 4-3 and 1-2 in the Pac-12. They lost 39-0 at USC, beat Sacramento State 49-3, won 26-10 at San Jose State, beat Rice 38-24, won 26-6 at Washington State, lost 38-31 to Boise State and then lost in San Diego. Two straight losses by a combined 10 points. That's close. We'll take close, and then we'll take the next one.

Part 2: Next Up, Oregon State at Fresno State

After the open week, Oregon State comes to Valley Children's Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 31. The kickoff time hasn't been announced yet, per ESPN. Halloween at home! I'm going as a raisin. Don't ask.

The Beavers

Oregon State is 5-2 and 3-0 in the Pac-12, and it can really throw it. The Beavers score 42.7 points per game and gain 527 yards per game, including 384.9 through the air, per ESPN. Braden Atkinson has completed 189 of 273 passes for 2,604 yards, 24 touchdowns and two interceptions. And Jesse Legree has 46 catches for 1,040 yards and 14 touchdowns. Per the AP, he was the first wide receiver in the country to reach 1,000 yards this season.

They beat Washington State 48-30 on Saturday, with Atkinson throwing for 347 yards and three touchdowns. And they're off this week too, so nobody gets a rest advantage.

But here's the thing about the Beavers. Their defense allows 23.1 points per game and 345.3 yards. And look at who they've been beating lately: UTEP, Colorado State, San Diego State and Washington State, per ESPN. Colorado State's defense ranks last in FBS, and San Diego State's ranks 133rd, per the AP. When the Beavers played Houston and Texas Tech in September, they lost both, 33-20 and 35-24. Our Bulldogs allow 20.9 points per game. Defense travels. Or, in this case, it stays home in Fresno.

Our Bulldogs

Mandal has completed 123 of 195 passes for 1,393 yards, eight touchdowns and just one interception, per ESPN. One! Freeman leads the receivers with 32 catches for 445 yards. Rayshon Luke leads the backs with 333 yards. The Bulldogs score 27.6 points per game.

The honest note: Fresno State's run defense allows 170.7 yards per game, and the Beavers' AJ Newberry has 431 rushing yards. The Bulldogs need to slow the run and get after Atkinson.

The Series

Fresno State leads the series 9-6, per CollegeFootballData.com, and beat Oregon State 36-27 in 2025. Let's make it 10.

Town Report: Fresno vs. Corvallis

Fresno. Fresno had 542,107 people at the 2020 census, per Wikipedia, the fifth-most populous city in California and the most populous inland city in the state. The name is Spanish for "ash tree," for the ash trees lining the San Joaquin River. The town was founded in 1872 as a Central Pacific Railroad station.

And look at the neighbors. Yosemite National Park is about 60 miles north, Kings Canyon about 60 miles east and Sequoia about 75 miles southeast. Three national parks in a day trip. We have the Forestiere Underground Gardens, the William Saroyan House Museum, the Armenian Museum of Fresno and the Shinzen Japanese Gardens at Woodward Park. The Fulton Mall downtown was one of the nation's first pedestrian malls, in 1964. And per Wikipedia, Fresno gets sunshine for 81 of every 100 possible daylight hours a year.

And the Red Wave? Per Wikipedia, Fresno State fans have been called the Red Wave for decades because they show up entirely in red.

Corvallis. Corvallis is a nice college town of 59,922, per the 2020 census. Its name comes from the Latin for "heart of the valley." Cute. But per Wikipedia, when Oregon's legislature was handing out that name, there was also a petition to rename Salem as Corvallis. So "heart of the valley" was almost the capital's name. Corvallis is the one that got stuck with it, babe.

And Wikipedia says Corvallis has mild, wet winters "with persistently overcast skies." Persistently! Fresno gets sunshine for 81 of every 100 possible daylight hours. Corvallis has persistently overcast.

Here's my go-to fact, though. Per Wikipedia, Reser Stadium is the tallest man-made structure in Corvallis and Benton County history. The tallest thing they've ever built in that whole county is a place to watch football. We built a city, babe. They built bleachers.

The Wait

Here's my plan for the open week. Rest. Heal. Find my reading glasses. Watch Oregon State tape until I can see Legree in my sleep. And come back on Halloween ready to slow down the first receiver in the country to reach 1,000 yards.

Not that Valley, babe. Ours.
